nodes.name: Buto V (Egypt, 2949 BC–2799 BC)
nodes.title: Buto V (Egypt, 2949 BC–2799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lower Egypt, 2949 BC–2799 BC] Buto V. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Later occupation of the Delta town at Tell el-Fara'in, spanning the early centuries of the pharaonic state. The site's waterlogged setting has preserved settlement remains of a kind rarely recovered in the Delta, where most ancient towns lie buried beneath river silt or modern fields.

nodes.name: Macedonian (Egypt, 331 BC–303 BC)
nodes.title: Macedonian (Egypt, 331 BC–303 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 331 BC–303 BC] Macedonian. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Alexander took Egypt from the Persians without a fight, was welcomed as a liberator, consulted the oracle of Ammon at Siwa and founded Alexandria on the coast. After his death his general Ptolemy took control of the country as satrap, keeping the Egyptian administrative machinery but installing a Greek-speaking ruling class at its head.

nodes.name: Late/Final A-group (Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC)
nodes.title: Late/Final A-group (Egypt, 3299 BC–3149 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lower Nubia, 3299 BC–3149 BC] Late/Final A-group. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

In Lower Nubia a wealthy elite emerged, best known from the large tombs at Qustul with their incense burners, imported Egyptian wine jars and stone vessels. Control of trade in gold, ebony, ivory and incense flowing north made these rulers rich enough to rival their contemporaries in Upper Egypt. Their culture disappears abruptly around the time Egypt unified, apparently swept aside by early pharaonic expansion up the Nile.

nodes.name: Ptolemaic (Egypt, 303 BC–29 BC)
nodes.title: Ptolemaic (Egypt, 303 BC–29 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 303 BC–29 BC] Ptolemaic. UEE notes that this chronology will be replaced/improved as the project goes forward, so may be outdated at some point in the near future -- but in use by contributors and DAI database, so useful to maintain a record of. Period definition from UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Willeke Wendrich.

Alexander's general Ptolemy seized Egypt after his death and founded a Greek-speaking dynasty that ruled from Alexandria for nearly three centuries. The city became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean, with its Library, Museum and lighthouse, while the countryside kept its temples and priesthoods - pharaonic architecture built by kings with Macedonian names. The line ended with Cleopatra VII, whose defeat alongside Mark Antony delivered Egypt to Rome.

properties.title: askos — 300BC-200BC
properties.notes:
Mouth of an askos, in form of figure of a slave. The upper part of an askos modelled as an actor: a slave seated on an altar, the upper edge of which survives at the rear. His arms are crossed on his chest, the hands below the edge of the mask. He wears a long-sleeved garment under a short-sleeved tunic, and probably trousers. The undergarment, except for the sleeves, is mottled to indicate fur, and is tied above the belly, with tassels hanging down. A himation is wrapped round, high at the waist behind and covering the buttocks, pulled tight and exposing his left thigh. A low vessel-mouth, damaged, rises from the top of the head and a short spout emerges from between his shoulders. Hollow; two-piece mould. Brown Nile silt with some white grits with an overall black slip: Memphis Black Ware.; | Type: askos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 9.00 centimetres; | Culture: Ptolemaic

Egypt, Coptos

properties.title: oinochoe — 270BC-240BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Faience oinochoe showing woman, named as Arsinoe II of Egypt, pouring libation. Trefoil mouth, with flat spreading lip. Triple-ribbed handles ending above and below in large masks of Seileni. Much restored: bluish-green enamel nearly all worn away; traces of gilding, e.g. round the foot. On the front is a woman to the front leaning over, holding out a small patera over an altar; round the top a wreath, below which are remains of an inscription. The woman stands on a base to left with left knee bent, holding out in right hand a large patera, and in left a cornucopia. Her hair is curly in front, and is drawn back in parallel tresses and wound round in a coil at the back, a fillet passing round the head, the gilt ends of which hang down behind; she wears earrings, a gilt armlet on left arm, long chiton, and himation twisted round the waist in a thick fold and falling to below the knees, the folds being carefully but conventionally indicated. Behind her is a cross-shaped object, and beyond, a tapering meta as the last. The handles end above and below in large masks of Seileni, partly bald, with open mouths, and beards in thick separate locks; the upper one is smaller than the lower and | Type: oinochoe | Medium: glazed composition; gold | Dimensions: 30.48 centimetres about ; 32.40 centimetres; | Culture: Ptolemaic

Egypt, Canosa di Puglia, Italy

properties.title: oinochoe — 220BC-200BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Faience oinochoe decorated in high relief. Trefoil mouth (restored); handle modern. Hard gritty paste, largely composed of sand and silica, with a coating of pale blue enamel or faience. On the front is a woman to the front leaning over to her right, with left hand on side, holding out a small patera over an altar; she has a high sphendone, shoes, long chiton, and himation round waist gathered up on the left side. The altar is square with pilasters round the base, and on the top are cakes of pyramidal form. Behind the woman is a meta in the form of a tapering obelisk, round which are knotted three wreaths or sashes. On the shoulder is an inscription.; | Type: oinochoe | Medium: glazed composition | Dimensions: 29.21 centimetres; | Culture: Ptolemaic

Egypt, Canosa di Puglia, Italy

nodes.name: Republican (Serbia, 168 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Republican (Serbia, 168 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 168 BC–1 BC] Republican. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.

nodes.name: Classical Period (Macedonia, 500 BC–350 BC)
nodes.title: Classical Period (Macedonia, 500 BC–350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 500 BC–350 BC] Classical Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Crete's Bronze Age glory was long gone; the island was now a mosaic of quarrelsome city-states such as Knossos, Gortyn and Lyttos, largely outside the great power struggles of mainland Greece. Its most famous monument is the Gortyn law code, inscribed on stone and preserving detailed rules on inheritance, marriage and the status of slaves. Cretan archers and mercenaries were in demand abroad, and the island had a reputation for piracy.

nodes.name: Medieval (Slovenia, AD 601–AD 1499)
nodes.title: Medieval (Slovenia, AD 601–AD 1499)
nodes.description: [Slovenia, AD 601–AD 1499] Medieval. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Transitional Period (Romania, 3800 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.title: Transitional Period (Romania, 3800 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 3800 BC–3500 BC] Transitional Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The unravelling of Old Europe's tell-dwelling farming societies. The great painted-pottery cultures of the Carpathian and Danubian lands broke up, copper metallurgy and settlement patterns changed, and new communities appear with cord-decorated pottery, more herding, horse bones and burials under mounds - developments long linked to contact with, or movement from, the Pontic steppe, and leading directly into the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Klasike/Qytetare ilire (Albania, 480 BC–336 BC)
nodes.title: Klasike/Qytetare ilire (Albania, 480 BC–336 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 480 BC–336 BC] Klasike/Qytetare ilire. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Illyrian communities in what is now Albania shifted from hillforts to genuine towns with fortification walls, streets and public buildings, minting coins and absorbing goods and ideas from the Greek colonies at Apollonia and Epidamnos. Local dynasts built up kingdoms strong enough to fight Macedon. The urban centres of this era became the foundation for the later Roman cities of Illyricum.

nodes.name: Early Medieval (Serbia, AD 565–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Medieval (Serbia, AD 565–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 565–AD 1000] Early Medieval. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

nodes.name: Late Medieval (Bulgaria, AD 1000–AD 1396)
nodes.title: Late Medieval (Bulgaria, AD 1000–AD 1396)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 1000–AD 1396] Late Medieval. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Bulgaria spent much of this stretch inside the Byzantine Empire after the fall of the First Bulgarian state, then broke free in 1185 to build a Second Empire ruled from Tarnovo, whose churches, painted tombs and silver coinage mark a confident revival. Ivan Asen II briefly made it the dominant power in the Balkans before Mongol raids, noble feuding and territorial splintering wore it down. Ottoman armies took Tarnovo and then Vidin, ending Bulgarian independence for nearly five centuries.

nodes.name: Пізньолатенський період (Ukraine, 299 BC–AD 50)
nodes.title: Пізньолатенський період (Ukraine, 299 BC–AD 50)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 299 BC–AD 50] Пізньолатенський період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Zarubintsy culture occupied the middle Dnipro and Prypiat, its fibulae, pottery and fortified settlements showing strong Celtic La Tène influence transmitted through Central Europe. Bastarnae and other groups moved through the region, and Sarmatian horsemen displaced the Scythians on the open steppe, confining the last Scythians to Crimea. Trade with the Greek Black Sea cities and, increasingly, with Rome brought coins and wine amphorae far inland.

nodes.name: Modern (Kosovo, AD 1850–AD 1944)
nodes.title: Modern (Kosovo, AD 1850–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 1850–AD 1944] Modern. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

nodes.name: Romaine (Morocco, 1 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Romaine (Morocco, 1 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, 1 BC–AD 400] Romaine. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Rome absorbed the old Mauretanian kingdom into the province of Tingitana, holding the northern plains and coast while the interior remained beyond direct control. Towns like Volubilis, Lixus and Tingis grew rich on olive oil, grain and the export of wild animals, leaving mosaics, bronzes and forums that are still the best-preserved ancient ruins in the country; the army largely withdrew in the later third century, though a coastal foothold persisted.

nodes.name: Classical (Italy, 479 BC–351 BC)
nodes.title: Classical (Italy, 479 BC–351 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 479 BC–351 BC] Classical. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.

nodes.name: Eneolothic (Slovenia, 3299 BC–2301 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolothic (Slovenia, 3299 BC–2301 BC)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 3299 BC–2301 BC] Eneolothic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper Age communities in the Ljubljana Marshes built pile-dwelling villages on wooden platforms above the wetlands, leaving waterlogged deposits that preserve wood, textiles and tools normally lost. From one of them comes the oldest known wooden wheel and axle, evidence that wheeled transport was in use here in the late fourth millennium. Copper tools, Bell Beaker pottery and long-distance contacts mark the transition towards the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Roman Republican (Slovenia, 349 BC–AD 29)
nodes.title: Roman Republican (Slovenia, 349 BC–AD 29)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 349 BC–AD 29] Roman Republican. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Rome pushed north-east from the colony at Aquileia into the world of the Iron Age Alpine and Adriatic peoples, trading before it conquered. Local hillforts and cemeteries fill with Italic wine vessels, coinage and weapons, showing communities drawn into Mediterranean commerce well before annexation. By the time of Augustus the region had been incorporated outright, and the town of Emona was founded to hold the route into Italy.

nodes.name: Edad del Hierro (Spain, 999 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: Edad del Hierro (Spain, 999 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description: [Spain, 999 BC–AD 1] Edad del Hierro. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Perandorake e hershme (Albania, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.title: Perandorake e hershme (Albania, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 1–AD 100] Perandorake e hershme. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Illyria and Epirus settled into provincial life under the early emperors, with the Via Egnatia carrying traffic from the Adriatic ports of Dyrrachium and Apollonia towards Macedonia and Constantinople's future site. Roman colonies, forums, theatres and aqueducts reshaped older Greek and Illyrian towns such as Buthrotum, and Latin spread inland alongside Greek on the coast. Local elites bought into Roman citizenship and civic building.

nodes.name: Пізньоантичний період (Ukraine, AD 280–AD 530)
nodes.title: Пізньоантичний період (Ukraine, AD 280–AD 530)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 280–AD 530] Пізньоантичний період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Chernyakhov culture spread across the forest-steppe — a mixed population of Goths, Sarmatians and local farmers using wheel-made pottery, Roman coins and imported wine. Gothic power was shattered by the Huns around 375, sending refugees into the Roman Empire and beginning the migrations that reshaped Europe. The Greek cities of the coast shrank and the Bosporan Kingdom faded, while Slavic groups emerge into visibility in the written sources for the first time.

nodes.name: Contemporary (Italy, AD 1790–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporary (Italy, AD 1790–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 1790–AD 2000] Contemporary. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Bulgaria, 6300 BC–4900 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Bulgaria, 6300 BC–4900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 6300 BC–4900 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Archaic (Italy, 579 BC–481 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Italy, 579 BC–481 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 579 BC–481 BC] Archaic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Serbia, 4100 BC–3060 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Serbia, 4100 BC–3060 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 4100 BC–3060 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Bronz i vonë (Albania, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.title: Bronz i vonë (Albania, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 1500 BC–1100 BC] Bronz i vonë. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Mycenaean pottery, swords and rapiers turn up in tumulus burials in the interior, showing that the communities of the region were tied into Aegean exchange networks. Burial under earthen mounds, often used and reused over centuries by the same groups, is the defining feature of the period and continued long afterwards, which is why archaeologists have argued about its links to the later Illyrian tribes.

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age (Bulgaria, 3500 BC–1900 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age (Bulgaria, 3500 BC–1900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 3500 BC–1900 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

nodes.name: Helenistike (Albania, 336 BC–168 BC)
nodes.title: Helenistike (Albania, 336 BC–168 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 336 BC–168 BC] Helenistike. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The age when the Illyrian south was drawn into the Hellenistic world: fortified cities such as Byllis, Amantia and Phoinike were built with monumental walls, theatres and stoas, coinage circulated widely, and local dynasts ruled alongside the Greek colonies of the coast. It closed with Rome's defeat of Macedon and the capture of the Illyrian king Gentius, which brought the region under Roman control.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Slovenia, 4999 BC–3301 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Slovenia, 4999 BC–3301 BC)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 4999 BC–3301 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Ottoman Period (Bulgaria, AD 1396–AD 1878)
nodes.title: Ottoman Period (Bulgaria, AD 1396–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 1396–AD 1878] Ottoman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

nodes.name: Roman Period (Romania, 1 BC–AD 300)
nodes.title: Roman Period (Romania, 1 BC–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 1 BC–AD 300] Roman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (Serbia, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (Serbia, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 1500 BC–1100 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

nodes.name: Roman Republican (Italy, 349 BC–AD 29)

nodes.name: Late Antique (Italy, AD 401–AD 599)
nodes.title: Late Antique (Italy, AD 401–AD 599)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 401–AD 599] Late Antique. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The western empire dissolved into barbarian kingdoms: Ostrogothic rule under Theoderic preserved much of Roman administration at Ravenna, until Justinian's twenty-year Gothic War devastated the peninsula and the Lombards seized the north in 568. Cities shrank, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and bishops and monasteries took over civic leadership. It was also an age of extraordinary art - Ravenna's mosaics - and of the Rule of St Benedict.

properties.title: lamp — 375-425
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with an oval body and a long nozzle (now broken) with a wide shallow channel between the wick-hole and the filling-hole area. At the rear is a pierced grooved handle, mainly missing. The flat shoulders are decorated with sunken panels containing stylized palm branches in relief; two transverse grooves cross the shoulder on each side at the nozzle end of the panels. The filling-hole area is decorated with a dramatic mask with a high onkos; the mouth and eyes are pierced to act as filling-holes. The base-ring extends into a long handle-spine, defined by a deep groove. Within the base-ring is a sunken branch, incised into the archetype. Covered with a glossy orange-red slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 9.40 centimetres; 6.80 centimetres; | Culture: Roman Imperial

Italy

nodes.name: Moderne (Albania, AD 1850–AD 1944)
nodes.title: Moderne (Albania, AD 1850–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 1850–AD 1944] Moderne. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Albanian lands remained Ottoman provinces while the Rilindja movement built a written language and a national idea across religious divisions. Independence was declared in 1912 amid the Balkan Wars, but the new state's borders left large Albanian populations outside them, and the interwar years under Ahmet Zogu were poor and unstable. Italian occupation in 1939 and then German control ended in 1944 with the victory of the communist partisans.

nodes.name: Iron Age (Slovenia, 999 BC–751 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Slovenia, 999 BC–751 BC)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 999 BC–751 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

nodes.name: Готи (Ukraine, AD 250–AD 375)
nodes.title: Готи (Ukraine, AD 250–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 250–AD 375] Готи. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Gothic groups moving south from the Vistula came to dominate the lands between the Danube and the Don, and are usually linked with the widespread Chernyakhov culture of villages, wheel-made pottery and Roman coin finds. From here they raided deep into the Balkans and Asia Minor by land and sea, forcing the Roman Empire onto the defensive. Their power collapsed abruptly when the Huns arrived from the east.

nodes.title: Bronz i mesëm (Albania, 1800 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.description: [Albania, 1800 BC–1500 BC] Bronz i mesëm. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Slovenia, 2299 BC–1001 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Slovenia, 2299 BC–1001 BC)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 2299 BC–1001 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

nodes.name: Perandorake e mesme (Albania, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.title: Perandorake e mesme (Albania, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 100–AD 300] Perandorake e mesme. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The high point of provincial prosperity in the Adriatic lands, when cities rebuilt their theatres, baths and water systems and coastal estates exported oil, wine and timber. Inscriptions show local families rising into the imperial administration and army, while eastern cults and early Christian communities took root in the port towns. The third-century crisis brought raids, walls around cities and the end of the building boom.

nodes.name: Раннє Середньовіччя (Ukraine, AD 450–AD 880)
nodes.title: Раннє Середньовіччя (Ukraine, AD 450–AD 880)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 450–AD 880] Раннє Середньовіччя. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Slavic-speaking communities expanded across the forest-steppe, leaving the simple sunken-floored houses and hand-made pottery of the Prague-Korchak and Penkivka groups, while Avar and later Khazar power pressed from the south and east. The Black Sea steppe saw waves of nomadic confederations, and the Crimean coast stayed tied to Byzantium. By the end of the period trade along the Dnipro and the arrival of Scandinavian merchants and warbands were setting the stage for Kyivan Rus'.

nodes.name: Roman Imperial (Slovenia, AD 31–AD 399)
nodes.title: Roman Imperial (Slovenia, AD 31–AD 399)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, AD 31–AD 399] Roman Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The eastern Alpine lands became a settled part of the empire, crossed by the road from Aquileia to the Danube and guarded by the fortified Claustra Alpium Iuliarum. Emona (Ljubljana) and Celeia (Celje) were laid out on grid plans with walls, drains and cemeteries, and local elites adopted Latin names and Roman gods alongside their own. The route made the region a corridor for armies and, later, for invaders heading into Italy.

nodes.name: Eneolithic (Romania, 4900 BC–3800 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolithic (Romania, 4900 BC–3800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 4900 BC–3800 BC] Eneolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

nodes.name: Новітня доба (Ukraine, AD 1914–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Новітня доба (Ukraine, AD 1914–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1914–AD 2000] Новітня доба. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

War, revolution and the short-lived Ukrainian People's Republic gave way to Soviet rule, which brought both a brief flowering of Ukrainian culture and then terror: forced collectivisation, the Holodomor famine of 1932–33, and purges. The Second World War devastated the country, with Nazi occupation, the Holocaust, partisan and nationalist insurgency, and millions dead. Independence came in 1991 with the collapse of the USSR, leaving a state to build from Soviet institutions — and a lasting legacy in Chornobyl.

nodes.title: Classic/Urban illyrian (Serbia, 480 BC–336 BC)
nodes.description: [Serbia, 480 BC–336 BC] Classic/Urban illyrian. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Edad del Bronce (Spain, 2299 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Bronce (Spain, 2299 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 2299 BC–1000 BC] Edad del Bronce. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Metalworking in copper and tin spread across the peninsula, and in the southeast the El Argar culture built fortified hilltop towns with rectangular houses, buried its dead in jars beneath house floors, and marked out sharp differences of wealth in silver and bronze grave goods. Elsewhere communities raised cairns and stelae, worked gold, and traded along Atlantic and Mediterranean routes. It was the first period in Iberia with clearly stratified societies controlling metal and land.

nodes.name: Iron Age (Italy, 999 BC–751 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Italy, 999 BC–751 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 999 BC–751 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

nodes.name: Класичний період (Ukraine, 499 BC–329 BC)
nodes.title: Класичний період (Ukraine, 499 BC–329 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 499 BC–329 BC] Класичний період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Greek city-states on the northern Black Sea coast — Olbia, Chersonesos, Panticapaeum — grew rich exporting grain, fish and slaves to the Aegean, while the Bosporan Kingdom consolidated control of the Kerch Strait. Inland, the Scythian royal horde reached its height, defeating Darius I's invasion and burying its kings with astonishing gold work in mounds like Solokha and Chortomlyk. Herodotus's account of Scythia dates from this time and remains the earliest written description of the region.

nodes.name: Contemporaine (Morocco, AD 1789–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporaine (Morocco, AD 1789–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, AD 1789–AD 2000] Contemporaine. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Morocco moved from a sovereign sultanate courted and squeezed by European powers to a French and Spanish protectorate imposed in 1912, then back to independence in 1956 under the Alaouite monarchy. The period saw Tangier as an international zone, the Rif war, huge growth of coastal cities like Casablanca, and rural depopulation as migration to Europe began.

nodes.name: Early Medieval (Kosovo, AD 565–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Medieval (Kosovo, AD 565–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 565–AD 1000] Early Medieval. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

nodes.name: Late Antiquity (Bulgaria, AD 300–AD 476)
nodes.title: Late Antiquity (Bulgaria, AD 300–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 300–AD 476] Late Antiquity. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Roman provinces along the lower Danube and in Thrace became a frontier zone under constant pressure, with Goths, Huns and other groups crossing the river while emperors fortified cities and roads. Christianity spread fast: basilicas and bishoprics appeared at Serdica, Philippopolis and elsewhere, and Serdica hosted a major church council. After the empire split, these lands fell to the eastern half, setting up their long Byzantine future.

nodes.name: Сармати (Ukraine, 299 BC–AD 300)
nodes.title: Сармати (Ukraine, 299 BC–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 299 BC–AD 300] Сармати. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Iranian-speaking nomads from the east displaced the Scythians as masters of the steppe, fighting as armoured lancers on horseback and burying their dead under mounds with weapons, mirrors, and gold worked in a distinctive style inlaid with coloured stones. Their tribal confederations traded with and raided the Greek coastal cities and later harassed Rome's Danube frontier. Sarmatian women's graves sometimes contain weapons, feeding ancient stories of Amazons.

nodes.name: Mauretaine (Morocco, 350 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Mauretaine (Morocco, 350 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, 350 BC–1 BC] Mauretaine. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Berber kingdom of the far Maghreb, ruled by kings such as Bocchus, whose territory stretched from the Atlantic coast into what is now western Algeria. Drawn steadily into Roman politics through the Jugurthine and civil wars, it ended as a client kingdom under Juba II, a scholar-king educated in Rome who filled his capital at Volubilis and Caesarea with Greek and Roman art. Rome annexed it outright a few decades later.

nodes.name: Eneolithic (Bulgaria, 4900 BC–3800 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolithic (Bulgaria, 4900 BC–3800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 4900 BC–3800 BC] Eneolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

nodes.name: Arkaike/Para qytetare ilire (Albania, 600 BC–480 BC)
nodes.title: Arkaike/Para qytetare ilire (Albania, 600 BC–480 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 600 BC–480 BC] Arkaike/Para qytetare ilire. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Illyrian tribes in the Albanian interior built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their elites under tumuli filled with weapons, bronze jewellery and imported goods. Contact with the Greek colonies of Apollonia and Epidamnos brought pottery, coinage habits and craft ideas inland, and some strongholds grew into recognisable towns. These communities became the kingdoms that later confronted Macedon and Rome.

nodes.name: Tardoantiguo (Spain, AD 401–AD 600)
nodes.title: Tardoantiguo (Spain, AD 401–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 401–AD 600] Tardoantiguo. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Roman authority in Iberia dissolved as Suebi, Vandals and Alans crossed the Pyrenees, and the Visigoths, first as imperial allies and then as masters, established a kingdom centred on Toledo. Cities contracted, villas turned into farming settlements or burial grounds, and bishops became the main figures of urban authority. Byzantine forces held a strip of the southeast, and Latin Christian culture survived in monasteries and church councils that shaped medieval Spain.

nodes.name: Mesolítico (Spain, 9999 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolítico (Spain, 9999 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 9999 BC–5000 BC] Mesolítico. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

With the Ice Age fauna gone, Iberian foragers turned to red deer, rabbit, shellfish and plants, and their stone tools shrank into geometric microliths set in wood and bone. On the Cantabrian coast the Asturian groups piled up limpet shells in enormous middens; in the east, painted rock shelters of the Levantine tradition show archers, honey-gatherers and hunts in lively narrative scenes. In the Tagus and Sado estuaries these last hunter-gatherers buried their dead in cemeteries, and their descendants met the first farmers arriving by sea.

nodes.name: Late Archaic Period (Macedonia, 600 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Late Archaic Period (Macedonia, 600 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 600 BC–500 BC] Late Archaic Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Argead kings consolidated a territory around the Thermaic Gulf while Greek colonies on the Chalcidice coast tied the region into Aegean trade, importing painted pottery and exporting timber and silver. Rich burials with gold masks and mouthplates show a wealthy local elite absorbing Greek fashions on its own terms. The century closes with Persian armies moving through and Macedonian kings accepting nominal submission.

nodes.name: Punique (Morocco, 1000 BC–350 BC)
nodes.title: Punique (Morocco, 1000 BC–350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, 1000 BC–350 BC] Punique. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Phoenician sailors from Tyre, and later Carthaginians, established trading stations down the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts - Lixus, Mogador, Rusaddir - to tap gold, ivory and the murex shellfish used to make purple dye. Contact brought iron, the potter's wheel, alphabetic writing and new burial customs to local Mauri communities. The result was a mixed coastal culture that would shape Mauretania long into the Roman era.

nodes.name: Medieval (Macedonia, AD 600–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Medieval (Macedonia, AD 600–AD 1400)
nodes.description: [Macedonia, AD 600–AD 1400] Medieval. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Contemporary (Macedonia, AD 1912–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporary (Macedonia, AD 1912–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, AD 1912–AD 2000] Contemporary. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

nodes.name: Eneolithic (Macedonia, 4500 BC–2200 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolithic (Macedonia, 4500 BC–2200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 4500 BC–2200 BC] Eneolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

nodes.name: Кіммерійці (Ukraine, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Кіммерійці (Ukraine, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 899 BC–699 BC] Кіммерійці. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The first steppe people in the region named in written sources, known from Assyrian records and from Homer as much as from their bronze horse-gear and daggers. Pressed from the east, Cimmerian bands rode south through the Caucasus and shattered the kingdom of Urartu and Phrygia, killing a Lydian king before being crushed in Anatolia. On the steppe itself they were absorbed or driven out by the incoming Scythians.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Macedonia, 6400 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Macedonia, 6400 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 6400 BC–4500 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Republikane (Albania, 168 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Republikane (Albania, 168 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 168 BC–1 BC] Republikane. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Roman power replaced the Illyrian kingdoms after the defeat of King Gentius, and the lands of present-day Albania were absorbed into the Republic's Balkan holdings. The Via Egnatia was driven across the region, linking the Adriatic ports of Dyrrachium and Apollonia to Macedonia and, ultimately, to the East. Those coastal cities grew rich as gateways between Italy and the Greek world, and Roman legions repeatedly used them as staging grounds in the civil wars.

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age (Kosovo, 2100 BC–1800 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age (Kosovo, 2100 BC–1800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 2100 BC–1800 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

nodes.name: Пізньоримський та гунський період (Ukraine, AD 175–AD 450)
nodes.title: Пізньоримський та гунський період (Ukraine, AD 175–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 175–AD 450] Пізньоримський та гунський період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The steppe and forest-steppe were drawn into the orbit of the late Roman world: Roman silver coins, glass and amphorae travelled far north, while the Chernyakhiv culture spread across a vast area under Gothic and mixed Sarmatian, Dacian and early Slavic influence. From the late 4th century the arrival of the Huns shattered this order, sending Goths and others westward into the Roman provinces. Finds from these centuries include polychrome gold jewellery, hoards buried in haste, and the abandoned villages of communities that vanished within a generation.

nodes.name: Perandorake e vonë (Albania, AD 300–AD 565)
nodes.title: Perandorake e vonë (Albania, AD 300–AD 565)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 300–AD 565] Perandorake e vonë. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Diocletian's reorganisation made these lands a strategic corridor between the empire's halves, guarded by fortified towns and controlling the road from the Adriatic to Constantinople. Christianity became dominant, and basilicas with mosaic floors were built at Butrint, Byllis and Lin. Gothic and Hunnic raids, earthquakes and plague thinned the cities, and Justinian's fortress-building was the last great imperial investment before the Slavic migrations.

nodes.name: Contemporary (Serbia, AD 1944–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporary (Serbia, AD 1944–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 1944–AD 2000] Contemporary. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

nodes.name: Modern Period (Romania, AD 1800–AD 1918)
nodes.title: Modern Period (Romania, AD 1800–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 1800–AD 1918] Modern Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Crete entered the century in political limbo, an autonomous state under great-power supervision, and was formally joined to Greece in 1913. German paratroopers seized the island in the fierce battle of 1941, and the brutal occupation and mountain resistance that followed are still central to local memory. Since the 1960s mass tourism and intensive olive and greenhouse agriculture have reshaped the coast, while excavation at Knossos, Phaistos and elsewhere turned the Minoan past into a national and international symbol.

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Kosovo, 336 BC–168 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Kosovo, 336 BC–168 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 336 BC–168 BC] Hellenistic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

nodes.name: Енеоліт (Ukraine, 5499 BC–3199 BC)
nodes.title: Енеоліт (Ukraine, 5499 BC–3199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 5499 BC–3199 BC] Енеоліт. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper metallurgy arrived alongside a farming boom, and the Trypillia culture built some of the largest settlements on earth at the time — planned rings of houses at Talianky and Maidanetske holding thousands of people, periodically burned and rebuilt. Painted pottery, clay figurines and models of houses survive in huge numbers. On the steppe to the east, herders raised kurgan burial mounds and began using wheeled vehicles and domestic horses, a way of life that would spread across Eurasia.

nodes.name: Early Iron Age (Kosovo, 1100 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age (Kosovo, 1100 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 1100 BC–800 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

nodes.name: Late Medieval Period (Romania, AD 1000–AD 1396)
nodes.title: Late Medieval Period (Romania, AD 1000–AD 1396)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 1000–AD 1396] Late Medieval Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Carpathian lands were reorganised as Hungarian kings extended control over Transylvania, planting German 'Saxon' townsmen and Székely border guards whose fortified churches still dot the landscape. South and east of the mountains, the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia emerged in the fourteenth century and asserted themselves against Hungarian overlordship. By the end, Ottoman armies were pressing north of the Danube, and the crusade defeated at Nicopolis set the terms of the region's next two centuries.

nodes.name: Transitional Period (Macedonia, 1200 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Transitional Period (Macedonia, 1200 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 1200 BC–1000 BC] Transitional Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The unravelling of Old Europe's tell-dwelling farming societies. The great painted-pottery cultures of the Carpathian and Danubian lands broke up, copper metallurgy and settlement patterns changed, and new communities appear with cord-decorated pottery, more herding, horse bones and burials under mounds - developments long linked to contact with, or movement from, the Pontic steppe, and leading directly into the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Italy, 4999 BC–3301 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Italy, 4999 BC–3301 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 4999 BC–3301 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Late Iron Age (Bulgaria, 500 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Late Iron Age (Bulgaria, 500 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 500 BC–1 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

nodes.name: Migrations Period (Romania, AD 275–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Migrations Period (Romania, AD 275–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 275–AD 1200] Migrations Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

After Rome abandoned Dacia, wave after wave of peoples passed through or settled the Carpathian and Danubian lands: Goths, Huns, Gepids, Avars, Slavs, Bulgars, Magyars, Pechenegs and Cumans. Towns and stone building largely gave way to villages, and the archaeological record is dominated by cemeteries, hoards and rich horse-warrior graves. Out of this churn came the Slavic settlement of the region and the medieval kingdoms of Hungary and Bulgaria.

nodes.name: Доба ранньої бронзи (Ukraine, 3199 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.title: Доба ранньої бронзи (Ukraine, 3199 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 3199 BC–2299 BC] Доба ранньої бронзи. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The age of the Yamna (Pit-grave) culture, when mobile herders buried their dead beneath earthen kurgans that still dot the steppe, used ox-drawn wagons and carried early metal tools. Their expansion westward is central to the argument that Indo-European languages spread from these grasslands. On the western fringe, groups like Usatove linked the steppe to the farming societies of the Danube.

nodes.name: Доба пізньої бронзи (Ukraine, 1799 BC–1299 BC)
nodes.title: Доба пізньої бронзи (Ukraine, 1799 BC–1299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 1799 BC–1299 BC] Доба пізньої бронзи. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The steppe filled with settled pastoral communities of the Zrubna (Timber-grave) and Sabatynivka cultures, living in substantial villages, working local copper and casting bronze on a near-industrial scale for export. Fortified settlements and huge quantities of metalwork show connections reaching to the Carpathians, the Caucasus and the Mycenaean world. Farther north, forest-steppe groups such as Trzciniec-Komarów combined farming with the same bronze-using traditions.

nodes.name: Hellenistic Period (Macedonia, 350 BC–AD 30)
nodes.title: Hellenistic Period (Macedonia, 350 BC–AD 30)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 350 BC–AD 30] Hellenistic Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.

nodes.name: Римський період (Ukraine, 49 BC–AD 280)
nodes.title: Римський період (Ukraine, 49 BC–AD 280)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 49 BC–AD 280] Римський період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Rome's shadow fell across the region without conquest: garrisons and fleets supported the Greek Black Sea cities, and imperial coin, glass, bronze vessels and wine flowed inland in exchange for grain and slaves. Sarmatian nomads held the open steppe, while settled farming communities of the forest-steppe grew wealthier on this trade. Hoards of Roman silver, some containing thousands of denarii, are among the most striking traces left behind.

nodes.name: Нова доба (Ukraine, AD 1569–AD 1914)
nodes.title: Нова доба (Ukraine, AD 1569–AD 1914)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1569–AD 1914] Нова доба. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Union of Lublin transferred Ukrainian lands to the Polish Crown, bringing serfdom, magnate estates and religious conflict — and provoking the Cossack risings. Partitions of Poland and wars with the Ottomans then split the territory between the Russian and Habsburg empires, with the steppe and Crimea colonised anew and Odesa founded as a boom port. A literary and scholarly revival, from Kotliarevsky and Shevchenko to Galician cultural societies, turned a peasant vernacular into a national movement.

nodes.name: Доба фінальної бронзи (Ukraine, 1299 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Доба фінальної бронзи (Ukraine, 1299 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 1299 BC–999 BC] Доба фінальної бронзи. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Bilozerka culture and its neighbours mark the last bronze-using generations on the steppe, with cemeteries of flat graves, standardised metalwork and growing contact with the Carpathian and Caucasian worlds. Climate shifts and a turn toward more mobile herding reshaped settlement, and the first iron objects begin to appear. Out of these communities emerged the mounted Cimmerians of the early Iron Age.

nodes.name: Modern (Italy, AD 1501–AD 1788)
nodes.title: Modern (Italy, AD 1501–AD 1788)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 1501–AD 1788] Modern. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

properties.title: albarello — 1500-1530
properties.notes:
Albarello, slightly waisted, with everted rim and foot, and prominent ridges at the top and bottom of the main section of the body. Earthenware, covered inside and outside with a presumed tin-glaze. Painted with a leaf-garland with flowers enclosing a band with the words "GIO LOGODIO"; above is a winged cherub-head; below is a roundel with a (?) heron pecking at the ground. The garland is flanked by ribbons. On the rim and foot alla porcellana designs.; | Type: albarello | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 9.50 centimetres base ; 22.90 centimetres;

Italy, Deruta

properties.title: bowl — 1533 (probably)
properties.notes:
Broad-rimmed bowl or plate with well, earthenware covered on the front and back with a presumed tin-glaze. Painted decoration on the front with red and gold lustre, in the centre a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, on the right a standing river god with a river issuing from a vase on his shoulder, on the left a man apparently carrying the infants to be exposed. Figure to the left from an engraving by Marcantonio Raimondi. River god after Caraglio after Raphael.; | Type: bowl | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 26.60 centimetres; 4.00 centimetres;

Urbino, Gubbio, Italy

properties.title: bowl — 1525-1535

The figures are from engravings.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 27.00 centimetres; 2.60 centimetres;

Urbino, Italy

properties.title: dish — 1515-1525 (circa)
properties.notes:
Dish or shallow bowl, the foot cut away. Earthenware, covered front and back with presumed tin glaze. Painted with a group of people in a landscape with a castle or town: one man gesturing to another on a plinth, the latter has his foot on the head of one of four bound, naked prisoners. Scene depicts either Caesar and Ariovistus or Fabius Maximus and Hannibal. Probably after Ripanda, based on a fresco by Genga. Scale pattern on reverse.; | Type: dish | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 25.20 centimetres; 3.90 centimetres;

properties.title: plate — 1510-1515 (circa)

Deep plate of earthenware covered front and back with presumed tin glaze. Painted on the front with the Death of the Virgin: the Virgin Mary in a canopied bed surrounded by the twelve Apostles. After Israel von Meckenem after Martin Schongauer. Edge painted orange. On the reverse 'acanthus' ornament near the rim and within this a band of scale pattern.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 263.00 millimetres; 40.00 millimetres;

Faenza, Italy

properties.title: plate — 1522-1523
properties.notes:
Plate or dish of earthenware with a foot-ring. Presumed tin glaze on front and lead glaze on back. Painted decoration on upper surface; in the well a shield of arms for Pope Hadrian VI: quarterly, 1 & 4, or three wolfhooks vert, 2 & 3 argent a lion rampant azure, crowned orange-brown. Arms flanked by pair of sconces, flowers and fruit, above it, crossed keys and triple crown. Rim with overlapping scales and foliage patterns.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 42.50 centimetres; 8.20 centimetres;

Deruta, Italy

properties.title: plate — 1542
properties.notes:
Plate, earthenware with a presumed tin-glaze on the front and back. The front is painted with Hercules stepping onto a block, he has a lion-skin over his shoulder and carries on either shoulder a large pillar. To the right a shield of arms: a tree proper, on a blue-black chief a cross patée; shield surmounted by a green-black prelatial hat with tassels on either side. On the reverse an inscription.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 26.20 centimetres; 3.30 centimetres;

Urbino, Italy

properties.title: plate — 1525 (circa)
properties.notes:
Plate or dish of earthenware, with foot ring, covered front and back with presumed tin glaze, the front painted. In the well two putti supporting a shield of arms for Calini of Brescia (blue, in bend a yellow ladder with between the rungs a white swallow-tailed flag). On rim a scene from the musical competition between Pan and Apollo, with Midas and Tmolus; derived from Ovid.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 41.60 centimetres; 5.20 centimetres;

Urbino, Italy

properties.title: jar — 1519 (11 October)
properties.notes:
Bulbous jar covered with a presumed tin-glaze inside and out. On either side of the jar is a shield of arms, each shield is surrounded by a green wreath tied with rings of fruit. Supporting the wreaths are two pairs of dragon-like monsters. Lower body is painted with four urns of fruit. On the neck two shields bearing a badge comprising two "F"s and a double traversed cross, between the shields two masks.; | Type: jar | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 14.40 centimetres rim ; 36.50 centimetres;

Castel Durante, Italy

properties.title: bowl — 1520 (circa)
properties.notes:
Broad-rimmed bowl, earthenware covered with a presumed tin-glaze on the front and back. Front is painted, in the well a landscape, on the sides in bianco sopra bianco ogee arches and flowers, on the rim a pair of musicians each playing a lira da braccia, and a reclining naked woman with two children one of whom holds a lute. Composition echoing an engraving after Marcantonio.; | Type: bowl | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 29.10 centimetres; 4.50 centimetres;

Urbino (?, vicinity), Castel Durante, Italy, France

properties.title: plate — 1510-1520 (circa)

Plate, slightly convex in centre. Earthenware covered front and back with presumed tin glaze over a slip. Painted decoration including red: in centre Mucius Scaevola, his hand in a flame on an altar. On it hangs a shield of arms for Giocondo?: blue, on a yellow fess between 3 yellow mullets, a blue fleur de lis. Behind him, soldiers; facing him, Lars Porsena, crowned. Faenza, Siena (?, possibly), Italy, Sweden

properties.title: plate — 1543-1545 (circa)

Plate, earthenware covered with a presumed tin-glaze on the front and back. Urbino, Italy

properties.title: bowl — 1533

Broad-rimmed bowl, earthenware covered with a presumed tin-glaze on the front and back. Urbino, Italy

Plate, broad rim, slight foot-ring. Urbino, Italy

properties.title: dish — 1525-1530 (circa)

Dish with emplacement for ewer; earthenware covered entirely with a presumed tin-glaze. Painted on the front, in the centre Athena playing the pipes, around the scene a wreath, on the base in a landscape Apollo playing a violin, Marsyas watching his pipes thrown to the floor, right Apollo flaying Marsyas, at the top the Gods having dinner (subject from Ovid); outside a scrolling pattern in bianco sopra bianco. Urbino, Italy

properties.title: albarello — 1540-1550 (circa)

Albarello, earthenware covered on the outside with a presumed tin-glaze and a brownish glaze inside. Painted decoration in bands. In front of her the letters "TB" and on the other side a merchant's mark, based on the letter P and a double cross and the letters E and F. Round the foot lines and a row of x's.; | Type: albarello | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 8.80 centimetres base ; 20.90 centimetres;

Abruzzo, Castelli (?, perhaps), Italy, France, Spain

properties.title: plate — 1525
properties.notes:
Broad-rimmed bowl or plate with well. Earthenware covered front and back with a presumed tin-glaze. Painted decoration with yellowish and reddish lustre, three men in academic dress in landscape. In base the mark.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 261.00 millimetres; 56.00 millimetres;

Gubbio, Italy

properties.title: dish — 1510 (circa)
properties.notes:
Dish, earthenware covered on the front with a presumed tin-glaze, the back has a thin coat of glaze or slip outside the foot. Front is painted with concentrically arranged decoration. The scene is bordered with a running interlace design. On the rim grotesques and three shields of arms.; | Type: dish | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 42.00 centimetres; 6.00 centimetres;

Siena, Italy

properties.title: dish — 1544
properties.notes:
Dish or bowl on low foot; earthenware, covered front and back with a presumed tin glaze; painted decoration on the front depicts the Roman legend of Coriolanus persuaded by his mother to spare Rome; on the left, in front of the City of Rome and accompanied by a group of women and a child, is the mother; to the right is Coriolanus; behind him a group of soldiers and some tents, one lettered "SPQR"; in the centre a white horse held by an African boy.; | Type: dish | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 26.70 centimetres; 5.30 centimetres;

Urbino, Italy

properties.title: plate — 1531
properties.notes:
Plate, earthenware covered front and back with a presumed tin-glaze. Painted on the front Aeneas carrying Anchises away from Troy (both are naked) with Ascanius walking ahead (a cloak over his shoulder and a casket in his hand). A shield of arms (perhaps of Squarzioni) hangs from a tree showing Hercules and the lion; the subject is from the Aeneid after an engraving after Raphael.; | Type: plate | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 258.00 millimetres; 31.00 millimetres;

Urbino, Italy

properties.title: apothecary-jar — 1502
properties.notes:

Deruta, Italy

Urbino, Gubbio, Italy

Urbino, Italy

Deruta, Italy

Faenza, Siena (?, possibly), Italy, Sweden

Faenza (?, perhaps), Italy, Spain

Faenza, Italy

nodes.name: Bronze age (Italy, 2299 BC–1001 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze age (Italy, 2299 BC–1001 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 2299 BC–1001 BC] Bronze age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Italy shifted from scattered farming hamlets to dense, organised settlements: pile-built villages around the northern lakes, the embanked terramare of the Po plain, and transhumant herding communities in the Apennines. Bronze axes, swords and fibulae circulated along routes linking the peninsula to central Europe, the Aegean and Mycenaean traders who reached southern coasts and Sicily. The collapse of the terramare and the spread of cremation urnfields at the end of the era set up the Villanovan and Etruscan world.

nodes.name: Eneolithic (Kosovo, 3100 BC–2100 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolithic (Kosovo, 3100 BC–2100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 3100 BC–2100 BC] Eneolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

nodes.name: Mesjetë /Bizantine (Albania, AD 1000–AD 1389)
nodes.title: Mesjetë /Bizantine (Albania, AD 1000–AD 1389)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 1000–AD 1389] Mesjetë /Bizantine. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Byzantine control over the Albanian lands was repeatedly challenged by Bulgarians, Normans crossing from Italy, Venetians and Serbs, and the coastal cities of Durrës and Vlora changed hands again and again. Out of this contest emerged the first native polities, the Principality of Arbanon and later the Angevin Kingdom of Albania, and the earliest written references to Albanians as a distinct people. Fortified towns, Orthodox churches with fresco cycles and Catholic cathedrals on the coast reflect a land caught between Rome and Constantinople.

nodes.name: Eneolithic (Serbia, 3100 BC–2100 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolithic (Serbia, 3100 BC–2100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 3100 BC–2100 BC] Eneolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Bulgaria, 1900 BC–1600 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Bulgaria, 1900 BC–1600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 1900 BC–1600 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

nodes.name: Bronz i hershëm (Albania, 2100 BC–1800 BC)
nodes.title: Bronz i hershëm (Albania, 2100 BC–1800 BC)
nodes.description: [Albania, 2100 BC–1800 BC] Bronz i hershëm. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Macedonia, 2200 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Macedonia, 2200 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 2200 BC–1200 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

nodes.name: Tard Antiquité (Morocco, AD 400–AD 600)
nodes.title: Tard Antiquité (Morocco, AD 400–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, AD 400–AD 600] Tard Antiquité. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

With Roman administration withdrawn from most of Mauretania Tingitana, the region's towns shrank and local Mauri chieftaincies and Berber confederations took over, while Christian congregations persisted in the northern ports. Vandal raiders and later Byzantine garrisons touched the Mediterranean coast, but the interior went its own way. This was the political landscape the Arab armies would encounter in the following century.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Kosovo, 4100 BC–3060 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Kosovo, 4100 BC–3060 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 4100 BC–3060 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Medieval/Byzantine (Serbia, AD 1000–AD 1389)
nodes.title: Medieval/Byzantine (Serbia, AD 1000–AD 1389)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 1000–AD 1389] Medieval/Byzantine. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Byzantine authority over the Serbian lands gave way to independent principalities and then, under the Nemanjić dynasty, to a kingdom and briefly an empire under Stefan Dušan. Wealth from silver mines paid for fresco-covered monastery churches such as Studenica and Gračanica, some of the finest medieval painting in Europe. The empire fragmented after Dušan's death, and the defeat at Kosovo in 1389 opened the way to Ottoman domination.

nodes.name: Early Iron Age (Bulgaria, 1000 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age (Bulgaria, 1000 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 1000 BC–500 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

nodes.name: Late Iron Age (Serbia, 800 BC–600 BC)
nodes.title: Late Iron Age (Serbia, 800 BC–600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 800 BC–600 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

nodes.name: Архаїчний період (Ukraine, 646 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Архаїчний період (Ukraine, 646 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 646 BC–499 BC] Архаїчний період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Greek settlers from Miletos and other Ionian cities planted colonies along the northern Black Sea shore — Berezan, Olbia, Panticapaeum, Theodosia — turning the coast into a frontier of the Greek world. They exported grain, fish and slaves southward and imported wine, oil and painted pottery, while dealing daily with the Scythian nomads of the steppe. The mixing produced the distinctive Graeco-Scythian art and the wealthy city-states that shaped the region for the next thousand years.

nodes.name: Давня Русь (Ukraine, AD 880–AD 1250)
nodes.title: Давня Русь (Ukraine, AD 880–AD 1250)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 880–AD 1250] Давня Русь. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

A state formed when Scandinavian Rus rulers and Slavic tribes came together along the Dnipro trade route from the Baltic to Byzantium, with Kyiv as its capital. Volodymyr's conversion in 988 brought Byzantine Christianity, Cyrillic literacy, stone churches and law codes such as the Ruska Pravda; Yaroslav the Wise married his daughters into half the courts of Europe. Princely rivalries split the realm into competing principalities, and the Mongol storming of Kyiv in 1240 ended its unity, though its churches, chronicles and dynastic memory shaped everything that followed.

nodes.name: Late Iron Age (Kosovo, 800 BC–600 BC)
nodes.title: Late Iron Age (Kosovo, 800 BC–600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 800 BC–600 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. nodes.name: Enéolithique (Morocco, 3300 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.title: Enéolithique (Morocco, 3300 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, 3300 BC–2300 BC] Enéolithique. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper objects and new prestige goods appear alongside a long-established way of life based on herding, farming and coastal foraging. Communal burials and the distinctive Bell Beaker pottery found on the Atlantic coast show that Morocco's communities were tied into exchange networks reaching across the Strait of Gibraltar to Iberia.

nodes.name: Козаччина (Ukraine, AD 1450–AD 1775)
nodes.title: Козаччина (Ukraine, AD 1450–AD 1775)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1450–AD 1775] Козаччина. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Runaway peasants and frontiersmen on the lower Dnipro formed self-governing warrior communities, fortified at the Zaporozhian Sich, raiding Ottoman coasts and electing their own hetmans. Khmelnytsky's 1648 rising against Polish rule created a Cossack state, then drew Muscovy into the region and set off decades of war known as the Ruin. Cossack autonomy was steadily eroded by St Petersburg until Catherine II destroyed the Sich in 1775 — but the era became the central myth of Ukrainian national identity.

nodes.name: Transitional Period (Bulgaria, 3800 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.title: Transitional Period (Bulgaria, 3800 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 3800 BC–3500 BC] Transitional Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The unravelling of Old Europe's tell-dwelling farming societies. The great painted-pottery cultures of the Carpathian and Danubian lands broke up, copper metallurgy and settlement patterns changed, and new communities appear with cord-decorated pottery, more herding, horse bones and burials under mounds - developments long linked to contact with, or movement from, the Pontic steppe, and leading directly into the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Age de Bronze (Morocco, 2300 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Age de Bronze (Morocco, 2300 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, 2300 BC–1000 BC] Age de Bronze. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

In the far northwest of Africa the Bronze Age is thin and hard to see: metal remained rare, and communities largely continued older herding and farming ways of life. Its clearest traces are the rock engravings of the High Atlas, where daggers, halberds and axes of unmistakably European type were pecked into the stone, and Bell Beaker pottery that shows contact across the Strait of Gibraltar. Together they hint at exchange linking Morocco with Iberia long before written history.

nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Kosovo, 1800 BC–1500 BC)
