Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

nodes.name: Early Iron Age (Serbia, 1100 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age (Serbia, 1100 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 1100 BC–800 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

nodes.name: Bashkëkohore (Albania, AD 1944–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Bashkëkohore (Albania, AD 1944–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 1944–AD 2000] Bashkëkohore. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Enver Hoxha's communist party took power at the end of the Second World War and held Albania in Europe's most rigid isolation — collectivised farms, banned religion, hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers, and successive ruptures with Yugoslavia, the USSR and finally China. The regime collapsed in 1990–91, followed by mass emigration, the ruinous pyramid-scheme crisis of 1997 and a difficult transition to a market economy.

nodes.name: Eneolit (Albania, 3100 BC–2100 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolit (Albania, 3100 BC–2100 BC)
nodes.description: [Albania, 3100 BC–2100 BC] Eneolit. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Republican (Kosovo, 168 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Republican (Kosovo, 168 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 168 BC–1 BC] Republican. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (Kosovo, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (Kosovo, 1500 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 1500 BC–1100 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Serbia, 336 BC–168 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Serbia, 336 BC–168 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 336 BC–168 BC] Hellenistic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

nodes.name: Contermporary (Slovenia, AD 1790–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contermporary (Slovenia, AD 1790–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, AD 1790–AD 2000] Contermporary. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Slovene lands passed from Habsburg rule, briefly interrupted by Napoleon's Illyrian Provinces, into the Yugoslav kingdom after 1918, and the period saw a national language and literature deliberately built up in the face of German and Italian dominance. Occupation and partisan warfare in the Second World War were followed by socialist Yugoslavia and, in 1991, independence after a ten-day war.

nodes.name: Mesolithique (Morocco, 10000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolithique (Morocco, 10000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.description: [Morocco, 10000 BC–5000 BC] Mesolithique. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age (Serbia, 2100 BC–1800 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age (Serbia, 2100 BC–1800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 2100 BC–1800 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

nodes.name: Roman Period (Macedonia, AD 30–AD 300)
nodes.title: Roman Period (Macedonia, AD 30–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, AD 30–AD 300] Roman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

nodes.name: Medieval/Byzantine (Kosovo, AD 1000–AD 1389)
nodes.title: Medieval/Byzantine (Kosovo, AD 1000–AD 1389)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 1000–AD 1389] Medieval/Byzantine. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Byzantine authority over the Serbian lands gave way to independent principalities and then, under the Nemanjić dynasty, to a kingdom and briefly an empire under Stefan Dušan. Wealth from silver mines paid for fresco-covered monastery churches such as Studenica and Gračanica, some of the finest medieval painting in Europe. The empire fragmented after Dušan's death, and the defeat at Kosovo in 1389 opened the way to Ottoman domination.

nodes.name: Contemporáneo (Spain, AD 1790–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporáneo (Spain, AD 1790–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1790–AD 2000] Contemporáneo. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Napoleonic invasion and the guerrilla war against it shattered the old order, and Spain spent the nineteenth century losing an American empire while lurching between liberal constitutions, dynastic civil wars and coups. The Second Republic, the Civil War of 1936-39 and forty years of Franco's dictatorship dominate the twentieth century, followed by a negotiated return to democracy and rapid modernisation.

nodes.name: Early Iron Age (Romania, 1000 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age (Romania, 1000 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 1000 BC–500 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

nodes.name: Moderne (Morocco, AD 1492–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Moderne (Morocco, AD 1492–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, AD 1492–AD 1789] Moderne. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Albanian lands remained Ottoman provinces while the Rilindja movement built a written language and a national idea across religious divisions. Independence was declared in 1912 amid the Balkan Wars, but the new state's borders left large Albanian populations outside them, and the interwar years under Ahmet Zogu were poor and unstable. Italian occupation in 1939 and then German control ended in 1944 with the victory of the communist partisans.

nodes.name: Iron Age (Macedonia, 1000 BC–600 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Macedonia, 1000 BC–600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 1000 BC–600 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

nodes.name: Mesjetë e hershme (Albania, AD 565–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Mesjetë e hershme (Albania, AD 565–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 565–AD 1000] Mesjetë e hershme. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Slavic migrations and the collapse of the late Roman urban network reduced most inland towns to hilltop refuges, while Durrës survived as a Byzantine stronghold and the seat of a theme. Christianity persisted but the region became a border zone fought over by Byzantium and the expanding Bulgarian empire. Archaeologically it is a thin, difficult period of scattered cemeteries and reused fortifications, from which the medieval Albanian population emerges.

nodes.name: Roman Imperial (Italy, AD 31–AD 399)
nodes.title: Roman Imperial (Italy, AD 31–AD 399)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 31–AD 399] Roman Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The eastern Alpine lands became a settled part of the empire, crossed by the road from Aquileia to the Danube and guarded by the fortified Claustra Alpium Iuliarum. Emona (Ljubljana) and Celeia (Celje) were laid out on grid plans with walls, drains and cemeteries, and local elites adopted Latin names and Roman gods alongside their own. The route made the region a corridor for armies and, later, for invaders heading into Italy.

nodes.name: Neolit (Albania, 4100 BC–3060 BC)
nodes.title: Neolit (Albania, 4100 BC–3060 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 4100 BC–3060 BC] Neolit. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Farming villages settled Albania's river valleys and the lake basins around Korçë, with Maliq and similar sites building up as mounds of debris from generations of mudbrick houses. Their painted and dark burnished pottery links them to the wider Balkan and Aegean Neolithic world, and copper begins to appear towards the end of the period. Livestock, grain storage and long-distance exchange in obsidian and fine wares mark the shift from scattered settlement to established communities.

nodes.name: Mid Imperial (Kosovo, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.title: Mid Imperial (Kosovo, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 100–AD 300] Mid Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The inland Roman province of Dardania was at its most developed, its wealth resting on silver, lead and iron mines in the surrounding mountains. The town of Ulpiana, raised to municipal status under Trajan, acquired baths, walls and a forum, and roads linked the region to the Adriatic and the Danube. Latin inscriptions, funerary monuments and imported goods show a provincial elite living in Roman style alongside a strongly local population.

nodes.name: Залізний вік (Ukraine, 999 BC–AD 450)
nodes.title: Залізний вік (Ukraine, 999 BC–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 999 BC–AD 450] Залізний вік. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Iron working spread as waves of mounted nomads — Cimmerians, then Scythians, then Sarmatians — dominated the steppe, burying their leaders with gold, weapons and horses in great mounds. Greek colonies along the Black Sea shipped grain south and left cities like Olbia, Chersonesos and the Bosporan capital Panticapaeum. In the forest-steppe, settled farming communities culminated in the Chernyakhov culture, trading with Rome until the Hunnic upheavals of the 5th century.

nodes.name: Late Antique (Slovenia, AD 401–AD 599)
nodes.title: Late Antique (Slovenia, AD 401–AD 599)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, AD 401–AD 599] Late Antique. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The western empire dissolved into barbarian kingdoms: Ostrogothic rule under Theoderic preserved much of Roman administration at Ravenna, until Justinian's twenty-year Gothic War devastated the peninsula and the Lombards seized the north in 568. Cities shrank, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and bishops and monasteries took over civic leadership. It was also an age of extraordinary art - Ravenna's mosaics - and of the Rule of St Benedict.

nodes.name: Romano imperial (Spain, AD 1–AD 400)
nodes.title: Romano imperial (Spain, AD 1–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1–AD 400] Romano imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The mature phase of Roman Hispania, when the peninsula was a settled, prosperous group of provinces rather than a war zone. Mines at Las Médulas and Río Tinto, oil shipped in amphorae whose sherds built Rome's Monte Testaccio, and grand cities at Mérida, Italica and Tarraco date from these centuries, as does the spread of Christianity in the later part of the span.

nodes.name: Eneolothic (Italy, 3299 BC–2301 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolothic (Italy, 3299 BC–2301 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 3299 BC–2301 BC] Eneolothic. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper Age communities in the Ljubljana Marshes built pile-dwelling villages on wooden platforms above the wetlands, leaving waterlogged deposits that preserve wood, textiles and tools normally lost. From one of them comes the oldest known wooden wheel and axle, evidence that wheeled transport was in use here in the late fourth millennium. Copper tools, Bell Beaker pottery and long-distance contacts mark the transition towards the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Neolítico (Spain, 4999 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.title: Neolítico (Spain, 4999 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 4999 BC–3300 BC] Neolítico. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The first farmers in the peninsula grew cereals and pulses and kept sheep, goats and cattle, spreading along the Mediterranean coast with distinctive shell-impressed Cardial pottery and inland through cave and open-air settlements. Burial in caves and, increasingly, in megalithic tombs marks a new concern with ancestors and place. Rock art and the earliest large communal monuments belong to these centuries.

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Serbia, 1800 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Serbia, 1800 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 1800 BC–1500 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

nodes.name: Early Imperial (Serbia, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.title: Early Imperial (Serbia, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 1–AD 100] Early Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Danube frontier was consolidated under the first Roman emperors, with legions stationed at Singidunum and Viminacium and a road network binding the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia to Italy. Veteran colonies, mining districts and river forts drew in traders and settlers, and Latin, Roman law and urban planning spread among local Illyrian, Celtic and Thracian communities. The region's importance grew until it eventually produced emperors of its own.

nodes.name: Ранньоримський період (Ukraine, 49 BC–AD 175)
nodes.title: Ранньоримський період (Ukraine, 49 BC–AD 175)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 49 BC–AD 175] Ранньоримський період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Greek cities on the Black Sea coast such as Olbia and Chersonesos became clients and then garrisons of Rome, pulling grain, hides and slaves into imperial trade networks. Sarmatian horsemen dominated the steppe while the Zarubintsy communities of the forest-steppe farmed and traded northward. Roman denarii, wheel-made tableware and wine amphorae turn up hundreds of kilometres beyond any frontier, a measure of how far imperial goods reached.

nodes.name: Calcolítico (Spain, 3299 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.title: Calcolítico (Spain, 3299 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 3299 BC–2300 BC] Calcolítico. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Copper metallurgy spread across the Iberian peninsula alongside the first walled settlements, such as Los Millares in the southeast, with bastioned enclosures, collective tholos and megalithic tombs, and rich grave goods of ivory, ostrich eggshell and Atlantic amber. Communal burial and long-distance exchange point to societies growing more unequal and more organised, while irrigation and metalworking reshaped the countryside. Near its end came the Bell Beaker phenomenon, whose distinctive drinking vessels and archer's kit turn up from Portugal to central Europe. The fortified towns and copper daggers of these centuries set the stage for the Bronze Age El Argar culture.

nodes.name: Archaic/Protourban illyrian (Kosovo, 600 BC–480 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic/Protourban illyrian (Kosovo, 600 BC–480 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, 600 BC–480 BC] Archaic/Protourban illyrian. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Illyrian communities in the interior fortified hilltop settlements and buried their leading families under tumuli with weapons, bronze ornaments and imported goods. Greek pottery and metalwork arriving from the Adriatic colonies show these groups plugged into wider Mediterranean trade, and some settlements begin to take on genuinely urban form. It is the world in which the Dardanian and other Illyrian polities that later fought Macedon and Rome took shape.

nodes.name: Гуни (Ukraine, AD 375–AD 450)
nodes.title: Гуни (Ukraine, AD 375–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 375–AD 450] Гуни. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Mounted nomads from the Asian steppe shattered the Gothic kingdoms of the Pontic region and set whole peoples fleeing westward across the Danube, the trigger for the great migrations that broke the western Roman Empire. For a few decades a Hunnic confederation, culminating under Attila, extracted tribute from Constantinople and terrorised Gaul and Italy. Their legacy in the region is archaeological — cauldrons, gold-sheathed saddles, artificially elongated skulls — rather than institutional, as the empire dissolved after Attila's death.

nodes.name: Early Medieval Period (Romania, AD 476–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Medieval Period (Romania, AD 476–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 476–AD 1000] Early Medieval Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

With Roman authority gone, the lands north of the Danube passed through the hands of Gepids, Avars, Slavs, Bulgars and finally the Magyars, who arrived at the end of the ninth century. Towns disappeared in favour of small farming villages with sunken-floored houses and hand-made pots, though hoards of Byzantine coins show trade never wholly stopped. The Slavic settlement of the region and the arrival of the Hungarians in the plain set the ethnic map that later Transylvanian history was built on.

nodes.name: Пізнє Середньовіччя (Ukraine, AD 1250–AD 1569)
nodes.title: Пізнє Середньовіччя (Ukraine, AD 1250–AD 1569)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1250–AD 1569] Пізнє Середньовіччя. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

After the Mongol conquest the lands were reshaped politically: Galicia-Volhynia flourished briefly as a kingdom, then was divided as the Grand Duchy of Lithuania absorbed most of the Rus' principalities and Poland took the west. Castles, brick churches and chartered towns with Magdeburg-law privileges mark the period, alongside the Crimean Khanate's rise in the south. It closes with the Union of Lublin, which folded these territories into a single Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

nodes.name: Contemporary (Bulgaria, AD 1878–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporary (Bulgaria, AD 1878–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 1878–AD 2000] Contemporary. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

nodes.name: Скіфи (Ukraine, 749 BC–249 BC)
nodes.title: Скіфи (Ukraine, 749 BC–249 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 749 BC–249 BC] Скіфи. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Mounted nomads from the steppe built a powerful confederation that dominated the region for centuries, extracting tribute from farming populations and trading grain to the Greek colonies of the Black Sea coast in exchange for wine and luxury goods. Their royal kurgans, some the size of small hills, held gold pectorals, sword scabbards and vessels showing scenes of Scythian life, much of it made by Greek craftsmen for Scythian patrons. Herodotus described their customs, horse sacrifices and burial rites in detail, and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed him.

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Romania, 1900 BC–1600 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Romania, 1900 BC–1600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 1900 BC–1600 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

nodes.name: Early Medieval (Bulgaria, AD 476–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Medieval (Bulgaria, AD 476–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 476–AD 1000] Early Medieval. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

nodes.name: Néolithique (Morocco, 5000 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.title: Néolithique (Morocco, 5000 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, 5000 BC–3300 BC] Néolithique. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Herding of sheep, goats and cattle, together with pottery and cultivated grain, spread across the Moroccan coast, the Rif and the Atlas, taking hold among populations descended from earlier hunter-gatherers. Cardial-impressed pottery in the north points to contact across the Strait with Iberia, while cave sites and shell middens show a mixed economy of farming, herding, fishing and gathering. Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.

nodes.name: Hekur i zhvilluar (Albania, 800 BC–600 BC)
nodes.title: Hekur i zhvilluar (Albania, 800 BC–600 BC)
nodes.description: [Albania, 800 BC–600 BC] Hekur i zhvilluar. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Mid Imperial (Serbia, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.title: Mid Imperial (Serbia, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 100–AD 300] Mid Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The inland Roman province of Dardania was at its most developed, its wealth resting on silver, lead and iron mines in the surrounding mountains. The town of Ulpiana, raised to municipal status under Trajan, acquired baths, walls and a forum, and roads linked the region to the Adriatic and the Danube. Latin inscriptions, funerary monuments and imported goods show a provincial elite living in Roman style alongside a strongly local population.

nodes.name: Orientalizing (Slovenia, 749 BC–581 BC)
nodes.title: Orientalizing (Slovenia, 749 BC–581 BC)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 749 BC–581 BC] Orientalizing. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Rich hillforts and enormous burial mounds in the Dolenjska region mark a wealthy Hallstatt-era elite trading with Italy and the eastern Alps. Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. The imagery borrows from Etruscan and Near Eastern art but tells local stories.

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (Bulgaria, 1600 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (Bulgaria, 1600 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 1600 BC–1000 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

nodes.name: Ottoman Period (Romania, AD 1396–AD 1878)
nodes.title: Ottoman Period (Romania, AD 1396–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 1396–AD 1878] Ottoman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

nodes.name: Late Antiquity (Macedonia, AD 300–AD 600)
nodes.title: Late Antiquity (Macedonia, AD 300–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, AD 300–AD 600] Late Antiquity. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Roman provinces along the lower Danube and in Thrace became a frontier zone under constant pressure, with Goths, Huns and other groups crossing the river while emperors fortified cities and roads. Christianity spread fast: basilicas and bishoprics appeared at Serdica, Philippopolis and elsewhere, and Serdica hosted a major church council. After the empire split, these lands fell to the eastern half, setting up their long Byzantine future.

nodes.name: Hekuri i hershëm (Albania, 1100 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Hekuri i hershëm (Albania, 1100 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description: [Albania, 1100 BC–800 BC] Hekuri i hershëm. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

nodes.name: Moderno (Spain, AD 1480–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Moderno (Spain, AD 1480–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1480–AD 1789] Moderno. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The union of Castile and Aragon under the Catholic Monarchs, the fall of Granada and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 created a single confessional monarchy that immediately became an Atlantic empire. American silver funded Habsburg wars in the Netherlands, Italy and Germany while sustaining the literary and artistic Golden Age of Cervantes, Velázquez and the great cathedrals. Decline, the loss of the Portuguese crown and a war of succession brought in the Bourbons and a century of centralising reform.

nodes.name: Late Iron Age (Romania, 500 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Late Iron Age (Romania, 500 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 500 BC–1 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

nodes.name: Late Imperial (Kosovo, AD 300–AD 565)
nodes.title: Late Imperial (Kosovo, AD 300–AD 565)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 300–AD 565] Late Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Diocletian and Constantine's reforms reorganised this inland Balkan territory as part of a militarised late Roman state, with new fortifications guarding the roads linking the Adriatic to Constantinople. Christianity became dominant, leaving basilicas and episcopal centres, and Justinian founded a grand new city near his birthplace in the province of Dardania. Repeated Gothic, Hunnic and Avar-Slav incursions eroded urban life and set up the region's transformation in the following centuries.

nodes.name: Contemporary (Kosovo, AD 1944–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Contemporary (Kosovo, AD 1944–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 1944–AD 2000] Contemporary. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

French invasion swept away the old patchwork of duchies and republics, and the ideas it left behind fed the Risorgimento and the unification of the peninsula under Piedmont in 1861. Industrialisation in the north, mass emigration from the south, two world wars, twenty years of Fascism and the birth of the Republic in 1946 all fall within this stretch.

nodes.name: Medievale (Morocco, AD 600–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Medievale (Morocco, AD 600–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Morocco, AD 600–AD 1500] Medievale. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Arab armies brought Islam to the Maghreb in the seventh century, and Morocco became the base of a succession of dynasties: the Idrisids, who founded Fez, then the Almoravids and Almohads, whose Berber empires ruled from the Sahara to central Spain. Trans-Saharan caravans carried gold, salt and slaves north, funding mosques, madrasas and walled cities. The Marinids and their successors held the country while Christian kingdoms completed the reconquest of Iberia, pushing Portuguese and Spanish forces onto the Moroccan coast.

nodes.name: Елліністичний період (Ukraine, 329 BC–49 BC)
nodes.title: Елліністичний період (Ukraine, 329 BC–49 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 329 BC–49 BC] Елліністичний період. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Greek cities of the northern Black Sea — Olbia, Chersonesos and the Bosporan kingdom around the Kerch strait — reached their commercial peak, shipping grain to the Aegean and burying their rulers in monumental tumuli. Scythian power on the open steppe gave way to a smaller kingdom in the Crimea and to incoming Sarmatians, keeping the cities under constant pressure. In the 1st century BC the region was pulled into the wars of Mithridates VI and then into the Roman sphere.

nodes.name: Archaic/Protourban illyrian (Serbia, 600 BC–480 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic/Protourban illyrian (Serbia, 600 BC–480 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, 600 BC–480 BC] Archaic/Protourban illyrian. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Illyrian communities in the interior fortified hilltop settlements and buried their leading families under tumuli with weapons, bronze ornaments and imported goods. Greek pottery and metalwork arriving from the Adriatic colonies show these groups plugged into wider Mediterranean trade, and some settlements begin to take on genuinely urban form. It is the world in which the Dardanian and other Illyrian polities that later fought Macedon and Rome took shape.

nodes.name: Roman Period (Bulgaria, 1 BC–AD 300)
nodes.title: Roman Period (Bulgaria, 1 BC–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, 1 BC–AD 300] Roman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

nodes.name: Osmane (Albania, AD 1389–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Osmane (Albania, AD 1389–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Albania, AD 1389–AD 1850] Osmane. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Ottoman rule reshaped Albanian society over more than four centuries: Skanderbeg's long resistance in the fifteenth century became the founding national legend, but after his death the highlands and coastal towns were absorbed into the empire's provincial system. Large numbers converted to Islam, Albanians rose to the highest offices in Istanbul and Cairo, and semi-independent pashas such as Ali of Tepelena carved out near-sovereign domains. Mosques, bridges, bazaars and hillside citadels from these centuries still dominate towns like Berat and Gjirokastër.

nodes.name: Late Roman Period (Romania, AD 400–AD 700)
nodes.title: Late Roman Period (Romania, AD 400–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 400–AD 700] Late Roman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.

nodes.name: Ottoman (Serbia, AD 1389–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Ottoman (Serbia, AD 1389–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 1389–AD 1850] Ottoman. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

nodes.name: Ottoman Period (Macedonia, AD 1371–AD 1912)
nodes.title: Ottoman Period (Macedonia, AD 1371–AD 1912)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, AD 1371–AD 1912] Ottoman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

nodes.name: Ottoman (Kosovo, AD 1389–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Ottoman (Kosovo, AD 1389–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 1389–AD 1850] Ottoman. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

nodes.name: Early Roman Period (Romania, AD 300–AD 476)
nodes.title: Early Roman Period (Romania, AD 300–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 300–AD 476] Early Roman Period. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

nodes.name: Доба середньої бронзи (Ukraine, 2299 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.title: Доба середньої бронзи (Ukraine, 2299 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, 2299 BC–1799 BC] Доба середньої бронзи. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Kurgan burial continued, but the rite changed: the Catacomb culture cut side-chambers off the grave shaft, modelled clay over the faces of the dead and left richly furnished tombs. Later the Babyno (multi-cordoned ware) groups spread across the steppe with simpler pottery and increasing evidence of horse gear. Metalwork grew more varied as copper from the Caucasus and the Balkans moved along steppe routes.

nodes.name: Late Imperial (Serbia, AD 300–AD 565)
nodes.title: Late Imperial (Serbia, AD 300–AD 565)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 300–AD 565] Late Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Diocletian and Constantine's reforms reorganised this inland Balkan territory as part of a militarised late Roman state, with new fortifications guarding the roads linking the Adriatic to Constantinople. Christianity became dominant, leaving basilicas and episcopal centres, and Justinian founded a grand new city near his birthplace in the province of Dardania. Repeated Gothic, Hunnic and Avar-Slav incursions eroded urban life and set up the region's transformation in the following centuries.

nodes.name: Orientalizing (Italy, 749 BC–581 BC)
nodes.title: Orientalizing (Italy, 749 BC–581 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 749 BC–581 BC] Orientalizing. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

Rich hillforts and enormous burial mounds in the Dolenjska region mark a wealthy Hallstatt-era elite trading with Italy and the eastern Alps. Their tombs yielded bronze situlae, buckets decorated in relief with feasting, processions, and boxing matches, along with imported amber, glass, and ornate helmets. The imagery borrows from Etruscan and Near Eastern art but tells local stories.

nodes.name: Early Imperial (Kosovo, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.title: Early Imperial (Kosovo, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[Kosovo, AD 1–AD 100] Early Imperial. Period definition from FASTI - Home — AIAC, 2004.

The Danube frontier was consolidated under the first Roman emperors, with legions stationed at Singidunum and Viminacium and a road network binding the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia to Italy. Veteran colonies, mining districts and river forts drew in traders and settlers, and Latin, Roman law and urban planning spread among local Illyrian, Celtic and Thracian communities. The region's importance grew until it eventually produced emperors of its own.

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Italy, 322 BC–30 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Italy, 322 BC–30 BC)
nodes.description:
[Late Roman Empire, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic. added post-GeoDia. Period definition from Rome, the late empire : Roman art AD 200-400. — Bianchi Bandinelli, Ranuccio., 1971.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

hints.label: Hellenistic
hints.source: Rome, the late empire : Roman art AD 200-400.

nodes.name: Late Empire (Italy, AD 192–AD 421)
nodes.title: Late Empire (Italy, AD 192–AD 421)
nodes.description:
[Late Roman Empire, AD 192–AD 421] Late Empire. Period definition from Rome, the late empire : Roman art AD 200-400. — Bianchi Bandinelli, Ranuccio., 1971.

Rome passed from the assassination of Commodus into a century of civil war, plague and currency collapse, then was rebuilt by Diocletian and Constantine as a more bureaucratic, militarised state with new capitals and a Christian emperor. Italy itself lost its privileged position — the court moved to Milan and then Ravenna — and Rome was sacked by the Goths in 410. Visitors see the shift in art too, from naturalistic portraiture to the frontal, hieratic style that leads into Byzantine imagery.

hints.label: Late Empire
hints.source: Rome, the late empire : Roman art AD 200-400.

nodes.name: Achaemenid rule (Iran, 499 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: Achaemenid rule (Iran, 499 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 499 BC–299 BC] Achaemenid rule. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Persian governors administered the empire's provinces through tribute, garrisons and local intermediaries, tying distant regions to the court by road networks and a common silver currency. It was an age of monumental royal building, trilingual inscriptions and religious tolerance, punctuated by satrapal revolts and the long contest with the Greeks.

hints.label: Achaemenid rule
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Akkad (Iran, 2333 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.title: Akkad (Iran, 2333 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2333 BC–2099 BC] Akkad. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The kings of Akkad extended their reach eastward across the Zagros, campaigning into Elam and taking Susa, where Akkadian became a language of administration alongside Elamite. Sargon and his grandson Naram-Sin claimed dominion from the Gulf to the Mediterranean and imposed governors and garrisons on conquered cities. Mesopotamian art, script and royal titles left a deep imprint on the Iranian plateau long after the empire itself collapsed.

hints.label: Akkad
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Susa II archaeological period (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC)
nodes.title: Susa II archaeological period (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 3499 BC–3099 BC] Susa II archaeological period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Prehistoric Susa II, corresponds to Mesopotamian Ubaid period. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

A phase of intense contact with Uruk-period Mesopotamia, visible in mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder-seal administration and clay tokens sealed in hollow clay balls. These recording devices mark the transition from counting to writing. Susa served as the western gateway of a trade system reaching deep into highland Iran.

hints.label: Susa II archaeological period
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Isin-Larsa (Iran, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.title: Isin-Larsa (Iran, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Isin-Larsa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Named for the two Mesopotamian cities that fought over the legacy of the fallen Ur III empire, this horizon in the east coincides with the rise of the Sukkalmah rulers of Elam, who traded, intermarried and intrigued with the kings of southern Iraq. Cuneiform contracts, cylinder seals and standardised pottery show how closely the Iranian lowlands were tied into Babylonian economic life. It ends with Hammurabi's conquests reshaping the region.

hints.label: Isin-Larsa
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Iron Age (Iran, 1199 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Iran, 1199 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1199 BC–299 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

hints.label: Iron Age
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Chalcolithic Age (Iran, 3999 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic Age (Iran, 3999 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 3999 BC–2899 BC] Chalcolithic Age. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Copper working moved from occasional ornaments to real industry, with smelted tools and the beginnings of alloying. Large sites on the Susiana plain and the Iranian plateau grew into centres with monumental platforms, mass-produced pottery and stamp seals for controlling goods — the machinery of administration taking shape just before writing.

hints.label: Chalcolithic Age
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Isin II (Iran, 1099 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Isin II (Iran, 1099 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1099 BC–899 BC] Isin II. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The second dynasty of Isin ruled Babylonia after the collapse of Kassite power, its most famous king, Nebuchadnezzar I, raiding deep into Elam and carrying home the statue of Marduk that Elamite armies had taken. That victory was celebrated in poetry for centuries and pushed Marduk to the head of the Babylonian pantheon. For Elam it marked the end of a period of dominance and the beginning of a long dark age in the written record.

hints.label: Isin II
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Early Dynastic II (Iran, 2749 BC–2599 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic II (Iran, 2749 BC–2599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2749 BC–2599 BC] Early Dynastic II. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

A middle phase in which independent city-states hardened into rivals, each with its patron deity, temple estate and palace. Later Mesopotamian tradition placed its legendary kings, including Gilgamesh of Uruk, in roughly this era. Temple sculpture of wide-eyed worshippers in fringed skirts, made to stand in perpetual prayer on behalf of the donor, belongs to this world.

hints.label: Early Dynastic II
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 599 BC–549 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Elamite II (Iran, 599 BC–549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 599 BC–549 BC] Neo-Elamite II. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Elam's final decades, following the Assyrian sack of Susa, when fragmented kingdoms and princes ruled the lowlands while Persian groups established themselves in Anshan and the highlands. Elamite scribal and administrative traditions passed directly to these newcomers, and within a lifetime Cyrus the Great had absorbed the whole region into Persia.

hints.label: Neo-Elamite II
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3499 BC–2699 BC)
nodes.title: Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite (Iran, 3499 BC–2699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 3499 BC–2699 BC] Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. This period corresponds to Proto-Literate period in Mesopotamia. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

At Susa and across the Iranian plateau, administrators adopted an accounting script of their own — Proto-Elamite — written on clay tablets that record livestock, grain and labour but remain largely undeciphered. The system spread remarkably far east, to Tepe Yahya and Shahr-i Sokhta, tracing a network of trading centres handling metal, stone and textiles. When it fell out of use, writing in Iran lapsed for centuries before Elamite cuneiform appeared.

hints.label: Protoliterate: Proto-Elamite
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Iran, 2899 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Iran, 2899 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

hints.label: Bronze Age
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Early Dynastic III (Iran, 2599 BC–2333 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic III (Iran, 2599 BC–2333 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2599 BC–2333 BC] Early Dynastic III. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The richest phase of the early city-state era, ending with conquest by Sargon of Akkad. Royal inscriptions become genuinely historical — border disputes between Lagash and Umma are recorded in detail — and cuneiform is used for literature, hymns and law. The Royal Cemetery of Ur, with its lyres, gold headdresses and mass retainer burials, dates to these centuries.

nodes.name: Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 599 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 599 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 599 BC–499 BC] Neo-Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Judah under Babylonian rule was a diminished, largely rural province, its capital and temple in ruins and its royal house deported. Excavations show towns in the south and the Shephelah abandoned or shrunken while some settlements north of Jerusalem, around Benjamin, carried on. This bleak interval ended when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and permitted exiles to return.

Altintepe, Iran

hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Achaemenid (Iran, 549 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: Achaemenid (Iran, 549 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 549 BC–299 BC] Achaemenid. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Cyrus the Great and his successors welded Iran, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Egypt into the largest empire the world had yet seen, governed through satraps, royal roads and a standardised silver coinage. Persepolis and Susa displayed the empire's wealth in carved processions of tribute-bearers from every subject people. Alexander's invasion brought it down, but its administrative model outlived it.

hints.label: Achaemenid
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 1499 BC–899 BC] Middle Elamite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Elam's most powerful era, when kings ruling from Susa and Anshan wrote in Elamite rather than Akkadian and built on a monumental scale. Untash-Napirisha founded the sacred city of Chogha Zanbil with its huge stepped ziggurat, still the best-preserved in the world, and later Shutrukid rulers sacked Babylon and carried off the stele of Hammurabi's laws and the victory monument of Naram-Sin as trophies for Susa. Assyrian and Babylonian counterattacks eventually broke the dynasty.

hints.label: Middle Elamite
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Late Uruk (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC)
nodes.title: Late Uruk (Iran, 3499 BC–3099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–3099 BC] Late Uruk. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The world's first cities took shape in the Mesopotamian lowlands, and their institutions, goods and administrators reached deep into the Iranian plateau and Khuzestan. Mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and the earliest clay tablets with proto-cuneiform signs mark the birth of bureaucratic record-keeping. When the Uruk network contracted, Susa and its neighbours went their own way, developing the Proto-Elamite script and state.

hints.label: Late Uruk
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.title: Susa I archaeological period (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Susa I archaeological period. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. This period designates prehistoric Susa and corresponds to Ubaid period in Mesopotamia. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Susa's earliest urban phase, dominated by a monumental mud-brick terrace and an extensive cemetery beside it. Its painted funerary beakers, with geometric animals stretched to fit the vessel, are icons of Iranian prehistory, and the copper tools and seals buried with them point to emerging craft specialisation and social hierarchy on the Susiana plain.

hints.label: Susa I archaeological period
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Kassite (Iran, 1599 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Kassite (Iran, 1599 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–1099 BC] Kassite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

After the Hittite raid that toppled Hammurabi's dynasty, Kassite kings—outsiders of uncertain origin—ruled Babylonia for close to four centuries, the longest single dynasty in Mesopotamian history. They stabilised the south, corresponded as equals with Egypt's pharaohs in the Amarna letters, built the new capital of Dur-Kurigalzu, and left the carved kudurru stones that recorded royal land grants.

hints.label: Kassite
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Ur III (Iran, 2099 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Ur III (Iran, 2099 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC] Ur III. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The Third Dynasty of Ur built a tightly administered state that reached across the Iranian lowlands, holding Susa and planting garrisons and governors in the Zagros foothills. Its scribes produced tens of thousands of accounting tablets recording livestock, labour and grain in obsessive detail, the densest bureaucratic archive of the ancient world. The empire fell when Elamite forces sacked Ur, an event lamented in Sumerian poetry for centuries afterwards.

nodes.name: Old Babylonian (Iran, 1799 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Old Babylonian (Iran, 1799 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1799 BC–1699 BC] Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.

hints.label: Old Babylonian
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Jamdat Nasr (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.title: Jamdat Nasr (Iran, 3099 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Jamdat Nasr. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The phase between the first Uruk cities and the Early Dynastic world, marked by distinctive polychrome painted jars and by the spread of proto-cuneiform tablets recording rations, land and livestock. Writing was still pictographic and administrative rather than literary, but the bureaucratic habits of temple economies were taking shape. Sites across the Iranian plateau show how far Mesopotamian styles and accounting practices travelled.

hints.label: Jamdat Nasr
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Prehistoric (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.title: Prehistoric (Iran, 3999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 3999 BC–3499 BC] Prehistoric. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Late Chalcolithic communities on the Iranian plateau and in Khuzestan used mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, copper metallurgy and clay tokens and seals to track goods. Susa emerged as a major centre in close contact with Mesopotamian Uruk, and the accounting systems developed here fed directly into the invention of writing.

hints.label: Prehistoric
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Elamite I (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Elam, 899 BC–599 BC] Neo-Elamite I. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

The first phase of Elam's revival, when local rulers reasserted themselves in Susiana and the highlands and began intervening in Babylonian politics against Assyria. Written sources are thin and largely Assyrian, but rock reliefs and rebuilt sanctuaries show royal ambition returning after centuries of obscurity.

hints.label: Neo-Elamite I
hints.source: The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre

nodes.name: Neo-Assyrian (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Assyrian (Iran, 899 BC–599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 899 BC–599 BC] Neo-Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from The royal city of Susa : ancient Near Eastern treasures in the Louvre — Musée du Louvre., 1992.

Assyrian armies pushed repeatedly into the Zagros in these centuries, campaigning for horses, tribute and control of the trade routes across the Iranian plateau, and leaving royal inscriptions and reliefs that give the first written glimpses of the Medes and Persians. Local fortified centres and elite burials, such as those at Hasanlu and Ziwiye, reflect both Assyrian pressure and the wealth it drew in. The eventual Median coalition that helped destroy Assyria grew out of this long confrontation.
