nodes.name: Iron IIC (Israel, 721 BC–585 BC)
nodes.title: Iron IIC (Israel, 721 BC–585 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 721 BC–585 BC] Iron IIC. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Judah alone remained, a client of Assyria and then of Babylon, with Jerusalem swollen by refugees and the Negev and Shephelah reorganised for trade and agriculture. Literacy is unusually visible in ostraca from Arad and Lachish, written as the Babylonian armies closed in. The period ends with the destruction of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple and the deportation of 586 BC.

hints.label: Iron IIC
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Late Bronze IIA-B (Israel, 1399 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze IIA-B (Israel, 1399 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 1399 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze IIA-B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The peak and then the collapse of Egypt's empire in Canaan. Local kings corresponded with the pharaoh in cuneiform, Egyptian officials occupied residences at key towns, and imported Mycenaean and Cypriot wares filled elite tombs. Within a generation or two around 1200 BC the cities burned, Egyptian rule ended, and the political map of the Levant was redrawn.

hints.label: Late Bronze IIA-B
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Early Bronze I (Israel, 3299 BC–3049 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze I (Israel, 3299 BC–3049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 3299 BC–3049 BC] Early Bronze I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Farming villages coalesced into large unwalled settlements, and olive and vine cultivation, donkey caravans and copper from the Arabah began to knit the region into wider trade. Egyptian traders and settlers established themselves in the southern coastal plain, leaving pottery and serekhs of the earliest pharaohs, including Narmer. Out of this came the region's first true towns.

hints.label: Early Bronze I
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Pottery Neolithic B (Israel, 4999 BC–4299 BC)
nodes.title: Pottery Neolithic B (Israel, 4999 BC–4299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 4999 BC–4299 BC] Pottery Neolithic B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The later Pottery Neolithic in the southern Levant, largely the Wadi Rabah horizon, when villages grew again and pottery became finer: burnished dark wares, bow-rim jars and carinated bowls. Farmers began exploiting olives and other tree crops alongside cereals and herds, and stamp seals and small quantities of copper hint at growing exchange and ownership. Much of what defines the following Chalcolithic villages is already taking shape here.

hints.label: Pottery Neolithic B
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I (Israel, 2299 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I (Israel, 2299 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 2299 BC–1999 BC] Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

A non-urban interval between two ages of cities: people lived in small unwalled villages, campsites and copper-working camps, and buried their dead in vast shaft-tomb cemeteries. Bronze daggers and javelins and a distinctive hand-finished pottery mark the material culture, but there are no fortifications, palaces or writing. The debate over whether these were newcomers from the north or the descendants of the collapsed Early Bronze towns is still unresolved.

hints.label: Early Bronze IV/Middle Bronze I
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Middle Bronze (Israel, 2299 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze (Israel, 2299 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 2299 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Canaan revived after a long rural interlude, with substantial cities ringed by massive earthen ramparts and glacis, and a material culture of fine wheel-made pottery, bronze weapons and scarab seals. Trade linked the coast to Egypt, Cyprus and Syria, and Canaanite settlers in the Nile Delta eventually gave rise to Hyksos rule in Egypt. Many of the biblical cities - Hazor, Megiddo, Jericho, Shechem - reached their greatest size in these centuries.

hints.label: Middle Bronze
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Late Bronze I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Late Bronze I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Following the fall of the fortified Middle Bronze Age towns, Canaan became a patchwork of small Egyptian-dominated city-states paying tribute to the pharaohs. Urban life was thinner than before, but international trade thrived, bringing Cypriot and Aegean pottery, and Egyptian scarabs and statuary appear in local temples.

[Palestine, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Canaan was an Egyptian province of walled city-states, each with its ruler answering to a pharaoh's garrison and paying tribute. The Amarna letters capture their rivalries and pleas for help, while Cypriot, Mycenaean and Egyptian goods in the tombs show how deeply the region was tied into eastern Mediterranean trade. Widespread destructions and the appearance of new groups, including the earliest mention of Israel, close the age.

hints.label: Late Bronze
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Early Bronze (Israel, 3299 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze (Israel, 3299 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 3299 BC–2299 BC] Early Bronze. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The southern Levant saw its first experiment with urban life: villages grew into walled towns with temples, palaces, granaries and planned streets at places like Arad, Megiddo and Bet Yerah. Olive oil and wine were produced for export, and trade with Egypt was intense enough that Egyptian rulers' names appear on jars in Canaan. Around 2500–2300 BC the towns were abandoned and people returned to villages and pastoralism, a collapse still debated by archaeologists.

hints.label: Early Bronze
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Canaanite culture (Syria, 1899 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: Canaanite culture (Syria, 1899 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, 1899 BC–1599 BC] Canaanite culture. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. removed Neo-Assyrian (722-586 B.C.) and Neo-Babylonian (586-539 B.C.) since not explicit, and added new sources Amitai, Barton, Savage, King/Stager, and Richard. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

In the Middle Bronze Age the Levant filled with fortified city-states, ringed by massive earthen ramparts and glacis and ruled by kings who exchanged letters and gifts with Mari, Egypt and Aleppo. Bronze weaponry, painted Levantine pottery, scarabs and rich tomb goods reflect a prosperous merchant world running along the coast from Ugarit and Byblos southwards. It was in this milieu that the first alphabetic writing appeared, the ancestor of the Phoenician, Greek and Latin alphabets.

hints.label: Canaanite culture
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Iron (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC)
nodes.title: Iron (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The centuries between the collapse of the Late Bronze Age palace world and the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem. Egyptian control of Canaan ended, Philistine towns took shape on the coast, small kingdoms including Israel, Judah, Moab, Ammon and the Aramaean states emerged inland, and alphabetic writing spread. Assyrian and then Babylonian armies swallowed them all, ending with the fall of Jerusalem and the Judaean exile.

hints.label: Iron
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Bronze (Israel, 3299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze (Israel, 3299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 3299 BC–1199 BC] Bronze. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The land of Canaan moved from its first walled towns in the Early Bronze Age, through the collapse and pastoral interlude that followed, to the powerful fortified city-states of the Middle Bronze Age with their sloping earthen ramparts and chariot-owning elites. In the Late Bronze Age these cities became vassals of Egypt, and the Amarna letters preserve their rulers' pleading correspondence with the pharaoh. The whole system unravelled around 1200 BC, clearing the ground for the Philistines, Israelites and Arameans of the Iron Age.

hints.label: Bronze
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Early Bronze II-III (Israel, 3049 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze II-III (Israel, 3049 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 3049 BC–2299 BC] Early Bronze II-III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Massive mudbrick fortifications went up at Arad, Bet Yerah, Megiddo and elsewhere, enclosing temples, palaces and streets in the southern Levant's first genuine urban centres. Olive oil and wine flowed to Egypt, and imported Khirbet Kerak ware shows contacts stretching to the Caucasus. The system unravelled in the later third millennium, when the towns were emptied and the countryside reverted to villages and herding.

hints.label: Early Bronze II-III
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC)
nodes.title: Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 999 BC–924 BC] Iron IIA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Monumental building returns: fortified gates, palaces and administrative centres at sites like Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, traditionally credited to Solomon and hotly debated ever since. Pharaoh Sheshonq I campaigned through the region around 925 BC, leaving a list of conquered towns at Karnak. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature.

hints.label: Iron IIA
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Iron II (Israel, 999 BC–585 BC)
nodes.title: Iron II (Israel, 999 BC–585 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 999 BC–585 BC] Iron II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The age of the kingdoms — Israel in the north, Judah in the south, alongside Philistine, Phoenician, Aramaean and Transjordanian neighbours. Cities gained casemate walls, gateways, palaces and rock-cut water tunnels; Hebrew inscriptions, seals and ostraca show a functioning bureaucracy. Assyrian conquest ended Samaria in 720 BC, and Babylon ended Jerusalem in 586 BC, deporting Judah's elite.

hints.label: Iron II
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Phoenician culture (Syria, 1099 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Phoenician culture (Syria, 1099 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Phoenicia, 1099 BC–999 BC] Phoenician culture. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, West Bank. removed Neo-Assyrian (722-586 B.C.) and Neo-Babylonian (586-539 B.C.) since not explicit, and added new sources Amitai, Barton, Savage, King/Stager, and Richard. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

As Egyptian and Hittite power receded, the coastal cities of Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad turned to the sea, building a trading network that eventually reached Spain. Their greatest export was the alphabet, an efficient consonantal script that Greeks and later Romans adapted. Cedar, purple-dyed cloth, ivory and metalwork made these small city-states wealthy without any territorial empire.

hints.label: Phoenician culture
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Pottery Neolithic A (Israel, 5999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: Pottery Neolithic A (Israel, 5999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 5999 BC–4999 BC] Pottery Neolithic A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan.". Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

The first phase in which southern Levantine villagers made and used fired pottery, associated with the Yarmukian and Jericho IX assemblages. Settlements were smaller and more scattered than the crowded pre-pottery towns, with pit houses, storage pits and a mixed economy of cereals and herded sheep, goats, pigs and cattle. Distinctive incised herringbone designs filled with red paint, and coffee-bean-eyed clay figurines, make its material culture instantly recognisable.

hints.label: Pottery Neolithic A
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Iron IIB (Israel, 924 BC–721 BC)
nodes.title: Iron IIB (Israel, 924 BC–721 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, 924 BC–721 BC] Iron IIB. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Rows 637-658 were previously incorrectly attributed to Winks and Mattern-Parkes, 2004 in GeoDia, and thus also in Krueger, 2013, pp.43-44. Spatial_coverage_name per n.1 page 33: "Like the editors of IEJ, I find the name 'Palestine' the most suitable geographical term denoting the modern states of Israel and Jordan."1992, page 30. Period definition from Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E — Mazar, Amihai, (1942- ).,, 1992.

Israel under the Omrides and then Jeroboam II became a substantial regional power with ivory-decorated palaces at Samaria, before Assyrian armies destroyed it and deported its population in 720 BC. Judah survived as a vassal, and Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BC is documented from both sides — by Assyrian palace reliefs and by the excavated siege ramp and mass grave. Royal administration is visible in stamped jar handles and standardised weights.

hints.label: Iron IIB
hints.source: Archaeology of the land of the Bible, 10,000-586 B.C.E

nodes.name: Pueblo III (United States, AD 1150–AD 1300)
nodes.title: Pueblo III (United States, AD 1150–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Southwestern Colorado / San Juan Basin, AD 1150–AD 1300] Pueblo III. Period definition from Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin — 1999.

After Chaco's decline people drew together into large, tightly packed towns, many of them tucked into canyon alcoves - the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde and Canyon de Chelly belong to this time. Defensive placement, towers and reservoirs suggest competition for land and water. By about 1300 the Four Corners country was emptied entirely, its inhabitants moving south and east in one of the great migrations of North American history.

hints.label: Pueblo III
hints.source: Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin

nodes.name: Basketmaker II (United States, 999 BC–AD 500)
nodes.title: Basketmaker II (United States, 999 BC–AD 500)
nodes.description:
[Southwestern Colorado / San Juan Basin, 999 BC–AD 500] Basketmaker II. Period definition from Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin — 1999.

Early farming communities of the Colorado Plateau, growing maize and squash while still hunting with the atlatl and gathering wild plants. They stored grain in slab-lined cists, lived in shallow pithouses and rockshelters, and produced the superb coiled baskets and sandals — preserved in dry caves — that give the period its name. Pottery and the bow had not yet arrived.

hints.label: Basketmaker II
hints.source: Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin

nodes.name: Basketmaker III (United States, AD 500–AD 750)
nodes.title: Basketmaker III (United States, AD 500–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Southwestern Colorado / San Juan Basin, AD 500–AD 750] Basketmaker III. Period definition from Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin — 1999.

Pottery arrives in quantity, the bow and arrow replaces the atlatl, and beans join maize in the diet, allowing bigger and more permanent settlements. People lived in deep pithouses clustered into hamlets, often with an oversized structure for communal use that foreshadows the later kiva. These villages are the direct foundation of the Pueblo world that followed.

hints.label: Basketmaker III
hints.source: Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin

nodes.name: Pueblo II (United States, AD 900–AD 1150)
nodes.title: Pueblo II (United States, AD 900–AD 1150)
nodes.description:
[Southwestern Colorado / San Juan Basin, AD 900–AD 1150] Pueblo II. Period definition from Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin — 1999.

The era of Chaco Canyon, when massive multi-storey great houses, great kivas and a network of engineered roads linked communities across tens of thousands of square miles. Small farmsteads spread over almost every arable pocket of the Colorado Plateau, tied to regional centres by shared architecture and ritual. Trade brought turquoise, macaws and copper bells from as far as Mesoamerica.

hints.label: Pueblo II
hints.source: Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin

nodes.name: Pueblo I (United States, AD 750–AD 900)
nodes.title: Pueblo I (United States, AD 750–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Southwestern Colorado / San Juan Basin, AD 750–AD 900] Pueblo I. Period definition from Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin — 1999.

Farming families across the Colorado Plateau moved out of scattered pithouses into rows of aboveground rooms built of jacal and stone, clustered into the first true villages. Populations grew fast, some settlements reaching hundreds of people, and pottery, turkey-keeping and bean cultivation spread. Many of these villages were short-lived, breaking up and reforming elsewhere - a pattern of movement that would define Puebloan history.

hints.label: Pueblo I
hints.source: Colorado prehistory : a context for the Southern Colorado River Basin

nodes.name: Etruscan (Italy, 615 BC–508 BC)
nodes.title: Etruscan (Italy, 615 BC–508 BC)
nodes.description:
[pre-Roman Italy, 615 BC–508 BC] Etruscan. "Etruscans" entry. Period definition from The Oxford classical dictionary. — 2003.

The years of Etruscan dominance over Rome, when the city was ruled by kings of the Tarquin line and transformed from a cluster of hill villages into a genuine urban centre with drained marshland, a paved Forum and a great temple on the Capitol. Etruscan craftsmen, engineers and religious practices, from divination by entrails to the alphabet itself, shaped Roman institutions permanently. Tradition ends the era with the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus and the founding of the Republic.

nodes.name: Aksumite (Ethiopia, AD 300–AD 700)
nodes.title: Aksumite (Ethiopia, AD 300–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 300–AD 700] Aksumite. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. Derived from Cerulli 1968. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

From a highland capital in northern Ethiopia, Aksum controlled the Red Sea trade in ivory, gold and incense, minted its own gold, silver and bronze coinage, and traded with Rome, Arabia and India. King Ezana adopted Christianity in the fourth century, making Aksum one of the earliest Christian states and founding the church that still shapes Ethiopian life. The giant carved stelae over royal tombs, some over thirty metres tall, remain the most striking monuments of the kingdom, which later lost ground as Islamic powers took over Red Sea commerce.

hints.label: Aksumite
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Postaksumite I (Ethiopia, AD 1200–AD 1433)
nodes.title: Postaksumite I (Ethiopia, AD 1200–AD 1433)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 1200–AD 1433] Postaksumite I. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. Derived from Cerulli 1968. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

Centuries after Aksum's decline, the Christian highland state re-formed further south: the Zagwe kings cut the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela out of living stone, and from 1270 the Solomonic dynasty claimed descent from Solomon and Sheba to legitimise its rule. Kings such as Amda Seyon campaigned against neighbouring Muslim sultanates over the trade routes to the Red Sea, and the court moved with the army rather than sitting in a fixed capital. Monasteries became the main producers of manuscripts, painting and the chronicles on which Ethiopian history is built.

hints.label: Postaksumite I
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Postaksumite II (Ethiopia, AD 1434–AD 1632)
nodes.title: Postaksumite II (Ethiopia, AD 1434–AD 1632)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 1434–AD 1632] Postaksumite II. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. Derived from Cerulli 1968. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

Power in the Ethiopian highlands rested with the Solomonic kings, who ruled from mobile tented camps rather than fixed capitals, while monasteries and rock-cut and built churches anchored Christian life in the countryside. The period was torn open by the invasion of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi in the 1520s-40s, which destroyed churches and treasuries across the plateau and drew in Portuguese musketeers on the emperors' side. Jesuit missionaries followed, until their expulsion and the restoration of the Orthodox faith closed the era just before Gondar was founded as a permanent royal city.

hints.label: Postaksumite II
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Zamana Masāfǝnt (Ethiopia, AD 1769–AD 1855)
nodes.title: Zamana Masāfǝnt (Ethiopia, AD 1769–AD 1855)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 1769–AD 1855] Zamana Masāfǝnt. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. Derived from Cerulli 1968. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

Ethiopian emperors at Gondar were reduced to figureheads while regional warlords, above all the Yejju Oromo rulers of Begemder, fought each other for the position of ras and controlled the throne. Provinces went their own way, trade routes were disrupted and the church split over doctrinal disputes. The fragmentation ended when Tewodros II defeated the great lords and reunified the empire by force.

hints.label: Zamana Masāfǝnt
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Modern Period (Ethiopia, AD 1855–AD 1974)
nodes.title: Modern Period (Ethiopia, AD 1855–AD 1974)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 1855–AD 1974] Modern Period. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. Derived from Cerulli 1968. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

Crete entered the century in political limbo, an autonomous state under great-power supervision, and was formally joined to Greece in 1913. German paratroopers seized the island in the fierce battle of 1941, and the brutal occupation and mountain resistance that followed are still central to local memory. Since the 1960s mass tourism and intensive olive and greenhouse agriculture have reshaped the coast, while excavation at Knossos, Phaistos and elsewhere turned the Minoan past into a national and international symbol.

hints.label: Modern Period
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Gondarine (Ethiopia, AD 1632–AD 1769)
nodes.title: Gondarine (Ethiopia, AD 1632–AD 1769)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 1632–AD 1769] Gondarine. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. Derived from Cerulli 1968. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

For the first time in centuries Ethiopian emperors stopped moving with a mobile camp and built a permanent capital, ringing Fasil Ghebbi with stone castles, churches and baths. The court sponsored a brilliant school of manuscript illumination and church wall painting, hosted Jesuit-influenced architecture and fierce theological disputes over the nature of Christ, and drew trade from the Red Sea. Royal power then drained away to regional warlords, opening the long era of princes.

hints.label: Gondarine
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: South-Arabian, Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite (Ethiopia, 999 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: South-Arabian, Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite (Ethiopia, 999 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, 999 BC–AD 1] South-Arabian, Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. This definition was not derived from Cerulli 1968, but provided directly by Bausi. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

Highland Ethiopia and Eritrea drew close to the Sabaean world across the Red Sea, producing the polity known as D'MT with monumental stone temples at Yeha, South Arabian script and inscriptions, and altars to the moon god Almaqah. Local traditions persisted alongside imported forms, and after D'MT's decline smaller chiefdoms coalesced. Out of them grew Aksum, whose kings would dominate the region and its Red Sea trade.

hints.label: South-Arabian, Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Early Aksumite (Ethiopia, AD 1–AD 300)
nodes.title: Early Aksumite (Ethiopia, AD 1–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Ethiopia and Eritrea, AD 1–AD 300] Early Aksumite. Spatial coverage: Eritrea, Ethiopia. This definition was not derived from Cerulli 1968, but provided directly by Bausi. Period definition from Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea — Alessandro Bausi, 2017.

A highland kingdom in northern Ethiopia grew rich by funnelling ivory, gold and slaves to the Red Sea port of Adulis and on to Roman Egypt, India and Arabia. Aksum built monumental stone palaces and raised carved granite stelae over elite tombs, developed the Ge'ez script, and by the late third century was striking its own gold coinage — one of only a handful of states in the world to do so. It set the stage for Ezana's conversion to Christianity and Aksum's imperial reach across the sea into Yemen.

hints.label: Early Aksumite
hints.source: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

nodes.name: Early Iron Age (Pompeii, 849 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age (Pompeii, 849 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 849 BC–699 BC] Early Iron Age. Period definition from The complete Pompeii — Berry, Joanne, 1971-, 2007.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

nodes.name: Khirokitia Culture (Cyprus, 6050 BC–4550 BC)
nodes.title: Khirokitia Culture (Cyprus, 6050 BC–4550 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 6050 BC–4550 BC] Khirokitia Culture. Compiled from several sources, including Bolger (2003: 214)[1]; Hood (personal communication 2004); Peltenberg (2003b: 99)[2]; and Peltenburg et al. (2001a: 65)[3]. Table includes conventional (uncalibrated) and calibrated equivalents, which are rounded and approximate. [1]Gender in Ancient Cyprus: Narratives of Social Change on a Mediterranean Island. AltaMira, Walnut Creek, CA. [2]Conclusions: Mylouthkia I and the Early Colonists of Cyprus. In Edgar Peltenburg (ed.), The Colonisation and Settlement of Cyprus. Investigations at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia, 1976-1996. Studies in Mediterranean Archaeology vol. 70:4. Paul Astroms Forlag, Savedalen, pp. 83-103. [3]Well-Established Colonists: Mylouthkia I and the Cypro-Pre-Pottery Neolithic B. In Stuart Swiny (ed.), The Earliest Prehistory of Cyprus: From Colonization to Exploitation. Archaeological Reports No. 5, American Schools of Oriental Research, Boston, pp. 61-93. Period definition from The neolithic revolution in the Near East : transforming the human landscape — Alan H. Simmons, 2007.

Cyprus's aceramic Neolithic villagers built clusters of round stone-and-mud houses, sometimes walled off from the outside, and buried their dead beneath the floors of their homes. They farmed grain, herded sheep, goats and pigs, ground stone into elegant vessels and carved stylised human figures, all without making pottery. Their settlements show an island society that developed largely on its own terms after the first farmers crossed from the mainland.

hints.label: Khirokitia Culture
hints.source: The neolithic revolution in the Near East : transforming the human landscape

nodes.name: Sotira Culture (Cyprus, 4150 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.title: Sotira Culture (Cyprus, 4150 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 4150 BC–3050 BC] Sotira Culture. Compiled from several sources, including Bolger (2003: 214)[1]; Hood (personal communication 2004); Peltenberg (2003b: 99)[2]; and Peltenburg et al. (2001a: 65)[3]. Table includes conventional (uncalibrated) and calibrated equivalents, which are rounded and approximate. In Edgar Peltenburg (ed.), The Colonisation and Settlement of Cyprus. Investigations at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia, 1976-1996. Studies in Mediterranean Archaeology vol. 70:4. Cyprus's Late Neolithic, named after the hilltop village of Sotira-Teppes, where dozens of round and sub-rectangular houses with plastered floors and hearths crowded inside an enclosure. Potters now made dark burnished bowls decorated with combed and painted patterns, a break from the earlier aceramic villages. Farming, herding and the seasonal use of caves and coastal sites continued until the settlements gave way to the Chalcolithic communities of Erimi.

hints.label: Sotira Culture
hints.source: The neolithic revolution in the Near East : transforming the human landscape

nodes.name: Epoca Bronzului (Romania, 3500 BC–1051 BC)
nodes.title: Epoca Bronzului (Romania, 3500 BC–1051 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 3500 BC–1051 BC] Epoca Bronzului. Romanian Academy. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Metalworkers in the Carpathian basin turned local copper and imported tin into swords, axes and ornaments of remarkable quality, buried in hoards that still turn up by the hundred. Cultures such as Otomani, Wietenberg and Monteoru built fortified settlements and tells, worked gold on a lavish scale, and traded amber and metal along routes running to the Aegean and central Europe.

nodes.name: Vroeg Romeinse Tijd (Netherlands, 12 BC–AD 69)
nodes.title: Vroeg Romeinse Tijd (Netherlands, 12 BC–AD 69)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 12 BC–AD 69] Vroeg Romeinse Tijd. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Roman armies pushed to and across the Rhine, turning the river into a supplied and fortified frontier and drawing the local tribes into the empire as taxpayers, allies and above all recruits. Towns, roads and forts appeared, and imported goods spread quickly through the countryside. The period closes with the Batavian revolt of AD 69, when Roman-trained auxiliaries turned on their masters and burned much of the frontier.

nodes.name: Modern (Denmark, AD 1660–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Modern (Denmark, AD 1660–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1660–AD 2000] Modern. ARENA1/ADS. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

nodes.name: Jüngere Eisenzeit (Austria, 450 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Jüngere Eisenzeit (Austria, 450 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[Austria, 450 BC–1 BC] Jüngere Eisenzeit. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The La Tène centuries, when Celtic-speaking communities in the eastern Alps buried warriors with iron swords and imported wine equipment, mined salt at Hallein, and eventually gathered into fortified hilltop towns. Out of these groups grew the kingdom of Noricum, famous for its steel and closely tied to Rome by trade before being absorbed into the empire under Augustus.

nodes.name: Mittel Neolithikum (Austria, 4800 BC–4251 BC)
nodes.title: Mittel Neolithikum (Austria, 4800 BC–4251 BC)
nodes.description:
[Austria, 4800 BC–4251 BC] Mittel Neolithikum. Austrian Academy of Sciences. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Farming communities of the Danube basin in this period built enormous circular ditched enclosures, the Kreisgrabenanlagen, with precisely aligned entrance causeways that are among Europe's oldest monumental architecture. The Lengyel culture's painted pottery, longhouse villages and copper ornaments show settled communities with growing social complexity. Why the enclosures were built, and why they were abandoned within a few centuries, remains debated.

nodes.name: Modern (Iceland, AD 1900–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Modern (Iceland, AD 1900–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Iceland, AD 1900–AD 2000] Modern. ARENA1/ADS. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

nodes.name: železna doba (Slovenia, 750 BC–31 BC)
nodes.title: železna doba (Slovenia, 750 BC–31 BC)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, 750 BC–31 BC] železna doba. ZRC SAZU, Institute of Archaeology. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

Iron-using communities in the Slovenian lands built fortified hilltop centres such as Stična and Vače, surrounded by great barrow cemeteries. Their aristocrats commissioned bronze situlae decorated with banquets, processions and boxing matches, some of the finest figural art north of the Adriatic, and traded with Etruria and the Balkans. Celtic Taurisci arrived from the 4th century BC, and the whole region was absorbed by Rome under Augustus.

nodes.name: Nieuwe Tijd Midden (Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1849)
nodes.title: Nieuwe Tijd Midden (Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1849)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1849] Nieuwe Tijd Midden. Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed. Period definition from ARIADNE Data Collection — ARIADNE Consortium, 2015.

The Republic after its commercial peak: wars with England and France, a slow slide from dominance in trade, and enormous investment in drainage, dykes and country estates. French invasion swept the old order away, producing the Batavian Republic, annexation to Napoleon's empire, and then the unified Kingdom of the Netherlands. Material culture from these centuries is abundant and well dated, from clay pipes and delftware to the timbers of merchant ships.
