nodes.name: Late Byzantine (Cyprus, AD 965–AD 1191)
nodes.title: Late Byzantine (Cyprus, AD 965–AD 1191)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 965–AD 1191] Late Byzantine. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Nikephoros Phokas's reconquest in 965 ended centuries of contested Arab-Byzantine condominium and made Cyprus a securely imperial province again, governed from Nicosia and Famagusta. Wealth from grain, sugar and trade paid for the mountain monasteries and churches whose frescoes are the island's greatest medieval treasure. It ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island in 1191, beginning three centuries of Latin rule.

nodes.name: Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3150 BC–2663 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic (Egypt, 3150 BC–2663 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 3150 BC–2663 BC] Early Dynastic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

nodes.name: Ceramic Neolithic B (Jordan, 5000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.title: Ceramic Neolithic B (Jordan, 5000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, 5000 BC–4500 BC] Ceramic Neolithic B. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The later Pottery Neolithic of the southern Levant, associated with the Wadi Rabah tradition — dark burnished bowls, bow-rim jars and incised decoration made by villagers farming grain and herding sheep, goats and cattle. Settlements are modest and scattered compared with the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic towns that preceded them, but the material culture leads directly into the copper-using Chalcolithic.

nodes.name: Neo Babylonian Period (Israel, 586 BC–539 BC)
nodes.title: Neo Babylonian Period (Israel, 586 BC–539 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 586 BC–539 BC] Neo Babylonian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After Nebuchadnezzar II's armies burned Jerusalem and its temple, Judah ceased to exist as a kingdom and became a Babylonian province administered from Mizpah, with much of its elite deported to Babylonia. Settlement in the Judean hills thinned sharply, while the exile communities produced much of the writing and editing that shaped the Hebrew Bible. The experience of loss and displacement reframed Israelite religion around law, memory and a temple-less devotion that would outlast the empire that caused it.

nodes.name: Middle Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 3600 BC–2700 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Chalcolithic (Cyprus, 3600 BC–2700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 3600 BC–2700 BC] Middle Chalcolithic. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cyprus at its most distinctive before metals took hold: villages of round, mud-and-timber houses at Erimi, Lemba and Kissonerga, with wells, storage pits and cemeteries set apart from the living. Craftworkers carved blue-green picrolite into cruciform figurines with outstretched arms, worn as pendants and buried with the dead, and modelled clay figures of women giving birth. The island stayed largely self-contained, developing its own idiom while the mainland moved into the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Cypro Geometric III (Cyprus, 900 BC–750 BC)
nodes.title: Cypro Geometric III (Cyprus, 900 BC–750 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 900 BC–750 BC] Cypro Geometric III. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Phoenicians established themselves at Kition and rebuilt its great temple, while local centres grew into the kingdoms that would dominate the island for centuries. Trade with the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant revived strongly, and Cypriot copper again moved widely across the eastern Mediterranean.

nodes.name: Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324)
nodes.title: Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, AD 132–AD 324] Late Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.

nodes.name: Late Hellenistic Period (Turkey, 187 BC–133 BC)
nodes.title: Late Hellenistic Period (Turkey, 187 BC–133 BC)
nodes.description:
[Turkey, 187 BC–133 BC] Late Hellenistic Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Seleucid power collapsed into dynastic civil war, and the old Phoenician harbour cities — Tyre, Sidon, Berytus — bought or seized autonomy, minting their own coins and trading across the Mediterranean. Greek civic institutions and temple architecture were grafted onto older Canaanite religious traditions, producing the hybrid sanctuaries later rebuilt on a colossal scale at Baalbek. Pompey's arrival ended the experiment, folding the coast into the Roman province of Syria.

nodes.name: Early Roman Period (Lebanon, 63 BC–AD 138)
nodes.title: Early Roman Period (Lebanon, 63 BC–AD 138)
nodes.description:
[Lebanon, Syria, 63 BC–AD 138] Early Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

nodes.name: Intermediate Bronze Age (Jordan, 2200 BC–2000 BC)
nodes.title: Intermediate Bronze Age (Jordan, 2200 BC–2000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, 2200 BC–2000 BC] Intermediate Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The great walled cities of the third millennium — Ebla, Mari and their neighbours — shrank or were abandoned, monumental building stopped, and much of the population shifted toward mobile pastoralism and small settlements. Archaeologists link the collapse to a sharp arid episode and the disruption of long-distance trade, while texts of the era speak of Amorite groups moving through the region. Urban life revived after 2000 BC on very different political foundations.

nodes.name: PPNA (Israel, 6000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.title: PPNA (Israel, 6000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 6000 BC–5000 BC] PPNA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The first villages of the Levant belong to this phase: round mud-brick houses, communal storage and the beginnings of cultivated wheat, barley and pulses, still without pottery. Jericho's stone tower and wall and the carved pillars of Göbekli Tepe further north show unprecedented investment in building. Hunting and gathering continued alongside the new crops, and the groundwork was laid for full farming economies.

nodes.name: Cypro Classical I (Cyprus, 480 BC–400 BC)
nodes.title: Cypro Classical I (Cyprus, 480 BC–400 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 480 BC–400 BC] Cypro Classical I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cypriot kings manoeuvred between Persian overlords and Greek liberators, most famously Evagoras of Salamis, who Hellenised his court and challenged Persia directly. Coinage, Greek-style sculpture and Attic imported pottery spread through the island as its elites aligned themselves increasingly with the Aegean world.

properties.title: amphora — 600BC-480BC
properties.notes:
Pottery amphora in Bichrome V ware decorated with a painted female head in a Hathor pose; ovoid-globular body; low ring base; slim vertical loop-handles at each side; neck missing (possibly broken and then deliberately levelled off); between the handles is a central frieze framed below by alternating light and dark bands and above with registers of floral and abstract motifs; on both sides of the vase, the central frieze depicts a Hathor head between two stylised trees: details of her hair are incised; the flanking panels are in-filled with cross-hatching.; | Type: amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 16.60 centimetres; | Culture: Cypro-Archaic II

Cyprus, Phocaea, Myrina, Greece

nodes.name: Arab Conflict (Cyprus, AD 647–AD 965)
nodes.title: Arab Conflict (Cyprus, AD 647–AD 965)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 647–AD 965] Arab Conflict. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Beginning with Mu'awiya's naval raids, Cyprus was fought over between the Byzantine empire and the caliphate and for long stretches held in an unusual condominium, its tribute divided between the two powers and neither garrisoning it permanently. The island's harbours and forests made it strategically valuable to both fleets, and coastal towns were repeatedly sacked and populations deported. Nikephoros Phokas's reconquest in 965 restored full Byzantine control.

nodes.name: Persian Period (Israel, 539 BC–332 BC)
nodes.title: Persian Period (Israel, 539 BC–332 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 539 BC–332 BC] Persian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.

nodes.name: Chalcolithic (Israel, 4500 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic (Israel, 4500 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 4500 BC–3500 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

nodes.name: Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1750 BC–1450 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1750 BC–1450 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1750 BC–1450 BC] Middle Cypriot III/Late Cypriot I. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

The decisive shift on Cyprus, when villages gave way to towns, fortifications were built across the island, and copper became an export industry. Coastal centres such as Enkomi were founded to ship metal abroad, Cypriot pottery turns up throughout the eastern Mediterranean, and the island — probably the Alashiya of cuneiform letters — begins corresponding with the great powers as a kingdom in its own right.

nodes.name: Hasmonean Period (Israel, 167 BC–37 BC)
nodes.title: Hasmonean Period (Israel, 167 BC–37 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, 167 BC–37 BC] Hasmonean Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Judaean self-rule under the descendants of Judas Maccabeus, who held both the crown and the high priesthood and pushed the kingdom's borders out to something close to the biblical ideal. Its politics produced the rival factions of Pharisees and Sadducees and, in the desert, the community associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls. Fratricidal quarrels among the last Hasmoneans opened the door to Rome and to Herod, who married into the family and then destroyed it.

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 3000 BC–2000 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age (Turkey, 3000 BC–2000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Turkey, 3000 BC–2000 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

nodes.name: Early Roman Period (Egypt, 31 BC–AD 135)
nodes.title: Early Roman Period (Egypt, 31 BC–AD 135)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 31 BC–AD 135] Early Roman Period. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

properties.title: lamp — 1stC BC (probably)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery plastic lamp in the form of a bull's head, with a filling-hole in the centre of the forehead, surrounded by a moulded edge. Between the horns is another hole, perhaps a thumb-grip. The oval nozzle projects from the bull's muzzle, and has a flat rim round the wick-hole. The raised base is pointed-oval in shape and flat below. Covered with a red slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 8.00 centimetres; 4.70 centimetres; | Culture: Ptolemaic

Egypt

properties.title: lamp — 1stC BC
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a low circular body and a ring-handle, now broken. The nozzle tip is rounded and fluked, and is flanked by raised ridges with voluted ends. On each side is a pierced dolphin-lug. The discus is decorated with a band of relief ovules, within which is a reclining Eros holding a torch, which extends along the nozzle-top, its flame near the wick-hole. The filling-hole is surrounded by a garland; there are three subsidiary filling-holes or air-holes. There is a well-defined base-ring. Covered with a black slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 15.80 centimetres; 11.10 centimetres; | Culture: Ptolemaic

Egypt

nodes.name: Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917)
nodes.title: Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, AD 1516–AD 1917] Ottoman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2700 BC–2200 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2700 BC–2200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, 2700 BC–2200 BC] Early Bronze Age III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from The Levantine Ceramics Project — Andrea Berlin, 2012.

Fortified towns in the southern Levant reached their peak, with thick town walls, temples, palaces and the huge circular storage structure at Beth Yerah. Distinctive burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, related to northern traditions, spreads through the region. By the close of the period nearly all these towns had been abandoned, and urban life vanished for centuries.

nodes.name: Late Iron Age (Spain, 549 BC–205 BC)
nodes.title: Late Iron Age (Spain, 549 BC–205 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 549 BC–205 BC] Late Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of the Iberians — Ruiz, Arturo., 1998.

Thracian tribes coalesced into powerful kingdoms, above all the Odrysian, whose rulers were buried in stone-built tholos tombs with gold and silver drinking sets, chariots and horses. Greek colonies on the Black Sea and Aegean coasts pumped wine, coin and artistic styles inland, while Macedonian and later Celtic incursions repeatedly redrew the political map. Rome absorbed the region at the end of the period.

nodes.name: Iron Age (Spain, 799 BC–549 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Spain, 799 BC–549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 799 BC–549 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from The archaeology of the Iberians — Ruiz, Arturo., 1998.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

nodes.name: Caloosahatchee IIA (Florida, AD 500–AD 800)
nodes.title: Caloosahatchee IIA (Florida, AD 500–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 500–AD 800] Caloosahatchee IIA. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Coastal villages grew larger and shell architecture more deliberate, with mounds, ridges and water courts shaped from discarded shell. Changing pottery, including wares linked to the interior Lake Okeechobee region, shows regular contact across the peninsula, and the settlement hierarchy that would underpin the later Calusa chiefdom begins to be visible.

hints.label: Caloosahatchee IIA
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Glades I, 1000 B.C.-A.D. 750 (Florida, 1000 BC–AD 750)
nodes.title: Glades I, 1000 B.C.-A.D. 750 (Florida, 1000 BC–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 1000 BC–AD 750] Glades I, 1000 B.C.-A.D. 750. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The first stage of a distinctive south Florida way of life built not on farming but on fish, shellfish, turtles and wild plants of the Everglades, coasts and Keys. Sand-tempered plain pottery appears at the start of the period, and huge shell and black-earth middens accumulate at favoured camps. Decorated wares emerge late in the sequence, the first sign of the regional styles that archaeologists use to track the centuries that follow.

hints.label: Glades I, 1000 B.C.-A.D. 750
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Prehistoric, indet. (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Late Prehistoric, indet. (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Late Prehistoric, indet.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages of maize, bean and squash farmers occupied river terraces across the region, some in Mississippian-style towns with mounds and plazas, others in the circular stockaded settlements of the Fort Ancient tradition. Pottery was tempered with crushed shell, hunting relied on the bow, and long-distance trade brought marine shell inland. Much of it ends in the disruption and depopulation that preceded sustained European contact.

hints.label: Late Prehistoric, indet.
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: or Turin (Iowa, 5500 BC–4250 BC)
nodes.title: or Turin (Iowa, 5500 BC–4250 BC)
nodes.description: [Iowa, 5500 BC–4250 BC] or Turin. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

hints.label: or Turin
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Woodland (Alabama, AD 350–AD 950)
nodes.title: Late Woodland (Alabama, AD 350–AD 950)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 350–AD 950] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

hints.label: Late Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Pioneer (Illinois, AD 1781–AD 1841)
nodes.title: Pioneer (Illinois, AD 1781–AD 1841)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1781–AD 1841] Pioneer. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

American settlers pushed into Illinois from the Ohio valley and the Upland South, clearing river-bottom timber before venturing onto the prairie. Territorial status in 1809 and statehood in 1818 were followed by the removal of Native nations after the Black Hawk War of 1832, opening the north to Yankee and European migrants. Log cabins, lead mining at Galena and the first canal and rail schemes belong to these decades, along with the move of the capital to Springfield.

hints.label: Pioneer
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 18th Century::2nd quarter (1725 - 1749) (Virginia, AD 1725–AD 1749)
nodes.title: 18th Century::2nd quarter (1725 - 1749) (Virginia, AD 1725–AD 1749)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1725–AD 1749] 18th Century::2nd quarter (1725 - 1749). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Settlement spread rapidly beyond the tidewater into the piedmont and the Shenandoah Valley, much of it by German and Scots-Irish families moving south from Pennsylvania. Tobacco inspection acts tightened quality control and made warehouse receipts a form of currency, strengthening the big planters at the expense of small ones. In the older counties the plantation landscape of brick houses, separate kitchens and quarters for the enslaved was taking its familiar form, and imported ceramics, glass and tea wares appear in growing quantity even in modest households.

hints.label: 18th Century::2nd quarter (1725 - 1749)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: High Rim Horizon (Iowa, AD 900–AD 1100)
nodes.title: High Rim Horizon (Iowa, AD 900–AD 1100)
nodes.description: [Iowa, AD 900–AD 1100] High Rim Horizon. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

hints.label: High Rim Horizon
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 17th Century::4th quarter (1675 - 1699) (Virginia, AD 1675–AD 1699)
nodes.title: 17th Century::4th quarter (1675 - 1699) (Virginia, AD 1675–AD 1699)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1675–AD 1699] 17th Century::4th quarter (1675 - 1699). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Frontier grievances and resentment of the governor's circle exploded in Bacon's Rebellion of 1676, which burned Jamestown and ended with mass hangings, and its aftermath pushed the planter elite toward a labour force of enslaved Africans rather than restless English servants. Statutes hardened race into law, and direct shipments from Africa rose sharply in the 1680s and 1690s. The colony's centre of gravity shifted inland as Jamestown was abandoned for a new capital at Middle Plantation, renamed Williamsburg in 1699, alongside the founding of the College of William and Mary.

hints.label: 17th Century::4th quarter (1675 - 1699)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Lewis (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Lewis (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.description: [Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Lewis. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

hints.label: Lewis
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Seminole, 2nd War to 3rd 1835-1855 (Florida, AD 1835–AD 1855)
nodes.title: Seminole, 2nd War to 3rd 1835-1855 (Florida, AD 1835–AD 1855)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1835–AD 1855] Seminole, 2nd War to 3rd 1835-1855. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Resistance to removal broke into the Second Seminole War, the longest and most expensive Indian war the United States fought — years of swamp campaigning, burned towns, and the seizure of Osceola under a flag of truce. Thousands of Seminole and Black Seminole were shipped to Indian Territory, and the war left a lasting mark on Florida's forts, roads and settlement pattern. A few hundred people held out in the southern wetlands.

hints.label: Seminole, 2nd War to 3rd 1835-1855
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: General Archaic (Georgia, 8050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.title: General Archaic (Georgia, 8050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, 8050 BC–1050 BC] General Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A catch-all label for the long stretch after the Ice Age hunters, when people in the Southeast settled into the modern forests and river valleys and lived by hunting deer, gathering nuts and collecting shellfish. Enormous shell mounds accumulated along the rivers and coast, ground stone tools and spear-throwers came into use, exchange networks moved copper and marine shell inland, and by the end of the period local people were making some of the earliest pottery in North America.

hints.label: General Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Nebraska (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300)
nodes.title: Nebraska (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300] Nebraska. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming families along the Missouri and its tributaries lived in scattered square earthlodges, growing maize, beans and squash and hunting bison. Storage pits, cord-marked pottery and bone hoes made from bison scapulae are the typical finds. Drought and shifting conditions after 1300 pushed these communities away, and their descendants are generally linked to later Plains villagers.

hints.label: Nebraska
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Safety Harbor, A.D. 1000-1500 (Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Safety Harbor, A.D. 1000-1500 (Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500] Safety Harbor, A.D. 1000-1500. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The late prehistoric culture of Florida's central Gulf coast, centred on Tampa Bay, where communities built flat-topped temple mounds facing plazas with separate burial mounds and huge shell middens behind them. People lived chiefly on fish, shellfish and wild plants rather than maize, showing that ranked chiefdoms could arise without farming. These were the towns of the Tocobaga and their neighbours, the people met by the Narváez and de Soto expeditions before disease and slaving destroyed them.

hints.label: Safety Harbor, A.D. 1000-1500
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 17th Century (1600 - 1699) (Virginia, AD 1600–AD 1699)
nodes.title: 17th Century (1600 - 1699) (Virginia, AD 1600–AD 1699)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1600–AD 1699] 17th Century (1600 - 1699). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

England's first lasting American colony began at Jamestown in 1607 as a barely surviving commercial venture and became, through tobacco, a wealthy and expanding plantation society. Its labour came first from English indentured servants and increasingly from enslaved Africans, whose status hardened into hereditary slavery in law by the century's end. Repeated wars with the Powhatan chiefdom drove Native communities from the tidewater, and Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 exposed the tensions between frontier settlers, elites and the colonial government.

hints.label: 17th Century (1600 - 1699)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Transitional, 1000 B.C.-700 B.C. (Florida, 1000 BC–700 BC)
nodes.title: Transitional, 1000 B.C.-700 B.C. (Florida, 1000 BC–700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 1000 BC–700 BC] Transitional, 1000 B.C.-700 B.C.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The bridge between Florida's Late Archaic and the Woodland cultures that followed. Potters moved on from the plain fibre-tempered wares of the Orange tradition to chalky, sand- and sponge-spicule-tempered vessels, while communities kept exploiting the rich estuaries and rivers, leaving the shell middens and mounds that dominate the state's coastal archaeology.

[Iowa, AD 1850–AD 1950] late 19th -20th cent residential. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Railroads filled the state with grid-plan towns and square-mile farmsteads, and the houses left behind are studied through their foundations, privies, wells and refuse pits. Mass-produced ceramics, bottles and tinned goods in those deposits track the arrival of national markets and catalogue shopping in rural households. Excavated backyards reveal the daily life of immigrant families and working-class neighbourhoods rarely recorded in written sources.

nodes.name: 18th Century (1700 - 1799) (Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1799)
nodes.title: 18th Century (1700 - 1799) (Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1799)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1799] 18th Century (1700 - 1799). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia became the wealthiest and most populous mainland British colony, its economy built on tobacco and, increasingly, on the labour of enslaved people who by mid-century made up around forty per cent of the population. Williamsburg's new capital, brick plantation houses and imported English ceramics and glass mark the rise of a self-consciously genteel planter class. The same men led the colony into revolution, and the century closed with Virginians dominating the new United States government. Archaeologically it is a period of sharp contrasts, between mansion assemblages and the quarters of the enslaved.

nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1830–AD 1860] Antebellum Period (1830 - 1860). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Nat Turner's rebellion opened the period with an emancipation debate in the legislature and closed it with the harshest slave codes Virginia had known. Worn-out tobacco land pushed planters into wheat and into selling enslaved people south, making the state the largest exporter of human beings in the country, while Richmond built ironworks, flour mills and railroads. John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry and his hanging brought the sectional crisis to Virginia soil months before secession.

The Soviet collapse triggered base closures and defense consolidation across a state built around the military, while Northern Virginia boomed as a hub of federal contracting and internet infrastructure. The attack on the Pentagon in 2001 reversed the drawdown and fed two decades of war spending. Archaeologically, this is the era in which suburban sprawl, highway widening and data centres became the main threat to older sites - and the recent past itself started being recorded.

Pottery becomes elaborately incised, with designs so distinctive that they serve as a clock for the whole region, and imported goods and ideas arrive from northern Florida and beyond. Settlements grow larger and more permanent on shell works and midden ridges, some with canals and artificial ponds, all still supported by fishing and gathering rather than crops.

[Florida, AD 1880–AD 1897] Post-Reconstruction 1880-1897. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

With federal oversight withdrawn, white Democratic governments entrenched segregation, poll taxes and convict leasing, while Black Floridians lost the political foothold gained after the Civil War. At the same time the state was remade economically: Henry Flagler's and Henry Plant's railroads opened the peninsula to citrus, phosphate mining and winter tourism, and Cuban cigar makers built Ybor City into an industrial town from 1886. The great freezes of the mid-1890s pushed the citrus belt south and set off another round of settlement.

The Early Woodland centuries in central Kentucky, when the first thick, coarse pottery came into use and people began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and sumpweed alongside hunting. Burial mounds and earthworks of the Adena tradition appear, signalling new ideas about ancestors, ceremony and territory.

[South Carolina, AD 1600–AD 1700] 17th Century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Quarrels between crown and parliament over money and religion escalated into civil war, the execution of Charles I in 1649 and a decade of republican rule, before the monarchy returned in 1660 and was again reshaped by the Glorious Revolution of 1688. Plague and the Great Fire devastated London in the 1660s, and the rebuilt city became a commercial capital served by joint-stock companies, coffee houses and the new Bank of England. The Royal Society gave institutional form to experimental science, and colonies in the Caribbean and North America made England a slave-trading Atlantic power.

[Iowa, AD 1935–AD 2000] Mid-late 20th century commerce. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small-town Iowa business districts, built up in the railroad era, were reshaped by the automobile: highway-side motels, filling stations, drive-ins and later chain stores drew trade away from the courthouse square. Farm consolidation and mechanisation shrank the rural population that had supported many of these places, and interstate construction left bypassed towns behind. The material record is one of storefront remodelling, neon and porcelain-enamel signage, and abandoned service stations.

nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1200] Cahokia. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The largest city north of Mexico before European contact, laid out around vast earthen platform mounds on the Mississippi floodplain, with Monks Mound covering more ground at its base than the Great Pyramid. Its sudden expansion around 1050 drew in thousands of people, reorganised the landscape into plazas and neighbourhoods, and sent Mississippian goods, crops, religious symbols and settlers far up the river valleys - including into the Iowa country. Excavations have revealed woodhenge sun calendars and mass burials that testify to the power of its rulers.

A Woodland-period culture of the lakes and wetlands of north-central Florida, whose people camped beside ponds and marshes and drew heavily on fish, turtles, waterfowl and shellfish rather than farming. They built low sand burial mounds, sometimes with elaborate pottery vessels placed with the dead, showing links to the wider Weeden Island ceremonial world. Their settlements gave way to the maize-growing Alachua tradition, ancestral to the Timucua encountered by Spanish explorers.

[Florida, AD 100–AD 300] Santa Rosa-Swift Creek. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Middle Woodland culture of the Florida panhandle coast, whose people fished and gathered shellfish in the bays and built low sand burial mounds. Their pottery carries the swirling complicated-stamped designs of Swift Creek potters in Georgia, made with carved wooden paddles. Copper, mica and panpipes found in the mounds show the community was plugged into the long-distance Hopewell exchange network reaching to the Ohio valley.

Henry VIII's break with Rome dissolved the monasteries, transferred enormous wealth to the crown and gentry, and began a century of religious upheaval that swung between Protestant and Catholic before settling under Elizabeth I. Population rose sharply, prices soared, and enclosure of common land pushed people towards the towns. The defeat of the Spanish Armada, the first ventures across the Atlantic, and the London playhouses of Shakespeare and Marlowe all belong to the reign's later years.

[Georgia, AD 1540–AD 1640] Protohistoric. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hernando de Soto's expedition cut through the interior Southeast and the Mississippian chiefdoms it described soon fell apart, undone by disease, violence and the collapse of the mound-building order. Communities dispersed, merged and moved, laying the groundwork for the Creek, Cherokee and other historic nations. Sites of this period mix late Native ceramics with the occasional Spanish bead or iron blade.

[Iowa, AD 300–AD 750] early Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Settlements dispersed into smaller camps and hamlets, and the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular and notched points in the record. The elaborate long-distance trade and mound ceremonialism of the preceding centuries faded, while cord-marked pottery became thinner and more standardised. Maize begins to appear in small quantities, foreshadowing the farming villages to come.

[Florida, 5000 BC–2000 BC] Mt. Taylor. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Foragers along the St. Johns River piled up enormous mounds of freshwater snail and mussel shell, some of them deliberately shaped rather than mere refuse heaps. They fished, hunted and gathered without pottery, using bone points, shell tools and ground stone, and buried their dead within the middens and in nearby ponds. These shell works are among the earliest large-scale constructions in the southeastern United States, evidence that hunter-gatherers could build monuments.

Early Woodland communities of the Ohio Valley and its fringes who built conical earthen burial mounds and buried their dead with copper bracelets, tubular pipes and carved stone tablets. They gathered and cultivated native seed plants, made some of the region's first pottery, and traded for exotic materials over long distances. Their mound-building and ritual exchange laid the groundwork for the far larger Hopewell networks that followed.

[Indiana, 1000 BC–AD 1200] Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A long stretch in which people of the Eastern Woodlands adopted pottery, built burial mounds, and gradually shifted from foraging to cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder, with maize arriving late. Trade networks moved copper, marine shell and exotic stone across half a continent, and Hopewell-style earthworks and elaborate grave goods appear in the middle centuries. By its end, settled villages, the bow and arrow and maize agriculture had set the stage for the town-building societies that followed.

Cold War spending, the growth of the federal workforce and cheap automobile commuting turned farmland into subdivisions, especially in the northern counties. Virginia's political leadership answered school desegregation with Massive Resistance, closing public schools in several localities before the policy collapsed. The buildings and refuse of this quarter-century — ranch houses, shopping plazas, motels — are the material record most often encountered by archaeologists working on modern sites.

nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1200] Mill Creek. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming villages on the small rivers of northwestern Iowa packed earth-lodge houses behind ditches and palisades, grew maize, beans and squash, and hunted bison on the nearby prairies. Their pottery and the presence of Cahokia-style goods show contact with the Mississippian world to the southeast. Drought and worsening conditions after about AD 1200 emptied the area, and the descendants are generally linked to the later Mandan and Hidatsa of the Missouri.

Spain ceded Florida to the United States, opening a century of land speculation, plantation slavery, railroad building and, later, tourism and citrus. The Seminole wars and forced removals cleared Indigenous communities from much of the peninsula, while drainage schemes reshaped the wetlands. Statehood, secession and Reconstruction were followed by land booms that turned a thinly settled frontier into one of the fastest-growing places in the country.

The Apalachee were a powerful farming people of the Florida panhandle whose towns became the breadbasket of Spanish Florida, supplying maize to St. Augustine from a chain of missions. Carolina-backed raids in 1704 shattered the missions, and survivors scattered — some westward to French Mobile, which is why Apalachee sites turn up in Alabama. Their pottery, made in Native forms but often for Spanish and French tables, marks the collision of three worlds.

[Missouri, AD 800–AD 1100] Early Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming along the Mississippi and its tributaries supported larger, more permanent villages, and communities began raising flat-topped earthen mounds around open plazas. Shell-tempered pottery, the bow and arrow, and a new emphasis on hereditary leadership all spread in these centuries. The trend culminated in Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico, just across the river from Missouri's American Bottom settlements.

Along the St. Johns River and Atlantic coast, communities lived on fish and shellfish, leaving huge shell middens, and made a distinctive chalky pottery tempered with freshwater sponge spicules. Villages became more permanent and burial mounds appear, with imported goods showing contact with Hopewellian networks to the north. Spain handed Florida to the United States in 1821, opening a violent century of frontier settlement: the Seminole Wars and forced removals, statehood in 1845, plantation slavery, secession and Civil War, then Reconstruction and the first railroads and citrus and cattle economies. Sites from these decades range from timber forts and homesteads to freedmen's settlements and early tourist towns. Material remains show mass-produced American and British goods arriving by steamboat and rail into what had been a Spanish borderland.

Beginning with Ponce de León's landing and consolidated by the founding of St. Augustine in 1565, Spain held Florida as a strategic shield for the treasure fleets rather than a profitable colony. A chain of Franciscan missions reached across northern Florida into Georgia, drawing Timucua and Apalachee communities into Catholic parishes; disease and English-backed slave raids destroyed them by the early 1700s. Spain handed the province to Britain in 1763 in exchange for Havana.

Sea levels stabilised and coastal and riverine communities grew larger and more settled, harvesting shellfish on a huge scale and heaping the remains into ridges, rings and mounds. Fibre-tempered Orange ware, among the earliest pottery in North America, appears in these centuries. The scale of the shell architecture and the appearance of formal cemeteries point to communities that were increasingly permanent and socially organised.

[Illinois, 1000 BC–200 BC] Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

A span that runs from the tightening of slavery after Nat Turner's rebellion, through secession and the state's role as the Confederacy's capital and chief battleground, to the upheavals of emancipation and Reconstruction. Farms, towns and households were rebuilt on new terms, with freedpeople negotiating wages, tenancy and land. Artefacts from these decades trace the shift from imported English ceramics to American factory goods arriving by rail.

nodes.name: Middle-Late Archaic, indet. (Kentucky, 8000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Middle-Late Archaic, indet. (Kentucky, 8000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 8000 BC–1000 BC] Middle-Late Archaic, indet.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Foragers settled into the river valleys, returning so often to the same spots on the Green and Ohio rivers that their discarded mussel shells built up into mounds metres deep, with hundreds of burials cut into them. They ground stone axes and pestles, exchanged copper from the Great Lakes and shell from the Gulf, and began tending native plants such as squash, sumpweed and chenopod — the first steps toward farming in eastern North America.

hints.label: Middle-Late Archaic, indet.
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 250–AD 650] Millville. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Middle Woodland communities of the upper Mississippi valley living in small riverside settlements, making pottery in styles related to the Havana tradition of the Illinois valley and burying their dead in mounds on the bluffs. They gathered nuts and mussels, hunted deer and tended native seed crops, and took part in the exchange networks that carried exotic stone and copper up the river corridor.

nodes.title: Woodland (1200 B.C. - 1606 A.D.) (Virginia, AD 1200–AD 1606)

[Virginia, AD 1200–AD 1606] Woodland (1200 B.C. - 1606 A.D.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The era in the Chesapeake and Virginia interior when pottery came into use, settlements grew more permanent, and maize, beans and squash were added to a diet of fish, shellfish, deer and wild plants. Villages along the rivers grew into the chiefdoms that the Powhatan paramountcy drew together, the political world English colonists met at Jamestown. Shell middens, ossuaries and distinctive ceramic wares are the main traces left behind.

hints.label: Woodland (1200 B.C. - 1606 A.D.)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Ft. Walton A.D. 1000-1500 (Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Ft. Walton A.D. 1000-1500 (Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500] Ft. Walton A.D. 1000-1500. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities on the Florida panhandle took up intensive maize farming and the Mississippian way of life, building flat-topped earthen mounds around open plazas and organising themselves under hereditary chiefs. Their pottery, incised and modelled in striking shapes, and their shell and copper ornaments connect them to a wide southeastern exchange network. The Apalachee whom Spanish expeditions met in the sixteenth century were their descendants.

hints.label: Ft. Walton A.D. 1000-1500
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Lamar (Florida, AD 1350–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1350–AD 1600] Lamar. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The last Mississippian-era culture of the interior Southeast, marked by complicated stamped pottery, folded and pinched rim decoration, and platform-mound towns ruled by chiefs. These were the societies Hernando de Soto's expedition marched through, and the diseases and disruption that followed shattered many of them. Their survivors coalesced into the historic Creek and other southeastern nations.

hints.label: Lamar
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Fort Ancient (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Fort Ancient (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Fort Ancient. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize-farming villagers of the middle Ohio valley, living in circular settlements of houses around an open plaza, often stockaded and set on river terraces. They grew maize, beans and squash, hunted deer and elk, made shell-tempered pottery and shell ornaments, and traded for marine shell and, in the final phase, European brass and glass beads. Their large late villages such as Madisonville were abandoned around the time epidemic disease and the fur trade reached the interior.

hints.label: Fort Ancient
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

[Kentucky, AD 900–AD 1100] LW & Miss - FA. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming took hold across the Ohio Valley, and scattered Late Woodland hamlets gave way to more permanent villages, often clustered around open plazas. The bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, and shell-tempered pottery spread from the Mississippian centres downriver. In the middle Ohio drainage these developments produced the Fort Ancient tradition, whose farming towns lasted until European contact.

hints.label: LW & Miss - FA
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Glades III, A.D. 1000-1700 (Florida, AD 1200–AD 1700)

[Florida, AD 1200–AD 1700] Glades III, A.D. 1000-1700. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The centuries in which the Calusa of the southwest coast and the Tequesta of Biscayne Bay built powerful chiefdoms on the wealth of estuaries, without ever taking up agriculture. Massive shell-mound towns with canals and courts appear, and later levels contain Spanish glass, metal and ceramics. The period closes with epidemic disease, slave raiding and the collapse of these societies under colonial pressure.

A holding category for artefacts and sites - scattered flakes, plough-damaged scatters, undiagnostic sherds - that are plainly pre-contact but cannot be tied to any particular era. Such material makes up a large share of what surveys actually recover, and it is a reminder that most archaeological evidence is fragmentary and mute about its own date.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Archaic (8500 - 1201 B.C.) (Virginia, 8500 BC–1201 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (8500 - 1201 B.C.) (Virginia, 8500 BC–1201 BC)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 8500 BC–1201 BC] Archaic (8500 - 1201 B.C.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

As the ice sheets retreated and oak-hickory forests spread, small bands shifted from hunting big game to a broad diet of deer, nuts, fish and shellfish, moving on a seasonal round through river valleys and the coastal plain. Ground and polished stone tools, atlatl weights, storage pits and carved soapstone bowls appear, along with the first cemeteries and long-distance exchange in copper and marine shell. By the end of the era populations were larger and more settled, setting the stage for pottery, gardening and the Woodland way of life.

hints.label: Archaic (8500 - 1201 B.C.)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Historic American Indian (Kentucky, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1650–AD 1950] Historic American Indian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers Native life after sustained European contact, when epidemics, the deerskin and fur trade, and colonial warfare reshaped older societies. Shawnee, Cherokee and Chickasaw groups hunted, camped and fought over the Ohio Valley, and their sites yield glass beads, brass kettles and gunflints alongside traditional tools. The period closes with forced removal and the near-erasure of Native communities from the region.

hints.label: Historic American Indian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: ca. 1930s-1940s (Iowa, AD 1930–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1930–AD 1950] ca. 1930s-1940s. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Depression and war reshaped rural life: drought and collapsing crop prices drove farm foreclosures, New Deal programmes brought rural electrification, soil conservation and federal art and building projects, and then wartime demand emptied the countryside of young men while raising commodity prices again. Objects from these decades often show make-do repair, home canning and salvage alongside the first wave of tractors and factory-made consumer goods.

hints.label: ca. 1930s-1940s
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Terminal Late Woodland (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Terminal Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

In the Ohio Valley these centuries saw the bow and arrow replace the spearthrower and maize move from a garden crop to a staple. Settlements grew larger and more permanent, and the social groundwork was laid for the fortified Fort Ancient villages that followed.

hints.label: Terminal Late Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Pelican Lake (Iowa, 1050 BC–AD 350)
nodes.title: Pelican Lake (Iowa, 1050 BC–AD 350)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 1050 BC–AD 350] Pelican Lake. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Archaic hunting tradition of the northern Plains, recognised chiefly by its small, finely corner-notched dart points, which mark the last centuries before the bow replaced the atlatl. Its people followed bison in communal drives and pounds, leaving deep kill and processing sites alongside campsites with hearths and boiling pits. The complex sets the stage for the Besant and later Plains Woodland groups that followed.

hints.label: Pelican Lake
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Red Ocher (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Red Ocher (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC] Red Ocher. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A burial tradition of the upper Midwest in which the dead were laid in low mounds or natural knolls and covered with powdered red hematite. Graves held finely flaked 'turkey-tail' blades of Indiana hornstone, hammered copper awls and beads, and marine shell from the Gulf coast — evidence that goods travelled across half a continent long before farming villages existed here. It marks the point where mortuary ceremony and long-distance exchange became central to life in the region, foreshadowing the great Woodland mound-building cultures.

hints.label: Red Ocher
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

An administrative category for Illinois sites with Native American artefacts that cannot be assigned to a particular phase — a scatter of flakes, an isolated point, a plough-damaged midden. The span it covers runs from the first hunters after the glaciers through the Archaic and Woodland periods to the Mississippian towns around Cahokia.

nodes.name: 18th Century::1st half (1700 - 1749) (Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1749)
nodes.title: 18th Century::1st half (1700 - 1749) (Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1749)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1749] 18th Century::1st half (1700 - 1749). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Williamsburg was laid out as a capital of brick public buildings and a formal main street, and the great tidewater families consolidated estates worked by a now largely enslaved and increasingly American-born workforce. Tobacco inspection laws of the 1730s standardised the export trade, while settlers, including German and Scots-Irish migrants coming down the Great Wagon Road, pushed into the piedmont and the Shenandoah Valley. Households of any means were furnished with English earthenwares, wine bottles and imported tea equipage, goods that were becoming ordinary rather than exceptional.

hints.label: 18th Century::1st half (1700 - 1749)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

[Virginia, AD 1825–AD 1849] 19th Century::2nd quarter (1825 - 1849). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Nat Turner's 1831 rising in Southampton County prompted a genuine legislative debate on ending slavery, and then, when that failed, a crackdown on literacy, movement and free Black life. Railroads, canals and Richmond's Tredegar ironworks began to industrialise parts of the state, while western counties grumbled about a constitution weighted toward eastern slaveholders. Mass-produced whitewares and cheap imported goods start to dominate domestic assemblages.

nodes.name: Modern (Post 1950) (Florida, AD 1950–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Modern (Post 1950) (Florida, AD 1950–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1950–AD 1950] Modern (Post 1950). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Air conditioning, mosquito control and interstate highways turned Florida from a lightly settled state into one of the fastest-growing in the country, filled by retirees, northern transplants and Cuban and Caribbean migrants. Cape Canaveral launched the space programme, Disney World remade central Florida into a tourist economy, and drained wetlands became suburbs and citrus groves. Archaeologically the period is visible as sprawl, dredged canals and the loss of coastal sites to development and rising seas.

hints.label: Modern (Post 1950)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Reconstruction 1866-1879 (Florida, AD 1866–AD 1879)
nodes.title: Reconstruction 1866-1879 (Florida, AD 1866–AD 1879)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1866–AD 1879] Reconstruction 1866-1879. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Florida was readmitted to the Union in 1868 under a new constitution that enfranchised Black men, who voted in large numbers and sent Black legislators to Tallahassee for the first time. Freedpeople moved into wage labour, sharecropping and turpentine and timber camps, while the Ku Klux Klan and paramilitary intimidation worked to reverse their gains. The disputed 1876 election, decided partly on Florida's returns, ended federal protection and opened the way to white Democratic 'Redemption'.

hints.label: Reconstruction 1866-1879
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Woodland (Illinois, AD 300–AD 900)
nodes.title: Late Woodland (Illinois, AD 300–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 300–AD 900] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

Florida entered the Union as the twenty-seventh state, its politics dominated by cotton planters in the northern counties and its population swelling with enslaved labourers. The last Seminole resistance was crushed and survivors pushed into the Everglades, while steamboats, sawmills and the first railroads opened the interior. The state seceded within weeks of Lincoln's election.

The final subdivision of the Glades sequence, identified in the field by Spanish beads, metal and olive-jar sherds mixed into native middens. It covers the era of missions, raids and epidemics that ended with the flight or destruction of south Florida's indigenous communities.

nodes.title: Manasota, 700 B.C.-A.D. 700 (Florida, 700 BC–AD 700)

[Florida, 700 BC–AD 700] Manasota, 700 B.C.-A.D. 700. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A coastal way of life on Florida's central Gulf shore, built around fishing, shellfish gathering and huge accumulations of discarded shell. Its people made plain sand-tempered pottery and, in later centuries, began raising sand burial mounds, a shift that marks the spread of new ceremonial ideas along the peninsula. Out of these communities grew the Weeden Island and Safety Harbor societies encountered by the first Spanish ships.

nodes.title: Pensacola (Florida, AD 1300–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1300–AD 1700] Pensacola. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Gulf Coast expression of Mississippian culture, centred on towns with earthen platform mounds such as Bottle Creek, whose people made distinctive shell-tempered pottery decorated with incised scrolls and hands-and-eyes motifs. They combined maize farming with rich estuarine fishing and shellfish gathering, and traded along the coast and up the river valleys. The final generations met Spanish expeditions, and the diseases that came with them.

hints.label: Pensacola
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Hopewellian (Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.title: Hopewellian (Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC] Hopewellian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Woodland societies of the eastern United States who raised burial mounds and geometric earthworks and moved exotic materials, copper, mica, obsidian and marine shell, across enormous distances. Their finely made platform pipes and cut-mica silhouettes are among the most striking art of prehistoric North America. The label is applied loosely to sites sharing that ceremonial and exchange tradition rather than to a single people.

hints.label: Hopewellian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

A catch-all classification used in Florida archaeology for material of European or Euro-American origin that cannot be tied to a single colonial or national component. It covers everything from Spanish olive jar sherds and gun flints to nineteenth-century bottle glass and machine-cut nails, spanning the Spanish, British, territorial and modern eras.

nodes.title: Oto (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)

[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Oto. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Chiwere Siouan people closely related to the Ioway and Missouria, the Otoe farmed maize along the rivers and rode out to the plains for bison, appearing in French records from the earliest exploration of the Mississippi valley. Trade, epidemics and pressure from expanding neighbours pushed them steadily westward, and nineteenth-century treaties stripped their lands until they were removed to a reservation in Nebraska and then to Indian Territory. Descendant communities remain federally recognised in Oklahoma.

hints.label: Oto
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Pottawattamie (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)

[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Pottawattamie. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers the historic era in western Iowa, from the first French traders' accounts of the region's Native nations to the twentieth century. The Potawatomi, pushed west out of the Great Lakes by treaty and removal, were settled near the Missouri River bluffs in the 1830s and moved on again within a generation, leaving the name attached to the county. Sites of this span include trading posts, mission and agency buildings, emigrant trail camps and early farmsteads.

nodes.title: Oneota (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673] Oneota. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages of maize farmers and bison hunters spread across the prairie-forest border, leaving distinctive shell-tempered globular jars with trailed decoration, deep storage pits, and cemeteries. Communities were large and mobile enough to shift between river-valley gardens and seasonal hunts on the plains. Their descendants met the first French explorers and traders, and the archaeological trail leads directly to the historic Ioway, Oto, and Ho-Chunk nations.

hints.label: Oneota
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Tri Pt Only (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Tri Pt Only (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Tri Pt Only. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A dating label rather than a culture: sites known only from small triangular arrowheads, the type made after the bow replaced the spearthrower across the Eastern Woodlands. Such points were used by Mississippian and Fort Ancient farming villagers, and where nothing else survives they are the sole clue that a place was occupied in these centuries.

hints.label: Tri Pt Only
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: early Middle Woodland (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 50)
nodes.title: early Middle Woodland (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 50)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 200 BC–AD 50] early Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities along the Mississippi and its tributaries joined the Havana–Hopewell exchange world, importing obsidian, marine shell and copper and burying their dead in log-tomb mounds. Pottery became elaborate, with zoned decoration and rocker-stamping, and gardens of native seed plants supplemented hunting and gathering. The mound groups of eastern Iowa's river bluffs date largely from this era.

hints.label: early Middle Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Contact (Indiana, AD 1650–AD 1900)
nodes.title: Contact (Indiana, AD 1650–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[Indiana, AD 1650–AD 1900] Contact. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

European traders, missionaries and soldiers moved into the Wabash and Maumee country, and Miami, Potawatomi, Delaware and Shawnee communities were drawn into the fur trade and the imperial rivalry between France, Britain and the young United States. Archaeologically the period shows itself in trade silver, glass beads, gun parts and kettles found alongside traditional material. It ends with treaty cession, forced removal west and the settling of the land by farmers.

hints.label: Contact
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Hopewell/Havana (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Hopewell/Havana (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400] Hopewell/Havana. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Illinois valley expression of the Hopewell world, marked by thick grit-tempered pottery, conical burial mounds on river bluffs, and log-lined tombs holding copper ear spools, platform pipes and cut mica. These communities cultivated native seed crops such as goosefoot and marsh elder long before maize arrived. Their influence spread up the Mississippi into Iowa, carrying both pottery styles and mortuary ceremony.

hints.label: Hopewell/Havana
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Spanish-1st or 2nd (Florida, AD 1513–AD 1821)
nodes.title: Spanish-1st or 2nd (Florida, AD 1513–AD 1821)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1513–AD 1821] Spanish-1st or 2nd. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers the whole span of Spanish claims to the peninsula, from Ponce de León's landing to the handover to the United States. Its physical traces range from mission churches and the coquina fortress of St. Augustine to shipwrecks and Native villages transformed by cattle, wheat and Catholicism.

hints.label: Spanish-1st or 2nd
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Gulf Formational (Alabama, 500 BC–100 BC)
nodes.title: Late Gulf Formational (Alabama, 500 BC–100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, 500 BC–100 BC] Late Gulf Formational. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Peoples of the Gulf Coast and Tombigbee drainage settled into more permanent riverine and shell-midden villages, making sand- and grog-tempered pottery and gathering at earthwork sites. Contacts to the north brought exotic goods and burial-mound customs that anticipate the Hopewell-influenced Middle Woodland societies that followed.

hints.label: Late Gulf Formational
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: First Spanish, Early 1600-1699 (Florida, AD 1600–AD 1699)
nodes.title: First Spanish, Early 1600-1699 (Florida, AD 1600–AD 1699)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1600–AD 1699] First Spanish, Early 1600-1699. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Franciscan mission chain spread west and north from St Augustine into Apalachee and Timucua country, tying Indigenous towns to the colony through labour drafts and maize tribute. St Augustine remained a small, subsidised garrison guarding the treasure fleet route, rebuilt in coquina stone as the Castillo de San Marcos after a pirate raid. English settlement at Charles Town from 1670 began the slave-raiding pressure that would destroy the missions.

hints.label: First Spanish, Early 1600-1699
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)
