nodes.name: Mormon (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Mormon (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Mormon. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Latter-day Saints expelled from Nauvoo in 1846 crossed the state on foot and by wagon, cutting the Mormon Trail and leaving behind way stations, cabins, wells and graves at Garden Grove, Mount Pisgah and the settlement at Kanesville. Thousands wintered there before continuing west, and Council Bluffs became a staging ground for later emigrant companies. The archaeological traces are modest - hearths, foundations, cemeteries - but they mark one of the largest organised religious migrations in American history.

hints.label: Mormon
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early National Period (1790 - 1829) (Virginia, AD 1790–AD 1829)
nodes.title: Early National Period (1790 - 1829) (Virginia, AD 1790–AD 1829)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1790–AD 1829] Early National Period (1790 - 1829). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The new republic's formative decades, when four of the first five presidents were Virginians and the state's planter class dominated national politics. Meanwhile tobacco exhausted the soils of the Tidewater and Piedmont, and Virginia turned increasingly to selling enslaved people to the expanding cotton states—a trade that tore apart families and reshaped the South. Archaeologically it is a period of shifting plantation layouts, new towns, and mass-produced English ceramics reaching ordinary households.

hints.label: Early National Period (1790 - 1829)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Yankeetown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Yankeetown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Yankeetown. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Woodland society of the lower Ohio valley, recognised by pottery decorated with fine incised and filleted bands unlike anything made by its neighbours. Its people lived in riverside villages, farmed maize alongside native seed crops, and traded along the Ohio. They stand at the threshold of the Mississippian world, and their descendants helped build the mound centre at Angel.

hints.label: Yankeetown
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Any Archaic Period (South Carolina, 8050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.title: Any Archaic Period (South Carolina, 8050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, 8050 BC–1050 BC] Any Archaic Period. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers adapting to post-glacial forests, rivers and an expanding coastline, using notched and stemmed spear points, ground stone tools and increasingly local resources as territories contracted. Over these millennia groups gathered seasonally at shellfish and riverine sites, some leaving large shell rings, and by the end were making some of the earliest pottery in North America. The label is used when material can be assigned to the Archaic but not to a finer subdivision.

hints.label: Any Archaic Period
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic, Undifferentiated (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.title: Historic, Undifferentiated (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Undifferentiated. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A catch-all for sites that clearly belong to the centuries after European contact but cannot be pinned to a particular nation, colony or community. Often it means a scatter of glass, iron and refined earthenware with nothing diagnostic enough to say who left it. Such sites still matter in bulk, mapping where people lived and worked across a landscape being rapidly transformed.

hints.label: Historic, Undifferentiated
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Belle Glade, 700 B.C.-A.D. 1700 (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Belle Glade, 700 B.C.-A.D. 1700 (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700] Belle Glade, 700 B.C.-A.D. 1700. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A distinctive society of the wet interior of southern Florida, centred on Lake Okeechobee and the Kissimmee floodplain, whose people built circular ditches, long linear embankments and mounds in a landscape that flooded every year. They lived on fish, turtles, birds and wild plants rather than farming, and left behind carved wooden effigies of extraordinary quality from the mortuary pond at Fort Center. The tradition ended only with Spanish contact and the collapse of Florida's native populations.

hints.label: Belle Glade, 700 B.C.-A.D. 1700
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: early 19th century (Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1850)
nodes.title: early 19th century (Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1850] early 19th century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Ioway, Sauk, Meskwaki and Dakota communities were pressed by the westward push of American settlement and the fur trade, then dispossessed by treaty — most sharply in the Black Hawk Purchase of 1832, which opened the land east of the Missouri to settlers. Steamboats on the Mississippi and Missouri brought waves of newcomers, and lead mining boomed near Dubuque. Iowa became a territory in 1838 and a state in 1846, its prairie broken by the plough within a generation.

hints.label: early 19th century
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 18th Century (South Carolina, AD 1700–AD 1800)
nodes.title: 18th Century (South Carolina, AD 1700–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 1700–AD 1800] 18th Century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Georgian England grew rich on Atlantic trade, colonial expansion and a booming market in consumer goods, while enclosure and new crop rotations remade the countryside and pushed people toward the towns. Canals, coke-smelted iron, steam engines and mechanised spinning laid the groundwork for industrial production in the century's later decades. Everyday material culture changed dramatically: tea drinking, cheap printed cottons, mass-produced Staffordshire ceramics and clay pipes turn up in enormous quantities on sites of the period. Politically it was the century of the Union with Scotland, Hanoverian rule, the Jacobite risings and the loss of the American colonies.

hints.label: 18th Century
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Oneota/Ioway/Oto (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Oneota/Ioway/Oto (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Oneota/Ioway/Oto. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The stretch when archaeology gives way to written record: French traders and missionaries arriving on the Mississippi encountered the Ioway and Oto, whose villages continued Oneota ways of life. Fur trading brought guns, kettles, and glass beads into the material record, followed by epidemics, warfare, and pressure from the east. Treaties in the nineteenth century stripped the tribes of their Iowa homelands and moved them to reservations in Kansas, Nebraska, and Oklahoma.

hints.label: Oneota/Ioway/Oto
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Marion (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.title: Marion (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC] Marion. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

An Early Woodland horizon marked by the appearance of thick, cord-roughened pottery in the upper Mississippi valley, alongside continued hunting, fishing and the gathering of native seed plants. The heavy jars are among the first ceramics used in the region, a sign of new ways of cooking and storing food, and burial mounds begin to appear on bluff edges above the rivers.

hints.label: Marion
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Archaic (South Carolina, 3050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.title: Late Archaic (South Carolina, 3050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, 3050 BC–1050 BC] Late Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.

hints.label: Late Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Faulkner (Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.title: Faulkner (Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC] Faulkner. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Middle Archaic hunting and gathering way of life, named for its distinctive side-notched points, in which groups moved between river valleys and uplands exploiting deer, nuts, fish and freshwater mussels. Populations grew and settlements became more repeatedly occupied, laying the groundwork for the shell mounds and cemeteries of later Archaic times.

hints.label: Faulkner
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Oneota, Correctionville phase (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.title: Oneota, Correctionville phase (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673] Oneota, Correctionville phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A western Iowa expression of Oneota, known from village and midden sites in the Little Sioux and Big Sioux drainages, where shell-tempered pottery, scapula hoes, and bison bone testify to a mix of gardening and plains hunting. It shows how Oneota communities on the prairie edge leaned more heavily on the bison herds than their neighbours further east.

hints.label: Oneota, Correctionville phase
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Quaker (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Quaker (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Quaker. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Members of the Religious Society of Friends, who worshipped in silence without clergy or ritual and refused oaths, war and social deference. Friends were among the earliest and most persistent American abolitionists, and their meetinghouses and farms in the Midwest served as stations on the Underground Railroad. Their plain furniture, unadorned buildings and burial grounds with uniform markers reflect a deliberate rejection of display.

hints.label: Quaker
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: late Early Woodland (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.title: late Early Woodland (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC] late Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Thick, cord-marked pottery came into general use, and communities began raising conical burial mounds over their dead on bluff edges above the rivers. Native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash were tended alongside hunting and gathering, a homegrown farming tradition centuries before maize. Exotic copper and marine shell in graves show goods already moving across long distances.

hints.label: late Early Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Weaver-like (Iowa, AD 400–AD 650)
nodes.title: Weaver-like (Iowa, AD 400–AD 650)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 400–AD 650] Weaver-like. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A label archaeologists use for assemblages that resemble the late Middle Woodland Weaver pottery of the Illinois valley without being firmly assigned to it. The material reflects the same post-Hopewell world of plain cord-marked jars, small dispersed camps and locally oriented communities.

hints.label: Weaver-like
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Malabar (Florida, AD 390–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Malabar (Florida, AD 390–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 390–AD 1400] Malabar. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The archaeological tradition of Florida's Indian River coast and adjacent St. Johns marshes, whose people fished, gathered shellfish and hunted rather than farming, leaving deep shell middens and sand burial mounds. Their sand-tempered and chalky plain pottery marks them off from neighbours to the north and south. These communities were the ancestors of the Ais and related groups encountered by the Spanish.

hints.label: Malabar
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Prehistoric (Missouri, 12000 BC–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, 12000 BC–AD 1673] Prehistoric. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Late Chalcolithic communities on the Iranian plateau and in Khuzestan used mass-produced wheel-thrown pottery, copper metallurgy and clay tokens and seals to track goods. Susa emerged as a major centre in close contact with Mesopotamian Uruk, and the accounting systems developed here fed directly into the invention of writing.

hints.label: Prehistoric
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: War of 1812 (Iowa, AD 1812–AD 1815)
nodes.title: War of 1812 (Iowa, AD 1812–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1812–AD 1815] War of 1812. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The upper Mississippi became a contested frontier as British traders and their Sauk, Fox and Winnebago allies fought American attempts to plant forts and control the river. American expeditions were beaten back at Campbell's Island and Credit Island, and Black Hawk fought alongside the British — a grievance that resurfaced in the 1832 war that bears his name. Peace left the region firmly in American hands and opened the way for treaty cessions and settlement.

hints.label: War of 1812
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Civil War (1861 - 1865) (Virginia, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War (1861 - 1865) (Virginia, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War (1861 - 1865). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia became the war's main battlefield the moment Richmond was made the Confederate capital, barely a hundred miles from Washington. More engagements were fought on its soil than anywhere else - Manassas, the Peninsula, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, the Wilderness, the long siege of Petersburg - and its western counties broke away in 1863 to enter the Union as a separate state. The surrender at Appomattox Court House in April 1865 effectively ended the Confederacy.

hints.label: Civil War (1861 - 1865)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Sioux (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Sioux (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Sioux. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Dakota bands hunted, fished and gathered wild rice across the lakes and prairies of the region, drawn into the French fur trade from the seventeenth century and later pushed westward by Ojibwe expansion and American settlement. Treaties in the 1830s and 1851 stripped away their land in the area, and the killings at Spirit Lake in 1857 hastened their removal. Village sites, burial mounds and trade goods from the period document both the older lifeway and its rapid disruption.

hints.label: Sioux
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Titterington Phase (Iowa, 2950 BC–2750 BC)
nodes.title: Titterington Phase (Iowa, 2950 BC–2750 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 2950 BC–2750 BC] Titterington Phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Archaic hunter-gatherer complex of the mid-Mississippi valley, recognised by long Sedalia lanceolate points and heavy chipped-stone gouges and adzes used for woodworking. Groups moved seasonally between upland camps and river bottoms, harvesting nuts, deer and freshwater mussels, and cemeteries with red ochre burials show growing attachment to particular places. It belongs to the long build-up towards settled river-valley life and early native plant cultivation.

hints.label: Titterington Phase
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Meskwaki (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Meskwaki (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Meskwaki. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Also known as the Fox, this Algonquian-speaking people were pushed west from the Great Lakes by decades of brutal warfare with the French and their allies, and later by U.S. treaties that stripped them of land in Illinois and Iowa. Removed to Kansas in the 1840s, many refused to stay: in 1857 they pooled money from annuities and horse sales and bought back land along the Iowa River, becoming one of the few Native nations to own its territory outright rather than hold it in reservation trust. That settlement near Tama still exists, and its origin story is the reason Meskwaki archaeology in Iowa spans the whole colonial and early modern era.

hints.label: Meskwaki
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: African-American (Florida, AD 1500–AD 1950)
nodes.title: African-American (Florida, AD 1500–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1500–AD 1950] African-American. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers the long presence of people of African descent in Florida, from enslaved and free Africans in Spanish St Augustine to Fort Mose, the first legally sanctioned free black town in what became the United States. Later came plantation slavery under British and American rule, alliance and intermarriage with the Seminoles, emancipation, and the segregated communities of the Jim Crow era. Archaeological sites range from slave quarters and cemeteries to twentieth-century town lots.

hints.label: African-American
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Jonathan Creek (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Jonathan Creek (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Jonathan Creek. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Mississippian town on the Tennessee River drainage, defended by repeatedly rebuilt palisade walls with bastions, with a plaza and rectangular pole-and-thatch houses inside. Excavated in the 1940s ahead of the flooding of Kentucky Lake, its overlapping house and stockade patterns gave archaeologists one of the clearest pictures of how such fortified communities grew, burned and were rebuilt - and of the endemic warfare that shaped life in the late prehistoric Southeast.

hints.label: Jonathan Creek
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 650–AD 750] Fox Lake. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Woodland-era way of life in the prairie lake country, built around seasonal camps on lakeshores and marsh edges where people fished, hunted bison and small game, and gathered wild plant foods. Its signature is thick, grit-tempered pottery with cord-roughened and stamped surfaces, left in scatters of hearths and refuse around the water margins.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Creek) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Creek). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Creek (Muscogee) Confederacy was a loose alliance of talwas along the Coosa, Tallapoosa and Chattahoochee, each with its own square ground and council. Deerskin trade with Carolina made them wealthy and dangerous, until the Creek War of 1813–14 and the defeat at Horseshoe Bend broke their power and opened Alabama to settlement. Excavated town sites show European ceramics and gunflints sitting alongside traditional shell-tempered pots.

Depression, New Deal relief programmes and then war mobilisation reshaped work and landscape within two decades. Shipyards at Newport News and Norfolk, new military bases and the construction of the Pentagon drew tens of thousands of migrants into Virginia's cities, while CCC crews built parks and Skyline Drive in the mountains. Rural electrification and paved roads began closing the gap between farm and town.

The physical traces of American mobilisation in the Midwest: rifle ranges, drill grounds, temporary cantonments and depot buildings thrown up quickly and largely dismantled afterwards. Their foundations and refuse deposits record how rapidly a rural state was pulled into an industrial war effort.

The earlier stage of the Indian River tradition, defined by plain undecorated pottery and a way of life built on estuarine fishing and shellfishing. Burial mounds of sand appear, sometimes with imported stone and shell items showing contact with communities far inland.

nodes.name: Mississippian (Illinois, AD 900–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Mississippian (Illinois, AD 900–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 900–AD 1500] Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming along the river bottoms supported the largest towns north of Mexico, built around flat-topped earthen mounds and open plazas. Cahokia, across the river from modern St Louis, grew to many thousands of people with a hundred mounds and a woodhenge of cedar posts, and its shell-tempered pottery and shell-and-copper regalia circulated across half a continent. The great centres were largely abandoned before Europeans arrived, leaving mounds that later settlers refused to credit to Native builders.

nodes.name: Archaic, indeterminate (Kentucky, 8000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic, indeterminate (Kentucky, 8000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 8000 BC–1000 BC] Archaic, indeterminate. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Along the Green and Ohio rivers, generations returned to the same spots to fish, collect mussels and bury their dead, building up shell mounds metres deep. Sites such as Indian Knoll have yielded thousands of burials, along with dog interments, spearthrower weights and ornaments of copper from the Great Lakes and shell from the Gulf. Late in the period these communities began tending goosefoot, sunflower and squash, the beginning of eastern North American agriculture.

hints.label: Archaic, indeterminate
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 450–AD 1000] Weeden Island 3. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

One division of the Weeden Island sequence of the northern Gulf coast, defined chiefly by pottery styles found in burial mounds and village middens. The tradition is famous for its finely decorated effigy and cut-out vessels, made to be smashed or cached as offerings rather than used in daily life. Everyday settlements relied on estuarine and riverine resources, with agriculture becoming significant only in some later communities.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Depression era (Iowa, AD 1929–AD 1941)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1929–AD 1941] Depression era. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Iowa farmers entered the slump already burdened by debt from the collapse of wartime crop prices, and the 1930s brought foreclosures, bank failures and corn selling below the cost of growing it. Anger boiled over in the Farm Holiday movement, when farmers blockaded roads, dumped milk and confronted judges to halt forced sales. New Deal programmes — crop price supports, the Rural Electrification Administration, soil conservation and WPA construction — reshaped the countryside and left buildings, roads and murals still in use.

nodes.title: Englewood (Florida, AD 900–AD 1100)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 900–AD 1100] Englewood. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A short transitional phase on Florida's central Gulf coast, bridging the older Weeden Island tradition and the later Safety Harbor culture. Its distinctive incised and punctated pottery, found in burial mounds and shell middens, marks a shift in ceramic styles and mortuary practice as communities along the coast reorganised.

nodes.name: Proto-historic (Illinois, AD 1500–AD 1650)
nodes.title: Proto-historic (Illinois, AD 1500–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1500–AD 1650] Proto-historic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Native communities here left no written records, but European trade goods — glass beads, brass and iron — arrived along Indigenous exchange routes well before any European did, and so did epidemic disease. Populations shifted and regrouped, with Illinois-speaking and Oneota groups rearranging themselves across the prairies and river valleys. By the time French explorers arrived in the 1670s they met a social landscape already transformed.

nodes.title: Caloosahatchee IV (Florida, AD 1350–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1350–AD 1500] Caloosahatchee IV. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The last fully pre-contact phase on the southwest Florida coast, immediately before Ponce de León's ships appeared. Calusa towns remained large and their leaders powerful enough to drive off early Spanish landings, sustained by fisheries rather than fields, and the elaborate carved wood, shell tools and ornaments of these generations are the material behind the famous Key Marco finds.

nodes.name: Late Archaic, indet. (Kentucky, 3000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Late Archaic, indet. (Kentucky, 3000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 3000 BC–1000 BC] Late Archaic, indet.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Foragers along the Green and Ohio rivers built up enormous shell middens through generations of harvesting mussels, fishing and hunting deer. They buried their dead in these mounds with copper from the Great Lakes and marine shell from the Gulf, evidence of long-distance exchange, and began tending native seed plants such as squash and goosefoot. This is the deep foundation for later mound-building societies.

hints.label: Late Archaic, indet.
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Quaker? (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Quaker? (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Quaker?. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Members of the Religious Society of Friends, who worshipped in silence without clergy or ritual and refused oaths, war and social deference. Friends were among the earliest and most persistent American abolitionists, and their meetinghouses and farms in the Midwest served as stations on the Underground Railroad. Their plain furniture, unadorned buildings and burial grounds with uniform markers reflect a deliberate rejection of display.

hints.label: Quaker?
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: War of 1812 (Iowa, AD 1812–AD 1815) [p086kj94g2n]

[Iowa, AD 1812–AD 1815] War of 1812. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The upper Mississippi became a contested frontier as British traders and their Sauk, Fox and Winnebago allies fought American attempts to plant forts and control the river. American expeditions were beaten back at Campbell's Island and Credit Island, and Black Hawk fought alongside the British — a grievance that resurfaced in the 1832 war that bears his name. Peace left the region firmly in American hands and opened the way for treaty cessions and settlement.

nodes.title: American Acquisition & Development 1821-45 (Florida, AD 1821–AD 1845)

Under the Adams-Onís treaty Florida passed from Spain to the United States, and Andrew Jackson took charge of a territory of Spanish towns, Seminole settlements and maroon communities. Tallahassee was laid out as a capital, cotton planters and enslaved labourers moved into the northern counties, and pressure for Indian removal produced the long and costly Second Seminole War. The territorial phase ended with admission to the Union as a slave state in 1845.

Worn-out tobacco land pushed Virginia planters toward wheat, mills and the sale of enslaved people southward, making the state a supplier of forced labour to the expanding cotton frontier. Gabriel's thwarted rising in Richmond hardened slave codes, while Jefferson's new university at Charlottesville advertised a different, more genteel self-image. Household sites from these years often mix imported English refined earthenwares with locally made storage wares.

[Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1899] 19th century urban. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Town-based archaeology of Iowa's steamboat landings, county seats and railroad depots, where merchants, artisans and immigrant families lived on tightly packed lots. Backyard privies, wells and cisterns, later filled with refuse, preserve unusually detailed records of what ordinary households ate, drank, bought and threw away.

nodes.title: Late Woodland (Florida, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 500–AD 1500] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

nodes.name: Old Copper Culture (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Old Copper Culture (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC] Old Copper Culture. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers around the Great Lakes hammered and annealed nuggets of pure native copper into knives, awls, spear points and fish hooks, some of the earliest metalworking anywhere in the world. The copper came mainly from Lake Superior deposits and travelled hundreds of miles through exchange networks. Over time metal shifted from tools toward ornaments and grave goods, marking growing distinctions in status among burials.

hints.label: Old Copper Culture

nodes.title: 20th Century::2nd half (1950 - 1999) (Virginia, AD 1950–AD 1999)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1950–AD 1999] 20th Century::2nd half (1950 - 1999). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Postwar prosperity remade the state: suburbs spread around Washington, Richmond and Hampton Roads, interstates cut through old farmland, and federal and military payrolls became a mainstay of the economy. Segregation was dismantled in the face of fierce official resistance, with schools closing rather than integrating before the courts forced the issue; in 1990 Virginia inaugurated the first elected Black governor in the United States. By the 1990s the northern counties were a hub of computing and telecommunications, and much of the archaeology of this era is about tract housing, shopping centres and demolished rural landscapes.

hints.label: 20th Century::2nd half (1950 - 1999)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 1870 - 1930 (Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1930)
nodes.title: 1870 - 1930 (Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1930)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1930] 1870 - 1930. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Railroads laced the state into a grid, and nearly every township got a shipping point, a grain elevator and a main street of brick storefronts within a wagon ride of the farms. Prairie sod gave way almost completely to corn, oats and hogs; barbed wire, tile drainage of the wetlands, and mail-order catalogues reshaped daily life, while German, Scandinavian, Czech and Dutch immigrant communities left their mark on churches and town names. Wartime demand made the 1910s boom years, and the crash in farm prices after 1920 began the long decline in the number of Iowa farms.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Depression/New Deal 1930-1940 (Florida, AD 1930–AD 1940)
nodes.title: Depression/New Deal 1930-1940 (Florida, AD 1930–AD 1940)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1930–AD 1940] Depression/New Deal 1930-1940. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Florida's crash came early, with the land boom bursting in the mid-1920s and hurricanes finishing the job, so the state entered the 1930s already broke. Federal programmes became a major employer: the CCC built state parks, the WPA produced roads, schools and the Federal Writers' Project guidebooks, and the Overseas Highway pushed toward Key West. The 1935 Labor Day hurricane, which killed hundreds of veterans working on that road, became a national scandal.

hints.label: Depression/New Deal 1930-1940
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: St. Johns IIa (Florida, AD 800–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 800–AD 1500] St. Johns IIa. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The stretch of the St. Johns tradition when check-stamped pottery replaced the older plain chalky wares along Florida's east coast and river valleys. Communities kept piling up the huge shell middens and sand burial mounds that still line the river, living off fish, shellfish, snails and wild plants rather than farming. These were the ancestors of the Timucua peoples the Spanish would meet centuries later.

nodes.name: Weeden Island A.D. 450-1000 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Weeden Island A.D. 450-1000 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 450–AD 1000] Weeden Island A.D. 450-1000. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A widespread culture of the Florida panhandle and neighbouring Georgia and Alabama, recognised above all by its mortuary pottery: red-painted, incised and punctated vessels, bird and animal effigies, and bowls with panels cut clean out of the walls, cached beside sand burial mounds. Villagers lived off estuaries, rivers and forests, with maize farming appearing only patchily and late. As settlements grew and platform mounds appeared, Weeden Island communities evolved into the Mississippian-era chiefdoms of the Gulf coast.

hints.label: Weeden Island A.D. 450-1000
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Apalachee (Florida, AD 1250–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Apalachee (Florida, AD 1250–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1250–AD 1600] Apalachee. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A powerful maize-farming chiefdom in the Florida panhandle, with platform-mound centres such as Lake Jackson, dense villages and extensive trade in copper and shell prestige goods. De Soto's expedition seized their principal town for the winter of 1539-40, and the epidemics and violence that followed shattered the old political order. Survivors were later gathered into a chain of Spanish missions around modern Tallahassee.

hints.label: Apalachee
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

Virginia moved from a rural, tobacco-and-agriculture economy under rigid legal segregation to a suburbanised state anchored by the federal government and the military. Its 1902 constitution stripped most Black Virginians of the vote; half a century later the state's 'Massive Resistance' to school desegregation closed public schools rather than integrate them. Hampton Roads shipyards and Northern Virginia's Cold War agencies drew in population and transformed the political map.

nodes.name: Archaic (Illinois, 8000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Illinois, 8000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, 8000 BC–1000 BC] Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

hints.label: Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Frontier (Illinois, AD 1841–AD 1871)
nodes.title: Frontier (Illinois, AD 1841–AD 1871)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1841–AD 1871] Frontier. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Prairie sod that had defeated earlier settlers was broken open by John Deere's steel plough, and the Illinois Central and other railroads turned a farming hinterland into the granary feeding Chicago's elevators, stockyards and lumberyards. Yankee, German and Irish migrants poured in, the state's politics produced Lincoln and the Civil War's western armies, and Chicago grew from lake port to national rail hub - until the fire of 1871 burned much of it down.

hints.label: Frontier
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle-Late Woodland, indet. (Kentucky, 1000 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Middle-Late Woodland, indet. (Kentucky, 1000 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 1000 BC–AD 1000] Middle-Late Woodland, indet.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Over these centuries people in the Ohio valley took up pottery, mound burial and gardening of native seed crops, joined long-distance exchange networks, and eventually adopted the bow and, late on, maize. Settlements grew from seasonal camps into hamlets and, by the end, into palisaded villages. The term is applied to sites whose material can be placed in this long span but not pinned to a phase.

hints.label: Middle-Late Woodland, indet.
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Pioneer (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1840)
nodes.title: Pioneer (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1840)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1840] Pioneer. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

American settlers pushed into Illinois from the Ohio valley and the Upland South, clearing river-bottom timber before venturing onto the prairie. Territorial status in 1809 and statehood in 1818 were followed by the removal of Native nations after the Black Hawk War of 1832, opening the north to Yankee and European migrants. Log cabins, lead mining at Galena and the first canal and rail schemes belong to these decades, along with the move of the capital to Springfield.

hints.label: Pioneer
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Woodland (Florida, 2500 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Woodland (Florida, 2500 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 2500 BC–AD 1500] Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A long stretch in which people of the Eastern Woodlands adopted pottery, built burial mounds, and gradually shifted from foraging to cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder, with maize arriving late. Trade networks moved copper, marine shell and exotic stone across half a continent, and Hopewell-style earthworks and elaborate grave goods appear in the middle centuries. By its end, settled villages, the bow and arrow and maize agriculture had set the stage for the town-building societies that followed.

hints.label: Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Mississippian (Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1000–AD 1500] Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming along the river bottoms supported the largest towns north of Mexico, built around flat-topped earthen mounds and open plazas. Cahokia, across the river from modern St Louis, grew to many thousands of people with a hundred mounds and a woodhenge of cedar posts, and its shell-tempered pottery and shell-and-copper regalia circulated across half a continent. The great centres were largely abandoned before Europeans arrived, leaving mounds that later settlers refused to credit to Native builders.

hints.label: Mississippian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Middle Woodland (Illinois, 200 BC–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, 200 BC–AD 300] Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

[Alabama, 1250 BC–AD 950] Woodland, Undifferentiated. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A catch-all label for sites in the Southeast that clearly belong to the Woodland era, with pottery, mound building and mixed foraging and gardening, but whose material is too sparse or mixed to place in a particular phase. Such collections still matter for mapping how densely the landscape was occupied.

hints.label: Woodland, Undifferentiated
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Prehistoric-Ceramic (Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Prehistoric-Ceramic (Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500] Prehistoric-Ceramic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Groups the Florida sites that produced pottery, beginning with fibre-tempered wares among late Archaic coastal foragers and continuing through the Woodland and later cultures that raised shell mounds, sand burial mounds and plazas. Ceramic styles are the main tool archaeologists use to date these sites and trace regional identities up to European contact.

hints.label: Prehistoric-Ceramic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Caloosahatchee III (Florida, AD 1200–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Caloosahatchee III (Florida, AD 1200–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1200–AD 1350] Caloosahatchee III. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Regional centres such as Mound Key reached their greatest scale, with canals, water courts and mounds raised high above the mangroves. The chiefly system that Spanish observers would later describe, in which coastal rulers drew tribute and captives from communities far inland, was by now firmly in place.

hints.label: Caloosahatchee III
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Quakers (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Quakers (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Quakers. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Members of the Religious Society of Friends, who worshipped in silence without clergy or ritual and refused oaths, war and social deference. Friends were among the earliest and most persistent American abolitionists, and their meetinghouses and farms in the Midwest served as stations on the Underground Railroad. Their plain furniture, unadorned buildings and burial grounds with uniform markers reflect a deliberate rejection of display.

hints.label: Quakers
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Eighteenth Century Spanish 1700-1763 (Florida, AD 1700–AD 1763)
nodes.title: Eighteenth Century Spanish 1700-1763 (Florida, AD 1700–AD 1763)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1700–AD 1763] Eighteenth Century Spanish 1700-1763. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

St Augustine spent these decades as a fortified frontier outpost, its stone Castillo de San Marcos sheltering the population through repeated British and Native attacks from Carolina and Georgia. The mission system that had spread across the interior was destroyed, and surviving Indigenous groups clustered near the town. Spain handed Florida to Britain in 1763, and most of the Spanish population evacuated to Cuba.

hints.label: Eighteenth Century Spanish 1700-1763
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Boom Times 1921-1929 (Florida, AD 1921–AD 1929)
nodes.title: Boom Times 1921-1929 (Florida, AD 1921–AD 1929)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1921–AD 1929] Boom Times 1921-1929. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Cheap land, new railways and highways, aggressive advertising and easy credit turned the state into a speculative frenzy, with lots in Miami and Coral Gables changing hands several times in a day, often unseen by their buyers. The bubble burst in 1926, helped along by a devastating hurricane, leaving half-built subdivisions and ruined banks — a preview of the national crash to come, and the origin of much of modern Florida's urban shape.

hints.label: Boom Times 1921-1929
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Middle Woodland (Georgia, 500 BC–AD 500)

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. nodes.name: Helton phase (Iowa, 4400 BC–3700 BC)
nodes.title: Helton phase (Iowa, 4400 BC–3700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 4400 BC–3700 BC] Helton phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Middle Archaic hunter-gatherer culture of the lower Illinois valley and neighbouring Mississippi drainage, known above all from the deep deposits at the Koster site. Groups returned to the same rich floodplain locations for long stays, building substantial dwellings, harvesting hickory nuts, fish and deer, and grinding seeds with stone tools. They left some of the earliest formal cemeteries in North America, and deliberate dog burials among the oldest known anywhere.

hints.label: Helton phase
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Belle Glade II (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Belle Glade II (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700] Belle Glade II. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The phase in which the Lake Okeechobee earthworks reached their most striking form, with great circular ditches, causeways and mounds shaped out of the wet prairie. At Fort Center a raised charnel platform stood over a pond, where the dead were laid out beneath carved wooden birds and animals — some of the finest wooden sculpture surviving from prehistoric North America.

hints.label: Belle Glade II
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Possible Paleoindian (Florida, 10000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.title: Possible Paleoindian (Florida, 10000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 10000 BC–5000 BC] Possible Paleoindian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Florida's earliest people hunted and foraged on a peninsula roughly twice its present width, since so much water was locked in glacial ice that the coastline lay far out on the continental shelf. They shared the landscape with mammoth, mastodon, giant tortoise and horse; sites like Page-Ladson in the Aucilla River preserve butchered bone and stone tools in waterlogged deposits. As the ice sheets melted, rising seas drowned much of this occupation, which is why so many finds now come from rivers, sinkholes and offshore.

hints.label: Possible Paleoindian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic, Native American (Choctaw) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Choctaw) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Choctaw). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Choctaw towns filled the country west of the Tombigbee, organised in tightly clustered districts of farmsteads around cleared bottomland fields. Skilled diplomats caught between the French, British and Spanish, they traded deerskins for cloth, guns and rum, and later ceded land treaty by treaty until removal in the 1830s. Distinctive Choctaw pottery and the burial-house customs described by early observers give their sites a recognisable signature.

hints.label: Historic, Native American (Choctaw)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Archaic (6500 - 3001 B.C.) (Virginia, 6500 BC–3001 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Archaic (6500 - 3001 B.C.) (Virginia, 6500 BC–3001 BC)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 6500 BC–3001 BC] Middle Archaic (6500 - 3001 B.C.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

As the climate warmed and oak-hickory forests replaced spruce and pine, hunter-gatherers shifted from wide-ranging pursuit of big game to intensively harvesting deer, nuts, fish and shellfish within smaller territories. New tools appear: ground and polished stone axes, grinding slabs, notched and stemmed points such as Stanly, Morrow Mountain and Guilford types. Camps became larger and were revisited season after season, a first step toward settled life.

hints.label: Middle Archaic (6500 - 3001 B.C.)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Glades Ib (Florida, 1000 BC–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 1000 BC–AD 750] Glades Ib. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The later part of the earliest Glades stage, distinguished by the first decorated pottery in south Florida, with incised designs around vessel rims. The subsistence base remained fishing, shellfishing and wild plants.

hints.label: Glades Ib
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Civil War 1861-1865 (Florida, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War 1861-1865 (Florida, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War 1861-1865. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The least populous Confederate state mattered chiefly as a larder, shipping cattle, salt and blockade-run supplies northward to the armies. Union forces held the major ports and coastal forts almost throughout, while the interior stayed in Confederate hands; the largest battle, Olustee in 1864, stopped a federal push toward Tallahassee. Thousands of Floridians, white and Black, served in Union units, and the state's slave system collapsed with emancipation.

hints.label: Civil War 1861-1865
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Industrial (1866-1899) (Missouri, AD 1866–AD 1899)
nodes.title: Early Industrial (1866-1899) (Missouri, AD 1866–AD 1899)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1866–AD 1899] Early Industrial (1866-1899). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

After the Civil War, railroads pushed across the state, St Louis and Kansas City boomed as manufacturing and meatpacking centres, and lead and zinc mining expanded in the southwest. Farms mechanised and mass-produced goods reached rural households through catalogues and rail freight. Sites from this era yield factory-made ceramics, bottles and hardware that mark the shift from local craft to national markets.

hints.label: Early Industrial (1866-1899)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Archaic (Illinois, 3000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Late Archaic (Illinois, 3000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, 3000 BC–1000 BC] Late Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.

hints.label: Late Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Antebellum (1821-1861) (Missouri, AD 1821–AD 1861)
nodes.title: Antebellum (1821-1861) (Missouri, AD 1821–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1821–AD 1861] Antebellum (1821-1861). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Admitted as a slave state under the compromise that briefly settled the sectional balance, Missouri grew rich on hemp, tobacco and river trade while St. Louis exploded into a immigrant-filled gateway city outfitting wagon trains for Santa Fe, Oregon and California. Slavery was concentrated along the Missouri River in "Little Dixie", even as German and Irish newcomers filled the cities with free-labour politics. The state supplied both the Dred Scott case and the armed settlers who made Kansas bleed, and entered the Civil War violently divided against itself.

hints.label: Antebellum (1821-1861)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Woodland (South Carolina, 1050 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Early Woodland (South Carolina, 1050 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, 1050 BC–500 BC] Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

hints.label: Early Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Plains Woodland (Iowa, 549 BC–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 549 BC–AD 1650] Plains Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities across the prairies took up pottery, built burial mounds and added squash, and later maize, to a diet still based on hunting, fishing and wild plants. The bow and arrow replaced the spear-thrower, and effigy and conical mound groups along the Mississippi and its tributaries mark territories and ceremonial life. These villages were the direct ancestors of the later Oneota and earth-lodge farming peoples of the eastern Plains.

hints.label: Plains Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Urban Industrial (Illinois, AD 1900–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Urban Industrial (Illinois, AD 1900–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1900–AD 1945] Urban Industrial. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Chicago's stockyards, steel mills and rail networks pulled workers from rural Illinois, southern and eastern Europe, and the Jim Crow South, producing crowded ethnic neighbourhoods and a militant labour movement. Coal mining and heavy manufacturing spread through downstate towns. The material record is one of factory-made abundance and municipal infrastructure: bottled goods, plumbing, streetcar lines and company housing.

hints.label: Urban Industrial
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 18th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1725 - 1774) (Virginia, AD 1725–AD 1774)
nodes.title: 18th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1725 - 1774) (Virginia, AD 1725–AD 1774)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1725–AD 1774] 18th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1725 - 1774). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The half-century in which colonial Virginia reached its height and then turned against Britain. Settlement filled the piedmont and the valley, tobacco inspection laws reshaped the export trade, and the Seven Years' War brought frontier fighting, debt and new imperial taxes. Genteel material culture spread widely in these decades, with white salt-glazed stoneware, creamware and tea equipage marking sites of the period, while the enslaved population grew and became largely American-born.

hints.label: 18th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1725 - 1774)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Mississippian (Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Middle Mississippian (Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1200] Middle Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming towns on the Ohio and Wabash built flat-topped mounds around open plazas, ringed themselves with palisades, and grew maize on the floodplains. Angel Mounds near Evansville was one of the largest, home to perhaps a thousand people and tied by trade and shared ritual style to Cahokia and other Mississippian centres. Shell-tempered pottery, chiefly burials and hierarchy between towns mark the region's most complex pre-contact societies.

hints.label: Middle Mississippian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Early Woodland (1200 B.C. - 299 A.D.) (Virginia, 1200 BC–AD 299)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 1200 BC–AD 299] Early Woodland (1200 B.C. - 299 A.D.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Pottery came into everyday use, first tempered with steatite and later with sand and shell, and settlements clustered along rivers and estuaries where fish, shellfish and nuts were abundant. Groups still moved seasonally but returned to favoured spots year after year, and some began tending native seed plants. Burials with copper and marine shell show goods moving along trade routes that stretched hundreds of miles.

nodes.name: Possible Meskwaki (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Possible Meskwaki (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Possible Meskwaki. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Meskwaki (called Fox by the French) appear in written records from the 1670s and spent the next century resisting French campaigns aimed at destroying them, eventually allying with the Sauk. Treaties in the 1830s and 1840s stripped them of Iowa land and forced removal to Kansas, but groups drifted back and in 1857 bought land outright near Tama - an unusual case of a tribe purchasing its own settlement rather than holding a federal reservation. Archaeological traces of these movements include village sites, trade goods and burials scattered across eastern Iowa.

hints.label: Possible Meskwaki
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Lane Farm (Iowa, AD 600–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 600–AD 700] Lane Farm. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Woodland phase of the wooded bluff country of the upper Mississippi, recognised chiefly by its cord-impressed pottery. Its people lived in small dispersed groups, hunted and gathered along the river valleys, and were part of the wider tradition that raised the region's low burial and effigy mounds.

hints.label: Lane Farm
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: WW I & Aftermath 1917-1920 (Florida, AD 1917–AD 1920)
nodes.title: WW I & Aftermath 1917-1920 (Florida, AD 1917–AD 1920)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1917–AD 1920] WW I & Aftermath 1917-1920. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

American entry into the war turned Florida into a training ground, with aviation fields, shipyards and army camps drawing federal money and outside labour. Wartime demand and the influenza epidemic of 1918 disrupted communities, while returning soldiers and a booming land market set the stage for the state's 1920s growth.

nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 100–AD 500] Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

nodes.name: Middle Mississippian (Georgia, AD 1200–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Middle Mississippian (Georgia, AD 1200–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, AD 1200–AD 1350] Middle Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming towns on the Ohio and Wabash built flat-topped mounds around open plazas, ringed themselves with palisades, and grew maize on the floodplains. Angel Mounds near Evansville was one of the largest, home to perhaps a thousand people and tied by trade and shared ritual style to Cahokia and other Mississippian centres. Shell-tempered pottery, chiefly burials and hierarchy between towns mark the region's most complex pre-contact societies.

nodes.title: Late Archaic (Alabama, 3950 BC–1250 BC)

[Alabama, 3950 BC–1250 BC] Late Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.

[Virginia, AD 1900–AD 1924] 20th Century::1st quarter (1900 - 1924). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The 1902 constitution disenfranchised nearly all Black voters and many poor whites, cementing one-party rule for decades. Tobacco, timber and coal drove the economy, while good-roads campaigns and the first automobiles began breaking rural isolation. The First World War turned Hampton Roads into a vast military complex, and the naval base at Norfolk, established in 1917, permanently reshaped the region.

nodes.title: Protohistoric (Indiana, AD 1400–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Indiana, AD 1400–AD 1650] Protohistoric. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hernando de Soto's expedition cut through the interior Southeast and the Mississippian chiefdoms it described soon fell apart, undone by disease, violence and the collapse of the mound-building order. Communities dispersed, merged and moved, laying the groundwork for the Creek, Cherokee and other historic nations. Sites of this period mix late Native ceramics with the occasional Spanish bead or iron blade.

Named for a mound site in Georgia, this Woodland culture spread across the Gulf Coast and interior Southeast, and is recognised above all by its pottery: vessels stamped before firing with carved wooden paddles bearing swirling, looping curvilinear designs. Because each paddle left a traceable signature, archaeologists can track individual paddles across distant sites and reconstruct networks of exchange and marriage. Communities built low burial and platform mounds and combined foraging with early cultivation of native seed plants.

nodes.name: Middle Archaic, indet. (Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Archaic, indet. (Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 6000 BC–3000 BC] Middle Archaic, indet.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers concentrated along the major rivers, especially the Green, where centuries of mussel harvesting built up huge shell mounds. These middens contain some of the earliest cemeteries in North America, with burials accompanied by atlatl weights, bone tools and marine shell traded from the Gulf coast. The scale and repeated use of these places point to growing attachment to territory and rising social complexity.

nodes.title: Historic Native American (Missouri, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1673–AD 1950] Historic Native American. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers the Native nations of the Missouri region from the first French descent of the Mississippi onward — Osage, Missouria, Illinois, Kansa and, later, peoples pushed west by removal. Sites from these centuries mix traditional material culture with glass beads, brass kettles, gunflints and horse gear, showing how deeply the fur trade reshaped daily life. The period ends with dispossession: by the 1830s most of these nations had been forced out of the state entirely.

[Missouri, AD 1804–AD 1820] Territorial (1804-1820). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The years between the Louisiana Purchase and statehood, when American settlers poured up the Missouri and Mississippi into land held by French and Spanish creole communities and by Osage, Sauk and Fox peoples. Lewis and Clark set out from here in 1804, St. Louis grew into the hub of the western fur trade, and the New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-12 shook the region violently. The territory's application to enter the Union as a slave state provoked the Missouri Compromise.

hints.label: Territorial (1804-1820)

[Virginia, 13050 BC–AD 1950] Prehistoric and Historic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A catch-all classification for sites that yield both Native American occupation and later colonial or American material, or that cannot be sorted between them. In practice it covers the whole Virginia sequence, from Paleoindian hunters at the end of the Ice Age through Woodland farming villages to plantations, mills and twentieth-century homes — often layered on the same well-drained river terrace.

[Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1860] Pioneer Iowa, Wisconsin Territory to early statehood. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Lead mining around Dubuque drew the first American settlers, and the Black Hawk Purchase of 1833 opened land along the Mississippi to homesteaders. Iowa passed from Michigan and Wisconsin territorial government to its own territory in 1838 and to statehood in 1846, as settlers broke the tough prairie sod and laid out county towns. By 1860 railroads had reached the Missouri River and the state's farming economy was established.

nodes.title: Woodland (Missouri, 1000 BC–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, 1000 BC–AD 900] Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A long stretch in which people of the Eastern Woodlands adopted pottery, built burial mounds, and gradually shifted from foraging to cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder, with maize arriving late. Trade networks moved copper, marine shell and exotic stone across half a continent, and Hopewell-style earthworks and elaborate grave goods appear in the middle centuries. By its end, settled villages, the bow and arrow and maize agriculture had set the stage for the town-building societies that followed.

[Iowa, AD 850–AD 950] Loseke Creek Variant. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The formal archaeological grouping for late Woodland sites of the middle Missouri and adjacent Iowa country, defined by cord-roughened ceramics with cord-impressed rim decoration. Communities were small and mobile, combining hunting and gathering with some horticulture, and marked their dead with earthen mounds. Archaeologists use the variant to track the transition from Woodland lifeways to the settled earth-lodge villages that followed.
