[Indiana, AD 1000–AD 1650] Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming along the river bottoms supported the largest towns north of Mexico, built around flat-topped earthen mounds and open plazas. Cahokia, across the river from modern St Louis, grew to many thousands of people with a hundred mounds and a woodhenge of cedar posts, and its shell-tempered pottery and shell-and-copper regalia circulated across half a continent. The great centres were largely abandoned before Europeans arrived, leaving mounds that later settlers refused to credit to Native builders.

nodes.title: Weeden Island 1 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 450–AD 1000] Weeden Island 1. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A ceramic tradition and way of life spread across the Florida panhandle and neighbouring Georgia and Alabama, best known for extraordinary mortuary pottery — modelled birds, animals and human figures, and vessels with cut-out panels — deposited in caches beside burial mounds. Villages sat near estuaries and river swamps, drawing on fish, shellfish and wild plants long before maize became important. Its later phases fed directly into the Mississippian-style chiefdoms of the region.

[Florida, AD 450–AD 750] Weeden Island I. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The earlier half of the Weeden Island sequence, when mortuary ceremonialism was at its most elaborate: sand burial mounds accompanied by caches of effigy vessels and cut-out pottery made specially for the dead. People lived in small villages exploiting estuaries, rivers and forests, without dependence on maize. The style spread widely across the northern Gulf coast, linking scattered communities in a shared ritual idiom.

Coastal hunting, fishing and shellfishing communities along the Atlantic and Gulf shores of the Southeast, recognised by their check-stamped and simple-stamped pottery made with carved wooden paddles. They left large shell middens and, later in the sequence, small burial mounds hinting at growing ceremonial life and exchange with interior groups. The tradition marks the spread of settled Woodland lifeways before maize agriculture reached the region.

nodes.title: Middle Gulf Formational (Alabama, 1200 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, 1200 BC–500 BC] Middle Gulf Formational. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities along the rivers and coasts of the Gulf South were making some of North America's earliest pottery, the fibre-tempered Wheeler wares, while still living by hunting, fishing and gathering shellfish. Exotic stone and beads found at their sites show links to the great earthwork centre at Poverty Point in Louisiana. These small-scale, seasonally mobile groups laid the ceramic and exchange foundations for the burial mound societies that followed.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: German Amana Colonists (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: German Amana Colonists (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] German Amana Colonists. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Community of True Inspiration, German Pietists who fled religious persecution, established seven communal villages on the Iowa River where property, kitchens and workshops were shared and worship was plain and frequent. They ran their own woollen mills, farms and craft shops with remarkable self-sufficiency until members voted in 1932 to end communal life and reorganise as a business corporation. Their sites yield German-made ceramics and locally produced goods alongside American mass-market wares.

nodes.title: Suwannee Valley Culture (Florida, AD 750–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 750–AD 1700] Suwannee Valley Culture. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The late prehistoric farming societies of north Florida, growing maize in dispersed hamlets and making plain and cob-marked pottery quite unlike the elaborate wares of neighbouring regions. These were the people the Spanish met as the northern Utina and other Timucua-speaking groups, and their villages became the sites of Franciscan missions along the Camino Real. Disease and mission life largely destroyed them within two centuries of contact.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.

nodes.title: The New Dominion (1946 - 1988) (Virginia, AD 1946–AD 1988)

[Virginia, AD 1946–AD 1988] The New Dominion (1946 - 1988). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Postwar Virginia was transformed by federal spending, as Pentagon and government work turned the northern counties into sprawling commuter suburbs and shifted political power away from the rural Southside. The Byrd Organization's policy of Massive Resistance closed public schools rather than desegregate them after Brown v. Board of Education, and its defeat, together with the Voting Rights Act, ended decades of one-party control. By the 1980s the state had elected a Republican governor and, soon after, the nation's first elected Black governor.

nodes.title: Caborn-Welborn (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)

[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Caborn-Welborn. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A late Mississippian people of the lower Ohio and Wabash confluence, whose scattered farming villages emerged as the great mound centre at Angel Mounds was abandoned. They lived in dispersed settlements without large mounds, made shell-tempered pottery, and hunted and farmed the rich bottomlands. The final generations acquired brass and glass from far-off European traders before the towns emptied, leaving the region largely vacant when the first colonists arrived.

nodes.title: Colonial (1700-1803) (Missouri, AD 1700–AD 1803)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1700–AD 1803] Colonial (1700-1803). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Lead mining, salt making and the fur trade drew French colonists across the Mississippi, producing settlements like Ste. Genevieve and, in 1764, St. Louis, with their distinctive vertical-log houses and long-lot fields. Spain governed after 1762 but the culture stayed French, and the town became the gateway for trade with Osage and other Native nations. The Louisiana Purchase ended colonial rule and opened the region to a flood of American settlers.

[Virginia, AD 1750–AD 1774] 18th Century::3rd quarter (1750 - 1774). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Fighting in the Ohio country pulled Virginia into the Seven Years' War, made a reputation for the young George Washington, and left Britain determined to tax its colonies. Protests over the Stamp Act and the Townshend duties turned Williamsburg's Capitol into a stage for resistance, and by 1774 the burgesses were meeting outside the governor's authority. Planter debt to British merchants deepened even as households filled with fashionable imported goods, above all the new creamware and tea sets that date sites of these years closely.

Early Woodland communities of the Ohio Valley and its fringes who built conical earthen burial mounds and buried their dead with copper bracelets, tubular pipes and carved stone tablets. They gathered and cultivated native seed plants, made some of the region's first pottery, and traded for exotic materials over long distances. Their mound-building and ritual exchange laid the groundwork for the far larger Hopewell networks that followed.

[Alabama, AD 950–AD 1150] Early Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming along the Mississippi and its tributaries supported larger, more permanent villages, and communities began raising flat-topped earthen mounds around open plazas. Shell-tempered pottery, the bow and arrow, and a new emphasis on hereditary leadership all spread in these centuries. The trend culminated in Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico, just across the river from Missouri's American Bottom settlements.

Tobacco planting spread across the tidewater on the backs of indentured servants and, increasingly, enslaved Africans brought directly from the Atlantic trade; laws passed in these decades made slavery hereditary and racial. Falling tobacco prices and land pressure fed the discontent behind Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, which burned Jamestown and ended with frontier attacks on Native communities. The capital moved to Williamsburg in 1699, and the colony's brick houses, imported ceramics and household goods show a settled gentry class taking shape.

nodes.title: Contact Era Prehistoric (South Carolina, AD 1500–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 1500–AD 1700] Contact Era Prehistoric. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Spanish and later English expeditions reached the interior chiefdoms of the Southeast, and the diseases they carried spread far ahead of the newcomers themselves. Large Mississippian towns with mounds and paramount chiefs broke apart, and survivors regrouped into the smaller nations recorded by later colonists. Sites of the period yield the first European metal, glass and ceramics mixed in with native pottery and stone tools.

hints.label: Contact Era Prehistoric
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Woodland (Illinois, 1000 BC–AD 900)
nodes.title: Woodland (Illinois, 1000 BC–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, 1000 BC–AD 900] Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A long stretch in which people of the Eastern Woodlands adopted pottery, built burial mounds, and gradually shifted from foraging to cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder, with maize arriving late. Trade networks moved copper, marine shell and exotic stone across half a continent, and Hopewell-style earthworks and elaborate grave goods appear in the middle centuries. By its end, settled villages, the bow and arrow and maize agriculture had set the stage for the town-building societies that followed.

hints.label: Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Archaic (Georgia, 3050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.title: Late Archaic (Georgia, 3050 BC–1050 BC)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, 3050 BC–1050 BC] Late Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherers in the Ohio Valley settled into river valleys for much of the year, harvesting mussels, nuts and deer and leaving deep shell and refuse middens. They began cultivating native seed plants such as goosefoot and squash, and traded copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf. Cemeteries with grave goods suggest growing attachment to particular places and differences in standing between individuals.

hints.label: Late Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Spanish-Second Period 1783-1821 (Florida, AD 1783–AD 1821)
nodes.title: Spanish-Second Period 1783-1821 (Florida, AD 1783–AD 1821)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1783–AD 1821] Spanish-Second Period 1783-1821. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Spain regained Florida after the American Revolution but never governed it firmly: the interior filled with Seminole towns, runaway slaves and American squatters, and the border with Georgia was effectively lawless. Andrew Jackson's raids and the Adams-Onís Treaty ended the experiment, transferring Florida to the United States.

hints.label: Spanish-Second Period 1783-1821
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic, Native American (Chatot) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Chatot) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Chatot). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A small nation of the lower Chattahoochee and Apalachicola country, missionised by the Spanish in the late 1600s and then driven west by slave raiding. They resettled near the French post at Mobile, where they lived as allies and neighbours of the colony. Their story is typical of the shattered smaller Gulf Coast groups that were absorbed or displaced within a couple of generations of contact.

hints.label: Historic, Native American (Chatot)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Belle Glade IV (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Belle Glade IV (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700] Belle Glade IV. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The final centuries of the Lake Okeechobee tradition, when interior towns were drawn into the orbit of the powerful Calusa of the southwest Florida coast and their tribute networks. European metal, glass beads and salvaged shipwreck material begin to appear alongside local pottery. Spanish missions, slave raiding and epidemic disease eventually emptied the region of its native population.

hints.label: Belle Glade IV
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Prehistoric (South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Late Prehistoric (South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1500] Late Prehistoric. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize farming, fortified riverside towns and platform mounds spread across the region, with communities organised into chiefdoms whose leaders were buried with shell, copper and finely made pottery. Bows replaced spearthrowers, and shell-tempered pots and triangular arrow points are the typical finds. These were the societies encountered and severely disrupted by the De Soto expedition and the diseases that followed.

hints.label: Late Prehistoric
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Protohistoric (Virginia, AD 1450–AD 1550)
nodes.title: Protohistoric (Virginia, AD 1450–AD 1550)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1450–AD 1550] Protohistoric. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hernando de Soto's expedition cut through the interior Southeast and the Mississippian chiefdoms it described soon fell apart, undone by disease, violence and the collapse of the mound-building order. Communities dispersed, merged and moved, laying the groundwork for the Creek, Cherokee and other historic nations. Sites of this period mix late Native ceramics with the occasional Spanish bead or iron blade.

hints.label: Protohistoric
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: General Woodland (Georgia, 1050 BC–AD 1150)
nodes.title: General Woodland (Georgia, 1050 BC–AD 1150)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, 1050 BC–AD 1150] General Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Pottery came into everyday use, communities grew more settled, and people began burying their dead in earthen mounds and tending native seed crops long before maize arrived. Distinctive complicated-stamped and check-stamped wares mark the period in the region, and long-distance exchange brought exotic materials into local burial ceremonies. The bow and arrow appeared late in the sequence, and rising populations along the rivers set the stage for the mound-building towns that followed.

hints.label: General Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early/Middle Woodland (1200 B.C. - 999 A.D.) (Virginia, 1200 BC–AD 999)
nodes.title: Early/Middle Woodland (1200 B.C. - 999 A.D.) (Virginia, 1200 BC–AD 999)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 1200 BC–AD 999] Early/Middle Woodland (1200 B.C. - 999 A.D.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Pottery, burial mounds and long-distance exchange in copper, mica and marine shell define these centuries, when groups settled more firmly along rivers and estuaries. Native seed plants were increasingly cultivated alongside hunting, fishing and shellfish collecting, and populations grew. The broad label is applied to sites whose material spans the era without falling neatly into either half.

hints.label: Early/Middle Woodland (1200 B.C. - 999 A.D.)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Prehistoric-Unspecified (Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500] Prehistoric-Unspecified. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A holding category for Native American sites in Florida that cannot be placed more precisely — surface scatters, disturbed shell middens, isolated finds. Together they map where people lived across the peninsula for more than eleven thousand years, even when the details are lost.

hints.label: Prehistoric-Unspecified
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Colonial (Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1781)
nodes.title: Colonial (Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1781)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1781] Colonial. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

French traders, soldiers and Jesuit missionaries moved down from Canada into the Illinois Country, founding Cahokia, Kaskaskia and Fort de Chartres among Illinois Indian villages and shipping wheat and flour downriver to New Orleans. Britain took the territory after 1763 and many French families crossed the Mississippi rather than live under it. George Rogers Clark's capture of Kaskaskia in 1778 brought the region into the American Revolution.

hints.label: Colonial
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Glenwood (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300)
nodes.title: Glenwood (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300] Glenwood. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Earthlodge farmsteads scattered through the loess bluffs above the Missouri River, part of the Central Plains tradition. Families lived in square, timber-framed lodges dug partly into hillsides, growing maize, beans and squash in bottomland gardens and hunting bison on the prairies. The settlements were abandoned as drier conditions set in, with these groups moving on to become part of the later Plains village peoples.

hints.label: Glenwood
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Angel (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Angel (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Angel. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The era of Mississippian town life in the lower Ohio valley, centred on the great walled settlement at Angel Mounds with its plazas, flat-topped earthen mounds and thousands of residents supported by maize agriculture. Such towns were the largest communities the region had ever seen, ruled by chiefs whose authority was expressed in mound architecture and shell-tempered pottery traded far along the rivers. They were abandoned well before Europeans arrived, leaving the valley to the dispersed Native communities encountered in the historic period.

hints.label: Angel
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 18th Century::4th quarter (1775 - 1799) (Virginia, AD 1775–AD 1799)
nodes.title: 18th Century::4th quarter (1775 - 1799) (Virginia, AD 1775–AD 1799)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1775–AD 1799] 18th Century::4th quarter (1775 - 1799). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Royal government collapsed in 1775, and Virginia declared rights and independence the following year; the war reached the colony directly with raids, the Yorktown campaign and Cornwallis's surrender in 1781. Thousands of enslaved Virginians fled to British lines seeking freedom, while the state's leaders went on to shape the federal Constitution. The capital moved to Richmond, the Anglican church was disestablished, and planters increasingly turned worn tobacco fields over to wheat.

hints.label: 18th Century::4th quarter (1775 - 1799)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Black Sand complex (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.title: Black Sand complex (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC] Black Sand complex. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

An Early Woodland complex of the upper Mississippi and Illinois river valleys, named for its incised and cordmarked pottery decorated with bold geometric designs. Groups lived in small floodplain settlements, gathered and stored nuts and native seed crops, and buried some of their dead in mounds. Their ceramics and burial customs lead directly into the elaborate Havana Hopewell societies that followed.

hints.label: Black Sand complex
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Wahpekute Dakota (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Wahpekute Dakota (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Wahpekute Dakota. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

One of the four Santee Dakota bands, ranging over southern Minnesota and northern Iowa, hunting bison on the prairies and harvesting wild rice and maple sugar. They were drawn into the fur trade with French and later American traders, and successive treaties from the 1830s stripped them of land, culminating in removal from Iowa and Minnesota.

hints.label: Wahpekute Dakota
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Archaic (3000 - 1201 B.C.) (Virginia, 3000 BC–1201 BC)
nodes.title: Late Archaic (3000 - 1201 B.C.) (Virginia, 3000 BC–1201 BC)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 3000 BC–1201 BC] Late Archaic (3000 - 1201 B.C.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Populations concentrated along rivers and estuaries, exploiting shellfish, fish runs and nuts intensively enough to support large, repeatedly occupied camps. Carved steatite bowls and broad-bladed Savannah River points travelled through wide exchange networks, and the first crude fired pottery appeared near the end. These riverine communities set the pattern for the Woodland societies that followed.

hints.label: Late Archaic (3000 - 1201 B.C.)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Pioneer (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1825)
nodes.title: Early Pioneer (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1825)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1825] Early Pioneer. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

French explorers reached the upper Mississippi and opened a fur-trading world in which Ioway, Meskwaki, Sauk and Dakota communities dealt with a shifting cast of French, British, Spanish and finally American traders. Goods such as guns, kettles and glass beads moved inland decades before any permanent European settlement, reshaping local economies and rivalries. Formal American control arrived with the Louisiana Purchase and the treaties that would soon strip Native nations of the land.

hints.label: Early Pioneer
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Seminole, 1st War to 2nd 1817-1834 (Florida, AD 1817–AD 1834)
nodes.title: Seminole, 1st War to 2nd 1817-1834 (Florida, AD 1817–AD 1834)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1817–AD 1834] Seminole, 1st War to 2nd 1817-1834. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Andrew Jackson's raids into Spanish Florida, ostensibly against Seminole raiders and the fugitive slaves living among them, helped force Spain to cede the territory to the United States. Under American rule the Seminole were pressed onto a poor inland reservation and squeezed by settlers and slave-catchers, and treaties signed under duress at Payne's Landing and Fort Gibson committed them to move west of the Mississippi.

hints.label: Seminole, 1st War to 2nd 1817-1834
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Weeden Island 2 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Weeden Island 2 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 450–AD 1000] Weeden Island 2. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Part of the Weeden Island ceramic tradition of the northern Gulf coast, whose potters made both plain domestic wares and elaborate effigy and cut-out vessels destined for mound-side burial offerings. Communities lived in villages built around fishing, shellfishing and wild plant foods, with ritual life focused on sand burial mounds. Over time these societies grew larger and more hierarchical, laying the ground for the Fort Walton chiefdoms.

hints.label: Weeden Island 2
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Mississippian (Alabama, AD 1150–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Middle Mississippian (Alabama, AD 1150–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1150–AD 1350] Middle Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming towns on the Ohio and Wabash built flat-topped mounds around open plazas, ringed themselves with palisades, and grew maize on the floodplains. Angel Mounds near Evansville was one of the largest, home to perhaps a thousand people and tied by trade and shared ritual style to Cahokia and other Mississippian centres. Shell-tempered pottery, chiefly burials and hierarchy between towns mark the region's most complex pre-contact societies.

hints.label: Middle Mississippian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Urban / Industrial (1900-1960) (Missouri, AD 1900–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Urban / Industrial (1900-1960) (Missouri, AD 1900–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1900–AD 1950] Urban / Industrial (1900-1960). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

St Louis and Kansas City drew in rural Missourians and Black migrants from the Deep South, filling brick tenements and working in shoe factories, meatpacking plants and rail yards. Electricity, automobiles and paved highways reshaped both cities and countryside, while the Depression and two world wars swung employment violently. Archaeologically the period shows up as mass-produced consumer goods, municipal sanitation, and the demolition layers of slum clearance.

hints.label: Urban / Industrial (1900-1960)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Woodland (Georgia, 1050 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Early Woodland (Georgia, 1050 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, 1050 BC–500 BC] Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

hints.label: Early Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 20th Century::4th quarter (1975 - 1999) (Virginia, AD 1975–AD 1999)
nodes.title: 20th Century::4th quarter (1975 - 1999) (Virginia, AD 1975–AD 1999)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1975–AD 1999] 20th Century::4th quarter (1975 - 1999). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Old industries such as tobacco, textiles and furniture declined while the corridor west of Washington filled with defence contractors, data networks and, by the 1990s, internet companies. Population shifted decisively to the suburbs, and preservation law began treating twentieth-century buildings and Cold War installations as heritage. Politics changed too, most visibly with the 1990 inauguration of the nation's first elected African American governor.

hints.label: 20th Century::4th quarter (1975 - 1999)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Middle Woodland (Alabama, 50 BC–AD 350)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, 50 BC–AD 350] Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

hints.label: Middle Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic (Missouri, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Historic (Missouri, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1673–AD 1950] Historic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Opens with the first European descent of the Mississippi and covers French lead mining and river villages, Spanish administration, and then American statehood, steamboats and railroads. Sites from these centuries include trading posts, farmsteads, Civil War fortifications and industrial works, and are studied with documents and maps alongside the ground itself. Native communities persisted and were pushed out during the same span, so the archaeology records both settlement and dispossession.

hints.label: Historic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Archaic (Illinois, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Archaic (Illinois, 6000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, 6000 BC–3000 BC] Middle Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

hints.label: Middle Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Orr phase (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.title: Orr phase (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673] Orr phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The last archaeological phase of Oneota in northeastern Iowa and adjacent Minnesota and Wisconsin, recognised by its thin shell-tempered pottery and, at later sites, European trade goods. Its villages are generally accepted as the direct remains of the Ioway, making it one of the clearest links between an archaeological culture and a named historic tribe.

hints.label: Orr phase
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Newtown. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Late Woodland farming hamlets of the central Ohio Valley, living in small circular villages after the great Hopewell earthwork and mound-building tradition had faded. Their people made cord-marked jars, took up the bow and arrow, and leaned increasingly on maize alongside native seed crops. Out of these communities grew the later Fort Ancient villages of the region.

hints.label: Newtown

[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Fox. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Meskwaki (called Fox by the French) were pushed west out of the Great Lakes by two brutal French campaigns of extermination in the 1710s and 1730s, and later ranged the Mississippi valley alongside the Sauk. Removed to Kansas after the 1842 treaty, a group of them did something almost unique in Native American history: they pooled money and bought their land back, purchasing acreage on the Iowa River in 1857 to found the Meskwaki Settlement, which their descendants still hold.

hints.label: Fox
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Industrial (Illinois, AD 1871–AD 1901)
nodes.title: Early Industrial (Illinois, AD 1871–AD 1901)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1871–AD 1901] Early Industrial. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Chicago rebuilt after the 1871 fire with steel-framed buildings, and the state's railroads, stockyards, coal mines and steel mills drew waves of European migrants into fast-growing industrial towns. Labour conflict was intense, from the Haymarket affair to the Pullman strike. Archaeologically, the period shows in worker housing, factory sites and mass-produced consumer goods.

hints.label: Early Industrial
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Woodland (Missouri, 1000 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Early Woodland (Missouri, 1000 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, 1000 BC–500 BC] Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

hints.label: Early Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Gulf Formational, Undifferentiated (Alabama, 500 BC–100 BC)
nodes.title: Gulf Formational, Undifferentiated (Alabama, 500 BC–100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, 500 BC–100 BC] Gulf Formational, Undifferentiated. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The stretch when people of the Gulf coastal plain and its river valleys began making and using pottery in quantity - first fibre-tempered, later sand-tempered wares - while still living largely by hunting, fishing and gathering. Settlements grew more permanent and long-distance exchange in stone and other goods expanded, setting up the burial-mound societies of the Woodland period that followed.

hints.label: Gulf Formational, Undifferentiated
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Early Woodland (Florida, 2500 BC–AD 100)

[Florida, 2500 BC–AD 100] Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: St. Johns II, A.D. 800-1500 (Florida, AD 800–AD 1500)
nodes.title: St. Johns II, A.D. 800-1500 (Florida, AD 800–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 800–AD 1500] St. Johns II, A.D. 800-1500. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Marked by check-stamped versions of the region's chalky pottery, this was a time of larger, more organised communities with platform and burial mounds and clear social ranking, influenced by but distinct from Mississippian chiefdoms inland. Fishing and shellfish remained the economic base rather than intensive maize farming. Its final generations were the Timucua chiefdoms met by French and Spanish expeditions.

hints.label: St. Johns II, A.D. 800-1500
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Woodland, indet (Kentucky, 200 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Middle Woodland, indet (Kentucky, 200 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 200 BC–AD 1000] Middle Woodland, indet. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities along the Ohio and its tributaries lived in small settlements, made thick grit-tempered pots, and buried their dead under earthen mounds. They grew squash, sunflower and native seed crops while still hunting and gathering heavily, and they traded for copper, marine shell and fine cherts through the exchange networks that linked Adena and Hopewell centres. The label is used when artefacts show only that a site falls somewhere in this broad ceramic-and-mound era.

hints.label: Middle Woodland, indet
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 1880 to 2008 (Iowa, AD 1880–AD 2008)
nodes.title: 1880 to 2008 (Iowa, AD 1880–AD 2008)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1880–AD 2008] 1880 to 2008. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A span that runs from the height of small-farm, small-town Iowa to the present-day landscape of consolidated grain and livestock operations. Steam and horse power gave way to tractors, hybrid seed and centre-pivot machinery; interstate highways and grain terminals replaced the local depot and creamery. Standing buildings and archaeological deposits from these years document ordinary rural and urban life, from farmstead outbuildings and privies to factory sites and demolished neighbourhoods.

hints.label: 1880 to 2008
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 19th Century (South Carolina, AD 1800–AD 1900)
nodes.title: 19th Century (South Carolina, AD 1800–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 1800–AD 1900] 19th Century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Steam, iron and coal turned England into the world's first industrial society: railways spread across the country from the 1830s, factory towns swelled, and by mid-century most people lived in urban places. Reform came in fits and starts, through the Reform Acts, factory and public health legislation, and the growth of trade unions, alongside grinding poverty, cholera and the workhouse. Britain's empire and global trade reached their greatest extent, and mass-produced goods, from transfer-printed china to bottled patent medicines, fill archaeological deposits of the period.

hints.label: 19th Century
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Indet. Mississippi (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Indet. Mississippi (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Indet. Mississippi. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Used for remains clearly of Mississippian type but not assignable to a named phase. Mississippian communities built platform mounds and plazas, farmed maize intensively on river bottomlands, made shell-tempered pottery, and were organised into ranked chiefdoms that rose and collapsed repeatedly. Western Kentucky sat within this world, linked by the Ohio and Mississippi rivers to centres like Cahokia and Angel.

hints.label: Indet. Mississippi
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Weeden Island 4 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Weeden Island 4 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 450–AD 1000] Weeden Island 4. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A subdivision of the long Weeden Island ceramic sequence in the Florida panhandle and adjacent Southeast, tracked through changing decoration on mound and village pottery. Ritual life centred on sand burial mounds accompanied by caches of elaborately modelled and perforated vessels. Settlement remained tied to rich coastal and river-valley food sources rather than to intensive farming.

hints.label: Weeden Island 4
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Twentieth C American (Florida, AD 1900–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Twentieth C American (Florida, AD 1900–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1900–AD 1950] Twentieth C American. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Railroads, drainage of the Everglades and aggressive land promotion turned a thinly settled state into a destination, with a speculative boom in the 1920s that collapsed spectacularly before the 1926 hurricane and the Depression. Military airfields and training bases in the 1940s brought in hundreds of thousands of servicemen, many of whom returned to stay. Sites from these decades range from Mediterranean Revival resorts and packing houses to New Deal camps and wartime airstrips.

hints.label: Twentieth C American
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: General Mississippian (Georgia, AD 900–AD 1540)
nodes.title: General Mississippian (Georgia, AD 900–AD 1540)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, AD 900–AD 1540] General Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The era of maize farming, flat-topped earthen mounds and hereditary chiefs in the Southeast. Towns like Etowah were laid out around plazas and mounds, ringed by palisades, and their elites were buried with copper plates, engraved shell and stone effigies bearing a shared body of religious imagery. The chiefdoms were still functioning when Hernando de Soto marched through in 1540, and collapsed rapidly afterwards under the diseases and disruption that followed.

hints.label: General Mississippian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 1870-1998 (Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1998)
nodes.title: 1870-1998 (Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1998)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1870–AD 1998] 1870-1998. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The span covers Iowa's transformation from newly railroaded farm country into an industrialised agricultural landscape. Horse-drawn work gave way to tractors and combines, rural electrification and paved highways closed the distance between farm and town, and hybrid corn and chemical fertiliser multiplied yields while steadily reducing the number of people needed to produce them. Hundreds of small towns and one-room schools shrank or disappeared, and the farm crisis of the 1980s accelerated consolidation into far fewer, far larger operations.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Moingona (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.title: Moingona (Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1673] Moingona. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages of the Oneota tradition along the central Des Moines River valley, whose people combined maize, bean and squash gardening with bison hunting and fishing. They left thick middens, storage and refuse pits, and distinctive shell-tempered pottery with trailed decoration. These communities are widely regarded as ancestral to the historic Ioway, and the sequence closes at the point when French explorers first reached the region.

hints.label: Moingona
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Loseke (Iowa, AD 850–AD 950)
nodes.title: Loseke (Iowa, AD 850–AD 950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 850–AD 950] Loseke. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Plains Woodland pottery complex of the Missouri valley and its eastern margins, known from cord-roughened jars decorated with single-cord impressions around the rim. Its people lived in small settlements, hunted bison and deer, gathered wild plants and built low burial mounds, and stand between the earlier Woodland mound-builders and the later village farmers of the Plains.

hints.label: Loseke
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Great Oasis or Oneota (Iowa, AD 900–AD 1673)
nodes.title: Great Oasis or Oneota (Iowa, AD 900–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 900–AD 1673] Great Oasis or Oneota. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A long span covering the shift from the early maize-farming Great Oasis hamlets to the Oneota villages that dominated the region until Europeans arrived. Oneota people made shell-tempered globular pots, lived in large seasonal settlements, and combined horticulture with bison hunting and wild rice gathering; their descendants include the Ioway, Otoe and Ho-Chunk. The end date marks the arrival of Marquette and Jolliet on the Mississippi.

hints.label: Great Oasis or Oneota
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic, Native American (Yuchi) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Yuchi) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Yuchi). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Yuchi spoke a language unrelated to any other, a linguistic isolate that hints at a long and separate history in the Southeast. Pushed from the Savannah River country by war and slave raiding, they resettled among the Creek towns while keeping their own square grounds, ceremonies and identity. They survived removal to Indian Territory as a distinct people despite being counted as Creeks.

hints.label: Historic, Native American (Yuchi)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Woodland (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Middle Woodland (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400] Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

hints.label: Middle Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Madison Phase (Iowa, AD 800–AD 900)
nodes.title: Madison Phase (Iowa, AD 800–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 800–AD 900] Madison Phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Woodland community pattern in the upper Mississippi valley, known from cord-impressed jars and the small triangular arrowheads that archaeologists still call Madison points. The bow had replaced the spearthrower, and people lived in scattered hamlets, hunting, fishing and tending small plots of native seed crops. These were the last generations before maize agriculture and Oneota village life reshaped the region.

hints.label: Madison Phase
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Hickory Pond, A.D. 800-1250 (Florida, AD 800–AD 1250)
nodes.title: Hickory Pond, A.D. 800-1250 (Florida, AD 800–AD 1250)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 800–AD 1250] Hickory Pond, A.D. 800-1250. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A phase of the Alachua tradition in north-central Florida, marked by cord-marked pottery and small villages set among the region's lakes and hardwood hammocks. Communities combined hunting, fishing and gathering with increasing cultivation of maize and other crops, a shift that supported larger and more permanent settlements.

hints.label: Hickory Pond, A.D. 800-1250
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Archaic (South Carolina, 6050 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Archaic (South Carolina, 6050 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, 6050 BC–3050 BC] Middle Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

hints.label: Middle Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Missouri Bluffs (Iowa, AD 900–AD 1100)
nodes.title: Missouri Bluffs (Iowa, AD 900–AD 1100)
nodes.description: [Iowa, AD 900–AD 1100] Missouri Bluffs. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

hints.label: Missouri Bluffs
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Archaic (Missouri, 7000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.title: Early Archaic (Missouri, 7000 BC–5000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, 7000 BC–5000 BC] Early Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Etruscan city-states were at their peak, exporting bucchero pottery and importing Greek vases, while Greek colonies in the south and Phoenician traders knitted Italy into a Mediterranean economy. Rome was still ruled by kings — this is the era of the Etruscan Tarquins, the draining of the Forum and the first great temple building. Monumental stone architecture, alphabetic writing and painted tombs mark a shift from tribal to urban society.

hints.label: Early Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: early Middle Archaic (Iowa, 5500 BC–4250 BC)
nodes.title: early Middle Archaic (Iowa, 5500 BC–4250 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 5500 BC–4250 BC] early Middle Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A warmer, drier climate expanded prairie at the expense of forest, pushing groups toward river valleys and increasing the importance of bison hunting. Ground and polished stone tools, grinding equipment for seeds and nuts, and the first substantial storage pits show a more scheduled, resource-specific way of life. Deeply buried sites in alluvial valleys preserve much of what is known about this time.

hints.label: early Middle Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: St. Johns Ib (Florida, 700 BC–AD 800)
nodes.title: St. Johns Ib (Florida, 700 BC–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 700 BC–AD 800] St. Johns Ib. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A continuation of the St. Johns way of life in which decorated wares from neighbouring traditions, including complicated-stamped and check-stamped pottery from the Gulf side, begin to appear alongside the local chalky ceramics. Sand burial mounds became more common, showing growing attention to formal treatment of the dead.

hints.label: St. Johns Ib
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: World War I to World War II (1917 - 1945) (Virginia, AD 1917–AD 1945)
nodes.title: World War I to World War II (1917 - 1945) (Virginia, AD 1917–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1917–AD 1945] World War I to World War II (1917 - 1945). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

For Virginia these decades brought a huge federal and military build-up, with Norfolk's naval and shipbuilding complex, Quantico, Fort Eustis and Langley reshaping whole districts, and drawing workers into rapidly built housing. Between the wars came the collapse of tobacco and farm prices, Depression relief and New Deal projects such as the Blue Ridge Parkway and Shenandoah National Park, and the beginnings of colonial restoration at Williamsburg. Archaeologically it is the period of concrete bases, worker housing, motor roads and abandoned farmsteads.

hints.label: World War I to World War II (1917 - 1945)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Swift Creek (Florida, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.title: Early Swift Creek (Florida, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 100–AD 300] Early Swift Creek. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Woodland communities in the Southeast made pottery stamped with carved wooden paddles bearing intricate curvilinear designs, each paddle so distinctive that archaeologists can trace individual pots — and the social ties behind them — across hundreds of kilometres. They built low burial mounds and participated in the wider exchange networks that carried exotic stone, copper and mica through the Hopewellian world. Village life was based on fishing, shellfish, hunting and gathered plants rather than farming.

hints.label: Early Swift Creek
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Perico Island (Florida, 500 BC–AD 800)
nodes.title: Perico Island (Florida, 500 BC–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 500 BC–AD 800] Perico Island. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Shell-mound people of the central Florida Gulf coast, living off fish, shellfish and estuary resources rather than farming, and piling up the vast middens and ridges that still mark the shoreline. They buried their dead in sand mounds with shell and bone tools, and their plain sand-tempered pottery marks the long transition from Archaic life to the later Manasota and Weeden Island traditions.

hints.label: Perico Island
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Woodland (South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1150)
nodes.title: Late Woodland (South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1150)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 500–AD 1150] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

hints.label: Late Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Glades IIc (Florida, AD 750–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Glades IIc (Florida, AD 750–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 750–AD 1200] Glades IIc. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The closing subdivision of the middle Glades sequence, when decoration on pottery becomes sparser, marking the transition to the late Glades chiefdoms.

hints.label: Glades IIc
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historical (Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Historical (Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1950] Historical. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Spans Illinois from the arrival of French missionaries and traders in the Illinois Country through statehood, prairie farming, and industrial Chicago. The archaeology includes French colonial villages of vertical-log houses, Native towns full of trade goods, lead-mining camps, steamboat wrecks, canal works and factory neighbourhoods. It tracks the transformation of tallgrass prairie into one of the most heavily engineered landscapes in the country.

hints.label: Historical
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Caloosahatchee IIB (Florida, AD 800–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Caloosahatchee IIB (Florida, AD 800–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 800–AD 1200] Caloosahatchee IIB. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Building on the shell mounds and canals of the estuary towns continued on a large scale, and the biggest sites developed into centres with plazas, elevated house mounds and engineered waterways. Exchange with the St Johns and Okeechobee regions is visible in the pottery, and the concentration of labour at a few places suggests leaders able to command it.

hints.label: Caloosahatchee IIB
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 19th cent. urban (Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1899)
nodes.title: 19th cent. urban (Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1899)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1899] 19th cent. urban. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Iowa's towns grew up along the Mississippi and Missouri and then along the rail lines, filling with German, Irish, Scandinavian and Czech immigrants who brought breweries, churches and fraternal halls. Urban lots from this era yield privy and cellar fills packed with bottles, ceramics and butchered bone, the everyday debris of households before municipal sewers and trash collection.

hints.label: 19th cent. urban
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: late Middle Woodland (Iowa, AD 50–AD 300)
nodes.title: late Middle Woodland (Iowa, AD 50–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 50–AD 300] late Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The great Hopewell exchange networks that had carried obsidian, mica and copper into the river valleys began to unravel, and elaborate mound burial grew simpler. Villages along the Mississippi and its tributaries stayed put longer, relying on fish, mussels and cultivated native seeds. What followed was a more local, dispersed way of life without the earlier long-distance ceremonial connections.

hints.label: late Middle Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Sac? (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Sac? (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Sac?. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Sauk, an Algonquian-speaking people who moved from the Great Lakes into the upper Mississippi valley, farmed maize in summer villages and hunted on the prairies in winter while trading furs and lead to European and American merchants. Sites are identified by combinations of trade goods with traditional material culture, and the question mark reflects how hard it can be to tell Sauk occupations from those of their Meskwaki and Ioway neighbours.

hints.label: Sac?
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Tenesaw) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description: [Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Tenesaw). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

hints.label: Historic, Native American (Tenesaw)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic Oneota (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Historic Oneota (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Historic Oneota. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The late Oneota villagers of the upper Mississippi valley step into written history when French explorers meet them and record names — Ioway, Oto, Winnebago. Their sites keep the familiar shell-tempered pottery and bison-scapula hoes but now include trade silver, iron axes and gun parts, letting archaeologists tie an archaeological tradition directly to named living nations. That link makes Oneota one of the clearest cases in North America of an excavated culture matched to its descendants.

hints.label: Historic Oneota
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late 19th-Early 20th Century (Iowa, AD 1850–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Late 19th-Early 20th Century (Iowa, AD 1850–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1850–AD 1950] Late 19th-Early 20th Century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Prairie sod was broken by Euro-American settlers, and railroads soon tied isolated farms to Chicago grain markets and mail-order catalogues. Corn, hogs and mechanised harvesting made the state a farming powerhouse, while small towns rose beside the depots and then began to shrink as tractors replaced hands. Archaeologists work with farmstead foundations, cisterns, barns and household trash dumps that trace this shift from homestead to industrial agriculture.

hints.label: Late 19th-Early 20th Century
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Pre-Contact (Virginia, 13050 BC–AD 1607)
nodes.title: Pre-Contact (Virginia, 13050 BC–AD 1607)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 13050 BC–AD 1607] Pre-Contact. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Spans the whole Native American occupation of the region, from Ice Age hunters tracking game across a colder landscape to the maize-farming towns of the Powhatan and their neighbours. Over these millennia people took up pottery, tobacco and cultivated crops, built shell middens and burial mounds, and gathered into palisaded riverside villages under paramount chiefs. It ends abruptly with the English landing at Jamestown and the diseases, land seizures and wars that followed.

hints.label: Pre-Contact
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 17th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1625 - 1674) (Virginia, AD 1625–AD 1674)
nodes.title: 17th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1625 - 1674) (Virginia, AD 1625–AD 1674)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1625–AD 1674] 17th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1625 - 1674). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

These decades saw Virginia settle into a royal colony organised around tobacco, county courts and parishes, with servants shipped from England providing most of the labour. Expansion up the rivers displaced the Powhatan peoples, whose 1644 uprising was crushed and followed by treaties confining them to reserved land. By the 1670s falling tobacco prices, a growing class of landless freedmen and rising imports of enslaved Africans were setting up the crisis of Bacon's Rebellion.

hints.label: 17th Century::2nd/3rd quarter (1625 - 1674)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Seminole-Colonization Period 1750-1816 (Florida, AD 1750–AD 1816)
nodes.title: Seminole-Colonization Period 1750-1816 (Florida, AD 1750–AD 1816)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1750–AD 1816] Seminole-Colonization Period 1750-1816. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Creek towns migrating into Florida settled the old Apalachee and Alachua prairies, ran cattle and horses, and traded deerskins with British and Spanish merchants while playing the two empires against each other. Escaped slaves from the plantations to the north established their own allied villages, a magnet that infuriated Georgia planters. Raids and reprisals across the border set up the invasions that followed.

hints.label: Seminole-Colonization Period 1750-1816
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: German Amana Colonist (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: German Amana Colonist (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] German Amana Colonist. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Community of True Inspiration, German Pietists who fled religious persecution, established seven communal villages on the Iowa River where property, kitchens and workshops were shared and worship was plain and frequent. They ran their own woollen mills, farms and craft shops with remarkable self-sufficiency until members voted in 1932 to end communal life and reorganise as a business corporation. Their sites yield German-made ceramics and locally produced goods alongside American mass-market wares.

hints.label: German Amana Colonist
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Glades IIIb (Florida, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1000–AD 1700] Glades IIIb. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A ceramic-defined subdivision of the late Glades sequence covering the generations immediately before European contact, when the Calusa and Tequesta chiefdoms were at their height.

hints.label: Glades IIIb
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Central Plains Tradition(?) (Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1250)
nodes.title: Central Plains Tradition(?) (Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1250)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1250] Central Plains Tradition(?). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize-farming villagers of the central Plains who built square earthlodges and dug deep storage pits, represented in western Iowa by the Glenwood earthlodge sites. The question mark marks a site whose pottery or house form only tentatively fits the tradition, a reminder that these labels are working interpretations rather than fixed identities.

hints.label: Central Plains Tradition(?)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Hoecake (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)

nodes.name: 20th Century (South Carolina, AD 1900–AD 1950)
nodes.title: 20th Century (South Carolina, AD 1900–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 1900–AD 1950] 20th Century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Two world wars drained the country's wealth and manpower, and the empire that had underwritten its power was dismantled within two decades of 1945. Out of the wars came the welfare state and the National Health Service; out of decolonisation came migration from the Caribbean and South Asia that remade Britain's cities. Heavy industry and coal collapsed, seaside and mill towns emptied, and the country reinvented itself around finance, services and pop culture.

hints.label: 20th Century
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: First Spanish Period 1513-1599 (Florida, AD 1513–AD 1599)
nodes.title: First Spanish Period 1513-1599 (Florida, AD 1513–AD 1599)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1513–AD 1599] First Spanish Period 1513-1599. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Ponce de León's landfall opened a century of Spanish attempts to hold the peninsula, most of them disastrous - Narváez and de Soto both ended in ruin. Menéndez de Avilés finally founded St Augustine in 1565 after destroying the French colony at Fort Caroline, giving Spain the oldest continuously occupied European town in the present-day United States. Jesuit and then Franciscan missionaries began working among the Timucua and Guale, while Old World disease devastated Indigenous populations.

hints.label: First Spanish Period 1513-1599
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)
