nodes.name: Prairie/Plains Late Archaic (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Prairie/Plains Late Archaic (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC] Prairie/Plains Late Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-gatherer bands in the tallgrass prairie and river valleys settled into predictable seasonal rounds, hunting bison and deer, harvesting mussels and nuts, and beginning to tend native seed plants such as goosefoot and marsh elder. Formal cemeteries and burials with red ochre, marine shell and copper from Lake Superior show growing attachment to territory and participation in far-reaching exchange networks. These habits of place and ceremony set the stage for the mound-building Woodland societies that followed.

hints.label: Prairie/Plains Late Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Woodland (Missouri, 500 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Middle Woodland (Missouri, 500 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, 500 BC–AD 400] Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

hints.label: Middle Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Blacksand (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.title: Blacksand (Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC] Blacksand. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

An Early Woodland complex of the upper Mississippi and Illinois river valleys, named for its incised and cordmarked pottery decorated with bold geometric designs. Groups lived in small floodplain settlements, gathered and stored nuts and native seed crops, and buried some of their dead in mounds. Their ceramics and burial customs lead directly into the elaborate Havana Hopewell societies that followed.

hints.label: Blacksand
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Seminole 1716-present (Florida, AD 1716–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Seminole 1716-present (Florida, AD 1716–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1716–AD 1950] Seminole 1716-present. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Seminole emerged as Creek-speaking groups moved south into a Florida largely emptied by Spanish-era epidemics and slave raids, absorbing surviving native peoples and escaped slaves from the Carolinas and Georgia. They built cattle herds and farms, fought three wars against the United States, and lost most of their people to forced removal westward. Those who stayed retreated into the Everglades and Big Cypress and never signed a treaty of surrender.

hints.label: Seminole 1716-present
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Upper Mississippian (Indiana, AD 1000–AD 1650)
nodes.description: [Indiana, AD 1000–AD 1650] Upper Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

nodes.name: Prehistoric/Unknown (15000 B.C. - 1606 A.D.) (Virginia, 15000 BC–AD 1606)
nodes.title: Prehistoric/Unknown (15000 B.C. - 1606 A.D.) (Virginia, 15000 BC–AD 1606)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, 15000 BC–AD 1606] Prehistoric/Unknown (15000 B.C. - 1606 A.D.). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A default classification for Virginia sites with Native American material of undetermined age, ending at the eve of English settlement at Jamestown. It spans everything from late Ice Age hunters pursuing game across a colder Chesapeake landscape to the Algonquian, Iroquoian and Siouan towns that colonists encountered.

hints.label: Prehistoric/Unknown (15000 B.C. - 1606 A.D.)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: pre 1873 (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1873)
nodes.title: pre 1873 (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1873)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1873] pre 1873. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Opens with the first European descent of the upper Mississippi and closes as railroads and farmsteads covered the prairie. Over these two centuries French and then American traders, soldiers and settlers displaced the Ioway, Sauk, Meskwaki and Dakota peoples through treaty cessions and removals, and the tallgrass prairie was broken into cropland. Archaeological sites from the era range from fur-trade posts and military forts to early farmsteads and vanished town sites.

hints.label: pre 1873
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Archaic (Missouri, 7000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Missouri, 7000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, 7000 BC–1000 BC] Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

hints.label: Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Proto-Historic (Missouri, AD 1500–AD 1750)
nodes.title: Proto-Historic (Missouri, AD 1500–AD 1750)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1500–AD 1750] Proto-Historic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Native nations of the Missouri region, chiefly the Osage, Missouria and Illinois, encountered Europeans indirectly long before meeting them face to face. Glass beads, brass kettles, guns and horses arrived through Indigenous exchange networks, along with epidemic disease that emptied villages and forced political realignment. By the time French traders established posts along the rivers, the social map had already been redrawn.

hints.label: Proto-Historic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Historic-Unspecified (Florida, AD 1500–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1500–AD 1950] Historic-Unspecified. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A working label for Florida sites datable to the post-contact centuries but not assignable to a specific group or occupation — Spanish, British, Seminole, American or some mixture. The giveaways are usually imported ceramics, bottle glass and nails rather than anything more precise. It is a reminder of how much of the archaeological record survives as fragments too generic to name.

hints.label: Historic-Unspecified
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: St. Johns IIc (Florida, AD 800–AD 1500)
nodes.title: St. Johns IIc (Florida, AD 800–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 800–AD 1500] St. Johns IIc. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The final phase of the St. Johns sequence, running up to and through the first European contacts. European glass beads, metal scraps and Spanish ceramics begin to appear in native middens alongside traditional chalky pottery, marking the beginning of the end for Timucua society through disease, mission life and slaving raids.

hints.label: St. Johns IIc
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Caloosahatchee I (Florida, 500 BC–AD 500)
nodes.title: Caloosahatchee I (Florida, 500 BC–AD 500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 500 BC–AD 500] Caloosahatchee I. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The long formative stretch of the southwest Florida coast, when people settled into intensive fishing and shellfishing of the estuaries and began piling the shell refuse that would eventually become mounds and ridges. Plain sand-tempered pottery came into use, and communities grew more permanent as they learned to exploit an exceptionally productive coastal environment without farming.

hints.label: Caloosahatchee I
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Red Ochre (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Red Ochre (Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 3000 BC–800 BC] Red Ochre. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A burial tradition of the upper Midwest in which the dead were laid in low mounds or natural knolls and covered with powdered red hematite. Graves held finely flaked 'turkey-tail' blades of Indiana hornstone, hammered copper awls and beads, and marine shell from the Gulf coast — evidence that goods travelled across half a continent long before farming villages existed here. It marks the point where mortuary ceremony and long-distance exchange became central to life in the region, foreshadowing the great Woodland mound-building cultures.

hints.label: Red Ochre
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Woodland (1000 - 1606) (Virginia, AD 1000–AD 1606)
nodes.title: Late Woodland (1000 - 1606) (Virginia, AD 1000–AD 1606)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1000–AD 1606] Late Woodland (1000 - 1606). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Settled villages along Virginia's rivers and the Chesapeake shore combined maize, beans and squash farming with fishing, oystering and hunting. Populations grew, some villages were palisaded, and the dead were gathered into communal ossuaries; along the coastal plain small groups coalesced into the paramount chiefdom that the English would meet as Powhatan's. The period closes on the eve of the Jamestown landing and the upheaval that followed.

hints.label: Late Woodland (1000 - 1606)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Gulf Formational (Alabama, 2500 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.title: Early Gulf Formational (Alabama, 2500 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, 2500 BC–1200 BC] Early Gulf Formational. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Coastal and riverine groups along the Gulf and lower Southeast started making pottery — thick, plain vessels tempered with plant fibre — while still living mainly by fishing, shellfishing and gathering. Enormous shell middens and rings accumulated at favoured spots, and long-distance exchange in stone and copper linked these communities to distant regions. The ceramic technology introduced here underlies all later Southeastern pottery traditions.

hints.label: Early Gulf Formational
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Hopewell (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400] Hopewell. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Middle Woodland communities along the Mississippi and its tributaries who buried their dead beneath earthen mounds with extraordinary imported goods. Obsidian from Yellowstone, copper from Lake Superior, mica from the Appalachians and marine shell from the Gulf travelled along an exchange network spanning half the continent. These were not cities or states but villages of gardeners and foragers, linked by shared ritual and a taste for exotic raw materials.

hints.label: Hopewell
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: Green River (Kentucky, 3000 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 3000 BC–1000 BC] Green River. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Hunter-fisher-gatherers along a stretch of river so rich in freshwater mussels that their discarded shells built up into mounds metres deep. Those mounds became cemeteries, and the burials preserve spear-throwers with carved weights, dog interments, and ornaments of marine shell and Great Lakes copper - evidence that goods moved across half a continent long before farming or pottery arrived. Sites like Indian Knoll gave archaeologists one of the first detailed pictures of Archaic life in eastern North America.

hints.label: Green River
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic, Native American (Seminole) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Seminole) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Seminole). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Seminoles coalesced in the 1700s from Creek towns moving south into Florida, joined by remnants of earlier peoples and by Africans escaping slavery. Their communities extended into the pine flatwoods and river swamps of the far south of the region, and their resistance in three wars against the United States was among the costliest the army ever fought. A nation that formed almost entirely within the historic era, they are a reminder that Native peoples were not static populations but constantly re-forming ones.

hints.label: Historic, Native American (Seminole)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Icarian (Iowa, AD 1852–AD 1879)
nodes.title: Icarian (Iowa, AD 1852–AD 1879)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1852–AD 1879] Icarian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Followers of the French utopian socialist Étienne Cabet, who left Europe to build the communist society he had described in his novel Voyage en Icarie. After the collapse of their settlement at Nauvoo, a remnant established a colony in Iowa where property was held in common, decisions were made by vote, and meals were taken together in a communal dining hall. Repeated schisms between older and younger members eventually broke it up, but it lasted longer than almost any other secular commune in America.

hints.label: Icarian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Havana/ Hopewell (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Havana/ Hopewell (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400] Havana/ Hopewell. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The regional expression of the Hopewell interaction sphere, in which valley communities built conical and occasionally geometric earthworks and placed exotic goods with their dead — copper from the Great Lakes, mica from the Appalachians, obsidian from the Rockies. Everyday life stayed dispersed and small-scale, based on hunting, fishing and gardens of native seed crops, which makes the reach of the exchange network all the more striking.

hints.label: Havana/ Hopewell
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Belle Glade I (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Belle Glade I (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700] Belle Glade I. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The opening stage of the Lake Okeechobee tradition, when small communities in the wet interior began settling on sand ridges and low mounds above the seasonal floods. Plain sand-tempered pottery appears, and the first earth embankments and circular ditches are dug at places like Fort Center. Fishing, hunting and gathering in the marshes supported people here for two thousand years without farming ever becoming central.

hints.label: Belle Glade I
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Baytown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Baytown (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Baytown. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Woodland way of life along the lower Mississippi and its tributaries, marked by plain, clay-grit-tempered pottery and small dispersed hamlets scattered across the floodplain rather than concentrated in large towns. People fished, hunted and gathered wild plants in the backswamps, building modest mounds and burial places. Out of these communities grew the more hierarchical Coles Creek and later Mississippian societies with their plazas and temple mounds.

hints.label: Baytown
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Weeden Island 5 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Weeden Island 5 (Florida, AD 450–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 450–AD 1000] Weeden Island 5. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The latest stretch of the Weeden Island ceramic tradition, when villages grew larger, some communities took up maize, and platform mounds began to appear alongside older burial mounds. The distinctive effigy and cut-out mortuary wares gradually gave way to the pottery of the Fort Walton and other Mississippian-period cultures. It marks the transition from Woodland ceremonialism to chiefdom-level society on the Gulf coast.

hints.label: Weeden Island 5
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Wahpkute band of the Santee Dakota Sioux (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Wahpkute band of the Santee Dakota Sioux (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Wahpkute band of the Santee Dakota Sioux. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Wahpekute, whose name is usually rendered 'shooters among the leaves', occupied the prairie and woodland edge of southern Minnesota and northern Iowa. Their seasonal round combined bison hunting, fishing and gathering with fur trading at posts along the rivers, and archaeological traces include camp sites, trade goods and burial places. Treaty cessions and the violence of the 1850s and 1862 ended their presence in the region.

hints.label: Wahpkute band of the Santee Dakota Sioux
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 18th Century::1st quarter (1700 - 1724) (Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1724)
nodes.title: 18th Century::1st quarter (1700 - 1724) (Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1724)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1700–AD 1724] 18th Century::1st quarter (1700 - 1724). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The new capital at Williamsburg took shape, with the Capitol, the Governor's Palace and the college giving the colony a monumental centre for the first time. Direct shipments from Africa peaked in these years, and slavery became the normal basis of tobacco production across the tidewater. It was also the era of Chesapeake piracy, ended with Blackbeard's death in 1718, and of the first serious settlement pressure west of the fall line.

hints.label: 18th Century::1st quarter (1700 - 1724)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Contact Period (1607 - 1750) (Virginia, AD 1607–AD 1750)
nodes.title: Contact Period (1607 - 1750) (Virginia, AD 1607–AD 1750)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1607–AD 1750] Contact Period (1607 - 1750). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

English settlement at Jamestown put a permanent European foothold on the Chesapeake, and within a few decades tobacco planting had reshaped the whole region: land taken from the Powhatan paramount chiefdom, indentured servants and then enslaved Africans brought in to work it. Epidemic disease, trade in copper, glass beads and guns, and two devastating wars broke Algonquian political power by the 1640s. Archaeologically it is a period of hybrid sites, where Native pottery turns up alongside English pipes and ironwork.

hints.label: Contact Period (1607 - 1750)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Orange (Florida, 2500 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.title: Orange (Florida, 2500 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 2500 BC–1500 BC] Orange. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Coastal and riverine shell-mound dwellers here made some of the earliest pottery in North America, thick vessels tempered with Spanish moss and palmetto fibre, often decorated with incised lines. The pots appear alongside enormous accumulations of oyster and clam shell, evidence of settled, resource-rich lives without agriculture. Their invention of ceramics spread widely across the Southeast.

hints.label: Orange
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Glades IIa (Florida, AD 750–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Glades IIa (Florida, AD 750–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 750–AD 1200] Glades IIa. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The first ceramic subdivision of the middle Glades sequence, defined by the appearance of distinctive incised designs on sand-tempered pottery used across the Everglades, the Keys and the southwest coast.

hints.label: Glades IIa
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic Non-Indian (Georgia, AD 1540–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Historic Non-Indian (Georgia, AD 1540–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Georgia, AD 1540–AD 1950] Historic Non-Indian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Everything left behind by newcomers to Georgia after Spanish entradas opened the interior — Spanish missions on the coast, English trading posts and forts, plantations worked by enslaved Africans, then farms, mills, railroads and towns. The archaeology here runs from potsherds and wine bottles to slave quarters, Civil War earthworks and tenant-farm sites. It is the material record of how a Native landscape became a colonial and then an industrialising one.

hints.label: Historic Non-Indian
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Mormon (alleged) (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Mormon (alleged) (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Mormon (alleged). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A cautious site-file designation for historic remains in the path of the 1846 Latter-day Saint migration that look like Mormon camps or farmsteads but lack documents or artefacts to prove it. The label reflects how hard it is to distinguish a few months' occupation by emigrants from that of ordinary frontier settlers using the same tools and building methods.

hints.label: Mormon (alleged)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 19th Century::3rd quarter (1850 - 1874) (Virginia, AD 1850–AD 1874)
nodes.title: 19th Century::3rd quarter (1850 - 1874) (Virginia, AD 1850–AD 1874)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1850–AD 1874] 19th Century::3rd quarter (1850 - 1874). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia went from prosperous slave state to the central theatre of the Civil War, with campaigns from Manassas to Appomattox destroying property and displacing whole communities. Emancipation freed roughly half a million people and the western counties left to form West Virginia. The years after 1865 brought military occupation, a new state constitution, and the beginnings of sharecropping and Black churches, schools and towns.

hints.label: 19th Century::3rd quarter (1850 - 1874)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Indet. Fort Ancient (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Indet. Fort Ancient (Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1000–AD 1700] Indet. Fort Ancient. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A catch-all label for material belonging to the Fort Ancient tradition that cannot be pinned to a particular phase. Fort Ancient people lived in circular villages around open plazas along the middle Ohio and its tributaries, farming maize, beans and squash, hunting deer and elk, and making shell-tempered pottery. Their descendants encountered European goods - glass beads, brass - before they ever met Europeans face to face.

hints.label: Indet. Fort Ancient
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Caloosahatchee 500 B.C.-1700 A.D. (Florida, 500 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Caloosahatchee 500 B.C.-1700 A.D. (Florida, 500 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 500 BC–AD 1700] Caloosahatchee 500 B.C.-1700 A.D.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The archaeological sequence of southwest Florida's estuaries, ending with the Calusa encountered by Spanish ships. These people never farmed maize seriously: fish, shellfish and other estuarine resources were rich enough to support dense, permanent towns, monumental shell mounds, canals and a powerful chiefdom that extracted tribute from much of the peninsula. Waterlogged sites such as Key Marco preserved wooden masks, carved animal figureheads and nets that almost never survive elsewhere.

hints.label: Caloosahatchee 500 B.C.-1700 A.D.
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Prehistoric-Aceramic (Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Prehistoric-Aceramic (Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 10000 BC–AD 1500] Prehistoric-Aceramic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers Florida sites that lack pottery: Paleoindian kill and quarry locations, and the long Archaic period of foragers who fished, collected shellfish and buried their dead in ponds. Waterlogged sites such as these preserve wood, cordage and even brain tissue, giving an unusually intimate view of people otherwise known only from stone tools.

hints.label: Prehistoric-Aceramic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Reconstruction and Growth (1866 - 1916) (Virginia, AD 1866–AD 1916)
nodes.title: Reconstruction and Growth (1866 - 1916) (Virginia, AD 1866–AD 1916)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1866–AD 1916] Reconstruction and Growth (1866 - 1916). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia emerged from the war with a wrecked economy and a transformed labour system, as freedpeople bargained over wages, founded churches and schools, and briefly held office before disfranchisement. Railroads, coalfields in the southwest, tobacco factories in Richmond and Danville and shipbuilding at Newport News pulled the state toward industry and cities. The 1902 constitution imposed poll taxes and literacy tests that stripped Black and many poor white Virginians of the vote, locking in segregation for half a century.

hints.label: Reconstruction and Growth (1866 - 1916)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Amana Colonists (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Amana Colonists (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Amana Colonists. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

German pietists of the Community of True Inspiration, persecuted at home, crossed to America and eventually built seven villages on the Iowa River where land, workshops and meals were shared in common. Their woollen mills, furniture shops and disciplined farming made the colonies prosperous and largely self-sufficient, with worship in plain meeting houses and no ordained clergy. Communal ownership ended in the Depression, when members reorganised the enterprise as a corporation.

hints.label: Amana Colonists
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Amana (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Amana (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Amana. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Community of True Inspiration began as a pietist movement in German-speaking Europe, guided by prophets who spoke inspired testimonies, and emigrated to escape conscription and state church pressure. Its members finally settled seven villages on the Iowa River, holding all property in common, eating in communal kitchens and running woollen mills and farms together. The communal system was voted out in 1932 and reorganised as a joint-stock company, though the church and the villages survive.

hints.label: Amana
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Woodland (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400) [p086kj9crzh]
nodes.title: Middle Woodland (Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400) [p086kj9crzh]
nodes.description:
[Iowa, 200 BC–AD 400] Middle Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Small communities built conical burial mounds and geometric earthworks and buried favoured dead with obsidian, mica, copper and marine shell brought from across the continent. The Mann site in southwestern Indiana was one of the biggest of these Hopewell-related centres, with earthworks and imported ritual goods. People still lived by hunting, fishing and gardening native seed plants rather than maize.

hints.label: Middle Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Seminole, 3rd War onward, 1856- (Florida, AD 1856–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Seminole, 3rd War onward, 1856- (Florida, AD 1856–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 1856–AD 1950] Seminole, 3rd War onward, 1856-. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A final short war ended with more deportations, leaving only a small population scattered through the Everglades and Big Cypress, living by hunting, fishing and trade in plumes, hides and alligator skins. Drainage schemes, the Tamiami Trail and the tourist economy gradually pulled them into contact with the surrounding state, and in the mid-twentieth century they organised as federally recognised tribes.

hints.label: Seminole, 3rd War onward, 1856-
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic, Native American (Mobile) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Mobile) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Mobile). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Native people of the lower Alabama and Mobile river country whose name still marks the bay, the river and the city. They lived on the delta when the French arrived in 1702, becoming close neighbours and allies of the new colony, and dwindled rapidly under epidemic disease and warfare. Their villages sit at the point where the Mississippian world of the interior met the Gulf.

hints.label: Historic, Native American (Mobile)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 17th Century::1st quarter (1600 - 1624) (Virginia, AD 1600–AD 1624)
nodes.title: 17th Century::1st quarter (1600 - 1624) (Virginia, AD 1600–AD 1624)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1600–AD 1624] 17th Century::1st quarter (1600 - 1624). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Jamestown was planted in 1607 and very nearly failed, with the 'starving time' winter of 1609-10 reducing the settlement to a handful of survivors. John Rolfe's success with West Indian tobacco after 1612 gave the colony an export crop, and with it came scattered riverside plantations, the first representative assembly in 1619, and the first documented Africans in the colony. The Powhatan attack of 1622 killed a quarter of the settlers and led to the Virginia Company losing its charter.

hints.label: 17th Century::1st quarter (1600 - 1624)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Santa Rosa (Florida, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.title: Santa Rosa (Florida, AD 100–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 100–AD 300] Santa Rosa. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Middle Woodland culture of the Florida panhandle coast, whose people fished and gathered shellfish in the bays and built low sand burial mounds. Their pottery carries the swirling complicated-stamped designs of Swift Creek potters in Georgia, made with carved wooden paddles. Copper, mica and panpipes found in the mounds show the community was plugged into the long-distance Hopewell exchange network reaching to the Ohio valley.

hints.label: Santa Rosa
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Weaver (Iowa, AD 400–AD 650)
nodes.title: Weaver (Iowa, AD 400–AD 650)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 400–AD 650] Weaver. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A late Middle Woodland complex marked by thick, cord-roughened jars and the disappearance of the elaborate Hopewell mortuary ceremonialism and long-distance trade that had preceded it. Communities lived in small, scattered settlements along river valleys, gathering wild plants, hunting and tending native seed crops. It represents the quieter, more locally focused world that followed the collapse of the Hopewell interaction sphere.

hints.label: Weaver
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Early Woodland (Alabama, 1250 BC–50 BC)
nodes.title: Early Woodland (Alabama, 1250 BC–50 BC)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, 1250 BC–50 BC] Early Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities in the river valleys began making thick, cord-marked pottery and burying their dead beneath earthen mounds, sometimes with copper ornaments and exotic stone brought from far away. They tended gardens of native seed crops such as goosefoot, marsh elder and squash while still hunting and gathering, allowing longer stays in one place. These mound-building and long-distance exchange habits grew into the elaborate Hopewell networks that followed.

hints.label: Early Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Swift Creek-Late (Florida, 300 BC–AD 450)
nodes.title: Swift Creek-Late (Florida, 300 BC–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 300 BC–AD 450] Swift Creek-Late. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The closing centuries of the complicated-stamped pottery tradition, when paddle designs grew more angular and cluttered and vessel shapes changed, giving archaeologists a fine-grained way to date sites. Along the Florida Gulf coast these communities overlapped with Weeden Island ceremonialism, with elaborate mortuary pottery deposited in burial mounds.

hints.label: Swift Creek-Late
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Belle Glade III (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Belle Glade III (Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 700 BC–AD 1700] Belle Glade III. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities around Lake Okeechobee continued to enlarge their linear embankments and mound-and-midden complexes, with settlements linked across the flooded interior. Pottery and imported goods show contact with the Gulf coast and with the mound-building societies to the north, while local subsistence still rested on fish, turtles, birds and wild plants rather than maize.

hints.label: Belle Glade III
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Archaic (Florida, 5000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Archaic (Florida, 5000 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 5000 BC–3000 BC] Middle Archaic. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

hints.label: Middle Archaic
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. nodes.name: Mississippian, Undifferentiated (Alabama, AD 950–AD 1490)
nodes.title: Mississippian, Undifferentiated (Alabama, AD 950–AD 1490)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 950–AD 1490] Mississippian, Undifferentiated. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming societies of the Southeast organised as chiefdoms, living in palisaded towns around plaza-and-mound complexes and growing maize, beans and squash. Moundville on the Black Warrior River is the outstanding example, with its ranked burials, engraved stone palettes and copper ornaments. Hereditary rank, craft specialists and long-distance exchange in marine shell and copper mark a decisive break from earlier village life.

hints.label: Mississippian, Undifferentiated
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Late Woodland (Missouri, AD 400–AD 900)
nodes.title: Late Woodland (Missouri, AD 400–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 400–AD 900] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

hints.label: Late Woodland
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: 18th Century::2nd half (1750 - 1799) (Virginia, AD 1750–AD 1799)
nodes.title: 18th Century::2nd half (1750 - 1799) (Virginia, AD 1750–AD 1799)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1750–AD 1799] 18th Century::2nd half (1750 - 1799). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

War with France on the Ohio frontier drew Virginia into imperial conflict and left the colony taxed, indebted and quarrelsome; two decades later its planters were leading the break with Britain. The Revolution ended with the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781, and afterwards Virginians wrote much of the new republic's constitutional framework while leaving slavery intact and expanding. Evangelical revivals unsettled the Anglican establishment, the capital moved to Richmond in 1780, and planters began shifting from exhausted tobacco land toward wheat.

hints.label: 18th Century::2nd half (1750 - 1799)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic Euro-american (Kentucky, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Historic Euro-american (Kentucky, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1650–AD 1950] Historic Euro-american. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The archaeology of European-descended settlement: fortified stations and log cabins, then farmsteads, mills, distilleries, iron furnaces and river towns. Excavated cellars, wells and refuse pits show how imported ceramics, glass and hardware spread inland, and how enslaved African Americans lived and worked on those same properties. Because written records survive too, sites can be tied to named families, making this a testing ground for combining documents with dirt.

hints.label: Historic Euro-american
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Sac (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Sac (Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Sac. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Sauk, an Algonquian-speaking people pushed westward out of the Great Lakes country, established villages along the Mississippi and its tributaries and lived by a cycle of maize farming, summer bison hunts on the prairies and winter trapping for the fur trade. Their expulsion from lands east of the Mississippi triggered the Black Hawk War of 1832, after which treaty cessions stripped away their Iowa holdings within two decades. Their sites are recognisable from trade silver, gunflints, glass beads and European kettles mixed with traditional tools.

hints.label: Sac
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Colony to Nation (1751 - 1789) (Virginia, AD 1751–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Colony to Nation (1751 - 1789) (Virginia, AD 1751–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1751–AD 1789] Colony to Nation (1751 - 1789). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia went from frontier war against the French and their allies to the leadership of the Revolution, supplying Washington, Jefferson, Madison and Henry. Tobacco debts to British merchants sharpened planter hostility to imperial taxation, and Dunmore's offer of freedom to enslaved men who joined the Crown exposed the contradiction at the heart of the cause. Yorktown ended the war on Virginia soil, and Virginians then drafted much of the federal Constitution.

hints.label: Colony to Nation (1751 - 1789)
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Historic Native American (Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Historic Native American (Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1650–AD 1950] Historic Native American. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers the Native nations of the Missouri region from the first French descent of the Mississippi onward — Osage, Missouria, Illinois, Kansa and, later, peoples pushed west by removal. Sites from these centuries mix traditional material culture with glass beads, brass kettles, gunflints and horse gear, showing how deeply the fur trade reshaped daily life. The period ends with dispossession: by the 1830s most of these nations had been forced out of the state entirely.

hints.label: Historic Native American
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Weeden Island II (Florida, AD 750–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Weeden Island II (Florida, AD 750–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 750–AD 1000] Weeden Island II. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The later phase of the tradition, when the lavish mortuary pottery became simpler, settlements grew larger and more permanent, and in some inland areas maize agriculture took hold. Platform mounds began to appear alongside the older burial mounds, a sign of emerging hereditary leadership. These changes lead straight into the Fort Walton and Mississippian chiefdoms that followed.

hints.label: Weeden Island II
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Middle Mississippian (Missouri, AD 1100–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Middle Mississippian (Missouri, AD 1100–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[Missouri, AD 1100–AD 1350] Middle Mississippian. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Farming towns on the Ohio and Wabash built flat-topped mounds around open plazas, ringed themselves with palisades, and grew maize on the floodplains. Angel Mounds near Evansville was one of the largest, home to perhaps a thousand people and tied by trade and shared ritual style to Cahokia and other Mississippian centres. Shell-tempered pottery, chiefly burials and hierarchy between towns mark the region's most complex pre-contact societies.

Uniquely in the Southeast, these societies grew populous and politically complex without maize agriculture, living off estuaries so productive that they supported towns of shell mounds, canals and chiefly courts.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. Jim Crow was written into law and the state constitution, poll taxes and literacy tests emptied the voter rolls, and Virginia's Black population left in large numbers for northern cities. Two world wars poured money and workers into Norfolk, Newport News and the shipyards, while the Depression hit tobacco and coal country hard. By 1949 the state was measurably more urban, more industrial and more dependent on federal spending than it had ever been.

Founded by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés to expel French Huguenots and guard the treasure fleets, it became the capital of Spanish Florida and the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the United States. Repeatedly burned and besieged by English raiders, it was rebuilt around the coquina-stone Castillo de San Marcos, and it sheltered a free Black community at Fort Mose. Its street plan and stone houses still reflect Spanish colonial ordinances.

Florida's warm weather and long coastline made it a vast military training zone, with hundreds of airfields, bases and hotels requisitioned for troops, while German submarines sank tankers within sight of the beaches. Millions of servicemen passed through, and many came back afterwards, driving the postwar population surge, air conditioning, and the suburban development that reshaped the state.

Farming communities in north-central Florida who grew maize in the sandy uplands, buried their dead in low sand mounds, and made distinctive cob-marked pottery. Their villages were the ones Spanish expeditions met as the Potano, a Timucua-speaking people, and the culture ends with the disruption brought by conquistadors, mission friars and epidemic disease.

War came to Virginia harder than to any other state: Richmond served as the Confederate capital, the western counties broke away in 1863, and four years of campaigning wrecked farms, bridges and towns. Emancipation remade the countryside into a patchwork of tenancy and sharecropping, and by the 1880s tobacco factories, coal, and railroads were pulling people into Richmond, Danville and Roanoke. The period closes with Redeemer governments and the legal machinery of segregation taking shape.

A catch-all for hunting and gathering communities of the long post-glacial millennia, when spear-throwers, ground stone tools and seasonal camps along rivers and shell-bearing shoals replaced big-game hunting. People gathered hickory nuts, mussels and deer, buried their dead in the great shell middens, and began the slow domestication of local seed plants. The label is used when a site's stone tools show only that it belongs somewhere in this vast span.

A slaveholding state that stayed in the Union, Missouri had rival Unionist and secessionist governments and sent troops to both armies. Beyond the conventional battles at Wilson's Creek and Westport lay a vicious guerrilla war of bushwhackers, jayhawkers and reprisals, culminating in Order No. 11, which depopulated four border counties. The bitterness outlived the war and produced outlaws such as the James and Younger brothers.

The Natchez of the lower Mississippi were among the last peoples to preserve a Mississippian-style hierarchy, with a paramount chief called the Great Sun, temple mounds and elaborate mortuary ritual — all described by French eyewitnesses. Their 1729 uprising against the French colony ended in devastating reprisals, and survivors took refuge among the Chickasaw, Creek and Cherokee, spreading Natchez families across the Southeast. They offer a rare written window into how a mound-building society actually worked.

A Plains Village culture of the prairie lakes country, whose people lived in small hamlets of earth-covered houses, grew maize, beans and squash on the floodplains, and hunted bison on the side. Their thin, globular, cord-roughened jars are the marker archaeologists use to trace them. Great Oasis stands at the point where Late Woodland foragers became settled farmers, and its communities fed into the Middle Missouri and Mill Creek traditions that followed.

Maize farming along the river bottoms supported the largest towns north of Mexico, built around flat-topped earthen mounds and open plazas. Cahokia, across the river from modern St Louis, grew to many thousands of people with a hundred mounds and a woodhenge of cedar posts, and its shell-tempered pottery and shell-and-copper regalia circulated across half a continent. The great centres were largely abandoned before Europeans arrived, leaving mounds that later settlers refused to credit to Native builders.

Tobacco processing, coal, and the Norfolk and Western railroad drew workers into growing industrial towns, while most rural Virginians, Black and white, farmed on shares. Settlement pushed up the James, York and Rappahannock rivers onto Native land, provoking the second great Powhatan uprising in 1644 and the treaty of 1646 that confined surviving tribes to reserved tracts. County courts, parishes and a working assembly gave the colony an administrative structure.

A Chiwere-Siouan people descended from the Oneota villagers of the upper Mississippi valley, first recorded by French traders and mapmakers in the late seventeenth century. They lived in bark lodges and earthlodges, farmed maize along the Iowa, Des Moines and Missouri rivers, and hunted bison on the prairies, becoming deeply entangled in the fur trade. Treaty cessions in the 1820s-1830s stripped them of the land that carries their name and pushed them onto reservations in Kansas-Nebraska and, later, Oklahoma.

A Late Woodland complex of the Missouri River bluffs and floodplain, known from small camps with storage pits and thin, cord-marked pottery decorated with trailed wavy lines. Its people combined hunting and gathering with small-scale cultivation of squash and gourds, an early step towards the farming villages that would follow on the Plains.

Maize farming along the Mississippi and its tributaries supported larger, more permanent villages, and communities began raising flat-topped earthen mounds around open plazas. Shell-tempered pottery, the bow and arrow, and a new emphasis on hereditary leadership all spread in these centuries. The trend culminated in Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico, just across the river from Missouri's American Bottom settlements.

A later stage of the St. Johns tradition, when contacts with Mississippian societies to the north and west brought new pottery styles, ornaments and status goods into northeastern Florida. Villages clustered around shell mounds and plaza-and-mound centres, and social ranking became more visible in burials. Interesting for how a society that never depended on maize farming still built monumental earthworks.

Everything from the first French explorers on the Mississippi to the modern era, lumped together as the historic period. Fur traders and missionaries gave way to treaties and forced removals that pushed the Ioway, Sauk and Meskwaki west, opening the land to settlers after 1833; statehood came in 1846. Prairie was broken into farms at extraordinary speed, and the archaeology of these centuries is trading posts, log cabins, railroad towns and abandoned farmsteads.

Begins with the shock of De Soto's entrada, which brought disease and violence to the Mississippian chiefdoms of the interior. Survivors coalesced into new confederacies — the Creek and Cherokee above all — that traded deerskins for guns, cloth and rum and were drawn into rivalries between Spanish, English and French colonists. Their towns produced a distinctive blend of native pottery and European goods, and the sequence ends with removal along the Trail of Tears.

The Lower Creek were the Muscogee towns of the Chattahoochee and Flint valleys, drawn into the Atlantic economy as suppliers of deerskins and captives to Carolina and Spanish Florida traders. Their diplomacy played English, Spanish and French interests against one another, while dissident and displaced townspeople who moved south into the Florida peninsula coalesced into the Seminole. Defeat in the Creek War of 1813–14 stripped away enormous tracts of land, and treaty pressure culminated in removal west of the Mississippi.

Deposits from Iowa's nineteenth-century towns, built first at river landings and then wherever the railroads reached. Their cellars, wells and privy shafts hold the discarded glass, ceramics and food waste of shopkeepers, tradesmen and immigrant labourers, offering a close-up view of frontier settlements turning into ordinary Midwestern cities.

Hunter-gatherers along the Gulf coast and river valleys of northern Florida began making some of the earliest pottery in North America, coil-built and tempered with plant fibre such as Spanish moss. The vessels are plain and thick-walled, made for cooking and storing shellfish, fish and plant foods gathered from the estuaries where their shell middens still stand. Pottery let people boil and store food in bulk, a shift that goes with longer stays in the same rich coastal spots.

[Virginia, AD 1650–AD 1674] 17th Century::3rd quarter (1650 - 1674). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia settled into a tobacco economy run on indentured labour, with planters claiming headrights of land for every servant they imported and pushing settlement up the rivers onto Powhatan and other Native land. Parliament's Navigation Acts tied the colony's crop to English ships and merchants, squeezing prices just as small planters were finishing their terms and finding the best land already taken. Africans were present in growing numbers, and colonial courts were beginning to treat their servitude as lifelong and hereditary. Excavated house sites from these decades are typically earthfast timber buildings, cheaply built by people who expected to move on.

hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.title: 19th Century (1800 - 1899) (Virginia, AD 1800–AD 1899)
nodes.description:
[Virginia, AD 1800–AD 1899] 19th Century (1800 - 1899). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Virginia's tobacco lands were worn out and its political weight in the nation slipping, while the domestic slave trade sold tens of thousands of people from the state to the cotton South. Richmond grew into an industrial city on flour milling, tobacco manufacture and the Tredegar Iron Works, and became the Confederate capital in 1861. The Civil War was fought largely on Virginia soil and ended at Appomattox, followed by emancipation, the creation of West Virginia, Reconstruction and its violent rollback, and the rise of segregation and tenant farming.

nodes.title: Protohistoric, Undifferentiated (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)
nodes.description:
[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Protohistoric, Undifferentiated. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The great Mississippian towns and their platform mounds went out of use, and the survivors of epidemic disease and Spanish entradas coalesced into new confederacies — the ancestors of the Creek, Choctaw and Chickasaw. Archaeologically the era is recognised by late shell-tempered pottery mixed with a trickle of European glass, brass and iron. The label 'undifferentiated' reflects how hard it is to tie particular sites to particular named peoples.

hints.label: Protohistoric, Undifferentiated

nodes.description:
[Iowa, 100 BC–AD 300] Hopewell. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Middle Woodland communities along the Mississippi and its tributaries who buried their dead beneath earthen mounds with extraordinary imported goods. Obsidian from Yellowstone, copper from Lake Superior, mica from the Appalachians and marine shell from the Gulf travelled along an exchange network spanning half the continent. These were not cities or states but villages of gardeners and foragers, linked by shared ritual and a taste for exotic raw materials.

[Iowa, 800 BC–200 BC] Black Sand. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

An Early Woodland complex of the upper Mississippi and Illinois river valleys, named for its incised and cordmarked pottery decorated with bold geometric designs. Groups lived in small floodplain settlements, gathered and stored nuts and native seed crops, and buried some of their dead in mounds. Their ceramics and burial customs lead directly into the elaborate Havana Hopewell societies that followed.

Tampa, Key West and Miami became embarkation camps and supply depots for the invasion of Cuba, pouring soldiers, money and railroads into a thinly settled state. The war left Florida with improved ports and a reputation as America's gateway to the Caribbean, setting up the land boom of the following decades.

A half-century that carried Virginia from Depression-era farms to a suburban, federally employed society. War industry and military bases swelled the Hampton Roads and Washington regions, cars and interstates dispersed settlement, and the tobacco-and-agriculture economy shrank. The same span saw the long confrontation over school desegregation, from the Brown decision through Massive Resistance to court-ordered busing.

The long-lived archaeological tradition of northeastern Florida, recognised by its distinctive chalky pottery made with freshwater sponge spicules. Its people never took up serious farming, instead thriving on fish, shellfish and wild plants, and leaving behind enormous shell middens and burial mounds along the river and coastal lagoons. Their descendants were the Timucua encountered by French and Spanish colonists in the sixteenth century.

[South Carolina, 1050 BC–AD 1150] Any Woodland Period. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Marked by widespread pottery use, more permanent settlements, burial mounds and the gradual adoption of cultivated plants alongside hunting and gathering. The bow and arrow appears, exchange networks carry exotic materials over long distances, and social groups grow larger and more organised. The label covers finds identifiable as Woodland but not attributable to a specific phase.

nodes.title: Archaic unspecified (Florida, 8500 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Florida, 8500 BC–1000 BC] Archaic unspecified. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Florida's hunter-fisher-gatherers adapted to rising seas and expanding wetlands, exploiting shellfish, fish and marsh plants in enormous quantity. Waterlogged sites preserve what usually rots away - woven fabrics, wooden tools, and at Windover the brains of people buried in a peat pond some 7,000 years ago. Along the St. Johns and the coast they piled shell mounds and, late in the period, made some of the earliest pottery in North America.

Small mobile bands hunted deer and gathered nuts and river mussels across the Ohio Valley, leaving behind changing styles of notched spear points and the grooved axes and atlatl weights of a maturing toolkit. Over these millennia groups returned repeatedly to rich river and shoal locations, building up the deep shell middens that later became burial places. The category covers material that is clearly Archaic but cannot be assigned to a finer phase.

[Iowa, AD 1800–AD 1950] 19th-20th cent urban. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Covers Iowa's towns from their river-landing beginnings to the age of paved streets, streetcars, municipal water and the automobile. Excavations in these settings often cut through layered fills where hand-blown bottles and transfer-printed ceramics give way to machine-made glass, tin cans and mass-produced goods shipped in by rail.

nodes.name: Early Woodland, indet (Kentucky, 1000 BC–200 BC)
nodes.title: Early Woodland, indet (Kentucky, 1000 BC–200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, 1000 BC–200 BC] Early Woodland, indet. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Ceramic vessels, earthen burial mounds and a growing reliance on cultivated native seed plants distinguish this era from the Archaic centuries before it. Adena-related communities in the Ohio Valley raised conical mounds and log-tomb burials over their dead, accompanied by copper, mica and marine shell obtained through long-distance exchange. The label "indeterminate" is used for finds that clearly belong to the era but cannot be tied to a particular local phase.

nodes.title: late Late Woodland (Iowa, AD 750–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 750–AD 1000] late Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, marked archaeologically by a sudden shift to small triangular points, and maize became a real part of the diet. Populations grew and gathered into larger villages, some fortified; in the northeast, groups built the animal-shaped effigy mounds. These changes set the stage for the Oneota and Mississippian farming societies that followed.

nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1900–AD 1950] 20th century. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Iowa's farms mechanised in these decades, with tractors and combines displacing horses and hired hands and steadily enlarging the average holding. A collapse in commodity prices after the First World War brought rural bankruptcies and bank failures well before the Depression deepened them, prompting New Deal price supports, soil conservation programmes and rural electrification. Wartime demand and postwar hybrid seed then pushed yields higher, while small towns and one-room schools began the long decline that followed.

Exhausted tobacco soils pushed many Virginians west and turned the state into the country's main exporter of enslaved people to the cotton South, a trade run out of Richmond and Alexandria. Gabriel's conspiracy in 1800 and Nat Turner's rebellion in 1831 provoked harsh new restrictions and a legislative debate on slavery that ended with the institution reaffirmed. Canals, turnpikes and the first railroads opened the piedmont and valley, wheat replaced tobacco on many farms, and Richmond's mills and ironworks made it an industrial exception in the South.

nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 700–AD 1200] Lake Benton. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

A Late Woodland complex of the prairie lake country, known from small campsites, cord-roughened pottery and low burial mounds. People hunted bison and deer, gathered wild plants, and moved seasonally between lake and prairie, with the bow and arrow largely replacing the spearthrower. It precedes the arrival of maize-farming villages in the region.

[Iowa, AD 1000–AD 1300] Nebraska Phase. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Part of the Central Plains tradition, these were dispersed homesteads of large square earthlodges set above river valleys, combining maize horticulture with bison hunting. Deep bell-shaped storage pits, cord-roughened jars and bone tools are the characteristic remains. The settlements were abandoned in the fourteenth century, with populations apparently moving north and west.

[Iowa, AD 1673–AD 1950] Sac and Fox. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Sauk and the Meskwaki (called Fox by the French) became close allies after French campaigns nearly destroyed the Meskwaki in the 1730s, and thereafter shared villages, hunting grounds and treaty negotiations. Together they controlled the lead-mining country of the upper Mississippi and traded heavily with British and American merchants. Removal followed the Black Hawk War, though a group of Meskwaki later bought land back in Iowa and remain there today.

nodes.title: Kolomoki (Florida, AD 200–AD 500)
nodes.description:
[Florida, AD 200–AD 500] Kolomoki. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Woodland communities in the Gulf coastal plain raised earthen mounds and buried their dead with extraordinary pottery — effigy vessels shaped as birds, animals and human heads, made to be broken and deposited rather than used. Complicated-stamped and Weeden Island wares from these ceremonies travelled through long-distance exchange networks across the Southeast. The scale of the mound-building shows people organising large labour projects long before maize farming and chiefdoms arrived.

Recognised by the arrival of check-stamped pottery from the St. Johns region, this stage saw larger and more permanent coastal settlements around the lagoons. Trade goods circulated along the Atlantic shore, and the societies that Spanish and French sailors would meet as the Ais and Surruque took shape by its close.

nodes.title: Historic, Native American (Cherokee) (Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770)

[Alabama, AD 1490–AD 1770] Historic, Native American (Cherokee). Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Cherokee towns spread into the ridges and river valleys of northeastern Alabama, where townhouses, farmsteads and later log cabins and ferry landings mark a nation adapting fast to a changing world. In the early 1800s Cherokees adopted a written syllabary, printed a newspaper, and built a constitutional government — and were forced west anyway on the Trail of Tears. Sites in the region record both the prosperity and the abrupt abandonment.

The founding decades: a fortified trading post at Jamestown, catastrophic mortality from disease and hunger, and the discovery that Virginia tobacco could be sold at a profit in London. The Virginia Company collapsed after the Powhatan attack of 1622 and the colony passed to royal control in 1624, while planters spread up the rivers and imported indentured servants by the shipload. The first Africans arrived in 1619, into a legal status not yet fully defined.

French mariners and Huguenot colonists challenged Spain's grip on the peninsula, most famously at Fort Caroline on the St Johns River, whose destruction and the massacre of its settlers prompted the Spanish to found St Augustine. Later French traders and officials pressed in from Louisiana along the Gulf coast, leaving a scatter of trade goods, faience and firearms in Native sites far from any French settlement.

[Georgia, AD 500–AD 1150] Late Woodland. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Villages in the Tennessee and Alabama river valleys grew larger and more permanent as the bow and arrow replaced the spearthrower, leaving small triangular points behind. The elaborate burial mounds and exotic trade goods of the preceding Hopewellian era faded, while maize gradually became a staple crop. These farming communities set the stage for the platform mounds, chiefdoms and shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian world that followed.

nodes.title: Post War (Illinois, AD 1945–AD 1950)

[Illinois, AD 1945–AD 1950] Post War. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Returning servicemen, cheap federal mortgages and the GI Bill fuelled a rush into new suburbs ringing Chicago while industry converted back to consumer production. The second wave of the Great Migration brought tens of thousands of Black southerners to the city, into neighbourhoods hemmed in by restrictive covenants and, soon, by high-rise public housing. Almost everything about the modern Illinois landscape - subdivisions, shopping strips, expressways - was set in motion in these few years.

nodes.title: Late Woodland, indet. (Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 500–AD 1000] Late Woodland, indet.. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Communities across Kentucky adopted the bow and arrow, made grit- and limestone-tempered pottery, and gathered into larger, sometimes stockaded settlements along river bottoms. Mound building and the far-flung exchange of the Hopewellian centuries largely ceased, while native seed crops were joined and then overtaken by maize. Out of these local traditions grew the Fort Ancient and Mississippian villages of the following centuries.

Spain ceded the peninsula to Britain in exchange for Havana, and the new rulers split it into East and West Florida with capitals at St Augustine and Pensacola. Land grants, indigo and rice plantations and a flow of loyalist refugees marked the two decades of British rule. Spain regained the colonies at the end of the American War of Independence.

[Florida, AD 700–AD 1702] Potano unspecified. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

The Potano were a Timucua-speaking people of north-central Florida, farmers of maize, beans and squash who lived in dispersed villages of round thatched houses linked to the archaeological Alachua tradition. They fought Hernando de Soto's army in 1539 and later accepted Spanish Franciscan missions, where labour drafts and epidemics thinned their numbers. Raids by Carolina colonists and their Creek allies at the start of the eighteenth century shattered the surviving mission towns and ended the Potano as a distinct people.
