hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Central Plains Tradition (Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1250)
nodes.title: Central Plains Tradition (Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1250)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1050–AD 1250] Central Plains Tradition. Period based on publications identified in the following Zotero collections:. Period definition from Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) — David G. Anderson, 2012.

Maize, bean and squash farmers who lived in scattered clusters of square earthlodges along the streams of the central Plains, storing crops in deep bell-shaped pits and hunting bison on foot. In western Iowa their easternmost settlements are the Glenwood earthlodges above the Missouri River. Drought and shifting conditions after the mid-1200s pushed these communities north and west, and their descendants include the Pawnee and Arikara.

hints.label: Central Plains Tradition
hints.source: Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)

nodes.name: Ubaid (Syria, 5799 BC–3999 BC)
nodes.title: Ubaid (Syria, 5799 BC–3999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 5799 BC–3999 BC] Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The first widespread village culture of southern Mesopotamia, marked by pale greenish painted pottery, mudbrick houses of tripartite plan and small temples rebuilt again and again on the same spot, most famously at Eridu. Irrigation let farmers work the dry alluvium, herds and fishing filled out the diet, and communities grew large enough to support differences in status visible in burials and buildings. Ubaid pottery and styles spread north into Syria and Anatolia and down the Gulf, setting the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.

hints.label: Ubaid
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1599 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Assyrian (Syria, 1599 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 1599 BC–999 BC] Middle Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Dates different in GeoDia. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Assyria emerged from vassalage to Mitanni to become a great power, its kings conquering northern Mesopotamia and, under Tukulti-Ninurta I, briefly capturing Babylon itself. An efficient provincial administration, meticulous royal archives and the Middle Assyrian Laws - unusually harsh, especially toward women - date from this era. Weakened by Aramaean pressure after 1100 BC, the kingdom nevertheless kept the institutions that its Neo-Assyrian successors used to build an empire.

hints.label: Middle Assyrian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2333 BC] Early Dynastic. in chronological discussion on p. 56, provides "ca." before date. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

hints.label: Early Dynastic
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC)
nodes.title: Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2192 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 2333 BC–2192 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.

hints.label: Akkadian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Uruk (Iraq, 3749 BC–3149 BC)
nodes.title: Uruk (Iraq, 3749 BC–3149 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 3749 BC–3149 BC] Uruk. in chronological discussion on p. 55, provides "ca." before date. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities in this period, with Uruk itself swelling to a size no settlement had reached before. Monumental temple platforms, mass-produced bevel-rim bowls for rationed labour, cylinder seals for accounting and finally the earliest writing all appear together, the machinery of a society organised around institutions rather than kin. Uruk-style material spread up the Euphrates into Syria and Anatolia, whether by colony, trade or imitation.

hints.label: Uruk
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Sassanian (Iraq, AD 227–AD 651)
nodes.title: Sassanian (Iraq, AD 227–AD 651)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, AD 227–AD 651] Sassanian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.

hints.label: Sassanian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Neo Assyrian (Syria, 999 BC–604 BC)
nodes.title: Neo Assyrian (Syria, 999 BC–604 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 999 BC–604 BC] Neo Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Assyrian kings drove west from the Tigris to take the cities of Syria one by one, turning Aramaean and Neo-Hittite kingdoms into taxed provinces under Assyrian governors and deporting whole populations to break resistance. Aramaic spread as the common language of administration and trade across the empire. When Nineveh fell in 612 BC the provinces passed rapidly to Babylon, and later to Persia.

hints.label: Neo Assyrian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3149 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.title: Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3149 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 3149 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr. in chronological discussion on p. 55, provides "ca." before date. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Named for a mound in central Iraq, this phase sits between Uruk and the Early Dynastic city-states. Distinctive polychrome painted jars in red and black appear alongside the earliest archives of proto-cuneiform tablets, which record grain, livestock and labour rather than stories. Settlements across southern Mesopotamia show a shared culture of seals, accounting and temple economies, the administrative machinery that would soon underpin Sumerian kingship.

hints.label: Jemdet Nasr
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Parthian (Syria, 125 BC–AD 227)
nodes.title: Parthian (Syria, 125 BC–AD 227)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 125 BC–AD 227] Parthian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. 226 A.D. in GeoDia. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The Arsacid empire out of Iran pressed to the Euphrates, making Syria the frontier zone of a rivalry with Rome that lasted nearly three centuries. Crassus lost his army and his head at Carrhae in 53 BC, and later Parthian raids and Roman counter-invasions repeatedly swept the caravan cities between the two powers. That contested ground was also enormously profitable: Palmyra, Dura-Europos and the Euphrates routes grew rich handling silk and spices moving between the empires, and their art blends Greek, Iranian and Semitic styles.

hints.label: Parthian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Chalcolithic (Syria, 5799 BC–3749 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic (Syria, 5799 BC–3749 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 5799 BC–3749 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Does not seem to be present in this work. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

hints.label: Chalcolithic
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 624 BC–538 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Babylonian (Iran, 624 BC–538 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 624 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian. In GeoDia as "Median". Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Judah under Babylonian rule was a diminished, largely rural province, its capital and temple in ruins and its royal house deported. Excavations show towns in the south and the Shephelah abandoned or shrunken while some settlements north of Jerusalem, around Benjamin, carried on. This bleak interval ended when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and permitted exiles to return.

Iran, West, Tepe Nush-i Jan, Iran

hints.label: Neo-Babylonian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2111 BC–2003 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2111 BC–2003 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 2111 BC–2003 BC] Neo-Sumerian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. In chronological discussion on p. 56, refers to this as the Third Dynasty of Ur. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The Third Dynasty of Ur reunited southern Mesopotamia after the Akkadian collapse and ran it through an extraordinarily detailed bureaucracy that has left tens of thousands of accounting tablets. Ur-Nammu and Shulgi built the great stepped ziggurats, issued one of the earliest law collections and promoted Sumerian as a language of high culture even as Akkadian took over daily speech. The state fell to famine, Amorite pressure and an Elamite attack, but its scribal schools shaped Mesopotamian literature for a thousand years.

hints.label: Neo-Sumerian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: Old Assyrian (Syria, 1999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Old Assyrian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian grouped together under one heading on p. 340. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Merchants from Assur ran a long-distance trade network carrying tin and woollen textiles by donkey caravan into Anatolia, exchanging them for silver and gold. Their archives at the Kanesh trading colony preserve thousands of clay letters, contracts and lawsuits, including those of women managing textile production at home. Shamshi-Adad I briefly welded northern Mesopotamia into a kingdom before Hammurabi's Babylon overshadowed it.

hints.label: Old Assyrian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Turkey, 330 BC–125 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Turkey, 330 BC–125 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 330 BC–125 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Turkey. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

hints.label: Hellenistic
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Old Babylonian. Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian grouped together under one heading on p. 340. Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.

hints.label: Old Babylonian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Persian (Iraq, 538 BC–330 BC)
nodes.title: Persian (Iraq, 538 BC–330 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Mesopotamia, 538 BC–330 BC] Persian. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. In GeoDia as "Achaemenid". Period definition from Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia — Bertman, Stephen., 2003.

Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and Judah became Yehud, a small tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire. Under governors and an increasingly powerful priesthood, much of the Hebrew Bible took shape and Aramaic became the everyday language. Coins, imported Greek pottery and administrative seal impressions show a province tied into imperial and Mediterranean networks.

hints.label: Persian
hints.source: Handbook to life in ancient Mesopotamia

nodes.name: Republican (Spain, 132 BC–26 BC)
nodes.title: Republican (Spain, 132 BC–26 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 132 BC–26 BC] Republican. Beginning-date corresponds with the end of the Celtiberian wars; outside of the Celtiberian homeland, the Republican period in Spain begins 218 B.C. (Second Punic War). Period definition from The romanization of central Spain : complexity, diversity, and change in a provincial hinterland — Curchin, Leonard A., 1950-, 2004.

The centuries in which Roman power pushed into the Balkans, beginning with the defeat of Macedon at Pydna and the creation of the province of Macedonia, and continuing with campaigns against Illyrian, Dardanian and Scordiscan peoples along the Danube frontier. For communities in the central Balkans this meant raiding, tribute, Roman roads and the first steady flow of Italian coinage and goods, well before formal provincial administration was settled under Augustus.

hints.label: Republican
hints.source: The romanization of central Spain : complexity, diversity, and change in a provincial hinterland

nodes.name: Archaic (Spain, 629 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Spain, 629 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iberia, 629 BC–499 BC] Archaic. See also Dominguez in C. Sanchez & G.R. Tsetskhladze, 2001. Greek Pottery from the Iberian Peninsula. Period definition from Greek Trade in Iberia: The Extent of Interaction — Paloma Cabrera, 1998.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

hints.label: Archaic
hints.source: Greek Trade in Iberia: The Extent of Interaction

nodes.name: Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.title: Jemdet Nasr (Iraq, 3099 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Uruk, 3099 BC–2899 BC] Jemdet Nasr. See also Charvat 2002. Period definition from The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies — Adams, Robert McC. (Robert McCormick), 1926-, 1972.

Named for a mound in central Iraq, this phase sits between Uruk and the Early Dynastic city-states. Distinctive polychrome painted jars in red and black appear alongside the earliest archives of proto-cuneiform tablets, which record grain, livestock and labour rather than stories. Settlements across southern Mesopotamia show a shared culture of seals, accounting and temple economies, the administrative machinery that would soon underpin Sumerian kingship.

hints.label: Jemdet Nasr
hints.source: The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies

nodes.name: Early Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–3199 BC)
nodes.title: Early Uruk (Iraq, 3499 BC–3199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Uruk, 3499 BC–3199 BC] Early Uruk. See also Liverani 2006. Period definition from The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies — Adams, Robert McC. (Robert McCormick), 1926-, 1972.

Southwestern Iran was drawn into the orbit of the emerging urban world of lowland Mesopotamia, adopting its mass-produced, undecorated pottery, its architecture and its systems of accounting with clay tokens and seals. Susa and its neighbours on the Susiana plain grew into centres with monumental buildings and clear differences in wealth. The exchange of highland metal, stone and timber for lowland goods set up a relationship that shaped Elamite civilisation for millennia.

hints.label: Early Uruk
hints.source: The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies

nodes.name: Late Uruk (Iraq, 3199 BC–3099 BC)
nodes.title: Late Uruk (Iraq, 3199 BC–3099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Uruk, 3199 BC–3099 BC] Late Uruk. See also Liverani 2006. Period definition from The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies — Adams, Robert McC. (Robert McCormick), 1926-, 1972.

The world's first cities took shape in the Mesopotamian lowlands, and their institutions, goods and administrators reached deep into the Iranian plateau and Khuzestan. Mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and the earliest clay tablets with proto-cuneiform signs mark the birth of bureaucratic record-keeping. When the Uruk network contracted, Susa and its neighbours went their own way, developing the Proto-Elamite script and state.

Nineveh, Iraq

hints.label: Late Uruk
hints.source: The Uruk countryside : the natural setting of urban societies

nodes.name: New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p0cp447qz64]
nodes.title: New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p0cp447qz64]
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

nodes.name: Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1069 BC–711 BC)
nodes.title: Third Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1069 BC–711 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 1069 BC–711 BC] Third Intermediate Period. unsure why GeoDia start_label said 2055 B.C. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

A long stretch of divided rule in which no single king controlled the whole Nile valley. Pharaohs of Libyan descent ruled the Delta while Thebes answered to a priestly dynasty of Amun, and royal tombs were tucked into the temple enclosure at Tanis - one of the few Egyptian royal burials found nearly intact. Kushite kings from Nubia later reunified the country, only for Assyrian invasion to end the period and usher in the Saite revival.

nodes.name: First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2133 BC–2039 BC)
nodes.title: First Intermediate Period (Egypt, 2133 BC–2039 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 2133 BC–2039 BC] First Intermediate Period. Robins' chronology is being used in preference to Freeman's, since it seems to represent the general textbook situation more accurately. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Central authority collapsed after the long reign of Pepi II, and Egypt broke into competing regional powers - provincial governors ruling as local dynasts, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Low Nile floods, famine and disorder colour the literature written afterwards, but tomb goods and inscriptions show provincial workshops and local elites flourishing. Funerary practices once reserved for kings spread to lesser officials, laying groundwork for the Coffin Texts. The Theban victory that ended the era produced the reunified Middle Kingdom.

nodes.name: Roman emperors (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 395)
nodes.title: Roman emperors (Egypt, 29 BC–AD 395)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 29 BC–AD 395] Roman emperors. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egypt became the emperor's private preserve, governed by a prefect and closed to senators, its harvests shipped north to feed Rome. Emperors from Augustus onward appear on temple walls at Dendera, Esna and Philae in pharaonic costume, offering to Egyptian gods in hieroglyphs. Alexandria stayed a vast, restive city of Greeks, Jews and Egyptians, while everyday papyrus documents record how Roman taxation and law reshaped village life.

nodes.name: Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC) [p0cp447b435]
nodes.title: Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC) [p0cp447b435]
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 2039 BC–1639 BC] Middle Kingdom. unsure why GeoDia start_label said 2055 B.C. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

nodes.name: Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1639 BC–1531 BC) [p0cp447757z]
nodes.title: Second Intermediate Period (Egypt, 1639 BC–1531 BC) [p0cp447757z]
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 1639 BC–1531 BC] Second Intermediate Period. unsure why GeoDia end_label said 1550 B.C. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

A divided Egypt, with the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the Delta from Avaris, a rump Theban kingdom in the south, and the Kushite kings of Kerma pressing the frontier. Trade with the Levant and the Aegean flourished at Avaris even as pharaonic art and building shrank. The Theban wars of liberation under Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and finally Ahmose reunified the country and launched the New Kingdom.

nodes.name: Late Period (Egypt, 711 BC–331 BC)
nodes.title: Late Period (Egypt, 711 BC–331 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 711 BC–331 BC] Late Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

nodes.name: Early Dynastic Period (Egypt, 2919 BC–2648 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic Period (Egypt, 2919 BC–2648 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 2919 BC–2648 BC] Early Dynastic Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Mesopotamia's cities came into their own: walled, densely populated, and ruled by kings who built temples and fought their neighbours. Writing spread beyond the storeroom into royal boasts, legal contracts and literature, giving the earliest named individuals in history. Excavated palaces, royal tombs and temple statuary from Ur, Lagash and Kish give an unusually vivid picture of daily and ceremonial life.

nodes.name: Predynastic Period (Egypt, 4999 BC–2919 BC)
nodes.title: Predynastic Period (Egypt, 4999 BC–2919 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 4999 BC–2919 BC] Predynastic Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Nile Valley societies moved from village agriculture to hierarchical chiefdoms with wealthy elite burials and specialised craft production. Trade linked Egypt to Nubia, the Levant and Mesopotamia, and rulers began using standardised symbols of power that would become the pharaonic crowns and regalia. Its close saw the political unification that launched dynastic Egypt.

nodes.name: Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2648 BC–2133 BC)
nodes.title: Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2648 BC–2133 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 2648 BC–2133 BC] Old Kingdom. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

nodes.name: Graeco-Roman Period (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 395)
nodes.title: Graeco-Roman Period (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 395)
nodes.description:
[Ancient Egypt, 331 BC–AD 395] Graeco-Roman Period. Period definition from The art of ancient Egypt — Robins, Gay., 2000.

Ptolemaic kings and then Roman prefects governed the Nile valley from Alexandria, running the country as an enormously profitable estate exporting grain, papyrus and glass. Traditional temple religion flourished under Greek and Roman patronage at Edfu, Dendera and Philae even as Greek became the language of government, and mixed Greek-Egyptian burial customs produced the strikingly lifelike Fayum portraits. The period closes with Egypt as a heartland of early Christianity and monasticism.

nodes.name: Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC) [p077fc55t8z]
nodes.title: Iron IIA (Israel, 999 BC–924 BC) [p077fc55t8z]
nodes.description:
[Bethsaida, 999 BC–924 BC] Iron IIA. Period definition from Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century — Savage, Carl E., 2011.

Monumental building returns: fortified gates, palaces and administrative centres at sites like Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, traditionally credited to Solomon and hotly debated ever since. Pharaoh Sheshonq I campaigned through the region around 925 BC, leaving a list of conquered towns at Karnak. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature.

hints.label: Iron IIA
hints.source: Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century

nodes.name: Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–721 BC)
nodes.title: Iron IIB (Israel, 899 BC–721 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bethsaida, 899 BC–721 BC] Iron IIB. Period definition from Biblical Bethsaida : an archaeological study of the first century — Savage, Carl E., 2011.

Israel under the Omrides and then Jeroboam II became a substantial regional power with ivory-decorated palaces at Samaria, before Assyrian armies destroyed it and deported its population in 720 BC. Judah survived as a vassal, and Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BC is documented from both sides — by Assyrian palace reliefs and by the excavated siege ramp and mass grave. Royal administration is visible in stamped jar handles and standardised weights.

The decades of the Babylonian Exile, when Jerusalem lay ruined and administration shifted north to Mizpah. Excavation shows the Judean heartland around Benjamin largely continuing while the city, the Shephelah and the Negev were emptied and burnt. It was in these years that exiled scribes reshaped Judah's traditions, and it ends with Cyrus's capture of Babylon and the permission to return.

nodes.name: Yugoslav War, 1991-1995 (Slovenia, AD 1991–AD 1995)
nodes.title: Yugoslav War, 1991-1995 (Slovenia, AD 1991–AD 1995)
nodes.description:
[Yugoslavia, AD 1991–AD 1995] Yugoslav War, 1991-1995. Spatial coverage: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro, Republic of Macedonia, Serbia, Slovenia. Extracted from heading "Yugoslav War, 1991-1995". Added to LCSH in 2003, revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Slovenia's declaration of independence triggered a ten-day conflict with the Yugoslav People's Army that ended with the federal troops' withdrawal and few casualties compared with what followed. The republic escaped the far bloodier wars in Croatia and Bosnia and turned quickly towards Europe. The break-up it began ended the multinational Yugoslav state built after the Second World War.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Tarragona, AD 1937–AD 1939)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Tarragona, AD 1937–AD 1939)
nodes.description:
[Tarragona (Spain), AD 1937–AD 1939] Bombardment, 1937-1939. Extracted from heading "Tarragona (Spain)--History--Bombardment, 1937-1939". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Republican-held port was hit again and again by Italian aircraft flying from Majorca and by warships offshore, aimed at the harbour, railway and the road link to Barcelona. Civilian districts were wrecked and much of the population fled; the raids ended only when Nationalist troops overran Catalonia.

nodes.name: Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD 1125)
nodes.title: Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD 1125)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1106–AD 1125] Henry V, 1106-1125. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry V, 1106-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Salian emperor came to power by deposing his own father, then spent years fighting the papacy over who could invest bishops with ring and staff. The struggle ended in the Concordat of Worms of 1122, a compromise that separated spiritual from secular investiture and set the pattern for church-state relations in Europe. His death without an heir opened the contest between Welf and Hohenstaufen families that shaped German politics for the next century.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Rome, AD 1943–AD 1944)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Rome, AD 1943–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Rome (Italy), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Rome (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 2007, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

nodes.name: Naval Revolt, 1893-1894 (Brazil, AD 1893–AD 1894)
nodes.title: Naval Revolt, 1893-1894 (Brazil, AD 1893–AD 1894)
nodes.description:
[Brazil, AD 1893–AD 1894] Naval Revolt, 1893-1894. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--Naval Revolt, 1893-1894". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Officers of the Brazilian navy turned their guns on Rio de Janeiro in an attempt to unseat President Floriano Peixoto, only four years after the monarchy had been overthrown. The rebellion fused monarchist sympathies, naval resentment of the army-dominated republic, and the southern federalist war in Rio Grande do Sul. Its defeat entrenched army primacy in Brazilian politics and cleared the way for the civilian oligarchic republic that followed.

nodes.name: Medieval period, 1066-1485 (England, AD 1066–AD 1485)

[Great Britain, AD 1066–AD 1485] Medieval period, 1066-1485. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Medieval period, 1066-1485". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Norman Conquest imposed a new French-speaking aristocracy, castles and a reordered church, and produced Domesday Book, the most detailed survey of any early medieval kingdom. Over four centuries came Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament, the growth of towns and the wool trade, Gothic cathedrals, the Black Death that killed perhaps a third or more of the population and broke the grip of serfdom, and the long wars in France. The dynastic bloodletting of the Wars of the Roses ends the period at Bosworth.

nodes.name: Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–AD 1556)
nodes.title: Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–AD 1556)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1519–AD 1556] Charles V, 1519-1556. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Charles V, 1519-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected emperor with money borrowed from the Fuggers, he confronted Luther at the Diet of Worms and spent the rest of his reign unable to contain the Reformation while also fighting France in Italy and the Ottomans on the Danube and in the Mediterranean. He beat the Lutheran princes at Mühlberg in 1547 but could not make the victory stick, and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 conceded that each prince would determine his territory's religion. Worn out, he abdicated and split his inheritance between his son and his brother, ending the dream of a single universal Christian empire.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Delaware, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Delaware, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Delaware, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Delaware--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.26 of LCSH 1987, and p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Wars of Independence, 1809-1825 (Bolivia, AD 1809–AD 1825)
nodes.title: Wars of Independence, 1809-1825 (Bolivia, AD 1809–AD 1825)
nodes.description:
[Bolivia, AD 1809–AD 1825] Wars of Independence, 1809-1825. Extracted from heading "Bolivia--History--Wars of Independence, 1809-1825". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The juntas of Chuquisaca and La Paz in 1809 were among the earliest revolts in Spanish America, and they were crushed brutally. Upper Peru then endured sixteen years of grinding guerrilla warfare by local 'republiquetas' while regular armies from Buenos Aires failed repeatedly to hold the highlands. Liberation came from outside, with Sucre's campaign after Ayacucho; the new republic took the name Bolivia in Bolívar's honour.

nodes.name: Augustus III, 1734-1763 (Poland, AD 1734–AD 1763)
nodes.title: Augustus III, 1734-1763 (Poland, AD 1734–AD 1763)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1734–AD 1763] Augustus III, 1734-1763. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Augustus III, 1734-1763". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His accession followed a war fought by France, Russia and Austria over who should be king of Poland, which tells you how far sovereignty had slipped. He spent almost all his reign in Dresden, leaving Poland to feuding magnate families while the Sejm was paralysed by the liberum veto - a single deputy could dissolve it, and repeatedly did. The drift left the Commonwealth defenceless against the partitions that began a decade after his death.

A tax revolt in the north grew into the FROLINAT rebellion against a southern-dominated government, and the fighting never fully stopped. Libya occupied the Aouzou Strip and backed rival factions, France repeatedly intervened, and the 1987 "Toyota War" saw Chadian pickup-mounted troops rout Libyan armour. Successive rulers took power by force, and rebellions from the east and north continued into the twenty-first century.

Overtaxed peasants and persecuted Christians on the Shimabara Peninsula and Amakusa islands rose behind the teenage figurehead Amakusa Shirō and held the ruined castle of Hara against a huge shogunal army, which finally starved and stormed it, killing the defenders almost to the last person. A Dutch ship shelled the walls from the sea, proof of Protestant usefulness. The shock hardened Tokugawa policy: the Portuguese were expelled, Christianity was hunted with picture-treading tests, and Japan's seclusion was locked in place for two centuries.

Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Simon bar Kokhba led a disciplined revolt against Rome that ran an independent Judaea for some three years, minting coins dated to "the freedom of Israel" and issuing orders preserved on letters found in Dead Sea caves. Hadrian sent his best general, Julius Severus, who reduced the rebels stronghold by stronghold, ending at Betar; ancient sources describe catastrophic slaughter and depopulation. Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina, rebuilt Jerusalem as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from it, closing the era of Jewish armed nationalism and pushing Judaism decisively towards the rabbinic study of law.

Independence from Belgium was followed within weeks by army mutiny, the secession of mineral-rich Katanga, and the murder of Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba. UN peacekeepers intervened on an unprecedented scale — Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash during the mission — while the Cold War powers backed rival factions. The crisis ended with Mobutu Sese Seko's coup and a kleptocratic dictatorship lasting three decades.

Under the first emperor born in the provinces, Rome reached its greatest territorial extent, absorbing Dacia and its gold, and briefly Armenia and Mesopotamia. Dacian plunder paid for a spectacular building programme - the Forum and Markets of Trajan, baths, a new harbour at Portus and roads across the empire - while the spiral frieze of Trajan's Column turned a military campaign into the most detailed picture of the Roman army ever carved.

Britain's longest reign until Elizabeth II covered the country's transformation into the world's first industrial superpower: railways, steamships, telegraphs, factory towns and a population that doubled. Abroad it meant the Raj, the scramble for Africa and an empire spanning a quarter of the globe; at home, reform acts that widened the vote, public health and schooling laws, and fierce arguments about poverty, faith and evolution. The monarchy itself was reinvented as a symbol of domestic respectability and imperial unity.

nodes.name: Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045 (Armenia, AD 885–AD 1045)
nodes.title: Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045 (Armenia, AD 885–AD 1045)
nodes.description:
[Armenia, AD 885–AD 1045] Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Bagratuni dynasty, 885-1045". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.5 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ashot I secured recognition as king from both the caliph and Byzantium, restoring an Armenian monarchy after centuries of foreign governors. The Bagratid century brought a building boom — above all at the capital Ani, the "city of a thousand and one churches" — along with flourishing trade, manuscript painting and the historians who recorded it. Family partitions weakened the kingdom, and Byzantine annexation left Armenia without defenders when the Seljuks arrived a generation later.

nodes.name: Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654 (Netherlands, AD 1652–AD 1654)
nodes.title: Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654 (Netherlands, AD 1652–AD 1654)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, Great Britain, AD 1652–AD 1654] Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654. Spatial coverage: England, Netherlands. Extracted from heading "Anglo-Dutch War, 1652-1654". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A war fought almost entirely at sea, sparked by English navigation laws aimed at Dutch carrying trade and by disputes over salutes in the Channel. Fleets of the Commonwealth under Blake met Tromp's convoys in a series of huge line-of-battle engagements that helped invent modern naval tactics. The English blockade throttled Dutch commerce and forced peace terms, but the underlying commercial rivalry was untouched.

nodes.name: French intervention, 1860-1861 (Lebanon, AD 1860–AD 1861)
nodes.title: French intervention, 1860-1861 (Lebanon, AD 1860–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[Lebanon, AD 1860–AD 1861] French intervention, 1860-1861. Extracted from heading "Lebanon--History--French intervention, 1860-1861". Added to LCSH in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After massacres of Maronite Christians by Druze in Mount Lebanon and the killing of thousands in Damascus, France landed an expeditionary force at Beirut with the consent of the other European powers and the Ottoman government. The intervention produced the Règlement Organique, which made Mount Lebanon an autonomous district under a Christian governor answerable to Istanbul. That settlement gave the region decades of relative peace and entrenched the practice of allotting office by religious community.

nodes.name: Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884 (China, AD 874–AD 884)
nodes.title: Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884 (China, AD 874–AD 884)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 874–AD 884] Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884. Extracted from heading "China--History--Huang Chao Rebellion, 874-884". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Huang Ch'ao Rebellion, 874-884." appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A failed examination candidate turned salt smuggler led a rebel army the length and breadth of China, sacking Guangzhou - where tens of thousands of Arab, Persian and Jewish merchants were reportedly massacred, wrecking the southern sea trade - and then taking Chang'an itself. The Tang emperor fled to Sichuan and only recovered his capital with the help of Turkic cavalry. The dynasty survived on paper for another twenty years, but real power had passed permanently to regional warlords.

nodes.name: Vladimir, 972-1015 (Russia, AD 972–AD 1015)
nodes.title: Vladimir, 972-1015 (Russia, AD 972–AD 1015)
nodes.description:
[Kievan Rus, AD 972–AD 1015] Vladimir, 972-1015. Spatial coverage: Belarus, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Ukraine. Extracted from heading "Kievan Rus--History--Vladimir, 972-1015". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975 (source uses term "Russia"). Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Vladimir seized Kiev with Varangian help, ruled a sprawling realm of Slavic and Finnic tribute-payers, and then made the decision that redirected the region's history: he accepted Byzantine Christianity, married the emperor's sister, and had the people of Kiev baptised in the Dnieper. Pagan idols were thrown down, Greek clergy and Church Slavonic books arrived, and stone churches such as the Tithe Church rose in the capital. The choice tied the Rus to Constantinople rather than Rome, shaping the alphabet, art and religion of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

nodes.name: Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864 (Vietnam, AD 1862–AD 1864)
nodes.title: Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864 (Vietnam, AD 1862–AD 1864)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1862–AD 1864] Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Trương Định Uprising, 1862-1864". Added to LCSH in 1993, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Nguyễn court ceded three southern provinces to France, the officer Trương Định refused the order to disband and kept fighting from the marshes of Gò Công, acclaimed by villagers as "Great General Pacifier of the West". His guerrilla bands harried French posts until he was betrayed and killed. The revolt showed that resistance to colonial rule in Cochinchina would come from local militias rather than the throne.

nodes.name: Louis XI, 1461-1483 (France, AD 1461–AD 1483)
nodes.title: Louis XI, 1461-1483 (France, AD 1461–AD 1483)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1461–AD 1483] Louis XI, 1461-1483. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XI, 1461-1483". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The 'Universal Spider', who preferred bribery, spies and patient diplomacy to battle, and wove alliances that undid his enemies. His long duel with Charles the Bold ended when the Burgundian duke died at Nancy, allowing Louis to seize the duchy; Anjou, Maine and Provence also fell in to the crown. He encouraged trade and fairs, organised a royal courier service, and left France far more unified and centrally governed than he found it.

nodes.name: Boleslaus II, 1058-1079 (Poland, AD 1058–AD 1079)
nodes.title: Boleslaus II, 1058-1079 (Poland, AD 1058–AD 1079)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1058–AD 1079] Boleslaus II, 1058-1079. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Boleslaus II, 1058-1079". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bolesław the Bold revived royal power after decades of collapse, intervening in Hungary and Rus and having himself crowned king in 1076 with papal backing during the Emperor's quarrel with Rome. Three years later he had Bishop Stanislaus of Kraków killed, a scandal that cost him the throne and sent him into exile. The murdered bishop became Poland's national saint, and the crown was lost again for another generation.

nodes.name: Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43 (Vietnam, AD 39–AD 43)
nodes.title: Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43 (Vietnam, AD 39–AD 43)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 39–AD 43] Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Trưng Sisters' Rebellion, 39-43". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two aristocratic sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, raised the Lac lords against Han Chinese officials and briefly ruled some sixty-five citadels across the Red River delta. General Ma Yuan crushed them and dismantled the old Vietnamese aristocracy, tightening direct Chinese rule for centuries. The sisters became the enduring emblem of Vietnamese independence and are still honoured with temples and a national holiday.

nodes.name: Gothic period, 414-711 (Spain, AD 414–AD 711)
nodes.title: Gothic period, 414-711 (Spain, AD 414–AD 711)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 414–AD 711] Gothic period, 414-711. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Gothic period, 414-711". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Visigoths settled in Hispania after their wanderings through Gaul and built a kingdom centred on Toledo, ruling a Hispano-Roman majority under their own kings. Their conversion from Arian to Catholic Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 fused crown and church, and the resulting law code, the Liber Iudiciorum, shaped later Iberian law. Internal succession disputes left the kingdom brittle, and it collapsed within a few years of the Muslim landing of 711.

nodes.name: Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Denmark, AD 1648–AD 1670)
nodes.title: Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Denmark, AD 1648–AD 1670)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1648–AD 1670] Frederick III, 1648-1670. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick III, 1648-1670". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign began with a disastrous war against Sweden that cost Denmark Scania and the provinces east of the Sound, permanently fixing the modern Scandinavian border. But when Copenhagen's citizens helped hold the city under siege, he used the crisis to break the nobility: in 1660-61 the elective monarchy was abolished and the King's Law of 1665 made him one of the most absolute rulers in Europe, on paper at least. He was also a passionate collector, founding the royal library and Kunstkammer.

nodes.name: Fyodor III, 1676-1682 (Russia, AD 1676–AD 1682)
nodes.title: Fyodor III, 1676-1682 (Russia, AD 1676–AD 1682)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1676–AD 1682] Fyodor III, 1676-1682. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Fyodor III, 1676-1682". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Theodore, 1678-1682" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign under a young and often ill tsar that nonetheless pushed through real reform, above all the abolition of mestnichestvo, the system that assigned offices by aristocratic pedigree rather than ability. Taxation was simplified, the war with the Ottomans over Ukraine was brought to a truce, and Western learning gained ground at court. His death without an heir triggered the succession crisis and streltsy revolt that brought his half-brother Peter the Great to the throne.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254–AD 1273)
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254–AD 1273)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1254–AD 1273] Interregnum, 1254-1273. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Interregnum, 1254-1273". Added to LCSH in 1986. Note that many of the periods for the Holy Roman Empire are reduplicated under the "Germany--History" heading, but are given different URIs. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the last Hohenstaufen emperors fell, no king could make his authority felt in Germany; rival foreign candidates, Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile, were elected and largely ignored. Princes, bishops and cities filled the vacuum, fortifying, coining and warring on their own account, and leagues formed to keep the roads safe. The election of Rudolf of Habsburg ended the drift, but the crown never recovered the ground lost to the territorial princes.

nodes.name: Turkish Wars, 1453-1571 (Veneto, AD 1453–AD 1571)
nodes.title: Turkish Wars, 1453-1571 (Veneto, AD 1453–AD 1571)
nodes.description:
[Venice, AD 1453–AD 1571] Turkish Wars, 1453-1571. Extracted from heading "Venice (Italy)--History--Turkish Wars, 1453-1571". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The fall of Constantinople set Venice against an expanding Ottoman Empire in a series of long, costly wars for its maritime empire. Negroponte fell in 1470, the Morean strongholds and finally Cyprus followed, and even the great victory at Lepanto in 1571 brought no territory back. Venice increasingly turned to its mainland Italian possessions as the eastern trade routes slipped away.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Ukraine, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Ukraine, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Ukraine--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 118 of LCSH 1986 and p.100 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Philadelphia, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Philadelphia, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Philadelphia (Pa.), AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Philadelphia (Pa.)--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.91 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789 (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789 (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1774–AD 1789] Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Abdul Hamid I, 1774-1789". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign opened with the humiliating treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, which handed Russia a foothold on the Black Sea and a claim to speak for Ottoman Orthodox subjects. Efforts to modernise the army and navy with French advisers began in earnest, but a new war with Russia and Austria was already going badly when he died.

nodes.name: Muromachi period, 1336-1573 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573)
nodes.title: Muromachi period, 1336-1573 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573] Muromachi period, 1336-1573. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Muromachi period, 1336-1573". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1990. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ashikaga Takauji's shogunate presided over a country where real power drained steadily to provincial military governors and, later, to self-made warlords. It was nevertheless the age of Noh drama, linked verse, the tea ceremony and the Golden and Silver Pavilions, funded partly by licensed trade with Ming China. Portuguese ships arrived in 1543 with firearms, and Jesuit missionaries followed, opening Japan's first sustained contact with Europe just as the old order was breaking apart.

nodes.name: Insurrection, 1868-1878 (Cuba, AD 1868–AD 1878)
nodes.title: Insurrection, 1868-1878 (Cuba, AD 1868–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[Cuba, AD 1868–AD 1878] Insurrection, 1868-1878. Extracted from heading "Cuba--History--Insurrection, 1868-1878". Added to LCHS in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ten Years' War began with Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freeing his slaves and calling for independence, and turned into a grinding guerrilla campaign that devastated the eastern countryside and killed perhaps 200,000 people. It ended in a negotiated peace rather than victory, but it forged a generation of fighters, hastened the abolition of slavery, and left the unfinished business that produced the 1895 war of independence.

nodes.name: Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C. (China, 220 BC–206 BC)
nodes.title: Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C. (China, 220 BC–206 BC)
nodes.description:
[China, 220 BC–206 BC] Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C.. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qin dynasty, 221-207 B.C.". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate lable "Ch'in dynasty, 221-207 B.C." appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fifteen years that reorganised China: the warring states abolished, walls between them torn down and frontier walls joined, a single script and currency imposed, and the empire divided into commanderies staffed by officials answerable to the throne. The First Emperor's tomb complex near Xi'an, with its thousands of individually modelled terracotta soldiers, gives a startling picture of the regime's scale and ambition. Rebellion broke out within a year of his death and the Han took over the machinery he had built.

nodes.name: Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945 (Burma, AD 1942–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945 (Burma, AD 1942–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Burma, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.12 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Japanese forces drove the British out within months, aided by the Burma Independence Army under Aung San, and installed a nominally independent state under Ba Maw in 1943. Reality meant harsh military rule, forced labour on the Thailand–Burma railway, and severe shortages. Aung San's forces switched sides in 1945, and the wartime rupture of British authority made a return to colonial rule impossible.

nodes.name: Federal Revolution, 1898-1899 (Bolivia, AD 1898–AD 1899)
nodes.title: Federal Revolution, 1898-1899 (Bolivia, AD 1898–AD 1899)
nodes.description:
[Bolivia, AD 1898–AD 1899] Federal Revolution, 1898-1899. Extracted from heading "Bolivia--History--Federal Revolution, 1898-1899". Added to LCSH and revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short civil war between the Conservative establishment in Sucre and Liberals based in La Paz, fought partly with the support of Aymara peasant forces under Pablo Zárate Willka. The Liberals won, La Paz became the seat of government and congress, and the indigenous allies were then turned on and their leaders executed.

nodes.name: Charles IV, 1788-1808 (Spain, AD 1788–AD 1808)
nodes.title: Charles IV, 1788-1808 (Spain, AD 1788–AD 1808)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1788–AD 1808] Charles IV, 1788-1808. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Charles IV, 1788-1808". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who preferred hunting to governing left affairs to his wife's favourite, Manuel Godoy, just as the French Revolution broke out next door. Spain's alliance with Napoleonic France ended in the destruction of its fleet at Trafalgar and then in French armies occupying the country. Forced to abdicate at Bayonne in favour of Napoleon's brother, he went into exile as Spain rose in the Peninsular War. Goya, his court painter, left the era's unsparing record.

nodes.name: James I, 1603-1625 (England, AD 1603–AD 1625)
nodes.title: James I, 1603-1625 (England, AD 1603–AD 1625)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1603–AD 1625] James I, 1603-1625. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--James I, 1603-1625". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Scottish king who inherited England from the childless Elizabeth, uniting the two crowns in one person though not the two states. He survived the Gunpowder Plot, quarrelled repeatedly with Parliament over money and royal prerogative, and commissioned the Bible translation that carries his name. He preferred peace abroad and favourites at home, and both choices stored up trouble for his son.

nodes.name: English Conquest, 1166-1186 (Ireland, AD 1166–AD 1186)
nodes.title: English Conquest, 1166-1186 (Ireland, AD 1166–AD 1186)
nodes.description:
[Ireland, AD 1166–AD 1186] English Conquest, 1166-1186. Extracted from heading "Ireland--History--English Conquest, 1166-1186". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.61 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The exiled king of Leinster, Diarmait Mac Murchada, recruited Cambro-Norman lords to help him regain his kingdom, and they came with mailed cavalry and archers. Richard de Clare ('Strongbow') took Waterford and Dublin, and Henry II crossed over in 1171 to assert lordship over both the newcomers and the Irish kings. It began eight centuries of English involvement in Ireland, and left a lasting patchwork of fortified manors, boroughs and Gaelic territories.

nodes.name: Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898 (India, AD 1897–AD 1898)
nodes.title: Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898 (India, AD 1897–AD 1898)
nodes.description:
[India, AD 1897–AD 1898] Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898. Extracted from heading "India--History--Tirah Campaign, 1897-1898". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2015. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A British Indian expedition of some 40,000 troops sent into the Afridi and Orakzai highlands after the great Pathan uprising had overrun the Khyber forts. The storming of the Dargai Heights, where the Gordon Highlanders took heavy losses, became one of the most celebrated actions of the frontier wars. The tribes were never decisively beaten, and the campaign helped convince the British to govern the north-west frontier through subsidies and militias rather than occupation.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1410-1412 (Aragon, AD 1410–AD 1412)
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1410-1412 (Aragon, AD 1410–AD 1412)
nodes.description:
[Aragon, AD 1410–AD 1412] Interregnum, 1410-1412. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--Interregnum, 1410-1412". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975; revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Martin I died without a legitimate heir, leaving six claimants and the real possibility of civil war across Aragon, Valencia and Catalonia. Rather than fight it out, delegates from the three realms met at Caspe and chose Ferdinand of Antequera by arbitration — a rare instance of a medieval succession settled by committee. It brought the Castilian Trastámara dynasty to Aragon and set the two crowns on the path that led to their union under Ferdinand and Isabella.

nodes.name: Regency, 1715-1723 (France, AD 1715–AD 1723)
nodes.title: Regency, 1715-1723 (France, AD 1715–AD 1723)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1715–AD 1723] Regency, 1715-1723. Extracted from heading "France--History--Regency, 1715-1723". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Philippe d'Orléans governed for the child Louis XV and deliberately unwound the late king's system, moving the court back to Paris, easing censorship and briefly handing government to councils of nobles. His backing of John Law's bank and Mississippi Company produced Europe's first modern stock bubble and its spectacular collapse, which left France suspicious of paper money for generations. Socially, it is remembered as a loosening — libertine, sceptical and fond of small elegant rooms — that opened the way to the Enlightenment.

nodes.name: Charles I, 1866-1914 (Romania, AD 1866–AD 1914)
nodes.title: Charles I, 1866-1914 (Romania, AD 1866–AD 1914)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 1866–AD 1914] Charles I, 1866-1914. Extracted from heading "Romania--History--Charles I, 1866-1914". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.98 of LCSH 1987, and p.83 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Prussian Hohenzollern prince was imported to rule the young union of Moldavia and Wallachia, and stayed for nearly half a century. He led Romanian troops alongside Russia against the Ottomans, winning full independence in 1878 and a royal crown in 1881, then presided over railways, banks, a new constitution and the fairy-tale castle at Peleș. His secret alliance with Austria-Hungary and Germany became untenable in 1914, and he died weeks after the war began.

nodes.name: Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600 (Roman Empire, AD 30–AD 600)
nodes.title: Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600 (Roman Empire, AD 30–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, Rome, AD 30–AD 600] Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600. Spatial coverage: Byzantine Empire, Roman Empire. Extracted from heading "Church history--Primitive and early church, ca. 30-600". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2010. Spatial coverage description given as "Church". Spatial coverage inferred from state of Church in this time period. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A small Jewish messianic movement grew into the official religion of the Roman Empire. Persecution, martyrdom and fierce internal argument over the nature of Christ gave way after Constantine to imperial patronage, great basilicas, monasteries and the ecumenical councils that fixed doctrine. The bishops of Rome, Constantinople, Antioch and Alexandria built the institutional church that would outlast the empire in the West.

nodes.name: Louis XV, 1715-1774 (France, AD 1715–AD 1774)
nodes.title: Louis XV, 1715-1774 (France, AD 1715–AD 1774)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1715–AD 1774] Louis XV, 1715-1774. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XV, 1715-1774". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inherited the throne as a five-year-old and reigned for nearly six decades, in which France fought the Wars of the Polish and Austrian Successions and then lost Canada and its Indian holdings in the Seven Years' War. Wealth and population grew and the Enlightenment flourished in Paris salons, but the monarchy quarrelled endlessly with the parlements over taxes and lost much of its prestige. He acquired Lorraine and Corsica, and left his grandson a kingdom with unreformed finances and a critical, increasingly hostile reading public.

nodes.name: German occupation, 1915-1918 (Lithuania, AD 1915–AD 1918)
nodes.title: German occupation, 1915-1918 (Lithuania, AD 1915–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Lithuania, AD 1915–AD 1918] German occupation, 1915-1918. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--German occupation, 1915-1918". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.72 of LCSH 1987, and p.58 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

German armies drove the Russians out and placed the country under the military administration of Ober Ost, which requisitioned timber, food and labour and controlled movement with permits. Berlin encouraged a Lithuanian council, the Taryba, hoping for a client state, but it declared full independence in February 1918 and made the claim stick once Germany collapsed.

nodes.name: Fernando I, 1412-1416 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1412–AD 1416)
nodes.title: Fernando I, 1412-1416 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1412–AD 1416)
nodes.description:
[Aragon, AD 1412–AD 1416] Fernando I, 1412-1416. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--Fernando I, 1412-1416". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975; revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Castilian prince chosen as king of Aragon by the Compromise of Caspe, an arbitration by nine electors that settled a disputed succession without civil war and installed the Trastámara dynasty in Aragon. His short reign tied the two crowns' ruling houses together, a link that led to the union under his grandson Ferdinand the Catholic. He also helped end the Great Schism by withdrawing support from the Aragonese antipope Benedict XIII.

nodes.name: Jin dynasty, 1115-1234 (China, AD 1115–AD 1234)
nodes.title: Jin dynasty, 1115-1234 (China, AD 1115–AD 1234)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1115–AD 1234] Jin dynasty, 1115-1234. Extracted from heading "China--History--Jin dynasty, 1115-1234". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Chin dynasty, 1115-1234" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by the Jurchen of Manchuria, who overthrew the Khitan Liao and then drove the Song out of northern China, capturing Kaifeng and two emperors in 1127. Ruling from Beijing over a mostly Chinese population, the Jin blended steppe military organisation with Chinese bureaucracy, taxation and examinations. Their destruction by the Mongols after decades of war opened the way for Khubilai Khan's conquest of the rest of China.

nodes.name: George I, 1714-1727 (United Kingdom, AD 1714–AD 1727)
nodes.title: George I, 1714-1727 (United Kingdom, AD 1714–AD 1727)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1714–AD 1727] George I, 1714-1727. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George I, 1714-1727". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A German prince from Hanover took the British throne because he was the nearest Protestant heir, passing over dozens of Catholic Stuarts and provoking the Jacobite rising of 1715. Uninterested in day-to-day government and often absent in Hanover, he left business to ministers, and Robert Walpole's rise in the wake of the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720 pushed Britain toward rule by a prime minister and cabinet.
