nodes.name: Vitellius, 69 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 69)
nodes.title: Vitellius, 69 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 69)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 69] Vitellius, 69. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Vitellius, 69". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed emperor by the Rhine legions, Vitellius won the throne by beating Otho at Bedriacum and lost it within months to the armies backing Vespasian. His brief reign, remembered by hostile sources mainly for gluttony, ended with street fighting in Rome, the burning of the Capitol and his own lynching. He was the third of the four emperors of 69, the year that proved an emperor could be made outside Rome by whichever army moved fastest.

nodes.name: Henry IV, 1589-1610 (France, AD 1589–AD 1610)
nodes.title: Henry IV, 1589-1610 (France, AD 1589–AD 1610)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1589–AD 1610] Henry IV, 1589-1610. Extracted from heading "France--History--Henry IV, 1589-1610". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Protestant king of Navarre inherited the French crown but had to conquer his kingdom, finally entering Paris only after converting to Catholicism. His Edict of Nantes gave Huguenots legal toleration and fortified towns, ending nearly forty years of religious war, and with Sully he restored royal finances, roads and canals. Stabbed by a Catholic fanatic in a Paris street, he became the founding figure of the Bourbon dynasty and, in popular memory, the good king who wanted a chicken in every pot.

nodes.name: Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C (Greece, 734 BC–459 BC)
nodes.title: Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C (Greece, 734 BC–459 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 734 BC–459 BC] Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Messenian Wars, 735-460 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 42 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sparta's long conquest of fertile Messenia across the Taygetus mountains turned an entire neighbouring people into helots, state-owned serfs who farmed Spartan land. The wealth freed Spartan citizens to train as full-time soldiers, but the constant threat of helot revolt shaped Spartan society into the militarised, inward-looking state it became. The great revolt after the earthquake of 464 BC dragged in Athens and helped poison relations between the two cities on the road to the Peloponnesian War.

nodes.name: Ramiro I, 1035-1063 (Spain, AD 1035–AD 1063)
nodes.title: Ramiro I, 1035-1063 (Spain, AD 1035–AD 1063)
nodes.description:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1035–AD 1063] Ramiro I, 1035-1063. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Ramiro I, 1035-1063". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The illegitimate son of Sancho the Great of Navarre inherited a small mountain county and turned it into the Kingdom of Aragon, expanding at the expense of his brothers and pressing south against the Muslim taifa of Zaragoza. He was killed besieging Graus, but the kingdom he founded became one of the great powers of medieval Iberia and the Mediterranean.

nodes.name: French occupation, 1918-1946 (Lebanon, AD 1918–AD 1946)
nodes.title: French occupation, 1918-1946 (Lebanon, AD 1918–AD 1946)
nodes.description:
[Lebanon, AD 1918–AD 1946] French occupation, 1918-1946. Extracted from heading "Lebanon--History--French occupation, 1918-1946". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.72 of LCSH 1987, and pg.58 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied victory over the Ottomans brought French troops to the coast and, under a League of Nations mandate, the creation of Greater Lebanon - the old autonomous mountain enlarged with Beirut, Tripoli, the Bekaa and the south, and with it a far more mixed population. A 1926 constitution introduced a republic whose offices were shared out by sect, the framework Lebanese politics still runs on. Independence was declared during the Second World War and confirmed when French troops finally withdrew.

nodes.name: Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221 (Anatolia, AD 1218–AD 1221)
nodes.title: Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221 (Anatolia, AD 1218–AD 1221)
nodes.description:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1218–AD 1221] Fifth Crusade, 1218-1221. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Fifth, 1218-1221". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rather than march on Jerusalem, the crusaders attacked Egypt, the heart of Ayyubid power, and besieged the Nile port of Damietta for eighteen months before taking it. The sultan al-Kamil twice offered to trade Jerusalem for their withdrawal; the papal legate Pelagius refused, and Francis of Assisi crossed the lines to preach to the sultan in person. The army then advanced upriver, was trapped by the Nile flood, and had to surrender everything it had won.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254–AD 1273) [p06c6g33rnp]
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1254-1273 (Germany, AD 1254–AD 1273) [p06c6g33rnp]
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1254–AD 1273] Interregnum, 1254-1273. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Interregnum, 1254-1273". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the last Hohenstaufen emperors fell, no king could make his authority felt in Germany; rival foreign candidates, Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile, were elected and largely ignored. Princes, bishops and cities filled the vacuum, fortifying, coining and warring on their own account, and leagues formed to keep the roads safe. The election of Rudolf of Habsburg ended the drift, but the crown never recovered the ground lost to the territorial princes.

nodes.name: Jangalī movement, 1914-1921 (Iran, AD 1914–AD 1921)
nodes.title: Jangalī movement, 1914-1921 (Iran, AD 1914–AD 1921)
nodes.description:
[Iran, AD 1914–AD 1921] Jangalī movement, 1914-1921. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Jangalī movement, 1914-1921". Added to LCSH in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A guerrilla movement based in the forests of Gilan, led by Mirza Kuchak Khan, which fought Russian and British intervention and the weakness of the Tehran government, calling for constitutional rule and an end to foreign control. With Bolshevik backing it proclaimed a short-lived Soviet republic in Gilan in 1920, then fractured over communist land policy. Reza Khan's army crushed it, and Kuchak Khan froze to death fleeing into the mountains.

nodes.name: Frederick I, 1523-1533 (Denmark, AD 1523–AD 1533)
nodes.title: Frederick I, 1523-1533 (Denmark, AD 1523–AD 1533)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1523–AD 1533] Frederick I, 1523-1533. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick I, 1523-1533". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He took the throne after the nobles deposed his nephew Christian II, promising to defend the Catholic Church and then quietly doing the opposite. At the Diet of Odense in 1527 he granted Lutheran preachers protection and let the reform movement spread through the towns. His death without a settled succession triggered the civil war known as the Count's Feud, out of which the Danish Reformation was imposed outright in 1536.

nodes.name: Tokugawa period, 1600-1868 (Japan, AD 1600–AD 1868)
nodes.title: Tokugawa period, 1600-1868 (Japan, AD 1600–AD 1868)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1600–AD 1868] Tokugawa period, 1600-1868. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Tokugawa period, 1600-1868". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Sekigahara the Tokugawa shoguns imposed two and a half centuries of peace, holding the daimyo in check through hostage residence in Edo and closing the country to most foreign contact. Cities grew enormous, a merchant class prospered, and with it came kabuki, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, haiku and a highly literate urban public. Commodore Perry's warships exposed the regime's weakness, and its fall in 1868 launched Japan's headlong modernisation.

nodes.name: Arab rebellion, 1936-1939 (State of Palestine, AD 1936–AD 1939)
nodes.title: Arab rebellion, 1936-1939 (State of Palestine, AD 1936–AD 1939)
nodes.description:
[Palestine, AD 1936–AD 1939] Arab rebellion, 1936-1939. Extracted from heading "Palestine--History--Arab rebellion, 1936-1939". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A general strike against British rule and Jewish immigration escalated into three years of armed insurgency across the countryside, with rural bands attacking police posts, railways and the Haifa oil pipeline. Britain answered with mass detentions, house demolitions and thousands of troops, and by 1939 the Arab leadership was exiled or dead and the villages disarmed. The revolt won the 1939 White Paper limiting Jewish immigration, but it also shattered Palestinian Arab political organisation on the eve of the decisive decade.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Emden, AD 1943–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Emden, AD 1943–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Emden (Lower Saxony, Germany), AD 1943–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1943-1945. Extracted from heading "Emden (Lower Saxony, Germany)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1945". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A North Sea port and shipyard town on the Ems, it was attacked for its harbour and submarine construction and lost the overwhelming majority of its old buildings, with the centre effectively erased in a single raid in September 1944. Postwar reconstruction produced an almost entirely modern town on a medieval street plan.

nodes.name: Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Germany, AD 1576–AD 1612)
nodes.title: Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Germany, AD 1576–AD 1612)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1576–AD 1612] Rudolf II, 1576-1612. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Rudolf II, 1576-1612". Added to LCSH in 1986. Identical entries exist under both "Germany--History" and "Austria--History", but with separate URIs. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Habsburg emperor moved his court to Prague and turned it into a magnet for astronomers, alchemists, painters and collectors – Tycho Brahe and Kepler worked under his patronage, and his cabinet of curiosities was the most famous in Europe. Politically he was indecisive and increasingly withdrawn, letting confessional tensions in the empire fester until his own family forced him to cede power. The Letter of Majesty he granted Bohemian Protestants in 1609, and its later breach, helped set up the revolt that began the Thirty Years' War.

nodes.name: Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C (Greece, 403 BC–402 BC)
nodes.title: Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C (Greece, 403 BC–402 BC)
nodes.description:
[Athens, 403 BC–402 BC] Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C. Extracted from heading "Athens (Greece)--History--Thirty Tyrants, 404-403 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Athens surrendered to Sparta, a pro-Spartan oligarchy of thirty men took control and ruled by execution, exile and confiscation, killing perhaps 1,500 citizens in a matter of months. Democratic exiles under Thrasybulus seized the Piraeus and overthrew them within a year. The restored democracy issued an amnesty, but the memory of the terror shaped Athenian politics and coloured the trial of Socrates, who had ties to several of the ringleaders.

properties.title: calyx-krater — 420BC-390BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: fragment of a red-figured calyx-krater. A woman in Phrygian costume (indicated only on the sleeves), with a bordered mantle decorated with trefoils at her back, to right, looking round in three-quarter face to left with an expression of anxiety in her features. In her arms she holds a suckling infant, and in order to bare her left breast she has let fall the upper part of her dress; the edge she still holds in her teeth, so as to cover her right breast. The infant, of whom only the right arm and side are seen, appears to face the spectator, but to press with his right arm around its mother's breast; on its wrist is a bangle, drawn in black, with the remains of a pigment beside it which has now faded. On the left is a portion of some object, of which too little is preserved to be intelligible. Large style, of late period. The fragment is from the upper part of the design, as the red line in the interior shows. Inner markings in fine brown. The forehead is wrinkled, a vertical line marks a hollow in the chin. The outline of the hair, both against forehead and background, is edged with fine black lines.; | Type: calyx-krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 11.50 centimetres; 133.00 grammes; 16.00 centimetres; | Culture: Apulian (Greek) (Greek) (Greek)

properties.title: guttus — 470BC-400BC
properties.notes:
Pottery Attic red figure guttus (oil flask with strainer) with a spout in form of a lion's head; wheel-made and with moulded and incised details; squat body, slightly splaying sides, with a convex top; flat base; the central strainer has a single hole in the middle and two outer rings of perforations; loop handle (mostly restored); vessel made of fine buff clay, decorated in red figure technique with animals on the shoulder below the strainer. On one side of the vessel is a couchant lion, facing left, whose head is formed by the spout: the details of the head are well rendered, with incised strokes for the mane; on the other side are two couchant animals facing each other: the beast on the left has pointed ears and a long tail, jaws wide open and a determined stare emphasised by the profile view of the face with a single eye (possibly a lion); its opposite number is more crudely drawn, and is either shown in profile, or else has two snouts/heads. Attica, Somme-Bionne, Greece

nodes.name: Ferdinand II, 1619-1637 (Austria, AD 1619–AD 1637)
nodes.title: Ferdinand II, 1619-1637 (Austria, AD 1619–AD 1637)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1619–AD 1637] Ferdinand II, 1619-1637. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Ferdinand II, 1619-1637". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Jesuit-educated hardliner whose determination to restore Catholicism to the Habsburg lands turned the Bohemian revolt into a European war. Victory at White Mountain let him execute or dispossess the Czech nobility and rebuild Bohemia as a Catholic, German-speaking crown land; his Edict of Restitution of 1629 then demanded the return of church property across the Empire and drove Protestant princes and Sweden into arms against him. He raised, and eventually murdered, the mercenary commander Wallenstein, whose private armies showed how war had become a business.

nodes.name: Qing dynasty, 1644-1912 (China, AD 1644–AD 1912)
nodes.title: Qing dynasty, 1644-1912 (China, AD 1644–AD 1912)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1912] Qing dynasty, 1644-1912. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qing dynasty, 1644-1912". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Ch'ing dynasty, 1644-1912" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and p.16 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Manchu invaders from beyond the Great Wall seized Beijing and went on to rule the largest Chinese empire ever assembled, pushing control deep into Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet. A long boom under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors tripled the population and filled palaces with porcelain, painting and encyclopedic scholarship, while ordinary men were made to shave their foreheads and wear the queue as a sign of submission. The nineteenth century brought opium, foreign gunboats, the catastrophic Taiping Rebellion and forced treaty ports, and the dynasty's collapse ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule.

nodes.name: Russian Conquest, 1831-1859 (Caucasus, AD 1831–AD 1859)
nodes.title: Russian Conquest, 1831-1859 (Caucasus, AD 1831–AD 1859)
nodes.description:
[Caucasus, Northern (Russia), AD 1831–AD 1859] Russian Conquest, 1831-1859. Extracted from heading "Caucasus, Northern (Russia)--History--Russian Conquest, 1831-1859". Added to LCSH in 2016, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Russia's push into the mountains of Dagestan and Chechnya met a religious and military resistance movement led by Imam Shamil, who welded the highland communities into an Islamic state. Decades of fortress-building, forest-clearing and scorched-earth campaigning ended with Shamil's surrender at Gunib, followed by mass deportations and emigration of Muslim highlanders to the Ottoman Empire – a displacement still remembered across the Caucasus and Turkey.

nodes.name: Xuantong, 1908-1912 (China, AD 1908–AD 1912)
nodes.title: Xuantong, 1908-1912 (China, AD 1908–AD 1912)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1908–AD 1912] Xuantong, 1908-1912. Extracted from heading "China--History--Xuantong, 1908-1912". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Hsuan t'ung, 1908-1912" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The nominal reign of the infant Puyi, last of the Qing, ending with the abdication of February 1912 and the founding of the Republic. Reform came too late to save the dynasty: railway nationalisation protests and the army mutiny at Wuchang triggered province after province to declare independence. Puyi kept his title and the Forbidden City for another twelve years as a private citizen-emperor.

nodes.name: Partition period, 1763-1796 (Poland, AD 1763–AD 1796)
nodes.title: Partition period, 1763-1796 (Poland, AD 1763–AD 1796)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1763–AD 1796] Partition period, 1763-1796. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Partition period, 1763-1796". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under Stanisław August Poniatowski, a cultured king installed with Russian backing, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth attempted reform and was dismembered for it. Russia, Prussia and Austria took slices in 1772 and 1793; the Constitution of 3 May 1791, Europe's first modern written constitution after America's, provoked invasion; Kościuszko's rising of 1794 was crushed. The third partition of 1795 removed the state from the map entirely, and Polish national identity survived for over a century without any Polish state.

nodes.name: Hannibal's War, 1644-1645 (Norway, AD 1644–AD 1645)
nodes.title: Hannibal's War, 1644-1645 (Norway, AD 1644–AD 1645)
nodes.description:
[Norway, AD 1644–AD 1645] Hannibal's War, 1644-1645. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Hannibal's War, 1644-1645". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Named after Hannibal Sehested, the Danish king's governor in Norway, this was the Norwegian front of the wider war between Denmark-Norway and Sweden. Norwegian troops raided across the border into Jämtland and Värmland with some success, but the peace settled at Brömsebro handed Jämtland and Härjedalen to Sweden for good. The campaign is remembered for Sehested's attempt to build a self-financing Norwegian army and administration.

nodes.name: Ivan IV, 1533-1584 (Russia, AD 1533–AD 1584)
nodes.title: Ivan IV, 1533-1584 (Russia, AD 1533–AD 1584)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1533–AD 1584] Ivan IV, 1533-1584. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Ivan IV, 1533-1584". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned as Russia's first tsar, Ivan the Terrible conquered the khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan, opening the Volga and the road to Siberia, and issued a new law code while summoning the first assembly of the land. His later years turned savage: the oprichnina, a private terror corps, tore through the nobility and sacked Novgorod, and a long, failed war for the Baltic drained the country. He struck his own heir dead in a rage, leaving a weak successor and the collapse into the Time of Troubles.

nodes.name: Claudius, 41-54 (Roman Empire, AD 41–AD 54)
nodes.title: Claudius, 41-54 (Roman Empire, AD 41–AD 54)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 41–AD 54] Claudius, 41-54. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Claudius, 41-54". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed emperor by the Praetorian Guard after Caligula's murder, Claudius was dismissed as a stammering scholar but proved an energetic administrator. He invaded Britain in AD 43, annexed Thrace and Mauretania, built the harbour at Portus and a great aqueduct system for Rome, and gave freedmen real power in a growing imperial bureaucracy. His death, widely rumoured to be poisoning by Agrippina, brought Nero to the throne.

nodes.name: Frederick I, 1720-1751 (Sweden, AD 1720–AD 1751)
nodes.title: Frederick I, 1720-1751 (Sweden, AD 1720–AD 1751)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1720–AD 1751] Frederick I, 1720-1751. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Frederick I, 1720-1751". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Hessian prince who gained the Swedish throne through marriage and promptly surrendered most royal power to the Riksdag, opening the parliamentary "Age of Liberty" in which the Hat and Cap factions governed. His reign saw a disastrous war with Russia that cost more Finnish territory, while the king himself was better known for hunting and mistresses than for ruling. Real authority lay with the Council and the estates, a constitutional experiment unusual in eighteenth-century Europe.

nodes.name: Angeli, 1185-1204 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1204)
nodes.title: Angeli, 1185-1204 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1204)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1204] Angeli, 1185-1204. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Angeli, 1185-1204". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three emperors of the Angelos family presided over the unravelling of the Byzantine state: revenues collapsed, provincial governors went their own way, and a Bulgarian revolt permanently detached the Balkans north of the Balkan range. Dynastic infighting — a brother blinding a brother, then a fugitive prince offering money for restoration — drew the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople. In 1204 the crusaders stormed and sacked the city, ending eight centuries of unbroken imperial rule there.

nodes.name: American Occupation, 1915-1934 (Haiti, AD 1915–AD 1934)
nodes.title: American Occupation, 1915-1934 (Haiti, AD 1915–AD 1934)
nodes.description:
[Haiti, AD 1915–AD 1934] American Occupation, 1915-1934. Extracted from heading "Haiti--History--American Occupation, 1915-1934". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.54 of LCSH 1987, and p. 43 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

US Marines landed after the lynching of President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam and stayed for nineteen years, taking control of customs revenue, rewriting the constitution to permit foreign land ownership, and building roads and hospitals with forced corvée labour. Peasant resistance under Charlemagne Péralte was crushed, and thousands died. The occupation left behind a centralised, US-trained Garde d'Haïti that dominated national politics for decades afterwards, and a bitter nationalist memory that shaped Haitian intellectual life.

nodes.name: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Indonesia, AD 1942–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Indonesia, AD 1942–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Indonesia, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Japanese occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.48 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch colonial regime collapsed in weeks, and Japan governed the archipelago as three separate military zones, extracting oil, rice and hundreds of thousands of romusha forced labourers. To mobilise support it released and promoted nationalists such as Sukarno and Hatta and trained Indonesian militias like PETA. When Japan surrendered, those leaders and those armed units declared independence, and the Dutch never regained control.

nodes.name: Indian occupation, 1969-1971 (California, AD 1969–AD 1971)
nodes.title: Indian occupation, 1969-1971 (California, AD 1969–AD 1971)
nodes.description:
[California, AD 1969–AD 1971] Indian occupation, 1969-1971. Extracted from heading "Alcatraz Island (Calif.)--History--Indian occupation, 1969-1971". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Activists of the group Indians of All Tribes landed on the abandoned Alcatraz prison island and held it for nineteen months, claiming it under a treaty provision on surplus federal land and demanding a cultural centre and university. The occupation drew national press, made Red Power visible to a mass audience, and helped push Washington away from the termination policy toward tribal self-determination. Painted slogans from the occupiers survive on the buildings and are now preserved as historic fabric.

nodes.name: Casimir IV, 1447-1492 (Poland, AD 1447–AD 1492)
nodes.title: Casimir IV, 1447-1492 (Poland, AD 1447–AD 1492)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1447–AD 1492] Casimir IV, 1447-1492. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Casimir IV, 1447-1492". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Casimir Jagiellon spent thirteen years fighting the Teutonic Knights, and the Second Peace of Toruń in 1466 handed Poland Gdańsk, Malbork and access to the Baltic while making the Order's remaining state a Polish fief. To pay for the war he conceded the Nieszawa statutes, entrenching the nobility's right to be consulted, a step towards the szlachta democracy of later centuries. His sons wore the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary as well, making the Jagiellonians the dominant dynasty of central Europe.

nodes.name: Federal Wars, 1858-1863 (Venezuela, AD 1858–AD 1863)
nodes.title: Federal Wars, 1858-1863 (Venezuela, AD 1858–AD 1863)
nodes.description:
[Venezuela, AD 1858–AD 1863] Federal Wars, 1858-1863. Extracted from heading "Venezuela--History--Federal Wars, 1858-1863". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.106 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The bloodiest conflict in Venezuela's republican history, pitting Federalists demanding regional autonomy and land reform against the Caracas Conservative order. Guerrilla campaigns across the plains killed perhaps a tenth of the population; the Treaty of Coche ended the fighting and produced a federal constitution that changed less on the ground than its slogans promised.

nodes.name: Soviet occupation, 1979-1989 (Afghanistan, AD 1979–AD 1989)
nodes.title: Soviet occupation, 1979-1989 (Afghanistan, AD 1979–AD 1989)
nodes.description:
[Afghanistan, AD 1979–AD 1989] Soviet occupation, 1979-1989. Extracted from heading "Afghanistan--History--Soviet occupation, 1979-1989". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Soviet troops entered to prop up a faltering communist government and found themselves fighting a decade-long guerrilla war against mujahideen fighters armed and financed by the United States, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Roughly a million Afghans died and five million fled abroad, while Soviet casualties and costs corroded confidence in Moscow. The withdrawal left behind a shattered country, a well-armed militia culture and networks of foreign volunteers that would shape the following decades.

nodes.name: Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592 (Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592)
nodes.title: Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592 (Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1527–AD 1592] Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Mạc dynasty, 1527-1592". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A palace guard commander seized the Vietnamese throne from the failing Lê rulers, holding the Red River delta and winning grudging recognition from Ming China. Loyalists proclaimed a restored Lê emperor in the south under the Nguyễn and Trịnh families, and the country split into rival regimes for two generations of civil war. Driven out of Thăng Long, the last of the family clung on in the mountains at Cao Bằng.

nodes.name: Maximus, 455 (Roman Empire, AD 455–AD 455)
nodes.title: Maximus, 455 (Roman Empire, AD 455–AD 455)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 455–AD 455] Maximus, 455. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Maximus, 455". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Petronius Maximus seized power after conniving at the murder of Valentinian III, then reigned barely eleven weeks. Forcing the dead emperor's widow into marriage broke the western court's fragile arrangements with Gaiseric, whose Vandal fleet sailed for Rome; Maximus was lynched by a mob as he fled, days before the city was sacked. The episode shows how thoroughly the western throne had become the plaything of court factions and barbarian fleets.

nodes.name: Qi dynasty, 479-502 (China, AD 479–AD 502)
nodes.title: Qi dynasty, 479-502 (China, AD 479–AD 502)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 479–AD 502] Qi dynasty, 479-502. Extracted from heading "China--History--Qi dynasty, 479-502". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised later that year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Southern Qi was the shortest-lived of the southern dynasties ruling from Jiankang on the Yangtze, a span of barely two decades marked by murderous succession struggles within the ruling Xiao clan. Despite the turmoil the court was a centre of Buddhist patronage and literary refinement, and the tonal experiments of the Yongming poets shaped the rules of later Chinese verse. A cousin of the last emperor seized the throne and founded the Liang, continuing the same aristocratic culture under a new name.

nodes.name: Clement V, 1305-1314 (Vatican City, AD 1305–AD 1314)
nodes.title: Clement V, 1305-1314 (Vatican City, AD 1305–AD 1314)
nodes.description:
[Papal States, AD 1305–AD 1314] Clement V, 1305-1314. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Clement V, 1305-1314". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Gascon elected under heavy French pressure, Clement never went to Rome and settled the papal court at Avignon, beginning nearly seventy years of French-dominated papacy. He bowed to Philip IV in suppressing the Knights Templar at the Council of Vienne, and their leaders were burned in Paris. The move damaged papal prestige and helped set up the later Great Schism.

nodes.name: Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873 (France, AD 1871–AD 1873)
nodes.title: Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873 (France, AD 1871–AD 1873)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1871–AD 1873] Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873. Extracted from heading "France--History--Occupation and evacuation, 1871-1873". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After defeat by Prussia, German troops remained garrisoned across the north and east while France paid off a five-billion-franc indemnity. The money was raised faster than Bismarck expected, through hugely oversubscribed public loans, and the last soldiers withdrew in September 1873. The experience left Alsace-Lorraine lost, the young Third Republic scarred, and a grievance that shaped French politics until 1914.

nodes.name: Edmund, 855-870 (England, AD 855–AD 870)
nodes.title: Edmund, 855-870 (England, AD 855–AD 870)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 855–AD 870] Edmund, 855-870. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edmund, 855-870". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edmund ruled East Anglia until the Great Heathen Army of the Danes overwhelmed his kingdom and killed him. Legend turned his death into martyrdom by arrows and beheading, and his shrine at Bury St Edmunds became one of the richest pilgrimage sites in England. He was venerated as a patron saint of the kingdom long before St George displaced him.

nodes.name: Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438 (Romania, AD 1437–AD 1438)
nodes.title: Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438 (Romania, AD 1437–AD 1438)
nodes.description:
[Transylvania (Romania), AD 1437–AD 1438] Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438. Extracted from heading "Transylvania (Romania)--History--Peasant Uprising, 1437-1438". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hungarian and Romanian serfs in Transylvania rose at Bobâlna against the bishop's tithe and tightening manorial demands, defeating noble forces before being ground down. The threat drove the nobility, the Székely and the Saxon towns into a mutual defence pact, the Union of the Three Nations, which became the constitutional basis of Transylvania for centuries. It froze the largely Orthodox Romanian peasantry out of political life, a grievance still cited in nationalist argument four hundred years later.

nodes.name: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Philippines, AD 1942–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Japanese occupation, 1942-1945 (Philippines, AD 1942–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Philippines, AD 1942–AD 1945] Japanese occupation, 1942-1945. Extracted from heading "Philippines--History--Japanese Occupation, 1942-1945". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.91 of LCSH 1987, and p.77 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch colonial regime collapsed in weeks, and Japan governed the archipelago as three separate military zones, extracting oil, rice and hundreds of thousands of romusha forced labourers. To mobilise support it released and promoted nationalists such as Sukarno and Hatta and trained Indonesian militias like PETA. When Japan surrendered, those leaders and those armed units declared independence, and the Dutch never regained control.

nodes.name: Social War, 90-88 B.C (ancient Rome, 89 BC–87 BC)
nodes.title: Social War, 90-88 B.C (ancient Rome, 89 BC–87 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 89 BC–87 BC] Social War, 90-88 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Social War, 90-88 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rome's Italian allies, who had supplied its armies for generations without gaining citizenship, rose in revolt, minted their own coinage and set up a rival capital. Rome won the war but conceded the cause, extending citizenship to the peninsula's free populations. The result was an Italy legally unified under Rome — and a generation of commanders and veteran armies that would soon be turned against the Republic itself.

nodes.name: Ivan VI, 1740-1741 (Russia, AD 1740–AD 1741)
nodes.title: Ivan VI, 1740-1741 (Russia, AD 1740–AD 1741)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1740–AD 1741] Ivan VI, 1740-1741. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Ivan VI, 1740-1741". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed emperor at two months old, he reigned only through regents before a palace coup by the guards put Peter the Great's daughter Elizabeth on the throne. The deposed baby was hidden away, his portraits and coins withdrawn from circulation, and he grew up in solitary confinement at Shlisselburg fortress, barely aware of who he was. He was killed by his guards in 1764 during a botched attempt to free him.

nodes.name: Maria I, 1777-1816 (Portugal, AD 1777–AD 1816)
nodes.title: Maria I, 1777-1816 (Portugal, AD 1777–AD 1816)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1777–AD 1816] Maria I, 1777-1816. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Maria I, 1777-1816". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Her accession ended the domineering rule of the Marquis of Pombal, who was dismissed and put on trial while exiled nobles returned to court. Devout and increasingly incapacitated by mental illness, she left government to her son John as regent, and when Napoleon's armies invaded, the whole court sailed for Brazil under British escort. She died in Rio de Janeiro, a Portuguese queen who spent her last years ruling from South America.

nodes.name: Vladislaus I, 1305-1333 (Poland, AD 1305–AD 1333)
nodes.title: Vladislaus I, 1305-1333 (Poland, AD 1305–AD 1333)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1305–AD 1333] Vladislaus I, 1305-1333. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus I, 1305-1333". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Władysław the Elbow-high spent decades in exile and rebellion before piecing the fragmented Polish duchies back together and having himself crowned in Kraków in 1320 — the first coronation in the old capital and the formal end of nearly two centuries of division. His reign was consumed by war with the Teutonic Knights over Pomerania and by alliance-building with Hungary and Lithuania. He left his son Casimir a kingdom that was smaller than the old Poland but was once again a kingdom.

nodes.name: Rebellion, 1914-1915 (South Africa, AD 1914–AD 1915)
nodes.title: Rebellion, 1914-1915 (South Africa, AD 1914–AD 1915)
nodes.description:
[South Africa, AD 1914–AD 1915] Rebellion, 1914-1915. Extracted from the heading "Africa, South--History--Rebellion, 1914-1915". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.1 of LCHS 1975; revised 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As South Africa's government prepared to invade German South West Africa on Britain's behalf, Afrikaner officers and former Boer generals, including De Wet, Beyers and Maritz, took up arms in protest. Botha and Smuts, themselves Boer War commanders, put the rising down within months with commando forces of their own. The episode split Afrikaner politics between those reconciled to the British Empire and a nationalist current that would later grow into the National Party.

nodes.name: Christian I, 1448-1481 (Norway, AD 1448–AD 1481)
nodes.title: Christian I, 1448-1481 (Norway, AD 1448–AD 1481)
nodes.description:
[Norway, AD 1448–AD 1481] Christian I, 1448-1481. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Christian I, 1448-1481". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Oldenburg king, elected in Denmark and then accepted in Norway, he spent his reign chasing an expensive union with Sweden and borrowing to pay for it. Short of cash for his daughter's dowry, he pledged Orkney and Shetland to the Scottish crown in 1468–69 — a loan never repaid, which is why those islands are Scottish today. He also secured papal permission for the University of Copenhagen, founded in 1479.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1989-1996 (Liberia, AD 1989–AD 1996)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1989-1996 (Liberia, AD 1989–AD 1996)
nodes.description:
[Liberia, AD 1989–AD 1996] Civil War, 1989-1996. Extracted from heading "Liberia--History--Civil War, 1989-1996". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles Taylor's incursion from Côte d'Ivoire toppled Samuel Doe and then fragmented into a war of warlord factions, notorious for drugged child soldiers and looting of timber, rubber and iron. A West African intervention force, ECOMOG, fought for years to contain it. Elections in 1997 made Taylor president, but the underlying conflict resumed within two years and spilled into Sierra Leone.

nodes.name: Insurrection, 1925-1927 (Syria, AD 1925–AD 1927)
nodes.title: Insurrection, 1925-1927 (Syria, AD 1925–AD 1927)
nodes.description:
[Syria, AD 1925–AD 1927] Insurrection, 1925-1927. Extracted from heading "Syria--History--Insurrection, 1925-1927". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Great Syrian Revolt began among the Druze of the Hawran under Sultan al-Atrash and spread to Damascus, Hama and the countryside, uniting rural fighters with urban nationalists against the French Mandate. France responded with aerial bombardment and artillery fire on Damascus, destroying whole quarters and shocking international opinion. The rebellion was defeated but became the founding episode of modern Syrian nationalism.

nodes.name: Augustus II, 1697-1733 (Poland, AD 1697–AD 1733)
nodes.title: Augustus II, 1697-1733 (Poland, AD 1697–AD 1733)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1697–AD 1733] Augustus II, 1697-1733. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Augustus II, 1697-1733". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony, converted to Catholicism to win the Polish crown and then dragged the Commonwealth into the Great Northern War against Sweden, losing the throne to Stanisław Leszczyński before Russian arms restored him. Real power drained to the magnates and to Russia, whose troops came and went as they pleased. He is better remembered in Dresden, where he built baroque palaces and founded the Meissen porcelain works after his alchemists cracked the Chinese formula.

nodes.name: House of Habsburg, 1477-1556 (Netherlands, AD 1477–AD 1556)
nodes.title: House of Habsburg, 1477-1556 (Netherlands, AD 1477–AD 1556)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1477–AD 1556] House of Habsburg, 1477-1556. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--House of Habsburg, 1477-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Mary of Burgundy's marriage to Maximilian of Austria carried the Low Countries into Habsburg hands, and under Charles V - born in Ghent - they were governed as part of an empire stretching to Spain and the Americas. Antwerp became the commercial capital of Europe, while the Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 bound the Seventeen Provinces together as a single inheritance. Charles's abdication in 1556 handed them to his Spanish son Philip II, a transfer that within a dozen years produced open revolt.

nodes.name: Henry VII, 1308-1313 (Germany, AD 1308–AD 1313)
nodes.title: Henry VII, 1308-1313 (Germany, AD 1308–AD 1313)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1308–AD 1313] Henry VII, 1308-1313. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry VII, 1308-1313". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A count of Luxembourg elected as a compromise candidate, he secured Bohemia for his family and then led the first imperial expedition to Italy in decades, seeking to revive the emperor's authority there. Dante hailed him as Italy's saviour and wrote him into the Paradiso; the Guelf cities and the pope resisted him. He died of fever near Siena before he could break Florence, and the imperial dream in Italy died with him.

nodes.name: Henry V, 1413-1422 (England, AD 1413–AD 1422)
nodes.title: Henry V, 1413-1422 (England, AD 1413–AD 1422)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1413–AD 1422] Henry V, 1413-1422. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry V, 1413-1422". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short, relentlessly focused reign that revived the English claim to the French crown and won the archers' victory at Agincourt in 1415. Systematic conquest of Normandy followed, and the Treaty of Troyes made Henry heir to France and regent for the mad Charles VI. He died of dysentery at thirty-five, leaving a nine-month-old son to hold together a dual monarchy that soon collapsed.

nodes.name: English Invasion, 1780-1781 (Nicaragua, AD 1780–AD 1781)
nodes.title: English Invasion, 1780-1781 (Nicaragua, AD 1780–AD 1781)
nodes.description:
[Nicaragua, AD 1780–AD 1781] English Invasion, 1780-1781. Extracted from heading "Nicaragua--History--English Invasion, 1780-1781". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A British scheme to cut Spanish America in two by seizing the San Juan River and Lake Nicaragua, opening a route to the Pacific. The force, which included a young Horatio Nelson, took Fort San Juan but was destroyed by malaria and dysentery rather than by fighting; the survivors withdrew after losing most of their men. It stands as one of the costliest British failures of the American Revolutionary War.

nodes.name: European intervention, 1861-1867 (Mexico, AD 1861–AD 1867)
nodes.title: European intervention, 1861-1867 (Mexico, AD 1861–AD 1867)
nodes.description:
[Mexico, AD 1861–AD 1867] European intervention, 1861-1867. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--European intervention, 1861-1867". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.77 of LCSH 1987, and p.62 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

France, Britain and Spain landed troops after Mexico suspended payments on its foreign debt; the others withdrew, but Napoleon III pressed on and installed the Habsburg archduke Maximilian as emperor. Benito Juárez's republican government never surrendered, and the improbable Mexican victory at Puebla on 5 May 1862 became a national holiday. French withdrawal under American pressure left Maximilian to be captured and shot at Querétaro, ending monarchy in Mexico for good.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1647-1648 (Naples, AD 1647–AD 1648)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1647-1648 (Naples, AD 1647–AD 1648)
nodes.description:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1647–AD 1648] Revolution, 1647-1648. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Revolution, 1647-1648". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A new tax on fruit set off a rising in the Naples markets led by the fisherman Masaniello, who briefly held the city before being murdered. The revolt widened into a broader assault on Spanish rule and noble privilege, and a Neapolitan Republic was proclaimed with French encouragement. Spanish forces under Don Juan José of Austria retook the city, but the episode became a byword across Europe for the sudden power of an urban crowd.

nodes.name: Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845 (Brazil, AD 1835–AD 1845)
nodes.title: Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845 (Brazil, AD 1835–AD 1845)
nodes.description:
[Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil), AD 1835–AD 1845] Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845. Extracted from heading "Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil : State)--History--Revolution of the Farrapos, 1835-1845". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cattle ranchers and gaúcho militias in Rio Grande do Sul rebelled against imperial taxes on their salted beef and hides, and declared the Riograndense Republic. The war spread into Santa Catarina and drew in the young Giuseppe Garibaldi, who learned his trade as a guerrilla and sailor in its service. It was the longest and most dangerous of the revolts against the Brazilian Empire, ending in a negotiated peace that left the province in the empire but confirmed its distinct identity.

nodes.name: Duarte, 1433-1438 (Portugal, AD 1433–AD 1438)
nodes.title: Duarte, 1433-1438 (Portugal, AD 1433–AD 1438)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1433–AD 1438] Duarte, 1433-1438. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Duarte, 1433-1438". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Edward, 1433-1438" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The scholarly son of John I, who wrote on ethics and horsemanship and codified Portuguese law, inherited a kingdom already committed to Atlantic expansion. His reign is remembered for the catastrophic assault on Tangier, where the army was trapped and his brother Fernando was left behind as a hostage to die in Moroccan captivity. Duarte died of plague barely a year later, leaving a six-year-old heir and a disputed regency.

nodes.name: Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Austria, AD 1576–AD 1612)
nodes.title: Rudolf II, 1576-1612 (Austria, AD 1576–AD 1612)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1576–AD 1612] Rudolf II, 1576-1612. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Rudolf II, 1576-1612". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Rudolph II, 1576-1612" appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987, and p.6 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Habsburg emperor moved his court to Prague and turned it into a magnet for astronomers, alchemists, painters and collectors – Tycho Brahe and Kepler worked under his patronage, and his cabinet of curiosities was the most famous in Europe. Politically he was indecisive and increasingly withdrawn, letting confessional tensions in the empire fester until his own family forced him to cede power. The Letter of Majesty he granted Bohemian Protestants in 1609, and its later breach, helped set up the revolt that began the Thirty Years' War.

nodes.name: Miguel I, 1828-1834 (Portugal, AD 1828–AD 1834)
nodes.title: Miguel I, 1828-1834 (Portugal, AD 1828–AD 1834)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1828–AD 1834] Miguel I, 1828-1834. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Miguel I, 1828-1834". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Dom Miguel seized his niece's throne and ruled as an absolutist, backed by the church and much of the countryside, abolishing the liberal charter and persecuting his opponents. The result was the Liberal Wars, in which his brother Pedro landed with a constitutionalist army; Miguel's defeat sent him into permanent exile and settled Portugal's future as a constitutional monarchy.

nodes.name: Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066 (England, AD 1042–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066 (England, AD 1042–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1042–AD 1066] Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward, the Confessor, 1042-1066". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward returned from long exile in Normandy to rule an England still shaped by its Danish conquest, balancing the power of Earl Godwine's family against Norman favourites. He poured resources into rebuilding Westminster Abbey, where he was buried and later venerated as a saint. Dying childless, he left a disputed succession that brought Harold Godwinson, Harald Hardrada and William of Normandy into collision in 1066.

nodes.name: Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–AD 1556) [p06c6g3bm3g]
nodes.title: Charles V, 1519-1556 (Germany, AD 1519–AD 1556) [p06c6g3bm3g]
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1519–AD 1556] Charles V, 1519-1556. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Charles V, 1519-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986. An identical entry exists under "Germany--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected emperor with money borrowed from the Fuggers, he confronted Luther at the Diet of Worms and spent the rest of his reign unable to contain the Reformation while also fighting France in Italy and the Ottomans on the Danube and in the Mediterranean. He beat the Lutheran princes at Mühlberg in 1547 but could not make the victory stick, and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 conceded that each prince would determine his territory's religion. Worn out, he abdicated and split his inheritance between his son and his brother, ending the dream of a single universal Christian empire.

nodes.name: Republic, 1836-1846 (Texas, AD 1836–AD 1846)
nodes.title: Republic, 1836-1846 (Texas, AD 1836–AD 1846)
nodes.description:
[Texas, AD 1836–AD 1846] Republic, 1836-1846. Extracted from heading "Texas--History--Republic, 1836-1846". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

For a decade Texas was an independent state with its own president, army, currency and diplomats in Washington, London and Paris, after Anglo settlers and Tejano allies broke away from Mexico at San Jacinto. Mexico never accepted the loss, the treasury was chronically broke, and frontier war with the Comanche was constant. Annexation by the United States ended the experiment and triggered the U.S.–Mexican War.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Kansas, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Kansas, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Kansas, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Kansas--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.69 of LCSH 1987, and p.67 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Ethelred II, 979-1016 (England, AD 979–AD 1016)
nodes.title: Ethelred II, 979-1016 (England, AD 979–AD 1016)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 979–AD 1016] Ethelred II, 979-1016. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Ethelred II, 979-1016". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign remembered for renewed Viking assaults, met with enormous payments of silver that flooded Scandinavia with English coin and left a rich numismatic record of the king's frequently changing coin types. Æthelred's ordered massacre of Danes in 1002 and the campaigns of Swein Forkbeard drove him briefly into exile in Normandy, a connection that would matter greatly in 1066. His death left England open to Cnut's conquest and a generation of Danish rule.

nodes.name: Henry IV, 1056-1106 (Germany, AD 1056–AD 1106)
nodes.title: Henry IV, 1056-1106 (Germany, AD 1056–AD 1106)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1056–AD 1106] Henry IV, 1056-1106. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Henry IV, 1056-1106". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign was consumed by the Investiture Controversy, the struggle with Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops — a contest about the very basis of royal authority. Excommunicated and facing revolt, he crossed the Alps in winter to stand penitent at Canossa and win absolution, then returned to depose Gregory and install an antipope. Decades of civil war followed, and he died deposed by his own son, with imperial prestige in Germany permanently weakened.

nodes.name: Robert III, 1390-1406 (Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406)
nodes.title: Robert III, 1390-1406 (Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406)
nodes.description:
[Scotland, AD 1390–AD 1406] Robert III, 1390-1406. Extracted from heading "Scotland--History--Robert III, 1390-1406". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.102 of LCSH 1987, and p.89 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Lamed by a horse-kick and reckoned unfit to rule, he left government largely to his brother and other kinsmen while the kingdom slid towards factional violence; his heir David died in suspicious captivity at Falkland. His surviving son James was captured by the English at sea in 1406, news that reportedly killed the king and left Scotland under regents for eighteen years.

nodes.name: Frederick William I, 1713-1740 (Germany, AD 1713–AD 1740)
nodes.title: Frederick William I, 1713-1740 (Germany, AD 1713–AD 1740)
nodes.description:
[Prussia, AD 1713–AD 1740] Frederick William I, 1713-1740. Spatial coverage: Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, Russia. Extracted from heading "Prussia--History--Frederick William I, 1713-1740". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.96 of LCSH 1987, and p.81 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The "Soldier King" turned Prussia into a barracks state, more than doubling the army, creating a disciplined salaried bureaucracy in the General Directory, and running the treasury with obsessive thrift while stamping out court luxury. He introduced compulsory schooling in principle, settled Protestant refugees on empty land, and collected exceptionally tall recruits for his Potsdam Giants. Brutal to his son, he nonetheless bequeathed him a full treasury and Europe's best-drilled army — the tools with which Frederick the Great made Prussia a great power.

nodes.name: Southern Han kingdom, 917-971 (China, AD 917–AD 971)
nodes.title: Southern Han kingdom, 917-971 (China, AD 917–AD 971)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 917–AD 971] Southern Han kingdom, 917-971. Extracted from heading "China--History--Southern Han kingdom, 917-971". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A regional state centred on Guangzhou, founded by the Liu family after the Tang collapse, which grew rich on the sea trade bringing Arab and Southeast Asian merchants to its harbour. Later rulers were remembered for extravagance and for staffing the government with eunuchs. Song forces conquered it, ending independent rule on China's southern coast.

nodes.name: Afonso III, 1248-1279 (Portugal, AD 1248–AD 1279)
nodes.title: Afonso III, 1248-1279 (Portugal, AD 1248–AD 1279)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1248–AD 1279] Afonso III, 1248-1279. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Afonso III, 1248-1279". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alfonso III, 1248-1279" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Seizing the throne from his brother, he completed the Portuguese Reconquista by taking the Algarve, giving the kingdom the borders it still has. He moved the capital to Lisbon and summoned townsmen to the Cortes, drawing the merchant class into royal government for the first time. His reign also began the long argument with Castile over who owned the newly won south.

nodes.name: Restoration, 1660-1688 (England, AD 1660–AD 1688)
nodes.title: Restoration, 1660-1688 (England, AD 1660–AD 1688)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1660–AD 1688] Restoration, 1660-1688. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Restoration, 1660-1688". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From the return of Charles II to the flight of his brother James II, the restored monarchy tried and failed to settle the religious question that had caused the Civil Wars. The Exclusion Crisis over a Catholic heir split politics into the first recognisable Whig and Tory parties, and James's Catholicising policies finally provoked the invitation to William of Orange. The era's culture was worldly and inventive: Wren's churches, Dryden's verse, Newton's mathematics, and comedies far bawdier than anything before or after.

nodes.name: Robert II, 996-1031 (France, AD 996–AD 1031)
nodes.title: Robert II, 996-1031 (France, AD 996–AD 1031)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 996–AD 1031] Robert II, 996-1031. Extracted from heading "France--History--Robert II, 996-1031". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as Robert the Pious, he spent his reign shoring up the still-fragile Capetian hold on a kingdom where great counts and dukes were the real powers, and secured the succession by crowning his son in his lifetime. His excommunication over an uncanonical marriage showed how far reforming churchmen could now press a king, and his reign coincided with the Peace of God movement and the first burnings for heresy in the medieval West.

nodes.name: Baudouin I, 1951-1993 (Belgium, AD 1951–AD 1993)
nodes.title: Baudouin I, 1951-1993 (Belgium, AD 1951–AD 1993)
nodes.description:
[Belgium, AD 1951–AD 1993] Baudouin I, 1951-1993. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Baudouin I, 1951-1993". Added to LCSH and revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the throne as a young man after his father's wartime conduct forced an abdication, and spent his reign as a stabilising figure in a country pulling apart along linguistic lines. His reign saw the abrupt independence of the Congo in 1960 and the long constitutional reforms that turned Belgium into a federal state. A devout Catholic, he briefly stood aside from his royal duties in 1990 so an abortion law could be signed without his name on it.

nodes.name: Separatist movement, 1918-1924 (Germany, AD 1918–AD 1924)
nodes.title: Separatist movement, 1918-1924 (Germany, AD 1918–AD 1924)
nodes.description:
[Rhineland (Germany), AD 1918–AD 1924] Separatist movement, 1918-1924. Extracted from heading "Rhineland (Germany)--History--Separatist movement, 1918-1924". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In the chaos after defeat, activists in the Rhineland and Palatinate, encouraged by French occupation authorities who wanted a buffer state, proclaimed short-lived independent republics. The movement peaked during the hyperinflation and Ruhr occupation of 1923, when Rhenish Republic governments briefly seized town halls. It collapsed under popular hostility, violent counter-attacks and the withdrawal of foreign backing, but the episode fed nationalist grievance narratives for years.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1917-1921 (Russia, AD 1917–AD 1921)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1917-1921 (Russia, AD 1917–AD 1921)
nodes.description:
[Soviet Union, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Estonia, Georgia (country), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia. Extracted from heading "Soviet Union--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.108 of LCSH 1987, and on p.87 of LCSH 1975 (source uses term "Russia"). Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1918-1923 (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1923)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1918-1923 (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1923)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1918–AD 1923] Revolution, 1918-1923. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Revolution, 1918-1923". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the Ottoman capital under Allied occupation and Anatolia parcelled out for partition, Mustafa Kemal built a rival government in Ankara and fought off the Greek invasion. Victory tore up the Treaty of Sèvres and produced Lausanne, new borders, and a massive population exchange with Greece. The sultanate and then the caliphate were abolished, and a secular nation-state replaced a six-hundred-year empire.

nodes.name: French occupation, 1923-1925 (Germany, AD 1923–AD 1925)
nodes.title: French occupation, 1923-1925 (Germany, AD 1923–AD 1925)
nodes.description:
[Ruhr (Germany), AD 1923–AD 1925] French occupation, 1923-1925. Extracted from heading "Ruhr (Germany : Region)--History--French occupation, 1923-1925". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Citing missed reparations deliveries of coal and timber, French and Belgian troops seized the Ruhr industrial basin. The German government called for passive resistance and printed money to pay idled workers, tipping the currency into hyperinflation that wiped out savings and fed extremist politics, including Hitler's failed Munich putsch. The crisis was defused by the Dawes Plan, which rescheduled reparations and brought American loans, and the troops went home.

nodes.name: Louis XIV, 1643-1715 (France, AD 1643–AD 1715)
nodes.title: Louis XIV, 1643-1715 (France, AD 1643–AD 1715)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1643–AD 1715] Louis XIV, 1643-1715. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XIV, 1643-1715". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Sun King turned France into Europe's dominant power and the model of absolute monarchy, governing without a chief minister and drawing the nobility to a gilded life at Versailles. Colbert's economic management, a huge standing army and Vauban's fortresses paid for near-constant warfare that ended in exhaustion during the War of the Spanish Succession. Revoking the Edict of Nantes drove hundreds of thousands of Protestants abroad; French language, cuisine and classical art meanwhile set the standard for courts everywhere.

nodes.name: Paul V, 1605-1621 (Vatican City, AD 1605–AD 1621)
nodes.title: Paul V, 1605-1621 (Vatican City, AD 1605–AD 1621)
nodes.description:
[Papal States, AD 1605–AD 1621] Paul V, 1605-1621. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Paul V, 1605-1621". Added to LCSH in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Camillo Borghese's pontificate pressed papal jurisdictional claims hard, most famously in the losing quarrel with Venice, and it also produced the first formal warning to Galileo in 1616 that Copernicanism was not to be held. In Rome he finished the job on St Peter's, adding Maderno's nave and façade, and rebuilt the ancient Trajanic aqueduct to feed the Acqua Paola fountain. Borghese family patronage, and the collections gathered by his nephew Scipione, seeded one of Europe's great art collections.

nodes.name: Sancho I, 1185-1211 (Portugal, AD 1185–AD 1211)
nodes.title: Sancho I, 1185-1211 (Portugal, AD 1185–AD 1211)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1185–AD 1211] Sancho I, 1185-1211. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Sancho I, 1185-1211". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sancho I earned the nickname 'the Populator' by filling a thinly held frontier with settlers, granting town charters and backing the new military orders to hold land against Almohad raids. He briefly took Silves in 1189 with the help of passing northern crusaders, only to lose it two years later. His long quarrels with the bishops over royal taxation of church property set the pattern for a century of crown–clergy conflict in Portugal.

nodes.name: House of Burgundy, 1384-1477 (Netherlands, AD 1384–AD 1477)
nodes.title: House of Burgundy, 1384-1477 (Netherlands, AD 1384–AD 1477)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1384–AD 1477] House of Burgundy, 1384-1477. Extracted from heading "Netherlands--History--House of Burgundy, 1384-1477". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987, and p.66 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Through marriage, purchase and inheritance the Valois dukes of Burgundy assembled Flanders, Brabant, Holland, Hainaut and their neighbours into a single princely bloc, imposing central councils and taxes on famously independent towns. Their court was the richest in Europe, paying for Van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden, polyphonic music, and the Order of the Golden Fleece. The experiment collapsed when Charles the Bold was killed at Nancy in 1477, but the united Low Countries he left behind became the core of the later Netherlands and Belgium.

nodes.name: Maximilian I, 1493-1519 (Germany, AD 1493–AD 1519)
nodes.title: Maximilian I, 1493-1519 (Germany, AD 1493–AD 1519)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1493–AD 1519] Maximilian I, 1493-1519. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Maximilian I, 1493-1519". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He gained the rich Burgundian Netherlands by marriage and then arranged his children's and grandchildren's marriages so shrewdly that his grandson Charles inherited Spain, the Low Countries, Austria and the Americas. At home he pushed through imperial reforms, an imperial court of justice and a common peace, though the Empire remained loosely governed and he was chronically short of money. He fought long and inconclusive wars in Italy, promoted the Landsknecht infantry, and used printed images and books to build his own legend.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1696-1697 (Poland, AD 1696–AD 1697)
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1696-1697 (Poland, AD 1696–AD 1697)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1696–AD 1697] Interregnum, 1696-1697. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1696-1697". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of John III Sobieski, the victor of Vienna, opened an election in which foreign money flowed freely and two candidates were proclaimed at once: the French prince de Conti and Augustus the Strong of Saxony. Augustus reached Kraków first and was crowned, beginning a Saxon connection that lasted, with interruptions, for two thirds of a century and left the Commonwealth increasingly at the mercy of its neighbours.

nodes.name: Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496 (Italy, AD 1494–AD 1496)
nodes.title: Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496 (Italy, AD 1494–AD 1496)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 1494–AD 1496] Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Expedition of Charles VIII, 1494-1496". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The French king marched an army the length of Italy to claim the throne of Naples, taking the city almost without a fight and exposing how vulnerable the Italian states were to a large modern army with mobile siege artillery. His success frightened Venice, Milan, the Pope and Spain into the League of Venice, which fought him at Fornovo as he retreated. The venture opened more than sixty years of Italian Wars and made the peninsula a battleground for foreign powers.
