nodes.name: Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775 (Russia, AD 1773–AD 1775)
nodes.title: Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775 (Russia, AD 1773–AD 1775)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1773–AD 1775] Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Rebellion of Pugachev, 1773-1775". Added to LCSH in 2003; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Yemelyan Pugachev, a Don Cossack deserter, claimed to be the murdered Tsar Peter III and drew Cossacks, serfs, Old Believers, Bashkirs and Ural factory workers into the largest popular revolt in Russian history. Rebel armies took Kazan and threatened the Volga heartland before Catherine II's troops, freed up by peace with the Ottomans, crushed them; Pugachev was quartered in Moscow. The shock hardened Catherine against reform, tightened noble control over serfs, and led to the reorganisation of provincial government to prevent anything similar.

nodes.name: Peter I, 1689-1725 (Russia, AD 1689–AD 1725)
nodes.title: Peter I, 1689-1725 (Russia, AD 1689–AD 1725)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1689–AD 1725] Peter I, 1689-1725. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Peter I, 1689-1725". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peter the Great dragged Russia into the European state system by force of will, building a navy, remodelling the army, shaving beards and taxing those who kept them, and founding a new capital on Baltic marshland at enormous human cost. Victory over Sweden at Poltava broke the northern balance of power and made Russia a great power; in 1721 he took the title of emperor. His reforms of administration, the church and the nobility set the framework of the Russian state for two centuries, and the argument over whether the westernisation was salvation or violence has never stopped.

nodes.name: Allied occupation, 1945-1955 (Austria, AD 1945–AD 1955)
nodes.title: Allied occupation, 1945-1955 (Austria, AD 1945–AD 1955)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1945–AD 1955] Allied occupation, 1945-1955. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Allied occupation, 1945-1955". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Austria was split into American, British, French and Soviet zones, with Vienna similarly quartered and patrolled by joint four-power teams. Treated as Hitler's first victim rather than an enemy state, the country kept its own government throughout and avoided the permanent partition that befell Germany. The State Treaty of 1955 withdrew all foreign troops in exchange for a pledge of permanent neutrality.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Belarus, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Belarus, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.description:
[Belarus, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Belarus--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

nodes.name: Grand duchy, 1806-1918 (Germany, AD 1806–AD 1918)
nodes.title: Grand duchy, 1806-1918 (Germany, AD 1806–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Hesse (Germany), AD 1806–AD 1918] Grand duchy, 1806-1918. Extracted from heading "Hesse (Germany)--History--1806-1918". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Napoleon dismantled the Holy Roman Empire, several German princes were promoted to grand dukes, creating states such as Baden, Hesse and the Mecklenburgs. They kept their crowns through the German Confederation and then as constituent states of Bismarck's empire, each with its own court, army contingent, constitution and postage stamps. All of them fell together in the revolution of November 1918.

nodes.name: Christian III, 1534-1559 (Denmark, AD 1534–AD 1559)
nodes.title: Christian III, 1534-1559 (Denmark, AD 1534–AD 1559)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1534–AD 1559] Christian III, 1534-1559. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian III, 1534-1559". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He won the throne in the civil war known as the Count's Feud and immediately arrested the Catholic bishops, confiscating church lands for the crown in 1536. The Lutheran Reformation was imposed from above, with a new church order drawn up with help from Wittenberg and the first complete Danish Bible printed in 1550. Royal finances and royal power both grew enormously on the back of former monastic estates.

nodes.name: Antislavery movement, 1830-1863 (Massachusetts, AD 1830–AD 1863)
nodes.title: Antislavery movement, 1830-1863 (Massachusetts, AD 1830–AD 1863)
nodes.description:
[Boston, Massachusetts, AD 1830–AD 1863] Antislavery movement, 1830-1863. Extracted from heading "Antislavery movements--Massachusetts--Boston". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised 1994. Earlier established form "Boston (Mass.)--History--Antislavery movement, 1830-1863" used as primary label, because it includes dates. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Boston became the engine room of radical abolition, with William Lloyd Garrison launching The Liberator in 1831 and demanding immediate, uncompensated emancipation rather than gradual reform. Black activists, women's antislavery societies, fugitive-slave rescues and speakers like Frederick Douglass made the state a centre of both organising and violent backlash. The movement's pressure helped push a reluctant nation toward emancipation, and Massachusetts raised the first Black regiments of the Civil War.

nodes.name: Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD 1197)

[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1190–AD 1197] Henry VI, 1190-1197. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Barbarossa's son married the heiress of Norman Sicily and seized the island kingdom, briefly encircling the papacy with Hohenstaufen power from the Baltic to Palermo. He financed the effort partly with the enormous ransom extorted from Richard the Lionheart, captured on his way home from crusade. His sudden death at thirty-one, leaving a three-year-old heir, wrecked his plan to make the empire hereditary and plunged Germany into civil war.

nodes.name: Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C (Greece, 354 BC–345 BC)
nodes.title: Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C (Greece, 354 BC–345 BC)

[Greece, 354 BC–345 BC] Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Third Sacred War, 355-346 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dispute over sacred land at Delphi escalated when the Phocians seized the sanctuary and melted down its treasures to hire mercenary armies. The decade of fighting exhausted the central Greek states and gave Philip II of Macedon his opening to intervene as the god's champion. His victory won Macedon a seat on the Delphic council and effective leadership in Greek affairs, a step towards the conquest of Greece itself.

nodes.name: John III Sobieski, 1674-1696 (Poland, AD 1674–AD 1696)
nodes.title: John III Sobieski, 1674-1696 (Poland, AD 1674–AD 1696)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1674–AD 1696] John III Sobieski, 1674-1696. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--John III Sobieski, 1674-1696". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier elected king on the strength of his victories over the Ottomans, he is famous for the ride to Vienna in 1683, where his winged hussars broke the Turkish siege in the largest cavalry charge in history. The victory made him a hero of Christendom and marked the beginning of the Ottoman retreat from central Europe. At home he failed to strengthen the monarchy against a fractious nobility, and built the palace of Wilanów as a private retreat.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1939-1945 (Wilhelmshaven, AD 1939–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1939-1945 (Wilhelmshaven, AD 1939–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Wilhelmshaven (Germany), AD 1939–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1939-1945. Extracted from heading "Wilhelmshaven (Germany)--History--Bombardment, 1939-1945". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Germany's principal North Sea naval base and warship yard was attacked by the RAF within days of the war's outbreak — among the very first bombing raids of the conflict — and was also the target of the first American heavy-bomber raid on Germany in January 1943. Repeated attacks on its docks, U-boat pens and shipbuilding left the town shattered by 1945.

Stephen seized the English throne on his uncle Henry I's death, breaking the oath he had sworn to support Henry's daughter Matilda. The result was two decades of civil war known as the Anarchy, with rival courts, unlicensed castles and a chronicler's famous complaint that Christ and his saints slept. It ended with a settlement making Matilda's son Henry II the heir, founding the Plantagenet dynasty.

nodes.name: Troubles, 1968-1998 (Northern Ireland, AD 1968–AD 1998)
nodes.title: Troubles, 1968-1998 (Northern Ireland, AD 1968–AD 1998)
nodes.description:
[Northern Ireland, AD 1968–AD 1998] Troubles, 1968-1998. Extracted from heading "Northern Ireland--History--1968-1998". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2017. Actual primary title "Northern Ireland--History--1968-1998" was replaced with variant. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Civil rights marches by Northern Ireland's Catholic minority met violent resistance, and within a few years the province was locked into a conflict between republican paramilitaries, loyalist gunmen, the police and the British Army. Around 3,500 people died in bombings, shootings and riots that reached Britain and the Republic as well. The Good Friday Agreement ended it with power-sharing institutions, a compromise that left the border question deliberately unresolved.

nodes.name: Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534 (China, AD 386–AD 534)
nodes.title: Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534 (China, AD 386–AD 534)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 386–AD 534] Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern Wei dynasty, 386-534". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.16 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by the Tuoba Xianbei, this was the state that finally ended a century of warlordism in northern China. Its emperors sponsored Buddhist carving at Yungang and Longmen, ordered a great persecution of Buddhism and then reversed it, and moved the capital to Luoyang as part of a programme of Chinese-style reform. Mutiny among the neglected northern garrisons brought it down in the 530s.

nodes.name: Isabel I, 1474-1504 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1474–AD 1504)
nodes.title: Isabel I, 1474-1504 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1474–AD 1504)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1474–AD 1504] Isabel I, 1474-1504. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile, Spain. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Isabel I, 1474-1504". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1998. Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Isabella's contested accession and her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon joined the two great Iberian crowns in a personal union that became the foundation of Spain. Her reign brought the fall of Granada in 1492, ending Muslim rule in Iberia, the establishment of the Spanish Inquisition and the expulsion of the Jews, and royal backing for Columbus's voyage west. She also curbed the Castilian nobility, reformed the coinage and courts, and left a monarchy strong enough to build an empire.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1992-2006 (Algeria, AD 1992–AD 2006)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1992-2006 (Algeria, AD 1992–AD 2006)
nodes.description:
[Algeria, AD 1992–AD 2006] Civil War, 1992-2006. Extracted from heading "Algeria--History--Civil War, 1992-2006". Added to LCSH in 2012, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The army cancelled elections that the Islamic Salvation Front was poised to win, and the country descended into a decade of insurgency and massacre. Armed Islamist groups and state forces both targeted civilians, and journalists, intellectuals and whole villages were slaughtered in what Algerians call the "black decade". An amnesty policy under President Bouteflika wound the conflict down while leaving responsibility for perhaps 150,000 deaths largely unexamined.

nodes.name: Dirty War, 1976-1983 (Argentina, AD 1976–AD 1983)
nodes.title: Dirty War, 1976-1983 (Argentina, AD 1976–AD 1983)
nodes.description:
[Argentina , AD 1976–AD 1983] Dirty War, 1976-1983. Extracted from heading "Argentina--History--Dirty War, 1976-1983". Added to LCSH in 2003, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A military junta seized power and set out to eliminate 'subversion' through clandestine detention centres, torture and the killing of thousands of people who simply disappeared, some thrown alive from aircraft into the sea. Babies born to detained women were taken and given to other families, a crime still being unravelled by DNA testing today. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo circled the square in white headscarves demanding answers, and the regime's collapse after defeat in the Falklands led to a democratic government that put its own former commanders on trial.

nodes.name: Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C (ancient Rome, 87 BC–62 BC)
nodes.title: Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C (ancient Rome, 87 BC–62 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 87 BC–62 BC] Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Mithridatic Wars, 88-63 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three wars between Rome and Mithridates VI of Pontus, who exploited resentment of Roman tax-farmers by orchestrating the massacre of tens of thousands of Italians across Asia Minor. Sulla, Lucullus and finally Pompey campaigned against him, and the fighting spilled into Greece and Armenia before Mithridates died a fugitive in the Crimea. Victory left Rome in direct control of Anatolia and Syria, and gave Pompey the wealth and clientele that fed the politics of the late Republic.

nodes.name: Chimurenga War, 1966-1980 (Zimbabwe, AD 1966–AD 1980)
nodes.title: Chimurenga War, 1966-1980 (Zimbabwe, AD 1966–AD 1980)
nodes.description:
[Zimbabwe, AD 1966–AD 1980] Chimurenga War, 1966-1980. Extracted from heading "Zimbabwe--History--Chimurenga War, 1966-1980". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.132 of LCSH 1987, and p.110 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Guerrilla armies of ZANU and ZAPU, based in Zambia and Mozambique and supplied by China and the Soviet bloc, fought the white minority government that had unilaterally declared independence from Britain. Fighting spread from border skirmishes to a rural war of ambushes, protected villages and cross-border raids that wore down the Rhodesian state and its economy under sanctions. The Lancaster House settlement ended it with elections that brought Robert Mugabe to power and created Zimbabwe.

Zambia, Mulilansolo

nodes.name: Ava kingdom, 1364-1527 (Burma, AD 1364–AD 1527)
nodes.title: Ava kingdom, 1364-1527 (Burma, AD 1364–AD 1527)
nodes.description:
[Burma, AD 1364–AD 1527] Ava kingdom, 1364-1527. Extracted from heading "Burma--History--Ava kingdom, 1364-1527". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded on the Irrawaddy by Thado Minbya, Ava saw itself as the heir of Pagan and spent decades trying to reconquer the Mon kingdom of Pegu in the south in the long, inconclusive Forty Years' War. Its court produced a golden age of Burmese poetry and chronicle writing even as Shan raids and rebellious vassals ate away at its power. Shan confederates sacked the city in 1527, splintering upper Burma.

nodes.name: Claudius II, 268-270? (Roman Empire, AD 268–AD 270)
nodes.title: Claudius II, 268-270? (Roman Empire, AD 268–AD 270)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 268–AD 270] Claudius II, 268-270?. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Claudius II, 268-270?". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-emperor raised by the army during the worst years of imperial breakdown, when Gaul and Palmyra had broken away and plague and invasion were constant. He won a crushing victory over the Goths at Naissus, earning the title Gothicus, before dying of plague after barely two years. His short reign began the run of tough Illyrian emperors who eventually put the empire back together.

nodes.name: Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609 (Poland, AD 1606–AD 1609)
nodes.title: Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609 (Poland, AD 1606–AD 1609)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1606–AD 1609] Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Rebellion of Zebrzydowski, 1606-1609". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A legal revolt, or rokosz, in which nobles led by Mikołaj Zebrzydowski took up arms against Sigismund III Vasa, accusing him of scheming for absolute rule and of Jesuit and Habsburg sympathies. The king won the battle at Guzów in 1607 but had to pardon the rebels and abandon his reform plans. The outcome entrenched the szlachta's veto over royal power, weakening central authority in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for the rest of its existence.

nodes.name: Luís I, 1861-1889 (Portugal, AD 1861–AD 1889)
nodes.title: Luís I, 1861-1889 (Portugal, AD 1861–AD 1889)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1861–AD 1889] Luís I, 1861-1889. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Luís I, 1861-1889". Added to LCSH in 2013, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cultured constitutional monarch who translated Shakespeare into Portuguese while parliament governed through the rotation of two rival parties. His reign saw railways and telegraphs spread, the death penalty and slavery in the colonies abolished, and Portugal stake ambitious claims in Africa that would soon collide with British interests.

nodes.name: Peter I, 1782-1830 (Montenegro, AD 1782–AD 1830)
nodes.title: Peter I, 1782-1830 (Montenegro, AD 1782–AD 1830)
nodes.description:
[Montenegro, AD 1782–AD 1830] Peter I, 1782-1830. Extracted from heading "Montenegro--History--Peter I, 1782-1830". Added to LCSH in 2005. Alternate label "Petar I, 1782-1830" appears on p.79 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Petar I Petrović-Njegoš ruled as prince-bishop, combining spiritual and political authority over a fractious set of clans. He beat back two Ottoman invasions at Martinići and Krusi, issued Montenegro's first written law code, and worked to replace blood feud with a central court. Canonised after his death as St Peter of Cetinje, he is treated as the founder of the modern Montenegrin state.

nodes.name: Joachim Murat, 1808-1815 (Naples, AD 1808–AD 1815)
nodes.title: Joachim Murat, 1808-1815 (Naples, AD 1808–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1808–AD 1815] Joachim Murat, 1808-1815. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Joachim Murat, 1808-1815". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's cavalry marshal and brother-in-law ruled Naples as king, abolishing feudal dues, imposing the Napoleonic Code and reorganising the army and administration. When the empire collapsed he tried to rally Italians to his cause with a call for national unity, was defeated at Tolentino, and was shot by firing squad. His brief reign left southern Italy with reformed institutions and an early taste of Italian nationalism.

nodes.name: Anschluss movement, 1918-1938 (Austria, AD 1918–AD 1938)
nodes.title: Anschluss movement, 1918-1938 (Austria, AD 1918–AD 1938)
nodes.description:
[Austria, Germany, AD 1918–AD 1938] Anschluss movement, 1918-1938. Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany. Extracted from heading "Anschluss movement, 1918-1938". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Habsburg empire dissolved, the German-speaking rump declared itself part of Germany, only to be forbidden union by the peace treaties and left as a small, economically shaky republic. Support for Anschluss ran across the political spectrum for years, but the 1930s brought paramilitary street fighting, a brief civil war, an authoritarian corporate state and the murder of Chancellor Dollfuss by Nazis. Under German military pressure Austria was annexed in March 1938, greeted by cheering crowds in Vienna and followed at once by persecution of Austrian Jews.

nodes.name: Vladislaus III, 1434-1444 (Poland, AD 1434–AD 1444)
nodes.title: Vladislaus III, 1434-1444 (Poland, AD 1434–AD 1444)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1434–AD 1444] Vladislaus III, 1434-1444. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus III, 1434-1444". Added to LCSH in 1999; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Crowned as a boy in Poland and later elected king of Hungary as well, Władysław was pushed by papal legates into leading crusading campaigns against the advancing Ottomans in the Balkans. He broke a sworn truce to march on Varna, where his army was destroyed and the young king was killed and his body never found. The defeat ended serious Western efforts to halt the Ottomans before Constantinople fell nine years later.

nodes.name: Sigismund I, 1506-1548 (Poland, AD 1506–AD 1548)
nodes.title: Sigismund I, 1506-1548 (Poland, AD 1506–AD 1548)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1506–AD 1548] Sigismund I, 1506-1548. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Sigismund I, 1506-1548". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sigismund the Old ruled a Jagiellonian Poland-Lithuania at its height, defeating the Teutonic Order and turning its state into the secular, vassal Duchy of Prussia at the Homage of 1525. His Italian queen, Bona Sforza, brought Renaissance architects, artists and cooks to Kraków, and Wawel Castle was rebuilt as an arcaded Italianate palace. Beneath the splendour, the gentry were already pressing for reform of royal lands and offices, a movement that would shape the next reign.

nodes.name: Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710 (France, AD 1702–AD 1710)
nodes.title: Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710 (France, AD 1702–AD 1710)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1702–AD 1710] Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710. Extracted from heading "France--History--Insurrection of the Camisards, 1702-1710". Added to LCSH and revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Protestant peasants and artisans of the Cévennes rose against the dragoons and priests sent to enforce Catholic conformity after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Fighting in small bands led by prophets and lay preachers, they held off royal armies far larger than themselves in a brutal guerrilla war of burned villages. The revolt failed but forced a de facto tolerance in the mountains, and its visionary preachers carried French prophetic Protestantism to London and beyond.

nodes.name: Charles I, 1516-1556 (Spain, AD 1516–AD 1556)
nodes.title: Charles I, 1516-1556 (Spain, AD 1516–AD 1556)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1516–AD 1556] Charles I, 1516-1556. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Charles I, 1516-1556". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Flemish-raised teenager inherited Castile, Aragon, Naples and the Indies, and within three years added the Holy Roman Empire, binding Spain into a dynastic system stretching from the Low Countries to Vienna. Castilian towns rose against the foreign king in the Comuneros revolt and were crushed; meanwhile Cortés took Mexico and Pizarro Peru, and American silver began funding endless European wars. Exhausted, he divided the inheritance and retired to a monastery at Yuste, leaving Spain to his son and the imperial title to his brother.

nodes.name: Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1295–AD 1312)
nodes.title: Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1295–AD 1312)
nodes.description:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1295–AD 1312] Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Ferdinand IV, 1295-1312". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the throne as a child amid rival claims and noble rebellion, and survived largely through the political skill of his mother, María de Molina, who held the kingdom together during the regency. As an adult he campaigned against Granada and captured Gibraltar in 1309, the first Christian seizure of the rock. His sudden death at twenty-six earned him the nickname "el Emplazado", the Summoned, from the legend that condemned men had called him to divine judgement.

nodes.name: Charles III, 898-922 (France, AD 898–AD 922)
nodes.title: Charles III, 898-922 (France, AD 898–AD 922)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 898–AD 922] Charles III, 898-922. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles III, 898-922". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Known as the Simple, meaning straightforward rather than stupid, he made the bargain that created Normandy, granting land around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo in exchange for baptism and defence of the Seine. He briefly recovered Lotharingia for the West Frankish crown. His reliance on a favoured counsellor alienated the great magnates, who deposed him in 922; he died a prisoner at Péronne.

nodes.name: Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925 (Iran, AD 1794–AD 1925)
nodes.title: Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925 (Iran, AD 1794–AD 1925)
nodes.description:
[Iran, AD 1794–AD 1925] Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Qajar dynasty, 1794-1925". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by Agha Mohammad Khan after decades of civil war, the Qajar state reunified Iran and made Tehran its capital, but lost the Caucasus to Russia and spent the nineteenth century balancing Russian and British ambitions. Concessions sold to foreigners, notably over tobacco, triggered mass protest led by merchants and clerics, and in 1906 forced the shah to accept a constitution and parliament. Qajar visual culture is instantly recognisable: life-size oil portraits of bejewelled princes, painted lacquer boxes, and the pioneering photographs of Nasir al-Din Shah's court.

nodes.name: Sixtus V, 1585-1590 (Vatican City, AD 1585–AD 1590)
nodes.title: Sixtus V, 1585-1590 (Vatican City, AD 1585–AD 1590)
nodes.description:
[Papal States, AD 1585–AD 1590] Sixtus V, 1585-1590. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Sixtus V, 1585-1590". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.89 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A ferocious reformer who hanged bandits by the hundred to restore order in the Papal States and rebuilt the papal government, fixing the College of Cardinals at seventy and dividing the Curia into permanent congregations — a structure that lasted for centuries. He remade Rome physically too, cutting straight avenues between the pilgrimage basilicas, raising the Vatican obelisk in a famous feat of engineering, and pushing the dome of St Peter's to completion. Visitors to Rome still walk his street plan.

nodes.name: Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673 (Poland, AD 1669–AD 1673)
nodes.title: Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673 (Poland, AD 1669–AD 1673)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1669–AD 1673] Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Michael Wisniowiecki, 1669-1673". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected as a compromise candidate by the lesser nobility, this weak and inexperienced king presided over factional paralysis in the Commonwealth. An Ottoman invasion in 1672 forced the humiliating Treaty of Buchach, ceding Podolia and promising tribute to the sultan. He died in 1673, one day before his hetman Jan Sobieski smashed the Turks at Chocim, a victory that carried Sobieski to the throne.

nodes.name: Mahmud I, 1730-1754 (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754)
nodes.title: Mahmud I, 1730-1754 (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1730–AD 1754] Mahmud I, 1730-1754. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mahmud I, 1730-1754". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Placed on the throne by the Patrona Halil uprising that ended the pleasure-loving Tulip Period, he then quietly disposed of the rebels. With the French convert Humbaraci Ahmed Pasha he began drilling artillery units on European lines, and his armies fought Russia and Austria to a successful close, regaining Belgrade in the Treaty of Belgrade of 1739. It was the Ottomans' last clearly victorious war for a century.

nodes.name: German occupation, 1941-1944 (Belarus, AD 1941–AD 1944)
nodes.title: German occupation, 1941-1944 (Belarus, AD 1941–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Belarus, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Belarus--History--German occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

nodes.name: Aurelian, 270-275 (Roman Empire, AD 270–AD 275)
nodes.title: Aurelian, 270-275 (Roman Empire, AD 270–AD 275)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 270–AD 275] Aurelian, 270-275. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Aurelian, 270-275". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Aurelian inherited an empire split three ways and put it back together in five years, crushing the Palmyrene realm of Zenobia in the east and reclaiming the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west. He also drove back Juthungi and Vandals, abandoned Dacia as indefensible, reformed the debased coinage and ringed Rome itself with the walls that still bear his name. Murdered by his own officers, he had bought the empire the breathing space Diocletian would use.

nodes.name: Mehmed III, 1595-1603 (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603)
nodes.title: Mehmed III, 1595-1603 (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1595–AD 1603] Mehmed III, 1595-1603. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mehmed III, 1595-1603". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Mohammed III, 1595-1603" appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign opened with the execution of nineteen brothers, the most extreme application of the Ottoman fratricide law and effectively its last. He personally led the army to victory at Mezőkeresztes in 1596 during the long, grinding war with Habsburg Austria in Hungary. At home the Celali revolts spread through Anatolia, and power increasingly shifted toward the palace household and the sultan's mother.

nodes.name: Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960 (China, AD 951–AD 960)
nodes.title: Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960 (China, AD 951–AD 960)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 951–AD 960] Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960. Extracted from heading "China--History--Later Zhou dynasty, 951-960". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Later Chou dynasty, 951-960" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Five Dynasties, and the one that laid the groundwork for reunification. Emperor Shizong reformed the army, curbed monastic landholding and campaigned successfully against the Southern Tang and the Khitan. His death left a child on the throne, and his general Zhao Kuangyin took power to found the Song.

nodes.name: Alfonso X, 1252-1284 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1252–AD 1284)
nodes.title: Alfonso X, 1252-1284 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1252–AD 1284)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1252–AD 1284] Alfonso X, 1252-1284. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso X, 1252-1284". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Learned King turned his court into a workshop of translation and compilation, producing the Siete Partidas law code, astronomical tables used across Europe, histories of Spain and the world, and the Cantigas de Santa María. He promoted Castilian over Latin for official writing, shaping the language itself. His ruinously expensive campaign to be elected Holy Roman Emperor failed, and he ended his reign deposed in all but name by his rebellious son.

nodes.name: Barons' War, 1263-1267 (England, AD 1263–AD 1267)
nodes.title: Barons' War, 1263-1267 (England, AD 1263–AD 1267)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1263–AD 1267] Barons' War, 1263-1267. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Barons' War, 1263-1267". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Simon de Montfort and a faction of English nobles took up arms against Henry III over his refusal to abide by the reforms he had sworn to at Oxford. After capturing the king at Lewes in 1264, Montfort ruled in his name and summoned a parliament that included townsmen as well as barons and knights — a precedent later cited in the growth of the Commons. Royal victory at Evesham in 1265 killed Montfort and dismembered his body, but the settlement that followed conceded much of what the rebels had demanded.

nodes.name: Uprising of 1357-1358 (France, AD 1357–AD 1358)
nodes.title: Uprising of 1357-1358 (France, AD 1357–AD 1358)
nodes.description:
[Paris, AD 1357–AD 1358] Uprising of 1357-1358. Extracted from heading "Paris (France)--History--Uprising of 1357-1358". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With King John II a prisoner of the English after Poitiers, the kingdom's government broke down: the Paris merchants' provost Etienne Marcel seized control of the capital and forced reforms on the dauphin, while in the countryside north of Paris peasants rose in the bloody revolt known as the Jacquerie. Both movements were crushed within months, the Jacquerie with great slaughter and Marcel by assassination. The episode showed how badly the Hundred Years' War had strained French royal authority, and it hardened noble attitudes toward the peasantry for generations.

nodes.name: Charles II, 840-877 (France, AD 840–AD 877)
nodes.title: Charles II, 840-877 (France, AD 840–AD 877)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 840–AD 877] Charles II, 840-877. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles II, 840-877". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The youngest son of Louis the Pious fought his brothers for a share of the Carolingian inheritance, settling it at Verdun in 843 with the western kingdom that became France. His reign was harried by Viking fleets on the Seine and Loire, bought off with tribute and eventually met with fortified bridges. He was a lavish patron of manuscripts and scholars, and took the imperial crown in 875; the concessions he made to his counts helped turn offices into hereditary lordships.

nodes.name: Basiliscus, 475-476 (Byzantine Empire, AD 475–AD 476)
nodes.title: Basiliscus, 475-476 (Byzantine Empire, AD 475–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 475–AD 476] Basiliscus, 475-476. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Basiliscus, 475-476". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brother-in-law of the previous emperor, Basiliscus drove Zeno out of Constantinople and held the throne for about twenty months. He alienated the capital by issuing an encyclical repudiating the Council of Chalcedon, lost the support of the church and the crowd, and was deposed when Zeno returned; he and his family were shut up in a Cappadocian fortress and left to die.

nodes.name: Wars with Persia, 1576-1639 (Turkey, AD 1576–AD 1639)
nodes.title: Wars with Persia, 1576-1639 (Turkey, AD 1576–AD 1639)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1576–AD 1639] Wars with Persia, 1576-1639. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Wars with Persia, 1576-1639". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long contest between the Ottoman sultans and Safavid Iran, fought over Iraq, the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia and sharpened by the Sunni–Shia divide. Fortunes swung dramatically: the Ottomans seized Tabriz and Georgian territory, then Shah Abbas I reconquered almost everything, before Murad IV retook Baghdad in 1638. The Treaty of Zuhab fixed a frontier close to the modern Iraq–Iran border and held, more or less, for centuries.

nodes.name: Henry III, 1574-1589 (France, AD 1574–AD 1589)
nodes.title: Henry III, 1574-1589 (France, AD 1574–AD 1589)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1574–AD 1589] Henry III, 1574-1589. Extracted from heading "France--History--Henry III, 1574-1589". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Returning from Poland to a kingdom torn by religious war, he tried to steer between militant Catholics and Huguenots and was distrusted by both, mocked for his favourites and his court ceremonial. When the Catholic League forced him out of Paris he had the Duke of Guise assassinated, then allied with his Protestant heir Henry of Navarre to besiege his own capital. A friar stabbed him to death in camp, ending the Valois dynasty.

nodes.name: Christian IX, 1863-1906 (Denmark, AD 1863–AD 1906)
nodes.title: Christian IX, 1863-1906 (Denmark, AD 1863–AD 1906)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1863–AD 1906] Christian IX, 1863-1906. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian IX, 1863-1906".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His accession was the spark for the Second Schleswig War, in which Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864 — a defeat that shrank the country to roughly its modern shape. At home he backed conservative governments that ruled by provisional decree for two decades before finally conceding parliamentary rule in 1901. His children married into the British, Russian, Greek and Norwegian royal houses, earning him the nickname "father-in-law of Europe".

nodes.name: Tang dynasty, 618-907 (China, AD 618–AD 907)
nodes.title: Tang dynasty, 618-907 (China, AD 618–AD 907)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 618–AD 907] Tang dynasty, 618-907. Extracted from heading "China--History--Tang dynasty, 618-907". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "T'ang dynasty, 618-907" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and on p.16 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded by the Li family after the Sui collapse, the Tang built a centralised bureaucracy on recruitment by examination and projected power across the Tarim Basin and into Korea. Its capital was a planned metropolis of a million people and a magnet for foreign religions and goods; Empress Wu Zetian ruled it as China's only reigning female emperor. After the An Lushan revolt the court survived on compromise with provincial commanders until peasant rebellion finished it.

nodes.name: Northern Expedition, 1926-1928 (China, AD 1926–AD 1928)
nodes.title: Northern Expedition, 1926-1928 (China, AD 1926–AD 1928)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1926–AD 1928] Northern Expedition, 1926-1928. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern Expedition, 1926-1928". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Chiang Kai-shek led Nationalist armies north from Guangdong against the warlords who had carved up China since 1916, taking Wuhan, Shanghai and finally Beijing. Midway through the campaign he turned on his Communist allies in the bloody Shanghai purge of 1927, splitting the revolutionary coalition and beginning a civil war that ran for two decades. The result was a Nationalist government at Nanjing whose authority over much of the country remained more nominal than real.

nodes.name: William I, 1871-1888 (Germany, AD 1871–AD 1888)
nodes.title: William I, 1871-1888 (Germany, AD 1871–AD 1888)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1871–AD 1888] William I, 1871-1888. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--William I, 1871-1888". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As the first emperor of a united Germany, Wilhelm presided over a state that within twenty years became Europe's leading industrial and military power. Real direction came from Bismarck, whose government fought the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf, banned socialist organisations, and then introduced the world's first national sickness, accident and old-age insurance. The old emperor's death opened the way to his grandson and the collapse of the Bismarckian system.

nodes.name: Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C (Egypt, 1199 BC–1069 BC)
nodes.title: Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C (Egypt, 1199 BC–1069 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 1199 BC–1069 BC] Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Twentieth dynasty, 1200-ca. 1070 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ramesses III fought off Libyan invasions and the Sea Peoples, recording the battles on the walls of Medinet Habu, but his reign also saw the first recorded labour strike, by the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, and a harem conspiracy that may have killed him. The eight later Ramesses presided over inflation, failing harvests and the systematic looting of the royal tombs, documented in remarkable court papyri. By the end, the high priests of Amun at Thebes were effectively independent, and the New Kingdom dissolved.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1917-1921 (Kyrgyzstan, AD 1917–AD 1921)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1917-1921 (Kyrgyzstan, AD 1917–AD 1921)
nodes.description:
[Kyrgyzstan, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Kyrgyzstan--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

nodes.name: Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD 1125) [p06c6g33ns4]
nodes.title: Henry V, 1106-1125 (Germany, AD 1106–AD 1125) [p06c6g33ns4]
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1106–AD 1125] Henry V, 1106-1125. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry V, 1106-1125". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Salian emperor came to power by deposing his own father, then spent years fighting the papacy over who could invest bishops with ring and staff. The struggle ended in the Concordat of Worms of 1122, a compromise that separated spiritual from secular investiture and set the pattern for church-state relations in Europe. His death without an heir opened the contest between Welf and Hohenstaufen families that shaped German politics for the next century.

nodes.name: Vladislaus II, 1138-1146 (Poland, AD 1138–AD 1146)
nodes.title: Vladislaus II, 1138-1146 (Poland, AD 1138–AD 1146)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1138–AD 1146] Vladislaus II, 1138-1146. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus II, 1138-1146". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The eldest son of Bolesław III inherited the position of senior duke under his father's succession testament, meant to keep Poland united under one overlord. Instead his attempt to subdue his half-brothers failed, he was driven into exile in Germany, and the seniority principle collapsed almost at once. Poland spent the next 175 years split among rival branches of the Piast family.

nodes.name: Diadochi, 323-276 B.C (Macedonia, 322 BC–275 BC)
nodes.title: Diadochi, 323-276 B.C (Macedonia, 322 BC–275 BC)
nodes.description:
[Macedonia, 322 BC–275 BC] Diadochi, 323-276 B.C. Extracted from heading "Macedonia--History--Diadochi, 323-276 B.C". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.74 of LCSH 1987, and p.59 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alexander's generals spent nearly fifty years fighting over his empire, and the wars destroyed his family: his mother, wife and both sons were all killed. Attempts to hold the whole conquest together failed at battles like Ipsus, and the territory settled into rival Macedonian kingdoms in Egypt, Asia and the homeland itself. Macedonia was fought over, invaded by Gauls in 279, and only stabilised when Antigonus Gonatas secured the throne for his dynasty.

nodes.name: Anti-Kine-Killing Movement, 1880-1894 (India, AD 1880–AD 1894)
nodes.title: Anti-Kine-Killing Movement, 1880-1894 (India, AD 1880–AD 1894)
nodes.description:
[India, AD 1880–AD 1894] Anti-Kine-Killing Movement, 1880-1894. Extracted from heading "India--History--Anti-Kine-Killing Movement, 1880-1894". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cow protection societies spread across north India and the Punjab, collecting signatures, prosecuting butchers and staging mass meetings against the slaughter of cattle by Muslims and by British army contractors. Backed by Arya Samaj preachers and rural notables, the campaign built one of the first mass-mobilising Hindu political networks, complete with printed tracts and touring lecturers. It also hardened religious boundaries, erupting in serious riots in 1893 that shaped communal politics for decades.

nodes.name: Sofʹi︠a︡ Alekseevna, 1682-1689 (Russia, AD 1682–AD 1689)
nodes.title: Sofʹi︠a︡ Alekseevna, 1682-1689 (Russia, AD 1682–AD 1689)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1682–AD 1689] Sofʹi︠a︡ Alekseevna, 1682-1689. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Sofʹi︠a︡ Alekseevna, 1682-1689". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Sophia, 1682-1689" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sophia ruled Russia as regent for her young brother Ivan V and half-brother Peter, an unusual position for a woman in Muscovy, and governed with her favourite Vasily Golitsyn. Her government signed a permanent peace with Poland and the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Qing China, but two costly failed campaigns against the Crimean Tatars drained her support. Peter overthrew her in 1689 and confined her to a convent, beginning his own reign.

nodes.name: Charles II, 1665-1700 (Spain, AD 1665–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Charles II, 1665-1700 (Spain, AD 1665–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1665–AD 1700] Charles II, 1665-1700. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Charles II, 1665-1700". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Physically frail and childless, the last Spanish Habsburg inherited at four and spent his life the object of court factions and foreign diplomacy. Spain's European position slipped as Louis XIV nibbled at the Netherlands and Franche-Comté, and the great question of the age became who would inherit the empire when he died. His final will left everything to a French Bourbon prince, triggering the War of the Spanish Succession and a general European conflict.

nodes.name: Anastasius I, 491-518 (Byzantine Empire, AD 491–AD 518)
nodes.title: Anastasius I, 491-518 (Byzantine Empire, AD 491–AD 518)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 491–AD 518] Anastasius I, 491-518. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Anastasius I, 491-518". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A former palace official chosen as emperor in his sixties, Anastasius overhauled Byzantine finance: he abolished the hated chrysargyron tax on trades, reformed the copper coinage into a usable small-change system, and left an enormous surplus in the treasury. He fought a war with Persia, fortified Dara, and built the Long Walls of Thrace. His Miaphysite sympathies provoked riots and Vitalian's revolt, leaving religious division as his main legacy.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1963-1974 (Guinea-Bissau, AD 1963–AD 1974)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1963-1974 (Guinea-Bissau, AD 1963–AD 1974)
nodes.description:
[Guinea-Bissau, AD 1963–AD 1974] Revolution, 1963-1974. Extracted from heading "Guinea-Bissau--History--Revolution, 1963-1974". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Amílcar Cabral's PAIGC turned the swamps and forests of Portuguese Guinea into the most effective of the African liberation wars, running schools, clinics and courts in liberated zones while fighting. Portuguese generals admitted the war was unwinnable; Cabral was assassinated in 1973, months before the party declared independence unilaterally. The strain of this war more than any other pushed Portuguese officers into the coup that ended their own dictatorship.

nodes.name: Mieszko III, 1173-1177 (Poland, AD 1173–AD 1177)
nodes.title: Mieszko III, 1173-1177 (Poland, AD 1173–AD 1177)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1173–AD 1177] Mieszko III, 1173-1177. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Mieszko III, 1173-1177". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Mieszko the Old, duke of Greater Poland, held the senior throne at Kraków during the era when Poland was split among Piast dukes. His heavy-handed rule, coin debasements and tight control of officials provoked the nobles and clergy, who expelled him in favour of his younger brother — an early demonstration that Polish magnates could unmake a ruler.

nodes.name: Austrian occupation, 1915-1918 (Poland, AD 1915–AD 1918)
nodes.title: Austrian occupation, 1915-1918 (Poland, AD 1915–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1915–AD 1918] Austrian occupation, 1915-1918. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Austrian occupation, 1915-1918". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.79 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Central Powers drove the Russians out, the conquered Polish lands were split into a German zone around Warsaw and an Austro-Hungarian zone administered from Lublin. The occupiers requisitioned food, timber and labour, but also permitted Polish schools and courts and, in 1916, proclaimed a nominal Kingdom of Poland to recruit soldiers. Those half-measures gave Polish politicians institutions to seize when the empires collapsed in November 1918.

nodes.name: Sonderbund, 1845-1847 (Switzerland, AD 1845–AD 1847)
nodes.title: Sonderbund, 1845-1847 (Switzerland, AD 1845–AD 1847)
nodes.description: [Switzerland, AD 1845–AD 1847] Sonderbund, 1845-1847. Extracted from heading "Switzerland--History--Sonderbund, 1845-1847". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.114 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.97 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

nodes.name: Louis VI, 1108-1137 (France, AD 1108–AD 1137)
nodes.title: Louis VI, 1108-1137 (France, AD 1108–AD 1137)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1108–AD 1137] Louis VI, 1108-1137. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis VI, 1108-1137". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spent his reign hammering the robber barons of the Île-de-France into submission, making the small royal domain around Paris genuinely governable for the first time. He allied with the towns and the Church, and his adviser Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis both shaped policy and wrote his life. He secured Aquitaine for his son by marriage to Eleanor just before his death, laying groundwork for the later expansion of Capetian power.

nodes.name: King George's War, 1744-1748 (Massachusetts, AD 1744–AD 1748)
nodes.title: King George's War, 1744-1748 (Massachusetts, AD 1744–AD 1748)
nodes.description:
[Massachusetts, AD 1744–AD 1748] King George's War, 1744-1748. Extracted from heading "Massachusetts--History--King George's War, 1744-1748". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 75 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

nodes.name: Rebellion, 66-73 (Israel, AD 66–AD 73)
nodes.title: Rebellion, 66-73 (Israel, AD 66–AD 73)
nodes.description:
[Israel, AD 66–AD 73] Rebellion, 66-73. Spatial coverage: Israel, State of Palestine. Extracted from heading "Jews--History--Rebellion, 66-73". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1989. Spatial coverage designation given as "Jews", spatial coverage extent inferred from knowledge of the Jewish Revolt. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Discontent with Roman taxation, procuratorial abuses and religious provocation exploded into open war; the rebels drove Roman forces from Jerusalem and struck their own coins, but fell into bitter factional fighting. Vespasian and then Titus reconquered the country, and in 70 the Temple was burned and Jerusalem destroyed, with the last holdouts at Masada falling in 73. The loss of the Temple transformed Judaism into a religion of synagogue, text and rabbinic law, and furnished Rome with the triumphal imagery of the Arch of Titus.

nodes.name: German occupation, 1941-1944 (Ukraine, AD 1941–AD 1944)
nodes.title: German occupation, 1941-1944 (Ukraine, AD 1941–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Ukraine--History--German occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p. 118 of LCSH 1986 and p.100 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

nodes.name: Charles XIII, 1809-1818 (Sweden, AD 1809–AD 1818)
nodes.title: Charles XIII, 1809-1818 (Sweden, AD 1809–AD 1818)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1809–AD 1818] Charles XIII, 1809-1818. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles XIII, 1809-1818". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An elderly, childless placeholder installed after officers deposed his nephew in a coup, he presided over the loss of Finland to Russia after six centuries of Swedish rule. In exchange Sweden got a new constitution dividing power between king and Riksdag that lasted until 1974, and Norway, seized from Denmark in 1814. Needing an heir, the Swedes elected a French marshal, Jean Baptiste Bernadotte, who ran the country long before he inherited the crown.

nodes.name: Joseph I, 1705-1711 (Germany, AD 1705–AD 1711)
nodes.title: Joseph I, 1705-1711 (Germany, AD 1705–AD 1711)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1705–AD 1711] Joseph I, 1705-1711. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Joseph I, 1705-1711". Added to LCSH and revised in 2000. An identical entry exists under "Austria--History", but with a separate URI. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inheriting the War of the Spanish Succession from his father, this emperor pushed the Habsburg cause hard, backing Marlborough and Prince Eugene in the campaigns that broke French power in Italy and the Low Countries. At home he sought terms with the Hungarian rebels of Ferenc Rakoczi. His sudden death from smallpox at thirty-two upended everything: his brother Charles inherited both Austria and the Spanish claim, and the allies, unwilling to see one man rule such an empire, began negotiating the peace of Utrecht.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1848-1849 (Slovenia, AD 1848–AD 1849)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1848-1849 (Slovenia, AD 1848–AD 1849)
nodes.description:
[Slovenia, AD 1848–AD 1849] Revolution, 1848-1849. Extracted from heading "Slovenia--History--Revolution, 1848-1849". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Metternich's system let Slovene intellectuals, students in Vienna and Graz among them, publish the programme of a 'United Slovenia', calling for the Slovene-speaking Habsburg lands to be joined in one administrative unit with Slovene as its language. Nothing came of it politically, and neo-absolutism soon closed the space for such demands. But it was the first Slovene national political programme, and it set the goal that Slovene politics pursued for the next seventy years.

nodes.name: French occupation, 1803-1813 (Germany, AD 1803–AD 1813)
nodes.title: French occupation, 1803-1813 (Germany, AD 1803–AD 1813)
nodes.description:
[Hannover (Germany), AD 1803–AD 1813] French occupation, 1803-1813. Extracted from heading "Hannover (Germany : Province)--History--French occupation, 1803-1813". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Imperial Recess swept away ecclesiastical principalities and most free cities, consolidating hundreds of statelets into a few dozen; three years later the Holy Roman Empire was abolished and Napoleon's client states formed the Confederation of the Rhine. Satellite kingdoms like Westphalia received the Civil Code, religious equality and the end of serfdom, while conscription and the Continental System bred resentment. Defeat at Leipzig ended French control but left a simplified map and reform agenda that shaped nineteenth-century Germany.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Kentucky, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Kentucky, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Kentucky, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Kentucky--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.69 of LCSH 1987, and p.67 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Stefan Batory, 1575-1586 (Poland, AD 1575–AD 1586)
nodes.title: Stefan Batory, 1575-1586 (Poland, AD 1575–AD 1586)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1575–AD 1586] Stefan Batory, 1575-1586. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Stefan Batory, 1575-1586". Added to LCSH in 2003. Alternate spelling "Stephen Bathory" appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Transylvanian prince elected king of Poland alongside Anna Jagiellon, remembered above all as a soldier. His campaigns drove Ivan the Terrible out of Livonia and secured the northern frontier, funded by a reformed army and newly organised registered Cossacks. He also founded the university at Vilnius, still one of the region's great institutions.

nodes.name: Angevin period, 1154-1216 (England, AD 1154–AD 1216)
nodes.title: Angevin period, 1154-1216 (England, AD 1154–AD 1216)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1154–AD 1216] Angevin period, 1154-1216. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Angevin period, 1154-1216". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry II, Richard I and John ruled an empire stretching from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, held together by an itinerant court and constant war. Henry's reforms — royal justices touring the shires, juries, the writ system — laid the foundations of English common law, though his quarrel with Thomas Becket ended in murder in Canterbury Cathedral. John lost Normandy and Anjou to the French king and, taxed to the limit, faced a baronial revolt that produced Magna Carta in 1215.

nodes.name: Armenian massacres, 1915-1923 (Armenia, AD 1915–AD 1923)
nodes.title: Armenian massacres, 1915-1923 (Armenia, AD 1915–AD 1923)
nodes.description:
[Armenia, AD 1915–AD 1923] Armenian massacres, 1915-1923. Spatial coverage: Armenia, Turkey. Extracted from heading "Armenian massacres, 1915-1923". Added to LCSH in 1986. Spatial coverage inferred from related subjects (Armenia -- History) and the historical context of the reference (events that happened in Turkey). Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ottoman government deported and destroyed its Armenian population, killing around a million people through massacres, forced marches into the Syrian desert and starvation. An ancient community was erased from most of Anatolia, and the survivors formed a worldwide diaspora. The events shaped the modern concept of genocide - Raphael Lemkin cited them when coining the word - and remain politically contested to this day.

nodes.name: Turkish rule, 1571-1878 (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1878)
nodes.title: Turkish rule, 1571-1878 (Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 1571–AD 1878] Turkish rule, 1571-1878. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--Turkish rule, 1571-1878". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the conquest from Venice the Latin church was dismantled and the Orthodox archbishop became the recognised leader of the Christian population, collecting taxes as well as souls. Muslim settlement created the island's mixed communities, and periodic revolts and heavy taxation marked the centuries. Britain took over the administration in 1878 while the Sultan retained nominal sovereignty.

nodes.name: Plague, 3rd century (Roman Empire, AD 200–AD 300)
nodes.title: Plague, 3rd century (Roman Empire, AD 200–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 200–AD 300] Plague, 3rd century. Extracted from heading "Plague--Rome--History--3rd century". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A devastating epidemic, described by Bishop Cyprian of Carthage, swept the Roman world from the late 240s, reportedly killing thousands a day in the capital and carrying off at least one emperor. It struck alongside civil war, currency debasement and frontier invasions, thinning the army and the tax base during the Crisis of the Third Century. Christian communities won converts by caring for the sick, while the state blamed the disaster on neglect of the old gods and persecuted them for it.

nodes.name: German occupation, 1941-1944 (Lithuania, AD 1941–AD 1944)
nodes.title: German occupation, 1941-1944 (Lithuania, AD 1941–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Lithuania, AD 1941–AD 1944] German occupation, 1941-1944. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--German Occupation, 1941-1944". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.73 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the deadliest occupations of the war, in which roughly a quarter of the population died. Ghettos and mass shootings destroyed Belarusian Jewry, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants in anti-partisan sweeps, and vast forest partisan armies tied down German divisions. The Red Army's Operation Bagration in summer 1944 shattered Army Group Centre and freed the republic, leaving cities like Minsk in ruins.

nodes.name: Süleyman II, 1687-1691 (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691)
nodes.title: Süleyman II, 1687-1691 (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1687–AD 1691] Süleyman II, 1687-1691. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Süleyman II, 1687-1691". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Suleiman II, 1687-1691"" appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Raised to the throne by a janissary revolt after catastrophic defeats in Hungary, this sultan inherited an empire in retreat, with the Habsburgs taking Belgrade and rebellion spreading in the provinces. His reign is remembered chiefly for handing power to the grand vizier Fazıl Mustafa Köprülü, whose tax reforms and counterattack recovered Belgrade in 1690 before he fell in battle the following year.

nodes.name: Period of Consolidation, 1462-1605 (Russia, AD 1462–AD 1605)
nodes.title: Period of Consolidation, 1462-1605 (Russia, AD 1462–AD 1605)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1462–AD 1605] Period of Consolidation, 1462-1605. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Period of Consolidation, 1462-1605". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From Ivan III to Boris Godunov, Moscow absorbed Novgorod and the other Russian principalities, threw off tribute to the Horde, and remade itself as an imperial capital with a new Kremlin and a claim to the Byzantine inheritance. Ivan IV took the title of tsar, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan, and opened Siberia to Russian expansion, while his terror and endless Livonian war exhausted the country. The line ended in dynastic failure and the Time of Troubles.

nodes.name: Mary I, 1553-1558 (England, AD 1553–AD 1558)
nodes.title: Mary I, 1553-1558 (England, AD 1553–AD 1558)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1553–AD 1558] Mary I, 1553-1558. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Mary I, 1553-1558". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

England's first undisputed queen regnant seized the throne from the supporters of Lady Jane Grey and set about undoing the Protestant Reformation, restoring papal authority and the Latin mass. Nearly three hundred Protestants were burned, including Archbishop Cranmer, which earned her the name Bloody Mary in later Protestant memory. Her marriage to Philip of Spain was deeply unpopular, it produced no child, and the war it dragged England into cost the loss of Calais, the last English foothold in France.

nodes.name: Taishō period, 1912-1926 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926)
nodes.title: Taishō period, 1912-1926 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926] Taishō period, 1912-1926. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Taishō period, 1912-1926". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.67 of LCSH 1987, and p.54 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cosmopolitan and unstable decade and a half, remembered for "Taishō democracy": party governments, mass movements, a lively press, and the modern girl in Western dress on the streets of Ginza. Japan profited from the First World War and joined the League of Nations as a great power, but economic slumps, the 1923 Kantō earthquake and rising anxiety about socialism set the stage for the militarism of the following reign.

nodes.name: Frederick II, 1559-1588 (Denmark, AD 1559–AD 1588)
nodes.title: Frederick II, 1559-1588 (Denmark, AD 1559–AD 1588)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1559–AD 1588] Frederick II, 1559-1588. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick II, 1559-1588". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A martial king who fought Sweden to a costly draw in the Northern Seven Years' War, then turned to profiting from the Sound dues and rebuilding. He raised Kronborg at Elsinore as a Renaissance showpiece guarding the strait, and famously gave the island of Hven and a generous income to Tycho Brahe, whose observatory at Uraniborg became the finest in Europe.

nodes.name: Charles XII, 1697-1718 (Sweden, AD 1697–AD 1718)
nodes.title: Charles XII, 1697-1718 (Sweden, AD 1697–AD 1718)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1697–AD 1718] Charles XII, 1697-1718. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles XII, 1697-1718". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Attacked at eighteen by a coalition of Denmark, Poland and Russia, he spent the rest of his life in the field and never returned to Stockholm. Brilliant early victories at Narva and elsewhere ended in disaster at Poltava, followed by five surreal years as a guest-prisoner of the Ottoman sultan. A bullet through the head at a Norwegian fortress ended both the king and Sweden's age as a great power.

nodes.name: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Maryland, AD 1600–AD 1775)
nodes.title: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Maryland, AD 1600–AD 1775)
nodes.description:
[Maryland, AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "Maryland--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.75 of LCSH 1987, and p.73 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Iowa, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Iowa, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Iowa, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Iowa--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987, and p.58 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Kentucky, AD 1861–AD 1865)

nodes.name: Pedro I, 1357-1367 (Portugal, AD 1357–AD 1367)
nodes.title: Pedro I, 1357-1367 (Portugal, AD 1357–AD 1367)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1357–AD 1367] Pedro I, 1357-1367. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Pedro I, 1357-1367". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Remembered as Pedro the Just, he rode a circuit of the kingdom hearing complaints and punishing corrupt officials, and clashed with the Church over clerical immunity. His reign is inseparable from the story of Inês de Castro, the Galician noblewoman his father had murdered: on taking the throne he hunted down her killers and had them executed, and built the paired tombs at Alcobaça that still face each other. A decade of peace and full treasuries left Portugal prosperous when his son Fernando inherited it.

nodes.name: German occupation, 1940-1944 (Luxembourg, AD 1940–AD 1944)
nodes.title: German occupation, 1940-1944 (Luxembourg, AD 1940–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Luxembourg, AD 1940–AD 1944] German occupation, 1940-1944. Extracted from heading "Luxembourg--History--German occupation, 1940-1944". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Grand Duchy was overrun in a day and, unlike other occupied states, was treated as German soil and attached to the Gau Moselland. French was banned, names were Germanised, and young men were conscripted into the Wehrmacht, prompting a general strike in 1942 that was answered with executions and deportations. The government-in-exile in London kept the country's legal existence alive until liberation in September 1944.
