nodes.name: Alexander I, 1801-1825 (Russia, AD 1801–AD 1825)
nodes.title: Alexander I, 1801-1825 (Russia, AD 1801–AD 1825)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1801–AD 1825] Alexander I, 1801-1825. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Alexander I, 1801-1825". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Came to the throne over his murdered father's body, flirted with liberal reform, then found himself Napoleon's chief antagonist: allied at Tilsit, invaded in 1812, and riding into Paris as the man who broke the Grande Armée. At the Congress of Vienna he redrew Europe and pushed his mystical Holy Alliance, but turned conservative at home, and his sudden death triggered the Decembrist revolt.

nodes.name: Capetians, 987-1328 (France, AD 987–AD 1328)
nodes.title: Capetians, 987-1328 (France, AD 987–AD 1328)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 987–AD 1328] Capetians, 987-1328. Extracted from heading "France--History--Capetians, 987-1328". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.28 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Hugh Capet's family held the French crown for over three centuries by a mixture of luck, fertility and the habit of crowning the heir during the father's lifetime. From a small domain around Paris they grew into rulers who seized Normandy and the south, built up royal courts and taxation, and made the Ile-de-France the centre of Gothic architecture and scholastic learning. The line's failure of male heirs in 1328 triggered the dynastic dispute behind the Hundred Years War.

nodes.name: New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847 (New Zealand, AD 1843–AD 1847)
nodes.title: New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847 (New Zealand, AD 1843–AD 1847)
nodes.description:
[New Zealand, AD 1843–AD 1847] New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847. Extracted from heading "New Zealand--History--New Zealand Wars, 1843-1847". Added to LCSH in 2004. Sources cited: Belich, J. The New Zealand wars and the Victorian interpretation of racial conflict, 1986: p. 204 (three local outbreaks of conflict took place between 1843 and 1847) p. 212 (The period 1847-60 was one of peace between Māori and Pākehā); Oxford hist. of N.Z., 1981: p. 148 (The central role of land in the wars between Māori and Pāehā has often been remarked; sometimes they have been called the Land Wars); The New Zealand Wars web site, Sept. 19, 2003 (The New Zealand Wars were fought in New Zealand between 1843 and 1872) what's in a name (the Maori Wars; the Land Wars; Nga Pakanga Nu Nui o Aotearoa; Nga pakanga o Aotearoa; the Anglo-Maori Wars; the Colonial New Zealand Wars; new Zealand Civil Wars; the overwhelmingly favourite name used these days is undoubtedly the New Zealand Wars). Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first armed clashes over land and sovereignty after the Treaty of Waitangi: the Wairau confrontation with settlers from Nelson, then Hōne Heke's repeated felling of the British flagstaff at Kororāreka and the northern campaign that followed, and fighting in the Hutt Valley and Whanganui. Māori built and abandoned purpose-designed gunfighter pā that absorbed artillery fire and frustrated British troops. The wars settled nothing, and left both sides rehearsing tactics for the far larger conflicts of the 1860s.

nodes.name: Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D (United States, 999 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D (United States, 999 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[eastern North America, 999 BC–AD 1000] Woodland period, ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D. "Here are entered works on the prehistoric culture of eastern North America which extended to the eastern Great Plains and existed ca. 1000 B.C.-ca. 1000 A.D. prior to contact with European influences.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Eastern North American societies took up pottery, buried their dead in mounds, and cultivated native starchy and oily seeds long before maize became a staple. Exchange networks carried Great Lakes copper, Gulf Coast shell and Rocky Mountain obsidian to ceremonial centres in the Ohio Valley. The bow and arrow spread in the later centuries, and rising populations and maize farming led on to the Mississippian towns.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1944-1949 (Greece, AD 1944–AD 1949)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1944-1949 (Greece, AD 1944–AD 1949)
nodes.description:
[Greece, AD 1944–AD 1949] Civil War, 1944-1949. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Civil War, 1944-1949". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As German occupation ended, the communist-led resistance and the British- then American-backed government army fought for control of the country. It was among the first open confrontations of the Cold War: the crisis prompted the Truman Doctrine and large-scale US aid. The government's victory kept Greece in the Western bloc, but left a divided society and decades of anti-communist repression.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Pennsylvania, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Pennsylvania, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Pennsylvania, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Pennsylvania--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 90 of LCSH 1987, and p.88 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Warlord period, 1916-1928 (China, AD 1916–AD 1928)
nodes.title: Warlord period, 1916-1928 (China, AD 1916–AD 1928)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1916–AD 1928] Warlord period, 1916-1928. Extracted from heading "China--History--Warlord period, 1916-1928". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Yuan Shikai's death left the Chinese republic with no centre: regional militarists with private armies fought shifting coalitions while a nominal government in Beijing sold offices and loans to foreigners. Amid the disorder came the May Fourth movement, the New Culture debates and the founding of the Communist Party. The Nationalists' Northern Expedition subdued or absorbed most of the warlords by 1928, though many kept their armies within the new order.

Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elizabeth I steered England to a Protestant settlement that was deliberately broad enough to keep most of her subjects inside the church, while refusing to marry and so leaving the succession open for forty-five years. Her reign saw the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the first English ventures into the Atlantic and the founding of the East India Company. It was also the age of Shakespeare, Marlowe and Spenser, when English became a literary language of the first rank.

nodes.name: War of Independence, 1810-1817 (Argentina, AD 1810–AD 1817)
nodes.title: War of Independence, 1810-1817 (Argentina, AD 1810–AD 1817)
nodes.description:
[Argentina , AD 1810–AD 1817] War of Independence, 1810-1817. Extracted from heading "Argentina--History--War of Independence, 1810-1817". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.5 of LCSH 1987. Alternate label, "Argentine Republic, 1810-1817" appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The May Revolution in Buenos Aires unseated the viceroy in the name of the captive Spanish king, and the provinces of the Río de la Plata slid from autonomy into open separation, formally declared at Tucumán in 1816. Campaigns north into Upper Peru failed repeatedly, so San Martín built an army at Mendoza and took the war over the Andes to Chile instead. Independence was won, but the question of whether Buenos Aires or the provinces would rule opened decades of civil war.

nodes.name: Northern Zhou dynasty, 557-581 (China, AD 557–AD 581)
nodes.title: Northern Zhou dynasty, 557-581 (China, AD 557–AD 581)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 557–AD 581] Northern Zhou dynasty, 557-581. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern Zhou dynasty, 557-581". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Northern Chou dynasty, 557-581" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Based in the northwest, the Yuwen emperors built an army of farmer-soldiers and a cohesive Guanlong aristocracy that would supply the ruling houses of the Sui and Tang. A state suppression of Buddhism in 574 stripped the monasteries of land, wealth and monks. Victory over the Northern Qi in 577 united the north, and four years later the dynasty was overthrown from within.

nodes.name: Germanic rule, 962-1268 (Italy, AD 962–AD 1268)
nodes.title: Germanic rule, 962-1268 (Italy, AD 962–AD 1268)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 962–AD 1268] Germanic rule, 962-1268. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Germanic rule, 962-1268". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 63 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Otto I's imperial coronation in Rome bound the German crown to Italy, and for three centuries emperors marched south to claim it. The result was chronic conflict: the Investiture Contest with the papacy, the northern communes' leagues against Frederick Barbarossa, and the Guelf and Ghibelline factions that split Italian cities. It ended with the execution of the last Hohenstaufen, Conradin, leaving Italy a patchwork of independent city-states and papal and Angevin territories.

nodes.name: Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832 (France, AD 1793–AD 1832)
nodes.title: Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832 (France, AD 1793–AD 1832)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1793–AD 1832] Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832. Extracted from heading "France--History--Wars of the Vendée, 1793-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peasants and rural gentry in western France rose against the revolutionary government's conscription levy and its attack on the Catholic Church, fighting a guerrilla war under the white flag of the Bourbons. The Republic's response — the "infernal columns" that burned farms and killed indiscriminately — left well over a hundred thousand dead and is still argued over as an early case of state mass killing. Smaller risings flared up again under Napoleon and the Restoration, keeping the west a symbol of counter-revolution deep into the nineteenth century.

nodes.name: Wars of Independence, 1809-1830 (Ecuador, AD 1809–AD 1830)
nodes.title: Wars of Independence, 1809-1830 (Ecuador, AD 1809–AD 1830)
nodes.description:
[Ecuador, AD 1809–AD 1830] Wars of Independence, 1809-1830. Extracted from heading "Ecuador--History--Wars of Independence, 1809-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Quito's junta of August 1809 claimed to be the first cry of independence in Spanish America, and its leaders were massacred a year later. Liberation finally came with Sucre's victory on the slopes of Pichincha above Quito in 1822, after which the territory joined Bolívar's Gran Colombia. When that union fell apart in 1830, Ecuador emerged as a separate republic.

nodes.name: Qin-Han dynasties, 221 B.C.-220 A.D (China, 220 BC–AD 220)
nodes.title: Qin-Han dynasties, 221 B.C.-220 A.D (China, 220 BC–AD 220)
nodes.description:
[China, 220 BC–AD 220] Qin-Han dynasties, 221 B.C.-220 A.D. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Four centuries in which the idea of a unified Chinese empire was invented and then made durable. The Qin supplied the bureaucratic apparatus; the Han softened it with Confucian learning, an examined officialdom and state ritual, pushed the frontier into Central Asia and opened the Silk Road, and presided on paper, lacquer, silk and iron. Han tombs are among archaeology's richest sources, and later Chinese would call themselves the Han people ever after.

nodes.name: Pedro V, 1853-1861 (Portugal, AD 1853–AD 1861)
nodes.title: Pedro V, 1853-1861 (Portugal, AD 1853–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1853–AD 1861] Pedro V, 1853-1861. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Pedro V, 1853-1861". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A young, conscientious king who put his energy into modernising a poor country: railways and telegraph lines were laid, roads and hospitals built, and he spent his own fortune on public works and famine relief. His refusal to leave Lisbon during an epidemic cost him his life at 24, and his death was mourned as a national tragedy. The reforming impulse of his reign, driven by the ministries of the Regeneração, outlived him.

nodes.name: Napoleonic Conquest, 1808-1813 (Spain, AD 1808–AD 1813)
nodes.title: Napoleonic Conquest, 1808-1813 (Spain, AD 1808–AD 1813)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1808–AD 1813] Napoleonic Conquest, 1808-1813. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Napoleonic Conquest, 1808-1813". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

French armies crossed the Pyrenees and put Joseph Bonaparte on the throne, triggering a brutal war of sieges, massacres and irregular "guerrilla" fighting that gave the word to the world. With the king a prisoner, patriot juntas filled the vacuum and a rump parliament at Cádiz drafted a liberal constitution in 1812. British and Portuguese forces under Wellington ground the French out, but Spanish America had meanwhile begun governing itself and never fully returned to Madrid's control.

nodes.name: Murad III, 1574-1595 (Turkey, AD 1574–AD 1595)
nodes.title: Murad III, 1574-1595 (Turkey, AD 1574–AD 1595)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1574–AD 1595] Murad III, 1574-1595. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Murad III, 1574-1595". Added to LCSH in 2005; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The sultan never left Istanbul on campaign, and power shifted toward the palace household - his mother and consort, the chief eunuchs and grand viziers who rose and fell rapidly. A long war seized Caucasian territory from the Safavids at ruinous cost, while debased silver coinage and inflation fed janissary mutinies and provincial unrest. His reign also opened formal trade with England and produced some of the finest Ottoman illustrated manuscripts.

nodes.name: Philip IV, 1621-1665 (Spain, AD 1621–AD 1665)
nodes.title: Philip IV, 1621-1665 (Spain, AD 1621–AD 1665)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1621–AD 1665] Philip IV, 1621-1665. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Philip IV, 1621-1665". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spain fought the Thirty Years' War, lost Portugal, faced revolt in Catalonia, and finally conceded Dutch independence in 1648 and defeat to France in 1659. The Count-Duke of Olivares's attempt to make all the kingdoms share the burden of war triggered the crises that broke Habsburg dominance. Yet the same decades produced Velázquez, Zurbarán and Calderón in a golden age of art.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1917-1921 (Tajikistan, AD 1917–AD 1921)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1917-1921 (Tajikistan, AD 1917–AD 1921)
nodes.description:
[Tajikistan, AD 1917–AD 1921] Revolution, 1917-1921. Extracted from heading "Tajikistan--History--Revolution, 1917-1921". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wartime hunger and defeat toppled the tsar in February; by October the Bolsheviks had seized power in Petrograd on the promise of peace, bread and land. What followed was a civil war fought across the whole of the former empire, with famine, epidemic and terror on both sides, and a death toll in the millions. Out of it came the Soviet Union, a one-party state whose existence reorganised international politics for the rest of the century.

nodes.name: Arab rule, 826-961 (Crete, AD 826–AD 961)
nodes.title: Arab rule, 826-961 (Crete, AD 826–AD 961)
nodes.description:
[Crete, AD 826–AD 961] Arab rule, 826-961. Extracted from heading "Crete--History--Arab rule, 826-960". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.24 of LCSH 1987, and on p.19 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A band of Andalusi exiles seized the island and founded an emirate at Chandax, today's Heraklion, ringed by a great ditch that gave the city its name. For over a century the island was the base for fleets that raided the Aegean and the Greek mainland, and Byzantium mounted repeated failed expeditions to dislodge them. Nikephoros Phokas finally took Chandax after a winter siege in 961, reopening the sea lanes and making his reputation as the empire's greatest soldier.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Mississippi, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Mississippi, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Mississippi, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Mississippi--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.78 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Period of military anarchy, 235-284 (Roman Empire, AD 235–AD 284)
nodes.title: Period of military anarchy, 235-284 (Roman Empire, AD 235–AD 284)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 235–AD 284] Period of military anarchy, 235-284. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Period of military anarchy, 235-284". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Some fifty emperors and usurpers in fifty years, most raised by their troops and killed by them, while Persian and Germanic invasions broke through the frontiers and the empire briefly split into three. Silver coinage collapsed, cities threw up walls, and long-distance trade contracted. Aurelian and finally Diocletian restored order, but the reformed state that emerged was more militarised, more bureaucratic and no longer ruled from Rome.

nodes.name: John Casimir, 1583-1592 (Germany, AD 1583–AD 1592)
nodes.title: John Casimir, 1583-1592 (Germany, AD 1583–AD 1592)
nodes.description:
[Palatinate (Germany), AD 1583–AD 1592] John Casimir, 1583-1592. Extracted from heading "Palatinate (Germany)--John Casimir, 1583-1592". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Source notes Palatinate is in modern Germany. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As administrator of the Palatinate for his young nephew, this Wittelsbach prince reversed his brother's Lutheran policy and re-established Calvinism, making Heidelberg a centre of the Reformed faith. He also sent mercenary armies to support the Huguenots in France and the Dutch rebels, tying the Palatinate to the militant Protestant cause across Europe.

properties.notes:
Stoneware 'Schnelle'; domed pewter lid-mount; unglazed; rilled concentric bands on neck and lower body; 3 applied rectangular panels, all identical, divided into 3 zones: top - armorial shield of an Elector of Brandenburg, surmounted by crown, framed by floral ornament; middle - figure of Venus in landscape, inscription, floral frame; bottom - armorial shield of Johan von Schönenburg, surmounted by crown, blossom frame; monogram.; | Type: tankard | Medium: stoneware (unglazed); pewter | Dimensions: 8.50 centimetres base ; 5.50 centimetres rim ; 25.00 centimetres max ; | Culture: Post-Medieval

Siegburg, Germany

nodes.name: Shang dynasty, 1766-1122 B.C. (China, 1765 BC–1121 BC)
nodes.title: Shang dynasty, 1766-1122 B.C. (China, 1765 BC–1121 BC)
nodes.description:
[China, 1765 BC–1121 BC] Shang dynasty, 1766-1122 B.C.. Extracted from heading "China--History--Shang dynasty, 1766-1122 B.C.". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The dates here follow the traditional chronology of later Chinese historians, who dated the dynasty from Tang's overthrow of the Xia to King Wu's victory at Muye. Archaeology at Erligang and Anyang has since shown a real state of walled cities, bronze foundries and chariot warfare, whose oracle-bone inscriptions are China's earliest deciphered writing. The gap between the transmitted dates and the excavated evidence is itself a good illustration of how ancient chronologies get built and revised.

nodes.name: Henry I, 1100-1135 (England, AD 1100–AD 1135)
nodes.title: Henry I, 1100-1135 (England, AD 1100–AD 1135)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1100–AD 1135] Henry I, 1100-1135. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry I, 1100-1135". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Seizing the treasury and crown within days of his brother William Rufus's death in the New Forest, Henry issued a Charter of Liberties promising to end abuses — a document later quarried for Magna Carta. He captured Normandy from his elder brother Robert, imprisoning him for life, and built up a professional royal administration whose exchequer accounts are the first of their kind in Europe. The drowning of his only legitimate son in the White Ship left the succession to his daughter Matilda, and his death was followed by nearly twenty years of civil war.

nodes.name: Early Stuarts, 1603-1649 (England, AD 1603–AD 1649)
nodes.title: Early Stuarts, 1603-1649 (England, AD 1603–AD 1649)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1603–AD 1649] Early Stuarts, 1603-1649. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Early Stuarts, 1603-1649". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne, uniting the crowns and commissioning the King James Bible, while English colonists took root in Virginia, New England and the Caribbean. Quarrels over taxation, royal prerogative and religion hardened under Charles I, who ruled for eleven years without Parliament before war broke out across the three kingdoms. It ended with the king tried and beheaded in Whitehall — an event without precedent in Europe.

nodes.name: King George's War, 1744-1748 (United States, AD 1744–AD 1748)
nodes.title: King George's War, 1744-1748 (United States, AD 1744–AD 1748)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1744–AD 1748] King George's War, 1744-1748. Extracted from heading "United States--History--King George's War, 1744-1748". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 122 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2012. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

nodes.name: British occupation, 1810-1815 (Mauritius, AD 1810–AD 1815)
nodes.title: British occupation, 1810-1815 (Mauritius, AD 1810–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[Réunion, AD 1810–AD 1815] British occupation, 1810-1815. Extracted from heading "Réunion--History--British occupation, 1810-1815". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain took the island from France to shut down the privateers preying on East India Company shipping in the Indian Ocean. The Treaty of Paris confirmed British possession while allowing the French-speaking planters to keep their language, law and Catholic religion. The sugar economy expanded sharply, and after the abolition of slavery the island became the first great destination for indentured labourers from India.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1962-1993 (Eritrea, AD 1962–AD 1993)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1962-1993 (Eritrea, AD 1962–AD 1993)
nodes.description:
[Eritrea, AD 1962–AD 1993] Revolution, 1962-1993. Extracted from heading "Eritrea--History--Revolution, 1962-1993". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Ethiopia dissolved Eritrea's federal autonomy and annexed it, and armed resistance began almost at once, later dominated by the disciplined and famously self-reliant EPLF. Three decades of fighting, including the great sieges and trench warfare around Nakfa, outlasted both Haile Selassie and the Derg. The EPLF took Asmara in 1991 and a referendum confirmed independence in 1993, making Eritrea Africa's newest state at the time.

nodes.name: Insurrection of Tupac Amaru, 1780-1781 (Peru, AD 1780–AD 1781)
nodes.title: Insurrection of Tupac Amaru, 1780-1781 (Peru, AD 1780–AD 1781)
nodes.description:
[Peru, Bolivia, AD 1780–AD 1781] Insurrection of Tupac Amaru, 1780-1781. Spatial coverage: Bolivia, Peru. Extracted from heading "Peru--History--Insurrection of Tupac Amaru, 1780-1781". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

José Gabriel Condorcanqui, claiming descent from the last Inca and taking the name Tupac Amaru II, executed a colonial official and set off the largest rebellion in Spanish America before independence. Tens of thousands of Andean villagers joined, driven by tribute demands, forced labour and the hated repartimiento of goods. The rising was crushed with public torture and dismemberment, and the crown banned Inca dress, portraits and titles, trying to erase the memory it had drawn on.

nodes.name: Christian IV, 1588-1648 (Denmark, AD 1588–AD 1648)
nodes.title: Christian IV, 1588-1648 (Denmark, AD 1588–AD 1648)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1588–AD 1648] Christian IV, 1588-1648. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian IV, 1588-1648". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A restlessly energetic builder-king whose long reign left more physical marks on Norway than any other's: Kongsberg's silver mines, Røros copper, and the towns of Kristiansand and Christiania, the latter laid out on a grid after Oslo burned in 1624. He gave Norway its first printed law code in Norwegian in 1604 and took a personal interest in northern trade and the Arctic. His wars against Sweden and his disastrous intervention in the Thirty Years' War drained the treasury and cost territory.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Empoli, AD 1943–AD 1944)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1943-1944 (Empoli, AD 1943–AD 1944)
nodes.description:
[Empoli (Italy), AD 1943–AD 1944] Bombardment, 1943-1944. Extracted from heading "Empoli (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1944". Added to LCSH in 1995, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Allied bombs fell on the rail yards and working-class quarter of San Lorenzo in July 1943, killing thousands and helping topple Mussolini within days. Rome was afterwards declared an open city, and the awkward question of bombing a capital that held the Vatican and the relics of antiquity shaped how the Allies fought the rest of the Italian campaign.

nodes.name: Helvetic Republic, 1798-1803 (Switzerland, AD 1798–AD 1803)
nodes.title: Helvetic Republic, 1798-1803 (Switzerland, AD 1798–AD 1803)
nodes.description:
[Switzerland, AD 1798–AD 1803] Helvetic Republic, 1798-1803. Extracted from heading "Switzerland--History--Helvetic Republic, 1798-1803". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.114 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

French armies swept away the old confederation of cantons and imposed a single centralised state on the French model, with one citizenship, one currency plan and an end to the rule of privileged towns over subject territories like Vaud and Aargau. The experiment was deeply unpopular, bankrupt and repeatedly overturned by coups, and Napoleon abandoned it with the Act of Mediation, restoring the cantons. But its abolition of feudal dues and subject status was never fully reversed, and it set the terms for the modern Swiss federal state.

nodes.name: Marcus Aurelius, 161-180 (Roman Empire, AD 161–AD 180)
nodes.title: Marcus Aurelius, 161-180 (Roman Empire, AD 161–AD 180)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 161–AD 180] Marcus Aurelius, 161-180. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Marcus Aurelius, 161-180". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Stoic philosopher who spent most of his reign on campaign, defending the Danube frontier against Marcomanni and Quadi while plague brought back from the East thinned the army and the cities. His private notebook, the Meditations, written in camp, became one of the most widely read works of ancient philosophy. By naming his son Commodus as heir he ended the run of adoptive emperors, and later writers dated Rome's decline from his death.

nodes.name: Later Lê dynasty, 1428-1787 (Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1787)
nodes.title: Later Lê dynasty, 1428-1787 (Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1787)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1428–AD 1787] Later Lê dynasty, 1428-1787. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Later Lê dynasty, 1428-1787". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.107 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Lê Lợi drove out the occupying Ming armies and founded a dynasty that gave Vietnam its most influential law code and a thoroughly Confucian bureaucracy under Lê Thánh Tông. Southward expansion crushed the Cham kingdom and pushed Vietnamese settlement toward the Mekong delta. From the sixteenth century the emperors reigned as figureheads while the Trịnh lords in the north and Nguyễn lords in the south ran a divided country.

nodes.name: Frederick V, 1746-1766 (Denmark, AD 1746–AD 1766)
nodes.title: Frederick V, 1746-1766 (Denmark, AD 1746–AD 1766)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1746–AD 1766] Frederick V, 1746-1766. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick V, 1746-1766". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A charming, hard-drinking king who left government largely to able ministers, above all J. H. E. Bernstorff and A. G. Moltke, and Denmark enjoyed peace and profitable neutral trade while wars raged elsewhere. The reign built the Frederiksstaden district of Copenhagen with the Amalienborg palaces and the Marble Church, founded academies of art and sciences, and dispatched the celebrated scientific expedition to Arabia from which only Carsten Niebuhr returned.

nodes.name: French occupation, 1798-1800 (Malta, AD 1798–AD 1800)
nodes.title: French occupation, 1798-1800 (Malta, AD 1798–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Malta, AD 1798–AD 1800] French occupation, 1798-1800. Extracted from heading "Malta--History--French occupation, 1798-1800". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.75 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon, sailing for Egypt, took the island in a few days and ended more than 250 years of rule by the Knights of St John. His administration abolished slavery and the nobility, reorganised courts and schools, and stripped churches of their silver - which provoked a general Maltese uprising that penned the French into Valletta. Blockaded by British and Maltese forces, the garrison starved into surrender, and the island passed to Britain.

nodes.name: Joseph, 1750-1777 (Portugal, AD 1750–AD 1777)
nodes.title: Joseph, 1750-1777 (Portugal, AD 1750–AD 1777)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1750–AD 1777] Joseph, 1750-1777. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Joseph, 1750-1777". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who largely left government to his formidable minister, the Marquis of Pombal. The reign was defined by the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, which destroyed the capital and was answered with a rationally planned, quake-resistant new city centre; by the expulsion of the Jesuits from Portugal and its empire; and by the crushing of noble opposition, the reorganisation of colonial trade and the ending of slavery within mainland Portugal.

nodes.name: Louis XII, 1498-1515 (France, AD 1498–AD 1515)
nodes.title: Louis XII, 1498-1515 (France, AD 1498–AD 1515)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1498–AD 1515] Louis XII, 1498-1515. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XII, 1498-1515". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Pursued the family claim to Milan and the Neapolitan crown, conquering Milan but eventually losing it after Pope Julius II turned the Holy League against him. At home he cut taxes and reformed justice, earning the title 'Father of the People' from the Estates. His Italian wars drew French armies deep into a Renaissance world whose art, architecture and manners they carried back north.

nodes.name: Lascarid dynasty, 1208-1259 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1208–AD 1259)
nodes.title: Lascarid dynasty, 1208-1259 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1208–AD 1259)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1208–AD 1259] Lascarid dynasty, 1208-1259. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Lascarid dynasty, 1208-1259". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With Constantinople in Latin hands after the Fourth Crusade, Theodore Laskaris had himself crowned emperor at Nicaea and built the most effective of the Byzantine successor states. John III Vatatzes turned it into a prosperous, well-governed realm with a strong army and full treasury, steadily reclaiming territory in Anatolia and the Balkans. The dynasty ended when the child John IV was pushed aside and blinded by Michael Palaiologos, who two years later walked into the recovered capital.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1572-1573 (Poland, AD 1572–AD 1573)
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1572-1573 (Poland, AD 1572–AD 1573)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1572–AD 1573] Interregnum, 1572-1573. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Interregnum, 1572-1573". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of Sigismund II Augustus ended the Jagiellonian line and turned the Polish–Lithuanian throne into an elective office chosen by the assembled nobility. The nobles used the vacancy to bind their next king with conditions: the Warsaw Confederation guaranteed religious peace between Catholics and Protestants, and the Henrician Articles set out rights the monarch had to swear to uphold. Henry of Valois was elected, and the Commonwealth's peculiar noble republic took shape.

Bowl of Chinese green Kinrande porcelain, covered with a bright apple-green glaze outside, on which are floral arabesques with formal flowers in thin gold leaf: the inside undecorated. Mark in blue, imitating a pierced Chinese coin. The mount is of silver gilt and engraved; a narrow band encircles the edge, and is connected with the base by four hinged ribs. The foot is of unusual design; the upper member is a drum with an edging of lozenges cast in relief, resting on a fringe of egg-and-tongue pattern; then a deep and wide cavetto and below, a simple round moulding, engraved with a double band of neat linear scrolls, interrupted by ovals containing single letters.; | Type: bowl | Medium: porcelain; gold; silver | Dimensions: 12.34 centimetres dia. of bowl ; 8.10 centimetres dia. of gold base ; 11.00 centimetres incl. gold mount ; 5.30 centimetres without gold mount ;

nodes.name: Revolution, 1820-1821 (Sicily, AD 1820–AD 1821)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1820-1821 (Sicily, AD 1820–AD 1821)
nodes.description:
[Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, AD 1820–AD 1821] Revolution, 1820-1821. Spatial coverage: Naples, Sicily. Extracted from heading "Kingdom of the Two Sicilies--History--Revolution, 1820-1821". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Palermo rose against Bourbon rule from Naples, demanding the restoration of the island's separate constitution and parliament, while liberal officers in Naples forced King Ferdinand to accept the Spanish constitution of 1812. The Sicilian movement split between autonomists and those wanting union with the mainland revolutionaries, and both were crushed when Austrian troops marched south on the orders of the Congress of Laibach. The episode hardened Sicilian resentment of Naples that resurfaced in 1848 and again in 1860.

nodes.name: Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814 (Europe, AD 1813–AD 1814)
nodes.title: Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814 (Europe, AD 1813–AD 1814)
nodes.description:
[Europe, AD 1813–AD 1814] Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814. Extracted from heading "Wars of Liberation, 1813-1814". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the Grande Armée destroyed in Russia, Prussia, Russia, Austria, Sweden and Britain combined against Napoleon in Germany, and the enormous Battle of the Nations at Leipzig drove the French back over the Rhine. The allies invaded France and entered Paris, forcing Napoleon's abdication and exile to Elba. In Germany the campaign was remembered as a national awakening, feeding a nationalism the restored princes then spent decades trying to contain.

nodes.name: Maurya dynasty, ca. 322 B.C.-ca. 185 B.C (India, 321 BC–184 BC)
nodes.title: Maurya dynasty, ca. 322 B.C.-ca. 185 B.C (India, 321 BC–184 BC)
nodes.description:
[India, 321 BC–184 BC] Maurya dynasty, ca. 322 B.C.-ca. 185 B.C. Extracted from heading "India--History--Maurya dynasty, ca. 322 B.C.-ca. 185 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.58 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The dynasty founded by Chandragupta and brought to its height by Ashoka united nearly the whole subcontinent under one administration for the first time, with a treasury, road network and bureaucracy described in the political treatise called the Arthashastra. Ashoka's patronage carried Buddhism far beyond India, and his lion capital from Sarnath is now the emblem of the Republic of India. The empire unravelled after his death and ended when the last king was assassinated by his own general.

nodes.name: Second Empire, 1852-1870 (France, AD 1852–AD 1870)
nodes.title: Second Empire, 1852-1870 (France, AD 1852–AD 1870)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1852–AD 1870] Second Empire, 1852-1870. Extracted from heading "France--History--Second Empire, 1852-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Louis-Napoleon converted his presidency into an empire by coup and plebiscite, ruling first through authoritarian control of press and parliament and later through cautious liberalisation. It was France's boom era: railways and investment banks, free-trade treaties, Haussmann's boulevards driven through medieval Paris, and world's fairs to display it all. Foreign adventure undid it - Crimea and Italy brought prestige, Mexico humiliation, and the Prussian war ended with the emperor's capture at Sedan and the birth of the Third Republic.

nodes.name: Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807 (United States, AD 1805–AD 1807)
nodes.title: Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807 (United States, AD 1805–AD 1807)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1805–AD 1807] Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807. Extracted from heading "Burr Conspiracy, 1805-1807". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Aaron Burr, lately vice-president and notorious for killing Alexander Hamilton in a duel, gathered men and boats on the Ohio for a venture whose aim is still argued over: invading Spanish Mexico, or detaching the western territories from the Union. Betrayed by his co-conspirator General Wilkinson, he was arrested and tried for treason before Chief Justice John Marshall. The acquittal set a deliberately narrow standard for treason in American law, requiring witnesses to an overt act.

nodes.name: Henry I, 1031-1060 (France, AD 1031–AD 1060)
nodes.title: Henry I, 1031-1060 (France, AD 1031–AD 1060)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1031–AD 1060] Henry I, 1031-1060. Extracted from heading "France--History--Henry I, 1031-1060". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The third Capetian king ruled a domain barely larger than the lands around Paris and Orléans, while dukes and counts around him — above all the Normans — grew far stronger. His repeated campaigns against the young William the Bastard of Normandy ended in defeat at Mortemer and Varaville, confirming Norman independence a decade before the conquest of England. His marriage to Anne of Kiev brought an unusual link between the French court and the Rus.

nodes.name: Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439 (China, AD 304–AD 439)
nodes.title: Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439 (China, AD 304–AD 439)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 304–AD 439] Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439. Extracted from heading "China--History--Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Non-Han peoples - Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Qiang and Jie - founded a rapid succession of short-lived states across northern China after the Jin court fled south. Mass migration carried Han elites to the Yangtze while Buddhism spread rapidly under rulers who patronised monks like Kumārajīva and Fotudeng. The Northern Wei finally reunified the north, beginning the long fusion of steppe and Chinese traditions that shaped the later Sui and Tang.

hints.label: Five Hu and the Sixteen kingdoms, 304-439

nodes.name: Jacobite Rebellion, 1745-1746 (Scotland, AD 1745–AD 1746)
nodes.title: Jacobite Rebellion, 1745-1746 (Scotland, AD 1745–AD 1746)
nodes.description:
[Scotland, AD 1745–AD 1746] Jacobite Rebellion, 1745-1746. Extracted from heading "Jacobite Rebellion, 1745-1746". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles Edward Stuart landed in the Hebrides with almost nothing, raised the Highland clans, took Edinburgh and routed a government army at Prestonpans before marching to within 130 miles of London. The retreat ended on Culloden Moor, where his exhausted army was destroyed in under an hour. The aftermath was systematic: punitive laws against Highland dress and weapons, the dismantling of clan chiefs' powers, roads and forts driven through the glens, and the end of armed Stuart hopes.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Maryland, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Maryland, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Maryland, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Maryland--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.75 of LCSH 1987, and p.73 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: English Invasions, 1806-1807 (Argentina, AD 1806–AD 1807)
nodes.title: English Invasions, 1806-1807 (Argentina, AD 1806–AD 1807)
nodes.description:
[Argentina , AD 1806–AD 1807] English Invasions, 1806-1807. Extracted from heading "Argentina--History--English Invasions, 1806-1807". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.3 of LCSH 1975. Source uses the term "Argentine Republic" in LCSH 1975, and "Argentina" in LCSH 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two British attempts to seize Buenos Aires and Montevideo while Spain was allied to Napoleon. The viceroy fled, and the city was retaken and then defended by locally raised militias fighting from rooftops — an experience that showed the colonists they could act without Spain and gave them arms and leaders. Within four years those same militias were central to the revolution of 1810.

nodes.name: Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C (Egypt, 2648 BC–2574 BC)
nodes.title: Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C (Egypt, 2648 BC–2574 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2648 BC–2574 BC] Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Third dynasty, ca. 2649-2575 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

This is the moment monumental stone architecture begins in Egypt: Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by Imhotep, replaced mudbrick mastabas with a six-tiered mountain of limestone inside a vast walled complex. A strong central administration, backed by expeditions to Sinai for copper and turquoise, made such projects possible. The techniques and ambitions worked out here led directly to the true pyramids of the following dynasty.

nodes.name: Decius, 249-251 (Roman Empire, AD 249–AD 251)
nodes.title: Decius, 249-251 (Roman Empire, AD 249–AD 251)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 249–AD 251] Decius, 249-251. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Decius, 249-251". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign remembered for one decree: every inhabitant of the empire was ordered to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate proving it, producing the first systematic, empire-wide persecution of Christians and a wave of martyrdoms and apostasies that split the church for decades. Surviving papyrus libelli from Egypt record ordinary people certifying their compliance. Decius then marched against the Goths and was killed with his son at Abritus, the first Roman emperor to die in battle against a foreign enemy.

nodes.name: Republic, 1931-1939 (Spain, AD 1931–AD 1939)
nodes.title: Republic, 1931-1939 (Spain, AD 1931–AD 1939)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1931–AD 1939] Republic, 1931-1939. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Republic, 1931-1939". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Second Republic arrived when Alfonso XIII left after republican victories in municipal elections, and it attempted rapid change: land reform, women's suffrage, regional autonomy for Catalonia, secular schooling and the separation of Church and state. Polarisation between left and right ran through elections, strikes and the 1934 Asturias rising. A military rebellion in 1936 became the Spanish Civil War, ending in Franco's dictatorship and a long exile for the republic's supporters.

nodes.name: Athelstan, 925-940 (England, AD 925–AD 940)
nodes.title: Athelstan, 925-940 (England, AD 925–AD 940)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 925–AD 940] Athelstan, 925-940. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Athelstan, 925-940". Added to LCSH in 2011, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Athelstan took Northumbria, received the submission of Welsh and Scottish rulers, and at Brunanburh in 937 beat a coalition of Norse, Scots and Strathclyde Britons - leaving him the first king who could plausibly be called king of all England. He issued law codes, reformed the coinage to a single national design, and ran a court that drew scholars and foreign envoys, marrying his sisters into the ruling houses of Europe. The kingdom he assembled outlasted him.

nodes.name: Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD 1197) [p06c6g3s9fz]
nodes.title: Henry VI, 1190-1197 (Germany, AD 1190–AD 1197) [p06c6g3s9fz]
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1190–AD 1197] Henry VI, 1190-1197. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry VI, 1190-1197". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Barbarossa's son married the heiress of Norman Sicily and seized the island kingdom, briefly encircling the papacy with Hohenstaufen power from the Baltic to Palermo. He financed the effort partly with the enormous ransom extorted from Richard the Lionheart, captured on his way home from crusade. His sudden death at thirty-one, leaving a three-year-old heir, wrecked his plan to make the empire hereditary and plunged Germany into civil war.

nodes.name: Henry I, 1214-1217 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1214–AD 1217)
nodes.title: Henry I, 1214-1217 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1214–AD 1217)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1214–AD 1217] Henry I, 1214-1217. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Henry I, 1214-1217". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A boy of ten inherited Castile and never reached adulthood, the kingdom being fought over by regents and the powerful Lara family. He died at thirteen when a roof tile fell on his head while playing. The crown passed to his sister Berenguela, who promptly handed it to her son Ferdinand III — the man who would unite Castile with León and conquer Córdoba and Seville.

nodes.name: Arab period, Spain, 711-1492 (Spain, AD 711–AD 1492)
nodes.title: Arab period, Spain, 711-1492 (Spain, AD 711–AD 1492)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 711–AD 1492] Arab period, Spain, 711-1492. Extracted from variant for heading "Spain--History--711-1516", where it is noted that an earlier LCSH form was "Spain--History--Arab period, 711-1492". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2011. The period is mapped to the  BNF entry " which explains the end-date of 1516 as the death of Ferdinand of Aragon. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Muslim army crossing from North Africa destroyed the Visigothic kingdom in a single campaign season, and within a few years most of the peninsula was al-Andalus. Córdoba under the Umayyads became the largest and most learned city in western Europe, a place where Arabic science, Hebrew poetry and Roman engineering met; after the caliphate fractured into taifa kingdoms, Christian realms pressed south, and the last emirate, Granada, fell in 1492. Its legacy runs through the Alhambra, the vocabulary of Spanish, and the transmission of Greek philosophy and mathematics back into Latin Europe.

nodes.name: Gustav III, 1771-1792 (Sweden, AD 1771–AD 1792)
nodes.title: Gustav III, 1771-1792 (Sweden, AD 1771–AD 1792)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1771–AD 1792] Gustav III, 1771-1792. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav III, 1771-1792". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.112 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A theatrical, French-educated king who seized back royal power in a bloodless coup in 1772, ending Sweden's parliamentary 'Age of Liberty'. He founded the Swedish Academy and the Royal Opera, promoted a distinctive neoclassical style in art and architecture, and pushed through religious toleration and a currency reform, while his war on Russia and his autocratic drift alienated the nobility. He was shot at a masked ball in his own opera house, a killing later retold on stage by Verdi.

nodes.name: Chen dynasty, 557-589 (China, AD 557–AD 589)
nodes.title: Chen dynasty, 557-589 (China, AD 557–AD 589)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 557–AD 589] Chen dynasty, 557-589. Extracted from heading "China--History--Chen dynasty, 557-589". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Ch'en dynasty, 557-589" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The shortest-lived of the four Southern Dynasties, ruling a diminished realm on the lower Yangtze while the militarised north grew steadily stronger. Its conquest by Sui forces marked the end of the long north–south split and the beginning of a reunified empire.

nodes.name: Southern Ming dynasty, 1644-1662 (China, AD 1644–AD 1662)
nodes.title: Southern Ming dynasty, 1644-1662 (China, AD 1644–AD 1662)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1644–AD 1662] Southern Ming dynasty, 1644-1662. Extracted from heading "China--History--Southern Ming dynasty, 1644-1662". Added to LCSH in 2007, revised in the same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Beijing fell and the last Ming emperor hanged himself, loyalist courts were proclaimed in succession at Nanjing, Fuzhou, Guangzhou and finally in the southwest, each undermined by factional quarrels as Qing armies advanced. Resistance drew in the Ming general Zheng Chenggong, who raided the coast and later took Taiwan from the Dutch. The last claimant, the Yongli emperor, fled to Burma and was handed over and executed, ending Ming rule.

nodes.name: Afonso VI, 1656-1683 (Portugal, AD 1656–AD 1683)
nodes.title: Afonso VI, 1656-1683 (Portugal, AD 1656–AD 1683)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1656–AD 1683] Afonso VI, 1656-1683. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Afonso VI, 1656-1683". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Alfonso VI, 1656-1683" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Physically and mentally impaired after a childhood illness, he reigned while others governed, and it was under his nominal rule that Portugal won the decisive victories of Ameixial and Montes Claros that secured independence from Spain. His marriage was annulled, his wife married his brother, and in 1667 that brother deposed him and ruled as regent. He spent his last years confined, first in the Azores and then at Sintra.

nodes.name: Japanese Invasions, 1592-1598 (Korean Peninsula, AD 1592–AD 1598)
nodes.title: Japanese Invasions, 1592-1598 (Korean Peninsula, AD 1592–AD 1598)
nodes.description:
[Korea, AD 1592–AD 1598] Japanese Invasions, 1592-1598. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Japanese Invasions, 1592-1598". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched two massive invasions aimed at conquering Ming China through Korea, overrunning much of the peninsula before stalling. Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet, including armoured 'turtle ships', cut Japanese supply lines, while Ming armies and Korean irregulars ground the invaders down. Korea was left devastated — its population, farmland, palaces and artisan workshops wrecked — and the war helped topple the Toyotomi regime in Japan.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1879-1884 (South Africa, AD 1879–AD 1884)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1879-1884 (South Africa, AD 1879–AD 1884)
nodes.description:
[Zululand, AD 1879–AD 1884] Civil War, 1879-1884. Extracted from heading "Zululand (South Africa)--History--Civil War, 1879-1884". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.132 of LCSH 1987, and p.110 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After British troops destroyed the Zulu kingdom's independence in 1879, Zululand was carved into thirteen chiefdoms, setting rival factions against one another. The restoration of King Cetshwayo in 1883 triggered open warfare between his uSuthu followers and Zibhebhu's Mandlakazi, who sacked the royal homestead at Ulundi; Cetshwayo died the following year. His son Dinuzulu bought Boer help with land, creating the short-lived New Republic and opening the way to full colonial annexation.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (United States, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (United States, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 122 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Alexander, 1879-1886 (Bulgaria, AD 1879–AD 1886)
nodes.title: Alexander, 1879-1886 (Bulgaria, AD 1879–AD 1886)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 1879–AD 1886] Alexander, 1879-1886. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Alexander, 1879-1886". Added to LCSH in 1986; appear on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first prince of newly autonomous Bulgaria, a German-born nephew of the Russian tsarina who quickly fell out with his Russian patrons. He backed the 1885 union with Eastern Rumelia, doubling the country's size, and defeated Serbia's attempt to overturn it. Pro-Russian officers kidnapped him in 1886 and forced his abdication, an early demonstration of how far Bulgarian politics would be pulled between St Petersburg and Vienna.

nodes.name: First Triumvirate, 60-53 B.C (ancient Rome, 59 BC–52 BC)
nodes.title: First Triumvirate, 60-53 B.C (ancient Rome, 59 BC–52 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 59 BC–52 BC] First Triumvirate, 60-53 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--First Triumvirate, 60-53 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Caesar, Pompey and Crassus struck a private alliance to push their agendas past a hostile Senate, dividing the great provincial commands among themselves. It funded Caesar's conquest of Gaul and Crassus's fatal expedition against Parthia. When Crassus died at Carrhae and the marriage tie between Caesar and Pompey lapsed, the arrangement dissolved into civil war.

nodes.name: Peloponnesian War, 431-404 B.C (Greece, 430 BC–403 BC)
nodes.title: Peloponnesian War, 431-404 B.C (Greece, 430 BC–403 BC)

A twenty-seven-year struggle between Athens' maritime empire and Sparta's land alliance that drew in most of the Greek world and ended with Athens starved into surrender, its walls pulled down and its fleet gone. Plague, the disastrous Sicilian expedition and repeated coups hollowed out the Athenian democracy even as Thucydides was writing its history. The war exhausted the city-states and opened the way for Theban and then Macedonian dominance.

nodes.name: Insurrection, 1815-1817 (Serbia, AD 1815–AD 1817)
nodes.title: Insurrection, 1815-1817 (Serbia, AD 1815–AD 1817)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 1815–AD 1817] Insurrection, 1815-1817. Extracted from heading "Serbia--History--Insurrection, 1815-1817". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A second rising, led by Miloš Obrenović, avoided outright war for independence and pressed instead for negotiated concessions. The Ottomans conceded a measure of self-government under Serbian officials, tax collection and an assembly, laying the foundations of the autonomous principality recognised in the 1830s. Miloš consolidated his position by having the returned Karađorđe killed, beginning a dynastic feud between the two families that shaped Serbian politics for a century.

nodes.name: Henry III, 1390-1406 (Castile and León, AD 1390–AD 1406)
nodes.title: Henry III, 1390-1406 (Castile and León, AD 1390–AD 1406)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1390–AD 1406] Henry III, 1390-1406. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile--History--Henry III, 1390-1406". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1998.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Coming to the throne at eleven amid a regency and anti-Jewish pogroms across Castile, he grew into a ruler who curbed the great nobles and rebuilt royal finances despite chronic ill health. He sent embassies far afield, including Ruy González de Clavijo's famous journey to the court of Timur at Samarkand. His reign also saw the first Castilian-sponsored ventures into the Canary Islands, an early step towards Atlantic empire.

nodes.name: Great Trek, 1836-1840 (South Africa, AD 1836–AD 1840)
nodes.title: Great Trek, 1836-1840 (South Africa, AD 1836–AD 1840)
nodes.description:
[South Africa, AD 1836–AD 1840] Great Trek, 1836-1840. Extracted from heading "Africa, South--History--Great Trek". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.1 of LCSH 1975; revised 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Thousands of Dutch-speaking farmers loaded ox-wagons and left the British Cape Colony, driven by resentment at British administration, the abolition of slavery and pressure for land. Their advance into the interior brought violent collisions with the Ndebele and the Zulu, most famously at Blood River, and produced the short-lived Natalia republic and the later Boer states of the Transvaal and Orange Free State. The trek became the founding myth of Afrikaner nationalism and reshaped the political map of southern Africa.

nodes.name: Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375 (Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, AD 1080–AD 1375)
nodes.title: Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375 (Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, AD 1080–AD 1375)
nodes.description:
[Cilicia, AD 1080–AD 1375] Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375. Extracted from heading "Cilicia--History--Armenian Kingdom, 1080-1375". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.22 of LCSH 1987. Revise in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Driven from their homeland by Seljuk invasions, Armenians founded a new state on the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia, where it became an indispensable ally, supplier and staging ground for the Crusader states. Its rulers married into Frankish families, adopted western titles and court fashions, and traded through the port of Ayas with Genoa and Venice. Cilician manuscript illumination, especially the work of Toros Roslin, is the high point of Armenian art; the kingdom fell to the Mamluks.

nodes.name: Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934 (China, AD 1930–AD 1934)
nodes.title: Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934 (China, AD 1930–AD 1934)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1930–AD 1934] Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934. Extracted from heading "China--History--Encirclement Campaigns, 1930-1934". Added to LCSH in 2012, revised in 2013. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Chiang Kai-shek launched five successive offensives to destroy the Communist base areas in Jiangxi and elsewhere. The first four were beaten off by guerrilla tactics, but the fifth used blockhouses, blockades and German military advice to strangle the Jiangxi Soviet. The Red Army broke out in October 1934 and began the Long March, a retreat that nearly destroyed it but brought Mao Zedong to the leadership.

nodes.name: Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D. (Armenia, 188 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D. (Armenia, 188 BC–AD 1)

[Armenia, 188 BC–AD 1] Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D.. Extracted from heading "Armenia--History--Artaxiad (Artashesian) dynasty, 189 B.C.-1 A.D.". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.4 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Artaxias broke free of Seleucid control and founded a dynasty that unified the Armenian highlands and built new capitals such as Artaxata. Under Tigranes the Great the kingdom briefly stretched from the Caspian to the Mediterranean, absorbing what was left of the Seleucid empire - until Roman armies under Lucullus and Pompey cut it back down. Thereafter Armenia became the perpetual buffer and battleground between Rome and Parthia.

nodes.name: Philip V, 1700-1746 (Spain, AD 1700–AD 1746)

nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1700–AD 1746] Philip V, 1700-1746. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Philip V, 1700-1746". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A French Bourbon grandson of Louis XIV whose accession triggered the War of the Spanish Succession, which cost Spain the Netherlands, Naples and Gibraltar. Victory at home let him abolish the separate laws of Aragon and Catalonia and impose centralised, French-style government. Spain shrank in Europe but its administration and navy were rebuilt.

nodes.name: Anne, 1702-1714 (United Kingdom, AD 1702–AD 1714)
nodes.title: Anne, 1702-1714 (United Kingdom, AD 1702–AD 1714)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1702–AD 1714] Anne, 1702-1714. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Anne, 1702-1714". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Stuart monarch presided over the union of the English and Scottish parliaments, creating the kingdom of Great Britain, and over Marlborough's victories at Blenheim and Ramillies in the War of the Spanish Succession. Bitter Whig and Tory rivalry, fought out in a newly unlicensed press and in the queen's own household, shaped modern party politics. None of her many pregnancies produced a surviving heir, so the crown passed by statute to the Protestant house of Hanover and Jacobite claimants were left to rebel.

nodes.name: Six Dynasties, 220-589 (China, AD 220–AD 589)
nodes.title: Six Dynasties, 220-589 (China, AD 220–AD 589)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 220–AD 589] Six Dynasties, 220-589. Extracted from heading "China--History--220-589". Added to LCSH in 1986. Primary title "China--History--220-589" too generic, so variant "Six Dynasties, 220-589" substituted for primary identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nearly four centuries of political fragmentation after the Han, when successive southern courts at Jiankang faced a shifting patchwork of northern regimes. Buddhism became a mass religion in China during these years, cave temples were carved, and the great families of the south turned their estates into centres of art and letters. The disunity ended only when the Sui conquered the south, but the cultural forms invented here shaped the Tang.

nodes.name: Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706 (Russia, AD 1705–AD 1706)
nodes.title: Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706 (Russia, AD 1705–AD 1706)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1705–AD 1706] Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Astrakhan Uprising, 1705-1706". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Streltsy soldiers, townspeople and Old Believers in the Volga delta rose against Peter the Great's taxes, forced shaving of beards and Western dress codes, killing the governor and running the city by an elected council. It took Field Marshal Sheremetev and regular troops to retake Astrakhan. The revolt showed how deeply Peter's reforms cut against ordinary Russians, and it distracted the state at a dangerous moment in the Great Northern War.

nodes.name: Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 640)
nodes.title: Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D (Egypt, 331 BC–AD 640)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 331 BC–AD 640] Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Greco-Roman period, 332 B.C.-640 A.D". Added to LCSH in1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and on p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From Alexander's arrival to the Arab conquest, Egypt was governed by Greek-speaking rulers: first the Ptolemies, then Roman and Byzantine officials. Alexandria became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean with its Library and Museum, while the countryside kept farming, worshipping and writing much as before, now recorded in Greek on papyrus. Christianity took hold early and deeply here, giving rise to the Coptic church and to desert monasticism.

nodes.name: Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632 (Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1632)
nodes.title: Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632 (Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1632)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1611–AD 1632] Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav II Adolf, 1611-1632". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.112 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Gustavus Adolphus turned a peripheral Baltic kingdom into a great power, overhauling the army with mobile field artillery, disciplined musket volleys and conscription, and reforming administration and taxation with his chancellor Axel Oxenstierna. His intervention in the Thirty Years' War rescued the Protestant cause in Germany and won stunning victories at Breitenfeld and the Lech, until he was killed leading a cavalry charge at Lützen. The blood-stained buff coat and horse relics of that battle became national relics, and his campaigns set the template for European warfare for a century.

nodes.name: War of the Pacific, 1879-1884 (Bolivia, AD 1879–AD 1884)
nodes.title: War of the Pacific, 1879-1884 (Bolivia, AD 1879–AD 1884)
nodes.description:
[Bolivia, Chile, Peru, AD 1879–AD 1884] War of the Pacific, 1879-1884. Spatial coverage: Bolivia, Chile, Peru. Extracted from heading "War of the Pacific, 1879-1884". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dispute over taxes on Chilean-run nitrate works in the Atacama escalated into war between Chile and the allied Bolivia and Peru. Chilean naval supremacy and an advance that reached Lima delivered total victory, and Bolivia lost its entire coastal province — leaving it landlocked, a grievance still pursued in international courts. Chile gained the nitrate fields that funded its state for a generation.

nodes.name: Louis XVI, 1774-1793 (France, AD 1774–AD 1793)
nodes.title: Louis XVI, 1774-1793 (France, AD 1774–AD 1793)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1774–AD 1793] Louis XVI, 1774-1793. Extracted from heading "France--History--Louis XVI, 1774-1793". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A well-meaning but indecisive king inherited a bankrupt treasury and a society straining against noble privilege. His attempt to solve the debt crisis by calling the Estates-General in 1789 unleashed the French Revolution, which stripped him of power, turned him into 'Citizen Louis Capet', and ended with his execution by guillotine. His reign closes a thousand years of French absolute monarchy and opens the modern age of republics and mass politics.

nodes.name: War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Estonia, AD 1918–AD 1920)
nodes.title: War of Independence, 1918-1920 (Estonia, AD 1918–AD 1920)
nodes.description:
[Estonia, AD 1918–AD 1920] War of Independence, 1918-1920. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--War of Independence, 1918-1920". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987, and p.25 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Days after declaring independence, the new Estonian state had to fight off an invasion by Soviet Russia, and later German Baltic forces in the south, with help from Finnish volunteers and a British naval squadron. The Treaty of Tartu in 1920 saw Soviet Russia renounce all claims to Estonia — the first such recognition it granted anyone. Radical land reform, breaking up the Baltic German estates, followed as a reward to the soldiers who had fought.

nodes.name: Casimir I, 1040-1058 (Poland, AD 1040–AD 1058)
nodes.title: Casimir I, 1040-1058 (Poland, AD 1040–AD 1058)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1040–AD 1058] Casimir I, 1040-1058. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Casimir I, 1040-1058". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Casimir the Restorer inherited a wrecked kingdom: pagan revolt, peasant uprising and a Bohemian raid had gutted the church and burned Gniezno. With German and Kievan backing he rebuilt the Piast monarchy from Kraków, which became the effective capital in place of the ruined Wielkopolska centres, and re-established bishoprics and monasteries. His patchwork recovery is why Poland survived as a state at all in the eleventh century.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1945-1949 (China, AD 1945–AD 1949)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1945-1949 (China, AD 1945–AD 1949)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1945–AD 1949] Civil War, 1945-1949. Spatial coverage: China, Taiwan. Extracted from heading "China--History--Civil War, 1945-1949". Added to LCSH in 1985, revised in 2014. Spatial coverage extend expanded to include Taiwan based off knowledge of the Chinese Civil War and Chiang Kai-Shek and the Kuomintang's flight to Taiwan after their defeat. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With Japan defeated, the truce between Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists and Mao Zedong's Communists collapsed into full-scale war across the Chinese mainland. Communist forces, helped by land reform in the countryside and Nationalist inflation and corruption, swept south in a series of huge campaigns. The Nationalists retreated to Taiwan, the People's Republic was proclaimed in 1949, and the two governments' rivalry remains unresolved.
