nodes.name: Henry III, 1573-1574 (Poland, AD 1573–AD 1574)
nodes.title: Henry III, 1573-1574 (Poland, AD 1573–AD 1574)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1573–AD 1574] Henry III, 1573-1574. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Henry III, 1573-1574". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The French prince chosen in Poland-Lithuania's first free royal election had to swear to the Henrician Articles, a contract guaranteeing noble privileges, religious toleration and regular parliaments, with the right of rebellion if he broke them. Those articles became the constitutional foundation of the Commonwealth for two centuries. He lasted only months before slipping out of Kraków by night on learning that he had inherited the French throne.

nodes.name: Middle Ages, 500-1500 (Europe, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Middle Ages, 500-1500 (Europe, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Europe, AD 500–AD 1500] Middle Ages, 500-1500. Extracted from heading "Biography--Middle Ages, 500-1500". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2005. Variants include the term "Medieval", but since individual headings use either "Medieval" (as for Social History) or "Middle Ages" (as here), we have entered them as two separate definitions. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A thousand years bracketed by the end of the western Roman Empire and the voyages and printing presses that opened the modern age. Christianity spread to the edges of the continent, Latin remained the language of learning while vernaculars found their first writers, and the manor, the town charter and the university all took form. Visitors usually recognise it through its buildings - castles, monasteries and Gothic cathedrals - but its lasting legacies include universities, banking and representative assemblies.

nodes.name: James II, 1685-1688 (England, AD 1685–AD 1688)
nodes.title: James II, 1685-1688 (England, AD 1685–AD 1688)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1685–AD 1688] James II, 1685-1688. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--James II, 1685-1688". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

England's last Catholic king inherited a broadly loyal country, crushed Monmouth's rebellion, then squandered support by packing the army and universities with Catholics and suspending the penal laws by prerogative. The birth of a Catholic son turned a temporary problem into a dynasty, and leading politicians invited William of Orange to intervene. James fled to France, and the Revolution settlement that followed made Parliament, not the crown, the final authority.

nodes.name: Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598 (France, AD 1562–AD 1598)
nodes.title: Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598 (France, AD 1562–AD 1598)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1562–AD 1598] Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598. Extracted from heading "France--History--Wars of the Huguenots, 1562-1598". Added to LCSH in 2011; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Eight rounds of civil war between Catholic and Calvinist (Huguenot) factions tore the French kingdom apart, mixing religious hatred with a struggle among the Guise, Bourbon and Valois houses for control of a weak crown. The St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, when thousands of Protestants were killed in Paris and provincial towns, became the era's defining atrocity. The fighting ended when the Protestant Henry of Navarre converted, took the throne as Henry IV, and issued the Edict of Nantes granting Huguenots limited toleration and fortified towns — a pragmatic settlement that put royal order above confessional unity.

nodes.name: Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815 (France, AD 1799–AD 1815)
nodes.title: Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815 (France, AD 1799–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1799–AD 1815] Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815. Extracted from heading "France--History--Consulate and First Empire, 1799-1815". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.39 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Napoleon's coup ended the Revolution's parliamentary phase and replaced it with one-man rule, crowned as empire in 1804. He gave France a lasting legal code, prefects, lycées and the Bank of France, and gave Europe fifteen years of war that redrew its map and spread revolutionary law wherever his armies went. Russia, Spain and finally Waterloo undid him, but the institutions largely survived the restoration of the monarchy.

nodes.name: Ferdinand I, 1037-1065 (Spain, AD 1037–AD 1065)
nodes.title: Ferdinand I, 1037-1065 (Spain, AD 1037–AD 1065)
nodes.description:
[Castile (Spain), AD 1037–AD 1065] Ferdinand I, 1037-1065. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Ferdinand I, 1037-1065". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

By inheriting Castile and taking León at the battle of Tamarón, he joined the two realms and made himself the dominant Christian ruler in Iberia. He forced the Muslim taifa kings to pay him tribute, wealth that funded churches and the growing cult of Santiago, then split his lands among his sons and set off the wars that Alfonso VI would eventually win.

nodes.name: Oscar II, 1872-1907 (Sweden, AD 1872–AD 1907)
nodes.title: Oscar II, 1872-1907 (Sweden, AD 1872–AD 1907)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1872–AD 1907] Oscar II, 1872-1907. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Oscar II, 1872-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cultivated monarch, patron of the sciences and sponsor of the mathematics prize that prompted Poincaré's work on the three-body problem, he presided over Sweden's industrial takeoff, mass emigration to America, and the rise of parliamentary politics. He arbitrated international disputes abroad while struggling at home with Norwegian demands, finally accepting the dissolution of the union in his last years.

properties.title: figure — 1890s
properties.notes:
Ceramic group of figures on a stand, made of pottery. In the centre is a man holding a drinking-horn in his left hand and a fan in his right, both signs of his status. Either side of him are two pregnant women, probably his wives, with elaborate hairstyles and scarification, and holding fans, the right-hand one holding a child. Seated in front is a servant or child with a gong and a fowl, possibly a sacrifice for the yam deity, Ifejioku; and a brazier.; | Type: figure | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 47.00 centimetres; 36.00 centimetres; 25.00 centimetres;

Osisa, Latvia

nodes.name: Pogroms, 1919-1920 (Ukraine, AD 1919–AD 1920)
nodes.title: Pogroms, 1919-1920 (Ukraine, AD 1919–AD 1920)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1919–AD 1920] Pogroms, 1919-1920. Extracted from heading "Pogroms--Ukraine". Added to LCSH in 1987, revised in 1994. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

During the Russian Civil War, Ukrainian territory saw the worst anti-Jewish violence before the Holocaust, carried out by Directory troops, Denikin's White forces, peasant warlords such as Hryhoriv and, less often, Red Army units. Estimates of Jewish dead run from tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand, with whole shtetl communities destroyed. The killings shaped Jewish emigration, self-defence movements and the assassination of Symon Petliura in Paris in 1926.

nodes.name: Alfonso VI, 1065-1109 (Spain, AD 1065–AD 1109)
nodes.title: Alfonso VI, 1065-1109 (Spain, AD 1065–AD 1109)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1065–AD 1109] Alfonso VI, 1065-1109. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso VI, 1065-1109". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His capture of Toledo in 1085 handed Christian Spain the old Visigothic capital and made the taifa kings his tributaries. Alarmed, they invited the Almoravids from North Africa, who crushed him at Sagrajas and turned the tide back; the frontier warlord Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, made his own career in the gap. Alfonso styled himself emperor of all Spain and brought the Roman liturgy and Cluniac monks into his realms.

nodes.name: Uprisings, 1846-1848 (Poland, AD 1846–AD 1848)
nodes.title: Uprisings, 1846-1848 (Poland, AD 1846–AD 1848)
nodes.description:
[Wielkopolska (Poland), AD 1846–AD 1848] Uprisings, 1846-1848. Extracted from heading "Wielkopolska (Poland)--History--Uprisings, 1846-1848". Added to LCSH in 1988, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Partitioned Poland's conspirators tried twice to rise. The 1846 Kraków rising ended in disaster when Galician peasants, encouraged by Austrian officials, massacred the very landowners who were leading the revolt; the Free City of Kraków was annexed by Austria in punishment. Two years later the European revolutions brought renewed risings in Poznań and Galicia, also defeated, though serfdom was abolished in Galicia as a consequence. The lesson drawn by later nationalists was that independence would need the peasantry on its side.

nodes.name: Christian VIII, 1839-1848 (Denmark, AD 1839–AD 1848)
nodes.title: Christian VIII, 1839-1848 (Denmark, AD 1839–AD 1848)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1839–AD 1848] Christian VIII, 1839-1848. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian VIII, 1839-1848".  Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.28 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had already been elected king of Norway in 1814 under the Eidsvoll constitution, a short-lived independence he was forced to surrender to Sweden. Danish liberals expected him to grant a constitution too, but he governed as an absolute monarch and only conceded reform on his deathbed. His reign ended just as the Schleswig question boiled over into war and Denmark's absolute monarchy gave way to the Constitution of 1849.

nodes.name: Insurrection, 1866-1868 (Crete, AD 1866–AD 1868)
nodes.title: Insurrection, 1866-1868 (Crete, AD 1866–AD 1868)
nodes.description:
[Crete (Greece), AD 1866–AD 1868] Insurrection, 1866-1868. Extracted from heading "Crete (Greece)--History--Insurrection, 1866-1868". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Cretan Christians rose against Ottoman rule demanding union with Greece, and the war became a cause célèbre across Europe after the defenders of Arkadi Monastery blew up their own powder magazine rather than surrender. The revolt failed militarily but won administrative concessions, and it set the pattern of periodic Cretan risings that kept the island's status an open European question for decades.

nodes.name: British occupation, 1811-1816 (Indonesia, AD 1811–AD 1816)
nodes.title: British occupation, 1811-1816 (Indonesia, AD 1811–AD 1816)
nodes.description:
[Indonesia, AD 1811–AD 1816] British occupation, 1811-1816. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--British occupation, 1811-1816". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.48 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Britain seized Java and the other Dutch possessions during the Napoleonic Wars, installing Thomas Stamford Raffles as lieutenant-governor. He overhauled the land revenue system, curbed forced deliveries, commissioned surveys of Javanese antiquities including Borobudur, and published a History of Java. The islands were returned to the Netherlands after Napoleon's defeat.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1970-1975 (Cambodia, AD 1970–AD 1975)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1970-1975 (Cambodia, AD 1970–AD 1975)
nodes.description:
[Cambodia, AD 1970–AD 1975] Civil War, 1970-1975. Extracted from heading "Cambodia--History--Civil War, 1970-1975". Added to LCSH in 2006; appears on p.15 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After Lon Nol deposed Prince Sihanouk, the country was drawn fully into the Vietnam War, with American bombing of the countryside on an enormous scale. The Khmer Rouge grew from a small maquis into an army capable of taking Phnom Penh in April 1975. Their victory opened four years of forced evacuation, execution and starvation in which roughly a quarter of the population died.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Milan, AD 1940–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1940-1945 (Milan, AD 1940–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Milan (Italy), AD 1940–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1940-1945. Extracted from heading "Milan (Italy)--History--Bombardment, 1940-1945". Added to LCSH in 2001, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

British night raids and American daylight raids grew into a round-the-clock campaign that destroyed the centres of Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and dozens of other cities, killed several hundred thousand civilians and made millions homeless. It absorbed a vast share of German industry and manpower in air defence, and it left a moral argument about area bombing that has never been settled.

nodes.name: Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771 (Sweden, AD 1751–AD 1771)
nodes.title: Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771 (Sweden, AD 1751–AD 1771)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1751–AD 1771] Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Adolphus Frederick, 1751-1771". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who reigned with almost no power during Sweden's Age of Liberty, when the Riksdag and the rival Hat and Cap parties governed the country. His attempt to reclaim royal authority failed so completely that ministers stamped documents with a facsimile of his signature when he refused to sign. The frustrations of his reign set the stage for his son Gustav III's coup and the return of royal absolutism.

nodes.name: Maximilian II, 1564-1576 (Germany, AD 1564–AD 1576)
nodes.title: Maximilian II, 1564-1576 (Germany, AD 1564–AD 1576)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1564–AD 1576] Maximilian II, 1564-1576. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Maximilian II, 1564-1576". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.44 of LCSH 1987, and p.35 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Habsburg emperor of famously ambiguous religion, sympathetic to Lutheran ideas yet never breaking with Rome, he presided over an unusually tolerant interlude in the Empire and allowed Protestant nobles wide latitude in Austria. He kept the peace with the Ottomans at a price, paying tribute for Hungary, and cultivated humanists, botanists and collectors at his court. The confessional compromise he embodied collapsed under his more militantly Catholic successors.

Germany

nodes.name: Carolingian rule, 774-887 (Italy, AD 774–AD 887)
nodes.title: Carolingian rule, 774-887 (Italy, AD 774–AD 887)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 774–AD 887] Carolingian rule, 774-887. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--Carolingian rule, 774-887". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 63 of LCSH 1987 as "Carlovingian rule". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charlemagne answered the pope's appeal by conquering the Lombard kingdom and taking its iron crown, ending two centuries of Lombard rule in the north. Frankish counts and bishops reshaped landholding and church life, while the alliance with Rome laid the foundations of the Papal States. Later Carolingians ruled Italy weakly from Pavia, and their extinction left the peninsula to competing local dynasties.

nodes.name: Papal rule, 1506-1797 (Bologna, AD 1506–AD 1797)
nodes.title: Papal rule, 1506-1797 (Bologna, AD 1506–AD 1797)
nodes.description:
[Bologna (Italy), AD 1506–AD 1797] Papal rule, 1506-1797. Extracted from heading "Bologna (Italy)--History--Papal rule, 1506-1797". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Julius II marched on the city in person and drove out the Bentivoglio family, bringing Bologna into the Papal States as its wealthiest possession after Rome. A cardinal legate ruled alongside a local senate of aristocratic families, and the arrangement funded the university, the great building projects of the Archiginnasio and San Petronio, and the painting workshops of the Carracci and Guido Reni. Charles V was crowned emperor here in 1530; the whole structure fell in 1797 when Napoleon's armies folded the city into a new Italian republic.

nodes.name: Napoleonic rule, 1796-1813 (Lombardy, AD 1796–AD 1815)
nodes.title: Napoleonic rule, 1796-1813 (Lombardy, AD 1796–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[Lombardy (Italy), AD 1796–AD 1815] Napoleonic rule, 1796-1813. Extracted from heading "Lombardy (Italy)--History--1796-1815". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1997. Earlier established form used as primary PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bonaparte's first Italian campaign swept away Austrian and ducal government, and Milan became the capital of a series of French satellite states, culminating in the Kingdom of Italy with Napoleon as king. Church lands were sold, the Napoleonic Code and conscription imposed, roads and administration modernised on the French model. The experience of a single Italian state under one law outlived the empire and fed the nationalist movement of the following decades.

nodes.name: Rebellion of Lubomirski, 1665-1666 (Poland, AD 1665–AD 1666)
nodes.title: Rebellion of Lubomirski, 1665-1666 (Poland, AD 1665–AD 1666)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1665–AD 1666] Rebellion of Lubomirski, 1665-1666. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Rebellion of Lubomirski, 1665-1666". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A powerful magnate, condemned and stripped of office by the royal court, raised an army and beat the king's forces in the field, most decisively at Matwy. His victory killed John Casimir's plan to elect a successor during his own lifetime and to reform the paralysed Polish parliament. The Commonwealth kept its free elections and liberum veto, and the noble anarchy that followed left it defenceless before its neighbours a century later.

nodes.name: Comneni dynasty, 1081-1185 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1185)
nodes.title: Comneni dynasty, 1081-1185 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1185)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1185] Comneni dynasty, 1081-1185. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Comneni Dynasty, 1081-1185". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alexios I salvaged an empire that had lost Anatolia to the Seljuks, buying help with trade privileges to Venice and appeals west that helped launch the First Crusade. His successors recovered coasts and prestige, ran a court culture of literature and learning, and tied the aristocracy to the throne by marriage. The system depended on strong emperors, and after Manuel I's death it unravelled fast, leaving the empire exposed to 1204.

nodes.name: Charles XI, 1660-1697 (Sweden, AD 1660–AD 1697)
nodes.title: Charles XI, 1660-1697 (Sweden, AD 1660–AD 1697)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1660–AD 1697] Charles XI, 1660-1697. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Charles XI, 1660-1697". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After a humiliating war he turned on the aristocracy, clawing back the crown lands they had been granted in the Great Reduction and having parliament declare him an absolute monarch answerable only to God. The confiscated estates funded the allotment system, which settled soldiers on farms and gave Sweden a standing army it could actually pay for. His reign ended in the catastrophic famine of the 1690s, which killed perhaps a third of the Finnish population.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Pennsylvania, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Pennsylvania, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Pennsylvania, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Pennsylvania--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 90 of LCSH 1987, and p.88 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: War of 1860-1861 (Italy, AD 1860–AD 1861)
nodes.title: War of 1860-1861 (Italy, AD 1860–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 1860–AD 1861] War of 1860-1861. Extracted from heading "Italy--History--War of 1860-1861". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Garibaldi sailed for Sicily with a thousand red-shirted volunteers, toppled the Bourbon kingdom in a few months, and handed the south to Victor Emmanuel II rather than claim it himself, while Piedmontese troops marched down through the Papal States to meet him. In March 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed, uniting nearly the whole peninsula under one crown for the first time since antiquity. Rome and Venice remained outside, and the abrupt annexation of the south left resentments and a brigand war that lasted years.

A coup by the Greek military junta against President Makarios triggered a Turkish invasion that left the north of the island under Turkish control and displaced roughly a third of the population in both directions. A UN-patrolled buffer zone still cuts across the island and through Nicosia, the last divided capital in Europe. Repeated negotiations, including the rejected 2004 Annan Plan, have failed to reunify it, and the abandoned resort of Varosha remains sealed behind fences.

[Great Britain, AD 1625–AD 1649] Charles I, 1625-1649. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Charles I, 1625-1649". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king convinced of his divine right ruled eleven years without Parliament, raising money through ship money and other levies that many considered illegal, and pushed ceremonial reforms that Puritans read as creeping popery. Attempts to impose a prayer book on Scotland forced him to recall Parliament, and the quarrel escalated into civil war across the three kingdoms. Defeated twice, he was tried by his own subjects and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall — an event without precedent in Europe. His art collection, one of the finest ever assembled, was sold off by the victors.

The first of the Salian emperors, elected when the Ottonian line died out, and a ruler who leaned on lesser knights and ministeriales rather than the great dukes. He secured hereditary rights for minor vassals in Italy, strengthening a service nobility loyal to the crown. His acquisition of the kingdom of Burgundy joined the three crowns of Germany, Italy and Burgundy under one emperor.

Sharif Hussein of Mecca rose against Ottoman rule with British money, weapons and liaison officers including T. E. Lawrence, while his son Faisal led irregular forces north along the Hejaz railway. The revolt tied down Ottoman troops and culminated in the entry into Damascus in 1918 and a short-lived Arab government there. Its promises of independence collided with the Sykes-Picot agreement and the mandates, a grievance that shaped Arab politics for the rest of the century.

The last Roman emperor, ruling a city surrounded by Ottoman territory and containing perhaps 50,000 people. He accepted union with the Roman church to buy western help that never adequately came, and refused Mehmed II's offer of surrender. He died fighting on the walls when the Ottomans broke through, ending an imperial line traced back to Augustus.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

Known as the Pastry War after a French baker's damage claim, this was a naval blockade and bombardment of Veracruz mounted to force Mexico to pay debts to French residents. It cost Santa Anna a leg - which he later had buried with military honours - and restored his political career. Mexico paid up, and the affair exposed how vulnerable the young republic was to gunboat diplomacy.

Peasants in Ostrobothnia and Savonia, worn down by the billeting and requisitions of Klaus Fleming's cavalry during the long war with Russia, rose in revolt armed largely with clubs and farm tools. They were also pawns in the struggle between Duke Charles and King Sigismund for the Swedish crown. Fleming's professional troops slaughtered them in a series of one-sided battles, and thousands of rebels died.

Emperor Go-Daigo's second attempt to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate began with betrayal and defeat — he was besieged at Kasagi and exiled to the Oki Islands — but guerrilla resistance by Kusunoki Masashige and others kept the revolt alive. When the shogunate's own generals turned, Ashikaga Takauji seized Kyoto and Nitta Yoshisada burned Kamakura, wiping out the Hōjō. The result was the short-lived Kenmu Restoration and, soon after, sixty years of civil war between two rival imperial courts.

Portuguese rule ended abruptly after the Carnation Revolution, and FRELIMO took power in a country whose settler population and technicians had largely fled. A Marxist-Leninist state faced an insurgency by RENAMO, backed by Rhodesia and then apartheid South Africa; the war killed around a million people, displaced millions more, wrecked railways, schools and clinics, and left the countryside strewn with landmines. Peace talks in Rome ended the fighting and led to multiparty elections.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

The Catholic Monarchs ruled Castile and Aragon jointly while keeping each kingdom's institutions intact, tamed the great nobles, and used the new Inquisition as an instrument of royal as much as religious authority. In a single year, 1492, they took Granada, expelled the Jews and sent Columbus west, decisions that ended Muslim rule in Iberia and opened an Atlantic empire. Their marriage alliances placed Habsburg Charles V in line for the whole inheritance, linking Spain to central Europe.

Across the Greek world single rulers seized power in cities that had been run by quarrelling aristocratic clans — Peisistratos and his sons at Athens, Polycrates on Samos — usually with popular backing against the nobility. Tyrants built temples, harbours and water systems, patronised poets, and promoted festivals that gave their cities a common civic identity. Their fall, when Hippias was driven out of Athens, opened the way to Cleisthenes' reforms and the beginnings of democracy.

This outfit, which resembles the Median costume, was most commonly used in Athenian art for Scythians, but since the figure is not bearded, it is most likely in this case to be intended to depict an Amazon archer. Later representations of Persians, Scythians and Amazons lose much of their individual identity. nodes.name: Bãi Sậy Uprising, 1883-1892 (Vietnam, AD 1883–AD 1892)
nodes.title: Bãi Sậy Uprising, 1883-1892 (Vietnam, AD 1883–AD 1892)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1883–AD 1892] Bãi Sậy Uprising, 1883-1892. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Bãi Sậy Uprising, 1883-1892". Added to LCSH in 2012, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A guerrilla resistance to French rule in the Red River Delta, named for the tangled reed marshes its fighters used as a refuge. Led principally by Nguyễn Thiện Thuật under the royalist Cần Vương banner, small bands ambushed patrols and tax collectors across Hưng Yên and Hải Dương for nearly a decade. Its slow strangulation by French columns and local auxiliaries marked the exhaustion of scholar-gentry armed resistance in the north.

nodes.title: Philip III, 1598-1621 (Spain, AD 1598–AD 1621)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1598–AD 1621] Philip III, 1598-1621. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Philip III, 1598-1621". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Government by favourite, as the Duke of Lerma ran Spain while the king hunted and attended court festivals. Peace with England and a truce with the Dutch eased the wars, but inflation, debased copper coinage and the expulsion of some 300,000 Moriscos damaged the economy. It was also the age of Cervantes, Lope de Vega and El Greco.

nodes.name: War of Independence, 1876-1878 (Romania, AD 1876–AD 1878)
nodes.title: War of Independence, 1876-1878 (Romania, AD 1876–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[Romania, AD 1876–AD 1878] War of Independence, 1876-1878. Extracted from heading "Romania--History--War of Independence, 1876-1878". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.98 of LCSH 1987, and p.83 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Romania entered the Russo-Turkish war on Russia's side, and its troops proved decisive at the long siege of Plevna. Victory converted formal Ottoman suzerainty into full sovereignty, recognised by the Congress of Berlin in 1878, though the price included surrendering southern Bessarabia to Russia in exchange for Dobruja. Within three years the principality was proclaimed a kingdom.

nodes.name: Gordianus III, 238-244 (Roman Empire, AD 238–AD 244)
nodes.title: Gordianus III, 238-244 (Roman Empire, AD 238–AD 244)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 238–AD 244] Gordianus III, 238-244. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Gordianus III, 238-244". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A boy of thirteen was raised to the purple after the chaotic 'Year of the Six Emperors', and the empire was effectively run by his praetorian prefect Timesitheus. His reign brought a brief lull in the third-century crisis before a Persian campaign on the Euphrates ended in his death and the accession of Philip the Arab; his coinage, struck in huge quantities, is among the most common Roman issues found across the provinces.

nodes.name: Taiping Rebellion, 1850-1864 (China, AD 1850–AD 1864)
nodes.title: Taiping Rebellion, 1850-1864 (China, AD 1850–AD 1864)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1850–AD 1864] Taiping Rebellion, 1850-1864. Extracted from heading "China--History--Taiping Rebellion, 1850-1864". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2000. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A failed examination candidate who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ raised an army in south China and founded the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace, capturing Nanjing and holding much of the Yangzi valley for over a decade. The war that followed killed perhaps twenty million people, making it the deadliest civil conflict in history. Its suppression by provincial armies under men like Zeng Guofan shifted military power away from the Qing centre and into regional hands, a change the dynasty never reversed.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Rhode Island, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Rhode Island, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Rhode Island, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Rhode Island--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.97 of LCSH 1987, and p.95 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Eudes, 888-898 (France, AD 888–AD 898)
nodes.title: Eudes, 888-898 (France, AD 888–AD 898)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 888–AD 898] Eudes, 888-898. Extracted from heading "France--History--Eudes, 888-898". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Odo, count of Paris and hero of the city's defence during the Viking siege of 885-86, was elected king of the West Franks in preference to the Carolingian heir. His reign showed that the crown could pass by the choice of the magnates to a man who could actually fight, and his family, the Robertians, would eventually become the Capetian dynasty. He spent his years contesting the throne with the young Charles the Simple and fending off further Norse raids.

nodes.name: War of Independence, 1810-1823 (Venezuela, AD 1810–AD 1823)
nodes.title: War of Independence, 1810-1823 (Venezuela, AD 1810–AD 1823)
nodes.description:
[Venezuela, AD 1810–AD 1823] War of Independence, 1810-1823. Extracted from heading "Venezuela--History--War of Independence, 1810-1823". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 126 of LCSH 1986 and p.106 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Caracas deposed its captain-general and in 1811 declared the first independent republic in Spanish America, which an earthquake and royalist counterattack destroyed within a year. Bolívar's proclamation of "war to the death", the switching allegiance of the llanero horsemen, and the British Legion turned the tide, and Carabobo in 1821 broke Spanish power on land. The final Spanish force surrendered after the naval battle on Lake Maracaibo, leaving a country exhausted, depopulated and dominated by its victorious generals.

nodes.name: Spanish dynasty, 1580-1640 (Portugal, AD 1580–AD 1640)
nodes.title: Spanish dynasty, 1580-1640 (Portugal, AD 1580–AD 1640)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1580–AD 1640] Spanish dynasty, 1580-1640. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Spanish dynasty, 1580-1640". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Portuguese royal line died out, Philip II of Spain claimed the throne and joined the two Iberian crowns and their global empires in a personal union. Portugal kept its own laws and institutions, but its ships, colonies and trade routes became targets in Spain's wars, and the Dutch seized much of Asia, Brazil and the African slave forts. Resentment at the costs of Castilian wars produced the 1640 revolt that put the House of Braganza on the throne and began a long war of independence.

nodes.name: Manchu Invasions, 1627-1637 (Korean Peninsula, AD 1627–AD 1637)
nodes.title: Manchu Invasions, 1627-1637 (Korean Peninsula, AD 1627–AD 1637)
nodes.description:
[Korea, AD 1627–AD 1637] Manchu Invasions, 1627-1637. Extracted from heading "Korea--History--Manchu Invasions, 1627-1637". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.70 of LCSH 1987, and p.56 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Twice within a decade the rising Manchu state struck south into Korea to secure its flank before attacking Ming China. The second campaign ended with King Injo emerging from the besieged fortress of Namhansanseong to kowtow to the Qing emperor at Samjeondo, sending his sons as hostages and breaking Joseon's loyalty to the Ming. The humiliation shaped Korean politics and thought for generations, feeding both resentment of the Qing and debate over how to strengthen the kingdom.

nodes.name: Later Shu kingdom, 934-965 (China, AD 934–AD 965)
nodes.title: Later Shu kingdom, 934-965 (China, AD 934–AD 965)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 934–AD 965] Later Shu kingdom, 934-965. Extracted from heading "China--History--Later Shu kingdom, 934-965". Added to LCSH in 1990, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

One of the southern states that broke away as northern China convulsed, ruled from Chengdu behind the mountain barriers of Sichuan. Sheltered from war, its court became a refuge for poets and painters and produced the first great anthology of ci lyric verse. Its ruler surrendered after a brief campaign by the newly founded Song.

nodes.name: Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925 (China, AD 907–AD 925)
nodes.title: Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925 (China, AD 907–AD 925)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 907–AD 925] Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925. Extracted from heading "China--History--Earlier Shu kingdom, 907-925". Added to LCSH in 1990, revised in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Tang dynasty fell, the general Wang Jian made himself emperor in Sichuan, whose mountains sheltered it from the wars convulsing the north. Poets, painters and officials fled there, and the court became a refuge for Tang culture and a centre of early printing. Wang's dissolute son lost it to the Later Tang armies in barely two months.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1954-1962 (Algeria, AD 1954–AD 1962)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1954-1962 (Algeria, AD 1954–AD 1962)
nodes.description:
[Algeria, AD 1954–AD 1962] Revolution, 1954-1962. Extracted from heading "Algeria--History--Revolution, 1954-1962". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The FLN's coordinated attacks on All Saints' Day 1954 opened a war that France fought as an internal matter, since Algeria was legally part of the republic and home to a million European settlers. Torture, massacres and the Battle of Algiers made the conflict a moral crisis in France, bringing down the Fourth Republic and returning de Gaulle to power. Independence came in 1962 after the Évian Accords, followed by the flight of nearly the entire settler population.

nodes.name: French rule, 1797-1815 (Bologna, AD 1797–AD 1815)
nodes.title: French rule, 1797-1815 (Bologna, AD 1797–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[Bologna (Italy), AD 1797–AD 1815] French rule, 1797-1815. Extracted from heading "Bologna (Italy)--History--French rule, 1797-1815". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Papal government ended abruptly as the city was folded into Napoleon's Cispadane and then Cisalpine republics and finally the Kingdom of Italy. Monasteries were suppressed and their property sold, the university and academies reorganised, and paintings by Raphael and the Carracci carted off to Paris - some never returned. Restoration handed the city back to the pope, but the taste of secular, code-based government left a lasting appetite for change that surfaced in the risings of the following decades.

nodes.name: Rebellion of the Three Feudatories, 1673-1681 (China, AD 1673–AD 1681)
nodes.title: Rebellion of the Three Feudatories, 1673-1681 (China, AD 1673–AD 1681)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1673–AD 1681] Rebellion of the Three Feudatories, 1673-1681. Extracted from heading "China--History--Rebellion of the Three Feudatories, 1673-1681". Added to LSCH in 1995, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Three Chinese generals who had helped the Manchus conquer the Ming were rewarded with near-independent southern domains; when the young Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish them, Wu Sangui and his allies revolted and for a time held most of southern China. Eight years of war ended in Qing victory and the elimination of the semi-autonomous feudatories, followed by the conquest of Taiwan in 1683. The victory secured Qing rule over all of China and confirmed Kangxi as one of its most effective emperors.

nodes.name: Leopold I, 1831-1865 (Belgium, AD 1831–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Leopold I, 1831-1865 (Belgium, AD 1831–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Belgium, AD 1831–AD 1865] Leopold I, 1831-1865. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Leopold I, 1831-1865". Appears on p.8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p. 9 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A German prince chosen to head the newly independent Belgian state, he gave the young constitutional monarchy credibility and secured its recognition and guaranteed neutrality through the 1839 Treaty of London. Uncle and mentor to both Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, he acted as an unofficial broker among Europe's courts, and Belgium industrialised rapidly under his rule while escaping the revolutions of 1848.

nodes.name: Berlin Blockade, 1948-1949 (Berlin, AD 1948–AD 1949)
nodes.title: Berlin Blockade, 1948-1949 (Berlin, AD 1948–AD 1949)
nodes.description:
[Berlin (Germany), AD 1948–AD 1949] Berlin Blockade, 1948-1949. Extracted from heading "Berlin (Germany)--History--Blockade, 1948-1949". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Soviet forces cut every road, rail and canal route into the western sectors of the city, hoping to force the Western Allies out. Instead, British and American aircraft flew in coal, flour and everything else a city of two million needed, landing at times every few minutes for nearly a year. The blockade failed, but it hardened the split between East and West, hastened the creation of two German states and led directly to the founding of NATO.

nodes.name: Henry VI, 1422-1461 (England, AD 1422–AD 1461)
nodes.title: Henry VI, 1422-1461 (England, AD 1422–AD 1461)

[Great Britain, AD 1422–AD 1461] Henry VI, 1422-1461. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry VI, 1422-1461". Added to LCSH in 1986. Crowned in the cradle in both England and France, he grew into a pious, politically hopeless king who suffered periods of catatonic mental collapse. Under him the English lost everything in France but Calais, and the resulting recriminations between court factions hardened into the Wars of the Roses. His deposition by Edward IV began three decades of dynastic bloodletting.

nodes.name: Movement to Protect the Constitution, 1917-1923 (China, AD 1917–AD 1923)
nodes.title: Movement to Protect the Constitution, 1917-1923 (China, AD 1917–AD 1923)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1917–AD 1923] Movement to Protect the Constitution, 1917-1923. Extracted from heading "China--History--Movement to Protect the Constitution, 1917-1923". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1996. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Beiyang government in Beijing dissolved parliament, Sun Yat-sen led dissident legislators south to Guangzhou and set up a rival regime claiming to defend the 1912 provisional constitution. Dependent on southern warlords who repeatedly turned on him, the movement failed to reunify the country, and China remained split among militarists. Its failure convinced Sun to build a disciplined party and army of his own, with Soviet help - the seed of the Nationalist Party's later Northern Expedition.

nodes.name: Frederick I, 1797-1816 (Germany, AD 1797–AD 1816)
nodes.title: Frederick I, 1797-1816 (Germany, AD 1797–AD 1816)
nodes.description:
[Württemberg (Germany), AD 1797–AD 1816] Frederick I, 1797-1816. Extracted from heading "Württemberg (Germany)--History--Frederick I, 1797-1816". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 131 of LCSH 1986 and p.109 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Württemberg ruler who rode Napoleon's coattails from duke to elector to king, doubling his territory with secularised church lands and absorbed imperial cities and free knights' estates. He dissolved the duchy's old representative estates and ruled as an autocrat over a newly enlarged, centralised state. Switching sides in 1813, he kept his crown at the Congress of Vienna, so a kingdom built by French power survived Napoleon's fall.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1830-1832 (Lithuania, AD 1830–AD 1832)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1830-1832 (Lithuania, AD 1830–AD 1832)
nodes.description:
[Lithuania, AD 1830–AD 1832] Revolution, 1830-1832. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--Revolution, 1830-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.72 of LCSH 1987, and p.58 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Insurrection against Russian rule spread from Warsaw into the former Grand Duchy, where noble-led detachments and peasant volunteers seized much of the countryside before regular Russian forces retook Vilnius and drove survivors into Prussia. The defeat brought sweeping punishment: Vilnius University was closed, estates were confiscated, and thousands went into exile, where Polish-Lithuanian emigre politics took root. The suppression pushed national feeling out of the manor houses and towards a new generation of writers and, eventually, peasant activists.

nodes.name: Francis I, 1515-1547 (France, AD 1515–AD 1547)
nodes.title: Francis I, 1515-1547 (France, AD 1515–AD 1547)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1515–AD 1547] Francis I, 1515-1547. Extracted from heading "France--History--Francis I, 1515-1547". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A king who opened his reign by winning Milan at Marignano and spent the rest of it losing ground to Emperor Charles V, including a year as Charles's prisoner after the disaster at Pavia in 1525. He shipped Italian Renaissance style into France wholesale — Leonardo da Vinci died in his service, and Chambord and Fontainebleau went up on his orders — while allying with the Ottoman sultan against fellow Christians, to Europe's scandal. His 1539 ordinance made French, not Latin, the language of law and administration.

properties.title: alarm clock — 1545
properties.notes:
Spring-driven table clock with astrolabic dial (now missing). The gear trains are arranged one above the other, with the striking train at the bottom. Spring-driven going train with gilded brass plates, barrel and fusee. Verge escapement with steel balance. Striking train, for hours only powered by a fixed barrel with engraved decoration on the visible side. The count-wheel is mounted on the lower side of the bottom plate, Alarum train located above the bell. At the top of the clock beneath the dial (now missing) is a rotating cage which operated the following indications:- A disc rotating once in a sidereal day; a sun-pointer showing the time on a twenty-four hour dial and the position of the sun in the zodiac; a moon pointer showing the position of the moon in the zodiac. Around the sides of the clock are three dials:- Upper left indicating the hours. Lower left indicating the day of week - this now has a red glass cabouchon replacing the hand. A dial at the right is for alarm-setting. There is a religious inscription in Latin around base of case.; | Type: alarm clock | Medium: brass (case, movement plates, wheels etc.) | Dimensions: 168.00 millimetres; 104.00 millimetres;

France

nodes.title: Valens, 364-378 (Byzantine Empire, AD 364–AD 378)

nodes.name: Eighteenth dynasty, ca. 1570-1320 B.C (Egypt, 1569 BC–1319 BC)
nodes.title: Eighteenth dynasty, ca. 1570-1320 B.C (Egypt, 1569 BC–1319 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 1569 BC–1319 BC] Eighteenth dynasty, ca. 1570-1320 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Eighteenth dynasty, ca. 1570-1320 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Egypt's imperial age began when Ahmose drove out the Hyksos and reunited the country, opening the New Kingdom. Its rulers - Hatshepsut, the conqueror Thutmose III, the heretic Akhenaten and the boy-king Tutankhamun - pushed Egyptian power to the Euphrates and Nubia, filled Karnak with obelisks and cut royal tombs into the Valley of the Kings. The Amarna episode, when Akhenaten abolished the old gods for the sun-disc Aten and built a new capital in the desert, was reversed within a generation, but its startlingly naturalistic art survives.

properties.title: stool — 1400BC-1350BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Ebony stool: the finest surviving example of its type, this stool combines precious materials and successful design with superlative craftsmanship. The leather seat dips in a double cove to give contoured support to the body from any of its four sides. Ivory inlay imitating garlands of lotus petals adorns the upper portions of the legs, contrasting brightly with the rich, dark tone of the ebony. Below the lotus garlands are miniature squares of ivory imitating through joints. The supporting lattice bracing, composed of two inner vertical struts on each side, flanked by two angled struts, is also of ivory. Stretchers of ebony terminating in ivory ferrules, which fan out in imitation of a papyrus umbel, hold the legs firmly in place. The legs taper toward the bottom and then flare out again to form a delicate, aesthetically balanced support. Incised rings ornament the tapered half.; | Type: stool | Medium: ebony; ivory | Dimensions: 37.50 centimetres; 43.80 centimetres; | Culture: 18th Dynasty

Thebes, Egypt

properties.title: cosmetic-jar — 1479BC-1352BC (circa)
properties.notes:
A pottery cosmetic-jar: in the form of a woman playing a lute, with her body twisted slightly to the left. She wears a long dress, and a bangle on her right wrist. The object does not stand on its own, so would have been impractical as a vessel. After moulding, the face, fingers, and toes were enhanced with a tool. A red slip covers the surface, which is vertically burnished. Black paint was applied, as usual, to the hair and eyes, and to outline the fingers and the toenails. On the woman's tunic dress, the short sleeves, keyhole neckline with its little tie strings, the stitching of the side seams and the fringe of the hem are all indicated in black paint. The lute is also realistically detailed, from the tassels for fixing the two strings, to the frets, holes in the sound box, and plectrum. A checkerboard pattern on the back of the sound box represents the tortoiseshell of which such objects were made. The handle, spout and base were moulded separately and then applied. The potter has taken great care to obliterate all tooling marks.; | Type: cosmetic-jar | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 23.00 centimetres; 0.24 kilograms; 7.50 centimetres; 5.70 centimetres; | Culture: 18th Dynasty

Thebes, Egypt

nodes.name: Edward II, 1307-1327 (England, AD 1307–AD 1327)
nodes.title: Edward II, 1307-1327 (England, AD 1307–AD 1327)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1307–AD 1327] Edward II, 1307-1327. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Edward II, 1307-1327". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Edward's reliance on favourites, first Piers Gaveston and then the Despensers, set him against his own barons and cost him the support of his queen. His defeat by Robert Bruce at Bannockburn in 1314 secured Scottish independence in practice. He was deposed by an invasion led by Isabella and Mortimer and died in captivity, the first English king forced from the throne.

nodes.name: John II, 1458-1479 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1458–AD 1479)
nodes.title: John II, 1458-1479 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1458–AD 1479)
nodes.description:
[Aragon, AD 1458–AD 1479] John II, 1458-1479. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon--History--John II, 1458-1479". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 3 of LCSH 1975; revised in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He came to the Aragonese throne already old and already king of Navarre, and spent his reign fighting a decade-long Catalan civil war against his own subjects, losing Roussillon to France in the process. His real achievement was diplomatic: the marriage he arranged in 1469 between his son Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile united the two crowns and made modern Spain possible.

nodes.name: Roman period, 55 B.C.-449 A.D (England, 54 BC–AD 449)
nodes.title: Roman period, 55 B.C.-449 A.D (England, 54 BC–AD 449)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, 54 BC–AD 449] Roman period, 55 B.C.-449 A.D. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Roman period, 55 B.C.-449 A.D". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Caesar's two raids put Britain on Rome's map; Claudius invaded in earnest in AD 43 and the island became a frontier province, walled off from the north by Hadrian's Wall. Towns, roads, baths, villas, coinage and writing arrived with the army and the tax collector, alongside new gods and eventually Christianity. When the field army and the money went in the early fifth century the towns emptied fast, and the traditional date for the coming of the Anglo-Saxons closes the period.

nodes.name: Clement VII, 1523-1534 (Vatican City, AD 1523–AD 1534)
nodes.title: Clement VII, 1523-1534 (Vatican City, AD 1523–AD 1534)
nodes.description:
[Papal States, AD 1523–AD 1534] Clement VII, 1523-1534. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Clement VII, 1523-1534". Added to LCSH in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Medici pope whose shifting alliances between France and the Emperor brought disaster: imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527 and held him prisoner in the Castel Sant'Angelo. Unable to defy Charles V, he refused Henry VIII's annulment, pushing England out of the Roman church. He also commissioned Michelangelo's Last Judgement and backed Copernicus's early circulation of his heliocentric ideas.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1383-1385 (Portugal, AD 1383–AD 1385)
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1383-1385 (Portugal, AD 1383–AD 1385)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1383–AD 1385] Interregnum, 1383-1385. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Interregnum, 1383-1385". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of Ferdinand I left only a daughter married to the king of Castile, and Lisbon's merchants and artisans revolted rather than accept absorption by Castile. John of Aviz, backed by the townsmen and the commander Nuno Álvares Pereira, was made king and destroyed a far larger Castilian army at Aljubarrota. The crisis founded the Aviz dynasty, sealed the alliance with England, and launched the voyages that became Portugal's overseas empire.

nodes.name: Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941 (Thailand, AD 1940–AD 1941)
nodes.title: Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941 (Thailand, AD 1940–AD 1941)
nodes.description:
[Indochina, Thailand, AD 1940–AD 1941] Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941. Spatial coverage: China, France, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam. Extracted from heading "Thai-Indochinese Conflict, 1940-1941". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2017. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With France defeated in Europe, Thailand attacked French Indochina to reclaim territories in Laos and Cambodia ceded decades earlier. Thai troops made gains on land while the French navy won a sharp victory at Ko Chang; Japan then imposed mediation, handing Thailand the disputed provinces and drawing Bangkok firmly into Tokyo's orbit on the eve of the Pacific War.

nodes.name: Constitutional period, 1789-1809 (United States, AD 1789–AD 1809)
nodes.title: Constitutional period, 1789-1809 (United States, AD 1789–AD 1809)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1789–AD 1809] Constitutional period, 1789-1809. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Constitutional period, 1789-1809". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 122 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The new federal machinery was switched on and tested: Washington's first administration, the Bill of Rights, a national bank, a Supreme Court that had to invent its own authority. Bitter argument between Federalists and Jeffersonian Republicans produced the first party system and the first peaceful transfer of power between opponents. The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled the country's territory at a stroke.

nodes.name: French Colony, 1555-1567 (Brazil, AD 1555–AD 1567)
nodes.title: French Colony, 1555-1567 (Brazil, AD 1555–AD 1567)
nodes.description:
[Brazil, AD 1555–AD 1567] French Colony, 1555-1567. Extracted from heading "Brazil--History--French Colony, 1555-1567". Appears on p.10 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.12 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Villegagnon's expedition planted a fortified settlement on an island in Guanabara Bay - France Antarctique - drawing both Catholics and Calvinist refugees in an experiment that collapsed into religious quarrelling. Portuguese forces drove the French out and founded Rio de Janeiro to hold the bay for good. The episode produced Jean de Léry's famous account of the Tupinambá, one of the earliest ethnographic descriptions of Brazil.

nodes.name: Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1878 (South Africa, AD 1877–AD 1878)
nodes.title: Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1878 (South Africa, AD 1877–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[South Africa, AD 1877–AD 1878] Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1878. Extracted from heading "Ngcayecibi, War of, South Africa, 1877-1878". Added to LCSH in 1990. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A brawl at a beer drink escalated into the ninth and last of the frontier wars between the Xhosa and the Cape Colony, drawing in both Gcaleka and Ngqika chiefdoms against colonial forces armed with breech-loading rifles. Xhosa defeat ended a century of resistance on the eastern frontier, killed the paramount chief Sarhili's independence and opened the Transkei to annexation. It was the opening move in the wider British campaign to subdue independent African polities across southern Africa.

nodes.name: House of Lancaster, 1399-1461 (England, AD 1399–AD 1461)
nodes.title: House of Lancaster, 1399-1461 (England, AD 1399–AD 1461)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1399–AD 1461] House of Lancaster, 1399-1461. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--House of Lancaster, 1399-1461". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry IV seized the crown from Richard II, and the usurpation shadowed the dynasty for sixty years. Henry V's victory at Agincourt and the treaty naming him heir to France marked the high point; under the pious, intermittently insane Henry VI those conquests evaporated and the nobility split into factions. Defeat at Towton in 1461 put the Yorkists on the throne and turned dynastic quarrel into the Wars of the Roses.

nodes.name: Peter II, 1727-1730 (Russia, AD 1727–AD 1730)
nodes.title: Peter II, 1727-1730 (Russia, AD 1727–AD 1730)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1727–AD 1730] Peter II, 1727-1730. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Peter II, 1727-1730". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Grandson of Peter the Great, he came to the throne at eleven and was governed by rival aristocratic factions, first Menshikov and then the Dolgorukovs, who moved the court back to Moscow and let his grandfather's navy rot. He died of smallpox at fourteen on the day set for his wedding, ending the male line of the Romanovs and opening a succession crisis that the nobility briefly tried to exploit to limit the monarchy.

nodes.name: Constantine I, the Great, 306-337 (Roman Empire, AD 306–AD 337)
nodes.title: Constantine I, the Great, 306-337 (Roman Empire, AD 306–AD 337)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 306–AD 337] Constantine I, the Great, 306-337. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Constantine I, the Great, 306-337". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Proclaimed by his father's troops at York, he fought his way to sole rule and dismantled the tetrarchy that Diocletian had built. He legalised and then favoured Christianity, called the Council of Nicaea to settle its doctrine, and founded Constantinople as a new imperial capital that would outlast Rome by a thousand years. His reformed gold solidus underpinned Mediterranean trade for centuries.

nodes.name: Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916 (Austria, AD 1848–AD 1916)
nodes.title: Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916 (Austria, AD 1848–AD 1916)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1848–AD 1916] Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916. Extracted from heading "Austria--history--Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916".  Appears under the alternate label "Francis Joseph I, 1848-1916" on p.6 of LCSH 1975, and on p.7 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Put on the throne at eighteen during the revolutions of 1848, he reigned for sixty-eight years while his empire was expelled from Italy and Germany, forced into partnership with Hungary in 1867, and steadily strained by its dozen nationalities. His Vienna tore down its walls for the Ringstrasse and became the city of Freud, Klimt and Mahler, even as the dynasty absorbed the suicide of his son and the assassination of his wife. His ultimatum to Serbia after the killing of his heir began the First World War.

nodes.name: Charles V, 1364-1380 (France, AD 1364–AD 1380)
nodes.title: Charles V, 1364-1380 (France, AD 1364–AD 1380)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1364–AD 1380] Charles V, 1364-1380. Extracted from heading "France--History--Charles V, 1364-1380". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.37 of LCSH 1987, and p.29 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Inheriting a kingdom humiliated at Poitiers and carved up by treaty, he recovered nearly all the lost territory without fighting a great battle, using Bertrand du Guesclin's raids, sieges and a rebuilt fleet to wear the English down. He reformed taxation and the coinage, fortified Paris and built the Bastille, and assembled a royal library of a thousand manuscripts, commissioning translations of Aristotle and Augustine into French. His careful, bookish style of kingship earned him the name the Wise.

nodes.name: Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979 (Iran, AD 1925–AD 1979)
nodes.title: Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979 (Iran, AD 1925–AD 1979)
nodes.description:
[Iran, AD 1925–AD 1979] Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Pahlavi dynasty, 1925-1979". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.60 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two shahs, father and son, remade Iran as a centralised modern state with a conscript army, railways, universities and a secularised legal system, financed increasingly by oil. Foreign involvement was constant, from the Anglo-Soviet occupation in 1941 to the CIA- and British-backed coup of 1953. The monarchy collapsed in 1979, replaced by an Islamic republic.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (West Virginia, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (West Virginia, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[West Virginia, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "West Virginia--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.130 of LCSH 1987, and p.127 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Maria Theresa, 1740-1780 (Austria, AD 1740–AD 1780)
nodes.title: Maria Theresa, 1740-1780 (Austria, AD 1740–AD 1780)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1740–AD 1780] Maria Theresa, 1740-1780. Extracted from the heading "Austria--History--Maria Theresa, 1740-1780". Appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.7 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Her inheritance of the Habsburg lands was immediately challenged, and the wars that followed cost her Silesia to Prussia but proved the monarchy could survive as a single state. She rebuilt it with a standing army, a professional bureaucracy, tax reform and compulsory schooling, centralising power in Vienna at the expense of the provincial estates. Mother of Joseph II and Marie Antoinette, she used dynastic marriages as deliberately as she used armies.

nodes.name: Achinese War, 1873-1904 (Indonesia, AD 1873–AD 1904)
nodes.title: Achinese War, 1873-1904 (Indonesia, AD 1873–AD 1904)
nodes.description:
[Indonesia, AD 1873–AD 1904] Achinese War, 1873-1904. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Achinese War, 1873-1904". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987, and p.48 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch invasion of the sultanate of Aceh in northern Sumatra turned into the longest and bloodiest colonial war in the Netherlands' history, dragging on for three decades. Guerrilla resistance led by local chiefs and Islamic scholars was eventually broken by mobile counter-insurgency columns and the harsh methods of Van Heutsz. Its end completed Dutch control of the Indonesian archipelago and left a legacy of Acehnese separatism that lasted into the twenty-first century.

nodes.name: Babylonian captivity, 598-515 B.C (Iraq, 597 BC–514 BC)
nodes.title: Babylonian captivity, 598-515 B.C (Iraq, 597 BC–514 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iraq, Babylonia, 597 BC–514 BC] Babylonian captivity, 598-515 B.C. Extracted from heading "Jews--History--Babylonian captivity, 598-515 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1987. Spatial coverage description from broader term "Jews--Iraq--Babylonia". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nebuchadnezzar II's armies deported Judah's king, nobles, priests and craftsmen to Babylonia in successive waves, destroying Jerusalem and its Temple in 586 BC. In exile, Judeans kept their identity through sabbath, circumcision, genealogy and the collection of prophetic and legal texts, while prophets such as Ezekiel and Second Isaiah reimagined their god as ruler of all nations. Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed a return, and the rebuilt Second Temple marked the end of the episode that turned a national cult into a portable religion.

nodes.name: Alfonso VII, 1126-1157 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1126–AD 1157)
nodes.title: Alfonso VII, 1126-1157 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1126–AD 1157)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1126–AD 1157] Alfonso VII, 1126-1157. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso VII, 1126-1157". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He restored royal authority after a period of civil war and had himself crowned Emperor of All Spain in León in 1135, claiming overlordship over the other Iberian rulers. He campaigned deep into Andalusia and took Almería, though it was soon lost to the Almohads. Dividing León and Castile between his two sons at his death undid much of what he had built.

nodes.name: Frederick I, 1152-1190 (Germany, AD 1152–AD 1190)
nodes.title: Frederick I, 1152-1190 (Germany, AD 1152–AD 1190)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1152–AD 1190] Frederick I, 1152-1190. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Frederick I, 1152-1190". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Barbarossa spent his reign trying to make imperial authority real in Italy, launching six expeditions south and destroying Milan, only to be beaten by the Lombard League at Legnano in 1176 and forced to recognise the cities' liberties. At home he broke his greatest rival, Henry the Lion, and redistributed his duchies, cementing the princes' power. He drowned in a river in Anatolia on the Third Crusade, and German legend later had him sleeping in a mountain, waiting to return.

nodes.name: Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913 (Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1913)
nodes.title: Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913 (Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1913)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1884–AD 1913] Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Yên Thế Uprising, 1884-1913". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peasant fighters in the forested hills north of Hanoi, led for most of three decades by Hoàng Hoa Thám (Đề Thám), waged guerrilla war against French colonial forces, negotiating truces and then resuming the fight. It outlasted every other armed resistance of its generation and tied down substantial French troops. Đề Thám's killing in 1913 ended it, but he became a national symbol for later anticolonial movements.

nodes.name: Francis II, 1792-1806 (Germany, AD 1792–AD 1806)
nodes.title: Francis II, 1792-1806 (Germany, AD 1792–AD 1806)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1792–AD 1806] Francis II, 1792-1806. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Francis II, 1792-1806". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Holy Roman Emperor, whose reign was one long losing struggle against revolutionary and Napoleonic France. After the catastrophe of Austerlitz and Napoleon's creation of the Confederation of the Rhine, he laid down the crown in 1806 and dissolved an institution that had existed in some form for a thousand years. He carried on as Francis I of Austria, a title he had created for himself two years earlier.

nodes.name: Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916 (Hungary, AD 1848–AD 1916)
nodes.title: Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916 (Hungary, AD 1848–AD 1916)
nodes.description:
[Hungary, AD 1848–AD 1916] Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Franz Joseph I, 1848-1916". Added to LCSH in 1986; on p.46 of LCSH 1975, and on p.57 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Put on the throne at eighteen during the revolutions of 1848, he reigned for sixty-eight years while his empire was expelled from Italy and Germany, forced into partnership with Hungary in 1867, and steadily strained by its dozen nationalities. His Vienna tore down its walls for the Ringstrasse and became the city of Freud, Klimt and Mahler, even as the dynasty absorbed the suicide of his son and the assassination of his wife. His ultimatum to Serbia after the killing of his heir began the First World War.

nodes.name: Daoguang, 1820-1850 (China, AD 1820–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Daoguang, 1820-1850 (China, AD 1820–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1820–AD 1850] Daoguang, 1820-1850. Extracted from heading "China--History--Daoguang, 1820-1850". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Tao kuang, 1820-1850" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987, and on p.16 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign spent watching Qing authority erode from within and without: opium imports drained silver from the economy, rebellions and floods strained the treasury, and the government's attempt to suppress the drug trade at Canton brought war with Britain. Defeat produced the 1842 Treaty of Nanjing, the cession of Hong Kong and the opening of treaty ports — the start of what Chinese historians call the century of humiliation. The emperor himself was frugal and cautious, and his indecision has often been blamed for the scale of the collapse that followed.

nodes.name: Rebellion, 1485-1487 (Naples, AD 1485–AD 1487)
nodes.title: Rebellion, 1485-1487 (Naples, AD 1485–AD 1487)
nodes.description:
[Naples (Kingdom), AD 1485–AD 1487] Rebellion, 1485-1487. Extracted from heading "Naples (Kingdom)--History--Rebellion, 1485-1487". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.80 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The barons of the kingdom of Naples, backed by Pope Innocent VIII, rose against King Ferrante of Aragon's centralising taxation and his squeeze on feudal privilege. Ferrante offered terms, then arrested and executed the ringleaders at a wedding feast and confiscated their estates. The affair left the monarchy hated by the nobility and the kingdom fatally divided when the French invaded in 1494.

nodes.name: Antonines, 96-192 (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 192)
nodes.title: Antonines, 96-192 (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 192)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 96–AD 192] Antonines, 96-192. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Antonines, 96-192". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius presided over the empire at its largest and, by later Roman reckoning, its most stable, with succession managed by adoption rather than birth. The century brought Trajan's Dacian and Parthian wars, Hadrian's frontier walls, monumental building across the provinces, and a flowering of Greek and Latin literature and philosophy. It closed badly, with plague, war on the Danube and the erratic reign of Commodus.

nodes.name: Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C (Egypt, 2685 BC–2180 BC)
nodes.title: Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C (Egypt, 2685 BC–2180 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2685 BC–2180 BC] Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Old Kingdom, ca. 2686-ca. 2181 B.C". Added to LCSH in 1999. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Egypt's first long era of unified, centralised rule, remembered above all for pyramid building and for the officials' tombs clustered around royal cemeteries. Wall reliefs in those tombs show farming, fishing, brewing and craftwork in remarkable detail, the everyday world that supported the court. When central authority weakened under Pepi II's successors, the provinces went their own way and the country slid into the First Intermediate Period.

nodes.name: Charles V, 1506-1555 (Belgium, AD 1506–AD 1555)
nodes.title: Charles V, 1506-1555 (Belgium, AD 1506–AD 1555)
nodes.description:
[Belgium, AD 1506–AD 1555] Charles V, 1506-1555. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Charles V, 1506-1555". Appears on p. 8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.9 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born in Ghent and Burgundian by upbringing, he ruled the Low Countries as their natural prince while governing half of Europe from elsewhere, leaving regents — his aunt Margaret and sister Mary — in charge at Mechelen and Brussels. He completed the Seventeen Provinces by conquest and inheritance and bound them together by the Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 as a single indivisible unit. Antwerp became the commercial capital of the world in these decades, while his edicts against Protestants sowed the grievances that later exploded into the Dutch Revolt. He abdicated in the palace at Brussels in 1555.
