London, Farringdon Street, United Kingdom

nodes.name: Taranaki War, 1860-1861 (New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1861)
nodes.title: Taranaki War, 1860-1861 (New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1861] Taranaki War, 1860-1861. Extracted from heading "New Zealand--History--Taranaki War, 1860-1861". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fighting broke out when the colonial government pushed through a disputed purchase of Māori land at Waitara over the objections of the Te Āti Awa chief Wiremu Kīngi. British regulars found themselves bogged down against skilfully engineered Māori pā, and the war ended in an inconclusive truce. It shattered any pretence of peaceful settlement under the Treaty of Waitangi and led on to the far larger invasion of the Waikato and mass confiscation of Māori land.

nodes.name: Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C (Egypt, 2179 BC–1550 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C (Egypt, 2179 BC–1550 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2179 BC–1550 BC] Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Middle Kingdom, ca. 2180-ca. 1551 B.C". Added to LCSH in 2010. The bibliographic notes suggest that the dates are derived from the end date for the Old Kingdom and the start date of the New Kingdom. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After a century of civil war and famine, Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt and his successors built a leaner, more bureaucratic state, moving the capital north to the Fayum region and draining land for agriculture. This was the classical age of Egyptian language and literature, producing the Tale of Sinuhe and the pessimistic wisdom texts still copied in schools a thousand years later, along with sober, watchful royal portrait sculpture. Royal power eventually frayed again, and rulers of Levantine origin, the Hyksos, took the Delta until Theban kings drove them out.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1955-1972 (Sudan, AD 1955–AD 1972)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1955-1972 (Sudan, AD 1955–AD 1972)
nodes.description:
[Sudan, AD 1955–AD 1972] Civil War, 1955-1972. Extracted from heading "Sudan--History--Civil War, 1955-1972". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Southern soldiers mutinied on the eve of independence, fearing domination by the Arab and Muslim north, and the Anyanya insurgency fought on for seventeen years. Hundreds of thousands died and many more fled. The Addis Ababa Agreement granted the south regional autonomy — a settlement that held for barely a decade before war resumed.

nodes.name: Titus, 79-81 (Roman Empire, AD 79–AD 81)
nodes.title: Titus, 79-81 (Roman Empire, AD 79–AD 81)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 79–AD 81] Titus, 79-81. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Titus, 79-81". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A reign of barely two years crowded with disasters: Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum within weeks of his accession, then fire and plague struck Rome itself. Titus, popular for his relief efforts and his generosity, opened the Colosseum with a hundred days of games and completed the great baths beside it. He had made his name sacking Jerusalem a decade earlier, an event still advertised on the arch that bears his name.

nodes.name: Leo V, 813-820 (Byzantine Empire, AD 813–AD 820)
nodes.title: Leo V, 813-820 (Byzantine Empire, AD 813–AD 820)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 813–AD 820] Leo V, 813-820. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Leo V, 813-820". Added to LCSH in 1997, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Armenian general who seized the throne after a crushing defeat by the Bulgars, he stabilised the northern frontier and defeated Khan Krum's successors. He revived iconoclasm in 815, arguing that the emperors who banned images had won victories while icon-venerating rulers lost them. He was murdered in the palace chapel on Christmas morning by supporters of his own former comrade, Michael the Amorian.

nodes.name: Henry VIII, 1509-1547 (England, AD 1509–AD 1547)
nodes.title: Henry VIII, 1509-1547 (England, AD 1509–AD 1547)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1509–AD 1547] Henry VIII, 1509-1547. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry VIII, 1509-1547". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The quest for a male heir and an annulment from Catherine of Aragon led to the break with Rome, the Royal Supremacy, and the dissolution of the monasteries, which transferred perhaps a fifth of England's land to the crown and its allies. Six marriages, two executed queens and the fall of ministers from Wolsey to Cromwell made the court lethally unpredictable. He also built a permanent navy and coastal forts, leaving a realm religiously divided and financially strained.

nodes.name: Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989 (Iraq, AD 1986–AD 1989)
nodes.title: Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989 (Iraq, AD 1986–AD 1989)
nodes.description:
[Iraq, AD 1986–AD 1989] Anfal Campaign, 1986-1989. Extracted from heading "Anfal Campaign, Iraq, 1986-1989". Added to LCSH in 2006, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A series of military operations by the Iraqi state against the Kurdish north, directed by Ali Hassan al-Majid, in which thousands of villages were bulldozed, their inhabitants deported to camps, and tens of thousands of men and boys shot in mass graves in the desert. Chemical weapons were used repeatedly, most notoriously on the town of Halabja in 1988. The campaign has been recognised as genocide by courts in Iraq and abroad, and it hardened Kurdish demands for autonomy that reshaped the country after 2003.

nodes.name: Theodosius II, 408-450 (Byzantine Empire, AD 408–AD 450)
nodes.title: Theodosius II, 408-450 (Byzantine Empire, AD 408–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 408–AD 450] Theodosius II, 408-450. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Theodosius II, 408-450". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Emperor from the age of seven, he reigned longer than any other Roman ruler while power lay largely with prefects, eunuchs and his formidable sister Pulcheria. His name is attached to the great land walls of Constantinople, which kept the city safe for a thousand years, and to the Theodosian Code of 438, the first official compilation of imperial law. His reign also saw the Council of Ephesus and the condemnation of Nestorius, and huge payments of gold to Attila to keep the Huns from the Danube frontier.

nodes.name: Frederick V, 1610-1623 (Germany, AD 1610–AD 1623)
nodes.title: Frederick V, 1610-1623 (Germany, AD 1610–AD 1623)
nodes.description:
[Palatinate (Germany), AD 1610–AD 1623] Frederick V, 1610-1623. Extracted from heading "Palatinate (Germany)--History--Frederick V, 1610-1623". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.88 of LCSH 1987, and p.74 of LCSH 1975. Source notes Palatinate is in modern Germany. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Calvinist Elector Palatine who accepted the crown of Bohemia offered by rebels against the Habsburgs, and lost it at the Battle of White Mountain little more than a year later, earning the nickname "the Winter King." His gamble helped ignite the Thirty Years' War; he was outlawed, stripped of the Palatinate and its electoral title, and spent his remaining years in exile in the Netherlands. His marriage to Elizabeth Stuart mattered enormously in the long run, since their descendants became the Hanoverian kings of Britain.

nodes.name: Weimar Republic, 1918-1933 (Germany, AD 1918–AD 1933)
nodes.title: Weimar Republic, 1918-1933 (Germany, AD 1918–AD 1933)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1918–AD 1933] Weimar Republic, 1918-1933. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--1918-1933". Added to LCSH in  1986, revised in 2003. Variant label used as primary, since it uses a name as well as a date range to define the period. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Germany's first democracy, born out of military defeat and revolution, with a constitution guaranteeing broad rights but a fragmented parliament and a president who could rule by decree. It survived hyperinflation, putsch attempts from left and right, and French occupation of the Ruhr, then enjoyed a few prosperous years of artistic and scientific brilliance — Bauhaus design, cabaret, expressionist film. The Depression destroyed its centre ground, and in 1933 Hitler was handed the chancellorship through the republic's own constitutional machinery.

nodes.name: Spanish colony, 1565-1763 (Florida, AD 1565–AD 1763)
nodes.title: Spanish colony, 1565-1763 (Florida, AD 1565–AD 1763)
nodes.description:
[Florida , AD 1565–AD 1763] Spanish colony, 1565-1763. Extracted from heading "Florida--History--Spanish colony, 1565-1763". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.35 of LCSH 1987, and p.27 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded to guard the treasure fleets' route through the Bahama Channel and to expel French Protestants, St Augustine anchored a colony of soldiers, friars and mission Indians rather than planters. The Franciscan missions of Timucua and Apalachee collapsed under English and Creek raids in the early 1700s, leaving Spanish Florida a garrison huddled behind the stone walls of the Castillo de San Marcos. Spain traded the province to Britain for the return of Havana at the end of the Seven Years' War.

nodes.name: Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589 (China, AD 386–AD 589)
nodes.title: Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589 (China, AD 386–AD 589)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 386–AD 589] Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589. Extracted from heading "China--History--Northern and Southern dynasties, 386-589". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Two centuries of formal division, with Xianbei and other non-Han dynasties in the north and successive Chinese courts at Jiankang in the south. It was a formative age for Chinese Buddhism, for aristocratic clan politics, for poetry and calligraphy, and for the mixing of steppe and Chinese military and landholding practices. Reunification by the Sui in 589 inherited institutions worked out on both sides of the divide.

nodes.name: Albert I, 1298-1308 (Germany, AD 1298–AD 1308) [p06c6g3pq8x]
nodes.title: Albert I, 1298-1308 (Germany, AD 1298–AD 1308) [p06c6g3pq8x]
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1298–AD 1308] Albert I, 1298-1308. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Albert I, 1298-1308". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Habsburg who seized the German throne by deposing and killing Adolf of Nassau in battle, then spent his reign clawing back crown lands and taxing the Rhine tolls, which set the electors and cities against him. He was murdered by his own nephew, and the crown passed out of Habsburg hands for a generation.

nodes.name: Frederick IV, 1699-1730 (Denmark, AD 1699–AD 1730)
nodes.title: Frederick IV, 1699-1730 (Denmark, AD 1699–AD 1730)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1699–AD 1730] Frederick IV, 1699-1730. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Frederick IV, 1699-1730". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spent much of his reign in the Great Northern War against Sweden, ending it with Denmark's hold on Schleswig confirmed but the old dream of recovering Scania gone. At home he abolished the last form of peasant bondage on Zealand, funded hundreds of village "cavalry schools" for rural children, and sent the first Danish missionaries to India. Copenhagen suffered plague and the catastrophic fire of 1728, while the king built Fredensborg and Frederiksberg palaces.

nodes.name: Ramiro II, 1134-1137 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1134–AD 1137)
nodes.title: Ramiro II, 1134-1137 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1134–AD 1137)
nodes.description:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1134–AD 1137] Ramiro II, 1134-1137. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Ramiro II, 1134-1137". Added to LCSH in 2009, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A monk pulled from the cloister to take the throne when his brother died childless and Aragon faced absorption by Navarre and Castile. He married, fathered a daughter, betrothed her to the count of Barcelona and promptly retired to religious life again, an arrangement that joined Aragon and Catalonia in the union that would dominate the western Mediterranean for centuries. Legend also credits him with the gruesome Bell of Huesca, beheading rebellious nobles and arranging their heads in a ring.

nodes.name: War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959 (Cyprus, AD 1955–AD 1959)
nodes.title: War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959 (Cyprus, AD 1955–AD 1959)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 1955–AD 1959] War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--War for Union with Greece, 1955-1959". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

EOKA, led by Colonel Grivas with Archbishop Makarios as its political face, launched a guerrilla and bombing campaign to drive out the British and unite the island with Greece. The British responded with detentions, hangings and a huge garrison, while Turkish Cypriots organised against enosis and intercommunal violence took hold. The 1959 settlement gave Cyprus independence rather than union, with British bases retained and a constitution dividing power between the two communities — a compromise that satisfied neither side.

nodes.name: House of Austria, 1516-1700 (Spain, AD 1516–AD 1700)
nodes.title: House of Austria, 1516-1700 (Spain, AD 1516–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1516–AD 1700] House of Austria, 1516-1700. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--House of Austria, 1516-1700". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Spanish Habsburgs, who inherited Castile, Aragon, the Netherlands and a growing American empire and for a time dominated Europe. American silver funded wars against the Ottomans, the Dutch rebels, France and England, but also fuelled inflation and repeated royal bankruptcies. The line ended with the childless, disabled Charles II, whose will triggered the War of the Spanish Succession and the partition of Spain's European possessions.

nodes.name: Despotate, 1204-1318 (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1318)
nodes.title: Despotate, 1204-1318 (Greece, AD 1204–AD 1318)
nodes.description:
[Epirus, AD 1204–AD 1318] Despotate, 1204-1318. Spatial coverage: Albania, Greece. Extracted from heading "Epirus (Greece and Albania)--History--Despotate, 1204-1318". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When the Fourth Crusade shattered Byzantium, a branch of the Komnenos Doukas family carved out a Greek successor state in Epirus and western Greece, ruling from Arta and briefly holding Thessalonica and an imperial title. It was one of three rival claimants to the Byzantine legacy, fighting Latin crusader lords, Bulgarians and the emperors of Nicaea, and losing the contest to restore the empire. The line ended in 1318 with the murder of the last Komnenos Doukas ruler, after which Italian and Serbian powers moved in.

nodes.name: Tripolitan War, 1801-1805 (United States, AD 1801–AD 1805)
nodes.title: Tripolitan War, 1801-1805 (United States, AD 1801–AD 1805)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1801–AD 1805] Tripolitan War, 1801-1805. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Tripolitan War, 1801-1805". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 122 of LCSH 1986 and p.103 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The young United States refused further tribute to the Pasha of Tripoli and sent its new navy across the Atlantic instead. The war produced the burning of the captured frigate Philadelphia in Tripoli harbour and a march overland from Egypt by a handful of marines and mercenaries to take Derna — the "shores of Tripoli" of the Marine Hymn. It established the US Navy as a permanent force and set a precedent for American military action far from home.

nodes.name: Pastry War, 1838-1839 (Mexico, AD 1838–AD 1839)
nodes.title: Pastry War, 1838-1839 (Mexico, AD 1838–AD 1839)
nodes.description:
[Mexico, France, AD 1838–AD 1839] Pastry War, 1838-1839. Spatial coverage: France, Mexico. Extracted from heading "Pastry War, 1838-1839". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

France sent a fleet to blockade Veracruz and bombard the fortress of San Juan de Ulúa over unpaid claims by French residents, one of them a pastry cook whose shop had been ransacked. Mexico, broke and unstable, eventually agreed to pay 600,000 pesos; Antonio López de Santa Anna lost a leg driving the landing party back and used the wound to rebuild his political career. The affair set the pattern of European powers collecting debts by gunboat that culminated in the French invasion of 1862.

nodes.name: Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1118)
nodes.title: Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1118)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1081–AD 1118] Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Alexius I Comnenus, 1081-1118". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alexios took over an empire losing ground on every front and rebuilt it, beating back Norman invasions, destroying the Pechenegs and stabilising the currency with a reformed coinage. His appeal to the West for troops helped trigger the First Crusade, which he tried to steer by extracting oaths from the crusade leaders. Trading privileges granted to Venice in exchange for naval help became a long-term drain, and his daughter Anna's Alexiad remains one of the great medieval biographies.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Lithuania, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Lithuania, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.description:
[Lithuania, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Lithuania--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1830-1832 (Poland, AD 1830–AD 1832)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1830-1832 (Poland, AD 1830–AD 1832)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1830–AD 1832] Revolution, 1830-1832. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Revolution, 1830-1832". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.94 of LCSH 1987, and p.79 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Insurrection against Russian rule spread from Warsaw into the former Grand Duchy, where noble-led detachments and peasant volunteers seized much of the countryside before regular Russian forces retook Vilnius and drove survivors into Prussia. The defeat brought sweeping punishment: Vilnius University was closed, estates were confiscated, and thousands went into exile, where Polish-Lithuanian emigre politics took root. The suppression pushed national feeling out of the manor houses and towards a new generation of writers and, eventually, peasant activists.

nodes.name: Tudors, 1485-1603 (England, AD 1485–AD 1603)
nodes.title: Tudors, 1485-1603 (England, AD 1485–AD 1603)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1485–AD 1603] Tudors, 1485-1603. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Tudors, 1485-1603". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry VII's victory at Bosworth ended the Wars of the Roses and began a dynasty that remade the English state: Henry VIII broke with Rome and dissolved the monasteries, Edward VI and Mary I pushed the country violently between Protestantism and Catholicism, and Elizabeth I settled a compromise church while fending off Spain. Royal administration, taxation and propaganda grew more centralised, and the crown began to look outward, chartering voyages that laid the groundwork for later empire. It is also the age of Shakespeare, Holbein portraits and the great brick prodigy houses.

nodes.name: Duchy, 1205-1458 (Greece, AD 1205–AD 1458)
nodes.title: Duchy, 1205-1458 (Greece, AD 1205–AD 1458)
nodes.description:
[Athens, AD 1205–AD 1458] Duchy, 1205-1458. Extracted from heading "Athens (Greece)--History--Duchy, 1205-1458". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1994. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Carved out of Attica and Boeotia by crusader knights after the sack of Constantinople, the duchy centred on Athens with the Acropolis as its ducal palace and the Parthenon as its cathedral. It passed from Burgundian lords to the Catalan Company, who seized it by massacring the Frankish chivalry at the Battle of Halmyros, and later to Florentine bankers, the Acciaioli. Two and a half centuries of Latin rule left western towers and Gothic detail on classical monuments before the Ottomans took the city.

nodes.name: Venetian rule, 1474-1570 (Cyprus, AD 1474–AD 1570)
nodes.title: Venetian rule, 1474-1570 (Cyprus, AD 1474–AD 1570)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 1474–AD 1570] Venetian rule, 1474-1570. Extracted from heading "Cyprus--History--Venetian rule, 1474-1570". Added to LCSH in 1991, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Venice took control of Cyprus through the widowed queen Caterina Cornaro, who was persuaded to abdicate in 1489, turning the old Lusignan kingdom into a colony run for sugar, cotton and salt. Fearing Ottoman attack, the Republic threw vast bastioned walls around Nicosia and Famagusta, still the island's most striking monuments. They failed: the Ottoman invasion of 1570 and the brutal siege of Famagusta ended Venetian Cyprus and helped provoke the Holy League's victory at Lepanto.

nodes.name: King George's War, 1744-1748 (Rhode Island, AD 1744–AD 1748)
nodes.title: King George's War, 1744-1748 (Rhode Island, AD 1744–AD 1748)
nodes.description:
[Rhode Island, AD 1744–AD 1748] King George's War, 1744-1748. Extracted from heading "Rhode Island--History--King George's War, 1744-1748". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.97 of LCSH 1987, and p.95 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The North American front of the War of the Austrian Succession brought border raids along the New England and New York frontier and a startling colonial success: a New England militia force, backed by the Royal Navy, captured the great French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton in 1745. To colonial fury, the peace treaty handed it straight back to France in exchange for Madras. The resentment fed directly into the final showdown of the French and Indian War.

nodes.name: Lothair II, 1125-1137 (Germany, AD 1125–AD 1137)
nodes.title: Lothair II, 1125-1137 (Germany, AD 1125–AD 1137)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1125–AD 1137] Lothair II, 1125-1137. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Lothair II, 1125-1137". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Elected king over the hereditary Hohenstaufen claimant, a choice that ignited the long Welf-Hohenstaufen feud later exported to Italy as Guelphs and Ghibellines. He backed Pope Innocent II in a disputed papal election and was crowned emperor in Rome in return, and campaigned in southern Italy against the Norman kingdom. His death without a son left the succession open and the rivalry unresolved.

nodes.name: Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931 (Spain, AD 1886–AD 1931)
nodes.title: Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931 (Spain, AD 1886–AD 1931)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1886–AD 1931] Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Alfonso XIII, 1886-1931". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

King from birth, he presided over the loss of Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines in 1898 and the national soul-searching that followed. Costly war in Morocco, culminating in the disaster at Annual, discredited the parliamentary system, and in 1923 he backed Primo de Rivera's dictatorship - a gamble that tied the crown to its failure. When republicans swept the 1931 municipal elections he left the country, and the Second Republic was proclaimed.

nodes.name: Pedro II, 1683-1706 (Portugal, AD 1683–AD 1706)
nodes.title: Pedro II, 1683-1706 (Portugal, AD 1683–AD 1706)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1683–AD 1706] Pedro II, 1683-1706. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Pedro II, 1683-1706". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He had already governed for fifteen years as regent after deposing his brother, and had secured Spain's formal recognition of Portuguese independence in 1668, closing the long war of restoration. His reign brought the Methuen Treaty of 1703, trading English cloth for Portuguese wine and binding the two economies together, and Portugal's entry into the War of the Spanish Succession on the Allied side. Gold strikes in Minas Gerais in the 1690s began the Brazilian bonanza that would finance the extravagance of his successors.

nodes.name: Constantius II, 337-361 (Roman Empire, AD 337–AD 361)
nodes.title: Constantius II, 337-361 (Roman Empire, AD 337–AD 361)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 337–AD 361] Constantius II, 337-361. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Constantius II, 337-361". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Constantine's son secured his share of the empire in a bloody purge of relatives and spent his reign fighting rivals in the west and Persians in the east. A committed supporter of the Arian position, he used imperial power to force his theology on the church, exiling bishops who refused. Late in life he appointed his cousin Julian to defend Gaul, then died marching against him.

nodes.name: Ming dynasty, 1368-1644 (China, AD 1368–AD 1644)
nodes.title: Ming dynasty, 1368-1644 (China, AD 1368–AD 1644)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1644] Ming dynasty, 1368-1644. Extracted from heading "China--History--Ming dynasty, 1368-1644". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Zhu Yuanzhang, a former monk and rebel commander, expelled the Mongols and founded a dynasty that made the examination-trained scholar-official the backbone of government. Cities grew, printing and vernacular fiction flourished, and merchants linked Chinese silk and porcelain to a world economy fuelled by New World silver. Peasant rebellion took Beijing in 1644, and the Manchus entered the passes to claim the throne.

nodes.name: Gustav V, 1907-1950 (Sweden, AD 1907–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Gustav V, 1907-1950 (Sweden, AD 1907–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[Sweden, AD 1907–AD 1950] Gustav V, 1907-1950. Extracted from heading "Sweden--History--Gustav V, 1907-1950". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.113 of LCSH 1987, and p.96 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sweden's longest-reigning king before Carl XVI Gustaf, whose 43 years spanned two world wars and the consolidation of parliamentary democracy. His 1914 Courtyard Speech, in which he defied the government over defence spending, was the last real attempt at personal rule and ended with the crown accepting that ministers, not the king, govern. He steered a careful neutrality in both wars, and in private life was a keen tennis player who competed internationally under the name 'Mr G'.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1975-1990 (Lebanon, AD 1975–AD 1990)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1975-1990 (Lebanon, AD 1975–AD 1990)
nodes.description:
[Lebanon, AD 1975–AD 1990] Civil War, 1975-1990. Extracted from heading "Lebanon--History--Civil War, 1975-1990". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A sectarian power-sharing arrangement, strained by the presence of armed Palestinian factions and shifting demographics, collapsed into fifteen years of militia warfare. Syria and Israel both invaded and occupied territory, Beirut was split along a Green Line, and events such as the Sabra and Shatila massacre and the 1983 barracks bombings drew in outside powers. The Taif Agreement ended the fighting by adjusting the confessional formula that still governs Lebanese politics.

nodes.name: Boleslaus III, 1102-1138 (Poland, AD 1102–AD 1138)
nodes.title: Boleslaus III, 1102-1138 (Poland, AD 1102–AD 1138)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1102–AD 1138] Boleslaus III, 1102-1138. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Boleslaus III, 1102-1138". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bolesław Wrymouth reunited Poland after a war with his half-brother, beat back a German invasion in 1109 and spent decades conquering and Christianising Pomerania, giving Poland access to the Baltic. His chaplain's chronicler, Gallus Anonymus, wrote the first history of the country at his court. His will, dividing the realm among his sons with seniority in Kraków, instead opened nearly two centuries of fragmentation.

nodes.name: Saxon House, 919-1024 (Germany, AD 919–AD 1024) [p06c6g359b4]
nodes.title: Saxon House, 919-1024 (Germany, AD 919–AD 1024) [p06c6g359b4]
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 919–AD 1024] Saxon House, 919-1024. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Saxon House, 919-1024". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.55 of LCSH 1987, and p.44 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry the Fowler and his Ottonian successors turned the east Frankish kingdom into the dominant power of Latin Europe, breaking the Magyar raids at the Lechfeld in 955 and reviving the imperial title when Otto I was crowned in Rome in 962. Bishops and abbots were used as instruments of royal government, tying church and crown together in a bond that would explode into the Investiture Contest a century later. The dynasty's manuscripts, ivories and great churches mark a deliberate revival of Carolingian and Byzantine imperial style.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD 1943–AD 1945) [p06c6g3hswp]
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1943-1945 (Italy, AD 1943–AD 1945) [p06c6g3hswp]
nodes.description:
[Vicenza (Italy : Province), AD 1943–AD 1945] Bombardment, 1943-1945. Extracted from heading "Vicenza (Italy : Province)--History--Bombardment, 1943-1945". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A North Sea port and shipyard town on the Ems, it was attacked for its harbour and submarine construction and lost the overwhelming majority of its old buildings, with the centre effectively erased in a single raid in September 1944. Postwar reconstruction produced an almost entirely modern town on a medieval street plan.

nodes.name: Later Three Years War, 1083-1087 (Japan, AD 1083–AD 1087)
nodes.title: Later Three Years War, 1083-1087 (Japan, AD 1083–AD 1087)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1083–AD 1087] Later Three Years War, 1083-1087. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Later Three Years War, 1083-1087". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.66 of LCSH 1987, and p.50 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Minamoto no Yoshiie intervened in a succession quarrel among the Kiyowara of northern Honshu and won, but the court refused to call it an official campaign and paid nothing. He rewarded his warriors from his own pocket, an act that bound eastern fighting men to the Minamoto for generations and helped make them the leading samurai house. The victory also opened the north to the Northern Fujiwara, who built their golden temples at Hiraizumi.

nodes.name: British occupation, 1765-1947 (India, AD 1765–AD 1947)
nodes.title: British occupation, 1765-1947 (India, AD 1765–AD 1947)
nodes.description:
[India, AD 1765–AD 1947] British occupation, 1765-1947. Extracted from heading "India--History--British occupation, 1765-1947". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.58 of LCSH 1987, and p.47 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The East India Company's acquisition of the revenues of Bengal turned a trading concern into a territorial power, and conquest spread across the subcontinent until the Crown took direct control after the 1857 rebellion. Railways, telegraphs, cash crops and English-language education reshaped Indian society while deindustrialisation and famine marked the cost. Nationalist mobilisation under the Congress and Gandhi ended in independence and the partition of 1947.

nodes.name: Danilo I, 1851-1860 (Montenegro, AD 1851–AD 1860)
nodes.title: Danilo I, 1851-1860 (Montenegro, AD 1851–AD 1860)
nodes.description:
[Montenegro, AD 1851–AD 1860] Danilo I, 1851-1860. Extracted from heading "Montenegro--History--Danilo I, 1851-1860". Added to LCSH in 1991. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Danilo refused ordination as prince-bishop and turned Montenegro into a secular principality, breaking a two-century tradition of clerical rule. He issued the country's first modern law code, taxed and disciplined the clans, and beat the Ottomans decisively at Grahovac in 1858, winning recognised borders; an exile shot him dead at Kotor two years later.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1895-1898 (Cuba, AD 1895–AD 1898)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1895-1898 (Cuba, AD 1895–AD 1898)
nodes.description:
[Cuba, AD 1895–AD 1898] Revolution, 1895-1898. Extracted from heading "Cuba--History--Revolution, 1895-1898". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Jose Marti's organised exile movement launched the final war for Cuban independence, with Maximo Gomez and Antonio Maceo carrying the fight westward across the island. Spain's General Weyler answered by herding rural civilians into fortified towns, where perhaps 150,000 died of hunger and disease, a policy that horrified American opinion. The explosion of the USS Maine brought the United States in, ending Spanish rule but placing Cuba under American occupation and, later, the Platt Amendment.

nodes.name: Nama Revolt, 1904-1908 (Namibia, AD 1904–AD 1908)
nodes.title: Nama Revolt, 1904-1908 (Namibia, AD 1904–AD 1908)
nodes.description:
[Namibia, AD 1904–AD 1908] Nama Revolt, 1904-1908. Extracted from heading "Namibia--History--Nama Revolt, 1904-1908". Added to LCSH in 2000, revised in 2001. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nama communities under Hendrik Witbooi and later the guerrilla leader Jakob Morenga rose against German colonial rule in the wake of the Herero war. German forces answered with extermination orders, mass deportation and camps such as Shark Island, where prisoners died in appalling numbers. Together with the Herero killings, the campaign is widely recognised as the first genocide of the twentieth century, and its consequences for land ownership in Namibia are still contested.

nodes.name: Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Barcelona, AD 1937–AD 1939)
nodes.title: Bombardment, 1937-1939 (Barcelona, AD 1937–AD 1939)
nodes.description:
[Barcelona (Spain), AD 1937–AD 1939] Bombardment, 1937-1939. Extracted from heading "Barcelona (Spain)--History--Bombardment, 1937-1939". Added to LCSH in 2005, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Republican-held port was hit again and again by Italian aircraft flying from Majorca and by warships offshore, aimed at the harbour, railway and the road link to Barcelona. Civilian districts were wrecked and much of the population fled; the raids ended only when Nationalist troops overran Catalonia.

nodes.name: Lý dynasty, 1010-1225 (Vietnam, AD 1010–AD 1225)
nodes.title: Lý dynasty, 1010-1225 (Vietnam, AD 1010–AD 1225)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1010–AD 1225] Lý dynasty, 1010-1225. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Lý dynasty, 1010-1225". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Lý Thái Tổ moved his capital to Thăng Long, the site of modern Hanoi, and built the first durable Vietnamese state after centuries of Chinese rule and short-lived native dynasties. Buddhism became the court religion while Confucian examinations and a Temple of Literature trained officials; armies fended off a Song invasion and pushed the frontier south against Champa. Much of what is thought of as classical Vietnamese culture — pagoda architecture, ceramics, the one-pillar pagoda, court ritual — takes shape here.

nodes.name: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Pennsylvania, AD 1600–AD 1775)
nodes.title: Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775 (Pennsylvania, AD 1600–AD 1775)
nodes.description:
[Pennsylvania, AD 1600–AD 1775] Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775. Extracted from heading "Pennsylvania--History--Colonial period, ca. 1600-1775". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 90 of LCSH 1987, and p.88 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Founded as a proprietary colony under the Calverts and intended as a refuge for Catholics, Maryland grew into a tobacco economy organised around scattered plantations on the Chesapeake rivers. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved Africans over the seventeenth century, hardening into racial slavery in law. Archaeology at St. Mary's City and Annapolis has made this one of the best-excavated colonial landscapes in North America.

nodes.name: Ahmed III, 1703-1730 (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730)
nodes.title: Ahmed III, 1703-1730 (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1703–AD 1730] Ahmed III, 1703-1730. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Ahmed III, 1703-1730". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign is remembered as the Tulip Era, when the Ottoman court cultivated gardens, pleasure palaces along the Golden Horn and a taste for French fashions, while embassies to Paris and Vienna brought back new ideas. Ibrahim Müteferrika's press, licensed in 1727, printed the first books in Turkish with movable type in the empire. Military defeat and economic strain fed resentment at courtly extravagance, and the Patrona Halil revolt of 1730 deposed the sultan and killed his grand vizier.

nodes.name: Justin II, 565-578 (Byzantine Empire, AD 565–AD 578)
nodes.title: Justin II, 565-578 (Byzantine Empire, AD 565–AD 578)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 565–AD 578] Justin II, 565-578. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Justin II, 565-578". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Justinian's nephew inherited an exhausted, overstretched empire and made it worse by refusing the subsidies that had kept the Persians and the Avars quiet. Most of Italy was lost to the invading Lombards, and a renewed war with Persia went badly enough that Justin descended into mental collapse, leaving his wife Sophia and the general Tiberius to govern in his name.

nodes.name: Conference of Carnuntum, 308 (Austria, AD 308–AD 308)
nodes.title: Conference of Carnuntum, 308 (Austria, AD 308–AD 308)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 308–AD 308] Conference of Carnuntum, 308. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Conference of Carnuntum, 308". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

With the tetrarchic system breaking down into rival claimants, the retired Diocletian was summoned back to a legionary fortress on the Danube to arbitrate. Licinius was made Augustus in the west, Maximian was ordered into retirement again, and Constantine was left with a subordinate rank he would not accept. The settlement lasted barely a moment and the empire slid on toward the wars that Constantine finally won.

nodes.name: Reconstruction, 1865-1877 (United States, AD 1865–AD 1877)
nodes.title: Reconstruction, 1865-1877 (United States, AD 1865–AD 1877)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1865–AD 1877] Reconstruction, 1865-1877. Extracted from heading "Reconstruction (U.S. history, 1865-1877)". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Confederacy's defeat, four million freedpeople sought land, schooling, families reunited and the vote, and constitutional amendments abolished slavery and promised citizenship and equal protection. Black men were elected to state legislatures and Congress under governments backed by federal troops, while the Ku Klux Klan and other paramilitaries used terror to overthrow them. The bargain settling the 1876 election withdrew federal enforcement, leaving the South to segregation and disfranchisement, but the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments remained on the books as the legal foundation of the later civil rights movement.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Illinois, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Illinois, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[Illinois, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Illinois--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.57 of LCSH 1987, and p.55 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572 (Poland, AD 1548–AD 1572)
nodes.title: Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572 (Poland, AD 1548–AD 1572)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1548–AD 1572] Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Sigismund II Augustus, 1548-1572". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last Jagiellonian king pushed through the Union of Lublin in 1569, merging Poland and Lithuania into a single Commonwealth with one elected monarch and one parliament. He kept religious peace at a moment when Protestantism was spreading fast among the nobility, and fought Russia for control of Livonia. He died childless, leaving a vast state whose kings would from then on be chosen by election.

nodes.name: William and Mary, 1689-1702 (England, AD 1689–AD 1702)
nodes.title: William and Mary, 1689-1702 (England, AD 1689–AD 1702)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1689–AD 1702] William and Mary, 1689-1702. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--William and Mary, 1689-1702". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Dutch stadtholder and his English wife took the throne after James II fled, accepting it on terms set out in the Declaration of Rights, which barred Catholic monarchs, banned taxation and standing armies without parliament, and made regular parliaments unavoidable. The settlement was resisted in Ireland and Scotland, where it was decided by Jacobite war, and it dragged England into William's long struggle against Louis XIV. Financing that war produced the Bank of England and the national debt, the machinery of Britain's rise as a great power.

nodes.name: Domitian, 81-96 (Roman Empire, AD 81–AD 96)
nodes.title: Domitian, 81-96 (Roman Empire, AD 81–AD 96)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 81–AD 96] Domitian, 81-96. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Domitian, 81-96". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last of the Flavian emperors ran an efficient, tightly controlled administration: he stabilised the coinage, pushed the frontier in Germany and Britain, and poured money into building in Rome. He also treated the Senate with open contempt, styled himself 'master and god', and executed enough aristocrats to earn lasting hatred from the writers who shaped his reputation. His assassination in the palace brought a smooth senatorial handover to Nerva and opened the era of the adoptive emperors.

nodes.name: Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648 (Poland, AD 1632–AD 1648)
nodes.title: Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648 (Poland, AD 1632–AD 1648)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1632–AD 1648] Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Vladislaus IV Sigismund, 1632-1648". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A soldier-king who began by relieving the Russian siege of Smolensk and forcing a favourable peace, then largely kept the Commonwealth out of the Thirty Years' War raging around it. He was a lavish patron of Italian opera and painting, tolerant in religion, and repeatedly frustrated by a parliament unwilling to fund his plans for war against the Ottomans. He died just as the Cossack uprising under Khmelnytsky broke out, leaving his successor a catastrophe.

nodes.name: Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912 (China, AD 1368–AD 1912)
nodes.title: Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912 (China, AD 1368–AD 1912)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1368–AD 1912] Ming-Qing dynasties, 1368-1912. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Five and a half centuries in which China was governed by broadly similar institutions under two very different ruling houses: the Han Chinese Ming and the Manchu Qing who supplanted them in 1644. Population roughly quadrupled on New World crops, the empire expanded to its greatest extent across Central Asia and Tibet, and Chinese goods drew silver from Europe and the Americas. The era closes with the Opium Wars, the Taiping devastation, and the 1911 revolution that ended imperial rule altogether.

nodes.name: Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736 (Iran, AD 1501–AD 1736)
nodes.title: Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736 (Iran, AD 1501–AD 1736)
nodes.description:
[Iran, AD 1501–AD 1736] Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--Ṣafavid dynasty, 1501-1736". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in 2009. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Shah Ismail's conquest gave Iran a single dynasty again and imposed Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion, a decision that still defines the country's religious map and its rivalry with the Sunni Ottomans. Under Shah Abbas I the capital moved to Isfahan, rebuilt around the great maidan with its tiled mosques, palaces and bazaar, while silk exports drew in European merchants and Armenian traders. Persian miniature painting, carpet weaving and metalwork reached a peak, before Afghan invasion collapsed the state in the 1720s.

nodes.name: Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D (Roman Empire, 29 BC–AD 476)
nodes.title: Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D (Roman Empire, 29 BC–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 29 BC–AD 476] Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Empire, 30 B.C.-476 A.D". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From Augustus to the last western emperor, Rome governed the Mediterranean world as a single state, spreading cities, law, roads, coinage and Latin across three continents. Peace and trade in the first two centuries gave way to third-century military crisis, then to Diocletian's and Constantine's reorganisation and the rise of Christianity as the official religion. The western provinces fragmented into Germanic kingdoms in the fifth century, while the eastern half continued from Constantinople.

nodes.name: Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889 (Serbia, AD 1868–AD 1889)
nodes.title: Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889 (Serbia, AD 1868–AD 1889)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, AD 1868–AD 1889] Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889. Extracted from heading "Serbia--History--Milan Obrenović, 1868-1889". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Milan came to the throne as a boy and presided over Serbia's transformation from Ottoman vassal to sovereign state: independence recognised at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, a kingdom proclaimed in 1882, railways and a modern army built, and a disastrous war with Bulgaria in 1885. His autocratic style, scandalous marriage and quarrels with the Radicals wore down his support, and he abdicated in favour of his young son.

nodes.name: Đinh dynasty, 968-980 (Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980)
nodes.title: Đinh dynasty, 968-980 (Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 968–AD 980] Đinh dynasty, 968-980. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Đinh dynasty, 968-980". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Đinh Bộ Lĩnh defeated the twelve rival warlords, proclaimed the state of Đại Cồ Việt and set his capital in the limestone valley of Hoa Lư. It was the first durable Vietnamese monarchy after a thousand years of Chinese rule, with its own reign titles, court ranks and Buddhist clergy. The dynasty collapsed after Đinh Bộ Lĩnh's assassination, and his general Lê Hoàn took the throne in time to repel a Song invasion.

nodes.name: Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517 (Germany, AD 1493–AD 1517)
nodes.title: Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517 (Germany, AD 1493–AD 1517)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1493–AD 1517] Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517. Extracted from heading "Bundschuh Insurrections, 1493-1517". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1989. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A string of peasant conspiracies in the Upper Rhine and Black Forest that took as their emblem the Bundschuh, the laced peasant boot, raised on a banner against the knight's spur. Organisers such as Joss Fritz demanded the abolition of serfdom, an end to arbitrary dues and church courts, and the restoration of "godly law"; each plot was betrayed and its leaders broken on the wheel. They rehearsed the grievances and the symbolism that exploded in the German Peasants' War of 1525.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Ohio, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (Ohio, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[Ohio, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "Ohio River Valley--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.87 of LCSH 1987, and p.85 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905 (Japan, AD 1904–AD 1905)
nodes.title: Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905 (Japan, AD 1904–AD 1905)
nodes.description:
[Japan, Russia, AD 1904–AD 1905] Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905. Spatial coverage: Japan, Russia. Extracted from heading "Russo-Japanese War, 1904-1905". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A contest over Manchuria and Korea that opened with a surprise attack on Port Arthur and ended with the annihilation of the Russian Baltic Fleet at Tsushima. It was the first modern defeat of a European empire by an Asian state, electrifying nationalists from Turkey to India, and it triggered the 1905 revolution in Russia while confirming Japan's grip on Korea, annexed five years later.

nodes.name: Selim III, 1789-1807 (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807)
nodes.title: Selim III, 1789-1807 (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1789–AD 1807] Selim III, 1789-1807. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Selim III, 1789-1807". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Watching European armies pull ahead, Selim built the Nizam-ı Cedid, a new infantry corps drilled and uniformed on Western lines, alongside new schools, embassies abroad and reformed taxes to pay for it. Napoleon's invasion of Egypt and provincial warlords stretched him thin, and the Janissaries, whose obsolescence the new army advertised, revolted and deposed him; he was murdered the following year. His programme became the template every later Ottoman reformer worked from.

nodes.name: Catherine I, 1725-1727 (Russia, AD 1725–AD 1727)
nodes.title: Catherine I, 1725-1727 (Russia, AD 1725–AD 1727)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1725–AD 1727] Catherine I, 1725-1727. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Catherine I, 1725-1727". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A Livonian peasant woman taken captive in war who became Peter the Great's mistress, then his wife, then, on his death, the first woman to rule Russia in her own right. Real power lay with Menshikov and the Supreme Privy Council created during her short reign. Her accession, engineered by the guards regiments, set the pattern for the palace coups and female sovereigns that dominated eighteenth-century Russia.

nodes.name: Elizabeth, 1741-1762 (Russia, AD 1741–AD 1762)
nodes.title: Elizabeth, 1741-1762 (Russia, AD 1741–AD 1762)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1741–AD 1762] Elizabeth, 1741-1762. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Elizabeth, 1741-1762". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Peter the Great's daughter seized the throne in a guards' coup and ruled with a flair for spectacle, commissioning Rastrelli's Winter Palace and Smolny Cathedral and founding Moscow University and the Academy of Arts. She abolished the death penalty in practice, a striking gesture for the age. Her armies humbled Frederick the Great in the Seven Years' War and briefly occupied Berlin, only for her death to hand Prussia a reprieve when her admiring nephew Peter III made peace.

nodes.name: Carlist War, 1873-1876 (Spain, AD 1873–AD 1876)
nodes.title: Carlist War, 1873-1876 (Spain, AD 1873–AD 1876)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1873–AD 1876] Carlist War, 1873-1876. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Carlist War, 1873-1876". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last great Carlist rising exploited the chaos of Spain's brief First Republic, and for a time Carlos VII ran a state of his own in Navarre and the Basque provinces, with its own mint, courts and university. The restored Bourbon monarchy defeated him and abolished the traditional Basque fueros in reprisal, an act that fed the growth of Basque nationalism.

nodes.name: Alfred, 871-899 (England, AD 871–AD 899)
nodes.title: Alfred, 871-899 (England, AD 871–AD 899)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 871–AD 899] Alfred, 871-899. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Alfred, 871-899". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.47 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alfred ruled Wessex through the worst of the Viking onslaught, buying time after defeat, then breaking the Danish army at Edington and forcing its leader to accept baptism. He built a network of fortified burhs and a reorganised levy that made the kingdom hard to raid, issued a law code, and sponsored translations of Latin works into English so that his subjects could read them. His successors used that foundation to absorb the Danelaw and forge a single English kingdom.

nodes.name: New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872 (New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1872)
nodes.title: New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872 (New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1872)
nodes.description:
[New Zealand, AD 1860–AD 1872] New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872. Extracted from heading "New Zealand--History--New Zealand Wars, 1860-1872". Added to LCSH in 2002, revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

War resumed in Taranaki over a disputed land purchase and escalated into a full invasion of the Waikato aimed at breaking the Kīngitanga, the Māori King movement. Defeat was followed by mass confiscation of Māori land, which in turn fed guerrilla resistance under the prophets and leaders Te Ua Haumēne, Tītokowaru and Te Kooti. The fighting decided who controlled the North Island, and the confiscations remain the basis of Treaty settlement claims today.

nodes.name: Sancho II, 1223-1248 (Portugal, AD 1223–AD 1248)
nodes.title: Sancho II, 1223-1248 (Portugal, AD 1223–AD 1248)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1223–AD 1248] Sancho II, 1223-1248. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Sancho II, 1223-1248". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sancho II pushed the Portuguese frontier deep into the Alentejo and towards the Algarve, but lost control at home: clergy and nobles complained of lawlessness and appealed to Rome. In 1245 Pope Innocent IV declared him unfit to rule and authorised his brother Afonso to take over as regent, and after a short civil war Sancho died in exile in Toledo. It is one of medieval Europe's clearest cases of a pope deposing a reigning king.

nodes.name: Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699 (Austria, AD 1683–AD 1699)
nodes.title: Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699 (Austria, AD 1683–AD 1699)
nodes.description:
[Austria, Turkey, AD 1683–AD 1699] Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699. Spatial coverage: Austria, Turkey. Extracted from heading "Austro-Turkish War, 1683-1699". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Ottoman grand vizier Kara Mustafa besieged Vienna in 1683 until a relief army led by Jan Sobieski of Poland broke the siege in a massive cavalry charge from the Kahlenberg. What followed was not a defensive war but a reconquest: Buda fell in 1686, Belgrade and Transylvania changed hands, and Eugene of Savoy shattered the Ottoman army at Zenta. The Treaty of Karlowitz gave Hungary to the Habsburgs and marked the first great Ottoman territorial retreat in Europe.

nodes.name: Wenzel, 1378-1400 (Germany, AD 1378–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Wenzel, 1378-1400 (Germany, AD 1378–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1378–AD 1400] Wenzel, 1378-1400. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Wenzel, 1378-1400". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Wenceslaus IV inherited Bohemia and the German kingship from his father Charles IV but proved unable to hold either together, quarrelling with the Bohemian nobility and the archbishop of Prague and leaving imperial affairs to drift during the Great Schism. The German electors deposed him as King of the Romans in 1400, though he kept the Bohemian crown for another decades of turmoil. His weak and indecisive rule helped open the space in which Jan Hus's reform movement grew.

nodes.name: Tanzimat, 1839-1876 (Turkey, AD 1839–AD 1876)
nodes.title: Tanzimat, 1839-1876 (Turkey, AD 1839–AD 1876)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1839–AD 1876] Tanzimat, 1839-1876. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Tanzimat, 1839-1876". Added to LCSH in 1989, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A programme of state remaking launched by imperial edict, promising security of life and property to all subjects regardless of religion and dismantling old privileges. New law codes, secular schools, provincial councils, conscription, banks and a telegraph network were introduced on European models, while the empire went into debt to pay for them. The reforms produced a new class of Western-educated officials who eventually demanded more than the sultan intended, culminating in the first Ottoman constitution.

nodes.name: Revolt of Civilis, 69-70 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 70)
nodes.title: Revolt of Civilis, 69-70 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 70)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 70] Revolt of Civilis, 69-70. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Revolt of Civilis, 69-70". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Amid the chaos of the Year of the Four Emperors, the Batavian auxiliary commander Julius Civilis raised his people and neighbouring Germanic and Gallic tribes against Rome on the Rhine. Legions defected, forts burned, and a short-lived Gallic Empire was proclaimed before Vespasian's general Cerialis restored control. Rome afterwards reorganised its frontier armies to keep auxiliary units away from their homelands, and Tacitus made the episode a set piece on the limits of empire.

nodes.name: Alfonso VIII, 1158-1214 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1158–AD 1214)
nodes.title: Alfonso VIII, 1158-1214 (Kingdom of Castile, AD 1158–AD 1214)
nodes.description:
[Castile, AD 1158–AD 1214] Alfonso VIII, 1158-1214. Spatial coverage: Castile and León, Kingdom of Castile. Extracted from heading "Castile (Spain)--History--Alfonso VIII, 1158-1214". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.17 of LCSH 1987.  Source notes Castile is in modern Spain. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His crushing defeat by the Almohads at Alarcos in 1195 was answered seventeen years later at Las Navas de Tolosa, where a coalition of Iberian kings broke Almohad power and opened Andalusia to conquest. He also founded the first Castilian university at Palencia and married Eleanor, daughter of Henry II of England, tying Castile into wider European politics.

nodes.name: Third Crusade, 1189-1192 (Anatolia, AD 1189–AD 1192)
nodes.title: Third Crusade, 1189-1192 (Anatolia, AD 1189–AD 1192)
nodes.description:
[Europe, Anatolia, Levant, AD 1189–AD 1192] Third Crusade, 1189-1192. Spatial coverage: Anatolia, Europe, Levant. Extracted from heading "Crusades--Third, 1189-1192". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1999. The variant label "Third Crusades" has been used as the primary label for the sake of clarity. Spatial coverage inferred from the historical record. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Launched after Saladin destroyed the crusader army at Hattin and took Jerusalem, this campaign drew in three of Europe's greatest rulers. Frederick Barbarossa marched a vast German army overland across Anatolia, storming Konya before drowning in a Cilician river, after which his force largely dissolved; Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus came by sea. The crusaders retook Acre and the coast but never Jerusalem, settling for a truce that guaranteed Christian pilgrims access to the city.

nodes.name: Justinian II, 685-695 (Byzantine Empire, AD 685–AD 695)
nodes.title: Justinian II, 685-695 (Byzantine Empire, AD 685–AD 695)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 685–AD 695] Justinian II, 685-695. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Justinian II, 685-695". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty came to the throne at sixteen, resettled populations wholesale, pushed hard against Bulgars and Arabs, and called the Quinisext Council to legislate on church discipline. He was the first ruler to put an image of Christ on his coins. Heavy taxation and the brutality of his officials provoked a revolt that ended with his nose slit and exile to the Crimea.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Azerbaijan, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1905-1907 (Azerbaijan, AD 1905–AD 1907)
nodes.description:
[Azerbaijan, AD 1905–AD 1907] Revolution, 1905-1907. Extracted from heading "Azerbaijan--History--Revolution, 1905-1907". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Strikes, peasant land seizures and mutinies, including the Potemkin rising off Odessa, swept the Ukrainian provinces of the Russian Empire, accompanied by devastating pogroms against Jewish communities. The October Manifesto lifted the ban on Ukrainian-language publishing, and a burst of newspapers, Prosvita cultural societies and cooperatives followed, with Ukrainian caucuses appearing in the first two Dumas. Most of these gains were rolled back after 1907, but the organisational networks built in these years underpinned the independence movement of 1917.

nodes.name: Otto IV, 1198-1215 (Germany, AD 1198–AD 1215)
nodes.title: Otto IV, 1198-1215 (Germany, AD 1198–AD 1215)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1198–AD 1215] Otto IV, 1198-1215. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Otto IV, 1198-1215". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Welf candidate in the long double election against the Staufer Philip of Swabia, Otto won the crown only after Philip's murder and was made emperor by Pope Innocent III. He promptly turned on his papal patron by invading southern Italy, was excommunicated, and lost his cause at Bouvines, where his French and English coalition was broken by Philip Augustus. The young Frederick II took the empire, and Otto ended his life a deposed prince in Saxony.

nodes.name: Schism, 1837-1870 (United States, AD 1837–AD 1870)
nodes.title: Schism, 1837-1870 (United States, AD 1837–AD 1870)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1837–AD 1870] Schism, 1837-1870. Extracted from heading "Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A.--History--Schism, 1837-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

American Presbyterians split into Old School and New School factions over revivalism, doctrinal looseness and the churches' cooperation with interdenominational mission societies, with slavery straining every seam. Each faction later divided again along North-South lines as the Civil War approached, so that a single denomination became four. Reunion in the North came only in 1869-70, leaving a separate southern church that endured for over a century.

nodes.name: Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C (Greece, 358 BC–322 BC)
nodes.title: Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C (Greece, 358 BC–322 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 358 BC–322 BC] Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Macedonian Expansion, 359-323 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Philip II turned a peripheral northern kingdom into the dominant power in Greece, remodelling his army around the sarissa-armed phalanx and paying for it with Thracian gold mines. Victory at Chaeronea gave him control of the Greek city-states through the League of Corinth; his assassination handed the planned invasion of Persia to his son Alexander. Within thirteen years Macedonian armies had reached the Indus, and the independent Greek polis was finished as a political force.

nodes.name: British occupation, 1762-1763 (Cuba, AD 1762–AD 1763)
nodes.title: British occupation, 1762-1763 (Cuba, AD 1762–AD 1763)
nodes.description:
[Cuba, AD 1762–AD 1763] British occupation, 1762-1763. Extracted from heading "Cuba--History--British Occupation, 1762-1763". Added to LCSH in 2004; appears on p.25 of LCSH 1987, and on p.19 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A British expedition took Havana after a two-month siege in the Seven Years' War, seizing the treasure fleet and a third of the Spanish navy. Eleven months of free trade flooded the island with goods and enslaved Africans and gave Cuban planters a taste of open commerce. Britain handed Havana back in exchange for Florida, but the shock pushed Spain into reforming the colony's defences and economy.

nodes.name: Hova rule, 1810-1885 (Madagascar, AD 1810–AD 1885)
nodes.title: Hova rule, 1810-1885 (Madagascar, AD 1810–AD 1885)
nodes.description:
[Madagascar, AD 1810–AD 1885] Hova rule, 1810-1885. Extracted from heading "Madagascar--History--Hova rule, 1810-1885". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.74 of LCSH 1987, and p.60 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

From the highland capital of Antananarivo, Radama I used muskets and British advisers to bring most of Madagascar under Merina control, while missionaries reduced Malagasy to writing. His successor Ranavalona I expelled the foreigners and persecuted Christian converts for three decades; later rulers reversed course, adopted Christianity as the court religion and abolished slavery. Growing French pressure ended the kingdom's independence in the 1880s.

nodes.name: Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D (Spain, 217 BC–AD 414)
nodes.title: Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D (Spain, 217 BC–AD 414)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 217 BC–AD 414] Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Roman period, 218 B.C.-414 A.D". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.109 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rome landed troops in Iberia to cut Carthage off from its Spanish silver and manpower, and stayed for six centuries. Conquest was slow and bloody – Numantia, the Lusitanian wars, the final Cantabrian campaigns – but the peninsula ended up among the most thoroughly Romanised provinces, exporting olive oil, garum and metals across the Mediterranean and sending Trajan, Hadrian and Seneca to Rome. Aqueducts, bridges and amphitheatres at Mérida, Segovia and Tarragona survive from it, and Latin here became Spanish and Portuguese.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1775-1783 (South Carolina, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1775-1783 (South Carolina, AD 1775–AD 1783)
nodes.description:
[South Carolina, AD 1775–AD 1783] Revolution, 1775-1783. Extracted from heading "South Carolina--History--Revolution, 1775-1783". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.105 of LCSH 1987, and p.102 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The three Delaware counties, long governed under the Penn proprietorship, declared their separation from both Pennsylvania and the Crown and adopted their own constitution. The colony's regiment earned the nickname Blue Hen's Chickens for its discipline in campaigns from Long Island to the Carolinas, and the British marched through on their way to Philadelphia, fighting at Cooch's Bridge. Occupation of Wilmington and the capture of the state's president made the war close and immediate for a very small state.

nodes.name: Mehmed IV, 1648-1687 (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687)
nodes.title: Mehmed IV, 1648-1687 (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687)

[Turkey , AD 1648–AD 1687] Mehmed IV, 1648-1687. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Mehmed IV, 1648-1687".
