nodes.name: Republic, 1912-1949 (China, AD 1912–AD 1949)
nodes.title: Republic, 1912-1949 (China, AD 1912–AD 1949)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1912–AD 1949] Republic, 1912-1949. Extracted from heading "China--History--Republic, 1912-1949". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 2014. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Sun Yat-sen's revolution ended two millennia of imperial rule, but the republic that replaced it was fragmented almost at once between Yuan Shikai's ambitions and regional warlord armies. Nationalist reunification in 1928 brought a decade of state-building in Nanjing, cut short by full-scale war with Japan. Victory in 1945 gave way immediately to civil war and the establishment of the People's Republic.

nodes.name: Guangxu, 1875-1908 (China, AD 1875–AD 1908)
nodes.title: Guangxu, 1875-1908 (China, AD 1875–AD 1908)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1875–AD 1908] Guangxu, 1875-1908. Extracted from heading "China--History--Guangxu, 1875-1908". Added to LCSH in 2000. Alternate label "Kuang hsu, 1875-1908" appears on p.21 of LCSH 1987, and p.16 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign of a boy emperor who spent most of his life under the control of the Empress Dowager Cixi, in decades when the Qing empire lost a war to Japan, ceded ports to European powers and faced the Boxer uprising. His backing of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898 ended with the reformers executed or exiled and the emperor confined to a palace island. He died a day before Cixi, of arsenic poisoning, leaving the dynasty three years from its end.

nodes.name: Tawfīq, 1879-1892 (Egypt, AD 1879–AD 1892)
nodes.title: Tawfīq, 1879-1892 (Egypt, AD 1879–AD 1892)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, AD 1879–AD 1892] Tawfīq, 1879-1892. Extracted from heading "Egypt--History--Tawfīq, 1879-1892". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.29 of LCSH 1987, and on p.23 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The reign of Khedive Tawfiq, installed after his father Ismail was deposed over Egypt's crushing debts to European creditors. Nationalist officers under Ahmad Urabi rose against foreign control, Britain answered by bombarding Alexandria and invading in 1882, and Tawfiq was left ruling under a British occupation that would outlast him by decades; meanwhile Egypt lost Sudan to the Mahdist revolt.

nodes.name: Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009 (Vietnam, AD 980–AD 1009)
nodes.title: Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009 (Vietnam, AD 980–AD 1009)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 980–AD 1009] Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Early Lê dynasty, 980-1009". Added to LCSH in 1999, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The general Lê Hoàn seized the throne from the child heir of the Đinh and immediately faced a Song Chinese invasion, which he crushed in 981, confirming the independence of the young Vietnamese state. He also campaigned south against Champa, sacking its capital, and ruled from the fortified valley capital of Hoa Lư. The dynasty lasted only three reigns; its last, notoriously cruel ruler was replaced in 1009 by the founder of the long-lived Lý dynasty.

nodes.name: Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C (Greece, 322 BC–280 BC)
nodes.title: Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C (Greece, 322 BC–280 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 322 BC–280 BC] Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Macedonian Hegemony, 323-281 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Alexander's death set his generals against one another in forty years of war, while Greek cities such as Athens rebelled and were crushed, garrisoned and made to accept Macedonian-backed regimes. Antipater, Cassander, Demetrius the Besieger and others fought over Macedon and Greece until the battle of Corupedium settled the map into the three great Hellenistic kingdoms. Greece itself became a strategic prize rather than a maker of policy.

nodes.name: Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870 (Canada, AD 1869–AD 1870)
nodes.title: Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870 (Canada, AD 1869–AD 1870)
nodes.description:
[Canada, AD 1869–AD 1870] Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870. Extracted from heading "Red River Rebellion, 1869-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

When Canada bought Rupert's Land from the Hudson's Bay Company without consulting the people living there, the Métis of the Red River Settlement seized Fort Garry and formed a provisional government under Louis Riel. Their List of Rights forced Ottawa to negotiate, and the result was the Manitoba Act, which brought a new province into Confederation with guarantees for French language and Catholic schools. The provisional government's execution of the Orangeman Thomas Scott poisoned relations between Ontario and Quebec, drove Riel into exile, and set the stage for the North-West Rebellion fifteen years later.

nodes.name: Zeno, 474-491 (Byzantine Empire, AD 474–AD 491)
nodes.title: Zeno, 474-491 (Byzantine Empire, AD 474–AD 491)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 474–AD 491] Zeno, 474-491. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Zeno, 474-491". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An Isaurian general who married into the imperial house and ruled the East through revolts, a usurpation that briefly drove him from Constantinople, and the final extinction of the Western Empire in 476. He acknowledged Odoacer's rule in Italy and then encouraged Theodoric and his Ostrogoths to go and take it, ridding the Balkans of them. His Henotikon, an attempt to paper over the split with the anti-Chalcedonians, instead caused a lasting schism with Rome.

nodes.name: Selim I, 1512-1520 (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1520)
nodes.title: Selim I, 1512-1520 (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1520)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1512–AD 1520] Selim I, 1512-1520. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Selim I, 1512-1520". Added to LCSH in 2000; appears on p.117 of LCSH 1987, and p.99 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

In eight years he roughly doubled the Ottoman Empire. He broke the Safavid army with gunpowder weapons at Chaldiran, then destroyed the Mamluk Sultanate, adding Syria, Egypt and the Hijaz with the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. From then on the Ottoman sultan was guardian of Islam's central shrines, and the empire's centre of gravity shifted decisively into the Arab world.

nodes.name: Java War, 1825-1830 (Indonesia, AD 1825–AD 1830)
nodes.title: Java War, 1825-1830 (Indonesia, AD 1825–AD 1830)
nodes.description:
[Indonesia, AD 1825–AD 1830] Java War, 1825-1830. Extracted from heading "Indonesia--History--Java War, 1825-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.59 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta led a broad revolt against Dutch encroachment on land, custom and courtly authority, blending Javanese kingship with Islamic messianic appeal. Five years of guerrilla fighting cost around 200,000 Javanese lives and drained the Dutch treasury; Diponegoro was finally seized while under a flag of truce during negotiations. To recoup the cost the Dutch imposed the Cultivation System, forcing peasants to grow export crops.

nodes.name: Revolutionary period, 1868-1875 (Spain, AD 1868–AD 1875)
nodes.title: Revolutionary period, 1868-1875 (Spain, AD 1868–AD 1875)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1868–AD 1875] Revolutionary period, 1868-1875. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Revolutionary period, 1868-1875". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Generals and liberals drove Isabella II from the throne in the "Glorious Revolution", then spent six years failing to agree on what should replace her. An imported Italian king, Amadeo of Savoy, abdicated in disgust; the First Republic that followed had four presidents in eleven months while Carlist war raged in the north and cantonalist risings split the south. Exhaustion brought a military coup and the restoration of the Bourbons under Alfonso XII, which set up the long, managed two-party system of the Restoration.

nodes.name: Confederation, 1783-1789 (United States, AD 1783–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Confederation, 1783-1789 (United States, AD 1783–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[United States, AD 1783–AD 1789] Confederation, 1783-1789. Extracted from heading "United States--History--Confederation, 1783-1789". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Independence won, the thirteen states governed themselves through a Congress with no power to tax or regulate trade, and the war debt went unpaid. The Northwest Ordinance set the rules by which new territories would become equal states and barred slavery north of the Ohio, one of the era's lasting achievements. Debt riots in Massachusetts convinced enough leaders that the framework was failing to force a constitutional convention.

nodes.name: Uprising, 1652-1653 (France, AD 1652–AD 1653)
nodes.title: Uprising, 1652-1653 (France, AD 1652–AD 1653)
nodes.description:
[Bordeaux (Aquitaine, France), AD 1652–AD 1653] Uprising, 1652-1653. Extracted from heading "Bordeaux (Aquitaine, France)--History--Uprising, 1652-1653". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The final, bloodiest phase of the Fronde, when the Prince de Condé turned his army against the crown, fought in the streets of Paris and then took Spanish pay against his own king. The revolt collapsed, Mazarin returned in triumph, and the boy Louis XIV emerged with a lifelong distrust of Paris and of the great nobility. His answer was Versailles: a court that kept aristocrats close, ornamental and harmless.

nodes.name: Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735 (Sicily, AD 1700–AD 1735)
nodes.title: Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735 (Sicily, AD 1700–AD 1735)
nodes.description:
[Sicily, AD 1700–AD 1735] Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735. Extracted from heading "Sicily (Italy)--History--Savoyard and Austrian rule, 1700-1735". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The end of the Spanish Habsburg line turned Sicily into a bargaining chip among Europe's powers. The Treaty of Utrecht handed the island and its crown to Victor Amadeus II of Savoy in 1713; seven years later a further diplomatic swap transferred it to the Austrian Habsburgs, who governed from Vienna until a Spanish Bourbon army under the future Charles III took it by force. Two decades of absentee rulers left little affection and few reforms, but the conquest of 1734-35 created the independent Bourbon kingdom of Naples and Sicily that lasted until Italian unification.

nodes.name: Christian VII, 1766-1808 (Denmark, AD 1766–AD 1808)
nodes.title: Christian VII, 1766-1808 (Denmark, AD 1766–AD 1808)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1766–AD 1808] Christian VII, 1766-1808. Extracted from heading "Denmark--History--Christian VII, 1766-1808". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.27 of LCSH 1987, and on p.21 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The king was mentally ill for most of his reign, so power lay with others — most spectacularly with the royal physician Struensee, who for sixteen months issued reforms abolishing censorship and torture before being executed in 1772. Later, under Crown Prince Frederik, serfdom was ended and the timber and grain trade made Norwegian merchants rich during Europe's wars. Neutrality collapsed in 1807 when the British bombarded Copenhagen and seized the fleet, cutting Norway off from Denmark by sea.

nodes.name: Civil War, 68-69 (Roman Empire, AD 68–AD 69)
nodes.title: Civil War, 68-69 (Roman Empire, AD 68–AD 69)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 68–AD 69] Civil War, 68-69. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Civil War, 68-69". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Nero's suicide ended the Julio-Claudian line and four men claimed the throne in quick succession: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and finally Vespasian. Legions from Spain, the Rhine and the East marched on Italy, and Rome itself saw street fighting and the burning of the Capitol. The episode exposed what Tacitus called the secret of empire - that an emperor could be made away from Rome - and installed the Flavian dynasty.

nodes.name: Civil War, 49-45 B.C (ancient Rome, 48 BC–44 BC)
nodes.title: Civil War, 49-45 B.C (ancient Rome, 48 BC–44 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 48 BC–44 BC] Civil War, 49-45 B.C. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Civil War, 49-45 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 84 of LCSH 1975 with dates 49 and 48 B.C. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Caesar crossed the Rubicon with a single legion rather than surrender his command, and the Republic split between his supporters and those of Pompey and the Senate. Campaigns ranged across Italy, Spain, Greece, Egypt and North Africa, ending with victories at Pharsalus, Thapsus and Munda. Caesar emerged as dictator with no rival left standing - a concentration of power that provoked his murder and the wars that followed.

nodes.name: Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1282–AD 1328)
nodes.title: Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1282–AD 1328)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1282–AD 1328] Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Andronicus II Palaeologus, 1282-1328". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A long, financially strapped reign in which the emperor scrapped the fleet to save money and hired the Catalan Company as mercenaries, who promptly ravaged the empire's own provinces. Meanwhile Byzantine Anatolia slipped away to Turkish emirates, among them the small principality of Osman. Yet these same decades produced the mosaics and frescoes of the Chora church and a brilliant revival of classical scholarship, and they ended with the old emperor deposed by his own grandson.

nodes.name: Theodosians, 379-455 (Roman Empire, AD 379–AD 455)
nodes.title: Theodosians, 379-455 (Roman Empire, AD 379–AD 455)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 379–AD 455] Theodosians, 379-455. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Theodosians, 379-455". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A dynasty that began with a general summoned to salvage the Balkans after Adrianople and ended with the murder of Valentinian III. Under its rule Nicene Christianity became the empire's official faith, pagan sacrifice was outlawed, and the administrative division of 395 between Constantinople and Ravenna hardened into a permanent split. The western half meanwhile lost Britain, Africa and much of Gaul and Spain to Germanic kingdoms, and Rome itself was sacked in 410, while the east stabilised behind new walls and a codified body of law.

nodes.name: Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945 (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945)
nodes.title: Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945 (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1945] Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945. Extracted from heading "Vietnam--History--Nguyẽ̂n dynasty, 1802-1945". Added to LCSH in 1996, revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Vietnam's last imperial house, founded when Gia Long crushed the Tây Sơn and ruled the whole country from a new citadel at Huế. Its Confucian, China-facing court resisted Western contact and persecuted Catholic converts, which France used to justify conquest, reducing later emperors to salaried figureheads of a protectorate. Bảo Đại's abdication in 1945 closed a thousand years of Vietnamese monarchy.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1917-1918 (Estonia, AD 1917–AD 1918)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1917-1918 (Estonia, AD 1917–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Estonia, AD 1917–AD 1918] Revolution, 1917-1918. Extracted from heading "Estonia--History--Revolution, 1917-1918". Added to LCSH 1986; appears on p.32 of LCSH 1987, and p.25 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The collapse of Russian authority let Finland declare independence, but the new state immediately split between socialist Reds in the industrial south and the Whites of the countryside. The civil war lasted barely four months and was savage out of proportion to its length, with executions and prison-camp deaths outnumbering battlefield casualties. German intervention decided it for the Whites, and the bitterness between the two sides shaped Finnish politics for generations.

nodes.name: Alfonso II, 1162-1196 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1162–AD 1196)
nodes.title: Alfonso II, 1162-1196 (Kingdom of Aragon, AD 1162–AD 1196)
nodes.description:
[Aragon (Spain), AD 1162–AD 1196] Alfonso II, 1162-1196. Spatial coverage: Aragon, Kingdom of Aragon. Extracted from heading "Aragon (Spain)--History--Alfonso II, 1162-1196". Added to LCSH in 1992, revised in 1993. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first ruler to hold both the kingdom of Aragon and the county of Barcelona, creating the composite state known as the Crown of Aragon. He divided future conquest zones with Castile by the Treaty of Cazorla, tying Aragonese expansion to Valencia, and built up holdings north of the Pyrenees. A poet himself, he made his court a centre of troubadour culture.

nodes.name: Ferdinand I, 1521-1564 (Austria, AD 1521–AD 1564)
nodes.title: Ferdinand I, 1521-1564 (Austria, AD 1521–AD 1564)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1521–AD 1564] Ferdinand I, 1521-1564. Extracted from heading "Austria--History--Ferdinand I, 1521-1564". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.6 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Charles V's younger brother took the Austrian duchies and then, after the Hungarian king's death at Mohács, claimed the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary, forming the Danubian monarchy that lasted until 1918. He defended Vienna from Suleiman's siege, negotiated the Peace of Augsburg that let German princes choose Lutheranism or Catholicism, and succeeded his abdicating brother as emperor.

nodes.name: Albert II, 1993- (Belgium, AD 1993–AD 2015)
nodes.title: Albert II, 1993- (Belgium, AD 1993–AD 2015)
nodes.description:
[Belgium, AD 1993–AD 2015] Albert II, 1993-. Extracted from heading "Belgium--History--Albert II, 1993-". Added to LCSH and revised in 2006. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Took the Belgian throne unexpectedly on his brother's death and reigned through the country's sharpest strains: the Dutroux scandal, the steady federalisation of the state, and a record-breaking 541 days without a government. He abdicated in favour of his son Philippe, the first Belgian king to step down voluntarily.

nodes.name: Justinian II, 705-711 (Byzantine Empire, AD 705–AD 711)
nodes.title: Justinian II, 705-711 (Byzantine Empire, AD 705–AD 711)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 705–AD 711] Justinian II, 705-711. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Justinian II, 705-711". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Mutilated and exiled, Justinian escaped, married a Khazar princess, then took Constantinople back with a Bulgar army and spent his second reign hunting down those who had deposed him. The vendetta politics and a disastrous punitive expedition against Cherson turned the army against him; his execution ended the Heraclian line and left the empire in two decades of instability.

nodes.name: Uprising, 1918-1919 (Poland, AD 1918–AD 1919)
nodes.title: Uprising, 1918-1919 (Poland, AD 1918–AD 1919)
nodes.description:
[Wielkopolska (Poland), AD 1918–AD 1919] Uprising, 1918-1919. Extracted from heading "Wielkopolska (Poland)--History--Uprising, 1918-1919". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

As the German Empire collapsed, Poles in the Poznań region rose against German rule and, unusually among Polish insurrections, won. Well-organised local militias took most of Greater Poland within weeks and held it until the Treaty of Versailles confirmed the territory for the reborn Polish state. The victory gave interwar Poland its most prosperous province and a trained officer cadre.

nodes.name: Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960 (China, AD 618–AD 960)
nodes.title: Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960 (China, AD 618–AD 960)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 618–AD 960] Tang-Five dynasties, 618-960. Period used explicitly with respect to art: "Use as a chronological subdivision under headings for art forms qualified by the adjective Chinese.". Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A single label for the Tang empire and the fractured half-century that followed its fall, when five short-lived regimes succeeded one another in the north and ten kingdoms shared the south. Despite the political chaos, the interval saw printing spread, tea culture and porcelain industries flourish, and southern China grow into the empire's economic centre. It closed with the Song reunification, which deliberately built a civilian state to prevent any repeat of warlord rule.

nodes.name: Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254 (Germany, AD 1138–AD 1254) [p06c6g38h2x]
nodes.title: Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254 (Germany, AD 1138–AD 1254) [p06c6g38h2x]
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1138–AD 1254] Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Hohenstaufen, 1138-1254". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Under Frederick Barbarossa, Henry VI and Frederick II the Staufen ruled Germany, imperial Italy and eventually Sicily, and pursued a vision of universal empire that brought them into repeated, ruinous conflict with the papacy and the Lombard cities. Their courts fostered chivalric culture, Minnesang, and in Frederick II's Palermo a famously cosmopolitan mix of Latin, Greek and Arabic learning. The dynasty's extinction left Germany without an effective king and its princes and towns permanently stronger.

nodes.name: SLORC period, 1988-1997 (Burma, AD 1988–AD 1997)
nodes.title: SLORC period, 1988-1997 (Burma, AD 1988–AD 1997)
nodes.description:
[Burma, AD 1988–AD 1997] SLORC period, 1988-1997. Extracted from variant for header "Burma--History--1988-". Added to LCSH in 2009. The same header includes a second period, "Burma--History--SPDC period, 1997-", which we have not included here. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The State Law and Order Restoration Council took power after crushing the 1988 uprising, renamed the country Myanmar, and then annulled the 1990 election won overwhelmingly by Aung San Suu Kyi's party. It opened the economy to border trade and foreign investment while keeping political life closed, fighting or buying off ethnic insurgencies and holding Suu Kyi under house arrest. Renamed the SPDC in 1997, the same generals ran the country for another decade.

nodes.name: Rebellion, 1837-1838 (Canada, AD 1837–AD 1838)
nodes.title: Rebellion, 1837-1838 (Canada, AD 1837–AD 1838)
nodes.description:
[Canada, AD 1837–AD 1838] Rebellion, 1837-1838. Extracted from heading "Canada--History--Rebellion, 1837-1838". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Reformers in Lower Canada under Louis-Joseph Papineau and in Upper Canada under William Lyon Mackenzie took up arms against colonial oligarchies, the Château Clique and the Family Compact, that controlled patronage and blocked elected assemblies. Both risings were quickly defeated, with hangings and transportations to follow. London's response, Lord Durham's report, produced the union of the Canadas and eventually responsible government, a step on the road to Confederation.

nodes.name: Otto III, 983-1002 (Germany, AD 983–AD 1002)
nodes.title: Otto III, 983-1002 (Germany, AD 983–AD 1002)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 983–AD 1002] Otto III, 983-1002. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Otto III, 983-1002". Added to LCSH in 1998. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Made king as a three-year-old, he grew up under the regency of his Byzantine mother Theophanu and his grandmother Adelaide, and as an adult pursued a visionary programme of renewing the Roman Empire from Rome itself. He installed his tutor Gerbert of Aurillac as Pope Sylvester II, recognised new Christian kingdoms in Poland and Hungary at Gniezno, and dreamed of a Christian empire uniting Latin and Greek traditions. His death at twenty-one left the plan unfinished and Italy in revolt.

nodes.name: Jin dynasty, 265-419 (China, AD 265–AD 419)
nodes.title: Jin dynasty, 265-419 (China, AD 265–AD 419)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 265–AD 419] Jin dynasty, 265-419. Extracted from heading "China--History--Jin dynasty, 265-419".  Added to LCSH in 2000. Revised in 2000. Alternate label "Chin dynasty, 265-419" appears on p.20 of LCSH 1987, and appears on p.15 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born when the Sima family usurped the throne of Wei, the Jin briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, then tore itself apart in the War of the Eight Princes. Nomadic groups seized the north, and the court fled south to Jiankang, leaving a divided China for the next 270 years. The refugee aristocracy in the south nurtured a golden age of calligraphy, landscape poetry and the spread of Buddhism, and produced figures such as Wang Xizhi and Tao Yuanming.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1923-1924 (Mexico, AD 1923–AD 1924)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1923-1924 (Mexico, AD 1923–AD 1924)
nodes.description:
[Mexico, AD 1923–AD 1924] Revolution, 1923-1924. Extracted from heading "Mexico--History--Revolution, 1923-1924". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2007. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Adolfo de la Huerta and much of the federal army rebelled when Obregón chose Calles as his successor rather than allowing an open contest. Peasant militias and, importantly, US arms and recognition kept Obregón in power, and the rebellion was crushed within months. Its defeat broke the army's ability to make presidents and helped shift power to the civilian party machine that would become the PRI.

nodes.name: Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355 (Italy, AD 1287–AD 1355)
nodes.title: Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355 (Italy, AD 1287–AD 1355)
nodes.description:
[Siena (Italy), AD 1287–AD 1355] Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355. Extracted from heading "Siena (Italy)--History--Rule of the Nine, 1287-1355". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Siena was governed by a rotating council of nine merchants and bankers drawn from the middle ranks of the city, deliberately excluding the great noble families. Their regime paid for the Campo, the Palazzo Pubblico and much of the cathedral, and commissioned Lorenzetti's Allegory of Good and Bad Government as a portrait of their own ideals. Plague, banking failures and popular anger brought the government down in 1355, and Siena never recovered its former standing.

nodes.name: Bayezid II, 1481-1512 (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512)
nodes.title: Bayezid II, 1481-1512 (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512)
nodes.description:
[Turkey , AD 1481–AD 1512] Bayezid II, 1481-1512. Extracted from heading "Turkey--History--Bayezid II, 1481-1512". Added to LCSH in 1988 revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cautious consolidator after his father's conquests, he spent years neutralised by his brother Cem, a rival claimant held hostage in Europe. He rebuilt the treasury and legal administration, expanded the navy that would dominate the eastern Mediterranean, and sent ships to carry Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 to Ottoman territory, where they settled in Salonica and Istanbul. Ageing and challenged by rebellion, he was forced to abdicate by his son Selim.

properties.title: mosque-lamp — 1510 (circa)
properties.notes:
Lamp (mosque), made of blue, white painted and glazed pottery. The lamp has a bulbous body with a flattened shoulder, three small suspension handles and a tall flaring neck, standing on a high profiled foot. It is painted in shades of cobalt blue with three oblong lobed cartouches with naïve Naskh inscriptions each reading Allh, Muhammad, >Al set against an arabesque of spiralling tendrils on a brushed cobalt ground. Each cartouche has a blue line border with plaited ends and is set in a larger white cartouche with small split-palmettes on a lightly dotted ground. The handles, which separate the cartouches, are flanked by asymetrical cloud bands on a reserve cobalt ground. The lower body has a continuous reserve band of cloud scrolls alternating with flowerheads. The foot has a reserve band of interlaced split-palmettes above a cable band; a further reserve band of split-palmettes features at the shoulder. The neck with three eight-lobed cartouches with barely legible Naskh inscriptions reserve against spiralling foliage alternating with smaller lobed cartouches joined by knot medallions. The underside of the foot and base with a reticulated medallion within a dart border. properties.title: mosque-lamp — 1510 (circa)
properties.notes:
Lamp (mosque), made of blue, white painted and glazed pottery. The lamp has a slightly flattened bulbous body with three applied loop handles and a flaring trumpet neck, standing on a high foot with a moulded profile. It is painted in tones of cobalt blue with three bold indented chinoiserie trefoils filled with smaller trefoils, cloud bands and fine trails of foliage in reserve. Each handle is at the centre of a cloud band composition with knot motifs. The lower section of the body and neck bear undulating floral scrolls. Below the rim are three lobed oblong cartouches bearing inscriptions separated by knotted hastave on a finely dotted ground. The inscriptions are in naïve, rather incorrect Naskh and read: Allh Muhammad, >Al, with BBW squashed into a corner; Nasr min, Allh wa fath qarb wa bi'ism; al Mu'minn ya Muhammad (part of Quran LXI, 13). There are cable and split-palmette arabesque bands at the foot, and a further cable band at the juncture of the body and the neck. The base has an elaborate knot design set within a ring of stiff lappets. Three metal suspension cables with pierced spherical beads probably of 19th century manufacture.; | Type: mosque-lamp | Medium: pottery; metal (suspension) | Dimensions: 10.60 centimetres foot ; 18.00 centimetres max ; 16.60 centimetres rim ; 28.20 centimetres; | Culture: Ottoman dynasty

properties.title: pen-box — 1510 (circa (box)); 1789-1807 (metal mount)
properties.notes:
Pen-box, made of blue, white painted and glazed pottery. The pen box is in the form of a 13th-14th century Mesopotamian or Near Eastern inlaid brass prototype with a rectangular body of square section, with rounded ends and a recessed base. The interior with a lobed opening and two small integral ceramic inkpots. It is painted in tones of underglaze cobalt blue after an early Ming imitation of the Islamic metal original. The sides bear a pseudo-inscription in knotted foliated Kufic (recalling distantly, "al-shif", or similar combinations) against an arabesque of meandering foliage between narrow cable bands. The rounded ends with panels of symmetrical split-palmette reserved against a brushed and dotted cobalt ground. The top with a knot motif surrounded by leaves and a lobed oblong cartouche with a naïve Naskh inscription "Nasr min Allah wa fath qarib" (part of Qur'an, LXI, 13) painted in reserve. The base with cloud scrolls amongst undulating foliate stems. The interior with cable bands and a lozenge diaper. The ink pots with small silver mounts, one still with its cover. Lid missing and replaced by coarsely engraved beaten silver sheet bearing a tughra of Selim (evidently Selim | Type: pen-box | Medium: pottery; silver (lid) | Dimensions: 6.40 centimetres; 29.70 centimetres; 6.10 centimetres; | Culture: Ottoman dynasty

nodes.name: Isaurian dynasty, 717-811 (Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 811)
nodes.title: Isaurian dynasty, 717-811 (Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 811)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 811] Isaurian dynasty, 717-811. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Isaurian dynasty, 717-811". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1997. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Leo III seized power just as an Arab army and fleet closed on Constantinople; the siege broke, and with it the momentum of Umayyad expansion into Anatolia. The dynasty reorganised the provinces and army, issued the concise Ecloga law code, and — most divisively — banned religious images, launching a century of iconoclasm that pitted emperors against monks and popes and helped push the papacy towards the Franks. Surviving art from these years is largely crosses and ornament rather than saints' faces.

nodes.name: John II Casimir, 1648-1668 (Poland, AD 1648–AD 1668)
nodes.title: John II Casimir, 1648-1668 (Poland, AD 1648–AD 1668)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1648–AD 1668] John II Casimir, 1648-1668. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--John II Casimir, 1648-1668". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A former Jesuit cardinal who inherited a crown as the Khmelnytsky Cossack uprising exploded in Ukraine, followed by the Swedish invasion remembered as the Deluge, which overran most of the country. The wars gutted Poland-Lithuania's population and wealth, and the Truce of Andrusovo ceded Kyiv and left-bank Ukraine to Moscow. The liberum veto was first used to break a Sejm in his reign; worn out and thwarted in his reform plans, he abdicated and retired to France.

nodes.name: Time of Troubles, 1598-1613 (Russia, AD 1598–AD 1613)
nodes.title: Time of Troubles, 1598-1613 (Russia, AD 1598–AD 1613)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1598–AD 1613] Time of Troubles, 1598-1613. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Time of Troubles, 1598-1613". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Epoch of confusion, 1605-1613" appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The death of the last Rurikid tsar left Russia without an accepted ruler, and famine, civil war and a succession of pretenders claiming to be the murdered prince Dmitry tore the state apart. Polish and Swedish armies intervened, Moscow was occupied, and perhaps a third of the population died. A militia raised in Nizhny Novgorod retook the capital and an assembly elected Michael Romanov, founding the dynasty that ruled until 1917.

nodes.name: Elective monarchy, 1572-1763 (Poland, AD 1572–AD 1763)
nodes.title: Elective monarchy, 1572-1763 (Poland, AD 1572–AD 1763)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1572–AD 1763] Elective monarchy, 1572-1763. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Elective monarchy, 1572-1763". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.93 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

After the Jagiellonian line died out, the Polish-Lithuanian nobility chose each new king by open vote on a field outside Warsaw, extracting binding concessions before the crown was handed over. The system made the szlachta the most powerful gentry in Europe and produced a genuinely mixed constitution, but it also invited foreign bribery and let a single deputy's veto paralyse the parliament. The resulting weakness left the vast Commonwealth unable to resist its neighbours, setting up the partitions that erased it from the map.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1997- (Democratic Republic of the Congo, AD 1997–AD 2015)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1997- (Democratic Republic of the Congo, AD 1997–AD 2015)
nodes.description:
[Democratic Republic of the Congo, AD 1997–AD 2015] Civil War, 1997-. Extracted from heading "Congo (Democratic Republic)--History--1997-". Added to LCSH in 1998, revised in 2012. Alternate identifier used to supply PeriodO identifier. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rebellion in Zaire toppled Mobutu, and the new government's break with its Rwandan and Ugandan backers triggered a second, far larger war that drew in nine African states - often called Africa's World War. Millions died, mostly from disease and hunger rather than combat, and armed groups financed themselves through coltan, gold and diamonds. Even after formal peace and elections, militias continued to fight over the mineral-rich eastern provinces.

nodes.name: Ferdinand III, 1637-1657 (Germany, AD 1637–AD 1657)
nodes.title: Ferdinand III, 1637-1657 (Germany, AD 1637–AD 1657)
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1637–AD 1657] Ferdinand III, 1637-1657. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Ferdinand III, 1637-1657". Added to LCSH in 2008, revised in same year. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited the Thirty Years' War in its worst phase and, unlike his father, accepted that it could not be won, negotiating the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. The settlement recognised Calvinism, confirmed the near-sovereignty of the German princes and the independence of the Dutch and Swiss, and ended the emperor's hope of ruling Germany as a real monarch. Habsburg energies turned instead to consolidating the hereditary lands and Hungary.

nodes.name: Plantagenets, 1154-1399 (England, AD 1154–AD 1399)
nodes.title: Plantagenets, 1154-1399 (England, AD 1154–AD 1399)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1154–AD 1399] Plantagenets, 1154-1399. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Plantagenets, 1154-1399". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Henry II's accession joined England to a sprawl of French territories and brought reforms that became the common law, though his quarrel with Thomas Becket ended in murder. Baronial resistance produced Magna Carta and a permanent parliament, while later kings conquered Wales, fought Scotland and launched the Hundred Years War. The Black Death, the Peasants' Revolt and finally the deposition of Richard II closed the line and opened the way to dynastic civil war.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (California, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (California, AD 1861–AD 1865)
nodes.description:
[California, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "California--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.19 of LCSH 1987, and p.17 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Republic, 1873-1875 (Spain, AD 1873–AD 1875)
nodes.title: Republic, 1873-1875 (Spain, AD 1873–AD 1875)
nodes.description:
[Spain, AD 1873–AD 1875] Republic, 1873-1875. Extracted from heading "Spain--History--Republic, 1873-1875". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.110 of LCSH 1987, and on p.93 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Spain's First Republic lasted under two years and burned through four presidents, declared after Amadeo of Savoy gave up the throne in despair. It faced the Third Carlist War, a Cuban insurgency, and the cantonalist revolt in which cities like Cartagena declared themselves independent. A military coup restored the Bourbons under Alfonso XII, beginning the long Restoration settlement.

[Louisiana, AD 1861–AD 1865] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Louisiana--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 73 of LCSH 1987, and p.71 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Restoration, 1814-1830 (France, AD 1814–AD 1830)
nodes.title: Restoration, 1814-1830 (France, AD 1814–AD 1830)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1814–AD 1830] Restoration, 1814-1830. Extracted from heading "France--History--Restoration, 1814-1830". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.39 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1995. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Bourbons returned after Napoleon's fall, with Louis XVIII accepting a Charter that preserved much of the Revolution's legal and administrative settlement while restoring the monarchy and a privileged Catholic Church. Ultra-royalists pressed for a fuller reversal, and under Charles X the attempt to muzzle the press and rig the electorate provoked the July Revolution. The regime's collapse showed that no French government could simply undo 1789.

nodes.name: Second Seminole War, 1835-1842 (Florida, AD 1835–AD 1842)
nodes.title: Second Seminole War, 1835-1842 (Florida, AD 1835–AD 1842)
nodes.description:
[Florida , AD 1835–AD 1842] Second Seminole War, 1835-1842. Extracted from heading "Seminole War, 2nd, 1835-1842". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1990. Note that alternate label "Seminole Wars" includes the First and Third Seminole Wars as well. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The costliest Indian war in United States history began when Seminoles resisted forced removal west, fighting a guerrilla campaign in the swamps and hammocks under leaders such as Osceola, who was seized under a flag of truce. Thousands of US troops died, mostly of disease, and the war drained the treasury before most Seminoles were deported to Indian Territory. A few hundred stayed hidden in the Everglades, ancestors of today's Florida Seminole and Miccosukee communities.

nodes.name: Famine, 1932-1933 (Ukraine, AD 1932–AD 1933)
nodes.title: Famine, 1932-1933 (Ukraine, AD 1932–AD 1933)
nodes.description:
[Ukraine, AD 1932–AD 1933] Famine, 1932-1933. Extracted from heading "Ukraine--History--Famine, 1932-1933". Added to LCSH in 2004, revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Impossible grain quotas, forced collectivisation and the blacklisting of villages that failed to deliver produced mass starvation in the Ukrainian countryside, killing roughly four million people. Peasants were barred from leaving to search for food, and the regime denied the famine while continuing to export grain. Known as the Holodomor, it is recognised by many states as a genocide and remains central to Ukrainian national memory.

nodes.name: George III, 1760-1820 (United Kingdom, AD 1760–AD 1820)
nodes.title: George III, 1760-1820 (United Kingdom, AD 1760–AD 1820)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1760–AD 1820] George III, 1760-1820. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--George III, 1760-1820". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.49 of LCSH 1987, and p.39 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His long reign spanned the loss of the American colonies, the wars against revolutionary and Napoleonic France, and the union with Ireland in 1801. It was also the age of canals, steam engines, cotton mills and enclosure, when Britain became the first industrial nation. Recurrent bouts of madness left him incapacitated from 1810, and his son ruled as Prince Regent for the last decade.

nodes.name: Leopold II, 1790-1792 (Hungary, AD 1790–AD 1792)
nodes.title: Leopold II, 1790-1792 (Hungary, AD 1790–AD 1792)
nodes.description:
[Hungary, AD 1790–AD 1792] Leopold II, 1790-1792. Extracted from heading "Hungary--History--Leopold II, 1790-1792". Appears on p. 46 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.56 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

He inherited a monarchy in turmoil from his brother Joseph II and quickly rolled back the most provocative reforms, calming rebellion in Hungary and the Austrian Netherlands. A capable and pragmatic ruler who had modernised Tuscany for decades beforehand, he tried to manage the French Revolution diplomatically, issuing the Declaration of Pillnitz with Prussia on behalf of his sister Marie Antoinette. He died suddenly, weeks before the war he had hoped to avoid broke out.

nodes.name: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Mississippi, AD 1861–AD 1861)
nodes.title: Civil War, 1861-1865 (Mississippi, AD 1861–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[Mississippi, AD 1861–AD 1861] Civil War, 1861-1865. Extracted from heading "Columbus (Miss.)--History--Civil War, 1861-1865". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.23 of LCSH 1987, and p.20 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Kansas entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, fresh from the guerrilla violence of 'Bleeding Kansas', and threw itself into the war with the highest rate of enlistment of any state. It also raised some of the first Black regiments in Union service. Confederate irregulars struck back on its soil - Quantrill's raiders burned Lawrence and killed some 150 men and boys in 1863 - before Price's invasion was broken at Mine Creek in 1864.

nodes.name: Bulavin Uprising, 1707-1709 (Russia, AD 1707–AD 1709)
nodes.title: Bulavin Uprising, 1707-1709 (Russia, AD 1707–AD 1709)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1707–AD 1709] Bulavin Uprising, 1707-1709. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Bulavin Uprising, 1707-1709". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Don Cossacks under Kondraty Bulavin rose against Peter the Great's punitive expeditions to drag runaway serfs back from the steppe frontier. The revolt spread along the Don and Volga while Russia was fighting Sweden, but government troops crushed it, Bulavin died in 1708, and whole Cossack towns were burned. Its defeat ended the Don's traditional autonomy — the Cossack host was absorbed into the imperial state, and the followers of Ignat Nekrasov fled to Ottoman lands rather than submit.

nodes.name: American occupation, 1847-1848 (Mexico City, AD 1847–AD 1848)
nodes.title: American occupation, 1847-1848 (Mexico City, AD 1847–AD 1848)
nodes.description:
[Mexico City (Mexico), AD 1847–AD 1848] American occupation, 1847-1848. Extracted from heading "Mexico City (Mexico)--History--American occupation, 1847-1848". Added to LCSH and revised in 2004. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Winfield Scott's army fought its way inland from Veracruz, stormed Chapultepec and entered the Mexican capital in September 1847, holding it for nine months. Occupation troops policed a hostile city while diplomats negotiated. The resulting Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred roughly half of Mexico's territory to the United States, reshaping the map of North America and igniting the American quarrel over slavery in the new lands.

nodes.name: Henry II, 1154-1189 (England, AD 1154–AD 1189)
nodes.title: Henry II, 1154-1189 (England, AD 1154–AD 1189)
nodes.description:
[Great Britain, AD 1154–AD 1189] Henry II, 1154-1189. Extracted from heading "Great Britain--History--Henry II, 1154-1189". Added to LCSH in 1986. Appears on appears on p.48 of LCSH 1987, and p.38 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The first Plantagenet ended England's civil war and ruled an assemblage of lands stretching from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, held together by ceaseless travel. His legal reforms — itinerant royal justices, standardised writs, juries of presentment — laid the foundations of the English common law, while his attempt to bring clergy under royal courts led to the murder of Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. His last years were consumed by rebellions raised by his own sons and his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine.

nodes.name: Alexander III, 1881-1894 (Russia, AD 1881–AD 1894)
nodes.title: Alexander III, 1881-1894 (Russia, AD 1881–AD 1894)
nodes.description:
[Russia , AD 1881–AD 1894] Alexander III, 1881-1894. Extracted from heading "Russia--History--Alexander III, 1881-1894". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.107 of LCSH 1987 (source uses term "Soviet Union"), and on p.86 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Coming to the throne after his father was blown apart by revolutionaries, Alexander abandoned reform for repression: political trials, censorship, tightened control over universities and peasants, aggressive Russification of minorities and legal restrictions that helped drive Jewish emigration. At the same time the state pushed industrialisation and began the Trans-Siberian Railway, and turned diplomatically towards France. His reign avoided major war but stored up the grievances his son Nicholas II inherited.

nodes.name: Revolution, 1961-1975 (Angola, AD 1961–AD 1975)
nodes.title: Revolution, 1961-1975 (Angola, AD 1961–AD 1975)
nodes.description:
[Angola, AD 1961–AD 1975] Revolution, 1961-1975. Extracted from heading "Angola--History--Revolution, 1961-1975". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1992. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Revolts in the cotton districts and coffee plantations grew into a guerrilla war against Portuguese rule, fought by three rival movements with different regional and ethnic bases and different foreign backers. Portugal held the cities but bled in the bush until its own army overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon in 1974. Independence the next year came without a settlement between the movements, and the war simply continued as a Cold War proxy conflict lasting to 2002.

nodes.name: Henry III, 1039-1056 (Germany, AD 1039–AD 1056) [p06c6g3m8r9]
nodes.title: Henry III, 1039-1056 (Germany, AD 1039–AD 1056) [p06c6g3m8r9]
nodes.description:
[Germany , AD 1039–AD 1056] Henry III, 1039-1056. Extracted from heading "Germany--History--Henry III, 1039-1056". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.43 of LCSH 1987, and p.34 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Salian power reached its height under a ruler who marched into Italy, deposed three rival claimants to the papacy at the Synod of Sutri, and installed a series of German reforming popes. He made Bohemia and Hungary acknowledge his overlordship and promoted the Peace of God in the empire. Ironically, the reform movement he sponsored produced the papacy that would humiliate his son.

nodes.name: Innocent X, 1644-1655 (Papal States, AD 1644–AD 1655)
nodes.title: Innocent X, 1644-1655 (Papal States, AD 1644–AD 1655)
nodes.description:
[Papal States, AD 1644–AD 1655] Innocent X, 1644-1655. Spatial coverage: Papal States, Vatican City. Extracted from heading "Papal States--History--Innocent X, 1644-1655". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.89 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Giambattista Pamphilj's pontificate opened with an assault on the wealth of his Barberini predecessors and was dominated by the influence of his formidable sister-in-law, Olimpia Maidalchini. He denounced the Peace of Westphalia for conceding too much to Protestants, but Europe's rulers ignored him, a sign of the papacy's shrinking political weight. He rebuilt Piazza Navona as a family showpiece, commissioning Bernini's Four Rivers fountain, and sat for Velázquez's famously unflattering portrait.

nodes.name: Maximilian I, 1597-1651 (Germany, AD 1597–AD 1651)
nodes.title: Maximilian I, 1597-1651 (Germany, AD 1597–AD 1651)
nodes.description:
[Bavaria, AD 1597–AD 1651] Maximilian I, 1597-1651. Extracting from heading "Bavaria--History--Maximilian I, 1597-1651". Appears on p.8 of LCSH 1975, and appears on p.8 of LCSH 1987. Revised in 1994. Source notes Bavaria is in modern Germany. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Maximilian of Bavaria turned a middling duchy into a major Catholic power: he reorganised its finances and army, led the Catholic League to victory at White Mountain in 1620, and was rewarded with the Upper Palatinate and the electoral dignity stripped from his Protestant cousin. His long reign spans almost the whole Thirty Years' War, including the Swedish invasion that reached Munich itself, and ends with the Peace of Westphalia confirming Bavaria as an electorate. His patronage left Munich much of its early Baroque face.

nodes.name: John V, 1706-1750 (Portugal, AD 1706–AD 1750)
nodes.title: John V, 1706-1750 (Portugal, AD 1706–AD 1750)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1706–AD 1750] John V, 1706-1750. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--John V, 1706-1750". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Brazilian gold and diamonds poured into Lisbon and were spent on absolutist magnificence: the colossal palace-convent of Mafra, the Águas Livres aqueduct, the library at Coimbra, and lavish bribes to secure Lisbon's elevation to a patriarchate. He never summoned the Cortes, ruling in imitation of Louis XIV. The spending left the treasury exhausted and Portugal's economy dependent on colonial bullion and English manufactures.

nodes.name: Vespasian, 69-79 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 79)
nodes.title: Vespasian, 69-79 (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 79)
nodes.description:
[Rome, AD 69–AD 79] Vespasian, 69-79. Extracted from heading "Rome--History--Vespasian, 69-79". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 99 of LCSH 1987. Note that Rome refers to the Roman state not the city. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A commander of modest Italian family, Vespasian won the civil wars of 69 and founded the Flavian dynasty, restoring order and, above all, solvency to a state emptied by Nero. His son Titus stormed Jerusalem in 70 and destroyed the Temple; the spoils helped pay for the Colosseum, built on the site of Nero's private lake as a deliberate gift back to the Roman people. He was remembered for blunt humour, heavy taxation and for dying with a joke about becoming a god.

nodes.name: Henrique, 1578-1580 (Portugal, AD 1578–AD 1580)
nodes.title: Henrique, 1578-1580 (Portugal, AD 1578–AD 1580)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1578–AD 1580] Henrique, 1578-1580. Extracted from heading "Portugal--History--Henrique, 1578-1580". Added to LCSH in 1986. Alternate label "Henry I, 1578-1580" appears on p.95 of LCSH 1987, and p.80 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2008. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A cardinal in his sixties took the throne after his young great-nephew Sebastian vanished with the Portuguese army at Alcácer Quibir in Morocco. Childless and celibate, he spent his short reign vainly seeking a dispensation to marry and an heir, while the treasury drained paying ransoms for captured nobles. His death opened a succession crisis that Philip II of Spain settled by invasion, beginning sixty years of Habsburg rule over Portugal.

nodes.name: British Intervention, 1838-1842 (Afghanistan, AD 1838–AD 1842)
nodes.title: British Intervention, 1838-1842 (Afghanistan, AD 1838–AD 1842)
nodes.description:
[Afghanistan, AD 1838–AD 1842] British Intervention, 1838-1842. Extracted from heading "Afghanistan--History--British Intervention, 1838-1842". Added to LCSH in 2011. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Fearing Russian influence, Britain invaded to replace Dost Mohammad Khan with a compliant former ruler, Shah Shuja. The occupation of Kabul collapsed in a general uprising, and the winter retreat of 1842 destroyed an army of some 16,000 soldiers and camp followers. A punitive expedition burned Kabul's bazaar and withdrew, leaving Dost Mohammad back on the throne and Afghanistan with a reputation as a graveyard of empires.

nodes.name: Israeli intervention, 1982-1985 (Lebanon, AD 1982–AD 1985)
nodes.title: Israeli intervention, 1982-1985 (Lebanon, AD 1982–AD 1985)
nodes.description:
[Lebanon, AD 1982–AD 1985] Israeli intervention, 1982-1985. Earlier established form: Lebanon--History--Israeli intervention, 1982-1984. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Israel invaded to drive the PLO out of Lebanon, besieged Beirut, and saw its Phalangist allies massacre civilians at Sabra and Shatila. The PLO leadership was evacuated to Tunis, but the occupation of the south bogged down against a newly mobilised Shia population and helped bring Hezbollah into being. Israeli forces withdrew to a 'security zone' along the border, which they held for another fifteen years.

A covert airlift carried roughly eight thousand Ethiopian Jews, the Beta Israel, out of famine-stricken refugee camps in Sudan to Israel on chartered flights. Thousands had walked hundreds of miles to reach the camps and many died on the way. When the operation leaked to the press, Arab pressure forced Sudan to halt it, stranding families for years until later rescues reunited them.

Denmark was seized in a few hours and then governed with unusual lightness: the king stayed, parliament sat, and the country was presented as a model protectorate supplying food to Germany. Cooperation collapsed in August 1943 amid strikes and sabotage; when deportation of Denmark's Jews was ordered that October, the resistance and ordinary citizens ferried some 7,000 people to safety in Sweden.

nodes.name: Restoration, 1853-1870 (Japan, AD 1853–AD 1870)
nodes.title: Restoration, 1853-1870 (Japan, AD 1853–AD 1870)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1853–AD 1870] Restoration, 1853-1870. Extracted from heading "Japan--History--Restoration, 1853-1870". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 2010. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Commodore Perry's warships forced Japan open after two centuries of restricted contact, and the resulting crisis destroyed the Tokugawa shogunate. Domains such as Satsuma and Chōshū rallied around the slogan of honouring the emperor and expelling the barbarians, then seized power themselves and returned formal rule to the young Meiji emperor. Within a few years the samurai class, the domains and the old capital were all swept away in favour of a centralised state bent on industrial and military modernisation.

A creole junta in Santiago began as self-government under a captive king and hardened into revolution, until royalist armies from Peru crushed the Patria Vieja at Rancagua and drove the patriots over the Andes. They came back with San Martín's Army of the Andes, winning at Chacabuco and decisively at Maipú, after which O'Higgins governed the new republic and helped launch the naval expedition that carried the war to Peru. The southern frontier and Chiloé held out for royalism until 1826.

The Sengoku age, when the shogunate's authority collapsed and provincial warlords fought for territory with mass armies of pikemen and, after 1543, Portuguese-style firearms. Castles, castle-towns and new commercial networks grew out of the fighting, and Christian missionaries arrived alongside European traders. Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and finally Tokugawa Ieyasu reunified the country, ending in a shogunate that would keep the peace for 250 years.

nodes.name: Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C (Greece, 278 BC–277 BC)
nodes.title: Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C (Greece, 278 BC–277 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 278 BC–277 BC] Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C. Extracted from heading "Greece--History--Galatian Invasion, 279-278 B.C". Added in to LCSH in 1986; appears on p. 52 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Celtic war bands swept south through Macedonia and Thessaly, killed the Macedonian king and pushed into central Greece before being turned back near Delphi, a repulse the Greeks credited to Apollo himself and commemorated for centuries. Part of the horde crossed into Asia Minor at the invitation of a Bithynian king and settled in the highlands around Ankara, becoming the Galatians. Their defeat became a favourite theme of Hellenistic art and propaganda, most famously in the Pergamene statues of dying Gauls.

properties.title: duck askos — 325BC-275BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured askos (perfume or oil vase) in the form of a duck. Designs in relief and painted in black on pale red ground; probably of Etruscan manufacture. Handle over the back; spout on the tail. The beak and feathers of the duck are picked out with black, the wave- and other patterns being intermixed with the feathers; the neck and head are black, and round the neck are five rings. On the back, two crosses and two rosettes of dots; on the handle, maeander; round the spout, rays, wavy band, and black spots. On the breast is painted a female figure moving to left, looking back, with hair gathered in a double sphendone, short girt bordered chiton and apoptygma, and sandals, in right hand a phiale, in left an oinochoe. On one side of the body is a female figure in relief, reclining with head towards the first figure, looking back over left shoulder; she has a himation over her arms, sphendone, and black shoes, and her hair is gathered up in masses at the back and over the forehead; in her left hand is an alabastron, and with right she holds up her drapery. On the other side is a male figure in relief, similarly attired, with hair gathered up in the same manner; head to right | Type: duck askos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 15.00 centimetres; 22.90 centimetres; 9.40 centimetres; | Culture: Hellenistic Period (Etruscan) (Etruscan) (Etruscan)

nodes.name: Alexander, 1501-1506 (Poland, AD 1501–AD 1506)
nodes.title: Alexander, 1501-1506 (Poland, AD 1501–AD 1506)
nodes.description:
[Poland , AD 1501–AD 1506] Alexander, 1501-1506. Extracted from heading "Poland--History--Alexander, 1501-1506". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.92 of LCSH 1987, and p.78 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2003. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

A short reign dominated by war with Muscovy and the Tatars and by the ruler's chronic shortage of money. In 1505 he accepted the Nihil novi statute, which barred the king from making laws without the consent of the Sejm - a decisive shift of power to the nobility that shaped Polish politics for the next three centuries.

nodes.name: Joseph II, 1780-1790 (Hungary, AD 1780–AD 1790)
nodes.title: Joseph II, 1780-1790 (Hungary, AD 1780–AD 1790)
nodes.description:
[Hungary, AD 1780–AD 1790] Joseph II, 1780-1790. Extracted from heading "Austria--history--Joseph II, 1780-1790". Added to LCSH in 1986;  on p.46 of LCSH 1975, and on p.56 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The most impatient of the enlightened despots issued some six thousand decrees in ten years: serfdom abolished, religious toleration extended to Protestants and Jews, contemplative monasteries dissolved, censorship relaxed, torture ended, and German imposed as the language of administration everywhere. The pace and the disregard for local privilege provoked open revolt in the Austrian Netherlands and near-rebellion in Hungary, and he died revoking much of his own work - a warning about reform from above that Europe noted just as the French Revolution began.

nodes.description:
[France, Germany, AD 1870–AD 1871] Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871. Spatial coverage: France, Germany. Extracted from heading "Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Bismarck manoeuvred Napoleon III into declaring war and the German states, fighting together, destroyed the French armies in weeks; the emperor himself surrendered at Sedan. Paris held out through a winter siege and then exploded into the Commune, while in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles the German Empire was proclaimed. The annexation of Alsace and much of Lorraine left a grievance that shaped European politics until 1918.

nodes.name: Medieval and modern Iran, 640- (Iran, AD 640–AD 2015)
nodes.title: Medieval and modern Iran, 640- (Iran, AD 640–AD 2015)
nodes.description:
[Iran, AD 640–AD 2015] Medieval and modern Iran, 640-. Extracted from heading "Iran--History--640-". Added to LCSH in 1986, revised in 1995. Earlier established form used as primary label. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

The Arab conquest ended the Sasanian empire and brought Islam, but Persian language and administrative tradition survived and shaped the caliphate; later came Seljuk and Mongol invasions, the brilliance of Timurid Herat and Samarkand, and the Safavids, who made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion and built Isfahan into one of the world's great cities. Qajar rule saw Iran squeezed between Russia and Britain, then the constitutional revolution of 1906 and the Pahlavi drive to modernise on oil revenues. The 1979 revolution replaced the monarchy with an Islamic republic.

nodes.name: Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Norway, AD 1648–AD 1670)
nodes.title: Frederick III, 1648-1670 (Norway, AD 1648–AD 1670)
nodes.description:
[Norway, AD 1648–AD 1670] Frederick III, 1648-1670. Extracted from heading "Norway--History--Frederick III, 1648-1670". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.86 of LCSH 1987, and p.72 of LCSH 1975. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

His reign began with a disastrous war against Sweden that cost Denmark Scania and the provinces east of the Sound, permanently fixing the modern Scandinavian border. But when Copenhagen's citizens helped hold the city under siege, he used the crisis to break the nobility: in 1660-61 the elective monarchy was abolished and the King's Law of 1665 made him one of the most absolute rulers in Europe, on paper at least. He was also a passionate collector, founding the royal library and Kunstkammer.

nodes.name: Interregnum, 1886-1887 (Bulgaria, AD 1886–AD 1887)
nodes.title: Interregnum, 1886-1887 (Bulgaria, AD 1886–AD 1887)
nodes.description:
[Bulgaria, AD 1886–AD 1887] Interregnum, 1886-1887. Extracted from heading "Bulgaria--History--Interregnum, 1886-1887". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.13 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Prince Alexander of Battenberg was kidnapped by pro-Russian officers and, though briefly restored, abdicated under pressure from St Petersburg, leaving the young principality without a ruler. A regency dominated by Stefan Stambolov defied Russian attempts to control the succession and eventually found a candidate in Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. The episode marked Bulgaria's break from Russian tutelage and the start of Stambolov's hard-handed rule.

nodes.name: Rupert, 1400-1410 (Germany, AD 1400–AD 1410)
nodes.title: Rupert, 1400-1410 (Germany, AD 1400–AD 1410)
nodes.description:
[Holy Roman Empire, AD 1400–AD 1410] Rupert, 1400-1410. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Holy Roman Empire, Italy, Luxembourg. Extracted from heading "Holy Roman Empire--History--Rupert, 1400-1410". Added to LCSH in 1986. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Rupert of the Palatinate was raised to the German throne by electors who had just deposed Wenceslaus IV, but he never controlled more than his own Rhineland lands. His expedition to Italy to be crowned emperor collapsed in failure, and his short reign shows how far the monarchy had shrunk against the princes; the crown passed afterwards to the Luxembourg Sigismund.

nodes.name: Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1143–AD 1180)
nodes.title: Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180 (Byzantine Empire, AD 1143–AD 1180)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1143–AD 1180] Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180. Extracted from heading "Byzantine Empire--History--Manuel I Comnenus, 1143-1180". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.14 of LCSH 1987. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

An emperor who spent lavishly to restore Byzantine dominance, intervening in Italy, Hungary and the Crusader states and courting Western knights and customs at his court. His army's destruction in the pass of Myriokephalon in 1176 ended hopes of driving the Turks from Anatolia, and the debts and resentments he left behind helped unravel the empire within a generation.

nodes.name: Third Republic, 1870-1940 (France, AD 1870–AD 1940)
nodes.title: Third Republic, 1870-1940 (France, AD 1870–AD 1940)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1870–AD 1940] Third Republic, 1870-1940. Extracted from heading "France--History--Third Republic, 1870-1940". Added to LCSH in 1986; appears on p.40 of LCSH 1987, and p.31 of LCSH 1975. Revised in 2005. Period definition from Library of Congress Subject Headings — Library of Congress, 2015.

Born from the collapse of Napoleon III's empire and the bloody suppression of the Paris Commune, this republic became the longest-lasting French regime since 1789. It built free secular schooling, separated church and state, expanded a vast colonial empire, and tore itself apart over the Dreyfus Affair. It produced the Paris of Haussmann's boulevards, the Eiffel Tower and Impressionism, and ended with the German invasion of 1940.
