properties.notes:
Pottery lekythos with black on white painted decoration; double row of parallel lines on shoulder; meander within linear borders at shoulder body junction; double lattice panels framing an ivy berry tendril; plain slip; foot lost; surface worn.; | Type: lekythos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 20.95 centimetres; 7.40 centimetres shoulder ; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Deve Huyuk, Greece

nodes.name: Early Empire (Italy, 26 BC–AD 96)
nodes.title: Early Empire (Italy, 26 BC–AD 96)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 26 BC–AD 96] Early Empire. Spatial coverage: Egypt, France, Greece, Israel, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Tunisia. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 171. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

From Augustus's settlement of the state to the death of Domitian, one man held permanent control of army, treasury and law while the Republic's institutions were kept as scenery. Peace across the Mediterranean fuelled trade, urban building and a boom in monumental architecture — the Colosseum, aqueducts, the rebuilt Forum — and the frontier armies pushed into Britain and along the Rhine and Danube. It is also the period preserved in freeze-frame at Pompeii and Herculaneum.

nodes.name: Early Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 526–AD 726)
nodes.title: Early Byzantine Period (Turkey, AD 526–AD 726)
nodes.description:
[Turkey, AD 526–AD 726] Early Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Israel, Russia, Turkey, Ukraine. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 235. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

Crete began this stretch as a rich, densely settled Christian province of grain estates and mosaic-floored basilicas centred on Gortyn, and ended it in upheaval. Earthquakes, plague and the collapse of Mediterranean security shrank its cities, and in the 820s Arab settlers took the island and founded the Emirate of Crete. Byzantine rule was only restored in 961.

nodes.name: Cycladic Culture (Greece, 2999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: Cycladic Culture (Greece, 2999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 2999 BC–1599 BC] Cycladic Culture. For spatial coverage label, please see map on page 85. Period definition from Art history — Stokstad, Marilyn, 1929-, 2005.

The islanders of the central Aegean carved slender marble figurines with folded arms and blank faces - abstract to modern eyes and hugely influential on twentieth-century sculpture. They were skilled seafarers and metalworkers whose obsidian and silver moved across the Aegean, and their fortified settlements and long-boat imagery show a maritime world that flourished before Minoan Crete and Mycenae came to dominate it.

nodes.name: 1940-45, 2. Verdenskrig (Denmark, AD 1940–AD 1945)
nodes.title: 1940-45, 2. Verdenskrig (Denmark, AD 1940–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1940–AD 1945] 1940-45, 2. Verdenskrig. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

German forces occupied Denmark on 9 April 1940 after only hours of fighting, and for three years the Danish government pursued a policy of cooperation that kept parliament, police and monarchy in place. Strikes and sabotage forced the collapse of that policy in August 1943; the Germans imposed martial law, the navy scuttled its fleet, and in October almost all of Denmark's Jews were ferried to safety in Sweden. Resistance groups, an underground press and Allied air support grew through 1944-45 until the German surrender in Denmark took effect on 5 May 1945. Bunkers, coastal batteries and Atlantic Wall works from the occupation still dot the Jutland coast.

nodes.name: Yngre Bronzealder per.6 (Denmark, 700 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Bronzealder per.6 (Denmark, 700 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 700 BC–500 BC] Yngre Bronzealder per.6. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The last phase of the Bronze Age, with contacts running south to the Hallstatt world of central Europe and the first iron objects trickling in. Metalwork becomes plainer and scarcer as bronze supply lines faltered, setting up the shift to a local iron-based economy.

nodes.name: 1919-39,  Mellemskrigstiden (Denmark, AD 1919–AD 1939)
nodes.title: 1919-39,  Mellemskrigstiden (Denmark, AD 1919–AD 1939)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1919–AD 1939] 1919-39,  Mellemskrigstiden. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The 1920 plebiscites returned North Schleswig to Denmark, an outcome celebrated as Reunification but preceded by a constitutional crisis when the king dismissed the government. Social Democratic and Radical governments under Thorvald Stauning built the foundations of the Danish welfare state, above all in the Kanslergade Agreement of 1933, which combined social reform with support for depressed farmers. Unemployment, currency crises and a strong agricultural export trade dominated the economy, while functionalist architecture and modern design took hold in the towns.

nodes.name: Ældre Bronzealder (Denmark, 1700 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Bronzealder (Denmark, 1700 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1700 BC–1100 BC] Ældre Bronzealder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark's early Bronze Age was extraordinarily wealthy: amber and cattle went south, and bronze came back to be cast into distinctive Nordic swords, axes, lurs and spiral-decorated jewellery. Chiefs and their families were buried in thousands of turf barrows, and in some the airtight mound conditions preserved oak coffins with woollen clothing, hair and skin — the Egtved girl and the Borum Eshøj family among them. The Trundholm sun chariot and the era's rock art point to a religion centred on the sun's daily journey.

nodes.name: Efterreformatorisk tid (1536-1660) (Denmark, AD 1536–AD 1660)
nodes.title: Efterreformatorisk tid (1536-1660) (Denmark, AD 1536–AD 1660)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1536–AD 1660] Efterreformatorisk tid (1536-1660). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Beginning with the Lutheran Reformation and the crown's seizure of church property, this era saw the Danish king rule alongside a powerful noble council. Royal wealth funded Renaissance castles, new towns and Christian IV's ambitious building schemes, while disastrous wars with Sweden stripped away territory. It closed with the collapse of noble power and the introduction of hereditary absolute monarchy.

nodes.name: Ældre middelalder (1067 - 1100-tal) (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1199)
nodes.title: Ældre middelalder (1067 - 1100-tal) (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1199)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1199] Ældre middelalder (1067 - 1100-tal). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The Danish church took shape around new dioceses and the archbishopric of Lund, and villages across the country replaced wooden chapels with Romanesque stone churches. Decades of dynastic civil war ended with Valdemar I, whose ally Bishop Absalon fortified a fishing harbour that became Copenhagen. Royal power was now grounded in landed estates, taxes and an alliance with the church rather than in the loyalty of a warrior fleet alone.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur 1A (Denmark, 3300 BC–3200 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur 1A (Denmark, 3300 BC–3200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3300 BC–3200 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur 1A. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The earliest stage of Denmark's passage-grave era, marked by the Troldebjerg pottery style with its bands of stab-and-drag ornament. Communities were investing enormous labour in stone-built chambers meant to be entered and re-entered, a shift away from the closed long barrows of earlier generations.

nodes.name: Yngre Jernalder (Germansk jernalder og Vikingetid) (Denmark, AD 375–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Yngre Jernalder (Germansk jernalder og Vikingetid) (Denmark, AD 375–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 375–AD 1066] Yngre Jernalder (Germansk jernalder og Vikingetid). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Seven centuries running from the turmoil after Rome's collapse to the end of the Viking Age. Wealth shifted from bog offerings of weapons to gold hoards and hall-based aristocracies, then to towns, coinage and long-distance raiding and trade; it closes with a Christian kingdom of Denmark ruled from Jelling and Roskilde.

nodes.name: Historisk tid (1067 -) (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 2100)
nodes.title: Historisk tid (1067 -) (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 2100)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1067–AD 2100] Historisk tid (1067 -). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The conventional dividing line where Danish archaeology hands over to written history, at the close of the Viking Age. What follows is a kingdom of stone churches and royal towns, medieval castles and market places, the Reformation and the loss and reshaping of territory, down to the industrial and modern eras. Finds are dated by documents, coins and imported ceramics as much as by typology.

nodes.name: Udateret (Denmark, 250000 BC–AD 2100)
nodes.title: Udateret (Denmark, 250000 BC–AD 2100)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 250000 BC–AD 2100] Udateret. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

A catch-all label, Danish for 'undated', used for sites and finds that cannot be assigned to any archaeological period. The span simply runs from the earliest possible human presence to the present.

nodes.name: Yngre Middelalder (1300 - 1535) (Denmark, AD 1300–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Yngre Middelalder (1300 - 1535) (Denmark, AD 1300–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1300–AD 1535] Yngre Middelalder (1300 - 1535). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Plague and agrarian crisis emptied villages, while Margrete I bound Denmark, Norway and Sweden together in the Kalmar Union of 1397. Brick castles, market towns and Hanseatic trade shaped the landscape, and the era ends in the civil war known as the Count's Feud and the Lutheran Reformation.

nodes.name: Ældre Bronzealder per.1 (Denmark, 1700 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Bronzealder per.1 (Denmark, 1700 BC–1500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1700 BC–1500 BC] Ældre Bronzealder per.1. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The opening phase of the Nordic Bronze Age, when metal was still scarce and locally made bronzes were few — flint daggers imitating metal forms remained in use, and burials often reused older mounds. Contacts with Central Europe brought in the first Nordic-style axes and neck ornaments, and the tradition of raising turf barrows over single inhumations took hold. Everything that follows in the Danish Bronze Age grows out of these tentative beginnings.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur I (Denmark, 3300 BC–3100 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur I (Denmark, 3300 BC–3100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3300 BC–3100 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur I. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The opening of the passage-grave era, when Funnel Beaker communities began raising stone chambers with entry corridors that could be reopened for generation after generation of dead. Pottery of the Troldebjerg style, decorated in horizontal zones, was deposited in quantity outside the tombs during communal rites.

nodes.name: Grubekeramisk kultur (Denmark, 2900 BC–2600 BC)
nodes.title: Grubekeramisk kultur (Denmark, 2900 BC–2600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2900 BC–2600 BC] Grubekeramisk kultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Communities on the Danish coasts and islands who lived by sealing, fishing and hunting rather than farming, making round-bellied pots decorated with dense rows of impressed pits. They overlapped with the Funnel Beaker farmers around them but kept separate economies and burial customs. Their existence shows that the shift to agriculture in southern Scandinavia was reversible and uneven.

nodes.name: Mesolitikum (Denmark, 9000 BC–3900 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolitikum (Denmark, 9000 BC–3900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 9000 BC–3900 BC] Mesolitikum. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

As the ice retreated and the sea flooded the land bridges, Denmark's hunter-gatherers passed through the Maglemose, Kongemose and Ertebølle traditions, moving from inland lake and bog camps to a rich life on the coast. Waterlogged sites preserve an extraordinary record: dugout canoes, leister prongs, bows, fish weirs, and huge shell middens of oyster and cockle. Ertebølle communities were settled enough to build cemeteries and make pottery while still living entirely by hunting and fishing, and they traded with farming neighbours for generations before taking up farming around 4000 BC.

nodes.name: Oldtid (Denmark, 250000 BC–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Oldtid (Denmark, 250000 BC–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 250000 BC–AD 1066] Oldtid. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

A blanket Danish term for everything before the medieval period, from the first reindeer hunters following the retreating ice to the Viking kings. It takes in the Stone Age farmers who built megalithic tombs, the Bronze Age chiefs buried in oak coffins with lurs and sun-discs, the Iron Age bog bodies and weapon sacrifices, and finally the seafarers who raided and settled across the North Sea. Denmark's peat bogs preserved wood, cloth and human remains from these millennia in exceptional condition.

nodes.name: Vikingetid (Denmark, AD 750–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Vikingetid (Denmark, AD 750–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 750–AD 1066] Vikingetid. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark's Viking Age combined seaborne raiding and conquest in England and Francia with rapid state-building at home: the Danevirke rampart, the trading towns of Ribe and Hedeby, and the precisely engineered ring fortresses of Trelleborg type. At Jelling, Harald Bluetooth's rune-stone claims he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian. Under Cnut the Great the kingdom briefly ruled England and Norway together.

nodes.name: Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C1 (Denmark, AD 175–AD 250)
nodes.title: Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C1 (Denmark, AD 175–AD 250)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 175–AD 250] Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C1. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The generation of the Himlingøje chieftains, whose graves on Zealand contain Roman silver drinking vessels, glass and bronze, suggesting a dynasty that controlled access to imports and redistributed them across the region. Ornate silver brooches and gold rings mark a sharply stratified society.

nodes.name: Ældre Romersk Jernalder, B1 (Denmark, AD 1–AD 70)
nodes.title: Ældre Romersk Jernalder, B1 (Denmark, AD 1–AD 70)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1–AD 70] Ældre Romersk Jernalder, B1. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The opening phase of Roman contact, when imported bronze and glass vessels first appear regularly in graves. Its emblem is the chieftain's burial at Hoby on Lolland, furnished with a pair of Roman silver cups showing scenes from Homer — diplomatic gifts or plunder that ended up in a Danish grave. Ordinary people were still cremated with little more than a brooch or a pot.

nodes.name: Ældre Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 5400 BC–4800 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 5400 BC–4800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 5400 BC–4800 BC] Ældre Ertebøllekultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Coastal foragers of the last Danish Mesolithic settled at fjord mouths and river outlets, piling up the shell middens that gave archaeology the word 'kitchen midden'. They fished with weirs and leisters, hunted seals and boar, travelled in dugout canoes, and buried their dead in cemeteries — signs of a settled, territorial way of life without farming. Their descendants would take up cattle and cereals only around 4000 BC, making these centuries the long final chapter of hunting-and-gathering Scandinavia.

nodes.name: Jernalder (Denmark, 500 BC–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Jernalder (Denmark, 500 BC–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 500 BC–AD 1066] Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Iron replaced bronze as the working metal, and Danish farmers built long timber halls in village clusters surrounded by field systems. Contact with the Roman Empire brought coins, glass and weapons north, while great weapon deposits in bogs and preserved bog bodies record war and ritual. The later centuries brought kings, towns and ships, ending with the Viking expansion and Denmark's conversion to Christianity.

nodes.name: Stenalder (Denmark, 250000 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.title: Stenalder (Denmark, 250000 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 250000 BC–1700 BC] Stenalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark's Stone Age, from reindeer hunters at the edge of the ice through the rich coastal foragers who left the shell-heap kitchen middens, to the first farmers who cleared forest and raised thousands of dolmens and passage graves. Bog finds from these millennia — flint axes, amber beads, pottery and sacrificed bodies — are among the best-preserved prehistoric material anywhere.

nodes.name: Yngre Førromersk Jernalder (per.3A) (Denmark, 100 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: Yngre Førromersk Jernalder (per.3A) (Denmark, 100 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 100 BC–AD 1] Yngre Førromersk Jernalder (per.3A). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Iron-using farming villages of the type known from Hodde and Grøntoft, with rows of longhouses inside a common fence and small family cremation cemeteries. Contacts with the Celtic world to the south brought in objects like ornate cauldrons, and the first Roman goods begin to appear at the very end of the period.

nodes.name: Ældre Vikingetid (Denmark, AD 750–AD 900)
nodes.title: Ældre Vikingetid (Denmark, AD 750–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 750–AD 900] Ældre Vikingetid. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Danish kings fortified the Danevirke across the neck of Jutland and fostered the trading towns of Ribe and Hedeby, where silver, glass and furs changed hands with Frisia and the Frankish empire. Improved sailing ships turned coastal raiding into long-distance expeditions to England and the Continent, and the first Christian missions arrived under Ansgar. Pagan burial with weapons, horses and boats was still the norm, and runic memorials record the warriors and traders who paid for it.

nodes.name: Ældre middelalder (1200-tal) (Denmark, AD 1200–AD 1299)
nodes.title: Ældre middelalder (1200-tal) (Denmark, AD 1200–AD 1299)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1200–AD 1299] Ældre middelalder (1200-tal). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Valdemar II's Baltic campaigns and the great land survey of the Jordebog show a kingdom at its most confident, before defeat and dynastic quarrels curbed royal ambition. The Law of Jutland, promulgated in 1241, opened with the words 'with law shall the land be built' and became a foundation of Danish legal tradition. Brick building spread from churches to castles and town halls, and market towns won charters as trade with the Hanseatic ports grew.

nodes.name: Nyere tid, 1600-1700 tallet (Denmark, AD 1661–AD 1799)
nodes.title: Nyere tid, 1600-1700 tallet (Denmark, AD 1661–AD 1799)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1661–AD 1799] Nyere tid, 1600-1700 tallet. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Under absolute monarchy Denmark rebuilt after ruinous wars with Sweden, reorganised its army, taxes and land registers, and ran a colonial and trading empire reaching the Caribbean, West Africa and India. The countryside was surveyed and reshaped, and in the late 1700s the great agrarian reforms broke up village open fields and moved farms out onto their own land – a change still legible in the map today.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur V (Denmark, 2900 BC–2800 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur V (Denmark, 2900 BC–2800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2900 BC–2800 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur V. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The final Funnel Beaker phase, with the plain, coarsely made Store Valby pottery replacing the ornate wares of earlier generations. Megalithic tombs fell out of regular use and settlement patterns changed, shortly before the Single Grave culture with its corded beakers and battle axes transformed Danish society.

nodes.name: Mell. Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2600 BC–2450 BC)
nodes.title: Mell. Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2600 BC–2450 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2600 BC–2450 BC] Mell. Enkeltgravskultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The middle phase of the Single Grave culture in Jutland, part of the wider Corded Ware world. Individuals were buried singly under low round barrows, men with polished stone battle-axes and beakers, in a sharp break from the collective megalithic tombs of earlier farmers. Ancient DNA links this change to incoming steppe-derived populations who reshaped the genetic and linguistic map of northern Europe.

nodes.name: Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur B (Denmark, 3700 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.title: Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur B (Denmark, 3700 BC–3500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3700 BC–3500 BC] Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur B. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Farming communities became more settled and began to build for the dead: earthen long barrows covering timber mortuary houses, and then the first megalithic dolmens of large glacial boulders. Pottery grew more elaborate, with deep-cut ornament on beakers and flasks, and enormous quantities of flint were mined and traded. The shift is really a social one — from scattered pioneer farmsteads to groups who marked their claim on the land with permanent monuments.

nodes.name: Germansk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 375–AD 750)
nodes.title: Germansk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 375–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 375–AD 750] Germansk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The later Iron Age in Denmark, when power concentrated in a few wealthy centres such as Gudme and Sorte Muld and lavish gold treasures, bracteates and the great hoards of the fifth and sixth centuries were buried. Animal-style ornament and Nordic mythological imagery took shape here, weapon sacrifices in bogs continued, and long-distance contacts reached the Roman and Byzantine worlds. The elite halls, ships and seafaring skills of this period led directly into the Viking Age.

nodes.name: Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2800 BC–2350 BC)
nodes.title: Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2800 BC–2350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2800 BC–2350 BC] Enkeltgravskultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The Danish expression of the Corded Ware world, marked by a sharp break with the collective megalithic tombs that came before: the dead were now buried singly under small round barrows, men with polished stone battle-axes, women with amber and beakers. Settlement spread onto the light sandy soils of central and western Jutland, with more emphasis on cattle and pastoralism. Ancient DNA links this change to migration from the Pontic steppe, and it is central to arguments about how Indo-European languages reached Scandinavia.

nodes.name: Nyere tid, industrialismen (Denmark, AD 1801–AD 1913)
nodes.title: Nyere tid, industrialismen (Denmark, AD 1801–AD 1913)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1801–AD 1913] Nyere tid, industrialismen. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark lost its fleet, went bankrupt, and gave up Norway, then lost Schleswig and Holstein in 1864 – and turned inward, reclaiming heathland and remaking its economy. Steam power, railways, harbours and Copenhagen's factories drew people off the land, while farmers organised cooperative dairies and bacon factories that made Denmark an export food producer. Absolutism ended with the constitution of 1849, and mass politics, trade unions and emigration followed.

nodes.name: Yngre middelalder (1400-tal) (Denmark, AD 1400–AD 1499)
nodes.title: Yngre middelalder (1400-tal) (Denmark, AD 1400–AD 1499)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1400–AD 1499] Yngre middelalder (1400-tal). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The Kalmar Union held together, uneasily, under kings who leaned on German advisers and quarrelled endlessly with Swedish nobles. Wealth flowed from herring fisheries and the Sound tolls, paying for brick churches whose vaults were covered in the vivid, often comic wall paintings visitors still come to see. The Oldenburg dynasty took the throne in 1448 and would hold it for four centuries; Copenhagen gained a university in 1479.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur II (Denmark, 3100 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur II (Denmark, 3100 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3100 BC–3000 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur II. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

A phase of the passage-grave era distinguished by its pottery styles, with continued tomb building and lavish deposits of vessels at the chamber entrances. Flint axe production and amber exchange linked Danish communities to a wide northern European network.

nodes.name: Yngre Senneolitikum (Denmark, 1950 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Senneolitikum (Denmark, 1950 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1950 BC–1700 BC] Yngre Senneolitikum. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The later Late Neolithic, when superbly pressure-flaked flint daggers imitating metal originals were mass-produced and traded across Scandinavia. Copper and the first bronze objects circulate, two-aisled timber longhouses become the standard farm building, and the way of life is essentially that of the coming Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Senneolitikum (Denmark, 2350 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.title: Senneolitikum (Denmark, 2350 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2350 BC–1700 BC] Senneolitikum. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Farming communities across the south adopted the flint dagger, skilfully pressure-flaked in imitation of imported metal blades and produced almost industrially at the Scanian mine sites. Large gallery graves held collective burials, longhouses grew substantial, and the first copper and bronze objects trickled in through wide exchange networks. These contacts set up the metal-rich Bronze Age that followed.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur III (Denmark, 3000 BC–2900 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur III (Denmark, 3000 BC–2900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3000 BC–2900 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur III. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

A ceramic stage of the Funnel Beaker sequence in which decoration on beakers and bowls became denser and more elaborate. Existing megalithic tombs remained in use, receiving new burials and offerings rather than being replaced by new construction.

nodes.name: Yngre Romersk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 175–AD 375)
nodes.title: Yngre Romersk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 175–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 175–AD 375] Yngre Romersk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Danish elites grew spectacularly rich on connections with the Roman frontier, burying their dead in chamber graves with silver cups, glass and gaming sets, as at Himlingøje on Zealand. Defeated armies' equipment was destroyed and thrown into lakes at Illerup, Nydam and Vimose, evidence of organised warfare across the Baltic, and the first runic inscriptions appear.

nodes.name: Nyere tid, "digital gennembrud" (Denmark, AD 1990–AD 2100)
nodes.title: Nyere tid, "digital gennembrud" (Denmark, AD 1990–AD 2100)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1990–AD 2100] Nyere tid, "digital gennembrud". Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Computers, mobile phones and the internet moved from workplaces into every household, reshaping how Danes worked, shopped, banked and talked to the state. Public administration digitised early and thoroughly, and physical infrastructure – cables, masts, server halls – became part of the landscape record.

nodes.name: Yngre Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 4300 BC–3900 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 4300 BC–3900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 4300 BC–3900 BC] Yngre Ertebøllekultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The last hunter-fisher-gatherers of the Danish coasts, living beside enormous shell middens and using pointed-base pottery and blubber lamps - among the earliest ceramics made by non-farmers in Europe. They traded with and knew about farming neighbours to the south for centuries before crops and cattle finally arrived.

nodes.name: Romersk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 1–AD 375)
nodes.title: Romersk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 1–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1–AD 375] Romersk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Contact with the Roman world flooded southern Scandinavia with imported bronze vessels, glass, silver cups and coins, which local elites buried with their dead in richly furnished graves such as those at Himlingøje. Society grew visibly stratified, with chieftains controlling trade routes and warrior retinues. Enormous deposits of captured weapons and gear in bogs – Illerup Ådal, Vimose, Nydam – record defeated armies and give an unmatched picture of Iron Age warfare, right down to boats, mail shirts and the earliest runic inscriptions.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur IV (Denmark, 3000 BC–2900 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur IV (Denmark, 3000 BC–2900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3000 BC–2900 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur IV. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

A late stage of the Funnel Beaker sequence, defined chiefly by pottery styles found in settlements and in the deposits outside megalithic tombs. Monument building had largely given way to the continued reuse of chambers built by earlier generations.

nodes.name: Bronzealder (Denmark, 1700 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Bronzealder (Denmark, 1700 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1700 BC–500 BC] Bronzealder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Southern Scandinavia grew rich by trading Baltic amber south for copper and tin, and used the metal with extraordinary flair: lur horns, the Trundholm sun chariot, spiral-decorated razors and folding stools. Chieftains were buried under turf barrows in hollowed oak coffins, some of which sealed in clothing, hair and skin — the Egtved girl among them. Thousands of rock carvings of ships, sun discs and ploughmen record a religion built around the sun's daily voyage.

nodes.name: Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur C (Denmark, 3500 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.title: Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur C (Denmark, 3500 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3500 BC–3300 BC] Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur C. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Dolmen building reached its height and the first great causewayed enclosures were dug, ditched arenas where crowds gathered, feasted and handled the bones of the dead. Richly decorated Fuchsberg-style pottery, polished flint axes and amber were deposited in bogs in growing quantities. It is the moment when Neolithic Denmark's ritual landscape took the shape that would culminate in the passage graves of the following centuries.

nodes.name: Middelalder (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Middelalder (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1535] Middelalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark became a kingdom in the European mould, with a network of bishoprics, stone and then brick churches in nearly every parish, and towns living on herring, cattle and Baltic trade. Royal power under the Valdemars extended briefly over much of the southern Baltic before civil war and noble mortgages nearly dissolved the realm, which was rebuilt and then joined to Sweden and Norway in the Kalmar Union. The era ends with the Count's Feud and the Reformation, which stripped the church of its lands.

nodes.name: Yngre Bronzealder (Denmark, 1100 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Bronzealder (Denmark, 1100 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1100 BC–500 BC] Yngre Bronzealder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Cremation replaced the great oak-coffin inhumations of earlier centuries, and the dead were buried in urns, often dug into the sides of older barrows. Bronze came in enormous quantities from far-off ore sources and was worked into thin, showy sheet metal - shields, hanging vessels, and the curved trumpets called lurs, deposited in bogs in pairs. It is the great age of hoards and of the rock-carved ships and sun-symbols that hint at a shared northern religion.

nodes.name: Ældre Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2800 BC–2600 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2800 BC–2600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2800 BC–2600 BC] Ældre Enkeltgravskultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The early Single Grave culture marks a sharp break with the communal megalithic tombs of the preceding farmers: the dead were now buried individually under small round barrows, men with stone battle axes and beakers, women with amber and copper ornaments. Part of the wider Corded Ware horizon linked to migration from the steppe, it brought new burial customs, pottery and an emphasis on cattle herding, and saw settlement push into the light soils of central and western Jutland. Ancient DNA has shown these communities carried substantially new ancestry, making the period a key case study in prehistoric migration.

nodes.name: Nyere tid (1661 - ) (Denmark, AD 1661–AD 2100)
nodes.title: Nyere tid (1661 - ) (Denmark, AD 1661–AD 2100)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1661–AD 2100] Nyere tid (1661 - ). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark's kings imposed hereditary absolute rule, codified in law and administered through a professional bureaucracy – one of the most complete absolutisms in Europe. What followed was agrarian reform and the end of serfdom-like tenancy, the loss of Norway and later Schleswig, a democratic constitution in 1849, industrialisation, occupation and welfare state. Material from these centuries – farmhouses, factories, harbours, housing estates – makes up much of what archaeologists now record.

nodes.name: Yngre Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2450 BC–2350 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Enkeltgravskultur (Denmark, 2450 BC–2350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2450 BC–2350 BC] Yngre Enkeltgravskultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The final stage of the Single Grave (Corded Ware) tradition in Jutland, when new burials were inserted high into existing mounds - the 'over-grave' phase - each with its stone battle-axe and beaker. Within a century or two these communities merged into the Bell Beaker world, bringing metalwork and a new burial fashion.

nodes.name: Ældre Middelalder (1066 - 1300) (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1299)
nodes.title: Ældre Middelalder (1066 - 1300) (Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1299)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1067–AD 1299] Ældre Middelalder (1066 - 1300). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark became a European kingdom in this stretch: dioceses and parishes were laid out, some two thousand stone and brick churches went up, and coinage, towns and royal administration took hold. After decades of dynastic civil war the Valdemarian kings turned outward, conquering along the Baltic coast, while the provincial laws — the Law of Jutland of 1241 among them — put custom into writing. Brick, newly introduced, gave the country cathedrals and castles that still dominate its towns.

nodes.name: Ældre Germansk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 375–AD 600)
nodes.title: Ældre Germansk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 375–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 375–AD 600] Ældre Germansk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

With the Roman frontier collapsing, Scandinavian elites turned to their own sources of wealth and display: gold neck-rings, bracteate pendants stamped in imitation of imperial coins, and the great treasures of the Migration Period. Animal ornament in the twisting Style I became the visual language of the north, and central places such as Gudme drew craftsmen, traders and cult activity. Weapons taken from defeated armies were still being sunk in bogs, evidence of organised warfare among emerging petty kingdoms.

nodes.name: 1914-18, 1. Verdenskrig (Denmark, AD 1914–AD 1918)
nodes.title: 1914-18, 1. Verdenskrig (Denmark, AD 1914–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1914–AD 1918] 1914-18, 1. Verdenskrig. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark stayed neutral, mined its own waters to satisfy Germany, and grew rich selling food to both sides, though rationing, inflation and profiteering by so-called goulash barons strained society at home. Around 30,000 Danish-speaking men from German-ruled North Schleswig were conscripted into the German army, and thousands died. Copenhagen was ringed by hastily built defensive positions manned by a large security force, and in 1917 Denmark sold the Danish West Indies to the United States.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur (Denmark, 3300 BC–2800 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur (Denmark, 3300 BC–2800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3300 BC–2800 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The high point of Denmark's megalithic age, when passage graves were built by the thousand and their chambers were reopened again and again for new burials and offerings. Pottery grew ornate, with richly decorated pedestalled bowls and funnel beakers set out at the tomb entrances, and flint axes were produced on an almost industrial scale in the Thy and Zealand mines. Causewayed enclosures served as gathering places for feasting and rites that bound scattered farming hamlets together.

nodes.name: Ældre Romersk Jernalder, B2 (Denmark, AD 70–AD 175)
nodes.title: Ældre Romersk Jernalder, B2 (Denmark, AD 70–AD 175)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 70–AD 175] Ældre Romersk Jernalder, B2. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Roman imports arrived in greater quantity and reached more households, while the wealthiest inhumation graves grew steadily richer in weapons, vessels and jewellery. Local bronze- and iron-smithing flourished on Roman models, and regional power centres emerged in Funen, Zealand and eastern Jutland. The weapon deposits sunk in bogs show that this prosperity was contested by force.

nodes.name: Yngre Stenalder (Denmark, 3900 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Stenalder (Denmark, 3900 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3900 BC–1700 BC] Yngre Stenalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The whole Neolithic in Denmark, opening with the arrival of cereals, cattle and pottery and the clearance of the wildwood. It produced the dolmens and passage graves that still stand in the landscape, the causewayed enclosures and amber offerings of the Funnel Beaker farmers, the barrow burials of the Single Grave people, and finally the flint-dagger workshops of the Late Neolithic.

nodes.name: Ældre Bronzealder per.3 (Denmark, 1300 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Bronzealder per.3 (Denmark, 1300 BC–1100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1300 BC–1100 BC] Ældre Bronzealder per.3. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Barrow burial continued but the practice began to change, with cremation appearing alongside inhumation and grave goods becoming smaller and more standardised — razors, tweezers, fibulae and tutuli. Bronze casting remained skilled, and hanging vessels and engraved razors carry ship and sun imagery that echoes the rock art. The shift towards cremation and urn burial here anticipates the very different funerary world of the late Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Ældre Tragtbægerkultur (Denmark, 3900 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Tragtbægerkultur (Denmark, 3900 BC–3300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3900 BC–3300 BC] Ældre Tragtbægerkultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Farming arrived in Denmark with these communities, who cleared woodland with polished flint axes, kept cattle and sowed barley and wheat, and made the flaring funnel-necked pots that name the culture. They built long earthen barrows for the dead and dug causewayed enclosures for gatherings and rituals, laying the groundwork for the dolmens and passage graves that followed. Pollen records show the first sustained human reshaping of the Danish landscape.

nodes.name: Ældre Bronzealder per.2 (Denmark, 1500 BC–1300 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Bronzealder per.2 (Denmark, 1500 BC–1300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1500 BC–1300 BC] Ældre Bronzealder per.2. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The classic period of the Nordic Bronze Age, when Danish workshops produced their finest work: full-hilted swords, huge spiral-ornamented belt plates and neck collars, and the earliest lurs. This is the phase of the famous oak-coffin burials — the Egtved girl in her corded skirt, Skrydstrup and Borum Eshøj — whose waterlogged mounds preserved clothing, textiles and even flowers. The Trundholm sun chariot belongs here too, the clearest surviving image of the era's sun worship.

nodes.name: Ældre Jernalder (Denmark, 500 BC–AD 375)
nodes.title: Ældre Jernalder (Denmark, 500 BC–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 500 BC–AD 375] Ældre Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Villages of turf-and-timber longhouses, each with cattle stalled under the same roof, spread across Jutland and the islands behind banked 'Celtic fields'. Iron tools made heavier soils workable, populations grew, and warfare left its traces in sacrificed weapon hoards and in the preserved bodies of people staked down in peat bogs. Roman goods — bronze vessels, glass, coins — arrived in the graves of a rising warrior aristocracy, connecting the north to an empire it never joined.

nodes.name: Yngre Bronzealder per.5 (Denmark, 900 BC–700 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Bronzealder per.5 (Denmark, 900 BC–700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 900 BC–700 BC] Yngre Bronzealder per.5. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The high point of northern sheet-bronze craft: hanging vessels, ceremonial razors engraved with ships, and the paired lur trumpets deposited in wetlands. Cemeteries of small urn graves cluster around older barrows, and rock art and hoards suggest ritual centred on the sun, the ship and water.

nodes.name: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur 1B (Denmark, 3200 BC–3100 BC)
nodes.title: Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur 1B (Denmark, 3200 BC–3100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3200 BC–3100 BC] Mellemneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur 1B. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

A short ceramic phase within the passage-grave era, defined by shifts in funnel beaker decoration rather than by any break in the way people lived. Tomb building continued, and offerings of pots and flint accumulated in front of the chamber entrances.

nodes.name: Førromersk Jernalder (Denmark, 500 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: Førromersk Jernalder (Denmark, 500 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 500 BC–AD 1] Førromersk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Local bog iron freed communities from dependence on imported bronze, and farms with longhouses sheltering both people and cattle spread across the landscape. Burials became plain cremations, but the wetlands received extraordinary offerings: the Hjortspring boat with its war gear, the Gundestrup cauldron, and human bodies preserved in the peat. Contact with the La Tene world to the south prepared the ground for the flood of Roman imports that followed.

nodes.name: Ældre Senneolitikum (Denmark, 2350 BC–1950 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Senneolitikum (Denmark, 2350 BC–1950 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2350 BC–1950 BC] Ældre Senneolitikum. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Flint reached its technical peak with the lanceolate daggers — thin, pressure-flaked imitations of the metal blades of central Europe — traded across Scandinavia in huge numbers. Bell Beaker contacts brought the first copper and the first hints of bronze into Jutland, and the dead were now laid in stone-lined cists or reused megalithic chambers rather than new great tombs. Farms shifted to long two-aisled houses, the ancestor of the Bronze Age longhouse.

nodes.name: Yngre middelalder (1300-tal) (Denmark, AD 1300–AD 1399)
nodes.title: Yngre middelalder (1300-tal) (Denmark, AD 1300–AD 1399)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1300–AD 1399] Yngre middelalder (1300-tal). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Plague arriving in 1349 killed a third or more of the population, emptying villages and collapsing grain prices while wages for survivors rose. Royal power, pawned away piecemeal early in the century, was rebuilt by Valdemar Atterdag and then by his daughter Margrete, who by 1397 had brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one crown in the Kalmar Union. Deserted farmsteads and abandoned church buildings from these decades are still turning up in excavations.

nodes.name: Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C2 (Denmark, AD 250–AD 310)
nodes.title: Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C2 (Denmark, AD 250–AD 310)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 250–AD 310] Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C2. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The peak of the great war-booty sacrifices: the weapons, shields and horse gear of entire defeated armies were smashed and sunk in bogs such as Illerup Ådal. The finds reveal well-organised forces with officers and Roman-made swords, and carry some of the earliest runic inscriptions in Scandinavia.

nodes.name: Ældre Romersk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 1–AD 175)
nodes.title: Ældre Romersk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 1–AD 175)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1–AD 175] Ældre Romersk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Contact with the Roman Empire, reached by way of the Elbe and the amber routes, brought bronze vessels, glassware, silver drinking cups and Roman coins into Danish graves. The richest burials, furnished for feasting in the Roman manner, mark the appearance of a distinct aristocracy above the ordinary village farmers. At the same time, defeated armies' equipment began to be destroyed and deposited in lakes and bogs, evidence of large-scale organised conflict.

nodes.name: Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 5400 BC–3900 BC)
nodes.title: Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 5400 BC–3900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 5400 BC–3900 BC] Ertebøllekultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Denmark's last foragers, known from the great kitchen middens of shells and bone along the old shorelines. They hunted seal and wild boar, fished eel and cod from dugout canoes, made the first pottery in the region — coarse pointed-base pots and oval lamps — and buried their dead with red ochre and antler grave goods. Their world ended around 4000 BC when farming, imported from central Europe, transformed the landscape within a few generations.

nodes.name: Yngre Vikingetid (Denmark, AD 900–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Yngre Vikingetid (Denmark, AD 900–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 900–AD 1066] Yngre Vikingetid. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The age of the Jelling dynasty, when Harald Bluetooth claimed to have 'won all Denmark and made the Danes Christian', built the great ring fortresses and the Jelling monuments, and his successors Sven Forkbeard and Cnut conquered England. A unified kingdom with towns, coinage, churches and royal taxation emerged from raiding wealth.

nodes.name: Tragtbægerkultur (Denmark, 3900 BC–2800 BC)
nodes.title: Tragtbægerkultur (Denmark, 3900 BC–2800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3900 BC–2800 BC] Tragtbægerkultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The arrival of farming in southern Scandinavia: forests cleared for wheat, barley and cattle, and settlements marked by the funnel-necked pots that give the culture its name. These communities raised the region's first monuments - long barrows, dolmens and passage graves built of glacial boulders - and deposited pottery, amber and flint axes in bogs and at tomb entrances, evidence of a new relationship between the living, the dead and the land they now owned.

nodes.name: Mell. Førromersk Jernalder (per.2) (Denmark, 400 BC–100 BC)
nodes.title: Mell. Førromersk Jernalder (per.2) (Denmark, 400 BC–100 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 400 BC–100 BC] Mell. Førromersk Jernalder (per.2). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Iron smelted from local bog ore became commonplace, freeing communities from imported bronze and putting tools and weapons within reach of ordinary farmsteads. Villages of longhouses with byre and living quarters under one roof spread across Jutland, while the dead were cremated and buried plainly in urn fields. From this period come the Hjortspring boat find and the first great weapon offerings, evidence of organised warfare between emerging tribal groups.

nodes.name: Ældre Førromersk Jernalder (per.1) (Denmark, 500 BC–400 BC)
nodes.title: Ældre Førromersk Jernalder (per.1) (Denmark, 500 BC–400 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 500 BC–400 BC] Ældre Førromersk Jernalder (per.1). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Iron, smelted locally from bog ore, began to replace bronze that had to be imported, and the lavish metalwork of the Bronze Age gave way to plain, sparsely furnished cremation graves in flat urn cemeteries. Society looks poorer and more equal in the archaeological record, though farms grew tighter and field systems more organised. This austere phase set the pattern of village life — longhouses shared by people and cattle — that lasted for the next thousand years.

nodes.name: Yngre Bronzealder per.4 (Denmark, 1100 BC–900 BC)
nodes.title: Yngre Bronzealder per.4 (Denmark, 1100 BC–900 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 1100 BC–900 BC] Yngre Bronzealder per.4. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Cremation became the standard funeral rite, the burnt bones packed into small pottery urns or bronze boxes set into existing burial mounds rather than under new ones. Metalwork remains lavish and locally made, and the first great bog offerings of ornaments and weapons belong here.

nodes.name: Klokkebægerkultur (Denmark, 2350 BC–1950 BC)
nodes.title: Klokkebægerkultur (Denmark, 2350 BC–1950 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 2350 BC–1950 BC] Klokkebægerkultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The Beaker 'package' — bell-shaped drinking pots, barbed-and-tanged flint arrowheads, wristguards and the first copper daggers — arrived in northern Jutland and was absorbed into local farming life. Its most spectacular product was the Danish flint dagger, knapped in imitation of metal blades and traded widely across the Baltic. Visitors see the moment when Denmark, without ore of its own, began acquiring metal and the tastes that came with it, setting the stage for the Nordic Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Yngre Germansk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 600–AD 750)
nodes.title: Yngre Germansk Jernalder (Denmark, AD 600–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 600–AD 750] Yngre Germansk Jernalder. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The Vendel-age centuries, when powerful families ruled from hall complexes such as Lejre and Tissø and had their gear decorated in the interlaced animal styles. Trading places like Ribe were founded, ship technology and sails matured, and the political and commercial ingredients of the Viking Age were assembled.

nodes.name: Nyere tid, "elektronisk gennembrud" (Denmark, AD 1960–AD 1989)
nodes.title: Nyere tid, "elektronisk gennembrud" (Denmark, AD 1960–AD 1989)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1960–AD 1989] Nyere tid, "elektronisk gennembrud". Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Television, transistor radios, refrigerators and washing machines arrived in ordinary Danish homes within a couple of decades, alongside cars, suburban housing blocks and prefabricated concrete construction. Women entered paid work in large numbers and the welfare state expanded fast. It is the period that produced much of the built environment Danes still live in.

nodes.name: Yngre middelalder (1500-tal) (Denmark, AD 1500–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Yngre middelalder (1500-tal) (Denmark, AD 1500–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1500–AD 1535] Yngre middelalder (1500-tal). Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Three turbulent decades: Christian II's massacre of Swedish nobles in Stockholm in 1520 broke the Kalmar Union for good, and he was himself deposed in 1523. Lutheran preachers won over towns and much of the nobility while monasteries lost their grip on land and alms. The civil war known as the Count's Feud ended with Christian III's victory and the confiscation of the Catholic Church's estates, closing the medieval order.

nodes.name: Nyere tid, efterkrigstiden (Denmark, AD 1945–AD 1959)
nodes.title: Nyere tid, efterkrigstiden (Denmark, AD 1945–AD 1959)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 1945–AD 1959] Nyere tid, efterkrigstiden. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

After five years of German occupation Denmark rebuilt with Marshall aid, joined NATO in 1949, and began the long boom that would transform living standards. Rationing gradually ended, housing was built at speed, and the foundations of the modern welfare state were laid.

nodes.name: Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C3 (Denmark, AD 310–AD 375)
nodes.title: Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C3 (Denmark, AD 310–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, AD 310–AD 375] Yngre Romersk Jernalder, C3. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Roman imports thin out as the empire's northern frontier weakened, while gold becomes the prestige metal of choice. Continued bog deposits, including the Nydam boats, show warfare and seafaring on a scale that leads directly into the Migration Period.

nodes.name: Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur A (Denmark, 3900 BC–3700 BC)
nodes.title: Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur A (Denmark, 3900 BC–3700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 3900 BC–3700 BC] Tidligneolitisk Tragtbægerkultur A. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

The first farmers in Denmark: forest was cleared with pointed-butted flint axes, emmer and barley were sown, and cattle, sheep and pigs replaced much of the wild diet of the preceding shell-midden hunters. Settlements were small and shifting, and the characteristic thin-walled funnel-necked beakers were placed in bogs and pits as offerings. This short opening phase set in motion the landscape clearance and the flint-axe economy that shaped the next thousand years.

nodes.name: Mell. Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 4800 BC–4300 BC)
nodes.title: Mell. Ertebøllekultur (Denmark, 4800 BC–4300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Denmark, 4800 BC–4300 BC] Mell. Ertebøllekultur. Period definition from MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark Dateringskodetabel — MUD - Museernes Udgravningsdata Danmark.

Coastal foragers along the Danish shores lived on seals, fish, oysters and forest game, leaving the great shell middens that gave the culture its name. They stayed put long enough to build cemeteries and bury their dead with ochre, antler and shell ornaments, and they traded for stone axes from the farming communities already established to the south. Their dugout canoes, fish weirs and bone-tipped leisters show a sea-oriented life that ended only when farming finally crossed into Scandinavia.

nodes.name: Ancient (Cyprus, 8999 BC–AD 749)
nodes.title: Ancient (Cyprus, 8999 BC–AD 749)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 8999 BC–AD 749] Ancient. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A very broad bracket covering Cyprus from its first farming villages through the Bronze Age copper trade, the Iron Age city-kingdoms, and the Hellenistic, Roman and early Byzantine centuries. The island's copper gave it a name and a place in Mediterranean exchange from the third millennium BC onward, while its position kept drawing in Egyptians, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and Romans. The bracket closes with the mid-eighth-century earthquakes and Arab raiding that ended the ancient urban order.

hints.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

nodes.name: Late Cypriot II-Late Cypriot III (Cyprus, 1449 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Late Cypriot II-Late Cypriot III (Cyprus, 1449 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1449 BC–1049 BC] Late Cypriot II-Late Cypriot III. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Spans the height of Cyprus's copper-fuelled urban civilisation and the turbulence that followed it, from ashlar-built port towns trading with Egypt and the Hittites to their destruction, rebuilding and gradual reshaping under Aegean influence.

hints.label: Late Cypriot II-Late Cypriot III
hints.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

nodes.title: Late Cypriot-Archaic (Cyprus, 1649 BC–474 BC)
nodes.description: [Cyprus, 1649 BC–474 BC] Late Cypriot-Archaic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

hints.label: Late Cypriot-Archaic
hints.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

nodes.name: Ancient-Medieval (Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 1570)
nodes.title: Ancient-Medieval (Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 1570)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 3499 BC–AD 1570] Ancient-Medieval. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A catch-all span covering almost the whole of Cyprus's pre-Ottoman past, from village farmers of the Chalcolithic to the fall of Venetian Nicosia and Famagusta. The island's copper made it rich and made it a target: Bronze Age traders, Mycenaean settlers, Phoenician and Greek city-kingdoms, then Assyrian, Egyptian, Persian, Ptolemaic, Roman and Byzantine masters in turn. Crusader conquest in 1191 brought three centuries of French Lusignan rule, with Gothic cathedrals and Famagusta's merchant churches, before Venice took over and the Ottomans took it away in 1570.

hints.label: Ancient-Medieval
hints.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

nodes.name: Late Roman (Cyprus, AD 300–AD 749)
nodes.title: Late Roman (Cyprus, AD 300–AD 749)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 300–AD 749] Late Roman. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

hints.label: Late Roman
hints.source: Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town

nodes.name: Ancient Historic-Medieval (Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 1570)
nodes.title: Ancient Historic-Medieval (Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 1570)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 1570] Ancient Historic-Medieval. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A long sweep from the Iron Age city-kingdoms and their Assyrian, Persian, Ptolemaic and Roman overlords through the Byzantine centuries and the Arab raids that devastated the coastal cities. From 1191 the island passed to Crusader hands, becoming the Lusignan kingdom and later a Venetian possession, with Famagusta and Nicosia growing rich on eastern trade. The sequence ends with the Ottoman conquest of 1570-71.

A long sweep from the age of the Cypriot city-kingdoms through Ptolemaic rule to nearly a millennium as a Roman and then Byzantine province. Cyprus grew rich on copper, grain and its position on eastern Mediterranean shipping routes, and its cities acquired theatres, aqueducts, gymnasia and later great basilicas with mosaic floors. The period is conventionally closed by the earthquakes and Arab raids of the seventh and eighth centuries, which ruined coastal cities like Salamis and Kourion.

nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 749 BC–AD 749] Ancient Historic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Cyprus enters written history as a patchwork of city-kingdoms - Salamis, Kition, Paphos and others - paying tribute in turn to Assyria, Egypt and Persia, and blending Greek, Phoenician and indigenous traditions. Alexander's successors ended the kingdoms, and Ptolemaic then Roman rule made the island a prosperous provincial backwater famous for copper, grain and the cult of Aphrodite. Early Christianity took root strongly, leaving mosaic-floored basilicas before earthquakes and Arab raids closed the era.

[Cyprus, 749 BC–474 BC] Archaic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

[Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 1877] Late Medieval-Ottoman. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Richard the Lionheart seized Cyprus during the Third Crusade and sold it on, and the French Lusignan dynasty turned it into a Latin kingdom with Gothic cathedrals at Nicosia and Famagusta and a Greek Orthodox majority under Catholic rule. Venice took over in 1489 and ringed the towns with massive artillery walls, which failed to stop the Ottoman conquest of 1571. Three centuries of Ottoman administration followed, restoring the Orthodox archbishop as leader of the Christian population, until the island was handed to Britain.

Kosovo passed from the last decades of Ottoman rule - years of Albanian national awakening around the League of Prizren and repeated uprisings - into Serbian and then Yugoslav control after the Balkan Wars of 1912. Land was redistributed and colonists settled, tens of thousands emigrated, and rival Albanian and Serbian national claims hardened into the contest that would define the territory for the next century. The Second World War brought Italian and German occupation, partition, and brutal reprisals before Yugoslav partisans took control.

The Claudian invasion turned southern Britain into a province: legions pushed north and west, client kings were absorbed, and the revolt of Boudica was crushed. Towns with forums, baths and grid streets appeared where none had existed, roads linked new civitas capitals, and villas began to dot the countryside. By the end of the period the frontier had settled at Hadrian's Wall.

Their art blends Greek, Phoenician and Near Eastern styles, seen in the crowds of limestone votive figures dedicated at rural sanctuaries. The island's kings walked a constant tightrope, some joining Greek revolts against Persia, others staying loyal.

[Cyprus, 98 BC–AD 2008] Roman-Modern. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A catch-all span running from the island's absorption into the Roman world through Byzantine, Lusignan, Venetian, Ottoman and British rule to the present. Each left something on the ground: mosaic-floored villas at Paphos, painted mountain churches, Gothic cathedrals turned into mosques, and sugar mills and aqueducts. The layering makes Cypriot sites unusually deep and continuously occupied.

[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC] Late Cypriot. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Cyprus's boom as the Mediterranean's copper supplier, exporting oxhide ingots from harbour towns such as Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke and appearing in Egyptian and Hittite records as Alashiya. Ashlar buildings, imported Mycenaean and Levantine pottery, ivories and the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script mark an urban, cosmopolitan society. After 1200 BC, when the surrounding Bronze Age states collapsed, Aegean settlers arrived, new sanctuaries and iron-working appeared, and the foundations of the Iron Age Cypriot kingdoms were laid.

[Cyprus, AD 750–AD 1190] Early Medieval. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

Cyprus moved from British colony to independent republic in 1960, then split after the 1974 coup and Turkish invasion left the island divided by a buffer zone. Refugees on both sides rebuilt lives in new towns; tourism and offshore finance transformed the coasts. The south joined the European Union in 2004 while the north remained recognised only by Turkey.

A broad bracket covering Cyprus from Ptolemaic rule through its absorption into the Roman Empire. Cities were rebuilt with theatres, gymnasia, aqueducts and colonnaded streets, copper mining supplied the empire, and Paphos flourished as the seat of the Roman governor. Christianity took root early here, and repeated earthquakes punctuate the archaeology.

[Cyprus, 473 BC–99 BC] Classical-Hellenistic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

The island's rival city-kingdoms, long caught between Persian overlords and Greek ambitions, were finally abolished after Alexander's conquest, and Cyprus became a prized Ptolemaic possession governed from Alexandria. Its copper, timber and shipyards made it strategically valuable, and its cities filled with Greek-style theatres, gymnasia and sanctuaries alongside older Phoenician and Cypriot cults. Salamis, Kition and the new Ptolemaic capital at Nea Paphos show the blend of local, Greek and Egyptian tastes.

[Cyprus, 310 BC–AD 749] Hellenistic-Roman. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

A long bracket covering Cyprus from the Ptolemies through Roman and early Byzantine rule, ending with the devastating earthquake of AD 749. It spans the island's greatest prosperity - copper exports, grain, monumental cities, and later a dense landscape of basilicas and bishoprics - followed by the disruption of Arab raids from the seventh century.

[Cyprus, 98 BC–AD 749] Roman. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

[Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 1570] Late Medieval. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Bulgaria spent much of this stretch inside the Byzantine Empire after the fall of the First Bulgarian state, then broke free in 1185 to build a Second Empire ruled from Tarnovo, whose churches, painted tombs and silver coinage mark a confident revival. Ivan Asen II briefly made it the dominant power in the Balkans before Mongol raids, noble feuding and territorial splintering wore it down. Ottoman armies took Tarnovo and then Vidin, ending Bulgarian independence for nearly five centuries.

nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–750 BC] Cypro-Geometric. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

After the collapse of the Late Bronze Age palaces, Cyprus rebuilt around new coastal centres such as Salamis, Kition and Palaepaphos, with iron replacing bronze for tools and weapons. Greek-speaking settlers left their mark in dialect and burial customs, and a Cypriot syllabary continued to be written. Phoenicians established themselves at Kition, and by the end of the period the island's kingdoms were wealthy enough to attract Assyrian attention.

[Cyprus, 1049 BC–311 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

[Cyprus, 2499 BC–999 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

A catch-all span covering Cyprus from the rise of its copper industry to the present. The island's ore made it a hub of eastern Mediterranean trade, and its position drew in Mycenaeans, Phoenicians, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Crusaders, Venetians, Ottomans and the British in turn. Each left buildings, cemeteries and place-names layered on the same sites, which is why excavations here so often cut through four thousand years at once.

Britain took over the administration of the island from the Ottomans, keeping it as a base guarding the route to the Suez Canal; formal annexation came in 1914 and Crown Colony status in 1925. Roads, schools and a colonial bureaucracy were built, but so was resentment—the 1931 riots burned Government House, and the campaign for enosis, union with Greece, hardened. The tensions of this period set the terms for the conflicts that followed.

[Cyprus, 749 BC–99 BC] Archaic-Hellenistic. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Cyprus passed from a patchwork of tribute-paying city-kingdoms under Assyrian, Egyptian and Persian overlords to direct rule by the Ptolemies of Egypt, who abolished the local dynasties. Wealth came from copper, timber for warships and grain, and the island's sanctuaries - above all that of Aphrodite at Palaipaphos - drew pilgrims from across the Greek world. Its material culture mixes Greek, Phoenician and Egyptian elements more thoroughly than almost anywhere else.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

Under Persian suzerainty the island's kings played Greek and Persian interests against each other, most famously Evagoras I of Salamis, who fought a long war for independence and promoted Greek language and art. Cypriot syllabic writing survived alongside the Greek alphabet and Phoenician, and royal tombs at Salamis were furnished with chariots, horses and Homeric-looking grave goods. The kingdoms ended when Ptolemy I abolished them and absorbed Cyprus into his empire.

[Cyprus, AD 1191–AD 2008] Medieval-Modern. Period definition from Pyla-Koutsopetria I : archaeological survey of an ancient coastal town — 2014.

Wrested from its Byzantine governor by Richard the Lionheart and sold on, the island passed through Lusignan kings, Venetian fortress-builders, three centuries of Ottoman rule, and British administration from 1878. Each layer left visible marks: Gothic cathedrals converted to mosques, massive Venetian walls at Nicosia and Famagusta, and colonial-era infrastructure. Independence in 1960 was followed by intercommunal conflict and the division of the island in 1974.
