The term 'middle post-medieval' is not used, and there is debate as to what constitutes the late post-medieval period. For the 18th century, it is best to stick simply to 'post-medieval' and qualify it using calendar dates. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The centuries after 1500 brought the Reformation, overseas empire, and the shift from an agrarian to an industrial society, all leaving dense archaeological traces. Sites of this age are full of dateable mass-produced material - clay pipes, glass bottles, glazed and printed pottery - which makes them unusually precise chronological anchors. Field boundaries, mills, docks, mines and workers' housing from this span still form the framework of the modern landscape.

properties.title: albarello — 1475-1500 (circa)
properties.notes:
Albarello with almost vertical sides. Earthenware apparently tin-glazed inside and out (not the foot). Painted around the body with a peacock, a duck, a cock and a goose, each bird within a contour panel; Gothic-floral foliage in between. Around the foot, diagonal panels and stylised foliage, and in Gothic letters ".sy. de. citro".; | Type: albarello | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 19.20 centimetres base ; 36.60 centimetres;

Marches, The, Pesaro, Urbino, Duchy of, United Kingdom, Italy

properties.title: albarello — 1470-1500 (circa)
properties.notes:
Albarello with almost vertical sides. Earthenware apparently tin-glazed inside and out (not the foot). Painted one side with a man in a hood (monk?) facing a nun; between them a scroll "HUMILITAS ALTA PETIT". On the other side is a younger woman, her head covered, facing a man in a peaked hat. All figures within contour panels; floral tendrils between. Around the foot diamond panels and foliage; in Gothic letters "sy. de. fumoterre" beneath the older pair.; | Type: albarello | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 19.50 centimetres base ; 37.30 centimetres;

Marches, The, Pesaro, Urbino, Duchy of, United Kingdom, Italy

nodes.name: Early Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 200)
nodes.title: Early Roman (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 200)
nodes.description:
[United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 200] Early Roman. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

The Claudian invasion turned southern Britain into a province: legions pushed north and west, client kings were absorbed, and the revolt of Boudica was crushed. Towns with forums, baths and grid streets appeared where none had existed, roads linked new civitas capitals, and villas began to dot the countryside. By the end of the period the frontier had settled at Hadrian's Wall.

nodes.name: Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 410–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Early Medieval (United Kingdom, AD 410–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[United Kingdom, AD 410–AD 1066] Early Medieval. This period is diverse and must be qualified wherever possible with Early, Middle or Late. The currently accepted chronology (spring 2013) is given below, but this is likely to change in the near future. English Heritage do not specify the boundaries of these sub-periods. Period definition from Periods used on the database — Portable Antiquities Scheme, 2003.

Avar and Slav raids broke the Byzantine Danube frontier, emptying the old Roman towns and bringing permanent Slavic settlement to the central Balkans. Over the following centuries small Serb principalities emerged in the hills between Byzantine and Bulgarian spheres, and Christian missionaries introduced the Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters. Archaeologically the shift is stark: masonry cities give way to timber villages, cremation cemeteries and simple hand-made pottery.

nodes.name: La première époque (Italy, 699 BC–449 BC)
nodes.title: La première époque (Italy, 699 BC–449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 699 BC–449 BC] La première époque. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy. "On sait l'extrème difficulté qu'il y a de fixer l'époque des monumens anciens avec quelque dégré de précision, soit en les considérant d'après le style de l'Art, soit d'après les principes de la paléographie, lorsqu'ils présentent des caractères. Mais en combinant ce qu'ont rapporté les auteurs anciens avec les monumens de toute espèce, surtout les médailles et les inscriptions, il semble qu'on peut établir trois époques principales." (Millingen 1813, viii)

cf. Millingen 1813, n. 6: "V. Planches XX à XXII, XXXI, XXXII". Period definition from Peintures antiques et inédites de vases grecs, tirées de diverses collections, avec des explications — James V. Millingen, 1813.

properties.title: hydria — 550BC-540BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: black-figured hydria; scene of warriors fighting.; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 6.20 centimetres base ; 8.30 centimetres rim ; 16.20 centimetres; | Culture: Chalcidian

Reggio di Calabria, Italy

properties.title: krater — 600BC-550BC
properties.notes:
Slipped pottery krater, painted with geometric patterns in the so-called "coastal style". Round mouth, arcs with dots and lines. Ribbon handles with ladder pattern; within them, arrowheads. Body decoration mainly of thin bands; on shoulder, narrow panels of broken meander; on lower part, panels containing swastikas and combs alternately. Foot plain.; | Type: krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 17.00 centimetres lip ; 24.00 centimetres; | Culture: Peucetian

Bari, Italy

hints.label: La première époque
hints.source: Peintures antiques et inédites de vases grecs, tirées de diverses collections, avec des explications

nodes.name: Tufa Period (Pompeii, 199 BC–79 BC)
nodes.title: Tufa Period (Pompeii, 199 BC–79 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 199 BC–79 BC] Tufa Period. Period definition from Pompeii : an architectural history — Richardson, Lawrence, Jr., 1920-2013., 1988.

Named for the grey Nocera tufa that became the standard building stone, this was Pompeii's Samnite heyday, when the town filled with Hellenistic-style architecture: the colonnaded Forum, the Temple of Jupiter, the Stabian Baths and grand atrium houses like the House of the Faun with its Alexander mosaic. Wealth from Campanian agriculture and trade paid for a townscape modelled on the Greek east. Much of what visitors see at Pompeii today was already standing before the Roman colony was planted in 80 BC.

nodes.name: Early Roman Colony (Pompeii, 79 BC–29 BC)
nodes.title: Early Roman Colony (Pompeii, 79 BC–29 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–29 BC] Early Roman Colony. Period definition from Pompeii : an architectural history — Richardson, Lawrence, Jr., 1920-2013., 1988.

Sulla planted a colony of army veterans in the town after besieging it, and Pompeii was refounded under Roman law with new settlers taking land and office. Latin displaced Oscan in public inscriptions, and the newcomers built the stone amphitheatre and the small covered theatre — the earliest surviving permanent amphitheatre anywhere. Older Pompeian families and the incoming veterans coexisted uneasily in a rapidly Romanised town.

nodes.name: Julio-Claudian (Pompeii, 29 BC–AD 62)
nodes.title: Julio-Claudian (Pompeii, 29 BC–AD 62)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 29 BC–AD 62] Julio-Claudian. Period definition from Pompeii : an architectural history — Richardson, Lawrence, Jr., 1920-2013., 1988.

The line of emperors descended from or adopted into the families of Augustus and Livia, spanning Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. Under them the improvised rule of one man hardened into a permanent monarchy with a court, a praetorian guard and an imperial bureaucracy; Britain was invaded, Egypt's grain fed Rome, and the succession repeatedly turned on poisonings, adoptions and palace intrigue. The line ended with Nero's suicide and a year of civil war.

nodes.name: Siglos XVI y XVII (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Siglos XVI y XVII (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1500–AD 1700] Siglos XVI y XVII. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia under the Habsburgs was a kingdom without a king in residence, governed by a royal captain-general and represented by the Junta of the Kingdom, whose seven cities voted taxes and troops. Its Atlantic coast made it a front line: Drake sacked Vigo and besieged A Coruña, and shipyards and coastal forts multiplied. Inland, monasteries and the pilgrimage to Santiago remained the great landowners and the great draw, while Baroque granite facades reshaped the cities.

nodes.name: Primera Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–400 BC)
nodes.title: Primera Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–400 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 800 BC–400 BC] Primera Edad del Hierro. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Phoenician traders settled the southern coasts, bringing iron, the potter's wheel, the alphabet and wine, and the wealth of the mines fed the legend of Tartessos. Inland, urnfield communities in the northeast absorbed influences from beyond the Pyrenees while Greek merchants founded Emporion. Out of this mix emerged the Iberian and Celtiberian cultures that Carthage and Rome would later fight over.

nodes.name: Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–50 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 800 BC–50 BC)
nodes.description: [Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 800 BC–50 BC] Edad del Hierro. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

nodes.name: Edad Contemporánea (Galicia, AD 1900–AD 2100)
nodes.title: Edad Contemporánea (Galicia, AD 1900–AD 2100)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1900–AD 2100] Edad Contemporánea. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia's twentieth century: mass emigration to Argentina, Cuba and later Europe emptied villages, while agrarian unions, the Rexurdimento's literary legacy and the Statute of Autonomy of 1936 fed a Galician national movement that Franco's dictatorship suppressed. Coastal industry, fishing fleets and canneries grew around Vigo and A Coruña, and after 1978 the region gained an autonomous government and official status for the Galician language.

nodes.name: Indígena-Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200)
nodes.title: Indígena-Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 50 BC–AD 200] Indígena-Romano. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. The Indigenous-Roman and Early Roman subdivisions of Roman Period have identical dates, but they refer to very different cultural contexts. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

After Augustus finished the conquest of the northwest, the hillfort communities of the castros kept living behind their walls in round stone houses, but began using Roman pottery, coins and Latin names. Rome reorganised the region for gold: enormous hydraulic mines, roads and administrative districts reshaped the landscape. The result is a distinctly hybrid material culture, with native warrior statues and torcs alongside Roman altars and imported tableware.

nodes.name: Edad del Bronce Media (Galicia, 1700 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Bronce Media (Galicia, 1700 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 1700 BC–1200 BC] Edad del Bronce Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

In southeastern Spain the El Argar world reached its height and then collapsed around 1550 BC, ending the fortified towns and their sharply hierarchical jar burials. Across the interior and the Atlantic side, herding communities used mould-cast bronze weapons and buried their dead in cists, and new alloys and forms circulated along routes that reached the Mediterranean and northwestern Europe. The period sets up the far-reaching metal trade of the Late Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Neolítico (Galicia, 4500 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.title: Neolítico (Galicia, 4500 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 4500 BC–2300 BC] Neolítico. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. The Neolithic category is split between Early Prehistory and Late Prehistory. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The first farmers in the peninsula grew cereals and pulses and kept sheep, goats and cattle, spreading along the Mediterranean coast with distinctive shell-impressed Cardial pottery and inland through cave and open-air settlements. Burial in caves and, increasingly, in megalithic tombs marks a new concern with ancestors and place. Rock art and the earliest large communal monuments belong to these centuries.

nodes.name: Alto Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200)
nodes.title: Alto Romano (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 200)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 50 BC–AD 200] Alto Romano. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

With the Cantabrian wars finished, Hispania settled into provincial life under the Empire: new towns with forums and theatres, roads and bridges, the aqueducts of Segovia and Mérida, and vast exports of olive oil, wine, garum and silver to Rome. Latin, Roman law and urban citizenship spread widely, and the peninsula gave the empire Seneca, Martial, Trajan and Hadrian.

nodes.name: Edad del Bronce Inicial (Galicia, 2300 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Bronce Inicial (Galicia, 2300 BC–1700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2300 BC–1700 BC] Edad del Bronce Inicial. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galician communities took up bronze metallurgy, and the great age of megalithic tomb-building gave way to individual burials in cists and to settlement in small, dispersed farmsteads. Local smiths produced flat axes, halberds and daggers, and gold lunulae and torcs signal an emerging elite with links along the Atlantic seaways. Rock carvings of weapons, deer and cup-marks across the region belong to this world.

nodes.name: Siglos XVIII y XIX (Galicia, AD 1700–AD 1900)
nodes.title: Siglos XVIII y XIX (Galicia, AD 1700–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1700–AD 1900] Siglos XVIII y XIX. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Maritime trade, Catalan-run sardine salting and the naval arsenal at Ferrol brought new money to the coast, while the interior stayed locked in smallholdings and rents. Napoleonic armies invaded in 1809 and were driven out by local risings within months. The century closed with two lasting transformations: mass emigration to Cuba, Argentina and Uruguay, and the Rexurdimento, the literary revival that made Galician a written language again through writers such as Rosalía de Castro.

nodes.name: Prehistoria Reciente (Galicia, 2700 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Prehistoria Reciente (Galicia, 2700 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2700 BC–800 BC] Prehistoria Reciente. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia's landscape filled with monuments: megalithic tombs under earthen mounds, then, in the Bronze Age, thousands of open-air rock carvings of deer, weapons and cup-marks on granite outcrops. Metalworkers produced flat axes, halberds and remarkable gold ornaments, some deposited in hoards or bogs. By the end of the period people were gathering into fortified hilltop settlements, the seeds of the castro culture.

nodes.name: Edad Media central (Galicia, AD 700–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Edad Media central (Galicia, AD 700–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 700–AD 1200] Edad Media central. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The centuries of al-Andalus at its height and of the Christian counter-advance: the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba flourished and then shattered into taifa kingdoms, inviting Almoravid and Almohad intervention from North Africa. Northern kingdoms — León, Castile, Navarre, Aragon, Portugal — pushed south, repopulating conquered land with charters and towns, while the pilgrimage road to Santiago de Compostela drew people and Romanesque architecture across the Pyrenees. The decisive Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 opened Andalusia to conquest.

nodes.name: Prehistoria Temprana (Galicia, 2500000 BC–2700 BC)
nodes.title: Prehistoria Temprana (Galicia, 2500000 BC–2700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2500000 BC–2700 BC] Prehistoria Temprana. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The long span from the first stone tools to the arrival of farming, represented in Galicia by quartzite handaxes and river-terrace scatters, coastal shell middens left by foragers, and finally the earliest Neolithic communities. Their most visible legacy is the mámoas — mounded chambered tombs raised on hilltops and passes, which fixed communal memory into the landscape for millennia.

nodes.name: Neolítico Antiguo (Galicia, 4500 BC–2700 BC)
nodes.title: Neolítico Antiguo (Galicia, 4500 BC–2700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 4500 BC–2700 BC] Neolítico Antiguo. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Farming arrived in the Atlantic northwest slowly, and the most visible legacy is the mámoa — the earthen mound covering a stone burial chamber — which spread in thousands across the Galician uplands from the mid-fifth millennium. These tombs staked out grazing land and routes as much as they housed the dead. Settlement traces are slight by comparison, so the monuments and their engraved and painted stones carry most of the story.

nodes.name: Edad del Bronce Final (Galicia, 1200 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Bronce Final (Galicia, 1200 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 1200 BC–800 BC] Edad del Bronce Final. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Long-distance Atlantic exchange peaked, moving bronze weapons, cauldrons and gold ornaments between Iberia, Brittany, Britain and Ireland, while carved warrior stelae in the southwest depict shields, swords and mirrors as symbols of rank. In the south, contacts with the eastern Mediterranean prepared the ground for Phoenician colonies and the emergence of Tartessos. Hoards of scrap and finished metal from these centuries are among the richest in western Europe.

nodes.name: Neolítico Final (Galicia, 2700 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.title: Neolítico Final (Galicia, 2700 BC–2300 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2700 BC–2300 BC] Neolítico Final. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The closing phase of the Neolithic, when settlements grew larger, ditched and walled enclosures appeared, and copper metallurgy began to be practised alongside older stone technologies. Collective burial in megalithic tombs and artificial caves reached its peak, with rich grave goods hinting at emerging differences in status. Within a few generations these communities would build the fortified Chalcolithic towns of the south.

nodes.name: Epipaleolítico (Galicia, 7000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.title: Epipaleolítico (Galicia, 7000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 7000 BC–4500 BC] Epipaleolítico. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

After the ice sheets retreated, hunter-gatherers adapted to warmer forests and rising seas, hunting deer and rabbit, gathering shellfish in huge quantities and making tiny geometric flint blades to arm composite tools. Their shell middens and cemeteries show settled, territorial communities living in the same coasts and river valleys that farmers would occupy a few centuries later.

nodes.name: Edad del Bronce (Galicia, 2300 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Bronce (Galicia, 2300 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 2300 BC–800 BC] Edad del Bronce. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Metalworking in copper and tin spread across the peninsula, and in the southeast the El Argar culture built fortified hilltop towns with rectangular houses, buried its dead in jars beneath house floors, and marked out sharp differences of wealth in silver and bronze grave goods. Elsewhere communities raised cairns and stelae, worked gold, and traded along Atlantic and Mediterranean routes. It was the first period in Iberia with clearly stratified societies controlling metal and land.

nodes.name: Edad Moderna (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1900)
nodes.title: Edad Moderna (Galicia, AD 1500–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1500–AD 1900] Edad Moderna. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Galicia entered the era as a kingdom without its own parliament, governed from Castile and dominated by monasteries and a landholding gentry; peasants worked under the foro leasehold system that shaped rural life for centuries. Maize and potatoes from America transformed farming and allowed the population to grow, while the ports lived off fishing, and A Coruña and Ferrol became naval and Atlantic trade centres. Compostela remained a pilgrimage capital, rebuilt in exuberant Baroque granite.

nodes.name: Alta Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 700)
nodes.title: Alta Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 400–AD 700] Alta Edad Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Roman authority in Hispania gave way to Germanic kingdoms, above all the Visigoths, who ruled from Toledo, absorbed the Suevi and eventually converted from Arianism to Catholicism. Cities shrank, coinage and trade contracted, and the church became the chief institution of learning, producing figures such as Isidore of Seville. The period closed with the Muslim invasion of 711, which swept the Visigothic state away in a few campaigns.

nodes.name: Segunda Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 400 BC–50 BC)
nodes.title: Segunda Edad del Hierro (Galicia, 400 BC–50 BC)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 400 BC–50 BC] Segunda Edad del Hierro. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Iberian communities along the Mediterranean coast built walled hilltop towns, wrote in their own scripts, minted coins and carved stone sculpture such as the Dama de Elche, while Celtiberian peoples of the interior fielded the warriors Rome found so hard to beat. Greek and Punic contact fed the trade in wine, oil and fine pottery. The period ends with the long Roman conquest, from the Second Punic War through the sieges of Numantia and the final campaigns in the north.

nodes.name: Siglos XX y XXI (Galicia, AD 1900–AD 2100)
nodes.title: Siglos XX y XXI (Galicia, AD 1900–AD 2100)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1900–AD 2100] Siglos XX y XXI. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Emigration continued on a huge scale, first to the Americas and later to Germany and Switzerland, hollowing out villages and funding the schools and quays the emigrants sent money home to build. Statutes of autonomy were drafted in the Republic, suppressed under Franco, and finally achieved in 1981, with Galician recognised as a co-official language. Fishing remained the region's signature industry, and the Prestige tanker disaster of 2002 brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets.

nodes.name: Bajo Romano (Galicia, AD 200–AD 400)
nodes.title: Bajo Romano (Galicia, AD 200–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 200–AD 400] Bajo Romano. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Hispania passed through third-century insecurity into the reorganised empire of Diocletian and Constantine, split into new provinces under a vicarius and taxed more heavily. Cities shrank behind walls while enormous rural villas with mosaic floors — Carranque, La Olmeda, Centcelles — became the centres of aristocratic power and wealth. Christianity spread fast, producing bishops, the council of Elvira and the Priscillianist controversy, and the landowning elite that emerged here survived to serve the Visigothic kings.

nodes.name: Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Edad Media (Galicia, AD 400–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 400–AD 1500] Edad Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Visigothic kingdoms gave way in 711 to the Muslim conquest, and for centuries the peninsula was divided between al-Andalus — with Córdoba among the largest and most learned cities in Europe — and the Christian kingdoms of the north. Warfare, frontier settlement and dynastic marriage steadily pushed the border south until only Granada remained, while Jews, Muslims and Christians lived in an uneasy and often violent proximity that also transmitted Greek and Arabic learning to the rest of Europe. Castile and Aragon were united by Ferdinand and Isabella, who took Granada in 1492.

nodes.name: Baja Edad Media (Galicia, AD 1200–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Baja Edad Media (Galicia, AD 1200–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, AD 1200–AD 1500] Baja Edad Media. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

The great southward conquests after Las Navas de Tolosa left Castile and the Crown of Aragon holding almost all Iberia, with Muslim rule reduced to Granada paying tribute. Aragon turned seaward to Sicily, Sardinia and Naples while Castile developed wool exports, Cortes assemblies and violent noble factionalism; plague, pogroms against Jewish communities and civil wars punctuated the era. It closes with the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella, the fall of Granada and the voyages that carried Iberian power across the Atlantic.

nodes.name: Época Romana (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Época Romana (Galicia, 50 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain, 50 BC–AD 400] Época Romana. Spatial coverage: Asturias, Castilla y Leon, Galicia. The Indigenous-Roman and Early Roman subdivisions of Roman Period have identical dates, but they refer to very different cultural contexts. Period definition from SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories — César Parcero Oubiña, 2014.

Rome's conquest of the northwest completed the subjugation of Iberia and turned the region into the province of Gallaecia, exploited above all for gold — the vast hydraulic workings of Las Médulas being the most spectacular result. New cities such as Lucus Augusti and Bracara Augusta anchored a road network, while many hillfort communities carried on in Roman-influenced form for generations. Latin, Roman law and eventually Christianity took root here and shaped the region's later identity.

nodes.name: Archaic (Libya, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Libya, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lepcis Magna, 649 BC–499 BC] Archaic. Derived from Leptis Magna Forum Vetus excavations, "level 4"; absolute dates determined from Greek material (term. post quem: Late Proto-Corinthian). On Liby-phoenicians, see Birley (1988), Lancel (1995). Period definition from Western Phoenicians at Lepcis Magna — Theresa Howard Carter, 1965.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

nodes.name: Early Iron Age (Spain, 749 BC–449 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age (Spain, 749 BC–449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 749 BC–449 BC] Early Iron Age. Contemporary with Hallstatt B-D (S. Germany). Overlaps LBA III/ Tartessian period, 750-600 B.C. (- cf. M. Diaz-Andreu & S. Keay, 1997. The Archaeology of Iberia.); includes Iberian I (600-500 B.C.) and II (500-450 B.C.) (ibid.). See also T. Chapa & M. Belen, 1997. La Edad del Hierro. Period definition from Iron Age Archaeology of the Northwest Iberian Peninsula — César Parcero Oubiña, 2005.

Iron working replaced bronze as the everyday metal, and communities in the western Balkans built fortified hilltop settlements and buried their dead beneath earthen tumuli with weapons and ornaments. Distinctive bronze jewellery and imported goods show links to the Adriatic and the Aegean world. These groups form the archaeological background to the Dardanians known from later Greek and Roman writers.

hints.label: Early Iron Age
hints.source: Iron Age Archaeology of the Northwest Iberian Peninsula

nodes.name: Lerna III (Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.title: Lerna III (Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 2399 BC–2099 BC] Lerna III. Applies to Lerna; equivalent to Lerna III. CC307C, Spring 2011, group 1: Jelyne Jesusa and Kevin Sartin. Period definition from C-14 Dates for Sites in the Mediterranean Area — Ellen L. Kohler, 1961.

The Early Bronze Age settlement in the Argolid dominated by the House of the Tiles, a large two-storey corridor building with a fired roof that burned down and was sealed under a tumulus. Its clay sealings imply centralised storage and administration, evidence of unusual social complexity in mainland Greece well before the Mycenaeans. The destruction of the building is a key marker in debates about upheaval at the end of Early Helladic II.

hints.label: Lerna III
hints.source: C-14 Dates for Sites in the Mediterranean Area

nodes.name: I. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1520–AD 1566)
nodes.title: I. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1520–AD 1566)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1520–AD 1566] I. Süleyman. wikipedia: 17 shawwal 926 - 20 or 21 safar 974. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The empire's longest-reigning sultan took Belgrade and Rhodes, destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, besieged Vienna, and made the Ottoman navy dominant in the Mediterranean under Barbarossa. At home he was 'the Lawgiver', systematising secular law alongside religious law, while Mimar Sinan built the mosques that still define Istanbul's skyline and poetry and miniature painting flourished. His marriage to Hürrem Sultan and the executions of his own sons opened a new era of harem politics.

nodes.name: III. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730)
nodes.title: III. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1703–AD 1730)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1703–AD 1730] III. Ahmed. wikipedia: 9 r2 1115 - 18/19 r1 1143. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Ahmed III's long reign is remembered as the Tulip Era, a period of French-influenced garden palaces, poetry, tulip mania among the elite and the first Ottoman-run printing press in Turkish, set up by İbrahim Müteferrika. He sheltered Charles XII of Sweden after Poltava, recovered the Morea from Venice, but lost Belgrade and Serbia at Passarowitz in 1718. The lavishness ended in 1730 when the Patrona Halil revolt of janissaries and artisans burned the pleasure pavilions and forced him from the throne.

hints.label: III. Ahmed
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: I. Murat (Turkey, AD 1360–AD 1389)
nodes.title: I. Murat (Turkey, AD 1360–AD 1389)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1360–AD 1389] I. Murat. wikipedia: 9 j2 791. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He took Adrianople (Edirne) and made it his capital, turning the Ottoman beylik into a European power that reduced Serbian and Bulgarian princes to tributaries. The standing janissary corps and the timar system of cavalry fiefs took shape under him, along with the practice of levying Christian boys for state service. He was killed at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, a defeat for the Balkan coalition that became a founding memory of Serbian national identity.

hints.label: I. Murat
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: I. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754)
nodes.title: I. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1730–AD 1754)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1730–AD 1754] I. Mahmud. wikipedia: 19 r1 1143 - 27 safar 1168. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Raised to the throne by the Patrona Halil janissary revolt that ended the Tulip Era, he later crushed the rebels and ruled through a long round of frontier wars. Victory over Austria and Russia brought the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739, recovering Belgrade and northern Serbia, the last major Ottoman territorial gain. He employed the French convert Humbaracı Ahmed Pasha (Comte de Bonneval) to reorganise the bombardier corps, an early experiment in European-style military reform.

hints.label: I. Mahmud
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: VI. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1922)
nodes.title: VI. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1918–AD 1922)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1918–AD 1922] VI. Mehmed. wikipedia: 25 ramadan 1336 - 11 r1 1341. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Vahdettin took the throne as the empire collapsed, signing the Armistice of Mudros and presiding over an Istanbul occupied by Allied troops. His government accepted the punitive Treaty of Sèvres, which pushed Turkish nationalists in Anatolia to rally behind Mustafa Kemal and fight their own war of independence. When the nationalists won, the Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate; Mehmed left aboard a British warship, ending more than six centuries of Ottoman rule.

hints.label: VI. Mehmed
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1617–AD 1618)
nodes.title: I. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1617–AD 1618)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1617–AD 1618] I. Mustafa. first reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

A brother of Ahmed I who had spent his life confined in the palace and was widely regarded as mentally unfit, he was enthroned by court factions in place of a direct heir. His accession broke the rule of father-to-son succession and established succession by seniority within the dynasty. Deposed after a few months, he was briefly restored in 1622 before being set aside for good.

[Ottoman Empire, AD 1622–AD 1623] I. Mustafa. second reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

A brother of Ahmed I who had spent his life confined in the palace and was widely regarded as mentally unfit, he was enthroned by court factions in place of a direct heir. His accession broke the rule of father-to-son succession and established succession by seniority within the dynasty. Deposed after a few months, he was briefly restored in 1622 before being set aside for good.

nodes.name: I. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789)
nodes.title: I. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1774–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1774–AD 1789] I. Abdülhamid. wikipedia: 8 dh-q 1187 - 10 racab 1203. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He came to the throne days before the humiliating Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca gave Russia influence over Ottoman Orthodox subjects and opened the Black Sea. Russia annexed the Crimea in 1783, and his attempt to reverse the losses led to another disastrous war in 1787. He backed cautious modernisation of the navy, artillery and engineering schools, laying groundwork for the later reform programmes.

hints.label: I. Abdülhamid
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: Abdülaziz (Turkey, AD 1861–AD 1876)
nodes.title: Abdülaziz (Turkey, AD 1861–AD 1876)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1861–AD 1876] Abdülaziz. wikipedia: 16 d-h 1277 - 6 j1 1293. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Naval expansion, railways and a state visit to Paris and London marked an outward-looking reign, funded by European loans that ended in default. Financial collapse and Balkan revolts brought his overthrow by reforming ministers.

hints.label: Abdülaziz
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: IV. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1807–AD 1808)
nodes.title: IV. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1807–AD 1808)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1807–AD 1808] IV. Mustafa. wikipedia: 21 r1 1222 - 4 j2 1223. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mustafa IV owed his brief reign to a janissary revolt that overthrew his cousin Selim III and destroyed the New Order army Selim had built. When reformist troops marched on Istanbul to restore Selim, Mustafa had him killed, but was deposed anyway; the survivor of the purge, Mahmud II, took the throne and later executed him.

hints.label: IV. Mustafa
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: II. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691)
nodes.title: II. Süleyman (Turkey, AD 1687–AD 1691)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1687–AD 1691] II. Süleyman. wikipedia: 2 m 1099 - 25 ramadan 1102. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Süleyman II was pulled out of decades of confinement in the palace to replace his deposed brother at the low point of the war against the Holy League. Belgrade had fallen, mutinous troops filled the capital, and the treasury was empty; his grand vizier Fazıl Mustafa Pasha restored discipline, reformed taxation and retook Belgrade in 1690. The sultan died the following year with the war still unresolved.

hints.label: II. Süleyman
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: IV. Murad (Turkey, AD 1623–AD 1640)
nodes.title: IV. Murad (Turkey, AD 1623–AD 1640)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1623–AD 1640] IV. Murad. wikipedia: 15 dh-q 1032 - 15/16 shawwal 1049. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad IV seized real power in his twenties and used terror to restore it, executing officials, banning tobacco, coffee and alcohol, and reportedly prowling Istanbul in disguise to catch offenders. He led campaigns in person, retaking Baghdad from Safavid Persia in 1638. The Treaty of Zuhab that followed fixed an Ottoman-Persian border that has largely survived as the Iraq-Iran frontier.

hints.label: IV. Murad
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1444–AD 1446)
nodes.title: II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1444–AD 1446)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1444–AD 1446] II. Mehmed. first reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed II's first reign began as a boy of twelve, when his father abdicated in his favour. A crusading army under the king of Poland-Hungary promptly invaded, and although it was crushed at Varna in 1444, factional strife and a Janissary mutiny in the capital forced the child sultan aside and brought Murad II back. The humiliation shaped Mehmed's later determination to rule absolutely — and to take Constantinople.

hints.label: II. Mehmed
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: V. Murad (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1876)
nodes.title: V. Murad (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1876)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1876–AD 1876] V. Murad. wikipedia: 6 j1 1293 - 10 sha'ban 1293. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

One of the shortest reigns in Ottoman history: installed by reformist ministers who had deposed his uncle Abdülaziz, Murad suffered a mental breakdown within weeks and was removed after 93 days. His fall brought Abdülhamid II to the throne, whose long autocracy shaped the empire's final decades. Murad spent the rest of his life confined in the Çırağan Palace, a focus of plots that never came to anything.

nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1574–AD 1595] III. Murad. wikipedia: 8 ramadan 982 - 5 j1 1003. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad III ruled from the palace, never leaving Istanbul, while his mother Nurbanu, his wife Safiye and a shifting cast of viziers competed for influence — the period later Ottomans called the 'sultanate of women'. A long, expensive war with Safavid Iran gained Caucasian territory that was soon lost, and in 1593 the Long War with Austria began. Currency debasement, inflation and the sale of offices strained the empire's finances, though the court also produced some of the finest Ottoman illustrated manuscripts.

properties.title: bottle — 1575-1580 (circa)
properties.notes:
Bottle, pottery; pear-shaped, with a moulded shoulder and tall constricted neck with a torus moulding and slightly everted lip, standing on a splayed foot-ring. Painted in cobalt blue, viridian green and orange-red with black outlines. The body has cypress trees with forked tips set between symmetrical rose sprays and large incurving feathery blue leaves heightened with contrasting red and green with smaller stems of marguerites below. A meander band above the foot-ring. A more compressed version of the same design is repeated on the upper part of the neck above the torus moulding which has an undulating blue scroll. nodes.title: I. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1389–AD 1402)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1389–AD 1402] I. Bayezid. wikipedia: 19 j2 791 - 19 dh 804. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Nicknamed 'the Thunderbolt' for the speed of his campaigns, he absorbed the Anatolian beyliks, pressed deep into the Balkans and blockaded Constantinople, crushing a Western crusade at Nicopolis in 1396. His dispossession of the Turkish emirs drove them to Timur, who destroyed his army at Ankara in 1402 and took him prisoner. His death in captivity plunged the empire into an eleven-year civil war among his sons.

nodes.name: II. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1691–AD 1695)
nodes.title: II. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1691–AD 1695)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1691–AD 1695] II. Ahmed. wikipedia: 25 ramadan 1102 - 21 j2 1106. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Ahmed II inherited the Ottoman half of the Great Turkish War against the Habsburg-led Holy League and lost ground almost throughout. His ablest minister, the grand vizier Fazıl Mustafa Pasha, was killed at the battle of Slankamen in 1691, and the empire slid toward the defeats that ended in the Treaty of Karlowitz. A short, unlucky reign in which the Ottoman state was clearly on the defensive in Europe for the first time.

hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: I. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1603–AD 1617)
nodes.title: I. Ahmed (Turkey, AD 1603–AD 1617)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1603–AD 1617] I. Ahmed. wikipedia: 17 racab 1012 - 23 dh-q 1026. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He signed the Treaty of Zsitvatorok, which for the first time acknowledged the Habsburg ruler as an equal rather than a tributary, and struggled with Celali revolts across Anatolia and renewed war with Safavid Iran. He abandoned the custom of executing royal brothers, replacing it with confinement and eventual succession by seniority, a change that reshaped Ottoman dynastic politics. His great monument is the Sultan Ahmed (Blue) Mosque facing Hagia Sophia.

hints.label: I. Ahmed
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1446–AD 1451)
nodes.title: II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1446–AD 1451)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1446–AD 1451] II. Murad. second reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad II returned to the throne to steady an empire shaken by crusade and by the failure of his boy-successor. He beat John Hunyadi at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448, secured the Balkan frontier and left his son a consolidated state, a disciplined army and a treasury capable of the siege that followed. He was also a notable patron of Turkish letters and of the mosques of Edirne and Bursa.

hints.label: II. Murad
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: İbrahim (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1648)
nodes.title: İbrahim (Turkey, AD 1640–AD 1648)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1640–AD 1648] İbrahim. wikipedia: 16 shawwal 1049 - 18 racab 1058. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

A sultan who came to the throne as the last surviving male of the Ottoman line, having spent his youth confined in the palace. His reign is remembered for extravagance, erratic favouritism and the grip of court factions, and for launching the long war against Venice over Crete in 1645. Janissaries and jurists deposed and strangled him in 1648, putting his six-year-old son Mehmed IV on the throne.

nodes.name: III. Osman (Turkey, AD 1754–AD 1757)
nodes.title: III. Osman (Turkey, AD 1754–AD 1757)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1754–AD 1757] III. Osman. wikipedia: 27 safar 1168 - 15/16 safar 1171. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Osman III reached the throne after fifty years shut up in the palace's kafes, and the isolation showed: contemporaries described an irritable, eccentric ruler who disliked music and women's presence and changed his grand viziers constantly. His brief reign is remembered mainly for repeated great fires in Istanbul and for the completion of the baroque Nuruosmaniye Mosque begun by his brother.

nodes.name: I. Orhan (Turkey, AD 1324–AD 1360)
nodes.title: I. Orhan (Turkey, AD 1324–AD 1360)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1324–AD 1360] I. Orhan. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Under him the small frontier principality became a state: Bursa fell and became a capital, Nicaea and Nicomedia followed, and the first Ottoman silver coins and organised standing troops appeared. His alliance and marriage with the Byzantine claimant John VI Kantakouzenos brought Ottoman soldiers into Europe, and by 1354 they held Gallipoli. That foothold in Thrace opened the Balkans to permanent Ottoman conquest.

nodes.name: II. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1695–AD 1703)
nodes.title: II. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1695–AD 1703)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1695–AD 1703] II. Mustafa. wikipedia: 21 j2 1106 - 9 r2 1115. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mustafa II revived the old practice of leading armies in person, with disastrous results: the Habsburg commander Prince Eugene destroyed his army at Zenta in 1697. The resulting Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 handed Hungary and Transylvania to Austria — the first time the Ottomans ceded large territories by negotiation, and a turning point in their relations with Europe. He withdrew to Edirne, left government to his old tutor the şeyhülislam, and was deposed by a revolt of soldiers and clerics in 1703.

hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: I. Osman (Turkey, AD 1281–AD 1324)
nodes.title: I. Osman (Turkey, AD 1281–AD 1324)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1281–AD 1324] I. Osman. 680-724 Hijri. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The warrior chief whose small band in the Byzantine borderlands of northwest Anatolia gave its name to the Ottoman dynasty. His defeat of a Byzantine force at Bapheus in 1302 drew ghazi fighters and nomads to his banner and began the slow strangulation of Bursa. From these obscure beginnings grew an empire that would last six centuries; later chroniclers wrapped his career in the legend of a prophetic dream.

nodes.name: II. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1808–AD 1839)
nodes.title: II. Mahmud (Turkey, AD 1808–AD 1839)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1808–AD 1839] II. Mahmud. wikipedia: 4 j2 1223 - 18 r2 1255. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mahmud II broke the Janissary corps in 1826 in the bloody purge known as the Auspicious Incident, removing the obstacle that had destroyed earlier reformers, and rebuilt the army, bureaucracy and taxation on European lines. He also introduced the fez and frock coat, opened the first Ottoman newspaper and sent students abroad. His reign nonetheless lost Greece, saw Algeria taken by France, and nearly ended in defeat by his own governor of Egypt, Mehmed Ali; the centralising groundwork he laid produced the Tanzimat reforms announced months after his death.

nodes.name: II. Selim (Turkey, AD 1566–AD 1574)
nodes.title: II. Selim (Turkey, AD 1566–AD 1574)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1566–AD 1574] II. Selim. wikipedia: 14 r1 974 - 7 ramadan 982. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Selim II left the running of the empire largely to his grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, and the machine of state worked well enough without him. His reign brought the conquest of Cyprus and the crushing naval defeat at Lepanto in 1571 — after which the Ottoman fleet was rebuilt within a year — and the Selimiye Mosque at Edirne, which the architect Sinan regarded as his masterpiece. He is remembered by the unkind nickname 'the Sot' and as the first sultan who neither campaigned nor governed personally.

nodes.title: I. Selim (Turkey, AD 1512–AD 1520)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1512–AD 1520] I. Selim. wikipedia: 8 safar 918 - 8 shawwal 926. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

In eight years he doubled the size of the empire, crushing the Safavid Shah Ismail's cavalry with firearms at Chaldiran and then overthrowing the Mamluk sultanate to take Syria, Egypt and the Hejaz. Custody of Mecca and Medina gave the Ottoman sultans leadership of the Sunni world and control of the Red Sea and eastern trade routes. Known as 'the Grim' for his purges, he left his son Süleyman the wealthiest state in the region.

nodes.name: II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1451–AD 1481)
nodes.title: II. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1451–AD 1481)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1451–AD 1481] II. Mehmed. second reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed II's first reign began as a boy of twelve, when his father abdicated in his favour. A crusading army under the king of Poland-Hungary promptly invaded, and although it was crushed at Varna in 1444, factional strife and a Janissary mutiny in the capital forced the child sultan aside and brought Murad II back. The humiliation shaped Mehmed's later determination to rule absolutely — and to take Constantinople.

hints.label: II. Mehmed
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: III. Selim (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807)
nodes.title: III. Selim (Turkey, AD 1789–AD 1807)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1789–AD 1807] III. Selim. wikipedia: 11 racab 1203 - 21 r1 1222. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Selim III created the Nizam-ı Cedid, the 'New Order' — a European-style trained and uniformed army with its own tax fund — alongside new military schools, permanent embassies in European capitals and reforms of the fleet. His reign coincided with the French Revolution's shockwaves, Napoleon's invasion of Egypt and Serbian revolt. In 1807 a rebellion of auxiliary troops and Janissaries overthrew him; he was murdered the following year, but his programme was resumed by his cousin Mahmud II.

hints.label: III. Selim
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: IV. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687)
nodes.title: IV. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1648–AD 1687)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1648–AD 1687] IV. Mehmed. wikipedia: 18 racab 1058 - 2 m 1099. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Enthroned as a child during a palace crisis, Mehmed IV left government largely to the Köprülü grand viziers, who restored discipline and finances and made this a last age of Ottoman expansion — Crete taken from Venice, gains in Ukraine and Hungary. His own passion was hunting, which earned him the nickname Avcı. The catastrophic failure before Vienna in 1683 and the losses that followed cost him his throne in 1687.

nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1839–AD 1861] Abdülmecid. wikipedia: 18 r2 1255 - 16 dh 1277. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The Tanzimat era of decrees promising legal equality, a reformed bureaucracy and a modern conscript army. The Crimean War drew the empire into the European alliance system, while Dolmabahçe Palace and new ministries in Istanbul showed the westward turn in taste and government.

nodes.name: I. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1403–AD 1421)
nodes.title: I. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1403–AD 1421)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1403–AD 1421] I. Mehmed. at first in Anatolia only, after 816/1413 in Rumeli also. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

He won the civil war that followed his father's capture by Timur, defeating his brothers to reunite the shattered Ottoman state from Edirne and Bursa. He rebuilt the army and administration, put down the radical religious revolt of Şeyh Bedreddin, and kept the peace with Byzantium and Venice while consolidating Anatolia. Contemporaries called him the second founder of the empire; his tiled Green Mosque and tomb at Bursa date from his reign.

nodes.name: V. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1909–AD 1918)
nodes.title: V. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1909–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1909–AD 1918] V. Mehmed. wikipedia: 6 r2 1327 - 24 ramadan 1336. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed Reşad came to the throne after the Young Turks deposed his brother Abdülhamid II, and reigned as a constitutional figurehead while the Committee of Union and Progress ran the state. Under him the empire lost Libya and nearly all its Balkan territory, then entered the First World War alongside Germany; his proclamation of jihad in 1914 largely failed to rouse Muslims under Allied rule. The Armenian genocide and the defence of Gallipoli both fell within his reign. He died months before the armistice that dismantled the empire.

hints.label: V. Mehmed
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: II. Osman (Turkey, AD 1618–AD 1622)
nodes.title: II. Osman (Turkey, AD 1618–AD 1622)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1618–AD 1622] II. Osman. wikipedia: 21 r1 1027 - 8 racab 1031. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Known as Genç Osman, the Young Osman, he took the throne as a teenager and returned from an inconclusive campaign against Poland at Khotyn convinced that the Janissaries were useless and corrupt. His plan to raise a new army in Anatolia and, allegedly, to move the capital leaked out; the Janissaries rose, imprisoned him in the Yedikule fortress and strangled him. It was the first killing of a reigning Ottoman sultan by his own soldiers, and it made the corps a standing threat to every reformer for the next two centuries.

hints.label: II. Osman
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: II. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512)
nodes.title: II. Bayezid (Turkey, AD 1481–AD 1512)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1481–AD 1512] II. Bayezid. wikipedia: 20 r1 886 - 8 safar 918. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Bayezid II spent his early years fighting off his brother Cem, whose flight to Christian Europe made him a hostage-pawn of popes and kings. He consolidated his father's conquests rather than expanding, rebuilt Istanbul after the 1509 earthquake, invested heavily in the navy, and sent ships to carry Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 to Ottoman lands. He was forced to abdicate by his son Selim I, backed by the Janissaries, and died shortly afterwards.

hints.label: II. Bayezid
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: III. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603)
nodes.title: III. Mehmed (Turkey, AD 1595–AD 1603)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1595–AD 1603] III. Mehmed. wikipedia: 16 j1 1003 - 16 or 17 rajab 1012. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mehmed III began his reign by having nineteen of his brothers executed, the largest and last of the great Ottoman fratricides. He was the final sultan to command an army in the field, winning at Mezőkeresztes in 1596 during the long, grinding war with the Habsburgs. Behind the front, Anatolia was convulsed by the Celali rebellions of unpaid soldiers and displaced peasants, and real power at court passed to his mother, the valide sultan Safiye.

properties.title: jug — 1600 (circa)
properties.notes:
Jug, polychrome glazed pottery. The jug is of pear-shaped form with a splayed foot-ring, a cylindrical trumpet-shaped neck and a curved handle with a knop where it meets the body. It is painted in cobalt blue, viridian green and bole red, outlined in black, with two zones of large blue feathery leaves (two of which enclose a composite tulip-rosette stem) alternating with, and overlapping, rose and tulip sprays; there is a meander band above the foot. The shoulder has a frieze of interconnected lappets loosely based on a Chinese cloud collar. The juncture of the neck and the shoulder has a slightly raised luting line marked by a band of cable ornament. The handle has a blue ladder design with a green feathery leaf at the juncture with the body. Below the rim is an inscription in Ottoman Turkish with verses across four cartouches by the poet Baki in naskh script.; | Type: jug | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 14.60 centimetres foot ; 21.00 centimetres; 34.00 centimetres; | Culture: Ottoman dynasty

properties.notes:
Ewer; formed of a jug of Iznik ware, mounted with spout, cover and foot of silver, embossed, chased and gilt. The jug has a mottled turquoise ground on which are disposed scrollwise plantain-like leaves splashed with red (Armenian bole); round the neck a broad band of blue and green gadroons. The silver cover is embossed with cartouches having swags of fruit between; on the thumb-piece a cherub's head with formal wings; the spout represents an eagle's neck and head issuing from a grotesque mask. The handle is the original pottery handle of the jug; the foot mount has the a modified egg-and-tongue pattern. nodes.title: Abdülmecid (Turkey, AD 1922–AD 1924)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1922–AD 1924] Abdülmecid. as Caliph only. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

The Tanzimat era of decrees promising legal equality, a reformed bureaucracy and a modern conscript army. The Crimean War drew the empire into the European alliance system, while Dolmabahçe Palace and new ministries in Istanbul showed the westward turn in taste and government.

nodes.name: II. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1909)
nodes.title: II. Abdülhamid (Turkey, AD 1876–AD 1909)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1876–AD 1909] II. Abdülhamid. wikipedia: 10 sha'ban 1293 - 6 r2 1327. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Abdülhamid II came to the throne amid bankruptcy and revolt, allowed a constitution and parliament for barely a year, then shelved both and ruled for three decades through a palace bureaucracy, an extensive spy network and strict press censorship. He also modernised aggressively — telegraph lines, schools, the Hejaz Railway — and cultivated his role as caliph to appeal to Muslims beyond his borders. His reign saw the loss of the Balkans and Cyprus, the massacres of Armenians in the 1890s, and finally the Young Turk revolution of 1908, which restored the constitution and deposed him the next year.

hints.label: II. Abdülhamid
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: III. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1757–AD 1774)
nodes.title: III. Mustafa (Turkey, AD 1757–AD 1774)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1757–AD 1774] III. Mustafa. wikipedia: 16 safar 1171 - 8 dh-q 1187. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Mustafa III tried to rebuild Ottoman finances and modernise the artillery and navy with European advisers such as the Hungarian-French Baron de Tott, founding schools of mathematics and gunnery. He also rebuilt Istanbul after the earthquake of 1766 and raised the Laleli Mosque. Against his own better judgement he was pushed into war with Catherine the Great's Russia in 1768; the war went catastrophically, and he died before the punishing peace of Küçük Kaynarca.

hints.label: III. Mustafa
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1421–AD 1444)
nodes.title: II. Murad (Turkey, AD 1421–AD 1444)
nodes.description:
[Ottoman Empire, AD 1421–AD 1444] II. Murad. first reign. Period definition from The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual — 2014.

Murad II returned to the throne to steady an empire shaken by crusade and by the failure of his boy-successor. He beat John Hunyadi at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448, secured the Balkan frontier and left his son a consolidated state, a disciplined army and a treasury capable of the siege that followed. He was also a notable patron of Turkish letters and of the mosques of Edirne and Bursa.

hints.label: II. Murad
hints.source: The new Islamic dynasties : a chronological and genealogical manual

nodes.name: Period of the American and French Revolutions (United States, AD 1718–AD 1815)
nodes.title: Period of the American and French Revolutions (United States, AD 1718–AD 1815)
nodes.description:
[America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1718–AD 1815] Period of the American and French Revolutions. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Portugal, Spain, United States. "From the Death of Charles XII of Sweden to the Battle of Waterloo, A.D. 1718-1815."
"America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. The World, Elsewhere" pages 134-145. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

An age when the idea that governments derive authority from the governed moved from pamphlets to practice: British colonies in North America broke away and wrote a federal constitution, and France destroyed its monarchy and aristocratic order. Slave rebellion in Haiti produced the first independent Black republic, and Napoleon's wars carried the new legal and administrative models across Europe. The same decades saw steam engines, factories and the first stirrings of industrial society.

hints.label: Period of the American and French Revolutions
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Period of the New Western Empire (France, AD 800–AD 1066)
nodes.title: Period of the New Western Empire (France, AD 800–AD 1066)
nodes.description:
[New Western Empire/France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England/ England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere, AD 800–AD 1066] Period of the New Western Empire. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Scotland, Spain. "From the Crowning of Charlemagne at Rome to the Battle of Hastings, A.D. 800-1066" page 47
"New Western Empire/France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England/ England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere" pages 74-77. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Charlemagne's coronation in Rome revived the idea of a Western emperor and briefly united most of Latin Christendom under Frankish rule, with a court-driven revival of learning, script and church reform. The empire was divided among his heirs at Verdun and then battered by Viking, Magyar and Saracen raids, and defence devolved onto local counts and castles – the roots of feudal France. By the close of the period the Capetians held a shrunken royal title and Normandy's dukes were strong enough to conquer England.

hints.label: Period of the New Western Empire
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss (France, AD 1299–AD 1453)
nodes.title: Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss (France, AD 1299–AD 1453)
nodes.description:
[France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1299–AD 1453] Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Scotland, Spain. "From the Founding of the Turkish Empire to the Taking of Constantinople, A.D. 1299-1453." page 47
"France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere" pages 102-111. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

An older textbook label for the late Middle Ages: plague and the Hundred Years' War tore through France and England, the papacy split between rival claimants, and reformers like Wyclif and Hus attacked church wealth and doctrine a century before Luther. In the east Timur's armies shattered empires from Delhi to Anatolia, and the age closed with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople and the first printing with movable type.

hints.label: Period of Tamerlane, Wickliffe, and Huss
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Persian Period (Italy, 587 BC–329 BC)
nodes.title: Persian Period (Italy, 587 BC–329 BC)
nodes.description:
[Asia. Africa. Greece. Rome, Etc/Rome and Italy, 587 BC–329 BC] Persian Period. "From Captivity, to Alexander the Great, B.C. 588-330.....258 years.....The Persian Period." page 2.
"Asia. Africa. Greece. Rome, Etc.", pages 20-23. "Asia. Africa. Greece. Rome and Italy.", pages 18-19, 24-25. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Cambyses' conquest made Egypt the 27th Dynasty, a satrapy governed from Susa: Darius completed a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, codified Egyptian law and built temples such as Hibis in the oases. Native resentment produced repeated revolts, and Egypt eventually broke free under a line of local pharaohs for some sixty years before the Persians returned.

hints.label: Persian Period
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions (Spain, AD 1453–AD 1598)
nodes.title: Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions (Spain, AD 1453–AD 1598)
nodes.description:
[England. Scotland. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1453–AD 1598] Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions. Spatial coverage: Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain. "From the Taking of Constantinople to the Edict of Nantes, A.D. 1453-1598} Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions." page 47
"England. Scotland. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere" pages 112-121. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Printing, ocean navigation and gunpowder reshaped Europe just as Spain became its dominant power: Granada fell, Columbus crossed the Atlantic, and American silver funded Habsburg armies from Italy to the Netherlands. Luther's challenge split Western Christianity, and Spain answered with the Council of Trent, the Inquisition and the Armada. Visitors can trace how conquest, bullion and religious war together made and then overstretched a global empire.

hints.label: Period of the Reformation; Discoveries and Inventions
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV (Spain, AD 1598–AD 1718)
nodes.title: Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV (Spain, AD 1598–AD 1718)
nodes.description:
[America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1598–AD 1718] Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV. Spatial coverage: Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain. "From the Edict of Nantes to the Death of Charles XII of Sweden, A.D. 1598-1718." page 47
"America. England. France. Spain and Portugal. Germany. Italy. Ottoman Empire. The World, Elsewhere" pages 122-133. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Spain slid from superpower to junior partner. The later Habsburg kings, propped up by American silver and ruinous credit, lost the northern Netherlands and Portugal, saw Catalonia revolt, and watched French armies take the initiative under Louis XIV. When Charles II died childless, the resulting War of the Spanish Succession installed a Bourbon dynasty and stripped away the Italian and Netherlandish possessions, leaving a smaller, more centrally governed Spain.

hints.label: Period of the English Commonwealth and Wars of Louis XIV
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Period of The Crusades (France, AD 1066–AD 1299)
nodes.title: Period of The Crusades (France, AD 1066–AD 1299)
nodes.description:
[France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere, AD 1066–AD 1299] Period of The Crusades. Spatial coverage: England, France, Germany, Scotland, Spain. "From the Battle of Hastings to the Founding of the Turkish Empire, A.D. 1066-1299." page 47.
"France, Spain, Germany. Eastern Empire. England & Scotland. The World, Elsewhere" pages 78-101. Period definition from The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history — George Palmer Putnam, 1850.

Two centuries in which Latin Christendom went on the offensive - into Syria and Palestine, into Muslim Spain, into the Baltic - and came home with new tastes, texts and banking arrangements. The same centuries saw the Norman Conquest of England, the growth of towns and universities, Gothic cathedral building, and the rise of strong monarchies in France and England. By the end the crusader states were gone but Europe was far richer and better connected than before.

hints.label: Period of The Crusades
hints.source: The world's progress : a dictionary of dates, with tabular views of general history

nodes.name: Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Kingdom (Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2059 BC–1794 BC] Middle Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egypt was reunified after a century of division, and the pharaohs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties built a tightly run state from a new capital near the Faiyum, where they drained land and expanded irrigation. Great fortresses were planted through Lower Nubia, mining expeditions ranged into Sinai and Punt, and the language and literature of the age — the Tale of Sinuhe, the wisdom texts — became the classic Egyptian canon. Central control weakened after 1800 BC, ending with the Hyksos ascendancy in the Delta.

hints.label: Middle Kingdom
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Troy III-V (Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.title: Troy III-V (Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 2099 BC–1799 BC] Troy III-V. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Three modest phases in which Troy was a small, ordinary Anatolian town rather than a rich stronghold. Houses were cramped, imports scarce and the architecture unambitious, yet occupation was continuous and the pottery shows unbroken local tradition. These quiet centuries separate the treasure-filled Early Bronze Age citadel from the grand walled city that followed.

hints.label: Troy III-V
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Old Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1574 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.title: Old Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1574 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Anatolia, 1574 BC–1399 BC] Old Hittite Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The earliest phase of Hittite power, when kings ruling from Hattusa welded central Anatolian towns into a single state and raided as far as Aleppo and Babylon. Their surviving laws, land grants and royal proclamations, written in cuneiform on clay, record an Indo-European language and a court perpetually troubled by assassination and disputed succession. The kingdom contracted sharply afterwards before re-emerging as the empire that would fight Egypt at Kadesh.
