nodes.name: Predynastic (Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC)
nodes.title: Predynastic (Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 4999 BC–3049 BC] Predynastic. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Farming villages along the Nile grew into competing chiefdoms with cemeteries, craft workshops and long-distance trade in lapis, cedar and gold. Naqada-culture potters, flint-knappers and stone-vase makers reached extraordinary technical heights, and the imagery on their palettes and painted jars — kings smiting enemies, sacred boats, animal standards — is already the visual language of pharaonic Egypt. It ends with the unification of the Nile Valley under a single ruler.

hints.label: Predynastic
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Neolithic (Syria, 8549 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Syria, 8549 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Near East, 8549 BC–4999 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, West Bank. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

hints.label: Neolithic
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Achaemenids (Iran, 549 BC–329 BC)
nodes.title: Achaemenids (Iran, 549 BC–329 BC)
nodes.description:
[Persia, 549 BC–329 BC] Achaemenids. Gates discusses only the Achaemenids in Persia proper in this chapter. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The dynasty founded by Cyrus the Great that ruled from the Aegean to the Indus, tolerating local gods and customs while extracting tribute through satraps. Its kings left carved cliff reliefs at Bisitun and Naqsh-e Rostam and vast terraced palaces at Persepolis, whose burnt ruins mark Alexander's conquest. Greek writers such as Herodotus defined 'Persia' for the West through their wars with these rulers.

hints.label: Achaemenids
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Middle Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1399 BC–1349 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Hittite Kingdom (Turkey, 1399 BC–1349 BC)
nodes.description:
[Anatolia, 1399 BC–1349 BC] Middle Hittite Kingdom. Spatial coverage: Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

A period of crisis in which enemies closed in from every direction — Kaska tribes burned Hattusa itself — and the kingdom nearly disappeared. Tudhaliya III rebuilt from a temporary capital and passed a restored army to his son Suppiluliuma I, who turned survival into conquest. The near-collapse and the recovery that followed are documented in unusually vivid royal annals and prayers.

nodes.name: Late Period (Egypt, 759 BC–331 BC)
nodes.title: Late Period (Egypt, 759 BC–331 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 759 BC–331 BC] Late Period. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

hints.label: Late Period
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Classical (Greece, 399 BC–322 BC)
nodes.title: Late Classical (Greece, 399 BC–322 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 399 BC–322 BC] Late Classical. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. The chapter associated with this term covers sites in both Greece and Turkey, although map of conquests of Alexander also covers the Levant, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan, and parts of India and Pakistan. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

In the Greek cities of the south, this was the era of grand Apulian and Lucanian red-figure vases, tomb painting, and lavish burials, even as Oscan and Lucanian peoples took over cities like Poseidonia. Central Italy saw Etruscan power ebb and Rome fight its way through the Latin and Samnite wars, absorbing neighbours and building the first roads and aqueducts. By the end of the century the peninsula's future belonged to Rome rather than to the Greek or Etruscan cities.

nodes.name: Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1474 BC–1224 BC)
nodes.title: Late Cypriot II (Cyprus, 1474 BC–1224 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1474 BC–1224 BC] Late Cypriot II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The peak of Bronze Age Cyprus. Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke functioned as cosmopolitan port towns handling copper, and the island — almost certainly the 'Alashiya' whose kings corresponded with the pharaoh in the Amarna letters — dealt with Egypt and the Hittites as a power in its own right. Tombs yield Mycenaean pictorial kraters, ivory, faience and gold, and clay tablets carry the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script.

nodes.name: Roman Republic (Lazio, 508 BC–26 BC)
nodes.title: Roman Republic (Lazio, 508 BC–26 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 508 BC–26 BC] Roman Republic. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After expelling its kings, Rome developed a government of elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and citizen assemblies, and an army of property-owning citizens. It absorbed Italy, destroyed Carthage and took the Greek east, becoming the dominant Mediterranean power within two centuries. The wealth and slaves that flooded in wrecked the old order, producing land crises, political violence and the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Caesar. Its institutions and its collapse became the standard reference point for later republics.

nodes.name: Troy VIIb 1 (Troy, 1259 BC–1189 BC)
nodes.title: Troy VIIb 1 (Troy, 1259 BC–1189 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 1259 BC–1189 BC] Troy VIIb 1. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Survivors rebuilt among the burnt ruins, reusing walls and keeping the old pottery styles, so life on the mound continued rather than stopping. Alongside the familiar wares appear crude handmade pots of a type foreign to Anatolia, hinting at newcomers arriving in the unsettled years after the Bronze Age collapse.

nodes.name: Post-Palatial (Crete, 1424 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Post-Palatial (Crete, 1424 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 1424 BC–1049 BC] Post-Palatial. "(= Late Minoan IIIA, B, and C)". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the destruction of Knossos, the palace system that had administered Crete for centuries was gone, and with it the centralised storage, seal-based bureaucracy and Linear B records. Settlement shifted toward smaller centres and, increasingly, to defensible upland sites such as Karfi, while burial customs, dress and pottery drew closer to mainland Mycenaean styles. Trade continued but on a reduced scale, and the period slides into the Aegean's early Iron Age.

nodes.name: Hittite Empire (Turkey, 1349 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Hittite Empire (Turkey, 1349 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Anatolia, 1349 BC–1199 BC] Hittite Empire. Spatial coverage: Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

At its height the Hittite kingdom fought Egypt and Assyria for control of Syria, sacked and absorbed the kingdom of Mitanni, and clashed with Ramesses II at Kadesh before signing the earliest surviving peace treaty between great powers. Vassal kings across Anatolia and the Levant were bound by written oaths, and the capital Hattusa was rebuilt on a monumental scale. The whole structure collapsed around 1200 BC, the city burned and abandoned, leaving only small successor states in the southeast.

nodes.name: Early Classical (Greece, 479 BC–449 BC)
nodes.title: Early Classical (Greece, 479 BC–449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 479 BC–449 BC] Early Classical. Gates concentrates on Athens, so Greece is most appropriate coverage. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The generation after the defeat of Persia at Plataea and Mycale, when Athens built the Delian League and turned it toward empire. In art it is the 'Severe Style': figures like the Delphi Charioteer and the Riace bronzes abandoned the archaic smile for calm, weighted naturalism. The confidence and tribute money of these decades made the Parthenon and the high classical age possible.

On the left Apollo stands holding in his left a chelys, his right resting on his hip; he is a youthful beardless figure with long wavy hair, of which a single tress falls on each shoulder; he wears a long sleeved chiton and himation. Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. Dionysos pursuing Giant, (a) Dionysos, bearded, with long hair flying back and wreathed with ivy, rushes to right, his thyrsos couched as a lance, the butt end in front, and holding forward in his outstretched left a snake, which also moves forward with open mouth. He wears a chitoniscos with apoptygma, bordered with a pattern of zigzags and a fringe, and apparently made of some thick material, decorated with V-shaped marks; a mantle hangs from his left arm; and on his legs are high boots with flaps. From the stem of the thyrsos two shoots issue on each side close under the head. (b) A Giant, nude, with shield on left seen edgewise, retreats to right, looking back, and hurling a stone with outstretched right arm. He is bearded and has a helmet with raised cheek-pieces; his shield has for device three rings, and a fringed apron also decorated with rings attached to the lower side. His body is in three-quarter back view. Much shattered, and surface injured, left leg of Dionysos missing; otherwise the designs are fairly complete. Strong style. Brown (thinned black) for hair (except on crown), beards, and inner markings; the hair is pictorially treate | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 33.02 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Gela, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 460BC-450BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Paris and Hermes on Mount Ida. Mount Ida is indicated on left by a series of wavy lines; Paris is seated on the top, a wreathed youth with wavy hair falling to his neck, and a mantle about his lower limbs and left arm, playing upon the chelys with a plectrum. On the right Hermes stands en face, but looking towards Paris; he is bearded, and has a short chiton, a chlamys fastened on the right shoulder, and a petasos hanging at his back; his left arm is concealed by his mantle; in his right hand, which hangs at his side, is a caduceus. (b) Draped ephebos resting right on staff, standing en face, looking to left. Fine style. Purple ground-lines, cord of petasos, pegs of lyre, and wreath; brown inner markings. Ends of hair in thinned black. Eye in developed profile type. Below a, sets of three maeanders alternately to right and left, separated by dotted cross squares; below b, a strip of key pattern.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 34.29 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 460BC-450BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) A slinger. A beardless warrior in helmet with curved cheek-pieces, short undertied chiton, stands en face, but head turned to right, preparing to sling; his left is extended in front, holding the missile and one end, the other end is raised in his right above his right shoulder. His feet are carelessly drawn. On left are two spears upright, point upwards. (b) Warrior apparently attacking the last figure. He strides to left, brandishing spear and covering body with shield (device, a hare in silhouette to left running, on a thin black line): he wears a helmet with cheek-pieces raised, decorated with a lizard in silhouette, cuirass, and short chiton embroidered with stars and a border. Beneath the foot incised characters. Thinned reddish brown for hair of slinger, and on front and back of crest of both helmets. The cord of the sling is drawn as a thin black line over the red and black alike. Below each side, a strip of zigzags.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 31.75 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 460BC-450BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Warrior moving to left, looking back, spear carried in right over shoulder, shield (device, bull in silhouette charging on thin black ground-line to left) on left arm covering body. He is beardless, and has wavy hair falling on shoulders and in front of ear, short chiton, and chlamys (?). His helmet has nasal, cheek-pieces raised and decorated with a lizard in black silhouette. (b) A Barbarian warrior moving to right, looking back. He has small features and a short beard; he wears a short tied chiton, with a skin fastened round his neck and protecting his left arm, and a sort of helmet of skin with high spherical crown and flat rim all round. In his right he carries two spears, and he wears shoes. Brilliant varnish and colour. Fine graceful style. Light brown used for hair, beard, markings on crest of helmet, and markings on skin and cap in b. Sketch marks very plain. The upper surface of the lip is left red.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 31.75 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

properties.title: pelike — 470BC-460BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured pelike. (a) Dionysos running to right, looking back, holding out on left a cantharos, in right a thyrsos. He is bearded, with long wavy hair falling on shoulders, and wears a long sleeved chiton and mantle, a woollen fillet and a wreath. (b) Maenad standing to left, holding a thyrsos; she is wreathed, and wears an Ionic chiton and himation. On right hangs a wreath of ivy. Late stage of fine style. Purple wreath in b. properties.notes:

The hair is looped up with a broad fillet. On left, ΚΑΛΟΣ, καλός (now faint). (b) A Maenad in a long chiton and himation, and radiated fillet, standing to right holding upright in left a thyrsos; from its stem an ivy branch springs to right. On left ΚΑΛΕ, καλή (now faint). properties.title: rhyton — 470BC-460BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery rhyton in the form of a seated sphinx. Two Nikae pursuing a youth. On the right a youth, with a short mantle over his shoulders, holding a chelys in his left hand, runs to right, looking back at a Nike, who flies after him, extending both arms towards him. On the left a second Nike flies after, holding in her right a fruit (?) and raising her left in surprise. Each wears a long chiton with sleeves, undertied, and a saccos. In the field, HOΠAIΣ KAΛΟΣ HOΠAIΣ, ο παις κάλος ό παις. The body of the vase is in the form of a seated Sphinx. The colouring and gilding have been imperfectly restored; the gilding round the hair seems to be modern; round the neck by a red cord hang three raised ornaments gilt. The filled-in space between the legs is coloured vermilion on a white engobe (slip-paint), and there is no spout between the forelegs. The whole rests on a plinth, encircled with a band of herring-bone pattern, black on the red clay. From between the up-curved wings rises a trumpet-shaped vase, around which is the design. Late stage of good style. Purple inscription, fillet, and cord of chelys. Brown inner markings. Eye in early stage of profile. Below, a thin red line. Above, her | Type: rhyton | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 15.24 centimetres; 33.02 centimetres; 7.60 centimetres of base ; 20.40 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

properties.title: neck-amphora — 470BC-460BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Type of Menelaos pursuing Helen. Young warrior pursuing a woman with a sword. The woman flees to right, her right hand pressed to bosom with gesture of fear, her left enveloped in himation. She wears a long chiton, diploidion with apoptygma, tied at waist with a shawl instead of a girdle (?), and her hair is looped up with many ties of a fillet. She looks back at her pursuer, who strides forward with drawn sword, left extended holding scabbard. He is beardless, with wavy hair falling to shoulders and tied with fillet, and wears short chiton, cuirass, and a mantle on outstretched left. His cuirass has the sides decorated with vertical rows of dots (representing scales ?). (b) Woman running to right with arms outstretched on either side, looking back; she wears a sleeved chiton, himation, and saccos. Drawing of good period. Excessive drapery. Purple swordbelt and fillets, brown ends of hair, shading of flaps of cuirass, and folds of chiton in b. Below a, sets of three maeanders in alternate directions, separated by dotted crosses ; below b, key pattern to right.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 34.29 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

properties.title: kylix — 470BC-460BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured kylix. Interior: Within a circle of single maeanders, a woman seated to right at the door of a house; she wears a saccos, earrings, a chiton, and a mantle which is muffled closely around her neck, covering the right hand on the breast: the left under the drapery is extended towards a calathos (part seen) on the right, decorated with horizontal bands, wavy lines and dots. The seat is of irregular shape (a rock ?) and is covered with an end of the mantle, beneath which a striped cushion also appears. The door (part seen) is represented by thick vertical strokes in black, with brown shading lines between; over it a horizontal slab projects vertically, representing the portico. Surface and colour in good condition; drawing very rough. The surface has been ruddled, and sketch marks appear in a lighter colour. Eye in profile.; | Type: kylix | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 20.30 centimetres; 12.05 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Fikellura grave 178, Greece

properties.title: hydria — 470BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured hydria. A bald old man seated to right between two women, holding out a flower in his right hand: his beard is only indicated by an outline in black, his hair by an outline in brown: around his legs, which are tucked under the chair, are an himation and the folds of a chiton, which is not shown on the upper part of his body, his right breast and side being bare. At the back of his head is a rectangular object which may represent the handle of his staff resting against his left shoulder. Seated on a square box confronting him is a woman holding out to him with both hands a wreath, and behind him a second woman stands, raising her left in an attitude of surprise: both women wear sleeved chiton, himation, and saccos. The figures, on the principle of isocephalism, are all of the same height (Same height whether seated or standing). Purple flower and wreath: brown outline of hair of the old man and inner markings of anatomy. Below, a strip of key pattern: above, and round the lip, egg pattern. Design curves up on shoulder of vase.; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 22.86 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Vulci, Greece

properties.title: hydria — 480BC-460BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figure hydria (Six technique). On body and shoulder: Nike floating in air to right, about to alight between two large hydria; which rest on the ground on either side. In her left she holds a fluted phiale mesomphalos, and turns her head to look at a large thymiaterion in her right. She wears a sleeveless chiton, fastened on each shoulder with a long pin, with apoptygma tied at waist, a fillet, and a radiated stephane. Over her head NIKHΚΑΛΗ, Νίκη καλή; on each side hangs a wreath of laurel; the colour from these and from the inscription has entirely disappeared, leaving only a discoloration of the surface. Fine style. Below, a strip of sets of three maeanders separated by dotted crosses; above, a strip of palmettes; round lip, egg moulding; and below back handle, palmette. The fillet, inscription and wreaths seem to have been coloured purple. Eye of developed profile type, with eyelash.; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 0.30 metres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: trefoil-mouth oinochoe — 480BC-470BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured trefoil oinochoe. Bearded satyr and Maenad. On left a bearded satyr, seated on the ground with left leg bent under him, right leg extended, holds a diota upright between his legs, a thyrsos in left, and with right offers a cantharos to a Maenad, who rushes away with extended arms, looking back; on her right arm is a diminutive lion springing open-mouthed to left; in her left hand she holds a twisting snake; she wears an Ionic chiton, succinct, and a nebris knotted around her neck by the fore-paws; her short hair flies loose. Both figures are wreathed with vine. Drawing of the fine period at the end of the severe style. Purple wreaths and lion's tongue. Brown inner markings and marks on nebris, lion, and snake. The hair around the face is outlined with dots. Eye in archaic type. Below, a broad band of elaborate anthemion pattern, continuous; above the scene, a strip of egg moulding. On base of handle, an inverted palmette, from which spreads on each side a fine ornament composed of two palmettes and a flower.; | Type: trefoil-mouth oinochoe | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 27.94 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

properties.title: amphora — 470BC-450BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured amphora type B. (a) Menelaos pursuing Helen and startled by her beauty. Menelaos, a bearded warrior in helmet, short chiton, and cuirass, and carrying shield (seen in foreshortening) on left arm, drops his sword from his right hand, as, pursuing Helen to right, he recognises her. She turns as she flies, looking at him and raising her right hand in surprise; with her left she lifts the edge of her skirt; and on the left a woman flees to left, looking back, and raising both hands in surprise. Both women wear long chiton, himation, and earrings; Helen has long hair with radiated stephane; the hair of the other is looped up with a fillet. The cuirass of Menelaos has a four-rayed star on each shoulder-piece and on the breast one of sixteen rays; the centre of the body is ornamented with scale pattern, the sides with brick pattern; his helmet is decorated with tendrils and has raised cheek-pieces; both it and the foot of the left figure project over the border. (b) Three Maenads. The central figure holds in her left a thyrsos, and with her right a phiale to be filled from the oinochoe (silhouette against her drapery) of the one on left; this figure holds in her left  | Type: amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 55.20 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

properties.title: hydria — 450BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured hydria. Youth pursuing woman beside a house in presence of a king (or priest of Apollo ?). On left is a large pair of folding doors, with architrave, bands of nails, and two handles, beside which a youth (wearing petasos, mantle hanging like plaid over left shoulder, sword-belt, hair in short wavy curls), holding two spears couched in left, advances to seize with right a woman, who flees, looking back and raising her right in surprise; with her left she lifts the hem of her sleeved chiton; she wears himation and a radiated stephane around her looped-up hair. properties.title: skyphos — 460BC
properties.notes:

properties.title: column krater — 460BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured column-krater. (a) Contest of Apollo and Heracles for the tripod. Heracles, bearded, holding up club in right, runs to right with the tripod under his left arm; he looks back at Apollo, beardless, with long hair, who runs after him, grasping a leg of the tripod in each hand. On the right Athene and on left a veiled goddess stand looking on, the latter raising both hands in surprise. Athene places her right hand against the club of Heracles, and has a long bordered chiton and diplois, dotted aegis with large Gorgoneion, a helmet with raised cheek-pieces, and a spear held upright in left. The veiled goddess is dressed in a long chiton and a mantle which passes over the back of her head; it is difficult to decide whether she raises her left hand with the fingers spread out, or whether she holds a torch in her left hand, the drawing being very defective here. (b) A woman in long chiton and himation, with hair looped up, moving to right, looking back, between two draped ephebi staff in hand. Brown shading of tripod.; | Type: column krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 19.05 centimetres; 26.67 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

properties.notes:

Exterior: (a) On right a satyr reclining on a rock, on which are strewn ivy tendrils, and leaning back against a diota which is wreathed with ivy; his left leg is bent under him; on his left arm is his thyrsos; in his right he holds out a cantharos towards a Nymph, who approaches from left, her head thrown back, playing on a chelys; she has long hair and wears a sleeved chiton with apoptygma, and a himation on her left arm; behind her stands a tree with forked branches, but no leaves. properties.title: volute krater — 490BC-460BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured volute-krater (bowl for mixing wine and water) with figure scenes on confined to a narrow, frieze-like band that encircles the lower element of the neck. (a) Combat of Achilles and Hector in the presence of Athena and Apollo. On the left, Achilles (youthful) presses forward with shield advanced and spear shortened to deal a finishing stroke to Hector (bearded), who, bleeding from wounds in the chest and left thigh, sinks helplessly backwards, with shield extended to right and point of spear dropped; each has a helmet with raised cheek-pieces, and a sword at side attached to his cross-belt. properties.title: kylix — 480BC-470BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured kylix. Interior: Within a circle of single maeanders, an old shoemaker at work in his shop. He sits on a diphros, part seen, on which is a striped cushion, before a trapeza seen in perspective on the right. On this is the usual square of hard wood, upon which the shoemaker has laid a long strip of leather, and with his left spread over it he keeps it in position, while with his right he cuts it carefully with the crescent-shaped knife (τομεύς or περίτομεύς). He is bald on the crown, and has a short beard and wrinkled forehead, and wears a mantle around his legs. The table has an under shelf, closed in, with two rectangular openings. At his feet is a cubical wicker basket, inscribed καλός. In the field hang objects intended to characterise the workshop: on left two pieces of leather cut out for the sole and upper respectively of a boot, then a hammer, a boot, a sandal, and a second τομεύς. In the field, καλός. Exergue left red. The eye is of unusual form, having the dotted pupil and archaic form, but with the upper lid drawn in naturally. The edge of the hair against the flesh is dotted; the shape of the head and nose are peculiar. Pottery: red-figured pelike. (a) Arming of a youth. properties.title: rhyton — 460BC-450BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery rhyton in the form of a boar's head. The cup, one handled, on which the design stands is supported by a finely modelled boar's head, in two longitudinal halves. The surface covered with fine black glaze; a series of lightly incised lines mark the fringe of hair all around the cheeks and lower jaw. The front of the snout and the interior of the ears are left in the natural clay, but may have been covered with a brownish pigment used for the mouth and tusks (two on each side of the lower jaw). The eyeball is black within a circle left red; it is set in a white ground, with a raised rim coloured purple for the eyelid. The crest is purple. The design is divided into three by the ears and handle. Above the crest is a wreath of ivy, the interlacing stalks indicated by lightly incised lines. On each side, between handle and ear, is a boar to left. Below, a band of herring-bone pattern. The one on left moves to left with open mouth, as if grunting, and with right fore-leg raised. properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Woman and ape. On the left a woman in a long bordered chiton undertied with a broad sash, who has wrapped a bordered mantle tightly over the upper part of her body, arms, and head, so that only the forehead and eye show, stands looking at an ape which squats facing her on a high cube or box, possibly its crib: its left knee is raised, its right leg hangs over the side, and in its left hand it holds the end of a cord which seems to pass around the right thigh: with its right hand it appears to be scratching the inside of its right thigh. nodes.name: Old Palace (Protopalatial) (Crete, 1929 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Old Palace (Protopalatial) (Crete, 1929 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 1929 BC–1699 BC] Old Palace (Protopalatial). "(= Middle Minoan IB)". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first great palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia rose as centres of storage, craft production and ritual, surrounded by growing towns. Cretan scribes began keeping records in Cretan Hieroglyphic and Linear A, and potters produced eggshell-thin Kamares ware painted in white, red and orange. Earthquakes or conflict levelled these palaces, but they were promptly rebuilt on a grander scale.

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Greece, 322 BC–30 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 322 BC–30 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates notes "to the Battle of Actium". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

nodes.name: Troy I (Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.title: Troy I (Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 2899 BC–2399 BC] Troy I. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first fortified settlement on the mound of Hisarlık: a small walled citadel of long, narrow megaron houses overlooking the entrance to the Dardanelles. Its people used handmade dark burnished pottery and worked copper, living off farming, fishing and the traffic passing through the straits. Ten building phases show the place was rebuilt again and again on the same spot, beginning the deep layer-cake of ruins Schliemann later dug through.

nodes.name: Classical (Greece, 478 BC–322 BC)
nodes.title: Classical (Greece, 478 BC–322 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 478 BC–322 BC] Classical. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates notes "to the death of Alexander the Great". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Greek colonies in the south flourished as centres of philosophy, coinage and monumental temple building, while Etruscan power ebbed after naval defeat off Cumae. Rome, still a small republic, fought its Latin and Etruscan neighbours, survived a sack by Gallic raiders and slowly emerged as the dominant city of central Italy. The groundwork was laid for the peninsula's unification under Roman rule in the following century.

nodes.name: Troy VIIb 2 (Troy, 1189 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Troy VIIb 2 (Troy, 1189 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 1189 BC–1099 BC] Troy VIIb 2. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

A distinctive knobbed pottery, Buckelkeramik, with parallels in the Balkans, becomes common, suggesting a new population settling on the old citadel. The town was poor and provincial, its great walls now sheltering modest houses, and after its end the site was largely deserted for centuries before Greek settlers returned.

nodes.name: Halaf and Ubaid (Syria, 4999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.title: Halaf and Ubaid (Syria, 4999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Near East, 4999 BC–3499 BC] Halaf and Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, West Bank. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The distinctive painted Halaf wares gave way to plainer, mass-produced Ubaid pottery spreading north from southern Mesopotamia, a sign of village societies being drawn into a much wider cultural orbit. Settlements grew larger, some with tripartite houses and small temples rebuilt on the same spot for generations, and irrigation and ploughing supported bigger surpluses. These centuries set the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.

nodes.name: Harappan, or Mature (Pakistan, 2599 BC–1899 BC)
nodes.title: Harappan, or Mature (Pakistan, 2599 BC–1899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Indus Valley, 2599 BC–1899 BC] Harappan, or Mature. Spatial coverage: India, Pakistan. Indus Valley is defined as "a region now situated in modern Pakistan and north-west India". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The high point of the Indus civilisation, when planned cities of baked brick with drains, granaries and citadels spread from the Arabian Sea to the foothills of the Himalaya. Craftsmen produced carnelian beads, bronze figurines and steatite seals inscribed with a script no one can read; standardised weights and bricks imply strong shared conventions rather than visible kings. Trade reached Mesopotamia by sea before the cities were gradually abandoned.

nodes.name: Akkadian (Iraq, 2349 BC–2149 BC)
nodes.title: Akkadian (Iraq, 2349 BC–2149 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2349 BC–2149 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.

hints.label: Akkadian
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Geometric (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometric. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates discusses Greek cities that are now in the territory of Turkey, although he does not refer to Anatolia specifically. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Greece emerging from the post-Mycenaean dark age, its pottery covered in meanders, zigzags and banded panels, later giving way to silhouetted horses, chariots and mourners on the huge Dipylon grave markers of Athens. Communities coalesced into the first city-states, sanctuaries like Olympia and Delphi filled with dedications, the Phoenician alphabet was adapted to Greek, and settlers began sailing west to Italy and Sicily. The oral traditions that became the Iliad and Odyssey took shape in these years.

hints.label: Geometric
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Protoliterate (Uruk) (Iraq, 3499 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.title: Protoliterate (Uruk) (Iraq, 3499 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 3499 BC–2899 BC] Protoliterate (Uruk). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Uruk swelled into the world's first true city, with monumental temple platforms, mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls and an administration that used cylinder seals and clay tokens to track goods. To keep the accounts, scribes pressed signs into clay — the proto-cuneiform tablets that are the earliest writing known. Uruk-style material spread far up the Euphrates and into Iran, marking the first great expansion of an urban economy.

hints.label: Protoliterate (Uruk)
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Gutian (Iraq, 2149 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Gutian (Iraq, 2149 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2149 BC–1999 BC] Gutian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. According to Gates, Gutian domination of Mesopotamia was ended by Ur-Nammu, the first ruler of the Third dynasty of Ur (2100 B.C.-2000 B.C.), which contradicts the end date of 2000 BC (p. 55). Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the Akkadian empire collapsed, groups from the Zagros mountains known as the Gutians took control of parts of Babylonia, and later Mesopotamian scribes blamed them for ruin, famine and the fall of civilised order. Their actual rule is thinly documented, and southern cities such as Lagash appear to have flourished during it, which makes the 'Gutian dark age' a case study in how history is written by later winners. Their expulsion by Utu-hegal of Uruk was celebrated as a liberation and opened the way for the Third Dynasty of Ur.

hints.label: Gutian
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: New Palace (Neopalatial) (Crete, 1699 BC–1449 BC)
nodes.title: New Palace (Neopalatial) (Crete, 1699 BC–1449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 1699 BC–1449 BC] New Palace (Neopalatial). "(= Middle Minoan III, Late Minoan IA and B)". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Minoan Crete at its height: the palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros were rebuilt on a grand scale after earthquake destruction, surrounded by towns, villas and harbours. Frescoes of bull-leapers, dolphins and processions, fine pottery, and Linear A archives belong to these centuries, as does Cretan influence across the Aegean. The eruption of Thera and later destructions ended it, with power passing to Mycenaean Greeks at Knossos.

hints.label: New Palace (Neopalatial)
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Troy II (Troy, 2399 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.title: Troy II (Troy, 2399 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 2399 BC–2099 BC] Troy II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The citadel grew richer, with a monumental gateway, a ramp still visible today and larger megara inside sloping stone-and-mudbrick walls. Potters adopted the fast wheel, and gold, silver and lapis jewellery was buried here — the hoard Schliemann seized and named "Priam's Treasure", though it is a thousand years older than any Homeric war. The settlement ended in a great fire, which Schliemann mistook for the sack of Homer's Troy.

hints.label: Troy II
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Severans (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235)
nodes.title: Severans (Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 193–AD 235] Severans. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Septimius Severus won power in civil war and openly based his rule on the army, raising soldiers' pay and telling his sons to enrich the troops and ignore everyone else. His son Caracalla extended Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire in 212, a sweeping change to what it meant to be Roman. The dynasty brought African and Syrian families to the centre of imperial politics, and its collapse in 235 opened fifty years of civil war and invasion.

hints.label: Severans
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1339 BC)
nodes.title: Late Helladic IIIA (Greece, 1399 BC–1339 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 1399 BC–1339 BC] Late Helladic IIIA. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The height of Mycenaean expansion, with palaces functioning, chamber-tomb cemeteries filling, and standardised stirrup jars and kylikes shipped to Egypt, the Levant and Italy. Hittite records of a kingdom called Ahhiyawa probably refer to these Greeks, dealing as equals with the great powers of the Near East.

Greece, Cyprus

hints.label: Late Helladic IIIA
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193) [p083p5rcq8f]
nodes.title: High Empire (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193) [p083p5rcq8f]
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 193] High Empire. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

From Nerva to Commodus, the empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan and then settled into consolidation behind fixed frontiers like Hadrian's Wall. Cities across the provinces filled with baths, aqueducts and forums, provincials rose to the throne, and law and citizenship spread widely. The Antonine plague and Commodus's murder in 192 exposed how much depended on a single life, ushering in civil war.

hints.label: High Empire
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Flavians (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96)
nodes.title: Flavians (Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 69–AD 96] Flavians. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Vespasian emerged from the civil wars of 69 as the first emperor from an ordinary Italian family, restoring stability and imperial finances. His reign saw the crushing of the Jewish revolt and the sack of Jerusalem, funding the Colosseum built on the site of Nero's private lake. Titus faced the eruption of Vesuvius, and Domitian's autocratic rule ended in assassination, opening the way to the adoptive emperors.

hints.label: Flavians
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1339 BC–1184 BC)
nodes.title: Late Helladic IIIB (Greece, 1339 BC–1184 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 1339 BC–1184 BC] Late Helladic IIIB. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The palaces reached their fullest form, with the Lion Gate and the huge walls of Tiryns raised and Linear B scribes tallying grain, textiles, chariots and rowers. Late in the phase came fire, abandonment and hurried defensive works, ending in the destruction of every mainland palace and the loss of writing.

hints.label: Late Helladic IIIB
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Second Intermediate (Egypt, 1794 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.title: Second Intermediate (Egypt, 1794 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 1794 BC–1549 BC] Second Intermediate. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Central authority fragmented as a rapid succession of kings at Memphis and then Thebes lost control of the Delta, where rulers of Levantine origin - the Hyksos - established a kingdom at Avaris. Nubian Kerma took the south, so Egypt was divided three ways. The invaders' legacy was technological as much as political: the horse and chariot, composite bow and new bronze-working entered Egypt in these years and equipped the armies that later built an empire.

hints.label: Second Intermediate
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Troy VI (Troy, 1799 BC–1299 BC)
nodes.title: Troy VI (Troy, 1799 BC–1299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 1799 BC–1299 BC] Troy VI. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Troy was rebuilt on a grand scale, with sloping ashlar walls, watchtowers and great gates enclosing terraced mansions — the most impressive city ever built on the mound. Mycenaean pottery, horse bones and links to the Hittite world place it in the wider Late Bronze Age network, and Hittite texts probably name it Wilusa. A geological survey found the outer town, defended by a rock-cut ditch, making the city far larger than Schliemann realised; it fell to what excavators read as an earthquake.

hints.label: Troy VI
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Etruscan rule (Lazio, 599 BC–508 BC)
nodes.title: Etruscan rule (Lazio, 599 BC–508 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 599 BC–508 BC] Etruscan rule. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Rome and much of Latium fell under the sway of Etruscan dynasts, a period credited with the city's first monumental building: the Cloaca Maxima, the Circus Maximus and the Capitoline temple. Latin towns absorbed Etruscan religious ritual, insignia of office and the alphabet that would become Latin script. The overthrow of the last king in 509 BC is the traditional birth date of the Roman Republic.

hints.label: Etruscan rule
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Julio-Claudians (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 69)
nodes.title: Julio-Claudians (Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 69)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 14–AD 69] Julio-Claudians. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Rome's first imperial dynasty, ruling from Augustus's death to Nero's fall. Their reigns settled the awkward question of what an emperor actually was: a first citizen in theory, an autocrat in practice, with the army and the treasury in his hands. Conquests in Britain and along the Rhine and Danube, monumental building in the capital, and a spectacular record of family murder have kept them the most notorious rulers in Roman history.

hints.label: Julio-Claudians
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Early Dynastic (Archaic) (Egypt, 3049 BC–2674 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic (Archaic) (Egypt, 3049 BC–2674 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 3049 BC–2674 BC] Early Dynastic (Archaic). Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first two dynasties, when the Nile valley was consolidated into a single kingdom governed from Memphis. Kings such as Narmer, Djer and Khasekhemwy left palace-facade tombs, ivory labels bearing the earliest Egyptian writing, and grand ceremonial palettes. The administrative and religious system built in these centuries made the pyramid age possible.

hints.label: Early Dynastic (Archaic)
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Cypriot III (Cyprus, 1224 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Late Cypriot III (Cyprus, 1224 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1224 BC–1049 BC] Late Cypriot III. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Destructions and abandonments hit the coastal towns, and the island is resettled and rebuilt in a noticeably Aegean idiom: locally made Mycenaean-style pottery, megaron-plan buildings, new sanctuaries at Kition and Enkomi. Greek-speaking newcomers appear to have arrived and stayed, laying the basis for the later Greek city-kingdoms, while Cypriot smiths became early masters of iron.

hints.label: Late Cypriot III
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Third Intermediate (Egypt, 1069 BC–714 BC)
nodes.title: Third Intermediate (Egypt, 1069 BC–714 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 1069 BC–714 BC] Third Intermediate. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the New Kingdom collapsed, Egypt split between kings ruling from the Delta and the high priests of Amun controlling Thebes. Libyan dynasties from settled military families took the throne, royal burials moved into temple precincts at Tanis, and the country fractured further into competing local rulers. Egypt's weakness invited outside powers, and the era ends with Kushite kings from Nubia asserting control over the south.

hints.label: Third Intermediate
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC) [p083p5r7nws]
nodes.title: Early Dynastic (Iraq, 2899 BC–2333 BC) [p083p5r7nws]
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2899 BC–2333 BC] Early Dynastic. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egypt was unified under a single king and the machinery of the pharaonic state was invented: writing in hieroglyphs, a royal titulary, taxation and a capital at Memphis. The rulers of the first two dynasties were buried at Abydos and Saqqara in vast mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers. Everything characteristic of later Egypt, from the royal ideology to the art canon, is already visible here in first form.

hints.label: Early Dynastic
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1184 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Late Helladic IIIC (Greece, 1184 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 1184 BC–1049 BC] Late Helladic IIIC. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Life after the palaces: no kings, no scribes, no frescoes, but surviving communities at Tiryns, Lefkandi, Perati and in the islands, some prospering briefly. Painters produced lively pictorial vases of ships and warriors, and refugees and traders kept Aegean contacts alive. A final decline led into the Protogeometric period and the Iron Age.

hints.label: Late Helladic IIIC
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 BC) [p083p5r9sqt]
nodes.title: Late Helladic II (Greece, 1499 BC–1399 BC) [p083p5r9sqt]
nodes.description:
[Greece, 1499 BC–1399 BC] Late Helladic II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Chieftains stopped digging shaft graves and began building tholoi, great stone beehive chambers approached by long passages, a display of labour and permanence. Mycenaean goods spread through the Aegean and mainlanders took control of Knossos, where Linear B was adapted to write Greek.

hints.label: Late Helladic II
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1759 BC)
nodes.title: Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1759 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1759 BC] Isin-Larsa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Named for the two Mesopotamian cities that fought over the legacy of the fallen Ur III empire, this horizon in the east coincides with the rise of the Sukkalmah rulers of Elam, who traded, intermarried and intrigued with the kings of southern Iraq. Cuneiform contracts, cylinder seals and standardised pottery show how closely the Iranian lowlands were tied into Babylonian economic life. It ends with Hammurabi's conquests reshaping the region.

hints.label: Isin-Larsa
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Archaic (Greece, 599 BC–478 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Greece, 599 BC–478 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 599 BC–478 BC] Archaic. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates notes "to the end of the Persian Wars". Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

hints.label: Archaic
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Kassite (Iraq, 1529 BC–1149 BC)
nodes.title: Kassite (Iraq, 1529 BC–1149 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1529 BC–1149 BC] Kassite. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

After the Hittite raid that toppled Hammurabi's dynasty, Kassite kings—outsiders of uncertain origin—ruled Babylonia for close to four centuries, the longest single dynasty in Mesopotamian history. They stabilised the south, corresponded as equals with Egypt's pharaohs in the Amarna letters, built the new capital of Dur-Kurigalzu, and left the carved kudurru stones that recorded royal land grants.

hints.label: Kassite
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire (Iraq, 611 BC–538 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Babylonian Empire (Iraq, 611 BC–538 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, the Levant, 611 BC–538 BC] Neo-Babylonian Empire. Spatial coverage: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

For roughly seventy years Babylon replaced Nineveh as the centre of the Near East, ruling Mesopotamia and the Levant and rebuilding its capital on a monumental scale with glazed-brick gates, ziggurat and walls that Greek visitors later listed among the world's wonders. Temple archives from Sippar, Uruk and Babylon document a busy economy of land, silver and dependent labour. Cyrus the Great entered the city in 539 BC and the empire passed intact into Persian hands.

nodes.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire (Iraq, 999 BC–611 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Assyrian Empire (Iraq, 999 BC–611 BC)
nodes.description:
[northern Mesopotamia or Assyria (= today's north Iraq and north-east Syria), 999 BC–611 BC] Neo-Assyrian Empire. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Assyria rebuilt itself into the largest empire the Near East had yet seen, ruling from Iran to Egypt through a machine of provinces, governors, standing armies and mass deportations of conquered populations. Its kings built colossal palaces at Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh, lined with carved stone reliefs of war, hunt and ritual, and assembled the great library of Ashurbanipal. When the empire collapsed under Median and Babylonian attack its administrative and military template passed to its successors.

hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC)
nodes.title: High Classical (Greece, 449 BC–399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 449 BC–399 BC] High Classical. Gates concentrates on Athens, so Greece is most appropriate coverage. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The decades after the Persian wars when Athens, funded by its maritime empire, rebuilt the Acropolis and put up the Parthenon under Pheidias's direction. Sophocles and Euripides were writing for the theatre, Socrates was arguing in the agora, and sculptors worked out an idealised human figure that European art would copy for two thousand years. The same era brought the Peloponnesian War, plague, and the collapse of Athenian power in 404.

hints.label: High Classical
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Troy VIIa (Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC)
nodes.title: Troy VIIa (Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC)
nodes.description:
[Troy, 1299 BC–1259 BC] Troy VIIa. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The earthquake-damaged city was patched up and packed with small houses, their floors sunk with huge storage jars as though a population had crowded inside the walls expecting trouble. It ended in fire, with unburied bodies and sling stones in the ruins. This is the layer most archaeologists nominate as the historical basis for Homer's Trojan War.

hints.label: Troy VIIa
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Ur III (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Ur III (Iraq, 2099 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2099 BC–1999 BC] Ur III. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The Third Dynasty of Ur built a tightly administered state that reached across the Iranian lowlands, holding Susa and planting garrisons and governors in the Zagros foothills. Its scribes produced tens of thousands of accounting tablets recording livestock, labour and grain in obsessive detail, the densest bureaucratic archive of the ancient world. The empire fell when Elamite forces sacked Ur, an event lamented in Sumerian poetry for centuries afterwards.

hints.label: Ur III
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC)
nodes.title: Late Cypriot I (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1474 BC] Late Cypriot I. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Cyprus enters the Late Bronze Age as coastal towns like Enkomi grow rich on copper, smelted inland and shipped abroad in oxhide ingots. Distinctive Base Ring and White Slip pottery begins turning up across Egypt and the Levant, evidence of an island trading network reaching far beyond its shores. Fortified sites and warrior burials suggest the wealth also brought competition and insecurity.

hints.label: Late Cypriot I
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.title: Late Minoan II (Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 1449 BC–1399 BC] Late Minoan II. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Knossos alone functioned as a palace, and its rulers were Greek-speaking Mycenaeans who kept inventories on clay tablets in Linear B — the earliest readable Greek. Burials changed too, with 'warrior graves' containing swords, helmets and boar's-tusk gear appearing around the city. Pottery turned formal and imposing in the Palace Style, adapting old Minoan motifs to a stiffer, more heraldic taste.

hints.label: Late Minoan II
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Ubaid (Iraq, 4999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.title: Ubaid (Iraq, 4999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 4999 BC–3499 BC] Ubaid. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The first widespread village culture of southern Mesopotamia, marked by pale greenish painted pottery, mudbrick houses of tripartite plan and small temples rebuilt again and again on the same spot, most famously at Eridu. Irrigation let farmers work the dry alluvium, herds and fishing filled out the diet, and communities grew large enough to support differences in status visible in burials and buildings. Ubaid pottery and styles spread north into Syria and Anatolia and down the Gulf, setting the stage for the first cities of the Uruk period.

hints.label: Ubaid
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: First Intermediate (Egypt, 2189 BC–2059 BC)
nodes.title: First Intermediate (Egypt, 2189 BC–2059 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2189 BC–2059 BC] First Intermediate. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Central authority at Memphis broke down after the long reign of Pepi II, and provincial governors ruled their nomes as effectively independent lords, with rival royal lines at Herakleopolis and Thebes. Tomb art becomes rougher and more regional, but funerary texts and coffins once reserved for kings now appear for ordinary officials. Theban victory under Mentuhotep II ended the split and began the Middle Kingdom.

hints.label: First Intermediate
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC)
nodes.title: Old Kingdom (Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2674 BC–2189 BC] Old Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The age of the great pyramids, when Egyptian kings commanded the labour, quarries and administration needed to build at Giza and Saqqara. A centralised bureaucracy of viziers, nomarchs and scribes ran the country from Memphis, and royal workshops perfected the conventions of Egyptian art that lasted for millennia. Long reigns, low Nile floods and the growing independence of provincial governors eventually broke the system apart.

hints.label: Old Kingdom
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (= Late Cypriot) (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (= Late Cypriot) (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC] Late Bronze Age (= Late Cypriot). Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Cyprus turned its copper into international power, exporting oxhide ingots across the eastern Mediterranean and appearing in Egyptian and Hittite records as the kingdom of Alashiya. Coastal towns like Enkomi and Kition grew into planned cities with ashlar sanctuaries, harbours and workshops, while the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script came into use. Destructions and the arrival of Aegean settlers around 1200 BC reshaped the island's language and culture.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age (= Late Cypriot)
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p083p5rnq5h]
nodes.title: New Kingdom (Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC) [p083p5rnq5h]
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 1549 BC–1069 BC] New Kingdom. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Egypt at its most powerful and outward-looking, ruling an empire from Nubia to Syria and enriched by tribute, gold and trade. This is the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten's religious revolution, Tutankhamun and the Ramesside pharaohs, of rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the vast temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. Its collapse amid invasion and economic strain ended pharaonic Egypt's dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

hints.label: New Kingdom
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2124 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Sumerian (Iraq, 2124 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2124 BC–1999 BC] Neo-Sumerian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The Third Dynasty of Ur reunited southern Mesopotamia after the Akkadian collapse and ran it through an extraordinarily detailed bureaucracy that has left tens of thousands of accounting tablets. Ur-Nammu and Shulgi built the great stepped ziggurats, issued one of the earliest law collections and promoted Sumerian as a language of high culture even as Akkadian took over daily speech. The state fell to famine, Amorite pressure and an Elamite attack, but its scribal schools shaped Mesopotamian literature for a thousand years.

hints.label: Neo-Sumerian
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1529 BC)
nodes.title: Old Babylonian (Iraq, 1999 BC–1529 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1529 BC] Old Babylonian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

The horizon dominated by Hammurabi's Babylon in Mesopotamia, which reshaped politics and material culture across the wider region. In Iran the sukkalmah rulers of Elam were deeply entangled with these Mesopotamian kingdoms through diplomacy, warfare and trade, and shared much of their writing, sealing and administrative practice.

hints.label: Old Babylonian
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Orientalizing (Early Archaic) (Greece, 724 BC–599 BC)
nodes.title: Orientalizing (Early Archaic) (Greece, 724 BC–599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 724 BC–599 BC] Orientalizing (Early Archaic). Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates discusses Greek cities that are now in the territory of Turkey, although he does not refer to Anatolia specifically. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

Eastern motifs and craft techniques transformed Greek art as trade with the Levant intensified, replacing the tidy geometry of earlier pottery with animal friezes, floral scrolls, and monsters. Corinthian workshops mass-produced small scented-oil vessels for export, and metalworkers took up hammered bronze and granulation. The alphabet arrived by the same routes, making written Greek possible.

hints.label: Orientalizing (Early Archaic)
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Protogeometric (Greece, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Protogeometric (Greece, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 999 BC–899 BC] Protogeometric. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Gates discusses Greek cities that are now in the territory of Turkey, although he does not refer to Anatolia specifically. Period definition from Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome — Gates, Charles, 1950-, 2003.

In the aftermath of the Mycenaean collapse, potters in Athens imposed a new discipline on their work: compass-drawn concentric circles and semicircles, crisp horizontal bands, and dark glaze over the vessel's shoulders. It is the first sign of confidence returning after the palaces fell, and it coincides with the spread of iron tools and weapons. The style travelled with Aegean settlers to the coast of Asia Minor and set the pattern for Geometric art that followed.

hints.label: Protogeometric
hints.source: Ancient cities : the archaeology of urban life in the Ancient Near East and Egypt, Greece and Rome

nodes.name: Classical (Cypro-Classical) I (Cyprus, 474 BC–399 BC)
nodes.title: Classical (Cypro-Classical) I (Cyprus, 474 BC–399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 474 BC–399 BC] Classical (Cypro-Classical) I. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Cyprus remained a patchwork of city-kingdoms under Persian overlordship, torn between loyalty to the Great King and the pull of the Greek world. Evagoras of Salamis pushed Hellenizing culture and the Greek alphabet, minted fine coinage and led a long revolt against Persia before being forced back into submission. Sculpture and architecture on the island blend Greek, Levantine and Egyptian models.

nodes.name: Iron Age (Cyprus, 1049 BC–AD 250)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Cyprus, 1049 BC–AD 250)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–AD 250] Iron Age. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Cyprus, 2499 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Cyprus, 2499 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 2499 BC–1049 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) II (Cyprus, 1799 BC–1724 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) II (Cyprus, 1799 BC–1724 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1799 BC–1724 BC] Middle Bronze Age (Middle Cypriot) II. Period definition from Cypriot antiquities text panels — Andrew Jamieson, 2007.

Copper production intensified and Cypriot goods began appearing more regularly in Levantine and Egyptian contexts, drawing the island into eastern Mediterranean trade. New pottery styles, notably White Painted wares, spread across regional workshops. Settlement was still village-scale, but the wealth differences visible in tomb goods hint at emerging elites.

properties.title: juglet — 1800BC-1650BC
properties.notes:
Pottery juglet/feeder bottle in White Painted Stringhole ware; handmade; depressed globular body on a rounded bottom, tall narrow neck and beaked spout; single handle from shoulder to just above the base of the handle; large oval 'mouth' set into the bottom of the spout just above the handle; four pairs of string-holes, placed one above the other, at the eside of the bodies, with two more pairs at the base of the spout flanking the handle. Made of fine buff clay, fired to a buff-cream surface, with black painted decoration: vertical lines framing hatched lozenges on the body, horizontal stripes on the spout.; | Type: juglet | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 17.78 centimetres; 17.80 centimetres; | Culture: Middle Cypriot

Cyprus

properties.title: bottle — 1850 BC -1650 BC
properties.notes:
White Painted ware bottle/flask with applied terracotta figurine; hand-made; oval body on a low conical base; spout on the side of the vessel, with a ring handle on the front; on the shoulder is a human figure with right hand at the chin. Made of cream colouted clay decorated with blacl paint: vertical wavy lines framed by straight one on the front and back, with lattices in between; rings on the neck and foot; horizontal lines on the figurine.; | Type: bottle | Medium: clay | Dimensions: 15.24 centimetres; | Culture: Middle Cypriot

properties.title: dish — 1800 BC-1650 BC

properties.notes:
Pottery flask in White Painted IV ware; hand-made; bird-shaped body (with tail feathers) with an arching handle on top of the body; small cutaway spout, concave sides; made of orange-buff clay decorated with matt orange-brown paint: parallel diagonal lines on the body, horizontal parallel lines on the neck and bands around the handle.; | Type: flask | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 10.16 centimetres; 10.16 centimetres; | Culture: Middle Cypriot

Cyprus

properties.title: jug — 1950 BC-1750 BC
properties.notes:
Miniature bottle made in Black Polished ware; hand-made; tapering body; pierced handle; beaked mouth; incised panelled decoration filled with lime or gypsum.; | Type: jug | Medium: pottery; gypsum (?) | Dimensions: 13.00 centimetres; | Culture: Middle Cypriot

properties.title: kyathos — 1800BC-1650BC
properties.notes:
Pottery bowl or dipper (kyathos) in White Painted ware; hand-made; conical body with a flattened base; high vertical wish-bone handle ending in a schematically modelled human head wearing a cap; very thin, fine buff clay, similar coloured slip, decorated in dark red-black paint: body has a chequer-board of plain and hatched lozenges and latticed triangles, framed by indented vertical panels of arrow-heads; double zig-zags on the handle; zig-zags and vertical lines on the interior.; | Type: kyathos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 15.24 centimetres; | Culture: Middle Cypriot
