nodes.title: Nieuwe tijd (Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 2050)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1500–AD 2050] Nieuwe tijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The Dutch archaeological catch-all for the modern era, running from the Reformation and the revolt against Spain through the Republic, the Kingdom, industrialisation and the present. Material culture becomes mass-produced and datable to the decade: tin-glazed earthenware, clay pipes, brick housing, then factory ceramics and machine-made glass. Excavations of this period often deal with urban cesspits, harbour fills, polders and shipwrecks, where documents and dug evidence can be checked against each other.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd vroeg (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 70)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd vroeg (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 70)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 70] Romeinse tijd vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Roman forces campaigned across the Rhine and built supply bases and camps in the delta, treating the region first as a springboard for conquering Germania and then, after that project failed, as the frontier itself. Local tribes were reorganised into Roman-recognised groups, above all the Batavians, who paid tribute in soldiers rather than grain. Native farmsteads changed slowly, but imported pottery, coins and army demand for food began reshaping the rural economy.

nodes.name: IJzertijd laat (Netherlands, 249 BC–11 BC)
nodes.title: IJzertijd laat (Netherlands, 249 BC–11 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 249 BC–11 BC] IJzertijd laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Contact with the Celtic world to the south intensified: imported goods, the first coinage, and larger, more organised settlements. Tribal names enter history through Roman writers, among them the Batavi, Frisii and Eburones. Caesar's campaigns and the Augustan advance to the Rhine ended local independence in the south and made the river a frontier.

nodes.name: Neolithicum laat B (Netherlands, 2449 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum laat B (Netherlands, 2449 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 2449 BC–1999 BC] Neolithicum laat B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Bell Beaker communities dominate, burying their dead under barrows with finely decorated beakers, archers' wristguards, flint daggers and the occasional copper or gold ornament. Later Veluwe and Barbed Wire beaker styles carry the tradition through to the start of the Bronze Age, and metalworking becomes a regular, if still rare, part of life.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen laat B (Netherlands, AD 1250–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen laat B (Netherlands, AD 1250–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1250–AD 1500] Middeleeuwen laat B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Towns came into their own, with Dordrecht, Utrecht, Deventer and Kampen trading grain, cloth and beer across the Hanseatic and North Sea networks. Sinking reclaimed peat and storm surges reshaped the coast, drowning villages and enlarging the Zuiderzee, while communities organised water boards to fight back. Political fragmentation gave way to Burgundian control, setting up the later Netherlands as a single state.

nodes.name: Nieuwe tijd C (Netherlands, AD 1850–AD 2050)
nodes.title: Nieuwe tijd C (Netherlands, AD 1850–AD 2050)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1850–AD 2050] Nieuwe tijd C. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Railways, steam pumping, the great reclamation schemes and explosive urban growth transformed the Dutch landscape, followed by two world wars and post-war reconstruction. Archaeology here includes factory sites, defence lines, bunkers, crash sites and the drained Zuiderzee polders, where the seabed gave up hundreds of wrecks. It is the period where excavation shades into living memory and industrial heritage.

nodes.name: Neolithicum laat (Netherlands, 2849 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum laat (Netherlands, 2849 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 2849 BC–1999 BC] Neolithicum laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The dead were now buried singly under round barrows with a beaker, a battle axe or a dagger, first in the Corded Ware or Single Grave tradition and then in the Bell Beaker style. Copper and gold objects appear, along with flint daggers imitating metal ones, and wheeled transport and wool-bearing sheep reshaped the rural economy. This is the period in which the barrow landscapes of the sandy soils took their lasting form.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd laat A (Netherlands, AD 270–AD 350)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd laat A (Netherlands, AD 270–AD 350)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 270–AD 350] Romeinse tijd laat A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

After the crisis of the 250s–260s the Rhine frontier was rebuilt on a smaller scale, with fewer, stronger fortifications and a heavier reliance on soldiers recruited from beyond the river. Large parts of the countryside emptied out, and villa estates in the south fell out of use. Coin hoards and burnt farmsteads from these decades mark an unsettled landscape of raids and reorganisation.

nodes.name: Neolithicum vroeg (Netherlands, 5299 BC–4199 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum vroeg (Netherlands, 5299 BC–4199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 5299 BC–4199 BC] Neolithicum vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming entered the Low Countries, first as an intrusive settlement of loess-soil villages in the far south and then as a slow blurring of frontiers with the hunter-fisher communities of the wet north. Longhouses, cereal fields and cattle appear alongside people who still lived largely from the marshes and rivers. It is one of Europe's clearest examples of an agricultural frontier that stalled for centuries before advancing.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen vroeg C (Netherlands, AD 725–AD 900)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen vroeg C (Netherlands, AD 725–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 725–AD 900] Middeleeuwen vroeg C. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The Frankish takeover of Frisia and the Carolingian empire's expansion brought churches, tithes and royal estates to the region. Dorestad reached its peak as an emporium, its wooden quays stretching along the Rhine and its workshops handling Rhineland pottery, glass and coin. From the 830s Viking fleets raided repeatedly, and the trading town declined.

nodes.name: Mesolithicum (Netherlands, 8799 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolithicum (Netherlands, 8799 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 8799 BC–4899 BC] Mesolithicum. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Postglacial forests of birch, pine and oak filled the sandy soils and river valleys, and small mobile bands hunted, fished and gathered hazelnuts along the streams and lakeshores. Their toolkit shrank to microliths hafted into arrows and knives; dugout canoes and paddles from Dutch bogs show how much travel went by water. Meanwhile the North Sea rose steadily, drowning the vast hunting grounds of Doggerland and reshaping the coast into something recognisable.

nodes.name: Bronstijd vroeg (Netherlands, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.title: Bronstijd vroeg (Netherlands, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Bronstijd vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Metal arrived only in a trickle, and much daily equipment was still flint and stone; the crude "barbed wire" decorated beakers of this phase carry on Bell Beaker potting habits. Communities were small and mobile, burying a few individuals under earthen mounds that reused and extended older Neolithic barrow groups. The real transformation came later, when permanent longhouse farms took hold.

nodes.name: Bronstijd midden (Netherlands, 1799 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Bronstijd midden (Netherlands, 1799 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 1799 BC–1099 BC] Bronstijd midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farmsteads with long byre houses sheltering people and cattle under one roof became the standard settlement form, surrounded by fields and cattle enclosures. Communities of the Hilversum tradition in the south and the Elp group in the north raised round barrows, often in rows along tracks, before cremation and urnfields took over. All bronze had to be imported, arriving through exchange networks reaching to Britain, central Germany and beyond.

nodes.name: Neolithicum vroeg B (Netherlands, 4899 BC–4199 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum vroeg B (Netherlands, 4899 BC–4199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 4899 BC–4199 BC] Neolithicum vroeg B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

After the Bandkeramik villages were abandoned, the loess belt was occupied by successor groups while, in the wetlands to the north, Swifterbant communities began making pottery and keeping a few animals without giving up hunting and fishing. Excavated riverbank and dune sites preserve fishtraps, canoes and food remains in waterlogged detail. The result is an unusually clear record of foragers adopting farming on their own terms.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen laat (Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen laat (Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1500] Middeleeuwen laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The centuries of systematic reclamation, when peat bogs were drained on a huge scale, dikes closed off the coast, and windmills and water boards were invented to keep the new land dry. The drained peat shrank and sank, causing floods that formed the Zuiderzee and forced ever more engineering. Trading towns multiplied and grew rich, and by the close of the period the counties and duchies had been gathered under Burgundian rule.

nodes.name: Neolithicum midden B (Netherlands, 3399 BC–2849 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum midden B (Netherlands, 3399 BC–2849 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 3399 BC–2849 BC] Neolithicum midden B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The centuries when farming communities north of the great rivers built the hunebedden — the boulder-slab megalithic tombs of Drenthe — as part of the Funnel Beaker (TRB) world. To the west, in the delta wetlands, Vlaardingen and related groups mixed cereal growing and stock keeping with fishing and fowling, showing that the Dutch "Neolithic" arrived piecemeal rather than all at once. Pottery, polished flint axes and the first substantial burial monuments make this the period when the landscape began to be permanently marked.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen vroeg A (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 525)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen vroeg A (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 525)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 450–AD 525] Middeleeuwen vroeg A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The generations immediately after Roman authority vanished, when towns, villas and roads in the river area fell out of use and the population thinned dramatically. Terp mounds in the north stayed occupied, while newcomers from across the Rhine filtered into the emptied landscape. Coins and pottery become scarce, making this one of the least visible periods in Dutch archaeology.

nodes.name: Nieuwe tijd B (Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Nieuwe tijd B (Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1650–AD 1850] Nieuwe tijd B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The long stretch from the height of the Republic through its decline, French annexation, and the founding of the Kingdom. Land reclamation, peat cutting and windmill drainage reshaped the countryside, while towns filled with Delftware, refined white clay pipes and imported tea and tobacco wares. Datable pipe stems and pottery marks from this phase let archaeologists pin deposits to within a few decades.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd laat B (Netherlands, AD 350–AD 450)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd laat B (Netherlands, AD 350–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 350–AD 450] Romeinse tijd laat B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Roman authority faded from the Rhine delta in stages, with garrisons withdrawn or absorbed into Frankish forces and imperial coin drying up. Newcomers from the north and east settled the emptied river landscape, producing handmade pottery and burying their dead with weapons and brooches in a style already recognisably early medieval. What survived of Roman infrastructure – roads, ruined forts, church-linked memories at Maastricht – became raw material for the Frankish kingdoms.

nodes.name: IJzertijd (Netherlands, 799 BC–11 BC)
nodes.title: IJzertijd (Netherlands, 799 BC–11 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 799 BC–11 BC] IJzertijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Iron, smelted locally from bog ore, replaced imported bronze and put decent tools in far more hands. People lived on small family farms with byre-houses, laid out rectangular Celtic field systems, and in the northern salt marshes began raising dwelling mounds above the tides. The period closes with Roman armies on the Rhine and the Low Countries divided between an occupied south and a free north.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd midden (Netherlands, AD 70–AD 270)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd midden (Netherlands, AD 70–AD 270)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 70–AD 270] Romeinse tijd midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

With the Batavian revolt crushed, the Rhine frontier settled into two centuries of relative stability: forts rebuilt in stone, a military road along the river, and the towns of Ulpia Noviomagus and Forum Hadriani granted urban status. Rural families adopted Roman goods and building styles while keeping much of their older farming life, and villa estates spread across the loess soils of the south. The period ends with raids, frontier disruption and the abandonment of much of the limes.

nodes.name: Neolithicum vroeg A (Netherlands, 5299 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum vroeg A (Netherlands, 5299 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 5299 BC–4899 BC] Neolithicum vroeg A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Bandkeramik farmers settled the fertile loess of southern Limburg, building timber longhouses in small hamlets and bringing wheat, barley, cattle and pottery from central Europe. Their villages sat at the northwestern edge of the whole continental farming expansion, with foragers still occupying the sandy and marshy lands just beyond. Sites such as Elsloo and Sittard give a remarkably detailed picture of house plans, cemeteries and imported stone.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd vroeg A (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 25)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd vroeg A (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 25)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 25] Romeinse tijd vroeg A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Drusus and his successors used the Rhine delta as a launching point for campaigns into Germania, digging canals and planting military bases such as those at Nijmegen and Velsen. The loss of Varus's legions in AD 9 ended ambitions of a province beyond the river and forced Rome to think of the Rhine as a limit. For local communities the main change was the sudden arrival of an army that had to be fed, housed and supplied.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd laat (Netherlands, AD 270–AD 450)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd laat (Netherlands, AD 270–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 270–AD 450] Romeinse tijd laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Frontier defence contracted sharply: many limes forts were abandoned or replaced by heavily walled strongpoints, rural settlement thinned dramatically, and coin supply became erratic. Franks and other groups from beyond the Rhine settled inside the old province, sometimes as raiders, sometimes as Roman-sponsored soldiers and farmers. By the end of the period Roman government had effectively evaporated, leaving Frankish-led communities as the successors.

nodes.name: Bronstijd laat (Netherlands, 1099 BC–799 BC)
nodes.title: Bronstijd laat (Netherlands, 1099 BC–799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 1099 BC–799 BC] Bronstijd laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Burial practice shifted decisively to cremation in urns set within large, densely used urnfields, a custom shared across much of northwest Europe. Settlements of byre houses moved every generation or two across the sandy landscape, and bronze objects circulated in growing numbers alongside deliberate deposits in wet places. The first iron objects appear towards the end of the period.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 525–AD 725)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 525–AD 725)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 525–AD 725] Middeleeuwen vroeg B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Merovingian times, known largely from row-grave cemeteries where the dead were buried with swords, brooches and glass vessels. Frisian traders worked the coast and rivers while Frankish kings pushed north, and settlements of timber longhouses spread again across the sandy soils. Dorestad and Domburg began their careers as trading places, and the first missionaries arrived.

nodes.name: IJzertijd vroeg (Netherlands, 799 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: IJzertijd vroeg (Netherlands, 799 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 799 BC–499 BC] IJzertijd vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Iron working arrived while urnfield burial customs were still in use, and a handful of exceptionally rich graves — the Chieftain's Grave at Oss with its bent sword in a bronze situla is the famous one — show contacts with the Hallstatt elites of central Europe. Most people, though, lived in modest farmsteads and fields on the sandy uplands. Bog iron made metal locally available for the first time, without the long-distance networks bronze had required.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 25–AD 70)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd vroeg B (Netherlands, AD 25–AD 70)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 25–AD 70] Romeinse tijd vroeg B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The Rhine hardened into a defended border, with a line of forts, Corbulo's canal linking the rivers, and Claudius abandoning further conquest to the north. Batavian and Cananefate auxiliaries became a mainstay of the imperial army, and the emperors' German bodyguard was recruited here. The period ends violently with the Batavian revolt of AD 69–70, when Julius Civilis exploited Rome's civil war to besiege and burn frontier forts.

nodes.name: Bronstijd midden B (Netherlands, 1499 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Bronstijd midden B (Netherlands, 1499 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 1499 BC–1099 BC] Bronstijd midden B. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farmsteads with byre-houses spread widely across the sandy soils, and in the north the Elp culture built settlements that shifted every generation or two across a landscape of small fields and barrow cemeteries. Burial practice changed decisively as cremation replaced inhumation, laying the groundwork for the great urnfields of the following centuries. Bronze circulated more freely now, with local smiths casting socketed axes, sickles and ornaments.

nodes.name: Neolithicum laat A (Netherlands, 2849 BC–2449 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum laat A (Netherlands, 2849 BC–2449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 2849 BC–2449 BC] Neolithicum laat A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Dominated by the Single Grave or Corded Ware culture, in which individuals were buried in a crouched position under a round barrow, men with a stone battle axe and a corded beaker. The custom spread rapidly across the sandy soils of the north and east, replacing the collective megalithic burials of the preceding centuries and reflecting new populations and ideas moving in from the east.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 450)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd (Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 11 BC–AD 450] Romeinse tijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Roman armies pushed to the Rhine and turned it into the empire's northern frontier, leaving the Netherlands split between provincial territory in the south and free Germanic lands in the north. Forts, roads, harbours and the towns of Nijmegen and Voorburg brought coined money, wheel-thrown pottery, wine and writing to farming communities that had lived in timber longhouses for centuries. Local groups such as the Batavians supplied auxiliary soldiers to Rome in extraordinary numbers, and one of them, the revolt of AD 69, nearly broke Roman control of the region. Waterlogged sites along the limes preserve leather, wooden writing tablets and whole river barges.

nodes.name: Bronstijd midden A (Netherlands, 1799 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Bronstijd midden A (Netherlands, 1799 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 1799 BC–1499 BC] Bronstijd midden A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming communities in the low countries settled into long timber houses that sheltered people and cattle under one roof, while their dead were buried under round barrows ringed by posts. Bronze itself remained scarce and had to be imported as ingots or finished axes from Britain, central Europe and the Alps, so metal objects were prized and often deposited in rivers and bogs. Pottery of the Hilversum tradition in the south shows links across the North Sea to southern England.

nodes.name: Romeinse tijd midden A (Netherlands, AD 70–AD 150)
nodes.title: Romeinse tijd midden A (Netherlands, AD 70–AD 150)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 70–AD 150] Romeinse tijd midden A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Rebuilding after the Batavian revolt fixed the shape of the frontier: a chain of auxiliary forts along the Rhine linked by a paved military road, with legionary and civilian centres at Nijmegen. Trade in Gaulish samian ware, wine and metalwork reached deep into the countryside, and local men served across the empire in Batavian and Cananefatian units. Hadrian's reign brought town charters and monumental building to the two main urban settlements.

nodes.name: Mesolithicum laat (Netherlands, 6449 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolithicum laat (Netherlands, 6449 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 6449 BC–4899 BC] Mesolithicum laat. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

In the final Mesolithic centuries the flint industry shifted to broad trapezoidal points and regular blades, and settlements clustered along wetland margins and stream valleys. Communities here were in contact with the first farmers of the loess belt to the south, exchanging goods and ideas long before adopting farming themselves. The Swifterbant sites show the result: fisher-hunters who gradually added pottery, cattle and small-scale cereal growing to an older way of life.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen vroeg (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1050)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen vroeg (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1050)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1050] Middeleeuwen vroeg. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

After the Roman frontier collapsed, much of the river country was abandoned before being resettled by Frisian, Frankish and Saxon groups living in timber farmsteads and burying their dead with weapons and jewellery. Frankish conquest and missionaries such as Willibrord and Boniface brought Christianity and Carolingian administration, and Dorestad grew into one of northwest Europe's greatest trading places. Viking raids and settlement disrupted the region before local counts and bishops began to consolidate power.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen laat A (Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1250)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen laat A (Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1250)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 1050–AD 1250] Middeleeuwen laat A. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Landlords and monasteries organised the draining of the great peat bogs, laying out the long ribbon-shaped farm plots still visible in the Dutch landscape. Local lords built mottes and then stone keeps, brick came into use for churches, and the first city rights were granted. Counts of Holland, dukes of Brabant and bishops of Utrecht emerged as the region's dominant powers.

nodes.name: Middeleeuwen (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Middeleeuwen (Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, AD 450–AD 1500] Middeleeuwen. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

The thousand years between Roman withdrawal and the Habsburg era, during which the Low Countries were settled by Frisians, Franks and Saxons, Christianised, and drawn into the Carolingian world. Rising sea levels and human drainage made water management the central fact of life, producing dikes, dams and polders. By the end, the region held some of Europe's densest concentrations of towns, living on cloth, shipping and trade.

nodes.name: Bronstijd (Netherlands, 1999 BC–799 BC)
nodes.title: Bronstijd (Netherlands, 1999 BC–799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 1999 BC–799 BC] Bronstijd. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Metal reached the low countries in quantity, mostly as imported bronze axes, swords and ornaments, since the region has neither copper nor tin. Farming communities lived in long timber byre houses on sandy soils, raising cattle and burying their dead first under round barrows and later in cremation urnfields. Bogs and rivers received deliberate deposits of weapons and ornaments, some of the most striking finds in Dutch archaeology.

nodes.name: Neolithicum midden (Netherlands, 4199 BC–2849 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum midden (Netherlands, 4199 BC–2849 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 4199 BC–2849 BC] Neolithicum midden. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

In the wetlands and river country, Swifterbant and Hazendonk communities combined fishing, fowling and hunting with small-scale cattle keeping and cereal growing, leaving exceptionally well preserved sites in the peat and clay. On the northern sandy soils the Funnel Beaker culture raised the hunebedden, chambered tombs of glacial boulders used for collective burial with quantities of decorated pottery. Together they mark the point at which farming finally took hold across the whole country.

nodes.name: Neolithicum (Netherlands, 5299 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithicum (Netherlands, 5299 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Netherlands, 5299 BC–1999 BC] Neolithicum. Period definition from Het Archeologisch Basisregister (ABR) — Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 1992.

Farming reached the Netherlands in two very different ways: Linear Pottery farmers settled the fertile loess of southern Limburg in longhouse villages, while in the wetlands to the north hunter-fisher communities of the Swifterbant tradition adopted cattle and cereals slowly, over centuries. Later came the Funnel Beaker builders of the hunebedden, the great boulder tombs of Drenthe, and finally Corded Ware and Bell Beaker groups burying individuals under round barrows. Waterlogged sites preserve wooden trackways, dugout canoes and even ploughed field surfaces.

nodes.name: Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC) (Syria, 1200 BC–700 BC)
nodes.title: Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC) (Syria, 1200 BC–700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Northern Levant, 1200 BC–700 BC] Neo-Hittite Northern Levant (1200-700 BC). Syro-Hittite Northern Levant. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

After the fall of the Bronze Age empires, a patchwork of Syro-Hittite and Aramaean city-states filled northern Syria, ruling from citadels at Carchemish, Aleppo, Tell Halaf and Zincirli. They carved monumental basalt reliefs and inscribed monuments in Luwian hieroglyphs and alphabetic Aramaic, an art that fed directly into Assyrian palace sculpture. Their independence ended with the Assyrian conquests of the eighth century.

[Mesopotamia, 1600 BC–1000 BC] Later 2nd Millennium BC Mesopotamia (1600-1000 BC). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Middle Assyrian/Middle Babylonian/Kassite Mesopotamia, LBA-Early Iron Age Mesopotamia, incl. Sea Peoples. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

After the fall of Hammurabi's dynasty, power in the region was shared between Kassite Babylon, the rising Middle Assyrian kingdom and the Middle Elamite state on the Iranian side. It was an age of literate diplomacy, with kings exchanging letters and gifts across the Near East, and of monumental building such as the great ziggurat at Chogha Zanbil. Elamite armies eventually sacked Babylon and carried off trophies including the stele of Hammurabi, before the whole system unravelled around 1100 BC.

nodes.name: Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-1258) (Afghanistan, AD 1037–AD 1258)
nodes.title: Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-1258) (Afghanistan, AD 1037–AD 1258)

[Middle East, AD 1037–AD 1258] Seljuq-Khwarezmian Middle East (AD 1037-1258). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Turkic dynasties ruled the Iranian world in these centuries: first the Seljuqs, then the Khwarazmshahs, who inherited much of their territory and pushed into Afghanistan against the Ghurids. Persian remained the language of administration and poetry, and the period produced great brick minarets, madrasas and lustre ceramics. It ended catastrophically with the Mongol invasions, which shattered the Khwarazmian state and destroyed cities across the region.

nodes.title: Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720-540 BC) (Egypt, 720 BC–540 BC)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, 720 BC–540 BC] Neo-Assyrian/Babylonian Middle East (720-540 BC). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Two successive Mesopotamian empires dominated the region: Assyria, which invaded Egypt in the 670s and sacked Thebes, and then Babylon, which inherited the western provinces after Nineveh fell. For Egypt this meant foreign armies in the Nile Delta, the end of Kushite rule and the rise of the Saite dynasty as a client-turned-rival power. The whole eastern Mediterranean was drawn into a single imperial arena, a pattern the Persians would simply take over.

[Middle East, AD 1800–AD 2000] Colonial-Modern Middle East (AD 1800-2000). Spatial coverage: Djibouti, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Yemen. Late Ottoman-Colonial-Mandate Modern Middle east. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

France took the Gulf of Tadjoura coast in the 1880s, and Djibouti city grew as the port terminus of the railway to Addis Ababa, making it Ethiopia's outlet to the sea. Colonial rule set Afar and Issa communities against one another in a competition for political weight that outlasted independence in 1977. The port's strategic position at the mouth of the Red Sea has kept foreign fleets and garrisons there ever since.

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC) (Turkey, 2000 BC–1750 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC) (Turkey, 2000 BC–1750 BC)
nodes.description:
[Anatolia, 2000 BC–1750 BC] Early Bronze Age Anatolia (2000-1750 BC). Karum Anatolia. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Merchants from Assur established trading colonies in central Anatolia, above all the karum at Kanesh (Kültepe), exchanging tin and textiles for Anatolian silver and gold. Their thousands of clay tablets in Old Assyrian cuneiform are the first written records from Anatolia, naming local kings, their households and even family quarrels and debts. Out of the small competing kingdoms they describe came the Hittite state that would dominate the region.

nodes.title: Middle Byzantine (AD 850-1200) (Albania, AD 850–AD 1200)

[Albania, AD 850–AD 1200] Middle Byzantine (AD 850-1200). Spatial coverage: Albania, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Iraq, Italy, Kenya, Lebanon. Middle Byzantine period in areas where such designations are appropriate. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Byzantine rule was reimposed over much of the region through new themes and fortified towns, competing with Bulgarian expansion under Samuel and, later, Norman raids from across the Adriatic. Churches with brick-and-stone masonry and fresco decoration went up in towns such as Berat and along the Via Egnatia. It was a frontier zone where Latin and Greek Christianity met and where control changed hands repeatedly.

nodes.name: Ilkhanate Middle East (AD 1258-1335) (Afghanistan, AD 1258–AD 1335)
nodes.title: Ilkhanate Middle East (AD 1258-1335) (Afghanistan, AD 1258–AD 1335)

[Middle East, AD 1258–AD 1335] Ilkhanate Middle East (AD 1258-1335). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Egypt, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon. Ilkhanid, Hulagu, Early Mongol. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The Mongol state founded by Hülegü after he sacked Baghdad and ended the Abbasid caliphate, ruling Iran, Iraq and much of the eastern Islamic world from the northwest. Its rulers converted to Islam under Ghazan in 1295 and sponsored a spectacular fusion of Persian and Chinese artistic traditions - illustrated manuscripts, tilework and observatories - while Rashid al-Din compiled one of the first world histories. The realm fragmented after Abu Sa'id died without an heir, leaving competing warlord dynasties behind.

nodes.name: Middle Kingdom Egypt (2010-1640 BCE/BC) (Sudan, 2010 BC–1640 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Kingdom Egypt (2010-1640 BCE/BC) (Sudan, 2010 BC–1640 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2010 BC–1640 BC] Middle Kingdom Egypt (2010-1640 BCE/BC). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The Middle Kingdom period in Egypt, following the chronology of the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (compiled by Thomas Schneider):. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Egyptian kings pushed the frontier deep into Nubia, ringing the Second Cataract with massive mudbrick fortresses at Buhen, Mirgissa, Semna and elsewhere to control gold, cattle and the river trade in ebony, ivory and incense. Garrisons of scribes and soldiers lived in these outposts and sent back written dispatches on papyrus reporting every Nubian who approached. Upstream, the rival kingdom of Kerma grew rich on the same traffic, and after Egypt's central authority collapsed it took the forts for itself.

nodes.name: Persian-Medieval Caucasus (AD 600-1500) (Georgia, AD 600–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Persian-Medieval Caucasus (AD 600-1500) (Georgia, AD 600–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Caucasus, AD 600–AD 1500] Persian-Medieval Caucasus (AD 600-1500). Spatial coverage: Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Persian-Arabic-Early Medieval-Middle Medieval-Turco-Mongol/Late Medieval Caucasus. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Georgia passed from Byzantine-Persian rivalry to Arab rule centred on the emirate of Tbilisi, then re-emerged under the Bagratid kings who unified the country around 1008. The reigns of David the Builder and Queen Tamar brought territorial expansion, cave monasteries, frescoed churches and a courtly literature that produced Rustaveli's epic. Mongol armies and later Timur's campaigns broke that ascendancy, leaving the kingdom splintering into rival principalities.

nodes.name: Pottery Neolithic Middle East (6000-4500 BC) (Iraq, 6000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.title: Pottery Neolithic Middle East (6000-4500 BC) (Iraq, 6000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, 6000 BC–4500 BC] Pottery Neolithic Middle East (6000-4500 BC). Spatial coverage: Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Palestine, Sudan, Syria, Turkey. ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Farming villages spread across northern Mesopotamia and out onto the plains, producing the successive painted pottery styles known as Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf. Samarran communities pushed south into land needing simple irrigation, the first step towards the canal agriculture that would sustain later cities, while Halaf potters made some of the finest painted ware of the ancient Near East and traded obsidian over long distances. Stamp seals, tholos buildings and communal storage show societies beginning to track property and status.

nodes.name: Crusader-Ottoman Levant (AD 1099-1750) (Turkey, AD 1099–AD 1750)
nodes.title: Crusader-Ottoman Levant (AD 1099-1750) (Turkey, AD 1099–AD 1750)
nodes.description:
[Levant, AD 1099–AD 1750] Crusader-Ottoman Levant (AD 1099-1750). Crusader-Seljuq-Ayyubid-Mamluk-Ottoman Levant. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

A long bracket covering the arrival of the crusaders, the Turkish and Mongol upheavals that followed, Mamluk rule, and finally the Ottoman order imposed after 1516. Across it the region shifted from a patchwork of contested principalities to a single imperial administration of provinces, pious foundations and caravan routes. Material culture from this span includes castles, khans, glazed wares and the mosques and bridges of Ottoman public building.

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age Southern Levant (1400-1200 BC) (Egypt, 1400 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age Southern Levant (1400-1200 BC) (Egypt, 1400 BC–1200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southern Levant, 1400 BC–1200 BC] Late Bronze Age Southern Levant (1400-1200 BC). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine. Southern Levant [[-1400,-1200]]. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Canaan functioned as an Egyptian province, its city-state rulers reporting to the pharaoh and hosting Egyptian officials and troops. Trade linked the coast to Cyprus, the Aegean and the Nile. When Egyptian power withdrew around 1200 BC the whole framework fell apart, opening the way for Philistine settlement and the emergence of new peoples in the hill country.

nodes.name: Old Kingdom Egypt (2670-2168 BCE/BC) (Egypt, 2670 BC–2168 BC)
nodes.title: Old Kingdom Egypt (2670-2168 BCE/BC) (Egypt, 2670 BC–2168 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2670 BC–2168 BC] Old Kingdom Egypt (2670-2168 BCE/BC). The Old Kingdom period in Egypt, following the chronology of the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (compiled by Thomas Schneider):. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Beginning with Djoser's step pyramid and reaching its peak at Giza, this was the era in which Egyptian kingship expressed itself in stone on an unmatched scale. Expeditions went south into Nubia for gold and granite and east to Sinai for copper and turquoise, funnelling resources through a growing bureaucracy at Memphis. The Pyramid Texts, carved inside late Old Kingdom tombs, are the world's oldest substantial body of religious writing.

nodes.name: Neolithic Middle East (9000-4500 BC) (Iraq, 9000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic Middle East (9000-4500 BC) (Iraq, 9000 BC–4500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, 9000 BC–4500 BC] Neolithic Middle East (9000-4500 BC). Spatial coverage: Iraq, Syria, Turkey. ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The world's first farming villages appear here, from Jarmo in the Zagros foothills to the painted-pottery cultures of Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf across northern Mesopotamia. Samarran farmers took the decisive step of irrigating land beyond the rain-fed zone, opening the southern floodplain to settlement. Halaf potters produced some of the finest painted ceramics of the ancient world, traded with obsidian and stamp seals across hundreds of miles.

nodes.name: Mongol Middle East (AD 1258-1501) (Afghanistan, AD 1258–AD 1501)
nodes.title: Mongol Middle East (AD 1258-1501) (Afghanistan, AD 1258–AD 1501)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, AD 1258–AD 1501] Mongol Middle East (AD 1258-1501). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine. ME, Central Asia. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Hülegü's sack of Baghdad ended the Abbasid caliphate and installed the Ilkhanate, whose rulers converted to Islam within two generations and patronised Persian painting, historiography and astronomy. The eastern lands passed through Timur's brutal campaigns and then the cultured Timurid courts of Herat and Samarkand, centres of manuscript art and architecture. The era closes with the rise of the Safavids, who imposed Shi'a Islam on Iran and set a new religious frontier.

nodes.name: Late Nubian (1600-350 BC) (Egypt, 1600 BC–350 BC)
nodes.title: Late Nubian (1600-350 BC) (Egypt, 1600 BC–350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, 1600 BC–350 BC] Late Nubian (1600-350 BC). NK-Kushite-Meroitic. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Egyptian armies pushed south and held Kush for centuries, planting temple towns at Napata and elsewhere; when Egyptian power faded, Nubian rulers turned the relationship around and conquered Egypt as its 25th Dynasty. Their kings built steep pyramids at el-Kurru and Nuri and presented themselves as restorers of ancient Egyptian tradition. Driven back south by Assyrian invasion, the Kushite state survived at Napata and then shifted its centre to Meroe, developing its own script and royal culture.

hints.label: Late Nubian (1600-350 BC)

nodes.title: Classical (Greco-Roman; 550 BC-330 BC) (Afghanistan, 550 BC–330 BC)
nodes.description:
[Afghanistan, 550 BC–330 BC] Classical (Greco-Roman; 550 BC-330 BC). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria. The Classical period in Greek and Roman history. For the purposes of Pleiades, this period is said to begin in the year 550 and end in the year 330 before the birth of Christ. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The regions of Bactria, Arachosia and Gandhara were governed as Achaemenid satrapies, paying tribute in gold, camels and soldiers and linked by imperial roads to Persepolis. Persian administration encouraged irrigation, fortified towns and the use of Aramaic as a chancery language. Alexander's invasion broke the empire and opened the country to Greek settlers whose kingdoms would rule the region for generations.

nodes.name: Chalcolithic Mesopotamia (6200-3750 BC) (Iran, 6200 BC–3750 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic Mesopotamia (6200-3750 BC) (Iran, 6200 BC–3750 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 6200 BC–3750 BC] Chalcolithic Mesopotamia (6200-3750 BC). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Copper Age Mesopotamia, Halaf-Ubaid-Early Uruk Mesopotamia. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The long build-up to urban life, running from the painted Halaf wares of the northern plains through the Ubaid period, when irrigation farming filled the southern floodplain and small shrines at Eridu were rebuilt ever larger. Ubaid pottery and ideas spread from the Gulf to Anatolia, and the temple-centred communities of these centuries became the cities of Uruk-period Sumer.

nodes.name: Bronze Age Britain (ca. 2500 - ca. 800 BC/BCE) (United Kingdom, 2500 BC–800 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age Britain (ca. 2500 - ca. 800 BC/BCE) (United Kingdom, 2500 BC–800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Britain, 2500 BC–800 BC] Bronze Age Britain (ca. 2500 - ca. 800 BC/BCE). A long time period associated with Bronze Age Britain. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Beaker pottery, copper metallurgy and, as ancient DNA now shows, a large influx of people from continental Europe transformed British society, and the great sarsen settings at Stonehenge belong to the start of this period. Communal monument-building gave way to individual burial under round barrows, and then to a landscape carved up by field boundaries and cattle enclosures. By the end, hoards of bronze were being buried in staggering quantities just as iron began to arrive.

nodes.name: Hellenistic-Parthian Middle East (330 BC - AD 226) (Syria, 330 BC–AD 226)
nodes.title: Hellenistic-Parthian Middle East (330 BC - AD 226) (Syria, 330 BC–AD 226)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, 330 BC–AD 226] Hellenistic-Parthian Middle East (330 BC - AD 226). Seleucid-Early Roman-Arsacid Middle East. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Syria passed from Seleucid kings to Roman governors, while beyond the Euphrates the Parthians built a rival empire that Rome never subdued. Caravan cities such as Palmyra and Dura-Europos grew rich on the traffic between the two worlds, producing a distinctive art that mixes Greek, Roman and Iranian elements. The period closes with the Sasanian overthrow of the Parthians, which brought a far more aggressive power to Rome's eastern frontier.

hints.source: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places

nodes.name: Ottoman Empire (AD 1513-1918) (Cyprus, AD 1513–AD 1918)
nodes.title: Ottoman Empire (AD 1513-1918) (Cyprus, AD 1513–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, AD 1513–AD 1918] Ottoman Empire (AD 1513-1918). Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Djibouti, Egypt, Greece, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine. ME, Balkan, Northern Africa. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The Ottoman conquest of Cyprus swept away Venetian rule after a brutal siege of Famagusta, and the island was resettled with Anatolian Turks, creating the two-community population that shaped its later history. The Orthodox archbishop was restored and made responsible to the sultan for the Greek population, becoming a political as well as religious leader, while Latin churches were converted to mosques. Britain took over the administration in 1878, though nominal Ottoman sovereignty lasted until the empire's collapse.

hints.label: Ottoman Empire (AD 1513-1918)

nodes.name: Archaic (Greco-Roman; 750-550 BCE/BC) (Albania, 750 BC–550 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Greco-Roman; 750-550 BCE/BC) (Albania, 750 BC–550 BC)
nodes.description:
[Albania, 750 BC–550 BC] Archaic (Greco-Roman; 750-550 BCE/BC). Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Armenia, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Egypt, France, Georgia. The Archaic period in Greek and Roman history. For the purposes of Pleiades, this period is seen to begin in the year 750 and end in the year 550 before the birth of Christ. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Greek colonists from Corinth and Corcyra planted trading cities on the Illyrian coast — Epidamnos and Apollonia — where ships could reach the interior along river routes. Local Illyrian communities supplied grain, silver, timber and slaves, and adopted Greek pottery, weapons and eventually coinage, while keeping their own tumulus burials and tribal structure. The contact zone created here would later become the western terminus of the Via Egnatia.

hints.label: Archaic (Greco-Roman; 750-550 BCE/BC)

nodes.description:
[Egypt, 2000 BC–1000 BC] 2nd Millennium BC Egypt (2000-1000 BC). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Sudan. Egypt. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Egypt swung twice between unity and fragmentation: the Middle Kingdom's strong central rule gave way to Hyksos rulers in the Delta, whose expulsion launched the New Kingdom and an empire reaching into Syria and Nubia. These are the centuries of Hatshepsut, Akhenaten's experiment at Amarna, Tutankhamun, and Ramesses II's wars and monuments. By the millennium's end the state had lost its empire and split again between Tanis and the priesthood of Amun at Thebes.

[Egypt, 304 BC–AD 640] Ptolemaic-Roman Egypt (304 BC - AD 640). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Palestine, Sudan. Egypt. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Nearly a thousand years in which Egypt was governed from outside: first by Greek kings in Alexandria, then as Rome's most valuable province, the granary that fed the capital. Temples to the old gods were still being built under Roman emperors, even as Christianity took hold and gave rise to desert monasticism and the Coptic Church. The era closes with the Arab conquest, after which Egypt's language, religion and centre of gravity shifted decisively.

nodes.title: Roman Early Empire/Parthian Middle East (30 BC - AD 226) (Afghanistan, 30 BC–AD 226)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, 30 BC–AD 226] Roman Early Empire/Parthian Middle East (30 BC - AD 226). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Egypt, Greece, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon. Early Roman/Parthian. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

While Rome and Parthia divided the west, this region lay at the heart of the Kushan realm, which grew out of nomadic groups who had taken Bactria from the Greeks. Kushan rulers controlled the routes linking India, Central Asia and China, minting gold coinage on a Roman weight standard and drawing Mediterranean glass and bronzes deep into Asia. Their patronage produced the Gandharan Buddhist art that dressed the Buddha in classical drapery, and helped carry Buddhism north along the Silk Road.

nodes.name: Sassanian Middle East (AD 262-700) (Afghanistan, AD 262–AD 700)
nodes.title: Sassanian Middle East (AD 262-700) (Afghanistan, AD 262–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Middle East, AD 262–AD 700] Sassanian Middle East (AD 262-700). Sassanid. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Persian power reached into the lands south of the Oxus when Sasanian kings took over the western Kushan realm, installing viceroys who struck their own coinage blending Iranian and Indian imagery. Control was never continuous: Kidarite and then Hephthalite rulers seized the region, and the Sasanians only recovered ground in alliance with the Turks in the 560s. Buddhism flourished at Balkh and Bamiyan throughout, until the Arab conquests transformed the region in the seventh and eighth centuries.

nodes.title: Neolithic Period (British Isles; 4,000-2,500 BC) (United Kingdom, 4000 BC–2500 BC)

[British Isles, 4000 BC–2500 BC] Neolithic Period (British Isles; 4,000-2,500 BC). Spatial coverage: Ireland, United Kingdom. The Neolithic period in the British Isles, after Wikipedia, Neolithic British Isles,. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Farming, pottery and domesticated animals arrived from the Continent, and within a few centuries communities were clearing woodland and raising monuments in timber and stone. Long barrows and chambered tombs held the jumbled bones of the collective dead; causewayed enclosures hosted seasonal gatherings and feasts; flint was mined at depth at Grimes Graves. By the period's end henges and stone circles, including the first Stonehenge, dominated the landscape, and villages like Skara Brae preserve the furniture of everyday life.

nodes.title: Middle Minoan (Crete; 2000-1600 BC/BCE) (Greece, 2000 BC–1600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 2000 BC–1600 BC] Middle Minoan (Crete; 2000-1600 BC/BCE). The Middle Minoan period on Crete, as defined in C. Shelmerdine, The Cambridge Companion to the Aegean Bronze Age (2008), p. 4, figure 1.1. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The era of Crete's first palaces, when Knossos, Phaistos and Malia became sprawling storage, workshop and ceremonial complexes arranged around a central court. Writing appears, first as Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A, alongside seal-stones, the potter's wheel and the extravagantly painted Kamares pottery exported as far as Egypt. Destruction around 1700 BC was followed by rebuilding on an even larger scale.

nodes.title: New Kingdom Egypt (1548-1086) (Egypt, 1548 BC–1086 BC)

The New Kingdom period in Egypt, following the chronology of the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (compiled by Thomas Schneider):. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Egypt's imperial age, when armies pushed into the Levant and deep into Nubia and the wealth of an empire flowed into temple building on an unprecedented scale. Kings abandoned pyramids for hidden rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings, and the court produced everything from Akhenaten's monotheistic experiment to the treasures buried with Tutankhamun. It ended in a slow unravelling of central authority and the loss of foreign territory.

nodes.name: Rum/Crusader Anatolia (AD 1077-1307) (Greece, AD 1077–AD 1307)
nodes.title: Rum/Crusader Anatolia (AD 1077-1307) (Greece, AD 1077–AD 1307)
nodes.description:
[Anatolia, AD 1077–AD 1307] Rum/Crusader Anatolia (AD 1077-1307). Spatial coverage: Greece, Iraq, Syria, Turkey. Seljuk-Latin States/Francocracy. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

After the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert, Turkish emirs settled the Anatolian plateau and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum grew up around Konya, while passing Crusader armies and, after 1204, Latin and Greek successor states carved up the west. Anatolia shifted decisively from a Greek-speaking Christian heartland to a Turkish and increasingly Muslim one, with caravanserais, madrasas and a distinctive stone architecture marking the new order. Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 reduced the sultanate to a tributary, and its collapse left the field to the small frontier emirates – one of which became the Ottoman state.

MBA Levant-LBA Levant-Iron Age I Levant (not sure as these are all taken from southern Levant periodisation). Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Fortified Canaanite city-states like Hazor, Megiddo and Byblos flourished on trade between Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Aegean, and in this milieu the first alphabetic writing was invented. Egyptian domination in the Late Bronze Age is documented in the Amarna letters, where local kings beg pharaoh for troops. The system collapsed around 1200 BC, and out of its aftermath came the Philistine cities, early Israel and the Phoenician ports.

nodes.name: Khedivate Egypt (AD 1800-1922) (Cyprus, AD 1800–AD 1922)
nodes.title: Khedivate Egypt (AD 1800-1922) (Cyprus, AD 1800–AD 1922)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, AD 1800–AD 1922] Khedivate Egypt (AD 1800-1922). Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Djibouti, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon. Muhammed Ali-Khedivate Egypt, Alawiyya Egypt, Anglo-Egyptian. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Muhammad Ali and his heirs built an autonomous state inside the Ottoman Empire, with conscript armies, cotton plantations, factories and European-trained engineers. The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and the debts it helped pile up brought British occupation in 1882, leaving the khedives as figureheads over a country run from London. The era ended with nominal independence in 1922, but its irrigation works, railways and Cairo boulevards still shape Egypt.

nodes.title: Ubaid period in Mesopotamia (ca. 6500 to 3800 BC) (Iraq, 6500 BC–3800 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 6500 BC–3800 BC] Ubaid period in Mesopotamia (ca. 6500 to 3800 BC). Spatial coverage: Iraq, Turkey. The prehistoric Ubaid period of Mesopotamia, as defined by Wikipedia following Carter, Robert A. and Philip, Graham Beyond the Ubaid: Transformation and Integration in the Late Prehistoric Societies of the Middle East (Studies in Ancient Oriental Civilization, Number 63) The Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago (2010) ISBN 978-1-885923-66-0 p.2, at. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Over nearly three millennia, farming villages on the southern alluvium developed irrigation, standardised painted pottery made partly on the slow wheel, and temples that were enlarged over generations on platforms of their own ruins. Society grew more stratified, with elite households, artificial cranial shaping in some burials and evidence of sailing craft trading down the Gulf. By the end of the sequence the population was concentrating in a few large centres, the immediate prelude to the world's first cities.

[Levant, AD 1099–AD 1291] Crusader/Seljuq-Ayyubid Levant (AD 1099-1291). Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria. Latin. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The lifespan of the crusader states, from the taking of Jerusalem to the loss of Acre, set against Seljuq, Zangid and Ayyubid resistance on the Muslim side. Cyprus was drawn in as supply base, refuge and finally successor: conquered in 1191 and ruled by the Lusignans, it absorbed Latin refugees and much of the eastern trade after the mainland fell. The period left fortifications, harbours and Gothic churches across the eastern Mediterranean.

nodes.title: Samanid-Ghaznavid Iran (AD 819-1186) (Afghanistan, AD 819–AD 1186)
nodes.description:
[Iran, AD 819–AD 1186] Samanid-Ghaznavid Iran (AD 819-1186). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Palestine, Saudi Arabia, Sudan. Iran. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The era in which eastern Iran and Afghanistan became the heartland of a revived Persian culture under the Samanids of Bukhara, then the centre of an empire in its own right when the Turkish slave-general Sebuktegin and his son Mahmud made Ghazna a capital. Mahmud's repeated raids into northern India brought back plunder that paid for a court of poets and scholars, including Ferdowsi and al-Biruni, and opened the way for lasting Muslim rule in the subcontinent. Ghazna was burned by the Ghurids, who inherited both the empire and its Indian ambitions.

Egypt after the New Kingdom, fragmented between Delta pharaohs and the Theban priesthood of Amun, with power increasingly in the hands of Libyan military families. The old royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings were officially stripped and the mummies rebundled and hidden, while new dynastic burials were placed at Tanis. Nubian kings of the 25th Dynasty reunited the land and revived archaic art and architecture, until Assyrian armies sacked Thebes and drove them out.

Timur's conquests, launched from Central Asia, swept through Persia, Iraq, Anatolia and India with devastating force, and his descendants ruled the eastern Islamic lands from Herat and Samarkand. The dynasty's real legacy was cultural: Persian miniature painting, the poetry of Jami, monumental tiled architecture and Ulugh Beg's astronomy. Timurid taste travelled with a fugitive prince, Babur, to become the foundation of Mughal art in India.

The Georgian lands were split into the kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti and a patchwork of princedoms, fought over for two centuries by Safavid Iran and the Ottomans; Shah Abbas deported tens of thousands of Kakhetians and slave raiding drained the countryside. Seeking protection, Erekle II signed the Treaty of Georgievsk with Russia in 1783, and the tsars simply annexed the kingdom from 1801, abolishing the monarchy and the independence of the Georgian church. Russian rule brought roads, railways, Baku oil money and Tbilisi's rebuilding, and also the national and socialist movements that produced an independent republic in 1918.

Rising from Seljuk provincial service, the Khwarazm-Shahs took over Iran, Afghanistan and Transoxiana and briefly looked set to dominate the Islamic east, clashing with the Abbasid caliphs over who really ruled. Their empire proved brittle, held together by Turkic cavalry and mistrustful cities. Genghis Khan's invasion from 1219 destroyed it, opening the region to Mongol rule and paving the way for the sack of Baghdad in 1258.

Communities across Britain built roundhouse farmsteads, dug hillforts on ridgelines and worked iron for tools and weapons, while cremation gave way to varied burial customs and deposits in rivers and bogs. Contact with Gaul brought coinage, wheel-thrown pottery, wine and named dynasties in the south-east during the last century BC. Roman invasion in AD 43 ended political independence in the lowlands, though Iron Age ways of building and farming continued for generations.

Those urns preserve the shape of the thatched huts people actually lived in, examples of which have been excavated on Rome's Palatine hill. This is the world that later Romans remembered as the age of Alba Longa, immediately preceding the first villages on the site of Rome.

Pottery painted with disciplined bands of meander and zigzag marks a period of renewed confidence in the Aegean, with Athens producing monumental vases for elite graves. Contact with Phoenicia and the Near East brought gold, ivory and new ideas, including the alphabet, while population and settlement expanded. Village societies across the Iranian plateau and southwest lowlands produced some of the finest painted pottery of the ancient world while learning to smelt and cast copper. Over these millennia a few settlements — Susa above all — pulled ahead, acquiring temples, seals and clay accounting tokens, and by the end of the span Proto-Elamite tablets record the region's first writing.

Egypt was Constantinople's grain basket and a heartland of monasticism, its countryside dotted with monasteries and pilgrimage shrines like Abu Mina. Theological division after Chalcedon set the Coptic majority against the imperial church, and plague and Persian occupation weakened Byzantine control. The Arab conquest of the 640s ended Roman rule that had lasted nearly seven centuries.

Farming towns in the Helmand valley and the north, such as Mundigak, grew into walled centres with mudbrick platforms, wheel-made pottery and craft workshops. The region's real wealth was mineral: lapis lazuli from Badakhshan, together with tin and copper, moved west to Mesopotamia and east to the Indus cities, making these valleys a hinge of Bronze Age trade. By the end of the millennium the distinctive Oxus civilisation of Bactria was emerging, with monumental compounds and richly furnished burials.

[Malta, 5000 BC–2500 BC] Neolithic Period on Malta (ca. 5,000-2,500BC). The neolithic or so-called "New Stone Age" as expressed in remains of physical culture on the island of Malta, where it appears to have lasted from around 5,000 to 2,500 BC. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Settlers from Sicily brought farming to the islands, and their descendants built the megalithic temples - Ġgantija, Ħaġar Qim, Mnajdra, Tarxien - among the oldest free-standing stone buildings anywhere. Underground at the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum, chambers cut to imitate the temples above held the remains of thousands of dead. The culture produced fat-bodied figurines and carved spirals, then collapsed abruptly around 2500 BC for reasons still argued over.

Farming communities across France built the first great megalithic tombs — passage graves, dolmens and the long alignments of Brittany — turning burial into permanent architecture on the landscape. Pottery styles such as Chassey spread widely, flint was mined industrially at sites like Spiennes and Grand-Pressigny, and the first copper objects appeared. Lake-edge villages in the Alpine foreground preserve wooden houses, textiles and wheels in waterlogged deposits.

Two centuries of Persian rule ended when Alexander entered Egypt unopposed, was crowned in pharaonic style and laid out Alexandria at the western edge of the Delta. His body was later brought back and interred there by Ptolemy, who governed as satrap in the name of Alexander's heirs. In 305 Ptolemy dropped the pretence and took the crown himself, beginning the Ptolemaic dynasty.

[Afghanistan, AD 300–AD 640] Late Antique (AD 300-AD 640). Spatial coverage: Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, Andorra, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. The Late Antique period in Greek and Roman history. For the purposes of Pleiades, this period is said to begin in the year 300 and to end in the year 640 after the birth of Christ. Control of the region passed among Sasanian governors, Kidarites and then the Hephthalites, each minting coins that copied and adapted Iranian models. Buddhism flourished alongside Zoroastrian and Hindu cults, endowed by merchants on the routes linking India, Central Asia and Iran; the colossal Bamiyan Buddhas and the monasteries of Bactria date from these centuries. Excavated stupas, monastic complexes and hoards of silver and glass show how thoroughly the area was plugged into long-distance trade.

With the Seleucid kingdom collapsing, the Arsacids of Iran took Mesopotamia and became Rome's principal rival in the East, a standoff that shaped politics from the Euphrates to the Red Sea. In the lands south of Damascus the practical beneficiaries were the Nabataeans and other caravan states, who profited from incense and spice traffic while the great powers watched each other. Parthia's decentralised system of vassal kings gave way in AD 224-226 to the Sasanians, who fought Rome far more aggressively.

Before there were pharaohs, Egypt was a string of farming communities that gradually consolidated into rival centres at Naqada, Hierakonpolis and Abydos. Their graves, dug into desert sand, preserve fine ripple-flaked knives, slate cosmetic palettes and painted pottery, and mark the beginnings of the elaborate Egyptian concern with the afterlife. Political consolidation and the first writing at the end of the period produced the unified state of the First Dynasty.

In these years the Ottomans grew from a frontier emirate in Anatolia into the dominant power of the eastern Mediterranean, crossing into Europe, absorbing rival Turkish beyliks and reducing Byzantium to little more than its capital. Even a shattering defeat by Timur in 1402 only briefly interrupted the advance. The capture of Constantinople in 1453 completed the process and reshaped politics and trade across the region.

Cities, craft workshops and long-distance trade flourished across the Iranian plateau, from Elamite Susa in the southwest to Shahr-i Sokhta in the east and the chlorite-carving centres near Jiroft. Carved vessels, lapis lazuli and tin moved between Mesopotamia, the Gulf and the Indus, and Elam developed its own writing and kingship. By the end of the period many of these centres had contracted, and new peoples and material cultures were spreading in from the northeast.

Highland Anatolia was organised for the first time into a single state, with fortress-cities, rock-cut tombs, irrigation works still in use today, and a written language adapted from Assyrian cuneiform. Urartian kings campaigned against Assyria and against the tribes of the Caucasus, and their metalworkers produced armour and vessels of exceptional quality. The kingdom disappeared around 600 BC, but its fortifications remain the most conspicuous ancient monuments in the region.

Elam grew up in the lowlands of Khuzestan and the Zagros highlands as Mesopotamia's great eastern rival, with Susa and Anshan as its twin poles. Its scribes produced Proto-Elamite tablets, still largely undeciphered, and later a cuneiform script for a language unrelated to any other known tongue. Elamite armies sacked Babylon and carried off Hammurabi's law stele as loot; centuries later the Achaemenid Persians absorbed the region and kept Elamite as a language of imperial administration at Persepolis.

Egypt under the Fatimids became the richest state in the eastern Mediterranean, its capital Cairo a magnet for merchants trading Indian Ocean spices and Nile grain. Copper made Cyprus indispensable: its ox-hide ingots travelled to Egypt, the Levant and the Aegean, and Egyptian and Hittite records probably know the island as Alashiya. Towns such as Enkomi and Kition grew into walled, cosmopolitan ports with their own still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script. A Macedonian dynasty ruling an ancient kingdom, blending Greek administration and coinage with Egyptian religion and royal imagery. Alexandria drew scholars from across the Greek world - Euclid, Eratosthenes, the translators of the Hebrew Bible - and the grain of the Nile made the Ptolemies enormously rich. Their decrees, issued in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, produced the Rosetta Stone that would later unlock the Egyptian script.

A long bracket covering the transformation from irrigated farming villages to the first cities and states: Ubaid temple towns, the Uruk expansion with its mass-produced bowls and earliest writing, and the Early Dynastic city-states with their walls, palaces and rival kings. Over these millennia writing, the cylinder seal, the wheel, bronze metallurgy and organised warfare all appear. Highland Iran was drawn into the process as a source of copper, tin, lapis and chlorite, and developed its own urban centres in response.

The last Ottoman decades ended in the First World War, after which Britain and France carved the Arab provinces into mandates and drew borders that still define the region. Afghanistan, never Ottoman but caught between Russian and British ambitions, won full control of its foreign affairs after the Third Anglo-Afghan War and embarked on contested modernising reforms under Amanullah. Across the region this was the age of oil concessions, new national capitals and archaeology conducted under colonial permits.

A long umbrella span covering the region's absorption into the Roman east, its Christianisation, and the Arab conquests that followed. Cities were rebuilt with colonnaded streets and then with churches and mosaic pavements; the countryside filled with villages and oil and wine presses in the sixth century as never before. Continuity is the theme – many towns carried on with little visible break under Umayyad and early Abbasid rule.

nodes.title: Mamluk Middle East (AD 1258-1516) (Egypt, AD 1258–AD 1516)

[Middle East, AD 1258–AD 1516] Mamluk Middle East (AD 1258-1516). Western ME. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

A state run by an elite of slave-soldiers who bought, trained and promoted their own successors rather than inheriting power. They stopped the Mongol advance at Ayn Jalut, expelled the last Crusaders from the Levant in 1291, and sheltered a puppet caliph in Cairo, which became the wealthiest and most learned city in the Islamic world — its mosques, madrasas and inlaid metalwork are among the great achievements of medieval Islamic art. Plague, the shift of spice routes to the Portuguese and Ottoman firearms brought the sultanate down in 1516–17.

The Ottomans took Cyprus from Venice in 1571 after a brutal siege of Famagusta, ending Latin rule and restoring the Orthodox archbishopric, which became the community's political voice under the millet system. Latin churches were converted to mosques, Anatolian settlers were brought in, and heavy taxation on a depopulated island provoked repeated revolts. The wider empire in these centuries expanded to Vienna's gates before its advance was checked in 1683.

[Southern Levant, 2100 BC–1900 BC] Transition Early-Middle Bronze Age Southern Levant (2100-1900 BC). Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Palestine. southern Levant. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The walled towns of the Early Bronze Age had collapsed, and the southern Levant became a landscape of small unwalled villages, campsites and, above all, cemeteries of thousands of rock-cut shaft tombs. Metalwork - curved daggers, javelins, fenestrated axes - is abundant while monumental architecture is absent, and scholars still argue whether this reflects nomadic incomers, climatic downturn or the unravelling of trade with Egypt. Urban life returned, on a new plan, in the Middle Bronze Age that followed.

[Albania, AD 1200–AD 1453] Late Byzantine/Ottoman Rise (AD 1200-1453). Spatial coverage: Albania, Egypt, Greece, Italy, Kenya, Syria. Aegean, Balkan & Anatolia. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Byzantine authority here dissolved into a contest between the Despotate of Epiros, Angevin claimants, the Serbian empire of Stefan Dušan and Venice, which held the best harbours. Into the gap stepped local noble houses — Thopia, Balsha, Muzaka, Kastrioti — ruling small principalities from hilltop fortresses. Ottoman armies broke into the region after the battle on the Vjosë plain in 1385, and by the mid-fifteenth century most of the country was under Ottoman rule or in revolt against it.

The region's first towns appeared, ringed by mudbrick walls and served by temples, granaries and reservoirs at places like Arad, Megiddo and Bet Yerah. Trade in olive oil, wine and copper linked these towns to Egypt and Byblos, and Egyptian pottery and royal marks turn up in the earliest levels. Around 2500–2200 BC the towns were abandoned one by one, and the population dispersed into villages and herding camps until urban life revived some centuries later.

As Abbasid control loosened, local dynasties took power in the eastern Caucasus, among them the Shirvanshahs, Sajids, Sallarids and Shaddadids, who fortified towns and minted their own coins. Seljuk Turks arrived in the eleventh century, bringing Turkic settlement and language that reshaped the region's population. The twelfth century saw a cultural high point around Ganja and Nakhchivan, home to the poet Nizami and to brick tomb-towers such as the Momine Khatun mausoleum.

The crusader states clung to a narrow coastal strip of ports and castles while power on land shifted decisively away from them. Mongol armies swept into Syria and were stopped by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut in 1260; the Mamluk sultans then took the crusader cities one by one, ending with Acre in 1291. Sugar, glass and silk moved through the coastal ports to Italian merchant fleets, making the Levantine harbours the hinge of east-west trade.

A broad sweep in which the lands of the Hindu Kush passed from Persian satrapal rule to Alexander of Macedon, then to the Seleucids, the independent Greco-Bactrian kings, and finally to Saka and Parthian newcomers. Cities like Ai Khanum show Greek theatres and gymnasia standing in the Oxus valley alongside Iranian and Indian traditions. Trade routes hardened into the arteries that would later carry silk, Buddhism and coinage across Asia.

Safavid Iran pushed its authority east into Herat and the Kandahar corridor, contesting these cities repeatedly with the Mughals of India and the Uzbeks of Bukhara. Herat became a Safavid provincial capital and a centre of Persianate painting, poetry and tilework, and princes were routinely sent there to be trained as governors. The dynasty's grip failed when Ghilzai Afghans revolted at Kandahar and marched on Isfahan, sacking the capital in 1722.

[Eastern Mediterranean, 10000 BC–3300 BC] Neolithic Period in the Eastern Mediterranean (ca. 10,000-3,300 BC). Spatial coverage: Cyprus, Greece, Turkey. The so-called "Neolithic" or "New Stone Age" period as defined in the Eastern portion of the Mediterranean basin, lasting roughly from 10,000 - 3,300 BC. See further:. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Cyprus was colonised by boat, and the settlers brought their whole farming world with them - cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, deer and even cats, one of which was buried beside a person at Shillourokambos. Khirokitia, a village of round stone houses packed behind a massive wall, shows how substantial these communities became without ever adopting pottery at first. The island's isolation makes it an unusually clear case study in how the Neolithic package travelled overseas.
