The Abbasid caliphs shifted the Islamic world's centre of gravity east to Baghdad, drawing on Persian administrative traditions and eastern trade routes. In the far east of the empire, cities like Balkh and Herat prospered as hubs of scholarship, paper-making and caravan commerce. Real power gradually slipped to regional dynasties such as the Tahirids and Samanids, leaving the caliph a religious figurehead.

Farming took root along the Nile and in the Fayum depression, with grain stored in basket-lined pits and villages of reed and mud huts at Merimde in the Delta. West of the valley the Sahara was still grassland, and herders at places like Nabta Playa kept cattle, buried them ceremonially and set up stone alignments. As the desert dried, these people pushed towards the river, concentrating population in the narrow valley that would become Egypt.

A chronological bracket borrowed from Mediterranean history but applied here to the age of the Kushan empire, when Bactria and Gandhara sat astride the routes linking Han China, India and the Roman world. Roman glass, bronzes and coins travelled east along these roads; the Begram treasure mixes Alexandrian glassware, Indian ivories and Chinese lacquer in a single storeroom. It is the era in which Buddhist art absorbed classical models.

The tight, austere first stage of Geometric pottery, dominated by Athens: dark-glazed vases with narrow bands of meander and compass-drawn circles. Behind the pots lies a society rebuilding after the Bronze Age collapse — smaller, iron-using, and burying its dead with weapons and imported goods that show contact with Cyprus and the Levant resuming.

The collapse of the Hittite empire left Anatolia fragmented: Neo-Hittite city-states carried on Luwian traditions in the southeast, Phrygians rose around Gordion, and Urartu built a mountain kingdom in the east. Writing, monumental art and long-distance trade contracted sharply before recovering in new forms, including alphabetic scripts. Assyrian expansion from the south increasingly shaped the region's politics until Cimmerian raids and Lydian ascendancy reset it again.

A century and a half of divided rule between the fall of the Old Kingdom's pyramid-building state and the Theban reunification under Mentuhotep II. Nomarchs commissioned their own decorated tombs and armies, and regional art styles diverged sharply from Memphite court standards. Later Egyptian writers remembered it as an age of chaos, a memory that shaped their political thinking for centuries.

Egypt broke into competing kingdoms: Levantine rulers known as the Hyksos governed the Delta from Avaris, Theban dynasts held the Nile valley to the south, and Kerma controlled Nubia. Egyptian rulers now faced a world of chariot warfare and Levantine connections they had largely held at arm's length. The Theban counterattack that ended the period made reconquest and empire a permanent ambition of Egyptian kingship.

After the fall of Ur, Amorite dynasties took over the cities of southern Mesopotamia, and Hammurabi of Babylon eventually welded them into a single kingdom whose law collection remains the most famous legal text of the ancient world. In the north, merchants from Ashur ran donkey caravans carrying tin and textiles into Anatolia, leaving thousands of clay letters and contracts in their trading colonies. This was the great age of Akkadian literature, mathematics and scribal schooling, and its texts were still being copied a thousand years later.

Christian communities remained large and Greek-speaking administrators stayed in office for decades, but Arabic and Islamic coinage steadily took over. A broad span covering the rebirth of Canaanite cities, their fortified heyday, and their subjugation by New Kingdom Egypt. Massive ramparts, palaces and elite tombs mark the peak, while Levantine migrants in the Nile Delta gave rise to the Hyksos dynasties. By the end of the span Canaan was a patchwork of vassal city-states writing to pharaoh.

The Sasanian empire ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from Ctesiphon, with Zoroastrianism as state religion and a huge investment in canal irrigation that made the Iraqi plains among the most productive land on earth. Repeated wars with Rome and Byzantium culminated in Khusrau II's conquest of Syria and Egypt and then total defeat by Heraclius. Exhausted, the empire fell to Arab armies in the 630s and 640s, but its bureaucracy, art and court culture were absorbed wholesale into the caliphate.

Egyptian control of Canaan collapsed and the region fragmented into small kingdoms and city-states: Philistines on the coast, Phoenician ports in the north, Israel, Judah, Ammon, Moab and Edom inland, and Aramaean states beyond. Alphabetic writing spread, iron tools became common, and long-distance trade in oil, wine, silver and incense flourished. Successive Assyrian, Egyptian and Babylonian invasions eventually swallowed them all, ending with the Persian conquest.

Coin finds and building activity thin out sharply, and cemeteries rather than cities provide most of the evidence. Byzantine control was reasserted from the ninth century, but the region's population and place names had been permanently reshaped.

From Diocletian's accession to Constantine's death, the empire was rebuilt: multiple emperors, smaller provinces, a new tax system, a reformed coinage and an army separated from civil administration. For Egypt these decades meant the end of its long-standing peculiar institutions, the last hieroglyphic inscriptions, the Great Persecution that the Coptic calendar still dates from as the Era of Martyrs - and then, abruptly, imperial patronage of the Church.

A prosperous Roman province turned Christian early, filling its cities with basilicas and mosaic floors until earthquakes and Arab raids from the 640s brought centuries of insecurity and a shared Byzantine-Arab arrangement over the island. Byzantine rule was firmly re-established in 965, and rural churches with wall paintings survive in numbers from the centuries that followed. Richard the Lionheart seized the island in 1191 and it passed to the Lusignan dynasty, whose Gothic cathedrals and castles sit oddly alongside Orthodox village chapels.

After the astonishing megalithic temple culture collapsed, the islands were occupied by people with very different habits: they cremated their dead, built dolmens, and fortified hilltop villages such as Borġ in-Nadur with massive walls. Metal, weapons and Aegean-style pottery point to Malta being drawn into wider Mediterranean trading circuits. The mysterious 'cart ruts' gouged into the limestone, and the silo pits cut into abandoned temple floors, both belong to these centuries.

Phrygia fell to Cimmerian raiders and Lydia rose in its place, minting some of the world's first coins and pushing its rule to the Aegean Greek cities. Assyrian and then Babylonian power pressed from the southeast, while Ionian ports became centres of trade and early Greek philosophy. It ended with Cyrus the Great's defeat of Croesus in 546 BC, which folded the whole peninsula into the Persian Empire.

The Seleucid kings inherited the largest share of Alexander's empire, ruling from Mesopotamia and Syria over a patchwork of Greek colonies, old temple cities and mountain principalities. Greek foundations such as Antioch and Seleucia became huge cosmopolitan centres, while Babylonian astronomy and cuneiform scholarship continued under new masters. Afghanistan emerged from the collapse of the old imperial order to win full control of its foreign affairs from Britain in 1919, and Amanullah Khan's attempts at rapid Westernising reform provoked a backlash that set the pattern for the century. Decades of cautious monarchy and foreign-aid development gave way to a republican coup in 1973, a communist seizure of power in 1978 and the Soviet invasion of 1979. The war that followed killed perhaps a million people, drove millions more into exile, and left a landscape of armed factions from which the Taliban emerged in the mid-1990s.

Bactria became the most easterly outpost of the Greek world, with planned cities, theatres, gymnasia and Corinthian columns built on the Oxus - Ai Khanum is the spectacular excavated example. Local Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kings struck some of the finest portrait coinage of antiquity and carried Greek artistic conventions into India, where they fed into Gandharan Buddhist sculpture. The Hittite kingdom grew from a battered central Anatolian state into an empire that sacked Babylon's successors' allies, absorbed Syria and fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh. Its capital Hattusa held cuneiform archives in several languages, and its treaties and correspondence with Assyria, Babylon and Egypt are among the richest diplomatic records of the Bronze Age. The empire vanished abruptly around 1200 BC in the wider collapse of the eastern Mediterranean world.

Two successive Mesopotamian empires — Sargon's Akkad and then the Third Dynasty of Ur — pushed east into Khuzestan and the Zagros, garrisoning Susa and installing loyal governors there. Ur's kings ran an obsessively documented bureaucracy, and tens of thousands of tablets record the tribute, livestock and labour extracted from the eastern provinces. Highland powers, above all the Shimashki and later Elam, eventually turned the tables and sacked Ur, carrying its last king off as a prisoner.

After the failed siege of Vienna the empire went from expansion to a long defensive struggle, losing Hungary, the Black Sea steppe and eventually most of the Balkans. Nineteenth-century sultans answered with sweeping reform – a new army, legal codes, telegraphs and railways, and a short-lived constitution – while nationalist movements pulled provinces away. The age of the Sumerian city-states — Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Kish, Umma — each walled, each ruled by a king who answered to a city god. Warfare between neighbours over land and water is documented on carved stelae and in the earliest historical inscriptions, while temples grew into major landholding institutions. Cuneiform matured from bookkeeping into a script capable of poetry and law, and the period closed when Sargon of Akkad swept the cities into a single empire.

The century between the accession of Alexios Komnenos and the sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade, when Byzantium clawed back territory from the Seljuqs while Latin armies carved out states in Syria and Palestine. In the Caucasus it was the Georgian golden age: David IV broke Seljuq power at Didgori and Queen Tamar's kingdom reached from the Black Sea to the Caspian, funding monasteries, frescoes and epic poetry. The collapse of Byzantine authority in 1204 rearranged power across the whole region.

Afghanistan takes shape as a state, beginning with Ahmad Shah Durrani's empire of 1747 and its capital at Kandahar. Wedged between the Russian and British empires, it became the board for the Great Game, surviving three Anglo-Afghan wars and winning full independence in 1919, then attempting rapid modernisation under Amanullah and Zahir Shah. The Soviet invasion of 1979 and the decades of war, refugee flight and shifting regimes that followed made this small, mountainous country a fixture of global politics.

Between Egyptian occupations, distinct Nubian societies flourished along the Middle Nile: the cattle-herding C-Group in the north, the Pan-Grave people of the eastern deserts, and above all Kerma, which grew into a powerful kingdom with monumental mud-brick architecture and huge tumulus burials. Egypt built a chain of massive fortresses at the Second Cataract to control this frontier and its gold and trade routes. When Egyptian power collapsed, Kerma took the forts and raided deep into Egypt.

The Late Bronze Age Near East was carved up between the Egyptian empire in the south and the Hittites in the north, with Levantine city-states as tribute-paying vassals caught between them. Their rivalry peaked at the battle of Kadesh and was settled by one of the earliest surviving peace treaties. It was an age of intense diplomatic correspondence, long-distance trade and cosmopolitan palace culture that collapsed abruptly around 1200 BC.

A last age of native pharaohs, punctuated by two spells of Persian rule and closed by Alexander's arrival. Temple building continued on a huge scale, animal cults and their vast catacombs flourished, and sculptors looked back to the styles of a thousand years earlier. Greek visitors like Herodotus came at exactly this time, and much of what the classical world thought it knew about Egypt was gathered here.

Early Islamic, Rashidun-Umayyad (starts with death of Muhammed who only controlled Arabia). Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Within a century of Muhammad's death, Arab armies had taken Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Iran and pushed into Central Asia and Sind, creating an empire ruled from Damascus. The Umayyads kept much of the Byzantine and Sasanian administrative machinery at first, then Arabised the coinage and bureaucracy and built monuments such as the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus. Resentment among non-Arab converts and garrison troops in Khurasan fed the revolution of 747-750 that swept the dynasty away and brought the Abbasids to power.

The Illyrian kingdoms and the Greek colonies of Apollonia and Dyrrhachium were drawn into wars between Macedon and Rome, ending with Roman conquest in the second century BC. The Via Egnatia was driven inland from the Adriatic coast, making this the land bridge between Italy and the Greek East, and coastal cities gained forums, theatres and aqueducts. Roman veteran settlement and road traffic reshaped a previously tribal interior.

Egypt passed from the last Ptolemies to Rome after Cleopatra's defeat, becoming the emperor's personal province and the granary that fed the capital. Alexandria remained a great centre of learning and commerce, while emperors were carved as pharaohs on temple walls in the south. Christianity took root early and deeply, producing the Coptic church and the desert monasteries that shaped monastic life everywhere. Papyri preserved in the dry sand give an unmatched record of taxes, lawsuits, letters and shopping lists until the Arab conquest.

Southeastern Arabia's long prehistory, opening with some of the earliest evidence for humans leaving Africa and stone tool traditions scattered across what is now desert but was then grassland with lakes. Later coastal peoples built shell middens, fished with bone hooks and shell lures, and traded with the Ubaid communities of Mesopotamia. It ends as copper working and oasis settlement begin, launching the land the Sumerians called Magan.

The Uruk phenomenon reached the Susiana plain and the Iranian plateau, bringing bevel-rim bowls, cylinder seals and numerical tablets to sites such as Susa, Chogha Mish and Godin Tepe. Whether these were trading outposts, colonies or local emulation is still argued. Out of this contact the Iranian lowlands developed their own administrative tradition, the Proto-Elamite script, and their own urban centres.

The prepalatial millennium, when Cretan villages adopted metalworking, built the great communal tholos tombs of the Mesara plain and started using stamp seals to mark property. Craft skill rose sharply, seen in mottled Vasiliki pottery, translucent stone vessels and delicate gold jewellery. Settlements like Myrtos Fournou Korifi give an intimate picture of daily life just before the palaces of Knossos and Phaistos were built.

The Bronze Age arrives on the Greek mainland: farming villages adopt metal tools, the potter's wheel and long-distance exchange with the Cyclades and Anatolia. At its height, sites like Lerna and Tiryns built monumental "corridor houses" and used clay sealings to control stored goods, hinting at the first mainland elites. Widespread destructions and a shift in pottery and house forms toward the end of the era broke that trajectory, setting the stage for the Middle Helladic world from which Mycenaean Greece emerged.

The first two dynasties, when a single kingship stretched from the Delta to Aswan and the machinery of a state — writing, taxation, a royal capital at Memphis — was assembled for the first time. Kings were buried at Abydos in mudbrick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers, with vast enclosures for funerary rites nearby. The conventions of Egyptian art, from the striding royal figure to the hieroglyphic label, were fixed here and held for three thousand years.

This is the Umm an-Nar era, when southeastern Arabia was the land the Mesopotamians called Magan and supplied them with copper and diorite by sea. Communities built round stone towers with wells at their heart, irrigated date gardens, and buried their dead collectively in monumental circular tombs faced with dressed white stone. Imported Indus and Mesopotamian goods in these tombs show Oman sitting at the hinge of Gulf trade.

Urban centres on the plateau and in the southeast — Shahr-i Sokhta, Shahdad, Konar Sandal on the Halil river — grew rich on chlorite bowls, lapis lazuli, copper and tin moving between Mesopotamia, Central Asia and the Indus. Mesopotamian kings from Sargon onward campaigned into these lands, naming Elam, Marhashi and Anshan among their rivals and trading partners. Proto-Elamite writing had faded, but Elam's kingdoms consolidated in the southwest around Susa and Anshan, setting up the long rivalry with Sumer and Akkad.

A long, austere stretch between the disruptions of the Early Bronze Age and the rise of Mycenae. People lived in small unwalled villages, made grey and yellow Minyan pottery and matt-painted jars, and buried their dead in cist graves inside or beside the settlement. Contact with Minoan Crete grew through the period, and by its close the spectacular shaft graves at Mycenae announce a new and far more hierarchical mainland society.

Sicilian communities of this phase buried their dead in rock-cut chamber tombs cut in cliffsides, sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and lived in hilltop villages overlooking the coastal plains. Mycenaean and Cypriot pottery begins to appear on the island's eastern shores and offshore islets, evidence that Sicily had become a stop on Aegean voyages west toward metal sources. Local potters answered with distinctive burnished and painted wares of their own.

From their fortified capital at Hattusa, the first Hittite kings pushed out across the Anatolian plateau and into Syria, and one of them, Mursili I, marched all the way to Babylon and destroyed it. Royal succession was violent and contested, prompting edicts like that of Telipinu that tried to fix the rules of inheritance. The state archives preserve treaties, laws and annals in cuneiform, giving an unusually candid view of how an early empire justified itself.

The Hittite kingdom, ruled from the fortified mountain capital of Hattusa, grew into an empire that fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and produced the earliest surviving international peace treaty. Its clay archives preserve treaties, prayers, law codes and myths in eight languages, including the oldest recorded Indo-European texts. Around 1200 BC the capital burned and the empire dissolved.

The great palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros were at their peak, with light wells, frescoes, storage magazines and workshops supporting an export trade in oil, wine and fine pottery. The Thera eruption and a later wave of burnings ended most of it; Knossos carried on under Mycenaean administrators writing Greek in Linear B. By the close, palaces were gone, cremation and new burial customs had appeared, and survivors were living in refuge sites high in the mountains.

In the southwest the Elamite kingdom flourished, building the vast stepped temple-city of Chogha Zanbil and eventually carrying Babylon's most famous monuments home as loot. Across the northern and western highlands, communities left few texts but distinctive grey burnished pottery and rich cemeteries, and it is in these centuries that scholars look for the arrival of Iranian-speaking peoples.

A wealthy Canaanite port kingdom on the Syrian coast, trading between Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean and the Hittite empire whose vassal it became. Its scribes used a 30-sign cuneiform alphabet to write their own language, preserving the Baal Cycle and other myths that transformed understanding of Canaanite religion and of the background to the Hebrew Bible. The city was burned around 1190 BC in the wave of destructions that ended the Bronze Age, and was never reoccupied, leaving its archives where they fell.

Iranian-speaking groups consolidated across the plateau while Assyrian armies raided westward valleys and Urartu pressed from the north. Grey burnished pottery, iron weapons and rich warrior graves mark the era, and sites like Hasanlu preserve a fortified citadel destroyed and burned around 800 BC with its inhabitants still inside. Out of this fragmented world of local chiefdoms came the Medes and, soon after, the Persians.

Assyria rebuilt itself into the first true empire of the Near East, campaigning east into the Zagros and demanding tribute from the highland peoples. Assyrian records from these centuries give the earliest written mentions of the Medes and Persians, while Elam in the southwest and Urartu to the north competed for influence. Iron working, horse breeding and fortified hilltop settlements spread across the Iranian plateau in a landscape being drawn into imperial politics.

Madagascar was still, so far as the firm evidence goes, essentially empty of people — one of the last large habitable landmasses on Earth to be settled. Giant lemurs, elephant birds and pygmy hippos lived on an island shaped only by fire, cyclone and forest. Scattered claims of much earlier human butchery marks on bones remain contested, and the debate over when the first arrivals came is one of the liveliest in Indian Ocean archaeology.

The hillfort societies of northwestern Iberia, living in dense clusters of round drystone houses ringed by ramparts and ditches, at sites like Citânia de Briteiros and Santa Tegra. They worked local tin and gold into torcs and diadems, traded with Mediterranean and Atlantic partners, and left carved warrior statues and decorated stone lintels. Rome absorbed the region after the Cantabrian Wars, and many castros stayed occupied as Roman-period villages.

After Jerusalem's destruction the southern Levant became a chain of imperial provinces, first Babylonian and then Persian, governed through local elites and temple institutions rather than annexed kingdoms. Under Persian rule exiles returned, the Jerusalem temple was rebuilt, and coinage, Aramaic administration and Greek trade goods spread through the region. It is the setting for the emergence of Second Temple Judaism and for Ezra and Nehemiah, and it closed with Alexander's arrival.

Persian rule reached the Hindu Kush, organising Bactria, Arachosia and Gandhara as tribute-paying satrapies linked by royal roads to Susa. Local dynasts kept much authority while imperial styles of seal, coin and column spread eastward. Resistance in these eastern provinces gave Alexander his hardest fighting.

Eight and a half centuries in which Anatolia and the Levant passed from Persian satraps to Alexander's successors, then to Rome. Greek became the language of city life, and the Hellenistic and Roman centuries filled the landscape with colonnaded streets, theatres and temples. The span closes with Constantine's victory and the founding of a Christian capital on the Bosphorus.

Iron Age communities of the central Alps, known from hillside settlements, distinctive pottery and bronzework, and short inscriptions in an alphabet borrowed from the Etruscans that remain largely undeciphered. Roman writers cast them as fierce mountain people, and Augustus sent his stepsons Drusus and Tiberius to subdue the Alpine valleys in 15 BC, absorbing them into the province of Raetia.

Alexander's armies pushed to the Syr Darya, founding garrison towns at the edge of the steppe, and Greek rule was continued by Seleucid and then Greco-Bactrian kings to the south. Greek coins, fortified cities and imported goods circulated among the Saka nomads who dominated the grasslands, and it is in the exchange between settled Greek colonists and mobile pastoralists that the interest of the period lies. Nomadic confederations reshaped the region: the Kangju held the middle Syr Darya, while the Yuezhi, pushed west out of Gansu, overran Greek-ruled Bactria and coalesced into the Kushan Empire. The Kushans linked India, Iran and China, minted gold coinage on Roman weight standards, and carried Buddhism north along the trade routes. This is the era in which the Silk Road became a working system of long-distance exchange.

Seafarers from island Southeast Asia crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean to reach Madagascar, bringing rice, bananas and the Austronesian language that is still spoken across the island today; African migrants brought cattle, and the two streams mingled. Firmly dated settlements appear in the later centuries of the millennium, on the coasts and then inland. Their arrival coincides with the beginning of the end for the island's giant lemurs and elephant birds.

nodes.name: Roman Britain (43 - 410 CE/AD) (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410)
nodes.title: Roman Britain (43 - 410 CE/AD) (United Kingdom, AD 43–AD 410)
nodes.description:
[Britain, AD 43–AD 410] Roman Britain (43 - 410 CE/AD). Spatial coverage: Northern Ireland, United Kingdom. Simon Hornblower and Antony Spawforth, eds. (1998). The Oxford Companion to Classical Civilization. Oxford University Press. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Claudius's invasion turned the tribal societies of southern Britain into a Roman province, with legionary fortresses, straight roads, planned towns like London, Colchester and York, and villas farming for a market economy. The north was never fully absorbed, and Hadrian's Wall fixed a garrisoned frontier across the island. Visitors can still see mosaics, bathhouses, curse tablets and writing tablets that record ordinary life in Latin. When the army and administration were withdrawn in the early fifth century, towns and coinage collapsed within a generation.

The Kushan order gave way to a succession of steppe-derived powers — Sasanian governors, Kidarites, then Hephthalites — while Sogdian merchants built the trading networks that carried silk, silver and religions across Asia. Cities on the oasis edges grew walls and citadels, and Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism and Nestorian Christianity circulated along the same roads. It is the world that produced the Sogdian letters and the mixed steppe-and-city culture later encountered by the Türks.

Five centuries in which England took shape: a landscape of dispersed farms and timber halls gave way to nucleated villages and open fields, to minsters and parish churches, and to fortified burhs that grew into towns with mints and markets. Silver pennies, imported wine and quernstones show an economy plugged into the North Sea world. The period's art — illuminated gospel books, garnet-set metalwork, carved crosses — is among the finest produced in early medieval Europe.

Turkic khaganates dominated the steppe while Sogdian merchant cities such as Samarkand and Panjikent grew rich on the overland trade between China, India and Byzantium. Walled towns, fortified manors and brilliantly painted murals record a cosmopolitan world where Zoroastrians, Buddhists, Manichaeans and Nestorian Christians lived side by side and Sogdian served as a lingua franca. Arab armies moving into Transoxiana ended it, opening the region's long Islamic era.

Five centuries of Islamic rule running from the Arab conquest through the Umayyads and Abbasids to the Fatimids, who took Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo as their capital. Arabic gradually replaced Greek and Aramaic in administration and daily life, new coinages and trade networks tied the region to the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean, and Jerusalem gained the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa. The era closes with the disruption of the First Crusade and the Frankish states established along the coast.

Some of the earliest securely dated settlements on the island belong to these centuries, when villages of fishers and herders appear along the northern and western coasts. Their inhabitants came from two directions - Austronesian voyagers whose language and rice, bananas and outrigger canoes came from Southeast Asia, and Bantu-speaking peoples from the East African mainland - producing a culture found nowhere else. Imported glass beads and Middle Eastern pottery show these communities were already plugged into the Indian Ocean trading world.

Ruling from Bukhara and Samarkand, the Samanids turned Transoxiana into the wealthiest and most cultivated province of the eastern Islamic world. Their silver dirhams flowed north along the Volga in exchange for furs and slaves and are found by the thousand in Viking hoards in Scandinavia and Russia. Bukhara's library and court nurtured Ibn Sina and the poet Rudaki, while the frontier trade in Turkish slave soldiers created the military class that would eventually overthrow the dynasty.

nodes.title: Qarakhanid Period in Central Asia (AD 1000 - AD 1200) (Kazakhstan, AD 1000–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Central Asia, AD 1000–AD 1200] Qarakhanid Period in Central Asia (AD 1000 - AD 1200). Spatial coverage: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan. Period as defined by Sören Stark [[1000, 1200]]. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The Qarakhanids were the first Turkic dynasty to convert to Islam as a state, and their rule fused steppe Turkic political tradition with Persianate Islamic urban culture. Under them Balasagun, Kashgar, Samarkand and Bukhara grew rich on the caravan trade, and towns across Semirechye and the Talas valley filled with brick mausolea, minarets, bathhouses and mints. The period produced the first great works of Islamic Turkic literature, the Kutadgu Bilig and Mahmud al-Kashgari's dictionary of Turkic dialects, before the Qara Khitai and then the Mongols swept the dynasty away.

Settlement was spreading inland as cattle-keeping and rice cultivation took hold, laying the groundwork for the kingdoms that emerged later.

Saladin abolished the Fatimid caliphate in Cairo and welded Egypt and Syria into a single Sunni state that recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 and withstood the Third Crusade. His heirs ruled as a loose family confederation of princes in Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo and the Jazira, patronising madrasas, citadels and Sunni scholarship. Their Turkish slave-soldiers overthrew them in Egypt in 1250, founding the Mamluk sultanate.

nodes.title: Late Byzantine Period (AD 1200-1450) (Byzantine Empire, AD 1200–AD 1450)

[Byzantine Empire, AD 1200–AD 1450] Late Byzantine Period (AD 1200-1450). Late Byzantine Period in contexts where such designations are appropriate. [[1200, 1450]]. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

The Fourth Crusade shattered the empire in 1204, and the successor states of Nicaea, Epiros and Trebizond fought Latin lords for the pieces; Nicaea recovered Constantinople in 1261 but never recovered its old reach. Under the Palaiologan dynasty the state shrank to a few provinces, its economy dominated by Venetian and Genoese merchants, even as scholars, mosaicists and fresco painters produced some of Byzantium's finest art at places like the Chora church and Mystras. Ottoman advances through Anatolia and the Balkans hemmed in the capital until the walls fell in 1453; the scholars who fled west carried Greek texts that fed the Italian Renaissance.

Madagascar's northwest coast was tied into the Indian Ocean trading world, with settlements exchanging local products for Islamic glazed pottery, Chinese ceramics and glass beads. Muslim merchant communities were established along the shore, and chlorite-schist vessels quarried on the island travelled widely. Inland, herding and rice farming spread and the forests and giant fauna of the interior came under increasing human pressure.

Beginning as one of several Turkish frontier principalities in northwest Anatolia, the house of Osman grew into an empire straddling the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa, with Constantinople as its capital after 1453. Its sultans claimed the caliphate, ruled a mosaic of religious communities through the millet system, and built the domed mosque complexes of Sinan that still define Istanbul's skyline. Contraction after the seventeenth century, nationalist revolts and defeat in the First World War ended it, and the Turkish Republic replaced it in 1923.

Sakalava rulers built the kingdoms of Menabe and then Boina along the west coast, using cattle wealth and firearms to dominate their neighbours. On the east coast, European pirates and traders set up bases, and Malagasy ports were drawn into an Indian Ocean commerce in slaves, cattle and guns feeding the Mascarene plantations. A short-lived French colony at Fort-Dauphin failed, an early warning of how hard the island would be to hold.

Powerful coastal kingdoms dominated the island: the Sakalava realms of Menabe and Boina in the west, and the Betsimisaraka confederation welded together on the east coast by Ratsimilaho, son of an English pirate and a Malagasy noblewoman. Malagasy rulers grew rich supplying captives, cattle and rice to European slavers and to the sugar plantations of Mauritius and Réunion, and firearms flowed back in return. In the highlands the fragmented Imerina was reunified late in the century by Andrianampoinimerina, laying the foundation for the Merina kingdom that would dominate the following century.

The Merina kingdom of the highlands, armed and advised from abroad, conquered most of the island and built a centralised state at Antananarivo, complete with a written script, missionary schools and mass Christian conversion after 1869 — punctuated by Queen Ranavalona I's long persecution of the new faith. Stone royal tombs, the Rova palace complex, and imported trade goods mark the period's wealth and outward connections. It ends with French invasion and the abolition of the monarchy, folding Madagascar into a colonial empire.

France completed its conquest and abolished the monarchy in 1897, running the island as a colony built on forced labour and export crops; a 1947 insurrection was crushed with heavy loss of life. Rapid population growth and forest clearance in these decades reshaped the island's landscape and endangered its unique wildlife.

nodes.description:
[Caucasus, AD 1200–AD 1500] Late Medieval Caucasus (AD 1200–1500). Spatial coverage: Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Syria, Turkey. Turco-Mongol, Seljuq-Georgian-Ilkhanate-Turkmen Caucasus [[1200,1500]]. Period definition from Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places — Roger Bagnall, 2025.

Georgia entered this era at its height, a unified kingdom with wealth from trade and a burst of church building and manuscript painting, and left it in pieces. Mongol armies arrived in the 1220s and imposed tribute, Timur's campaigns devastated the countryside repeatedly, and by the end the crown had split into the rival kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti with semi-independent princes between them. The fall of Constantinople cut the old trade and religious links westward, leaving Georgia isolated between Ottoman and Persian power.

nodes.name: Assyrian Imperial (Turkey, 929 BC–609 BC)
nodes.title: Assyrian Imperial (Turkey, 929 BC–609 BC)
nodes.description:
[North Syria, 929 BC–609 BC] Assyrian Imperial. Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean — Hodos, Tamar., 2006.

The Neo-Assyrian kings turned Anatolia's southeastern kingdoms into provinces or tribute-payers, and their campaigns brought down the Neo-Hittite city-states and pressed against Urartu in the highlands. Royal inscriptions and palace reliefs record the machinery of it all: siege engines, mass deportations, standing armies and a road and messenger system that held a vast territory together. Assyrian collapse in 612–609 BC left a vacuum that Medes, Babylonians and later Lydians moved to fill.

hints.label: Assyrian Imperial
hints.source: Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean

nodes.name: Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 1099 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age I (Early Iron Age) (Turkey, 1099 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[North Syria, 1099 BC–899 BC] Iron Age I (Early Iron Age). Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean — Hodos, Tamar., 2006.

The centuries immediately after the fall of Hattusa, when centralised palace administration and cuneiform record-keeping vanished from Anatolia. Handmade and painted wares replace standardised Hittite pottery, settlements are smaller and more defensive, and written evidence is scarce. Continuity survived mainly in the south and south-east, where local dynasts kept Hittite royal titles and hieroglyphic script alive.

hints.label: Iron Age I (Early Iron Age)
hints.source: Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean

nodes.name: Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 899 BC–599 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age) (Turkey, 899 BC–599 BC)
nodes.description:
[North Syria, 899 BC–599 BC] Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age). Spatial coverage: Lebanon, Syria, Turkey. This period is used to designate the moment of Phoenician colonization in the West before the development of a distinctive Punic identity. Period definition from Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean — Hodos, Tamar., 2006.

Anatolia was divided among successor kingdoms: Neo-Hittite city-states in the southeast carrying on Bronze Age Hittite art and hieroglyphic writing, Urartu in the eastern highlands with its fortresses and canals, and Phrygia in the centre with its rock-cut monuments and tumulus burials at Gordion. Assyrian armies pressed westward for metal, horses and timber, absorbing one kingdom after another. The period's monumental reliefs and bilingual inscriptions are among the richest sources for how small states survived between empires.

hints.label: Iron Age II (Middle Iron Age)
hints.source: Local responses to colonization in the Iron Age Mediterranean

nodes.name: Roman (Israel, 62 BC–AD 325)
nodes.title: Roman (Israel, 62 BC–AD 325)
nodes.description:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 62 BC–AD 325] Roman. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

nodes.name: Iron I-II (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC)
nodes.title: Iron I-II (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron I-II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

The full sweep of the Iron Age here, from the collapse of Late Bronze Age Canaan through the rise of Israel, Judah, Philistia, Ammon, Moab and Edom, to their absorption by Assyria and Babylon. Over these six centuries alphabetic writing spread, olive oil and wine were produced for export, and cities grew walls, water systems and royal quarters. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem.

nodes.name: Byzantine (Israel, AD 325–AD 636)
nodes.title: Byzantine (Israel, AD 325–AD 636)
nodes.description:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, AD 325–AD 636] Byzantine. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.

nodes.name: Persian (Israel, 538 BC–331 BC) [p0qwcp63xkk]
nodes.title: Persian (Israel, 538 BC–331 BC) [p0qwcp63xkk]
nodes.description:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 538 BC–331 BC] Persian. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. see also Mazar, 1992. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Cyrus's conquest of Babylon allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and Judah became Yehud, a small tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire. Under governors and an increasingly powerful priesthood, much of the Hebrew Bible took shape and Aramaic became the everyday language. Coins, imported Greek pottery and administrative seal impressions show a province tied into imperial and Mediterranean networks.

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Israel, 321 BC–61 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Israel, 321 BC–61 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 321 BC–61 BC] Hellenistic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

nodes.name: MB I-II (Israel, 1999 BC–1649 BC)
nodes.title: MB I-II (Israel, 1999 BC–1649 BC)
nodes.description:
[Palestine and Neighboring Areas (Mesopotamia), Southern Levant, 1999 BC–1649 BC] MB I-II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria. Period definition from Near Eastern archaeology : a reader — 2003.

Town life returned to the southern Levant after the collapse and rural interlude of the preceding centuries. Fortified city-states with massive earthen ramparts and multiple-entry gates dominated the plains and valleys, supported by grain, olive oil and wine and by brisk trade with Egypt, Cyprus and Syria. This is the Canaanite world at its height, and the archaeological setting for the Middle Kingdom Egyptian texts that name its rulers.

nodes.name: Classical Iberian Period (Spain, 399 BC–199 BC)
nodes.title: Classical Iberian Period (Spain, 399 BC–199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Catalan area, 399 BC–199 BC] Classical Iberian Period. Equivalent to Iberian III (450-350 B.C.) and IV (350-200 B.C.) - cf. M. Diaz-Andreu & S. Keay, 1997. The Archaeology of Iberia; Dominguez in C. Sanchez & G.R. Tsetskhladze, 2001. Greek Pottery from the Iberian Peninsula. Period definition from Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).  — Belarte, M.C..

Iberian communities in eastern and southern Spain lived in dense hilltop towns, wrote in their own scripts, struck coinage and produced sharply painted pottery and stone sculpture for elite sanctuaries and tombs. Trade with Greeks, Phoenicians and Carthaginians brought wine, luxury goods and new ideas, while warrior aristocracies fought and hired themselves out as mercenaries. The Second Punic War brought Roman armies into the peninsula and began the long conquest that absorbed these societies.

hints.label: Classical Iberian Period
hints.source: Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).

nodes.name: Early Iberian Period (Spain, 524 BC–399 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iberian Period (Spain, 524 BC–399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Catalan area, 524 BC–399 BC] Early Iberian Period. Period definition from Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).  — Belarte, M.C..

Native communities of eastern and southern Spain, enriched by centuries of contact with Phoenician and Greek traders, developed into the Iberian culture: fortified hilltop towns, wheel-made painted pottery, an alphabet of their own, and stone sculpture of warriors, beasts and veiled ladies. Coastal trade brought wine, oil and luxury goods inland in exchange for metals and grain. These were the peoples Carthage and then Rome would encounter and absorb.

hints.label: Early Iberian Period
hints.source: Domestic Architecture and Social Differences in North-Eastern Iberia during the Iron Age (c.525-200 BC).

nodes.name: Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 43)
nodes.title: Iron Age (United Kingdom, 799 BC–AD 43)
nodes.description:
[Roman Britain, 799 BC–AD 43] Iron Age. May be an inference, not statement / assertion. Period definition from The Oxford illustrated history of Roman Britain — Salway, Peter., 1993.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

hints.label: Iron Age
hints.source: The Oxford illustrated history of Roman Britain

nodes.title: Sasanian (Iraq, AD 224–AD 651)
nodes.description:
[ancient Near East, AD 224–AD 651] Sasanian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Period definition from Sasanian Iran, 224- 651 CE : portrait of a late antique empire — Daryaee, Touraj, 1967-, 2008.

Mesopotamia was the wealthiest province and the political heart of the Sasanian Persian empire, whose capital Ctesiphon stood on the Tigris below modern Baghdad. Massive canal systems such as the Nahrawan turned the Sawad into a granary funding centuries of war with Rome and Byzantium. It was also home to the Babylonian rabbinic academies that produced the Talmud, and to large Christian communities. Exhausted by the last Byzantine war, the empire collapsed after Arab victories at Qadisiyya and Nahavand.

hints.label: Sasanian
hints.source: Sasanian Iran, 224- 651 CE : portrait of a late antique empire

nodes.name: Archaic (Spain, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic (Spain, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Spain, 899 BC–699 BC] Archaic. See also van Dommelen et al. (2008). Period definition from Colonial encounters in ancient Iberia Phoenician, Greek, and indigenous relations — 2009.

Etruscan power was at its height, its cities exporting bronze work and importing Greek pottery by the shipload, while Rome under its last kings acquired its first great temple on the Capitol, its drainage works and its census-based army. The expulsion of the Tarquins around 509 turned the city into a republic ruled by annual magistrates, and the decades after were a hard fight for survival among Latin and Etruscan neighbours. The painted tombs of Tarquinia and Cerveteri come from this world, giving us banquets, dancers and hunters in colour.

hints.label: Archaic
hints.source: Colonial encounters in ancient Iberia Phoenician, Greek, and indigenous relations

nodes.name: Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1739 BC)
nodes.title: Isin-Larsa (Iraq, 1999 BC–1739 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ur, Mesopotamia, 1999 BC–1739 BC] Isin-Larsa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Syria. Robins' chronology is being used in preference to Freeman's, since it seems to represent the general textbook situation more accurately. Period definition from Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1982.

Named for the two Mesopotamian cities that fought over the legacy of the fallen Ur III empire, this horizon in the east coincides with the rise of the Sukkalmah rulers of Elam, who traded, intermarried and intrigued with the kings of southern Iraq. Cuneiform contracts, cylinder seals and standardised pottery show how closely the Iranian lowlands were tied into Babylonian economic life. It ends with Hammurabi's conquests reshaping the region.

hints.label: Isin-Larsa
hints.source: Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur

nodes.name: Early Dynastic IIIa (Iraq, 2649 BC–2549 BC)
nodes.title: Early Dynastic IIIa (Iraq, 2649 BC–2549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mesopotamia, 2649 BC–2549 BC] Early Dynastic IIIa. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Removed due to inferences in GeoDia: al-'Ubaid (5500-4000 B.C.), Uruk (4000-3250 B.C.), Jamdat Nasr periods (3250-3000 B.C.), and Ur of the Chaldees (1150-800 B.C.). Note this quote p.15: "At an archaeological congress of excavators held at Baghdad in 1929 it was agreed that the early stages of human settlement in south Mesopotamia could be classified n successive phases which should be called, after the places where the evidence for each was first discovered, the al-'Ubaid period, the Uruk period, the Jamdat Nasr period, and then the Early Dynastic period, towards the end of which (in IIIb) comes the First Dynasty of Ur." p.16: "Archaeological excavation ... does not of itself offer an absolute chronology in years B.C./A.D.". Period definition from Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1982.

The phase of the great archives from Shuruppak (Fara) and Abu Salabikh, where cuneiform tablets first carry proverbs, word lists and literary texts rather than just accounts. The spectacular graves of the Royal Cemetery at Ur, with their sacrificed attendants and imported lapis lazuli and carnelian, belong here, showing how far Sumerian trade reached into Iran and beyond.

hints.label: Early Dynastic IIIa
hints.source: Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur

nodes.name: Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2153 BC)
nodes.title: Akkadian (Iraq, 2333 BC–2153 BC)
nodes.description:
[Ur, Mesopotamia, 2333 BC–2153 BC] Akkadian. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq. Removed due to inferences in GeoDia: al-'Ubaid (5500-4000 B.C.), Uruk (4000-3250 B.C.), Jamdat Nasr periods (3250-3000 B.C.), and Ur of the Chaldees (1150-800 B.C.). Note this quote p.15: "At an archaeological congress of excavators held at Baghdad in 1929 it was agreed that the early stages of human settlement in south Mesopotamia could be classified n successive phases which should be called, after the places where the evidence for each was first discovered, the al-'Ubaid period, the Uruk period, the Jamdat Nasr period, and then the Early Dynastic period, towards the end of which (in IIIb) comes the First Dynasty of Ur." p.16: "Archaeological excavation ... does not of itself offer an absolute chronology in years B.C./A.D.". Period definition from Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur — Woolley, Leonard, 1880-1960., 1982.

For roughly six generations the dynasty founded by Sargon ruled southern Mesopotamia and campaigned from the Gulf to the Mediterranean, replacing independent city-states with a centralised administration. Standardised weights, a unified calendar and the wide use of the Akkadian language in documents show how far the reach of government extended. Naram-Sin even had himself declared a god; after him the empire unravelled, and later tradition blamed the collapse on divine punishment and Gutian invaders.

hints.label: Akkadian
hints.source: Ur 'of the Chaldees' : a revised and updated edition of Sir Leonard Woolley's Excavations at Ur

nodes.name: The Tetrarchs (Italy, AD 284–AD 312)
nodes.title: The Tetrarchs (Italy, AD 284–AD 312)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 284–AD 312] The Tetrarchs. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy, Turkey. Period definition from Roman art : Romulus to Constantine — Ramage, Nancy H., 1942-, 2001.

Diocletian concluded that the empire was too large for one ruler and divided authority among four — two senior emperors and two juniors — each with his own army, court and regional capital. Sweeping reforms multiplied provinces and officials, fixed prices, reorganised taxation and made the emperor a remote, ceremonial figure; the last great persecution of Christians also belongs here. The system depended on cooperation among men who mostly wanted supreme power, and it dissolved in the wars that carried Constantine to the throne.

nodes.name: The Soldier Emperors (Italy, AD 235–AD 284)
nodes.title: The Soldier Emperors (Italy, AD 235–AD 284)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 235–AD 284] The Soldier Emperors. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy, Turkey. Period definition from Roman art : Romulus to Constantine — Ramage, Nancy H., 1942-, 2001.

For half a century emperors were made and unmade by their troops, most reigning only months before being killed; meanwhile Gothic and Persian invasions broke through the frontiers and plague and debased coinage wrecked the economy. Britain, Gaul and Palmyra broke away as separate regimes before being clawed back. Cities across the empire built walls for the first time in generations, a physical sign of how insecure life had become.

nodes.name: Constantine (Italy, AD 307–AD 337)
nodes.title: Constantine (Italy, AD 307–AD 337)
nodes.description:
[Italy, AD 307–AD 337] Constantine. Spatial coverage: Greece, Italy, Turkey. Period definition from Roman art : Romulus to Constantine — Ramage, Nancy H., 1942-, 2001.

Sole ruler after defeating Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge and Licinius in the east, he ended the tetrarchy and refounded the empire around a new capital on the Bosphorus. His patronage transformed Christianity from a persecuted sect into the favoured religion of the state, and the Council of Nicaea in 325 set the creed still recited today. His reforms of coinage, army and administration shaped the later Roman world.

nodes.name: Late Phrygian (Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC)
nodes.title: Late Phrygian (Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC)
nodes.description:
[Turkey, 539 BC–329 BC] Late Phrygian. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

Under Persian rule the old Phrygian heartland around Gordion became part of a satrapy, its Anatolian traditions continuing alongside imported Achaemenid tastes in metalwork, seals and tumulus burial. Phrygian remained in use in inscriptions, and the cult of the mother goddess Matar (later Cybele) spread far beyond the region. Alexander's passage through Gordion in 333 BC – the setting of the Gordian knot story – brought the era to a close.

hints.label: Late Phrygian
hints.source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Gordion, 1999 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Gordion, 1999 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Gordion, 1999 BC–1499 BC] Middle Bronze Age. added post-GeoDia. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

hints.label: Middle Bronze Age
hints.source: The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion

nodes.title: Initial Early Phrygian (Turkey, 949 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Turkey, 949 BC–899 BC] Initial Early Phrygian. Period definition from The archaeology of Midas and the Phrygians : recent work at Gordion — 2005.

The earliest layers of Phrygian occupation at Gordion, when the settlement on the Sangarios began to take on the plan of a citadel with megaron-style halls. Buildings and pottery from these levels underlie the more famous city of the Midas era and the great burial mounds that surround it. For archaeologists, the phase matters mainly for dating: it anchors the start of Phrygian material culture in central Anatolia after the collapse of Hittite power.

properties.title: jar — 9thC BC-8thC BC (about)
properties.notes:
