nodes.name: Mughal dynasty (India, AD 1526–AD 1805)
nodes.title: Mughal dynasty (India, AD 1526–AD 1805)
nodes.description:
[India, AD 1526–AD 1805] Mughal dynasty. 1526-1805; India. Period definition from British Museum.

Babur's victory at Panipat founded an empire that, under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, governed most of the subcontinent through a salaried military aristocracy and a cash revenue system assessed on measured land. Its courts fused Persian, Central Asian and Indian traditions into the architecture of Fatehpur Sikri and the Taj Mahal, miniature painting, and the Urdu language. After Aurangzeb's costly southern wars the empire fragmented, and later emperors ruled in name only under Maratha and then British protection.

nodes.name: Late Cypriot (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC) [p08m57hgrmh]
nodes.title: Late Cypriot (Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC) [p08m57hgrmh]
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1649 BC–1049 BC] Late Cypriot. 1650 BC-1050 BC.  The third major division of the Cypriot Bronze Age is marked by the appearance of new pottery types, such as White Slip, Base Ring and Monochrome in the North West of the island, which gradually replace older fabrics which continue in use from the Middle Bronze Age. Other important fabrics included Bichrome Wheelmade, Red Lustrous Wheelmade and various Plain and Painted Wheelmade wares; the latter are heavily influenced by imports from the Mycenaean world in particular (but also the Levant) which gradually displace the older hand-made wares by the 12th century.  The period is characterised by a thriving copper extraction industry, intense commercial interchange with surrounding regions – with imports visible from all around the Eastern Mediterranean - , and the emergence of more complex forms of social organisation, which can be called towns by LCIIC and LCIIIA. Literacy is attested in the form of documents written in a script called Cypro-Minoan, which has some links with Bronze Age Crete.  The last phase of the LC period, LCIII is a transitional period marked by major changes in the settlement pattern, burial practices, economy and material culture (including pottery types); the development of Proto-White Painted and Proto-Bichrome wares signal the beginning of the Iron Age in ceramic terms. The development of iron-making technology, in which Cypriot metallurgists played a leading role, develops apace at this time. Period definition from British Museum.

Cyprus's boom as the Mediterranean's copper supplier, exporting oxhide ingots from harbour towns such as Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke and appearing in Egyptian and Hittite records as Alashiya. Ashlar buildings, imported Mycenaean and Levantine pottery, ivories and the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script mark an urban, cosmopolitan society. After 1200 BC, when the surrounding Bronze Age states collapsed, Aegean settlers arrived, new sanctuaries and iron-working appeared, and the foundations of the Iron Age Cypriot kingdoms were laid.

nodes.name: Liu Shan (China, AD 223–AD 263)
nodes.title: Liu Shan (China, AD 223–AD 263)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 223–AD 263] Liu Shan. 223-263 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The son of Liu Bei and second and last emperor of Shu Han, who inherited a small mountain kingdom in Sichuan at sixteen and left its government largely to Zhuge Liang and his successors. When Wei armies broke through in 263 he surrendered without a final fight and was resettled in comfort at the enemy capital, allegedly saying he did not miss home at all. His reign ends one of the three kingdoms whose wars became China's most retold historical drama.

nodes.name: Johei Era (Japan, AD 931–AD 938)
nodes.title: Johei Era (Japan, AD 931–AD 938)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 931–AD 938] Johei Era. 931-938. Period definition from British Museum.

The years when Taira no Masakado's feuds in eastern Japan escalated into open rebellion against the court, while Fujiwara no Sumitomo turned to piracy in the Inland Sea. Together these revolts exposed how little real power the Kyoto government held in the provinces, and how much it depended on other warriors to suppress them.

nodes.name: Dien Ninh reign period (Vietnam, AD 1454–AD 1459)
nodes.title: Dien Ninh reign period (Vietnam, AD 1454–AD 1459)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1454–AD 1459] Dien Ninh reign period. Dien Ninh reign period (1454-1459). Period definition from British Museum.

The era name of the boy-emperor Lê Nhân Tông's personal rule, after his mother's long regency ended. Court politics remained tense between rival factions of the Lê aristocracy, and the reign closed violently when the emperor and his mother were killed in a palace coup by his elder brother. The usurper lasted less than a year before officials overthrew him and installed Lê Thánh Tông, whose reign became the dynasty's golden age.

nodes.name: Gaudo (Campania, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Gaudo (Campania, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Campania, 2999 BC–1999 BC] Gaudo. 3000BC-2000BC.  Used with Campania as production place. Period definition from British Museum.

Known above all from its cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs near Paestum, where the dead were laid in groups in artificial caves reached by shafts. The pottery is unmistakable: sharply carinated flasks, asymmetric bowls and double vessels in a dark burnished ware, buried alongside copper daggers and flint arrowheads. It marks the arrival of metal-using communities in southern Italy and a new emphasis on the warrior in burial display.

properties.title: askos — 2800BC-2400BC
properties.notes:
Pottery askos with decoration of fine incised lines imitating the stitching on containers made from animal organs or skins. In horizontal outline it is sub-rectangular, while on the flattened upper surface is a tapering cylindrical neck and strap handle; | Type: askos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 26.67 centimetres; | Culture: Gaudo

Campania, Paestum, Italy

nodes.name: Zhenzong (China, AD 998–AD 1022)
nodes.title: Zhenzong (China, AD 998–AD 1022)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 998–AD 1022] Zhenzong. 998-1022 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

After a costly stalemate with the Khitan Liao, the Song court bought peace with the Treaty of Chanyuan, paying annual silver and silk in exchange for a stable northern border that held for over a century. The emperor then staged elaborate and expensive Heaven-sent-text ceremonies and imperial sacrifices to shore up his prestige. Peace underwrote a boom in trade, printing and the examination-trained bureaucracy that defined Song government.

nodes.name: Sonso (Colombia, AD 700–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Sonso (Colombia, AD 700–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Calima region of Colombia in the Western Range of the Valle del Cauca department, AD 700–AD 1600] Sonso. The term refers to a period and a culture of the Calima region of Colombia in the Western Range of the Valle del Cauca department from 700 AD to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The last prehispanic phase of the Calima region in Colombia's western cordillera, following the goldworking heyday of Yotoco. Communities lived in dispersed hamlets on artificial house terraces cut into the slopes, farming maize on ridged fields, and buried their dead in deep shaft-and-chamber tombs. Its pottery and simpler gold ornaments were still in use when Spanish forces entered the valley.

nodes.name: Northern Zhou dynasty (China, AD 557–AD 581)
nodes.title: Northern Zhou dynasty (China, AD 557–AD 581)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 557–AD 581] Northern Zhou dynasty. 557-581. Period definition from British Museum.

Successor to the Western Wei in the Wei valley, this regime turned a weaker resource base into military advantage through the fubing militia and an aristocratic elite fusing Xianbei and Chinese families. It absorbed its eastern rival in 577 and briefly ruled all of northern China. Its usurpation by Yang Jian led directly to the Sui reunification of the empire.

nodes.name: Enkei Era (Japan, AD 1308–AD 1311)
nodes.title: Enkei Era (Japan, AD 1308–AD 1311)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1308–AD 1311] Enkei Era. 1308-1311. Period definition from British Museum.

A short Kamakura-period era name, beginning with the accession of Emperor Hanazono after the death of Go-Nijo. It falls within the awkward arrangement, brokered by the Hojo regents in Kamakura, under which the throne alternated between two rival imperial lines — a compromise that would eventually fracture into the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts.

nodes.name: Genryaku Era (Japan, AD 1184–AD 1185)
nodes.title: Genryaku Era (Japan, AD 1184–AD 1185)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1184–AD 1185] Genryaku Era. 1184-1185. Period definition from British Museum.

The closing act of the Genpei War: Minamoto no Yoshitsune's victories at Ichi-no-Tani and Yashima drove the Taira to sea, and at Dan-no-ura their fleet was destroyed and the child emperor Antoku drowned with the imperial sword. With the Taira annihilated, Minamoto no Yoritomo began installing stewards and constables across the provinces — the skeleton of Japan's first warrior government.

nodes.name: Tianshou (China, AD 1038–AD 1048)
nodes.title: Tianshou (China, AD 1038–AD 1048)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1038–AD 1048] Tianshou. 1038-1048. Period definition from British Museum.

Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Xia, converting the Tangut border state into a rival empire that refused to accept Song overlordship. He promoted a distinctive Tangut script, court dress and rituals, and fought the Song to a standstill in a series of battles that ended with Kaifeng paying annual silver, silk and tea in exchange for nominal submission. His murder by his own son plunged the new state into a long regency.

nodes.name: Jokyu Era (Japan, AD 1219–AD 1222)
nodes.title: Jokyu Era (Japan, AD 1219–AD 1222)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1219–AD 1222] Jokyu Era. 1219-1222. Period definition from British Museum.

Dominated by the Jokyu War of 1221, when the retired emperor Go-Toba raised troops to overthrow the Hojo regents who controlled the Kamakura shogunate. The imperial forces were crushed in weeks; Go-Toba was exiled to the Oki Islands, court estates were confiscated and handed to warrior loyalists, and the shogunate installed governors in Kyoto to watch the throne. Military government had definitively become the real power in Japan.

nodes.name: Jogan Era (Japan, AD 859–AD 877)
nodes.title: Jogan Era (Japan, AD 859–AD 877)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 859–AD 877] Jogan Era. 859-877. Period definition from British Museum.

A formative stretch of early Heian Japan in which the Fujiwara secured the regency for the first time under Yoshifusa, and esoteric Tendai and Shingon Buddhism reshaped religious art. Art historians still use 'Jōgan style' for the heavy, brooding wooden sculpture of these decades. The era also saw the great Sanriku earthquake and tsunami of 869, whose deposits were studied again after 2011.

nodes.name: Eiryaku Era (Japan, AD 1160–AD 1161)
nodes.title: Eiryaku Era (Japan, AD 1160–AD 1161)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1160–AD 1161] Eiryaku Era. 1160-1161. Period definition from British Museum.

The short era immediately after the Heiji Disturbance, in which Taira no Kiyomori destroyed his Minamoto rivals and made himself the dominant figure at court. The defeated Minamoto no Yoshitomo was killed and his young son Yoritomo exiled to Izu - a mercy that would cost the Taira everything twenty years later.

nodes.name: San Agustin Regional Classic (Colombia, AD 1–AD 900)
nodes.title: San Agustin Regional Classic (Colombia, AD 1–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Colombia, AD 1–AD 900] San Agustin Regional Classic. The terms refer to a period of the San Agustin cultural tradition of Colombia in the upper Magdalena valley in the Huila department from 1 AD to 900 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

The peak of monument building in the upper Magdalena, when the great stone sculptures were carved and installed inside mound-covered burial chambers made of massive slabs, some painted red, black and yellow. The scale of the tombs implies chiefs able to command a great deal of labour, while the imagery of jaguar mouths, twinned figures and staff-bearing guardians suggests a shamanic religion. Nothing comparable in stone was produced anywhere else in Colombia.

nodes.name: Meitoku Era (Japan, AD 1390–AD 1394)
nodes.title: Meitoku Era (Japan, AD 1390–AD 1394)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1390–AD 1394] Meitoku Era. 1390-1394. Period definition from British Museum.

The Yamana clan's revolt against the shogun was crushed in 1391, breaking the power of a family said to control a sixth of Japan's provinces. The following year Ashikaga Yoshimitsu negotiated the return of the southern emperor's regalia, ending the sixty-year split between rival imperial courts. It marks the high point of Ashikaga authority.

nodes.name: Yongzheng (China, AD 1723–AD 1735)
nodes.title: Yongzheng (China, AD 1723–AD 1735)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1723–AD 1735] Yongzheng. 1723-1735 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A famously hard-working and suspicious emperor who tightened Qing control: he created the Grand Council, merged the poll tax into the land tax, attacked corruption through secret palace memorials, and hid his chosen heir's name behind a palace tablet. Imperial kilns at Jingdezhen reached a technical peak under his eye, producing the delicate famille rose and monochrome wares collectors prize. His short reign paid for his son Qianlong's expansive one.

nodes.name: Kogen Era (Japan, AD 1256–AD 1257)
nodes.title: Kogen Era (Japan, AD 1256–AD 1257)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1256–AD 1257] Kogen Era. 1256-1257. Period definition from British Museum.

Marked by epidemic disease and by the retirement of the shogunal regent Hōjō Tokiyori, who took Buddhist vows but continued to steer policy from behind the scenes. The episode showed how real power in Japan had detached itself from formal office — an emperor who did not rule, a shogun who did not command, and a retired regent who did both.

nodes.name: Gia Long (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1819)
nodes.title: Gia Long (Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1819)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1802–AD 1819] Gia Long. (1802-1819) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

Nguyen Anh's defeat of the Tay Son ended decades of civil war and, for the first time, brought the whole length of the country from the Red River delta to the Mekong under one ruler. He took the reign name Gia Long, made Hue his capital and built a vast citadel there, adopted the name Vietnam for the realm, and issued a legal code closely modelled on Qing China. The dynasty he founded lasted until 1945.

nodes.name: Daido Era (Japan, AD 806–AD 810)
nodes.title: Daido Era (Japan, AD 806–AD 810)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 806–AD 810] Daido Era. 806-810. Period definition from British Museum.

The short reign of Emperor Heizei and the first year of his brother Saga, at the beginning of the Heian age. It closed with the Kusuko Incident of 810, in which the retired Heizei tried to seize back power and move the capital to Nara; his defeat confirmed Kyoto as the seat of government and gave the Fujiwara family a further foothold at court.

nodes.name: Northern Dynasties (China, AD 386–AD 581)
nodes.title: Northern Dynasties (China, AD 386–AD 581)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 386–AD 581] Northern Dynasties. 386-581. Period definition from British Museum.

A succession of regimes founded largely by Xianbei and other steppe elites ruled northern China while rival Chinese dynasties held the south. Their rulers adopted Chinese administration, promoted Buddhism on a huge scale — the cave temples at Yungang and Longmen date from this time — and devised the equal-field land system and fubing militia that later empires inherited. Intermarriage between steppe and Chinese aristocratic families produced the northwestern elite from which the Sui and Tang ruling houses emerged.

nodes.name: Later Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 951–AD 960) [p08m57hxm9p]
nodes.title: Later Zhou Dynasty (China, AD 951–AD 960) [p08m57hxm9p]
nodes.description:
[China, AD 951–AD 960] Later Zhou Dynasty. 951-960. Period definition from British Museum.

The last of the Five Dynasties, and the one that laid the groundwork for reunification. Emperor Shizong reformed the army, curbed monastic landholding and melted down bronze Buddhas for coin, then campaigned successfully against the Southern Tang and the Khitan. His death left a child on the throne, and his general Zhao Kuangyin took power to found the Song.

nodes.name: Tongzheng (China, AD 916–AD 916)
nodes.title: Tongzheng (China, AD 916–AD 916)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 916–AD 916] Tongzheng. 916. Period definition from British Museum.

A single-year reign title used by Wang Jian, the former bandit and general who had carved the rich Sichuan basin out of the collapsing Tang empire and ruled it as the Former Shu kingdom. His frequent changing of era names near the end of his life reflects the restless legitimacy-seeking of the Five Dynasties warlord states, each claiming imperial dignity over a fragment of the old empire.

nodes.name: Daoguang (China, AD 1821–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Daoguang (China, AD 1821–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1821–AD 1850] Daoguang. 1821-1850 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Qing emperor who confronted the opium crisis, sending Lin Zexu to destroy the drug stocks at Canton and provoking the First Opium War. Defeat brought the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842: Hong Kong ceded, five ports opened, an indemnity paid, and the tributary system of foreign relations broken. Silver drained abroad, the Yellow River and Grand Canal fell into disrepair, and the rural distress that produced the Taiping rebellion was already building.

nodes.name: Jogen Era 976-978 (Japan, AD 976–AD 978)
nodes.title: Jogen Era 976-978 (Japan, AD 976–AD 978)
nodes.description: [Japan, AD 976–AD 978] Jogen Era 976-978. 976-978. Period definition from British Museum.

nodes.name: Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Elamite (Iran, 1499 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Iran, 1499 BC–999 BC] Middle Elamite. circa 1500 BC-1000 BC. Period normally divided into three phases; Middle Elamite I c.1500 BC-1400 BC, Middle Elamite II c.1400 BC-1200 BC, Middle Elamite III c.1200 BC-1100 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Elam's most powerful era, when kings ruling from Susa and Anshan wrote in Elamite rather than Akkadian and built on a monumental scale. Untash-Napirisha founded the sacred city of Chogha Zanbil with its huge stepped ziggurat, still the best-preserved in the world, and later Shutrukid rulers sacked Babylon and carried off the stele of Hammurabi's laws and the victory monument of Naram-Sin as trophies for Susa. Assyrian and Babylonian counterattacks eventually broke the dynasty.

nodes.name: Ninevite 5 (Iraq, 2999 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.title: Ninevite 5 (Iraq, 2999 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.description:
[northern Mesopotamia, 2999 BC–2499 BC] Ninevite 5. Spatial coverage: Iraq, Mesopotamia, Syria, Turkey. Period within sequence excavated by Campbell-Thompson at Nineveh. Divided into incised and painted for pottery, but can be used as general chronological description c.3000-2500 B.C. for northern Mesopotamia. Period definition from British Museum.

The culture of northern Mesopotamia in the centuries after the Uruk expansion collapsed, when the region returned to smaller farming villages and modest towns while southern Sumer built cities. It is defined by its distinctive fine pottery — first painted, later carved and incised — found from the Tigris to the Khabur. By its end, sites like Tell Brak and Tell Leilan were growing into walled cities again, setting the stage for the Akkadian conquest of the north.

nodes.name: Early Iron Age late (Italy, 899 BC–779 BC)
nodes.title: Early Iron Age late (Italy, 899 BC–779 BC)
nodes.description:
[Italy, 899 BC–779 BC] Early Iron Age late. For Italy: Early Iron Age early c. 1000 BC to 880 BC. Early Iron Age late c. 900 BC to 780 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Villanovan settlements grew into genuine proto-urban centres of hundreds of hectares, with organised cemeteries ringing them. Graves become sharply unequal: some hold weapons, horse gear and imported bronzes, signalling the emergence of an aristocracy. The first Greek and Levantine pottery arrives on the Tyrrhenian coast, the beginning of contacts that would transform Italian art, writing and trade.

nodes.name: Tenpyo-hoji Era (Japan, AD 757–AD 765)
nodes.title: Tenpyo-hoji Era (Japan, AD 757–AD 765)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 757–AD 765] Tenpyo-hoji Era. 757-765. Period definition from British Museum.

Fujiwara no Nakamaro reached unmatched power, installing his own candidate as Emperor Junnin and remodelling the government on Chinese lines. His rebellion against the retired Empress Kōken failed in 764 and he was killed; she retook the throne as Empress Shōtoku with the monk Dōkyō at her side.

nodes.name: Tenmei Era (Japan, AD 1781–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Tenmei Era (Japan, AD 1781–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1781–AD 1789] Tenmei Era. 1781-1789. Period definition from British Museum.

The Tenmei famine killed hundreds of thousands, worsened by the catastrophic 1783 eruption of Mount Asama, and triggered rice riots that tore through Edo and Osaka. The crisis brought down the powerful senior councillor Tanuma Okitsugu and ushered in Matsudaira Sadanobu's austere Kansei reforms.

nodes.name: Early Helladic III (Greece, 2299 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Early Helladic III (Greece, 2299 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 2299 BC–1999 BC] Early Helladic III. 2300BC-2000BC. Period definition from British Museum.

After the destructions, Messenian settlements were smaller and simpler, with apsidal houses and new dark-on-light painted pottery of the Tiryns type. Population and long-distance contacts contracted sharply. The pottery and building traditions of this phase carry directly into the Middle Helladic period.

nodes.name: Western Ganga Dynasty (India, AD 350–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Western Ganga Dynasty (India, AD 350–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[parts of Karnataka in the Deccan, AD 350–AD 1000] Western Ganga Dynasty. The Western Ganga Dynasty (c. 350-1000) ruled parts of Karnataka in the Deccan. Period definition from British Museum.

A long-lived dynasty of southern Karnataka, ruling from Kolar and later Talakad, usually as the junior partner of larger neighbours such as the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas. They were exceptional patrons of Jainism, and under them Kannada emerged as a literary language. Their most famous legacy is the 17-metre monolithic statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, carved around 983 for the Ganga minister Chavundaraya and still bathed in milk and saffron at festivals today.

nodes.name: Bunka Era (Japan, AD 1804–AD 1818)
nodes.title: Bunka Era (Japan, AD 1804–AD 1818)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1804–AD 1818] Bunka Era. 1804-1818. Period definition from British Museum.

A high point of late Edo townsman culture, when Hokusai was at work, kabuki and comic fiction flourished, and the pleasure districts set the fashions of the age. Beyond the closed coast, foreign pressure was mounting: a Russian mission was rebuffed at Nagasaki, a British warship forced the harbour there, and Japanese surveyors began mapping the northern islands. Prosperity in the cities sat alongside rural distress and a shogunate increasingly unsure of how to answer the outside world.

nodes.name: Dawenkou culture (China, 4299 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.title: Dawenkou culture (China, 4299 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.description:
[China, 4299 BC–2399 BC] Dawenkou culture. Neolithic culture, circa 4300 BC-2400 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Farming communities in Shandong and the lower Yellow River who grew millet, kept pigs, and buried their dead with striking differences in wealth — some graves crammed with fine pottery, jade and ivory, others nearly bare. Distinctive customs included the deliberate extraction of upper teeth and the shaping of skulls. Their elegant wheel-thrown vessels and incised pottery marks anticipate the Longshan culture that followed, and the whole sequence feeds into the emergence of early Chinese states.

nodes.name: Eiso Era (Japan, AD 989–AD 990)
nodes.title: Eiso Era (Japan, AD 989–AD 990)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 989–AD 990] Eiso Era. 989-990. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era at the Heian court marked by the death of the regent Fujiwara no Kaneie and the passing of his offices to his son Michitaka, part of the fierce competition within the Fujiwara house to control the boy emperor Ichijo through marriage. The court culture of these decades produced the great writing of Sei Shonagon and Murasaki Shikibu.

nodes.name: Yarmukian (Levant, 5599 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: Yarmukian (Levant, 5599 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Levant, 5599 BC–4999 BC] Yarmukian. The Yarmukian Culture (5600-5000 BC) was first recognised at the site of  Shaar Hagolan (Central Jordan Valley) and was named after the nearby Yarmuk River. In this period the Levant region was characterized by regional cultures and sites are distinguished by distinct forms of material culture (pottery, flint etc). Period definition from British Museum.

One of the first pottery-making cultures of the Levant, following the great Pre-Pottery Neolithic villages. At sites like Sha'ar HaGolan people lived in substantial courtyard houses along planned streets and made pottery decorated with incised herringbone bands. They also left hundreds of pebble and clay figurines with slit 'coffee-bean' eyes, among the earliest large bodies of figurative art in the region.

nodes.name: Early Cycladic (Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Early Cycladic (Greece, 3199 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyclades, 3199 BC–1999 BC] Early Cycladic. The Early Cycladic period (3200BC – 2000BC) refers to material produced in the Cyclades during the Aegean Early Bronze Age. Although it is part of the tripartite scheme (Early, Middle and Late) into which the Aegean Bronze Age is conventionally divided, it is difficult to apply the same subdivisions (I,II,III) as for Early Minoan or Early Helladic. For this reason it is divided into partly overlapping cultural groups, initially defined by Colin Renfrew. The three main groups used to subdivide the period are Grotta-Pelos (q.v.), Keros-Syros (q.v.) and Phylakopi I (q.v.). Period definition from British Museum.

The islands of the Aegean supported small farming and fishing communities that became skilled sailors and metalworkers, moving obsidian, copper and marble around the sea. They are best known for the marble folded-arm figurines placed in graves, pared down to abstract simplicity and much admired by modern artists. Their trading networks laid the groundwork for the later Minoan and Mycenaean maritime world.

nodes.name: Tianqi (China, AD 1621–AD 1627)
nodes.title: Tianqi (China, AD 1621–AD 1627)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1621–AD 1627] Tianqi. 1621-1627 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The teenage Zhu Youjiao preferred carpentry to government, leaving affairs to his old wet nurse and the eunuch Wei Zhongxian, who built a secret police apparatus and had temples raised to himself while still alive. The reformist Donglin scholars who opposed him were purged, imprisoned and tortured to death, poisoning court politics for a generation. Famine, revolt and Manchu pressure on the frontier all deepened while the factions fought.

nodes.name: Yongle (China, AD 1403–AD 1424)
nodes.title: Yongle (China, AD 1403–AD 1424)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1403–AD 1424] Yongle. 1403-1424 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The Yongle Emperor seized the throne from his nephew and then spent two decades making the usurpation look like destiny: he moved the capital north, built the Forbidden City, reopened the Grand Canal and commissioned the vast Yongle Encyclopedia. Zheng He's treasure fleets sailed as far as East Africa, and armies pushed into Mongolia and Vietnam. The costs were enormous, and his successors pulled back from the sea.

properties.title: dish — 1403-1424
properties.notes:
Porcelain serving dish with a bracketed rim and underglaze blue decoration. This large serving dish has lobed sides and an upturned flat bracket-lobed rim with a thickened edge. It stands on a low foot ring. It is painted in uneven blue characteristic of the Yongle period with, in the centre, three bunches of grapes on a leafy vine with delicate tendrils surrounded by a bracket-lobed frame. In the cavetto are six lingzhi sprays alternating with six different flowers: camellia, chrysanthemum, gardenia, hibiscus or azalea, lotus and peony. Around the rim is a flower scroll with blooms each with six pointed petals. The exterior is further painted with individual flowers echoing those inside the dish and adding further varieties. The flat base is unglazed.; | Type: dish | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 41.00 centimetres; 7.00 centimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

Jingdezhen, China

properties.title: ewer — 1403-1424
properties.notes:
Porcelain sengmaohu (monk's cap ewer) incised beneath a monochrome tianbai glaze. This ewer has a globular body, tall neck, elongated spout with a jagged rim and a long handle with a ruyi-shaped thumb piece. It stands on a low foot ring and the base is glazed. Beneath the tianbai (sweet-white) glaze it is incised with formal lotus scrolls around the body and neck, lingzhi scrolls on the spout and handle and with classic scrolls around the foot. At the base of the neck is a collar of lotus lappets framing individual lingzhi with a band of lotus scroll below. Each of these lotus blooms supports one of the Eight Treasures of Buddhism. These auspicious emblems are the canopy, parasol, conch shell, wheel, endless knot, lidded jar, paired fish and lotus.; | Type: ewer | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 19.40 centimetres; 19.20 centimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

Jingdezhen, China

properties.title: moon-flask — 1403-1424
properties.notes:
Porcelain bianhu moon flask with underglaze blue decoration. This bianhu moon or pilgrim flask has a circular body with a flat base, a narrow cylindrical neck which flares out towards the mouth and two arched side handles which join the neck to the body, terminating at each end with a curlicue. The base is concave and unglazed. It is Painted in underglaze blue with fruiting and flowering lychee branches on both sides. White-crested waves, unrestrained by a border are painted around the lower section of the flask; the collar has ruyi heads and a band of lotus lappets around the neck; the rim and handles are also ornamented.; | Type: moon-flask | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 25.00 centimetres; 1.25 kilograms; 22.00 centimetres; 12.00 centimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

This magnificent shrine is modelled in the form of three tiered niches within a rocky or cloud frame. There are two 'anhua' slip five claw dragons chasing pearls under the glaze on the interior. The base is glazed.; | Type: bowl | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 66.00 millimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

There is a three-clawed dragon in reserve against a background of waves in underglaze cobalt blue on the exterior, a wide band of scrolling lotus flowers on the neck, and scrolling lotus leaves below the mouth rim.; | Type: flask | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 446.00 millimetres; 7.20 kilograms; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

Porcelain bowl with incised and anhua decoration beneath a monochrome tianbai glaze. The sides of this delicately potted bowl flare out from a low foot ring. Six V-shaped indentations are made to the rim, suggesting the petals of a flower. Inside, beneath the yellow-tinged white glaze around the sides, is an anhua design of two prancing dragons chasing each other's tails and separated by ruyi clouds. The five-clawed dragons are depicted in profile but with their heads twisted around to stare at the viewer rather than the dragon they pursue. Incised in the centre is a four-character Yongle reign mark written in seal-script characters. To achieve this thinness of body, the sides have been pared down before glazing. The porcelain is completely translucent and fingers can be seen through its walls when it is picked up.; | Type: bowl | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 21.80 centimetres; 7.00 centimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

It stands on a broad hollow stem which spreads towards the foot. Inside it is moulded with an anhua design of dragons in the cavetto and is covered with a clear glaze. Outside the decoration is reserved in white on a copper-red ground. Two five-clawed dragons with closed jaws are seen chasing their flaming pearls among ruyi clouds and the stem has a band of classic scroll framed by double white lines above the foot. The stem is glazed inside.; | Type: stem cup | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 15.00 centimetres; 10.10 centimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

Porcelain bottle vase of yuhuchun form, with a pear-shaped body, narrow neck and flaring mouth rim. There is a band of lingzhi fungi in underglaze blue below the mouth rim, plantain leaves and lotus flowers in underglaze blue on the neck, and lily plants with a butterfly in underglaze blue on the body. The base is glazed.; | Type: bottle | Medium: porcelain | Dimensions: 340.00 millimetres; | Culture: Ming dynasty; Yongle

Jingdezhen, China

nodes.name: Republic (China, AD 1912–AD 1949)
nodes.title: Republic (China, AD 1912–AD 1949)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1912–AD 1949] Republic. 1912-1949. Period definition from British Museum.

The Qing abdication left a republic on paper and warlords in practice: parliamentary government collapsed within years, and provincial militarists fought over the north while the Nationalists built a base in the south. Beneath the fighting came the May Fourth movement, vernacular literature, new universities, and the founding of both the Nationalist and Communist parties. Nanjing government, Japanese invasion and civil war followed, ending with the Communist victory and the Nationalist retreat to Taiwan.

nodes.name: Tu Duc (Vietnam, AD 1848–AD 1883)
nodes.title: Tu Duc (Vietnam, AD 1848–AD 1883)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1848–AD 1883] Tu Duc. (1848-1883) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

Tự Đức ruled as French warships arrived, and lost the southern provinces piece by piece until Cochinchina became a French colony and Tonkin fell in his last years. A conservative Confucian scholar-emperor, he persecuted Catholic missionaries and converts, giving France its pretext, and rejected the modernising proposals of reformers like Nguyễn Trường Tộ. He died childless as the court accepted a protectorate, and Vietnam's independence ended with him.

nodes.name: Late Christian Period I (Sudan, AD 1100–AD 1300)
nodes.title: Late Christian Period I (Sudan, AD 1100–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Nubia and Sudan, AD 1100–AD 1300] Late Christian Period I. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Sudan. The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1100-1300. Period definition from British Museum.

Makuria's last confident centuries, when Nubian kings still ruled from Old Dongola but faced repeated Egyptian raids and mounting tribute demands. Church building continued on a reduced scale, wall paintings took on a heavier, more schematic style, and pilgrimage centres such as Banganarti drew visitors from across the middle Nile. Handmade pottery replaced much of the fine wheelmade tradition, a sign of contracting workshops and trade.

properties.title: vessel — 12thC-13thC
properties.notes:
Redware pottery aquamanile vessel in form of animal; yellow glaze; partially reassembled from fragments.; | Type: vessel | Medium: pottery | Culture: Christian

Soba East, Sudan

nodes.name: Zhenglong (China, AD 1156–AD 1161)
nodes.title: Zhenglong (China, AD 1156–AD 1161)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1156–AD 1161] Zhenglong. 1156-1161 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The last era of Wanyan Liang, the Jin ruler who murdered his way to the throne, moved the capital south and razed the old Jurchen homeland centre. He launched a massive invasion of Southern Song, only for his fleet to be shattered at Caishi; his own officers then assassinated him in camp. The failure fixed the Huai River frontier between Jin and Song for decades.

nodes.name: Hoan Era (Japan, AD 1120–AD 1124)
nodes.title: Hoan Era (Japan, AD 1120–AD 1124)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1120–AD 1124] Hoan Era. 1120-1124. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign-era of the late Heian court, when real power lay not with the reigning emperor but with a retired sovereign ruling from his cloistered household, and with the Fujiwara regents at the palace. Provincial warrior houses were meanwhile accumulating land and armed followings that would soon dominate the country.

nodes.name: Taisho Era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926)
nodes.title: Taisho Era (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926] Taisho Era. 1912-1926. Period definition from British Museum.

A short reign, under an emperor too ill to govern, in which power drifted from the old oligarchs to political parties and the Diet. Cities boomed, mass newspapers and cinema spread, women entered offices and factories, and the era's liberal mood gave Japan its first genuine party cabinets and universal male suffrage. The great Kantō earthquake of 1923 levelled Tokyo and Yokohama and hardened the state's repressive instincts.

nodes.name: Joei Era (Japan, AD 1232–AD 1233)
nodes.title: Joei Era (Japan, AD 1232–AD 1233)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1232–AD 1233] Joei Era. 1232-1233. Period definition from British Museum.

In 1232 the Kamakura regent Hōjō Yasutoki issued the Goseibai Shikimoku, a plain-spoken code of fifty-one articles governing land disputes, inheritance and the duties of warriors. It was the first legal system written by and for the samurai rather than the imperial court, and it shaped Japanese law for centuries.

nodes.name: Guangxu (China, AD 1875–AD 1908)
nodes.title: Guangxu (China, AD 1875–AD 1908)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1875–AD 1908] Guangxu. 1875-1908 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of a boy emperor who spent most of his life under the thumb of the Empress Dowager Cixi, in decades when the Qing empire lost a war to Japan, ceded ports to European powers and faced the Boxer uprising. His backing of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898 ended with the reformers executed or exiled and the emperor confined to a palace island. He died a day before Cixi, of arsenic poisoning, leaving the dynasty three years from its end.

nodes.name: Early Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.title: Early Haftavan Period VIB (Iran, 1899 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Haftavan Tepe, Iran, 1899 BC–1549 BC] Early Haftavan Period VIB. Period at Haftavan Tepe, Iran, c.1900BC-1550BC. Period definition from British Museum.

A Middle Bronze Age phase in the Lake Urmia basin, named from the levels at Haftavan Tepe. Its signature is the handsome painted 'Urmia ware' — dark burnished vessels with geometric designs — which links the region to painted pottery traditions running through eastern Anatolia and the Caucasus, and to the mobile, pastorally inclined societies that succeeded the Kura-Araxes world.

nodes.name: Later Zhao (China, AD 319–AD 351)
nodes.title: Later Zhao (China, AD 319–AD 351)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 319–AD 351] Later Zhao. 319-351. Period definition from British Museum.

A state founded by Shi Le, a man sold into slavery as a youth who rose to command armies and rule much of northern China during the chaos after the fall of Western Jin. His court patronised the Central Asian Buddhist monk Fotudeng, an early foothold for Buddhism among northern rulers. The dynasty ended in massacre and civil war after the tyrannical reign of Shi Hu.

nodes.name: Ten'yo Era (Japan, AD 1144–AD 1145)
nodes.title: Ten'yo Era (Japan, AD 1144–AD 1145)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1144–AD 1145] Ten'yo Era. 1144-1145. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief era in the reign of the boy-emperor Konoe, when real authority lay with the retired emperor Toba, who governed as a cloistered sovereign from outside the formal court. The rivalries among Toba's sons and consorts nursed during these years erupted a decade later in the Hōgen Disturbance, opening the door to warrior rule.

nodes.name: Kyoroku Era (Japan, AD 1528–AD 1532)
nodes.title: Kyoroku Era (Japan, AD 1528–AD 1532)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1528–AD 1532] Kyoroku Era. 1528-1532. Period definition from British Museum.

A brief reign name in the middle of the Sengoku wars, when the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiharu was repeatedly driven out of Kyoto and depended on rival Hosokawa and Miyoshi warlords for protection. Real authority had passed to provincial daimyo who fought over the capital as a prize. The court continued to issue era names it had no power to enforce.

nodes.name: Bunpo Era (Japan, AD 1317–AD 1319)
nodes.title: Bunpo Era (Japan, AD 1317–AD 1319)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1317–AD 1319] Bunpo Era. 1317-1319. Period definition from British Museum.

The era of the Bunpō Compromise, a brokered agreement by which the Kamakura shogunate tried to settle the quarrel between the two branches of the imperial house by having them alternate on the throne. It brought Go-Daigo to power — the emperor who would reject the arrangement, overthrow the shogunate, and plunge Japan into the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts.

nodes.name: Cypro-Geometric III (Cyprus, 899 BC–749 BC)
nodes.title: Cypro-Geometric III (Cyprus, 899 BC–749 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 899 BC–749 BC] Cypro-Geometric III. 900 BC-750 BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Cypriot trade expanded sharply: Black-on-Red juglets, probably carrying perfumed oil, reached Greece, Crete, the Levant and the west, while Levantine and Aegean goods flowed back. Rich tombs and the rebuilding of sanctuaries show emerging royal families, the ancestors of the historical city-kingdoms that would soon submit to Assyria.

nodes.name: Xiaozong (China, AD 1163–AD 1190)
nodes.title: Xiaozong (China, AD 1163–AD 1190)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1163–AD 1190] Xiaozong. 1163-1190 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

Usually reckoned the ablest Southern Song emperor: he cleared the name of the executed general Yue Fei, tried one campaign against the Jin, then settled for a treaty on better terms that held for decades. The peace paid for a flourishing of trade, printing and Neo-Confucian scholarship, with Zhu Xi active at court and in the academies. He ended by abdicating to his son, as his own predecessor had done.

nodes.name: Wuzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1308–AD 1311)
nodes.title: Wuzong Yuan dynasty (China, AD 1308–AD 1311)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1308–AD 1311] Wuzong Yuan dynasty. 1308-1311 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A brief Yuan reign that came out of a contested succession settled by military backing, and spent freely on rewards to supporters, temple building and Buddhist patronage. To pay for it the court issued a new paper currency, which quickly lost value and worsened the fiscal disorder that dogged the dynasty. His death after three years reopened the succession struggles that steadily weakened Mongol rule in China.

nodes.name: Zhaodi (China, 85 BC–72 BC)
nodes.title: Zhaodi (China, 85 BC–72 BC)
nodes.description:
[China, 85 BC–72 BC] Zhaodi. 86-73BC (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

A child emperor of the Han ruled in name while the general Huo Guang held actual power, steering the empire away from the ruinously expensive wars and expansion of Emperor Wu. Taxes and labour levies were eased and frontier campaigning scaled back. The famous court debate on the state monopolies of salt and iron, later written up as the Discourses on Salt and Iron, pitted Legalist-minded officials against Confucian critics of state enterprise.

nodes.name: Kanpyo Era (Japan, AD 889–AD 898)
nodes.title: Kanpyo Era (Japan, AD 889–AD 898)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 889–AD 898] Kanpyo Era. 889-898. Period definition from British Museum.

Emperor Uda governed without a Fujiwara regent after Mototsune's death, raising the scholar Sugawara no Michizane to counterbalance the great house—a short-lived experiment later remembered as good government. In 894 the court cancelled the embassy to Tang China, ending two and a half centuries of official missions and turning the aristocracy inward toward a distinctly Japanese court culture.

nodes.name: Early Helladic I (Greece, 3199 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.title: Early Helladic I (Greece, 3199 BC–2899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 3199 BC–2899 BC] Early Helladic I. 3200BC-2900BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Small farming hamlets in the southwest Peloponnese take up metal and new pottery shapes, the first mainland stage of the Bronze Age. Settlements were modest and scattered, with burials in simple pits and cists rather than monumental tombs. It provides the baseline against which the wealthier, more centralised communities of the following centuries stand out.

nodes.name: Thieu Tri (Vietnam, AD 1841–AD 1847)
nodes.title: Thieu Tri (Vietnam, AD 1841–AD 1847)
nodes.description:
[Vietnam, AD 1841–AD 1847] Thieu Tri. (1841-1847) reign. Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of a Nguyen emperor who inherited his father Minh Mang's centralised, Confucian state and his hostility to Christian missionaries. Persecution of Catholics continued and gave France a pretext for intervention: in 1847 French warships destroyed the Vietnamese fleet at Da Nang, an early step toward colonial conquest. He died soon after, leaving the crisis to his son Tu Duc.

nodes.name: Bosnian (Egypt, AD 1550–AD 1811)
nodes.title: Bosnian (Egypt, AD 1550–AD 1811)
nodes.description: [fortress of Qasr Ibrim, AD 1550–AD 1811] Bosnian. The term Bosnian as a narrower term of Ottoman dynasty refers to a specific cultural period on the fortress of  Qasr Ibrim between 1550-1811 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

nodes.name: Genroku Era (Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704)
nodes.title: Genroku Era (Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1688–AD 1704] Genroku Era. 1688-1704. Period definition from British Museum.

A boom time for the merchant cities, when Osaka and Edo money paid for kabuki, the puppet theatre of Chikamatsu, the novels of Ihara Saikaku, Bashō's poetry and the first great wave of ukiyo-e prints. The shogunate under Tsunayoshi debased the coinage to cover its spending and issued the notorious edicts protecting dogs and other animals. The revenge of the forty-seven rōnin in 1702 gave the age its most enduring story.

nodes.name: Zhiyuan Shundi (China, AD 1335–AD 1340)
nodes.title: Zhiyuan Shundi (China, AD 1335–AD 1340)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1335–AD 1340] Zhiyuan Shundi. 1335-1340 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The early years of Toghon Temür, the last Yuan emperor, when real power lay with the chancellor Bayan, who abolished the civil service examinations and pushed harshly anti-Chinese measures that alienated the literati the dynasty needed. Bayan's own nephew overthrew him and reversed course. The reprieve came too late to steady a regime already sliding toward rebellion.

nodes.name: Middle Minoan II (Crete, 1849 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Minoan II (Crete, 1849 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 1849 BC–1699 BC] Middle Minoan II. 1850BC-1700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The high point of the first palaces, when Phaistos and Knossos ran centralised storage and craft production and kept records with seals and Cretan Hieroglyphic script. Kamares ware reached its technical peak, thin as an eggshell and painted with swirling white, red and orange designs, and it turns up in Egypt and along the Levantine coast as evidence of Cretan trade. The phase closed with widespread destruction, probably by earthquake.

nodes.name: Middle Minoan (Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Minoan (Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 1999 BC–1599 BC] Middle Minoan. 2000BC-1600BC. Period definition from British Museum.

Crete's first palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, huge multi-storey complexes built around a central court, packed with storage magazines for oil and grain and workshops for craft production. Administrators kept accounts on clay in Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A, potters threw eggshell-thin Kamares ware painted in white and red on black, and Cretan goods travelled to Egypt and the Levant. Earthquakes levelled the palaces around 1700 BC; they were rebuilt grander still.

nodes.name: Zhongxi (China, AD 1032–AD 1054)
nodes.title: Zhongxi (China, AD 1032–AD 1054)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1032–AD 1054] Zhongxi. 1032-1054 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The long Chongxi era of Emperor Xingzong of the Khitan Liao, a settled period of dual Khitan-Chinese administration, Buddhist temple building and the casting of Chongxi coinage. Taking advantage of Song troubles with the Tanguts, the Liao court extracted an increase in the annual payments agreed at Chanyuan without going to war. Repeated Liao campaigns against Western Xia, however, went badly.

nodes.name: Yuanzhen (China, AD 1295–AD 1297)
nodes.title: Yuanzhen (China, AD 1295–AD 1297)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1295–AD 1297] Yuanzhen. 1295-1297 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The first reign period of Temür Öljeytü, who succeeded his grandfather Kublai and inherited an empire that had stopped expanding. He ended the costly campaigns against Vietnam and Japan, patched up relations with rival Mongol khanates and tried to curb corruption and runaway spending. It was a short, comparatively peaceful interlude before the succession struggles that destabilised the later Yuan court.

nodes.name: Early Historic (India, 499 BC–AD 500)
nodes.title: Early Historic (India, 499 BC–AD 500)
nodes.description:
[India, 499 BC–AD 500] Early Historic. The term is used to broadly define the period in India between about 500 BC - AD 500 and follows the Iron Age. It includes the periods of the Mauryan empire and the Guptas. Period definition from British Museum.

Cities returned to the subcontinent on a large scale, with fortified capitals, punch-marked coins, writing in Brahmi and Kharoshthi, and organised craft and trade guilds. Buddhism and Jainism took shape and then spread under Mauryan patronage, leaving Ashoka's rock edicts, stupas and rock-cut monasteries. Ports on both coasts traded with Rome and Southeast Asia, and the era's texts, sculpture and inscriptions form the foundation of Indian history proper.

nodes.name: Susa III (Iran, 3099 BC–2699 BC)
nodes.title: Susa III (Iran, 3099 BC–2699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Khuzestan, 3099 BC–2699 BC] Susa III. Khuzestan, ca 3100BC-2700BC. Period definition from British Museum.

The Proto-Elamite horizon, when Susa and sites across the Iranian plateau used a still-undeciphered script of their own on thousands of accounting tablets. Distinctive glyptic art depicts animals acting as humans—lions enthroned, bulls holding vessels. The network collapsed after a few centuries, leaving Susa oriented once more toward Mesopotamia.

nodes.name: Cypro-Geometric (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC)
nodes.title: Cypro-Geometric (Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 1049 BC–749 BC] Cypro-Geometric. 1050 BC-750 BC.  The Cypro-Geometric period, some three hundred years in duration, is the first division of the Cypriot Iron Age. Settlements founded during the transitional LCIII period become the urban centres of the city-kingdoms into which the island is divided in historic times. Economic and cultural contacts with the Levantine world with are re-established (or become archaeologically visible) after a short period of isolation; contacts with the Aegean become apparent again somewhat later in this horizon. Important ceramic types include White Painted and Bichrome wares, which are decorated with geometric motifs and often occur in inventive shapes; slightly later, the distinctive Black-on-Red wares are developed on Cyprus, partly as a result of contact with the Levantine world; fine metalworking in bronze abounds, particularly in burials. Inscriptions point to the existence of Greek and Phoenician speakers on the island living alongside the local Cypriot population. Period definition from British Museum.

After the collapse of the Late Bronze Age palaces, Cyprus rebuilt around new coastal centres such as Salamis, Kition and Palaepaphos, with iron replacing bronze for tools and weapons. Greek-speaking settlers left their mark in dialect and burial customs, and a Cypriot syllabary continued to be written. Phoenicians established themselves at Kition, and by the end of the period the island's kingdoms were wealthy enough to attract Assyrian attention.

nodes.name: Quimbaya (Colombia, 499 BC–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Quimbaya (Colombia, 499 BC–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Colombia, 499 BC–AD 1600] Quimbaya. The term refers to a region of Colombia in the Middle Cauca valley and the Central Range in the Antioquia, Caldas, Risaralda and Quindio departments from 500 BC to 1600 AD. Period definition from British Museum.

Goldsmiths of the middle Cauca valley whose work is among the finest ever produced in the Americas: hollow-cast flasks and lime containers of astonishing smoothness, made in a gold-copper alloy called tumbaga and finished by chemically etching the copper from the surface. Their serene, rounded human figures and the famous Quimbaya Treasure made the name famous worldwide. Spanish arrival brought conquest, disease and the looting of tombs that still continues.

nodes.name: Yuanyou (China, AD 1086–AD 1093)
nodes.title: Yuanyou (China, AD 1086–AD 1093)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1086–AD 1093] Yuanyou. 1086-1093 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

With the young Emperor Zhezong on the throne, his grandmother Empress Dowager Gao ruled as regent and recalled Sima Guang and the conservatives, who dismantled most of Wang Anshi's New Policies within months. The reversal was itself reversed when Zhezong took power, and those who had served in these years were blacklisted as the "Yuanyou faction", their names carved on stone tablets of proscription. The bitter factionalism weakened the Song state on the eve of the Jurchen invasions.

nodes.name: Xuanhe (China, AD 1119–AD 1125)
nodes.title: Xuanhe (China, AD 1119–AD 1125)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1119–AD 1125] Xuanhe. 1119-1125 (era). Period definition from British Museum.

The final era of the Song emperor Huizong, an aesthete who catalogued the imperial painting and bronze collections, founded an academy of court artists and beggared the treasury shipping exotic rocks for his garden. Peasant and bandit uprisings spread while the court allied with the Jurchen Jin to destroy the Liao. The Jin turned on Song immediately after, and by 1127 Huizong and his son were prisoners in the north.

nodes.name: Hailingwang (China, AD 1149–AD 1161)
nodes.title: Hailingwang (China, AD 1149–AD 1161)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 1149–AD 1161] Hailingwang. 1149-1161 (reign). Period definition from British Museum.

The reign of Wanyan Liang, the Jin ruler stripped of imperial title after his death and demoted to "Prince of Hailing." He purged rival princes, moved the Jurchen capital south to Yanjing (modern Beijing) to govern his Chinese subjects more directly, and pushed sinicising reforms on the court. His huge invasion of the Southern Song collapsed at the Yangtze, and his own officers murdered him in camp, leaving the Song–Jin border much as it had been.

nodes.name: Jinki Era (China, AD 724–AD 729)
nodes.title: Jinki Era (China, AD 724–AD 729)
nodes.description:
[China, AD 724–AD 729] Jinki Era. 724-729. Period definition from British Museum.

The years around the accession of Emperor Shōmu, the ruler whose devotion to Buddhism would later produce the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji. The Nara court was consolidating its Chinese-style law codes, land registers and provincial administration, and the Fujiwara family was tightening its grip on the throne through marriage.

properties.notes:
Lead-glazed lidded box ('sancai' ware). The base is unglazed and the lid knobbed. Made of transparent, mottled, cobalt blue glazed earthenware.(buff).; | Type: box | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 7.10 centimetres; | Culture: Tang dynasty

Yaozhou, Chang'an, China

Figure (groom). Made of brown, green glazed earthenware.; | Type: figure | Medium: earthenware | Dimensions: 18.50 inches; | Culture: Tang dynasty

properties.title: figure — 728 (Date recorded for the death of general Liu Tingxun.)
