He is the Arabian prince from who the deposed High Priest Jason requested asylym in 168 BCE....Most of the Nabatean kings who reigned in Petra from that date until the abolishment of the Nabatean kingdom in 106 CE are known." (page 1181). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The Nabataeans emerge in the historical record as nomadic traders controlling the incense and spice routes from Arabia to the Mediterranean—first described when a Hellenistic army failed to subdue them. Over these centuries they settled, mastered desert water catchment, and began carving the tombs and cult places at Petra. Their wealth came from taxing caravans rather than farming, and their kingdom grew rich enough to strike its own coinage.

hints.label: Early Nabatean Period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3299 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic (Israel, 4499 BC–3299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 4499 BC–3299 BC] Chalcolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Corresponding cultural periods are Early phase and Ghassulian phase (derived from chronological table on page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

hints.label: Chalcolithic
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Ottoman period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917)
nodes.title: Ottoman period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, AD 1516–AD 1917] Ottoman period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Selim I's defeat of the Mamluks brought Palestine under Ottoman rule, and Suleiman the Magnificent rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem that still stand today. For most of four centuries the region was a quiet cluster of districts governed from Damascus and Sidon, its towns supported by pilgrimage, soap and grain, though the nineteenth century brought European consuls, missionary institutions, new farming colonies and the first Zionist settlements. British forces took the country in 1917.

hints.label: Ottoman period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (Israel, 1549 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Late Roman period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324)
nodes.title: Late Roman period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, AD 132–AD 324] Late Roman period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

After the crushing of the Bar Kokhba revolt, Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina, Jerusalem was rebuilt as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from the city. Jewish life regrouped in Galilee, where the Mishnah and later the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled and monumental stone synagogues began to appear. Cities like Caesarea and Beth Shean flourished on Roman roads and aqueducts, while a small Christian community grew that would soon, under Constantine, transform the whole country.

hints.label: Late Roman period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Late Arab period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 1516)
nodes.title: Late Arab period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 1516)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, AD 1291–AD 1516] Late Arab period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. The Late Arab period encompasses the Fatimid and Mameluke, which are not differentiated chronologically here. (page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Mamluk rule from Cairo replaced the Crusader states, and administration shifted decisively inland. Jerusalem gained a dense fabric of religious colleges and fountains around the Haram, caravanserais and bridges served the Cairo–Damascus post road, and the demolished harbours of the coast stayed empty. Ottoman conquest ended the era.

hints.label: Late Arab period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age I (Israel, 2199 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Middle Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Towns and cities were re-established across the southern Levant after centuries of largely village and pastoral life, with fortifications, wheel-made pottery and true bronze metallurgy returning. Coastal sites looked north to Byblos and the Syrian world for trade and inspiration. This revival set the framework of Canaanite city-states that Egyptian and biblical sources would later describe.

hints.label: Middle Bronze Age I
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Early Roman period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132)
nodes.title: Early Roman period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 36 BC–AD 132] Early Roman period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Encompasses the Herodian period, 37 BCE-70 CE (page 1529). Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Herod the Great, ruling as Rome's client king, rebuilt the Jerusalem Temple on a vast scale and founded Caesarea Maritima, Masada and other showpiece projects. Direct Roman rule and heavy taxation followed, along with the ferment of sects and messianic movements from which Christianity and rabbinic Judaism both emerged. Two catastrophic revolts frame the era's end: the destruction of the Temple in AD 70 and the crushing of Bar Kokhba's rising.

hints.label: Early Roman period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Late Hellenistic period (Israel, 166 BC–36 BC)
nodes.title: Late Hellenistic period (Israel, 166 BC–36 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 166 BC–36 BC] Late Hellenistic period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

The Maccabean revolt against Seleucid rule produced an independent Jewish state under the Hasmoneans, which expanded aggressively into Galilee, Idumaea and the coastal plain. Fortified palaces, ritual baths and the first distinctly Jewish coinage appear in the archaeological record, alongside Greek imports and architectural styles the Hasmoneans happily borrowed. Roman intervention and dynastic infighting ended the kingdom, clearing the way for Herod.

hints.label: Late Hellenistic period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Early Hellenistic period (Israel, 331 BC–166 BC)
nodes.title: Early Hellenistic period (Israel, 331 BC–166 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 331 BC–166 BC] Early Hellenistic period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Alexander's conquest ended two centuries of Persian rule and pulled the southern Levant into the contest between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek cities, gymnasia, coinage and language spread along the coast and into Jerusalem's elite, provoking tensions over Judaean religious practice. The period closes with Antiochus IV's decrees and the Maccabean revolt.

hints.label: Early Hellenistic period
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Late Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Canaan's towns recovered slowly from the upheavals that ended the Middle Bronze Age, now under Egyptian overlordship after repeated pharaonic campaigns. Settlements were smaller and rarely walled, and the wealth that remained came from trade: painted bichrome jugs, Cypriot base-ring flasks and Aegean vessels found their way into local tombs and temples.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age I
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Pottery Neolithic (Israel, 5499 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Pottery Neolithic (Israel, 5499 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 5499 BC–4499 BC] Pottery Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Based on chronological table on page 1529, this period coincides with part of the post-glacial period of the Ice Age in Europe and the Holocene geological epoch. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

After the great stone-built farming towns of the pre-pottery era broke up, people settled in smaller, looser villages of pit dwellings and courtyard houses, herding sheep and goats alongside their crops. Fired clay vessels came into everyday use for cooking and storage, decorated with incised herringbone bands and red paint, and small clay figurines appear in numbers. It is a period of apparent decline in scale that in fact laid the technical groundwork for the Chalcolithic villages that followed.

hints.label: Pottery Neolithic
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Iron Age IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age IIA (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Holy Land, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron Age IIA. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Period definition from The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim]. — 1993.

Villages grew into fortified towns with gates, palaces and storehouses, and the first real state institutions appear in the southern Levant. Scholars argue bitterly over whether these remains belong to a Solomonic kingdom or to the later Omride dynasty, and radiocarbon dating has become central to the fight. Distinctive red-slipped, burnished pottery marks the horizon at sites from Megiddo to Beersheba.

hints.label: Iron Age IIA
hints.source: The new encyclopedia of archaeological excavations in the Holy Land 4 [Petra - Ziqim].

nodes.name: Late Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800)
nodes.title: Late Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1600–AD 1800] Late Islamic 2. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Ottoman authority over the region was mostly exercised through subsidies to tribal leaders and control of the Hajj route rather than direct administration. Settlement was sparse and largely pastoral, with seasonal camps, small fortified farms and pilgrimage forts making up most of the built record. Coffee and tobacco consumption spread, leaving distinctive clay pipe bowls at almost every site.

hints.label: Late Islamic 2
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516)
nodes.title: Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516] Mamluk. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Under the Cairo sultanate this region became a well-run frontier province, its roads carrying the barid postal relay that linked Egypt to Damascus and its valleys filled with irrigated sugar plantations and refineries. Karak and other castles were rebuilt as administrative centres, and villages grew around the pilgrimage and trade routes. The whole system passed to the Ottomans in 1516.

hints.label: Mamluk
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Late Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Late Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1600] Late Islamic 1. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Late Mamluk sugar estates and villages contracted, and after 1516 the region passed to the Ottomans, who surveyed it for taxation and reorganised the annual Hajj caravan route through it. Fortified way-stations, cisterns and khans were built or refurbished along that road. Many settled sites were abandoned as tribal groups took control of the land.

hints.label: Late Islamic 1
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Middle Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1200–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Middle Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 1200–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1200–AD 1400] Middle Islamic 2. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Mamluk rule brought administrative reorganisation, a functioning postal and road system, and investment in sugar production, mills and market towns. Karak served as a provincial capital and place of exile for rival princes, and the pilgrimage route south was maintained with forts and cisterns. Prosperity faded in the later fourteenth century with plague, Bedouin unrest and economic decline.

hints.label: Middle Islamic 2
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: modern (Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918)
nodes.title: modern (Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1800–AD 1918] modern. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Europe in these centuries built centralised states and overseas empires, argued its way through the Reformation's aftermath, the Enlightenment and revolution, and then industrialised. Steam, railways, factories and mass literacy transformed daily life faster than at any earlier time, while nationalism redrew the map. The era ends in the wreckage of the First World War and the collapse of the continent's old dynastic empires.

hints.label: modern
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171)
nodes.title: Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171] Fatimid. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Cairo's Shi'i caliphs held the Jordanian lands as a frontier zone of their Syrian province, valuable for the pilgrimage and caravan routes running down the desert edge. Bedouin power and Seljuk pressure eroded that control, and the arrival of the Crusaders left the region divided between Frankish castles and Muslim rulers.

hints.label: Fatimid
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Umayyad (Jordan, AD 630–AD 750)
nodes.title: Umayyad (Jordan, AD 630–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 630–AD 750] Umayyad. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Under the caliphs at Damascus, the lands east of the Jordan sat close to the centre of an empire reaching from Spain to Central Asia, rather than on its margins. Umayyad princes built the so-called desert castles here, among them Qusayr Amra with its startling frescoes of bathers, hunters and kings, and Qasr al-Kharana and Qasr al-Mshatta. Towns like Jerash and Pella continued to thrive with new markets and mosques until the earthquake of 749, and the dynasty fell to the Abbasid revolution the following year.

hints.label: Umayyad
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Middle Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Middle Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1200] Middle Islamic 1. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Fatimid and then Crusader and Ayyubid power contested the region, and the great fortresses of Karak and Shobak were raised on the plateau to control the caravan and pilgrim roads. Saladin's victories brought the territory under Ayyubid rule and stimulated the sugar plantations of the Jordan Valley. Villages of this era are recognised by distinctive handmade painted pottery.

hints.label: Middle Islamic 1
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Early Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Islamic 2 (Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 800–AD 1000] Early Islamic 2. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

With the caliphate's centre shifted east to Baghdad, the region lost its patrons; many Umayyad estates were abandoned and settlement contracted. Abbasid and later Fatimid authority was exercised at a distance through provincial towns, while the countryside grew poorer and thinner on the ground. Pottery and glass of this era show the region plugged into wider Islamic trade networks even as its own towns shrank.

hints.label: Early Islamic 2
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 600)
nodes.title: late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 491–AD 600] late Byzantine. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Christian building reached its peak: town after town rebuilt with basilicas paved in mosaic, including the famous map of the Holy Land at Madaba. Pilgrim traffic, olive oil and wine production and imperial patronage under Justinian supported dense settlement even at the desert margins. Plague, earthquakes and Persian invasion would shortly break this prosperity, and within a generation the region passed to Muslim rule.

hints.label: late Byzantine
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Caliphal (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969)
nodes.title: Caliphal (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 630–AD 969] Caliphal. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. The Caliphal period encompasses the Umayyad and Abbasid periods. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Arab-Muslim armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and Jordan became part of the province of Bilad al-Sham, close to the Umayyad heartland at Damascus. The countryside is dotted with the results: the so-called desert castles such as Qusayr Amra and Qasr al-Kharana, with their bathhouses and painted walls, and towns where churches, mosques and mosaic floors sit side by side. When the Abbasids moved the centre of the caliphate to Iraq after 750, the area slipped to the margins, and its towns shrank.

hints.label: Caliphal
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263)
nodes.title: Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263] Ayyubid. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Saladin's Kurdish dynasty ruled Egypt, Syria and the lands east of the Jordan, and his defeat of the crusaders at Hattin in 1187 brought Jerusalem back under Muslim rule. In Transjordan the period left striking military architecture, above all the castle of Ajlun, built to watch the crusader lords and guard the iron mines and communications with Damascus. Family infighting weakened the realm until Mamluk soldiers seized Egypt and the Mongols swept through Syria.

hints.label: Ayyubid
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: High Islam (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918)
nodes.title: High Islam (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918] High Islam. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. Encompasses the Fatimid/Crusader, Ayyubid, and Mamluk periods.  (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Four centuries of Ottoman rule, when the region was governed from Damascus as a frontier of settled administration facing the desert tribes. Its central institution was the pilgrimage road to Mecca, guarded by a chain of forts and cisterns and later paralleled by the Hejaz Railway. Ottoman authority ended with the Arab Revolt and the First World War.

hints.label: High Islam
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Early Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 600–AD 800)
nodes.title: Early Islamic 1 (Jordan, AD 600–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 600–AD 800] Early Islamic 1. This periodization is archaeological, which Whitcomb separates from political periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

The Byzantine defeat at the Yarmuk in AD 636 handed the region to the new Muslim state, but the change on the ground was gradual: the same villages, farms and craft traditions continued, and Christian communities kept building and paving churches with mosaics. Under the Umayyads, ruling from nearby Damascus, elites built rural estates and pleasure palaces along the steppe fringe. Arabic gradually replaced Greek in administration, and coinage and inscriptions took on a new Islamic idiom.

hints.label: Early Islamic 1
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Abbasid (Jordan, AD 750–AD 969)
nodes.title: Abbasid (Jordan, AD 750–AD 969)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 750–AD 969] Abbasid. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Under Abbasid rule the Levant became a province rather than a heartland, as the capital moved from Damascus to Baghdad and Syrian elites lost their privileged position. Desert palaces were abandoned or repurposed, while pilgrimage roads to Mecca and the ports of the coast kept trade alive. Glazed pottery and glass from Iraq spread widely, marking sites of the period.

hints.label: Abbasid
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 630)
nodes.title: late Byzantine (Jordan, AD 491–AD 630)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 491–AD 630] late Byzantine. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization. (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Christian building reached its peak: town after town rebuilt with basilicas paved in mosaic, including the famous map of the Holy Land at Madaba. Pilgrim traffic, olive oil and wine production and imperial patronage under Justinian supported dense settlement even at the desert margins. Plague, earthquakes and Persian invasion would shortly break this prosperity, and within a generation the region passed to Muslim rule.

hints.label: late Byzantine
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918)
nodes.title: Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918] Ottoman. This periodization is political, which Whitcomb separates from archaeological periodization (page 386). Period definition from Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV. — 1992.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

hints.label: Ottoman
hints.source: Studies in the history and archaeology of Jordan IV.

nodes.name: Early Nabataean (Egypt, 167 BC–84 BC)
nodes.title: Early Nabataean (Egypt, 167 BC–84 BC)
nodes.description: [Central Negev, 167 BC–84 BC] Early Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

hints.label: Early Nabataean
hints.source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

nodes.name: Middle Nabataean (Egypt, 84 BC–AD 70)
nodes.title: Middle Nabataean (Egypt, 84 BC–AD 70)
nodes.description:
[Central Negev, 84 BC–AD 70] Middle Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

The Nabataean kingdom at its height, when its rulers grew rich taxing incense and spice caravans moving from Arabia to the Mediterranean and pushed their commercial reach into Sinai and the Egyptian frontier. Petra's rock-cut facades, sophisticated water engineering and distinctive eggshell-thin painted pottery date largely from these generations. Nabataean fortunes shifted as Rome absorbed the surrounding region, and the kingdom survived as a client until its annexation in AD 106.

hints.label: Middle Nabataean
hints.source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

nodes.name: Late Nabataean (Egypt, AD 70–AD 106)
nodes.title: Late Nabataean (Egypt, AD 70–AD 106)
nodes.description:
[Central Negev, AD 70–AD 106] Late Nabataean. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

The last generation of independent Nabataean rule, under Rabbel II, when the kingdom's centre of gravity shifted north toward Bostra and its caravan wealth faced growing Roman competition. Potters were still producing the astonishingly thin, painted 'eggshell' bowls that are the culture's signature. It ended in 106 when Trajan absorbed the kingdom as the province of Arabia.

hints.label: Late Nabataean
hints.source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

nodes.name: Roman Period (Egypt, AD 106–AD 295)
nodes.title: Roman Period (Egypt, AD 106–AD 295)
nodes.description:
[Central Negev, AD 106–AD 295] Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

hints.label: Roman Period
hints.source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

nodes.name: Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 295–AD 635)
nodes.title: Byzantine Period (Egypt, AD 295–AD 635)
nodes.description:
[Central Negev, AD 295–AD 635] Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Jordan, State of Palestine, Syria. Spatial coverage based on map on page 37 (fig 1.36). Period definition from Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal — Tali Erickson-Gini, 2010.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.

hints.label: Byzantine Period
hints.source: Nabataean settlement and self-organized economy in the Central Negev : crisis and renewal

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age II B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The Ramesside phase of Egyptian control in Canaan, marked by Egyptian-style administrative buildings at Beth Shean and elsewhere, hieratic inscriptions and anthropoid clay coffins. It ends with the unravelling of Egyptian power, the burning of major cities, and the first mention of Israel on the Merneptah stele.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age II B
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Early Roman Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132)
nodes.title: Early Roman Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 132)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 36 BC–AD 132] Early Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Rome annexed the island after a hard campaign and joined it administratively to Cyrenaica, with Gortyn as capital. Freed from the endemic warfare between Cretan city-states, the island prospered: aqueducts, theatres and bath buildings went up, harbours handled long-distance trade, and old Greek sanctuaries continued in Roman dress. Gortyn grew into one of the largest cities of the southern Aegean.

hints.label: Early Roman Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age I A (Israel, 1199 BC–1149 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 1199 BC–1149 BC] Iron Age I A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The opening decades after the Late Bronze Age collapse, marked by the burning or abandonment of Canaanite centres and the final withdrawal of Egyptian authority. Locally made Aegean-style Mycenaean IIIC pottery appears at Ashdod, Ekron and Ashkelon, the archaeological signature of Philistine settlement. Meanwhile small new villages begin to dot the central highlands.

hints.label: Iron Age I A
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age II (State of Palestine, 2999 BC–2699 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age II (State of Palestine, 2999 BC–2699 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 2999 BC–2699 BC] Early Bronze Age II. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The Castelluccio culture dominates the island: villages of huts on defensible hills, cemeteries of rock-cut chamber tombs sometimes closed with carved stone slabs, and painted pottery with bold dark designs on a pale ground. Carved bone plaques and imported beads point to contacts reaching Malta, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean, drawing Sicily into wider Bronze Age trade routes.

hints.label: Early Bronze Age II
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC) [p0hsq83b9gd]
nodes.title: Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–36 BC) [p0hsq83b9gd]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 331 BC–36 BC] Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Crete stayed outside the great kingdoms, divided among a hundred quarrelsome city-states whose feuds, mercenary service and piracy made the island notorious. Gortyn and Knossos dominated a landscape of walled hill towns, treaties and inscribed laws, and Cretan archers served in armies across the Mediterranean. Rome finally conquered the island in the 60s BC and made it a province.

hints.label: Hellenistic Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age II B (Israel, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 899 BC–699 BC] Iron Age II B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Two rival kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south, reached their fullest development, with royal capitals at Samaria and Jerusalem, ivory-inlaid furniture, olive oil industries and administrative ostraca. Assyrian pressure grew until Samaria fell in 722 BC and the northern kingdom's population was deported. Judah absorbed refugees, expanded rapidly, and survived Sennacherib's devastating campaign of 701 BC as an Assyrian vassal.

hints.label: Iron Age II B
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age II C (Israel, 699 BC–585 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 699 BC–585 BC] Iron Age II C. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Judah lived on as a client of Assyria and then Babylon, its countryside dotted with olive-oil and textile towns and its bureaucracy leaving thousands of stamped jar handles and inscribed seals. When Assyrian power collapsed, Judah gambled on revolt; Nebuchadnezzar's armies answered by razing Jerusalem and its temple and deporting the elite. The destruction layers of this moment are among the most vividly excavated in the region.

hints.label: Iron Age II C
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0hsq8329bf]
nodes.title: Iron Age (Israel, 1199 BC–585 BC) [p0hsq8329bf]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 1199 BC–585 BC] Iron Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

hints.label: Iron Age
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age I A-B (Israel, 3499 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 3499 BC–2999 BC] Early Bronze Age I A-B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Farming villages in the southern Levant expanded into large unwalled settlements, with growing craft specialisation in copper and pottery. Contact with Egypt intensified until Egyptian-style pottery, seal impressions and even Egyptian residents appear in the southern coastal plain. Within a few generations these communities would build the region's first fortified towns.

hints.label: Early Bronze Age I A-B
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–166 BC)
nodes.title: Early Hellenistic Period (Israel, 331 BC–166 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 331 BC–166 BC] Early Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Alexander's conquest ended two centuries of Persian rule and pulled the southern Levant into the contest between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek cities, gymnasia, coinage and language spread along the coast and into Jerusalem's elite, provoking tensions over Judaean religious practice. The period closes with Antiochus IV's decrees and the Maccabean revolt.

hints.label: Early Hellenistic Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Crusader and Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD 1099–AD 1291)
nodes.title: Crusader and Ayyubid Periods (Israel, AD 1099–AD 1291)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, AD 1099–AD 1291] Crusader and Ayyubid Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The First Crusade's capture of Jerusalem installed a Latin ruling class that built castles, churches and fortified towns across the country, while Muslim and Eastern Christian villagers continued to work the land. Saladin's Ayyubids destroyed the field army at Hattin in 1187 and reduced the kingdom to a coastal strip governed from Acre, sustained by Italian merchant colonies and the military orders. The Mamluk capture of Acre in 1291 ended the Latin presence and left much of the coast deliberately ruined.

hints.label: Crusader and Ayyubid Periods
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638) [p0hsq837tkh]
nodes.title: Byzantine Period (Israel, AD 324–AD 638) [p0hsq837tkh]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, AD 324–AD 638] Byzantine Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Crete under Constantinople, when the old Roman capital at Gortyn was rebuilt as a Christian city and large basilicas rose across the island. Arab forces took Crete in the 820s and ran it as an emirate from the fortified port of Chandax, a base for raiding the Aegean, until Nikephoros Phokas stormed the city in 961. The reconquered island was resettled and heavily churched, and its small painted chapels are the beginning of Crete's long fresco tradition, before Venice took over in 1204.

hints.label: Byzantine Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Roman and Byzantine Periods (Israel, 36 BC–AD 638)
nodes.title: Roman and Byzantine Periods (Israel, 36 BC–AD 638)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 36 BC–AD 638] Roman and Byzantine Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

From Herod's reign to the Arab conquest, this long stretch covers the destruction of the Second Temple, the rise of rabbinic Judaism, and the birth and eventual triumph of Christianity. Under Byzantine rule the region became a landscape of churches, monasteries and pilgrim routes, with mosaic-floored basilicas in almost every town. Population and agriculture reached a peak, with terraces and wine presses pushed far into the Negev, before Persian invasion and then Muslim armies ended imperial control.

hints.label: Roman and Byzantine Periods
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Herodian Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70)
nodes.title: Herodian Period (Israel, 36 BC–AD 70)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 36 BC–AD 70] Herodian Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from  Encompassed by Early Roman Period (37 BCE - 132 CE) (page xvi). Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Herod the Great, installed by Rome as king of the Jews, spent his reign building on a spectacular scale: the vastly enlarged Temple Mount platform, the harbour city of Caesarea Maritima, the desert palaces at Masada and Herodium. Under him and his heirs Judaea was a client kingdom balanced uneasily between Roman power and Jewish religious life, the setting for the events of the Gospels. It ended with revolt against Rome and the burning of the Temple in AD 70.

hints.label: Herodian Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC) [p0hsq83tspw]
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age I (Israel, 1549 BC–1399 BC) [p0hsq83tspw]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Late Bronze Age I. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Canaan's towns recovered slowly from the upheavals that ended the Middle Bronze Age, now under Egyptian overlordship after repeated pharaonic campaigns. Settlements were smaller and rarely walled, and the wealth that remained came from trade: painted bichrome jugs, Cypriot base-ring flasks and Aegean vessels found their way into local tombs and temples.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age I
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age I A (Israel, 2199 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 2199 BC–1999 BC] Middle Bronze Age I A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

A transitional, largely rural phase between the collapse of the Early Bronze Age towns and the urban revival that followed, known mostly from cemeteries of shaft graves and small seasonal camps rather than settlements. Pastoralism and mobility dominated, and copper daggers and simple pottery are the characteristic finds. Scholars have long argued over whether this reflects newcomers from the north or local people adapting to hard times.

hints.label: Middle Bronze Age I A
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel, 585 BC–331 BC) [p0hsq83g9mg]
nodes.title: Babylonian and Persian Periods (Israel, 585 BC–331 BC) [p0hsq83g9mg]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 585 BC–331 BC] Babylonian and Persian Periods. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Judah began this stretch as a wrecked Babylonian province, Jerusalem burned and its elite deported, and ended it as Yehud, a small temple-centred district of the Achaemenid Empire. Exiles returning under Persian permission rebuilt the Temple and, with Ezra and Nehemiah, reshaped Judaism around law, scripture and priesthood rather than monarchy. Aramaic spread as the everyday language, coinage and imperial administration arrived, and the Hebrew Bible took much of the shape it still has.

hints.label: Babylonian and Persian Periods
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917) [p0hsq83t3q2]
nodes.title: Ottoman Period (Israel, AD 1516–AD 1917) [p0hsq83t3q2]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, AD 1516–AD 1917] Ottoman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Ottoman armies took the island from Venice after a long war, with Candia (Heraklion) falling in 1669 only after one of the longest sieges in European history. Under the new rulers many Cretans converted to Islam, Venetian churches became mosques with slender minarets, and the countryside was reorganised around estates and tax farms. Repeated insurrections through the nineteenth century wore the administration down and led to autonomy at the century's end.

hints.label: Ottoman Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324) [p0hsq83459j]
nodes.title: Late Roman Period (Israel, AD 132–AD 324) [p0hsq83459j]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, AD 132–AD 324] Late Roman Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

The island prospered as part of a province joined with Cyrenaica, exporting wine and oil in its own amphorae and shipping them across the eastern Mediterranean. Gortyn, the provincial capital, grew large and elaborate, and by the fourth century Christian basilicas were rising in towns and harbours. Earthquakes, including the destructive event of AD 365, reshaped coastlines and forced settlements to be rebuilt.

hints.label: Late Roman Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Late Arab Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 1516)
nodes.title: Late Arab Period (Israel, AD 1291–AD 1516)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, AD 1291–AD 1516] Late Arab Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

With the fall of Acre in 1291 the last Crusader foothold was gone and the region was governed from Cairo by the Mamluk sultans. Coastal towns were deliberately left ruined to deter a European return, while inland Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed prospered, filling with madrasas, markets and pilgrim hostels built in banded Mamluk stonework. The period closes with the Ottoman victory that absorbed the whole area into a new empire.

hints.label: Late Arab Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 166 BC–36 BC)
nodes.title: Late Hellenistic Period (Israel, 166 BC–36 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 166 BC–36 BC] Late Hellenistic Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Seleucid power collapsed into dynastic civil war, and the old Phoenician harbour cities — Tyre, Sidon, Berytus — bought or seized autonomy, minting their own coins and trading across the Mediterranean. Greek civic institutions and temple architecture were grafted onto older Canaanite religious traditions, producing the hybrid sanctuaries later rebuilt on a colossal scale at Baalbek. Pompey's arrival ended the experiment, folding the coast into the Roman province of Syria.

hints.label: Late Hellenistic Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–2199 BC) [p0hsq83knpb]
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age III (Israel, 2699 BC–2199 BC) [p0hsq83knpb]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 2699 BC–2199 BC] Early Bronze Age III. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Fortified towns in the southern Levant reached their peak, with thick town walls, temples, palaces and the huge circular storage structure at Beth Yerah. Distinctive burnished red-and-black Khirbet Kerak ware, related to northern traditions, spreads through the region. By the close of the period nearly all these towns had been abandoned, and urban life vanished for centuries.

hints.label: Early Bronze Age III
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age II A (Israel, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron Age II A. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Small highland villages consolidated into towns with public architecture, casemate walls and six-chambered gates at sites such as Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer. This is the horizon traditionally linked to the biblical united monarchy of David and Solomon, and the dating of its pottery and buildings remains one of the fiercest debates in Levantine archaeology. Red-slipped and hand-burnished pottery is the period's signature find.

nodes.name: Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age I B (Israel, 1149 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 1149 BC–999 BC] Iron Age I B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Distinctive Philistine bichrome pottery and planned coastal towns mark the consolidation of the Philistine pentapolis, while the highland villages multiply and grow, with terraced fields, storage pits and four-room houses. Egyptian and Canaanite power in the lowlands fades for good. By the end of the phase, larger political units are forming that will become the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

hints.label: Iron Age I B
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 1099) [p0hsq8349nj]
nodes.title: Early Arab Period (Israel, AD 638–AD 1099) [p0hsq8349nj]
nodes.description:
[The Levant, AD 638–AD 1099] Early Arab Period. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Muslim armies took Palestine from Byzantium in the 630s, and the region was governed successively from Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo. The Umayyads built the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem and founded Ramla as a new provincial capital, while Christians and Jews continued to live under the protected-subject system. Earthquakes, Bedouin unrest and Fatimid–Seljuk conflict weakened the area before the Crusaders stormed Jerusalem in 1099.

hints.label: Early Arab Period
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Israel, 3499 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Israel, 3499 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 3499 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

hints.label: Bronze Age
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age II B (Israel, 1749 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.description:
[The Levant, 1749 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age II B. Spatial coverage: Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria. Derived from. Period definition from The archaeology of society in the Holy Land — 1995.

Fortified Canaanite cities were at their peak, with rampart defences, palace complexes and cemeteries containing weapons, jewellery and imported goods. Levantine populations settled in the eastern Nile Delta and Hyksos rulers of Semitic origin took power in northern Egypt. The period ends amid destructions as Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty pushed back into Asia.

hints.label: Middle Bronze Age II B
hints.source: The archaeology of society in the Holy Land

nodes.name: The Seleucid Era (Syria, 310 BC–63 BC)
nodes.title: The Seleucid Era (Syria, 310 BC–63 BC)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 310 BC–63 BC] The Seleucid Era. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Inferred from the following discussions: page 30 states that Seleucus I declared the official Year 1 of the Seleucid Era to be 311 BCE; Figure 1 on page 6 indicates the final Seleucid king, Philip II Barypous, ended his reign in 64 BCE; and page 234 explicitly states the dissolution of the Seleukid kingdom by Pompey in 64 BCE. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Seleucus I took the eastern share of Alexander's empire and built a Greek-ruled state stretching from the Aegean towards India, anchored on new foundations like Antioch and Seleucia on the Tigris. Greek settlers, coinage and city institutions were grafted onto Babylonian, Persian and Syrian populations, producing genuinely hybrid cultures. Continual wars with the Ptolemies, the loss of the east to the Parthians and the Maccabean revolt in Judaea whittled the kingdom down until Pompey annexed what was left as the Roman province of Syria.

hints.label: The Seleucid Era
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (Iraq, 322 BC–315 BC)
nodes.title: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1 (Iraq, 322 BC–315 BC)
nodes.description:
[Babylonia, 322 BC–315 BC] Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1. Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 1: From the death of Alexander the great in 323 BCE to Antigonus Monophthalmus' expulsion of Seleucus Nicator from Babylon in 316 BCE, records were dated by the years of king Philip III Arrhidaeus and then, after his posthumous eighth year, by the years of king Alexander IV;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

Babylonian scribes dated legal tablets and astronomical diaries by the regnal years of the reigning king, and after Alexander's death those formulae named his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus, a figurehead ruling under the generals. The dating clauses are therefore a running record of who was recognised as sovereign in Babylonia during the wars of the successors. Cuneiform bookkeeping outlasted the Persian empire and the Macedonian conquest with little change.

hints.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Philip I Philadelphus (Syria, 93 BC–82 BC)
nodes.title: Philip I Philadelphus (Syria, 93 BC–82 BC)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 93 BC–82 BC] Philip I Philadelphus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

One of the last Seleucid kings, ruling a rump state around Antioch while fighting his own brothers for scraps of a once-vast empire. Cities effectively governed themselves, and Armenian and then Roman power filled the vacuum. His abundant tetradrachms kept circulating long after the dynasty fell, copied even under Roman rule.

hints.label: Philip I Philadelphus
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (Iraq, 315 BC–310 BC)
nodes.title: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2 (Iraq, 315 BC–310 BC)
nodes.description:
[Babylonia, 315 BC–310 BC] Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2. Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 2: From late 316 to 311 BCE, the preiod of Antigonus Monophthalmus's undisputed dominance in Babylonia and Seleucus's exile in Ptolemy's Egypt, records were no longer dated by the reigning monarch, Alexander IV, who was absent in Macedonia. Instead, scribes introduced a year count of Antigonus in his official capacity as lúrab uqu, the Akkadian term for the Greek title stratêgos (general) of Asia....The beginning of this count, in an important precedent for the Seleucid Era, was retrojected to 317/316 BCE;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

After Philip Arrhidaeus was killed, Babylonian tablets began counting the regnal years of Alexander's posthumous son, Alexander IV, still a child in the custody of the Macedonian generals. The shift in the dating clause marks a change of recognised authority rather than any real change of ruler. These formulae are one of the sharpest tools chronologists have for pinning down the chaotic politics of the successor wars.

hints.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus (Syria, 68 BC–66 BC)
nodes.title: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus (Syria, 68 BC–66 BC)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 68 BC–66 BC] Antiochus XIII Asiaticus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The last Seleucid to be recognised as king, installed in Antioch by the Roman general Lucullus after Tigranes of Armenia's occupation collapsed. His authority never extended much past the capital, and Pompey deposed him and annexed Syria as a Roman province; he was killed soon after by an Arab dynast. With him ended the line founded by Alexander's general Seleucus more than 240 years earlier.

hints.label: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Alexander II Zabinas (Syria, 127 BC–122 BC)
nodes.title: Alexander II Zabinas (Syria, 127 BC–122 BC)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 127 BC–122 BC] Alexander II Zabinas. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A usurper set up by Ptolemy VIII of Egypt, who passed him off as an adopted heir of Antiochus VII; his nickname means roughly 'the bought one'. He beat and killed Demetrius II, ruled much of Syria briefly, then lost Egyptian support and was destroyed by Antiochus VIII, another turn in the fratricidal collapse of the Seleucid kingdom.

hints.label: Alexander II Zabinas
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Antiochus Hierax (Syria, 241 BC–226 BC)
nodes.title: Antiochus Hierax (Syria, 241 BC–226 BC)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 241 BC–226 BC] Antiochus Hierax. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

"The Hawk", younger brother of Seleucus II, was set up to govern Asia Minor and promptly made war on him, hiring Galatian mercenaries and splitting the empire in two. The fraternal war exhausted Seleucid authority in Anatolia and gave Attalus I of Pergamon the opening to defeat both Galatians and Hierax and build an independent kingdom. Hierax died a fugitive, but the damage let Parthia and Bactria consolidate their breakaway in the east.

hints.label: Antiochus Hierax
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Antiochus VI Dionysus (Syria, 143 BC–140 BC)
nodes.title: Antiochus VI Dionysus (Syria, 143 BC–140 BC)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 143 BC–140 BC] Antiochus VI Dionysus. Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

A child raised to the throne as a figurehead by the general Diodotus Tryphon, who used him to fight Demetrius II and issued coins in his name. Tryphon eventually murdered him and ruled outright, an act of usurpation that split the kingdom between rival courts. The chaos let Jonathan and Simon of the Hasmonean house play both sides and win effective independence for Judaea.

hints.label: Antiochus VI Dionysus
hints.source: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

nodes.name: Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign) (Syria, 144 BC–AD 139)
nodes.title: Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign) (Syria, 144 BC–AD 139)
nodes.description:
[Seleucid Empire, 144 BC–AD 139] Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign). Spatial coverage: Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Derived from Figure 1 ("The House of Seleucus, simplified") on page 6, which lays out the genealogy of the Seleucid kings. Demetrius II Nicator reigned twice, with other claimants forcing him out of power in between. Period definition from Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire. — Paul J. Kosmin, 2019.

The son of Demetrius I ousted the usurper Alexander Balas with Ptolemaic help, then lost ground to rivals and to mercenary troops who turned the population of Antioch against him. To keep Judaean support he conceded tax exemptions to Jonathan Maccabeus, effectively recognising Jewish autonomy. His eastern campaign against the Parthians ended in disaster: he was captured and held for years at the Arsacid court.

properties.title: amphora — 2ndC-3rdC
properties.notes:
