[Slovakia, 799 BC–449 BC] Hallstatt culture/period. Period definition from Interreg Iron-Age-Danube — University of Vienna, Institute of Prehistoric and Historical Archaeology, 2019.

The first fully iron-using culture of central Europe, named after a salt-mining village in the Austrian Alps whose cemetery yielded thousands of richly furnished graves. Wealth built on salt, copper and control of trade routes produced a warrior aristocracy buried under mounds with four-wheeled wagons, bronze feasting gear and imported Mediterranean luxuries. In the Carpathian Basin these communities lived in fortified hilltop settlements and later absorbed waves of horse-riding steppe newcomers; their descendants form the background to the historically attested Celts.

nodes.name: Iron Age IIa (Jordan, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age IIa (Jordan, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron Age IIa. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Villages and tribal groupings east of the Jordan hardened into the territorial kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom, each with a capital, a national god and its own script. Fortified towers and border sites spread across the plateau, and the trade routes carrying incense and copper north became the region's economic backbone.

hints.label: Iron Age IIa
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Babylonian/Persian (Jordan, 538 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: Babylonian/Persian (Jordan, 538 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 538 BC–299 BC] Babylonian/Persian. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After Babylonian campaigns broke the small kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom, the lands east of the Jordan became thinly settled districts of empire, first Babylonian and then Achaemenid. Urban life contracted, pastoral and tribal groups became more prominent, and Arab traders — the ancestors of the Nabataean power at Petra — took control of the incense routes. Aramaic administration, Persian-style imports and Greek pottery show a region tied loosely but firmly into a wider imperial economy.

hints.label: Babylonian/Persian
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 450)
nodes.title: Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 49 BC–AD 450] Roman. Derived from the start date of the Early Roman period and the end date of the Late Roman period, which are derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is not explicit.  

Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After Actium and the death of Cleopatra, Egypt became the personal possession of the emperor, governed by a prefect and squeezed for the grain that fed Rome. Greek remained the language of administration, temples went on being built in pharaonic style with emperors shown as pharaohs, and the desert quarries and Red Sea ports linked the Nile to India. The dry sands preserved tens of thousands of papyri and the startlingly lifelike Fayum mummy portraits, while Alexandria became a cradle of Christian thought.

hints.label: Roman
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Iron Age III (Jordan, 585 BC–538 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age III (Jordan, 585 BC–538 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 585 BC–538 BC] Iron Age III. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Lydia rose to dominate western Anatolia from Sardis, striking some of the world's first coins and drawing wealth from the Pactolus river, while Phrygia declined after Cimmerian raids. In the east, Urartu was worn down and the Assyrian empire fell, leaving Medes and Babylonians to divide the spoils. The era closed abruptly when Cyrus the Great took Sardis and made Anatolia Persian.

hints.label: Iron Age III
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Iron Age I (Jordan, 1199 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age I (Jordan, 1199 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 1199 BC–999 BC] Iron Age I. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The Hittite empire disappeared and Anatolia fragmented into small, often illiterate societies, with monumental hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions kept alive only by the Neo-Hittite successor states of the south-east. Phrygians moved into the central plateau and settlement clustered on defensible mounds, while in the east the tribal groups later unified as Urartu began to coalesce. From this fractured landscape came the kingdoms - Phrygia, Urartu, Lydia and the Syro-Hittite city-states - that dominated the following centuries.

hints.label: Iron Age I
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Chalcolithic (Jordan, 5499 BC–4299 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic (Jordan, 5499 BC–4299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 5499 BC–4299 BC] Chalcolithic. Derived from information on page xv of Levy 1995,  but Levy gives period in uncalibrated dates with unclear start and end points; there are also "slight adaptations to reflect the specific situation in southern Jordan." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

hints.label: Chalcolithic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Kingdom of Edom (Jordan, 999 BC–538 BC)
nodes.title: Kingdom of Edom (Jordan, 999 BC–538 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 999 BC–538 BC] Kingdom of Edom. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

A kingdom of herders, traders and copper workers in the arid highlands and Wadi Arabah south of the Dead Sea, with its centre at Bozrah and huge smelting operations at Khirbat en-Nahas and Faynan. It controlled caravan routes to Arabia and fought repeatedly with Judah, which the Hebrew Bible remembers bitterly. Assyrian tribute lists record its kings; after Babylon crushed Judah, Edomites moved west into the Negev, the region that became Idumaea.

hints.label: Kingdom of Edom
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: late prehistory (Jordan, 6349 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.title: late prehistory (Jordan, 6349 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 6349 BC–2499 BC] late prehistory. Derived from information on page xv of Levy 1995,  but Levy gives period in uncalibrated dates with unclear start and end points; there are also "slight adaptations to reflect the specific situation in southern Jordan." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After the collapse of the great early farming villages, people spread into smaller hamlets, adopted pottery, and turned increasingly to sheep, goats and orchard crops. Copper working began in earnest, with the extraordinary metalwork and painted shrines of the Chalcolithic at sites like Teleilat Ghassul. By the end of the span, walled towns with public buildings had appeared, the first urban experiment in the region.

hints.label: late prehistory
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (Jordan, 1549 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (Jordan, 1549 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 1549 BC–1199 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516) [p072r4qjq6g]
nodes.title: Mamluk (Jordan, AD 1263–AD 1516) [p072r4qjq6g]
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 1263–AD 1516] Mamluk. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Under the Cairo sultanate this region became a well-run frontier province, its roads carrying the barid postal relay that linked Egypt to Damascus and its valleys filled with irrigated sugar plantations and refineries. Karak and other castles were rebuilt as administrative centres, and villages grew around the pilgrimage and trade routes. The whole system passed to the Ottomans in 1516.

hints.label: Mamluk
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Hellenistic (Jordan, 299 BC–49 BC)
nodes.title: Hellenistic (Jordan, 299 BC–49 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 299 BC–49 BC] Hellenistic. Start date is derived from that of the Early Hellenistic and end date is derived from that of the Late Hellenistic. These periodizations are derived from Erickson-Gini 2010 ( ) and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Alexander's conquest replaced Persian rule with Greek-speaking kings, and the region was fought over by the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. Greek city foundations, coinage, gymnasia and language spread alongside older Semitic traditions, and the friction between them helped provoke the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state. Pompey's arrival in 63 BC brought the whole area into the Roman orbit.

hints.label: Hellenistic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1800)
nodes.title: Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 650–AD 1800] Islamic. Start date is derived from that of the Early Islamic and end date is derived from that of the Late Islamic, which are derived from Whitcomb 1992's ( Early Islamic I ( and Late Islamic 2 (. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Arab armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and over the following centuries its towns were reshaped by mosques, congregational plans and new trade routes running to Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo. Umayyad rulers built desert palaces and bath-houses here decorated with startling frescoes and mosaics; later the land passed through Crusader castles, Mamluk garrisons and finally Ottoman provincial administration and the pilgrimage road to Mecca. Village and nomadic life continued beneath these changes of regime, visible archaeologically in pottery, sugar mills and irrigation works.

hints.label: Islamic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Nabatean Kingdom (Jordan, 167 BC–AD 106)
nodes.title: Nabatean Kingdom (Jordan, 167 BC–AD 106)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 167 BC–AD 106] Nabatean Kingdom. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

From Petra, hidden in the sandstone canyons of southern Jordan, a dynasty of Arab traders controlled the incense route north from Arabia. They mastered desert hydrology, cutting cisterns and channels that let cities flourish where rainfall could not support them, and carved monumental facades blending Hellenistic columns with local design. Trajan annexed the kingdom peacefully as the province of Arabia Petraea.

hints.label: Nabatean Kingdom
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918) [p072r4qcqjb]
nodes.title: Ottoman (Jordan, AD 1516–AD 1918) [p072r4qcqjb]
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 1516–AD 1918] Ottoman. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

hints.label: Ottoman
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Umayyad-Abbasid (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969)
nodes.title: Umayyad-Abbasid (Jordan, AD 630–AD 969)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 630–AD 969] Umayyad-Abbasid. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Arab-Muslim armies took the region from Byzantium after the battle of Yarmuk, and under the Umayyads of Damascus it sat at the heart of the caliphate rather than on its edge - the era of the desert palaces at Qusayr Amra and Qasr al-Mshatta, with their frescoes and carved stone facades. Arabic replaced Greek in administration and the gold dinar replaced Byzantine coin. When the Abbasids moved the capital to Iraq in 750, the area became a provincial backwater, and a series of earthquakes finished off several of its Roman-era cities.

hints.label: Umayyad-Abbasid
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Early Hellenistic (Jordan, 299 BC–199 BC)
nodes.title: Early Hellenistic (Jordan, 299 BC–199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 299 BC–199 BC] Early Hellenistic. Derived from Erickson-Gini 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 (

Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Following Alexander's conquest, the region fell under Ptolemaic and then Seleucid rule, with Greek-style cities, coinage and administration layered over older Transjordanian communities. The Nabataeans of Petra were meanwhile building wealth from the incense trade. Greek architectural forms, imported amphorae and new fortified estates mark the change on the ground.

hints.label: Early Hellenistic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Iron Age (Jordan, 1199 BC–538 BC) [p072r4qxj42]
nodes.title: Iron Age (Jordan, 1199 BC–538 BC) [p072r4qxj42]
nodes.description:
[Petra, 1199 BC–538 BC] Iron Age. Start date is derived from that of Iron Age I and end date is derived from that of Iron Age III, which are in turn derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

hints.label: Iron Age
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171) [p072r4qfcxf]
nodes.title: Fatimid (Jordan, AD 969–AD 1171) [p072r4qfcxf]
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 969–AD 1171] Fatimid. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Cairo's Shi'i caliphs held the Jordanian lands as a frontier zone of their Syrian province, valuable for the pilgrimage and caravan routes running down the desert edge. Bedouin power and Seljuk pressure eroded that control, and the arrival of the Crusaders left the region divided between Frankish castles and Muslim rulers.

hints.label: Fatimid
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Early Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Islamic (Jordan, AD 650–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 650–AD 1000] Early Islamic. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Arab armies took the region from Byzantium in the 630s, and under the Umayyads it lay close to the heart of the new empire, dotted with the rural palaces and bath-houses known as the desert castles. Village life, churches and mosaic workshops carried on with surprising continuity, though the devastating earthquake of AD 749 wrecked many towns. When the Abbasids moved the capital to Iraq, the area slipped from imperial centre to provincial backwater.

hints.label: Early Islamic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Middle Islamic (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Middle Islamic (Jordan, AD 1000–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 1000–AD 1400] Middle Islamic. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Jordan sat between Crusader lordships, Ayyubid armies and finally the Mamluk sultanate, whose castles, sugar mills and postal routes reshaped the countryside. Karak and Shobak changed hands amid the wars of Saladin and his successors, and villages prospered on sugar cane, pottery and the pilgrimage road to Mecca. Handmade geometric-painted wares are the characteristic find of the period.

hints.label: Middle Islamic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Late Roman (Jordan, AD 250–AD 450)
nodes.title: Late Roman (Jordan, AD 250–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 250–AD 450] Late Roman. Derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is unclear.  
Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

hints.label: Late Roman
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Iron Age IIb-c (Jordan, 899 BC–585 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age IIb-c (Jordan, 899 BC–585 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 899 BC–585 BC] Iron Age IIb-c. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Ammon, Moab and Edom reached their peak as Assyrian vassals, paying tribute in exchange for a share of the caravan trade in incense and spices; their kings appear by name on Assyrian monuments. Ammonite palaces, distinctive stone statuary and inscribed seals date from these centuries. Babylonian campaigns after Assyria's fall brought the kingdoms to an end.

hints.label: Iron Age IIb-c
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Early Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.title: Early Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 4299 BC–2499 BC] Early Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

After the rich copper-working tell cultures of the Balkan Chalcolithic broke down, settlement in the Bulgarian lands was rebuilt on a different footing: fortified mounds such as Ezero and Yunatsite, alloyed copper and then true bronze, ox-drawn carts and the plough. Burial mounds of the kind raised by steppe pastoralists to the north spread across the Danube plain and the Thracian valleys, a sign of new populations and new ideas about rank. The dead were now marked by the tomb above ground rather than by the gold-filled graves of the earlier era.

hints.label: Early Bronze Age
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Jordan, 2499 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Jordan, 2499 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 2499 BC–1549 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

hints.label: Middle Bronze Age
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Byzantine (Jordan, AD 450–AD 650)
nodes.title: Byzantine (Jordan, AD 450–AD 650)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 450–AD 650] Byzantine. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Cyprus as a prosperous Christian province of the eastern Roman empire, covered in basilicas and mosaic floors and shipping copper, oil and wine across the Mediterranean. From the mid-seventh century Arab raids made the island a contested frontier, and for three centuries it was shared uneasily between Constantinople and the caliphate before Nikephoros Phokas took it back outright. The Byzantine centuries ended abruptly when Richard the Lionheart seized the island on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it on.

hints.label: Byzantine
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Jordan, 4299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 4299 BC–1199 BC] Bronze Age. Start date is derived from that of the Early Bronze Age, which is in turn derived from  page xvi with "slight adaptations to reflect the specific situation in southern Jordan" (page 627). End date is derived from that of the Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

hints.label: Bronze Age
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Middle Roman (Jordan, AD 100–AD 250)
nodes.title: Middle Roman (Jordan, AD 100–AD 250)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 100–AD 250] Middle Roman. Derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is unclear.  
Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Following Rome's annexation of the Nabataean kingdom, the new province of Arabia was tied together by the Via Nova Traiana running from the Red Sea to Syria. Cities such as Gerasa, Philadelphia and Bostra rebuilt themselves with colonnaded streets, theatres and temples, and garrisons secured the desert edge. It was the most prosperous and heavily built-up phase in the region's ancient history.

hints.label: Middle Roman
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Early Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 100)
nodes.title: Early Roman (Jordan, 49 BC–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 49 BC–AD 100] Early Roman. Derived from Erickson-Gini, 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( though the Roman period in Erickson-Gini 2010 ( does not correspond directly to any Roman period here and the periodization in Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 is unclear. 
Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

The Claudian invasion turned southern Britain into a province: legions pushed north and west, client kings were absorbed, and the revolt of Boudica was crushed. Towns with forums, baths and grid streets appeared where none had existed, roads linked new civitas capitals, and villas began to dot the countryside. By the end of the period the frontier had settled at Hadrian's Wall.

hints.label: Early Roman
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Late Hellenistic (Jordan, 199 BC–49 BC)
nodes.title: Late Hellenistic (Jordan, 199 BC–49 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 199 BC–49 BC] Late Hellenistic. Derived from Erickson-Gini 2010 ( and Erickson-Gini, Israel 2013 ( Page 627 recommends Schmid for "an alternative chronological schema that covers the Nabataean period (here Hellenistic to Roman)." (Schmid, S.G. 2000. "Die Feinkeramik der Nabataer: Typologie, Chronologie und kulturhistorische Hintergrunde." Petra Ez Zantur. Vol. 2, pt. 1. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern.). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Seleucid armies took the region from the Ptolemies at the start of this stretch, but imperial control soon frayed: Hasmonean rulers pushed east of the Jordan, the Greek-styled cities that would become the Decapolis asserted themselves, and the Nabataeans of Petra grew rich taxing incense and spice caravans. Greek language, coinage and civic architecture spread widely while local Semitic culture persisted underneath. The period closes as Rome moves into Syria and begins rearranging the whole region.

hints.label: Late Hellenistic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Late Islamic (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1800)
nodes.title: Late Islamic (Jordan, AD 1400–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 1400–AD 1800] Late Islamic. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Mamluk administration gave way to Ottoman rule, and much of the countryside shifted from villages to a more mobile, tribally organised way of life based on herding and seasonal cultivation. State attention concentrated on the pilgrimage road to Mecca, guarded by a chain of forts with cisterns where caravans watered. Handmade painted pottery and clay tobacco pipes are the period's most common archaeological markers.

hints.label: Late Islamic
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263) [p072r4qxqb4]
nodes.title: Ayyubid (Jordan, AD 1171–AD 1263) [p072r4qxqb4]
nodes.description:
[Petra, AD 1171–AD 1263] Ayyubid. "For reasons of practicality, very broad subdivisions within the Islamic periods are indicated with the chronology proposed by Whitcomb (1992), though they have been amended slightly with regard to the end date of the Byzantine and the start of the Early Islamic period." (page 627). Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Saladin's Kurdish dynasty ruled Egypt, Syria and the lands east of the Jordan, and his defeat of the crusaders at Hattin in 1187 brought Jerusalem back under Muslim rule. In Transjordan the period left striking military architecture, above all the castle of Ajlun, built to watch the crusader lords and guard the iron mines and communications with Damascus. Family infighting weakened the realm until Mamluk soldiers seized Egypt and the Mongols swept through Syria.

hints.label: Ayyubid
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Iron Age II (Jordan, 999 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age II (Jordan, 999 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 999 BC–499 BC] Iron Age II. Derived from  pages 228-49 and. Period definition from The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan — Alex R. Knodell, 2017.

Greek settlers pushed out from Syracuse and Naxos to found a chain of colonies around the coast, while Phoenicians held the western tip at Motya and Panormus. The indigenous Sikels, Sikanians and Elymians adopted Greek pottery, building styles and writing even as they lost land, and Sikel resistance culminated in Ducetius' short-lived confederation. Sicily's grain, its tyrants and its rivalry with Carthage made the island a major player in the wider Mediterranean world.

hints.label: Iron Age II
hints.source: The Brown University Petra Archaeological Project: Landscape Archaeology in the Northern Hinterland of Petra, Jordan

nodes.name: Incrustation Style (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC)
nodes.title: Incrustation Style (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 199 BC–89 BC] Incrustation Style. "The Tufa Period coincides throughout with the time of the first style of decoration." (page 41). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

The first of the Pompeian wall-painting styles, in which plaster was moulded and painted to imitate blocks of coloured marble veneer - a cheap way of giving an ordinary house the look of a Hellenistic palace. It marks the point at which Greek luxury tastes reached Italian domestic architecture on a large scale. Later styles abandoned the illusion of masonry for painted architecture and figured scenes.

hints.label: Incrustation Style
hints.source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

nodes.name: Architectural Style (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC)
nodes.title: Architectural Style (Italy, 79 BC–26 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–26 BC] Architectural Style. "The wall decoration of the fourth period is of the second Pompeian style, which came into vogue just after the founding of the colony, and which we shall call the Architectural Style." (page 42)

"The Architectural Style, already mentioned, remained in vogue to the time of Augustus." (page 43). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

Roman wall painters stopped imitating masonry and began dissolving walls altogether, framing rooms with painted columns, coffered ceilings, shrines and vistas onto imaginary buildings and gardens. This 'Second Style', best seen at Pompeii, Boscoreale and the Villa of Livia, is the first sustained European experiment in illusionistic perspective. Wealthy Romans used it to turn modest rooms into stage sets of aristocratic Hellenistic luxury.

hints.label: Architectural Style
hints.source: Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey.

nodes.name: Intricate Style (Italy, AD 50–AD 79)
nodes.title: Intricate Style (Italy, AD 50–AD 79)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, AD 50–AD 79] Intricate Style. "The fourth or Intricate Style came in about the year 50 A.D." (page 43). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

The last of the four Pompeian wall-painting styles, buried mid-development by the eruption of Vesuvius. Painters abandoned the sober architectural illusionism of earlier decades for crowded fantasy: impossible slender colonnades, theatrical stage-fronts, delicate ornamental panels and framed mythological pictures set like hung paintings. Its ornate, layered compositions survive in the House of the Vettii and the rebuilt houses of the post-earthquake years, giving an unusually precise snapshot of Roman taste in a single generation.

nodes.name: The third period (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC)
nodes.title: The third period (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC)
nodes.description: [Pompeii, 199 BC–89 BC] The third period. "Certain Oscan inscriptions, an early Latin monumental inscription, and a few words, dating from 78 B.C., scratched upon the plaster of the Basilica, oblige us to place the Tufa Period before the time of the Roman colony; yet not long before, for the next oldest buildings date from the first years of the colony. The time of peace that furnished the background for the period can only have been that between the Second Punic War and the Social War, about 200 to 90 B.C.; the Tufa Period was approximately the second century before Christ." (page 40). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

nodes.title: Ornate Style (Italy, 26 BC–AD 50)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 26 BC–AD 50] Ornate Style. "The Architectural Style, already mentioned, remained in vogue to the time of Augustus; it then gave place to the third or Ornate Style." (page 43). Period definition from Pompeii, its life and art. Translated into English by Francis W. Kelsey. — August Mau, 1899.

Roman wall painters abandoned illusionistic architecture for flat panels of deep red, black, and gold, framed by impossibly slender columns and candelabra, with tiny landscapes or mythological scenes floating at the centre. Egyptian motifs and delicate ornament reflect Augustan taste and the recent conquest of Egypt. Villas around the Bay of Naples preserve the best surviving examples.

nodes.name: Plague of Provence (France, AD 1720–AD 1722)
nodes.title: Plague of Provence (France, AD 1720–AD 1722)
nodes.description:
[Continental Europe, AD 1720–AD 1722] Plague of Provence. Period definition from Putting Africa on the Black Death map: Narratives from genetics and history — Monica H. Green, 2018-12-24.

Plague came ashore at Marseille in 1720 aboard a merchant ship from the Levant whose quarantine was cut short for commercial reasons, and it killed roughly half the city's people before spreading through Provence. Authorities sealed off the region with troops and a drystone barrier, the mur de la peste, parts of which still stand. It was the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in western Europe and a landmark case in the history of quarantine.

hints.label: Plague of Provence
hints.source: Putting Africa on the Black Death map: Narratives from genetics and history

nodes.name: Great Plague of Marseille (France, AD 1720–AD 1722)
nodes.title: Great Plague of Marseille (France, AD 1720–AD 1722)
nodes.description:
[Provence (France), AD 1720–AD 1722] Great Plague of Marseille. Source describes period as "one of the last well-documented European epidemics, the Great Plague of Marseille (1720–1722), that occurred in the Provence region of France at the end of the second pandemic.". Period definition from Eighteenth century Yersinia pestis genomes reveal the long-term persistence of an historical plague focus — Stephen A Forrest, 2016-01-21.

Plague came ashore with the merchant ship Grand-Saint-Antoine from the Levant, and quarantine rules bent for the sake of a valuable cargo of silk and cotton. Around half the city's population died, and the epidemic spread through Provence despite a stone plague wall built across the countryside to contain it. It was the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in western Europe, and it hardened maritime quarantine practice for the next century.

nodes.name: Fifth Syrian War (Syria, 201 BC–199 BC)
nodes.title: Fifth Syrian War (Syria, 201 BC–199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 201 BC–199 BC] Fifth Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus III of the Seleucids exploited the accession of the child king Ptolemy V to attack Egypt's possessions in Palestine and Phoenicia. His victory at Panium near the sources of the Jordan broke the Ptolemaic field army and transferred Coele-Syria and Judaea to Seleucid rule for the first time. Jerusalem's new masters granted the Temple privileges, but the shift set up the tensions that erupted a generation later in the Maccabean revolt.

nodes.name: Fourth Syrian War (Syria, 218 BC–216 BC)
nodes.title: Fourth Syrian War (Syria, 218 BC–216 BC)
nodes.description:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 218 BC–216 BC] Fourth Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus III of the Seleucids drove south to seize Coele-Syria and Phoenicia from Ptolemaic Egypt, and was stopped at Raphia in 217 BC by an Egyptian army stiffened with tens of thousands of native Egyptian troops. The victory saved Ptolemaic Syria for a generation, but arming and training Egyptians fed decades of revolt in the Nile valley. Antiochus returned twenty years later and took the province for good.

nodes.name: Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era (Yemen, 310 BC–AD 2015)
nodes.title: Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era (Yemen, 310 BC–AD 2015)
nodes.description:
[Yemen, 310 BC–AD 2015] Yemeni Jewish Seleucid Era. Derived from discussion on page 101: "To this day the Yemeni Jewish community dates its documents and activities according to Seleucus I's return to Babylon after the battle of Gaza [311 BCE, 1 SE]....". Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

The Seleucid year-count, known to Jews as the 'era of contracts', began with Seleucus I's seizure of Babylon and became the standard dating system across the Near East. Most Jewish communities abandoned it in the Middle Ages for the count from Creation, but the Jews of Yemen kept using it in deeds, marriage contracts and colophons into the twentieth century. It is the longest continuously used era in recorded history.

nodes.name: Third Syrian War (Syria, 245 BC–240 BC)
nodes.title: Third Syrian War (Syria, 245 BC–240 BC)
nodes.description:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 245 BC–240 BC] Third Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Ptolemy III of Egypt invaded Seleucid territory after his sister, married to the Seleucid king, was murdered along with her infant son in a succession struggle. Egyptian forces marched deep into Mesopotamia and briefly took Antioch and Seleucia, and Ptolemy returned with plunder that included cult statues carried off from Persia centuries earlier. Egypt kept the port of Seleucia Pieria and coastal gains, leaving the Seleucid realm weakened on its western flank.

nodes.name: Sixth Syrian War (Syria, 169 BC–167 BC)
nodes.title: Sixth Syrian War (Syria, 169 BC–167 BC)
nodes.description:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 169 BC–167 BC] Sixth Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus IV of Syria invaded Ptolemaic Egypt, captured the young king Ptolemy VI and stood at the gates of Alexandria before a single Roman envoy, Popillius Laenas, drew a circle in the sand and ordered him to withdraw. He did — a humiliation that marked Rome as the real arbiter of the eastern Mediterranean. Antiochus turned his energies on Judaea instead, and his measures against the Jerusalem Temple touched off the Maccabean revolt.

nodes.title: Second Syrian War (Syria, 259 BC–252 BC)
nodes.description:
[Syria and Asia Minor, 259 BC–252 BC] Second Syrian War. Spatial coverage: Israel, Lebanon, State of Palestine, Syria, Turkey. Period definition from The land of the elephant kings : space, territory, and ideology in the Seleucid Empire — 2018.

Antiochus II and Ptolemy II fought over the coast of Syria, Asia Minor and the Aegean islands, with cities changing hands and Rhodes and Macedon drawn in. It ended in a diplomatic bargain: Antiochus set aside his wife Laodice to marry Ptolemy's daughter Berenice, a match whose collapse would trigger the next war. The struggle shows how the Hellenistic kingdoms treated dynastic marriage as an instrument of war.

[Pompeii, 26 BC–AD 63] 5° periodo. "...più completo il Mau che suddivise l'edilizia pompeiana in fasi principali." (pages 88-89) "Dal 27 a.C. al terremoto del 63 d.C. Caratteristica la tecnica del reticolato. È il periodo coevo del II e III e dell'inizio del IV stile della pittura parietale." (page 89). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The Augustan and Julio-Claudian phase at Pompeii, when imperial patronage reshaped the town: a new aqueduct brought running water to street fountains and private houses, the forum was rebuilt in marble, and a temple to the imperial cult appeared. Painted decoration shifted to the delicate 'Third Style', and bakeries, fulleries and shops spread into once-grand houses.

nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 299 BC–179 BC] Periodo sannitico secondo. "Periodo sannitico secondo" translates to "Second Samnite Period." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Maiuri does not explain the gap between this period and the Third Samnite Period. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The wealthiest phase of Campania's Oscan towns, when trade after Rome's victory over Carthage paid for grand tufa-built houses with atria and peristyles, painted plaster in the 'First Style', temples, theatres and baths. Greek and Hellenistic taste is everywhere in the plans and decoration, even though public inscriptions remained in Oscan.

nodes.title: Periodo sannitico primo (Italy, 399 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 399 BC–299 BC] Periodo sannitico primo. "Periodo sannitico primo" translates to "First Samnite Period." "Periodo paleosannitica" translates to "Paleo-Samnite Period." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

Oscan-speaking Samnite communities dominated inland and coastal Campania, and towns such as Pompeii took on their first real urban shape – a defensive circuit, a street grid and the earliest public buildings in local limestone. It was also the era of the Samnite wars with Rome, which slowly drew these cities into the Roman alliance system.

nodes.name: 3° periodo (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC)
nodes.title: 3° periodo (Italy, 199 BC–89 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 199 BC–89 BC] 3° periodo. "...più completo il Mau che suddivise l'edilizia pompeiana in fasi principali." (pages 88-89)
"È il periodo del tufo corrispondente alla seconda età sannitica (200-90 a.C.) e al I stile ad incrostazione della pittura parietale pompeiana."
"Anche questa classificazione del Mau non è ormai più aderente alla realtà e alla luce della nuove scoperte, sopratutto riguardo al periodo  pre-sannitico che ci si presenta con una varietà più complessa e con materiali finora non ancora conosciuti, quali in tufo tenero, usato dapprima da solo e poi insieme calcare. In secondo luogo non tutte le case ad atrio calcareo possono considerarsi oggi d'età sannitica." (page 90). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

nodes.name: Periodo sannitico terzo (Italy, 119 BC–89 BC)
nodes.title: Periodo sannitico terzo (Italy, 119 BC–89 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 119 BC–89 BC] Periodo sannitico terzo. "Periodo sannitico terzo" translates to "Third Samnite Period." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Maiuri does not explain the gap between the preceding Second Samnite Period and this one. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The last decades of Oscan self-government, ending in the Social War when the allied Italian cities rose against Rome and Sulla besieged and stormed Pompeii. Defeat brought Roman citizenship, a colony of veterans, and the rapid replacement of Oscan by Latin in public life.

properties.title: cinerary urn — 200BC-100BC
properties.notes:
Terracotta cinerary urn, depicting Achilles (Achle) slaying Troilos (Truile), with a lid with a figure of a reclining man holding an embossed libation bowl. The head is finely modelled in the idealizing manner of contemporary portraiture.; | Type: cinerary urn | Medium: terracotta; human remains | Dimensions: 75.50 centimetres urn and lid ; | Culture: Etruscan

properties.title: cup — 125BC-75BC
properties.notes:

The ivy leaves and berries were applied as festoons of mould-made appliqués, with tendrils and leaves incised below.; | Type: cup | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 16.51 centimetres; | Culture: Roman Republican

properties.title: figure-mould — 100BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Terracotta mould for making statuettes of female figures. A woman with left foot advanced, hair arranged in neat parallel curls vertically over the forehead with a long twisted tress over each shoulder; wears a long under-chiton of crinkly material, and an upper chiton gathered at the waist which she draws aside with her left hand, leving her left shoulder free. Drapery elaborately treated with neat formal fold, recalling archaic femal figures from the Acropolis of Athens. Archaistic in style.; | Type: figure-mould | Medium: terracotta | Dimensions: 25.40 centimetres;

Italy, Taranto

"Anche questa classificazione del Mau non è ormai più aderente alla realtà e alla luce della nuove scoperte, sopratutto riguardo al periodo pre-sannitico che ci si presenta con una varietà più complessa e con materiali finora non ancora conosciuti, quali in tufo tenero, usato dapprima da solo e poi insieme calcare. In secondo luogo non tutte le case ad atrio calcareo possono considerarsi oggi d'età sannitica." (page 90). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

nodes.name: Epoca romana (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79)
nodes.title: Epoca romana (Italy, 79 BC–AD 79)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–AD 79] Epoca romana. "Epoca romana" translates to "Roman era." This period refers to the chronology of fortifications at Pompeii. Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

A century that carried Italy from the wreckage of Sulla's dictatorship through the civil wars of Caesar, Pompey, Antony and Octavian into the peace and monumental building of the early emperors. Rome became a city of marble, concrete vaults and a million inhabitants, fed by grain fleets and supplied by aqueducts. The period ends with the eruption of Vesuvius, which buried Pompeii and Herculaneum and preserved for us the ordinary streets, shops and painted rooms of Roman life.

nodes.name: 6° periodo (Italy, AD 63–AD 79)
nodes.title: 6° periodo (Italy, AD 63–AD 79)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, AD 63–AD 79] 6° periodo. "...più completo il Mau che suddivise l'edilizia pompeiana in fasi principali." (pages 88-89) 
"Sono gli ultimi 16 anni della città compresi fra due disastri, quello tellurico del 63 e la tremenda eruzione vesuviana del 79: ultime fase del IV stile." (page 90). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

The last sixteen years of Pompeii, between the earthquake that wrecked the town in AD 62/63 and the eruption that buried it. Much of the city was a building site — temples propped up, houses subdivided, the water system still broken — which is why so many rooms preserve fresh 'Fourth Style' paintings, stacked materials and unfinished repairs at the moment of destruction.

properties.notes:

properties.notes:
Lead glazed pottery goblet; pine scale decoration on upper body; indescent pale green glaze on exterior; honey-brown interior.; | Type: goblet | Medium: pottery; lead | Dimensions: 13.10 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Rome, Italy

properties.title: incense-burner — 76-100
properties.notes:
Fragmentary mould-made pottery incense-burner in the form of a miniature altar with a lamp attached to one side. The altar has a square body tapering to an expanding moulding with a bowl above, the edges of which are cut to form four petal-like corners. One corner and the base of the altar are restored in fired clay. At one side of the altar is an applied lamp with a rounded body, a short semicircular voluted nozzle, a wide rounded shoulder decorated with ovules, and a moulded rim. The discus is decorated with an eight-petalled rosette. The flat base is defined by two grooves and has an impressed ring-and-dot at the centre. Covered with an orange-red slip, fired brown in places.; | Type: incense-burner | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 12.80 centimetres as restored ; 6.50 centimetres lamp ; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: incense-burner — 70-120 (circa)
properties.notes:
Combined pottery incense-burner and lamp-stand, built up by hand from several mould-made elements. The base is a rectangular plinth, open underneath, with a panel on the front containing three masks in relief. On the centre of the plinth is a fluted column supporting a thymiaterion bowl. On each side is a support surmounted by a lamp with a ring handle, decorated on the discus with a rosette. Each support is decorated with a relief of Eros asleep, holding a downturned torch. At the rear are the remains of an incised inscription, which can be expanded to read "take this for the gods". Covered with an orange slip.; | Type: incense-burner | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 19.20 centimetres; 17.30 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Knidos, Crete, Italy

properties.title: jar — 70-100
properties.notes:

Gaul, Italy

properties.notes:

Rome, Italy

Fragment of a pottery jug. Rough unglazed red clay. Combat of two gladiators. Each has a visored helmet with grilled front, a short dagger (sica) in one hand, arm-guard on one arm, and oval shield on the other; round their waists are ornamented belts; their lower parts are wanting. On the left is seen the crest of a helmet, perhaps from a different subject.; | Type: jug | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 9.50 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Knidos, Italy

properties.notes:
Pottery juglet with a ribbed handle and a trefoil lip (broken); decorated on the shoulder with incised markings and on the body with chevrons between pairs of vertical lines; orange-brown fabric with dull olive-green glaze, with white encrustation on the base.; | Type: juglet | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 3.40 centimetres base ; 4.50 centimetres rim ; 14.00 centimetres max ; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.notes:
Piece of kiln-furniture: originally a pad of soft clay, this support was fired with the pottery in the kiln. It kept the lower vessel of a pile of bowls, stacked upside-down, from touching the floor of the kiln.; | Type: kiln-furniture | Medium: fired clay | Dimensions: 10.16 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Gaul, Lezoux, Italy

properties.title: lamp — 1stC
properties.notes:

Italy, St Martin's le-Grand

properties.title: lamp — 40-70 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp decorated on the discus with a pantheistic deity with many attributes; there is an air-slit. Within the slightly raised base is a foot-print containing the name CCLOD. Covered with a red slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 12.90 centimetres; 9.70 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy, Cyprus

properties.title: lamp — 70-125
properties.notes:
Pottery firmalampe, with ring-handle and two shoulder-lugs (unpierced). Multiple base-ring; ATIMETI in relief. Light brown clay; orange-brown slip. Plaster mould.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 81.00 millimetres; 44.00 millimetres; | Culture: Romano-British

Gaul, London, Italy

properties.title: lamp — 75-125
properties.notes:
Pottery lamp ('firmalampe'), with ring-handle and two shoulder-lugs (unpierced). Discus: slave mask. Multiple base-ring; illegible stamp in relief. Whitish-buff clay; grey-brown slip. Plaster mould.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 96.00 millimetres; 53.00 millimetres; | Culture: Romano-British

Colchester, Italy

properties.title: lamp — 30-80 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery plastic lamp in the form of a dolphin. The short rounded nozzle emerges from the dolphin's mouth and is edged by a raised rim. The filling-hole is pierced between the curved body and the tail-fin. Above the pectoral fin is an air-hole. The undefined flat base follows the shape of the dolphin. Covered with a finger-marked red-brown slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 11.10 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 30-70 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a voluted rounded-tipped nozzle, a narrow rounded shoulder and an inward-sloping moulded rim. The discus is decorated with a victorious chariot team. The charioteer holds a palm branch and a prize-wreath. Behind the team is a stand of lap-counting dolphins supported by fluted columns, a statue of Victoria (?), an Egyptian obelisk and a small polygonal building supported by columns. Within the base-ring is the impressed letter K. Covered with a finger-marked orange-brown slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 12.80 centimetres; 9.70 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 51-100
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery plastic lamp in the form of a sandalled left foot. The short rounded nozzle, which extends from below the big toe, is decorated with spirals and ring-and-dot patterns. The filling-hole is surrounded by a wreath. At the rear is a pierced handle, with a decorative ornament above in the form of a siren or sphinx. The lamp stands on a flat sole-shaped base. Covered with a dull orange-red slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 8.50 centimetres; 16.80 centimetres; 4.60 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy, Banghazi

properties.title: lamp — 70-120 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery plastic lamp in the form of a long narrow ship, curving up at both ends. Along each side is a row of six semicircular nozzles, separated from the flat deck by a kerb. On the deck are three filling-holes. The poop-deck and smaller fore-deck are stepped up and edged by rails. The lamp stands on an undefined pointed oval flat base. A few fragments have been restored. Covered with a red-brown slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 35.00 centimetres; 10.80 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 70-100
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery Firmalampe: a lamp with a circular bowl-shaped body, a rounded shoulder, a small flat discus with a raised rim, and a long nozzle with a channel along the top and a rounded tip. On the shoulder are three grooved lugs, pierced for suspension. One air-hole is pierced at the edge of the discus, and another at the end of the nozzle channel. The discus is decorated with a mask of Jupiter Ammon, flanked by two filling-holes. The lamp stands on a base-ring with an internal moulding; within is the name STROBILI in relief.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 11.30 centimetres; 7.80 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 1stC
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery plastic lamp in the form of a bull's head wearing a fillet with a central four-petalled rosette, through which is pierced the filling-hole. The semi-circular nozzle projects from the muzzle. At the rear is a pierced handle with a decorative ornament above, decorated on the flat face with a palmette in relief; a firing-slit is cut through the back. The lamp stands on an undefined flat oval base. Covered with a finger-marked orange-brown slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 9.10 centimetres; 20.30 centimetres; 12.30 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 51-100
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a ring-shaped body and ten radiating nozzles, three broken and restored. Each nozzle has a flat heart-shaped area surrounding the wick-hole. The convex top is decorated with a myrtle-wreath. There are two filling-holes, each in a sunken rectangular panel. Inside the body are two crossing `basket' handles, now missing. The lamp rested on an undefined flat area below. Covered with an orange-red slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 25.80 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 40-80 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a voluted rounded-tipped nozzle, a flat shoulder and an inward-sloping moulded rim. An air-slit is marked between the nozzle volutes. The discus is decorated with two satyrs treading grapes. Within the slightly raised base is a foot-print containing the letters CCLOD. Covered with a streaky orange-brown to dark brown slip. A fragment is missing from the underbody.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 11.00 centimetres; 7.90 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy, Herpes

properties.title: lamp — 70-100 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a rounded-tipped nozzle with shoulder-volutes, a wide shoulder and a plain moulded rim with an internal ridge. Between the volutes is a double decorative feature. At the rear is transverse vertical handle, pierced with two connected holes to allow suspension on a nail on the wall. The discus is decorated with trophy mounted on a tree-stump, consisting of a short belted tunic, a sheathed sword, a plumed helmet and two rectangular shields with crossed spears behind them. At its foot are a German prisoner and a sorrowing woman. The lamp stands on a slightly raised base.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 12.30 centimetres; 9.10 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy, Corfu

properties.title: lamp — 40-75 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a voluted nozzle with a rounded tip (now lost), a flat shoulder and an inward-sloping moulded rim. Between the nozzle volutes is an air-hole. The discus is decorated with two heavily cloaked seated slave boys; one has a lantern and the other sleeps with his head in the first boy's lap. Within the slightly raised base is a foot-print containing obscure letters, perhaps CTP. At one edge of the base is a mould-mark of a single stroke. Covered with a finger-marked orange-red and brown slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 9.90 centimetres; 8.10 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 30-70 (circa)
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a voluted rounded-tipped nozzle (now broken), a narrow rounded shoulder and an inward-sloping moulded rim. Between the nozzle volutes is an air-slit. The discus is decorated with Fortuna standing on a globe, holding a cornucopia and steering-oar. Next to her stands Mercury, wearing a winged hat and winged boots, holding a purse and winged caduceus. Behind Fortuna is a naked Hercules with his club and lion-skin, and a diminutive boar. The lamp stands on a slightly raised base. Covered with a streaky matt orange-brown slip.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 10.30 centimetres; 8.70 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 51-100
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery New Year lamp with a rounded-tipped nozzle with shoulder-volutes, a rounded shoulder decorated with ovules, and a raised rim with an internal moulding. Between the nozzle volutes is an air-hole. At the rear is a broken handle, which perhaps had a crescent-shaped decorative ornament. The discus is decorated with a figure of Victory holding a palm-branch and a shield with the inscription "AN./NV.NOV/FAV.STV./FELIC." She is surrounded by New Year gifts: a date, a fig, a fig-bundle and three coins. The lamp stands on a slightly raised base.; | Type: lamp | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 15.70 centimetres; 10.70 centimetres; | Culture: Roman

Italy

properties.title: lamp — 51-75
properties.notes:
Mould-made pottery lamp with a rounded-tipped nozzle, a wide rounded shoulder, and a groove surrounding the discus. Between the discus and the wick-hole area is a narrow channel with a pierced air-hole. At each side of the body is a small ear-handle, the right one slightly damaged. nodes.title: 4° periodo (Italy, 79 BC–27 BC)
nodes.description:
[Pompeii, 79 BC–27 BC] 4° periodo. "...più completo il Mau che suddivise l'edilizia pompeiana in fasi principali." (pages 88-89)
"Età romana repubblicana (a. 80 - 27 a.C.)" "...appare in esso il secondo stile del la pittura parietale." (page 89). Period definition from Introduzione allo studio di Pompei : (la città ed i monumenti publici) : corso universitario di Antichità Pompeiano dell'anno 1948-49 — Amedeo Maiuri, 1949.

Pompeii's late Republican phase, after Sulla planted a colony of Roman veterans on a town that had backed the losing side. Latin replaced Oscan in public inscriptions, the amphitheatre and covered theatre went up, and wealthy incomers built the large atrium houses whose walls carry the illusionistic 'Second Style' frescoes.

properties.title: The Actium Vase — 30BC-25BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Black-glazed pottery lidded 'stamnos' with relief decoration. The 'stamnos' (jar) has a sharply offset rim, a sloping neck and a sharply carinated shoulder. The body is full and rounded, tapering gently to a low ring foot. Above the shoulder rise two large horizontal handles with striated shafts, decorated with female masks at the terminals and at the mid-points. The lid has a conical knob and a shallow body with a small everted rim. The vessel has been reconstructed from many fragments and the black surface has been overpainted in several areas. The lid is decorated in relief, with ten olive leaves forming a wreath. The body of the 'stamnos' is also covered with relief decoration. Below the shoulder is a band of double ovolos and at the base of the body is a band of acanthus leaves. Between these are two zones of relief decoration separated by a band of concentric bulbs. The upper zone features seven olive trees, from which are suspended heavy festoons. Above each festoon is a cupid playing the syrinx and flanked by two light festoons of vine leaves. Above one of the cupids is a maker's name, BASSU(S), in cursive script. nodes.name: Talmudic Period (Egypt, AD 70–AD 640)
nodes.title: Talmudic Period (Egypt, AD 70–AD 640)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, Libya, Judea, Palestine, several other places, AD 70–AD 640] Talmudic Period. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Libya, State of Palestine. “This article presents a narrative history of the Jews between the destruction of the Second Temple (70 ce) and the Arab conquest of Palestine (c.640 CE). After the destruction, Palestine was made into a standard Roman province in a way which at least curtailed the Jews' traditional autonomy. Nevertheless, the Jews rebelled again, with disastrous results. The Diaspora Revolt (115–17 CE) seems to have ended in the decimation or destruction of the Jewish settlements in Egypt, Libya, and several other places, while the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132–5) brought an end to the Jews' hopes for the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple and, more tangibly, to Jewish settlement in the district of Judaea. The historiography of the past sixty years on the Jews in the ‘Talmud period’ can be divided into two very broad tendencies, which may be designated Israeli and non-Israeli" (Abstract). Period definition from Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE) — Seth Schwartz, 2004.

Framed by the destruction of the Second Temple and the Arab conquest, these centuries saw Judaism reinvent itself around rabbis, synagogues and study rather than sacrifice, producing the Mishnah and then the Talmuds. Egypt's once-vast Jewish community, centred on Alexandria, had been shattered by the revolt of 115-117 and rebuilt slowly under Roman and Byzantine rule. The same span covers the rise of Egyptian Christianity and the flight of a religious minority to the margins of an increasingly Christian empire.

hints.label: Talmudic Period
hints.source: Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE)

nodes.name: Diaspora Revolt (Egypt, AD 115–AD 117)
nodes.title: Diaspora Revolt (Egypt, AD 115–AD 117)
nodes.description:
[Egypt, Libya, Judea, Palestine, several other places, AD 115–AD 117] Diaspora Revolt. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Israel, Libya, State of Palestine. “This article presents a narrative history of the Jews between the destruction of the Second Temple (70 ce) and the Arab conquest of Palestine (c.640 CE). After the destruction, Palestine was made into a standard Roman province in a way which at least curtailed the Jews' traditional autonomy. Nevertheless, the Jews rebelled again, with disastrous results. The Diaspora Revolt (115–17 CE) seems to have ended in the decimation or destruction of the Jewish settlements in Egypt, Libya, and several other places, while the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132–5) brought an end to the Jews' hopes for the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple and, more tangibly, to Jewish settlement in the district of Judaea. The historiography of the past sixty years on the Jews in the ‘Talmud period’ can be divided into two very broad tendencies, which may be designated Israeli and non-Israeli" (Abstract). Period definition from Historiography on the Jews in the ‘Talmudic Period’ (70–640 CE) — Seth Schwartz, 2004.

While Trajan campaigned against Parthia, Jewish communities rose in Cyrenaica, Cyprus, Mesopotamia and Egypt in a bitter war marked by massacres on both sides. Fighting reached the Egyptian countryside and Alexandria, where the great Jewish population that had produced Philo and the Greek Bible was effectively destroyed. Papyri record ruined estates and a commemorative 'day of victory' still observed decades later; Egyptian Jewry did not recover for centuries.

nodes.name: Nabatean period (Jordan, 311 BC–AD 106)
nodes.title: Nabatean period (Jordan, 311 BC–AD 106)
nodes.description:
[Petra, 311 BC–AD 106] Nabatean period. "The Nabatean period extends from the earliest reference to the Nabateans in 312 B.C. by Diodorus Siculus to the Roman annexation in A.D. 106." (page 16). Period definition from Petra Great Temple. Volume III, Brown University excavations 1993-2008 : architecture and material culture — 2017.

Beginning as nomadic herders and caravaneers who repelled a Greek attack on their desert stronghold, the Nabataeans became settled city-builders with Petra at their centre. Their engineers dammed flash floods and piped water for miles; their masons cut temple facades directly into cliff faces. Wealth from the incense trade sustained them until Roman annexation folded the kingdom into the empire.
