nodes.name: Geometrische Zeit (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Geometrische Zeit (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometrische Zeit. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The period when Greek craftsmen filled their vases with ruled bands, meanders and compass circles, later adding stick-like figures in funeral processions and sea battles. Populations grew, iron replaced bronze for tools, communal sanctuaries appeared, and writing returned with an alphabet adapted from Phoenician. By its end Greeks were founding cities overseas and the city-state had taken shape.

nodes.name: frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC)
nodes.title: frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 899 BC–849 BC] frühgeometrisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Athenian potters imposed a strict new order on their vases — bands of meanders, concentric circles and zigzags covering black-glazed surfaces — in the first coherent Greek art style after the collapse of the Mycenaean world. Populations were growing again, iron working was routine, and cremation burials with modest metal goods hint at families asserting rank. The Lefkandi hero-burial shows how much wealth and long-distance contact could still be commanded.

nodes.name: mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC)
nodes.title: mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 849 BC–759 BC] mittelgeometrisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Athenian potters tightened the geometric repertoire inherited from the previous century, filling vases with meanders, zigzags and the first tentative silhouette animals. Behind the pottery lies a society climbing out of the post-Mycenaean slump: population growing, metalwork and burial goods richer, contacts with Cyprus and the Levant resuming. The stage is being set for the huge grave-marker amphorae and figured scenes of the Late Geometric, and for the eighth-century surge of colonisation and writing.

nodes.name: spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 759 BC–699 BC] spätgeometrisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Painters filled Athenian grave vases with meanders, chariot processions and rows of mourners – the first narrative scenes in Greek art after centuries of abstraction. Population and settlement grew sharply, sanctuaries filled with dedications, the alphabet was adopted from Phoenician traders, and Greeks began founding colonies in Italy and Sicily as the polis took shape.

nodes.name: früharchaisch (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC)
nodes.title: früharchaisch (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 699 BC–619 BC] früharchaisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Greek communities emerged from centuries of isolation to trade and settle across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, absorbing Near Eastern art, myth and technology in the process. The alphabet was put to work on Homer and on the first written laws; the first monumental stone temples and life-size statues appeared; and the citizen militia of massed hoplites began to reshape who held power in the polis.

nodes.name: mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC)
nodes.title: mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 619 BC–559 BC] mittelarchaisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Athens and Corinth turned out black-figure vases traded across the Mediterranean, sculptors carved the first life-size marble kouroi and korai, and cities replaced timber shrines with stone temples. Tyrants seized power in many poleis, while Solon's reforms reshaped Athenian law and citizenship. Colonies planted from the Black Sea to Spain spread Greek language, coinage and the alphabet.

nodes.name: Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC)
nodes.title: Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 449 BC–429 BC] Hochklassik. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The high point of Athenian art and confidence, funded by tribute from the Delian League under Pericles: the Parthenon and the Propylaia rose on the Acropolis, Phidias made his colossal cult statues, and Polykleitos worked out the canon of ideal bodily proportion. Sculpture achieved the balanced, idealised naturalism that later ages took as the definition of classical beauty. It ended with the outbreak of war with Sparta and the plague that killed Pericles himself.

Pottery: red-figured amphora, with twisted handles. (a) Mousaios, Terpsichore and Melousa. Terpsichore is seated in the centre on a chair to right, playing upon a harp (magadis), which she holds on her lap, bending over it, with her head in three-quarter face: she wears a long sleeved chiton, a mantle around her lap, and a curious stephane. Over her, her name, ΤΕΡΨΙΧΟΡΑ, Τερψίχορα. In front of her stands Mousaios, a youth in an himation, wreathed with laurel and holding in his left a chelys: he stands en face, but looks down at her, leaning against a long staff which has a shoot of laurel at the top and halfway up the stem. Over him, his name, MOYΣAIOΣ, Μουσαίος. On the left stands Melousa, in Doric chiton with apoptygma and saccos, who holds in her left a pair of flutes, of one of which she tries the mouthpiece with her right forefinger. Over her, ΜΕΛΕΛΟΣΑ, Μελ<ελ>ούσα. Above Terpsichore hangs a lyre of horse-shoe form. (b) A woman in long sleeved chiton, mantle and saccos, standing to left holding up her right hand, between two draped ephebi leaning on staves: the one on left wears a wreath. Large style. Below and above, strips of egg pattern.; | Type: pelike | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 17.78 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: lekythos — 440BC-430BC
properties.notes:
[Text from BM catalogue of vases] Pottery: red-figured lekythos. The sending of Triptolemos. On the left Triptolemos wreathed, wearing himation over left shoulder and legs, sits in the winged chariot to right, and holds out his right to receive the ears of corn which Demeter offers him with his right; the stalks of the corn are not indicated; she stands en face, wearing a long chiton, a mantle passed over the back of her head, and a wreath: in her left she holds across her body a long torch, the upper part of which is lost in the border of the design. Drawing of best period, but careless. The stalks of the corn have possibly been in purple, now faded, and can still be traced in the sketch-marks. Brown inner markings and details of wings and torch. Below, a strip of key pattern; above, of sets of three maeanders separated by dotted cross squares. On shoulder, an inverted palmette with two side palmettes issuing horizontally, black on red.; | Type: lekythos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 32.35 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Gela, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Type of Thetis bringing armour to Achilles. A youth on left, wreathed, with hair looped up and passed over ear, and a mantle in a doubled roll thrown over his left shoulder, holds out his right for a helmet which a woman offers him; she has also a shield with black device of a scorpion to left, and a long spear, and she wears a long chiton, himation, a radiated stephane, and a saccos which has a flap behind the left ear. (b) Bearded man in himation, wearing a fillet with a vertical piece over the forehead, standing to left, resting right hand on staff. Drawing of the best period. Purple wreath and fillet; brown inner markings. Edge of hair dotted. Eye in profile. Below a, pairs of maeanders set in alternate directions, separated by dotted cross squares; below b, a strip of key pattern.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 33.02 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: pelike — 440BC-430BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured pelike. (a) Departure scene (?) A bearded man with wrinkled forehead, wearing himation, leans forward against his staff, with right raised, conversing with a youth on the right, who stands en face, but looks towards him, holding out his right arm; in his left he holds upright a spear; he wears a chlamys fastened on his right shoulder, and a petasos hangs at his back. (b) A woman in Doric chiton with apoptygma moves in three-quarter face to right, holding up a phiale in her left hand; in her right, hanging at her side, is a trefoil oinochoe; her hair is looped up. Graceful style. Ends and outline of hair wavy. Eye in profile. Below and above a, a band, sets of three maeanders in alternate directions, separated by dotted cross squares; below and above b, a strip of key pattern. Below the lower insertion of each handle, an inverted palmette.; | Type: pelike | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 25.40 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: pelike — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured pelike. (a) Two Maenads conversing. The one on the left, holding in her left a chelys, leans forward, with her left foot raised on a rock, resting her right elbow upon her left knee, conversing, as the action of her right hand shows, with the Maenad confronting her, who holds upright with her right hand a thyrsos. Each wears a chiton and himation and earrings. The one on left wears a necklace, coloured brown, and has her hair looped up with a radiated fillet (left red); the other has her hair looped up with a purple fillet. (b) Bearded satyr, closely draped in an himation, wearing a fillet with vertical piece over the forehead, stands to left, holding upright in his right a thyrsos. Graceful style. Purple fillets, rays, and tuning-pegs of lyre. Brown inner markings. Eye in profile. Above and below a, a strip of maeander broken by two dotted cross squares; above and below b, a strip of key pattern. On the lower insertion of each handle, an inverted palmette.; | Type: pelike | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 25.40 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: kylix — 440BC-430BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured kylix, with low foot. Interior: Within two concentric thin red circles, two women conversing. The one on left is seated on a rock, closely muffled in drapery: the other stands en face, but looks at her, her right resting on a sceptre. Both wear a sleeved chiton, himation, and fillet looping up the hair. Exergue left red. Exterior: (a) A woman with sceptre, and a winged figure, Nike (?), running toward her. The woman is exactly like the figure holding sceptre in the interior, and stands in the same position on right. On left Nike, muffled in himation and wearing chiton and fillet, runs towards her. Between them hang two uncertain objects (a pair of boots ?). (b) The same repeated. Drawing rough. Eye in profile. Beneath and beside each handle a palmette, from which sprouts on each side a long tendril with three spirals, terminating in a flower. The foot on its under surface is decorated with a series of concentric circles, partly painted and partly moulded.; | Type: kylix | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 21.55 centimetres; 6.85 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: chous — 430BC-410BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured chous, with trefoil mouth. On body: three athletes. One on left, wreathed and holding along his left arm a rod, holds up his right hand as if addressing the one in the centre, who, standing to left in three-quarter face, looks down at a wreath which he holds in both hands. The athlete on the right stands with his back three-quarter turned to the spectator, looking to left over his left shoulder; he leans his left forearm on a tall stele, and holds in his right, hanging at his side, a strigil. Graceful style. Purple (now nearly white) wreaths. Brown inner markings. Eye of developed profile type. Below, a strip composed of sets of four maeanders separated by chequer squares; above, egg pattern; and on each side a thin red line, the whole forming a panel.; | Type: chous | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 18.00 centimetres; 15.00 centimetres; 15.80 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Capua, Greece

properties.title: hydria — 430BC-420BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured hydria. Woman at toilet. On a chair on right a woman in chiton and himation around lap is seated, leaning with her left arm on the back of the chair; she extends her right to receive a square box from the left hand of an attendant, who holds in her an alabastron. The attendant stands en face, looking to right; she wears a bordered Doric chiton with apoptygma tied at the waist: beside her, in the background diphros, on which is a striped cushion. Both have short hair looped up; the seated figure has rays in her hair. Above the scene, a festooned taenia. The box is ornamented with two rosettes. Purple ends of taenia and rays: brown inner markings very sparsely used. Eye in profile. Below, a strip of sets of three maeanders separated by chequer squares. Above, a strip of egg and tongue, black on red. Design extends over shoulder of vase.; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 18.40 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: hydria — 430BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured hydria. Toilet scene. On the left a nude woman wearing only a saccos stands with left leg crossed over right, and holding with both hands her chiton rolled up in bundle: around the right thigh is a black cord with ring attached. She is confronted by a woman in sleeved chiton, bordered himation, and fillet, who rests her right hand on the back of a cushioned chair placed to right in the background. Between them stands a calathos full of wool (?). On the left hangs in the field an embroidered cap, and on either side of the draped woman a taenia. Graceful style, with occasional carelessness. Purple ends of cap and taeniae, fillet, and wool. Brown inner markings. Eye in profile. Below, a band, sets of three maeanders separated by chequer squares. Above, egg and dart, black on red. Design rises over shoulder of vase.; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 17.78 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: lekythos — 435BC-425BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: White-ground lekythos. Hare-hunt beside a stele. The locality is indicated in faint brown lines as the rocky slope of a hill, which rises to the upper border on the left side. At the foot of the hill is a plain stele, surmounted by a cornice and resting on quadruple plinth; around it is tied a taenia, another is laid on top, and two more rest on the plinth and rocks below. Up the hill beside the stele runs a hare closely pursued by a large hound, urged on by a nude youth on right, who carries a mantle on his left arm and a club over his shoulder, and extends his right toward the hare. On the left, under the hill, a second youth strides forward with left foot raised on a rock, and hurling with his right a stone, apparently at the hare; from his left hangs a club, and he has a mantle over his left shoulder. Drawing of good period; brown outline; hair stippled black on brown; dress of left-hand figure in red wash with brown folds; skin of hare in light brown wash; ends of taenia black. Eye in profile. Above, a strip of maeander; on shoulder, three palmettes below egg pattern, black on white.; | Type: lekythos | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 31.75 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Ampelokepoi, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora, with twisted handles. (a) Three Greek warriors. On the right a hoplite stands en face, resting right on spear, with helmet tilted back, shield (no device), sword hanging from cross-belt, and short chiton which leaves the right shoulder free and is tied at waist: he looks to left towards two others who advance: the first is a horseman (hippeus) mounted on a prancing horse, in chlamys and petasos, with his spear under his right arm: the other is a javelin-thrower (?) wearing a hemispherical helmet and a chlamys, and carrying his spear sloped over his left shoulder. All these are beardless. Over the centre, ΚΑΛΟΣ, καλός. (b) A woman addressing two draped ephebi: the left hand one leans on a staff, the other stands en face, but looks to right; both wear fillets. Round shoulder, guilloche: round lip, egg pattern: on each side of neck, a palmette with four tendrils: below each handle, two palmettes back-to-back, surmounted by one smaller.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 55.88 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Europa carried off by the bull. The bull gallops to left with Europa sitting on his back; she faces to front, supporting herself with her right on the neck and her left on the flank of the bull, wearing sleeved chiton, and himation of which the end floats back, a saccos embroidered with pairs of dots, and earrings. She looks back to right. (b) A companion of Europa, in chiton and himation, hair looped up, who runs to left with outstretched right arm, looking round to right. Drawing of Europa careless, but of fine style, the bull heavy and clumsy; the reverse sketchy. Brown inner markings, hair on tail, and wavy strokes on neck of bull, also lower folds of chiton in b. Below a, sets of three maeanders in alternate directions, separated by dotted crosses ; below b, key pattern to right.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 32.00 centimetres; 1.24 kilograms; 18.50 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: kylix — 440BC-430BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured kylix, with low foot. Interior: Within a thin red circle, a youth, nude, wreathed, standing to right with knees beat, as if under the weight of the situla (bronxe vessel - ?), which he holds up in both hands; on right a stool, with a striped cushion on it, half seen. Red exergue. Exterior: (a) Eros flies to right towards a boy with long hair, who stands holding out a purse in his right, in an attitude as if singing. On the left, another boy appears to be tuning his chelys. All three are nude and wreathed. (b) Similar scene, except that the boy on right holds a cord. Minute style; glaze brownish. The wreaths, cord, and the plectra are in a colour which has turned whitish. Inner markings in faint brown. Eye fully developed profile type. Beneath each handle a palmette, from which branches out on each side a tendril terminating in a flower.; | Type: kylix | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 19.05 centimetres; 6.35 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: calyx-krater — 460BC-430BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured calyx-krater. (a) Eos pursuing Kephalos. Eos, in a long chiton, an himation which covers her left arm, hair looped up with fillet, runs to left, extending her right arm towards Kephalos, who is attired as a hunter, with chlamys, and petasos at back, and holds in his left two spears; he is wreathed and has hair looped up; he looks round, raising his right in astonishment. (b) A draped ephebos with staff to left. Good period. Purple fillet and strings of petasos. Brown inner markings. Eye in profile. Below a, sets of three maeanders in alternate directions, separated by dotted cross squares; below b, key pattern. Round the lip, laurel-wreath.; | Type: calyx-krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 25.40 centimetres; 250.00 millimetres; 24.13 centimetres; 243.00 millimetres; 1248.00 grammes; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 440BC-430BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Ajax seizing Cassandra (?). In place of the Palladion is an archaic image of Apollo, in the form of a long-haired, beardless youth, en face, with hands at sides and feet close together, a black line drawn horizontally across the waist; this figure stands on a square base, resting on a plinth on the left. Cassandra, in sleeved chiton with apoptygma tied, and himation over her shoulders, with hair flying loose in long wavy tresses, has fled to the statue; and with one foot on the plinth she is in the act of throwing both arms around its waist, but is dragged back by Ajax, who, with right foot raised, has seized her with his right hand by the hair. He is bearded, and has a helmet tilted back, shield (device, a lion in silhouette, springing to left), spear, and greaves decorated with spirals. Beneath his shield hangs an end of drapery which is not shown elsewhere. (b) Bearded man in himation, standing to right, resting right hand on a staff. Late stage of strong style. Brown inner markings and (very light yellowish) for hair of Apollo. Eyes of Apollo of archaic type. Greater part of figure of Ajax destroyed, only the head, right arm and shoulder,  | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 33.00 centimetres; 1.40 kilograms; 18.00 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Capua, Greece

properties.title: column krater — 430BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured column-krater. (a) Revel. Two ephebi and a woman dancing to right. The woman in the centre, with a long sleeved chiton and himation, and hair looped up behind with a fillet, plays on the flute. The youth on right stands en face, with legs wide apart, looking to left, and playing on a chelys, to which a flute-case (sybene) is attached; a mantle floats back from his arms, and he wears a woollen fillet with ivy-leaves attached. The figures at each side overlap the border. (b) The same repeated. Purple fillets. Brown inner markings and shading of lyre, etc. Round the lip, on each side, two groups of a lion springing (to left) and a goat browsing, confronted.; | Type: column krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 29.21 centimetres; 36.83 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: hydria — 460BC-440BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured hydria: Women with lyres, and Eros. Design in frieze extending round shoulder, with border of palmettes and single lotus flowers above and below. Egg pattern round lip. Musical scene in women's apartments: in the centre, a woman seated on a chair playing a lyre (chelys). Facing her, an attendant holding a box ornamented with chequers and a chelys; between them a crane. On the left, a woman standing by a stool with a thick cushion; above hangs a pair of writing tablets. Beyond is Eros flying towards the woman, holding a wreath; below him, a chest. Next, a woman wrapped in a mantle, looking round, and a Doric column closing the scene. On the right, another seated woman playing on a chelys; next, a woman to the front holding plectrum and flute-case (?) and another holding an open scroll (mostly wanting); between them, a stool over which drapery is spread. Underneath the foot is incised Y∆I∆PAX∏OI A/; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 41.00 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: olpe — 470BC-440BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured olpe (shape 5a). Youth to front, looking to left and holding out in right a chelys; himation covering left arm; hair wavy, falling to shoulders. On right is a square base surmounted by a plinth which is inscribed ΛΟΣΚ, κ(α)λός (?). Above hangs a plectrum decorated with trefoils. Late stage of fine style. Light brown inner markings. Eye in profile. Below, a strip of ivy-leaves, black on red.; | Type: olpe | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 29.21 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Fikellura grave 136, Greece

properties.title: bell krater — 430BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured bell-krater. Designs red on black ground; the red glaze completely worn away. Above the designs, laurel-wreath; below each, maeander and chequer; round the ends of the handles, egg-moulding. (a) Dionysiac group: A seated Satyr is playing on the flutes to a Maenad who stands before him on the right; her hair is gathered in a knot at the back, and she wears a long girt chiton; in left hand is a thyrsos, and in right she holds out a dish on which are two large bunches of grapes. Behind the Satyr stands a similar Maenad, and behind the first Maenad a Satyr advances with thyrsos in left hand and an askos of skin in right. Each thyrsos has a projecting spur. (b) Three ephebi conversing, wrapped in himatia, the centre one to right.; | Type: bell krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 35.56 centimetres; 33.02 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: column krater — 450BC-440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured column-krater. (a) Symposion. Two bearded men recline to left on two couches, leaning left arm on striped cushions; the one on the right has a broad radiated band (ampyx?) tied in a bow behind the ear, with end hanging down; he raises on his right a phiale, addressing his companion, who turns towards him, holding up in his right by the stem a large kylix; this one is wreathed, and has his left arm wrapped in his mantle; both have the legs draped. In the foreground between the two a flute-player stands, to right, playing on flutes; she wears a long chiton with apoptygma, and her hair is looped up with a radiated fillet. In the background hang a taenia (on left) and a ring-shaped object (wreath ?). In front of each couch is a table, on which is a dish with flowers. (b) Three draped ephebi. The one on left moves away to left, looking back at the other two; his right arm projects over the border of the design. The central one holds a staff. In the field hangs a pair of halteres (jumping-weights). Round the lip, in black silhouette on red, two pairs of animals, a lion and boar, stepping towards each other.; | Type: column krater | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 27.94 centimetres; 34.29 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: hydria — 450BC-440BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured hydria. Toilet scene. On the left a woman is seated in a chair, holding up on her left a calathos, her right closed, as if drawing something from it. Confronting her is a woman in a radiated stephane, holding up a mirror: and on the right a third woman (long hair tied in roll at end, fillet) looking down at a taenia, which she holds in both hands. All three wear long chiton and himation. The seated one has her hair looped up with a fillet, left red; above her hangs a taenia. Drawing graceful, with occasional carelessness. Purple fillet of right hand figure. Brown inner markings of chair and calathos. Eye in profile. Below, sets of two to four meanders separated by red cross squares. Above, a strip formed of a running helix pattern. Design curves up over shoulder of vase. The varnishing has been carelessly done, so that in parts a line is left red outside the artist's outline. On the foot incised characters PN.; | Type: hydria | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 29.00 centimetres; 1.70 kilograms; 24.00 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Greece

properties.title: kylix — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured kylix. Interior: Within a circle of single maeanders interspersed with five red cross squares, a woman en face, head turned to left, extending to left with her right hand part of a taenia which she holds in her left. She wears a sleeved chiton, himation and saccos. On left, part seen, a rectangular box. Exterior: (a) A woman, like that just described, between two draped ephebi; towards the one on left she holds out a toilet-box with her right; this figure rests his right hand on a staff; the other stands en face, with his right akimbo, but looks to left. Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: pelike — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured pelike. (a) Nike offering wine to a warrior. On the left Nike, in a chiton with apoptygma tied, and a radiated stephane, stands holding up in her right a phiale which she has filled from an oinochoe hanging at her side in her left, and which is only partially seen; her long hair falls down her back. On the right stands a young warrior en face, but looking at Nike and extending his right hand for the phiale; his left foot is turned to the right; he wears a short chiton, a cuirass with a star on the shoulder, and a crestless helmet tilted back; in his left he carries a long spear and a shield with device in black silhouette of a scorpion to left. On the lower insertion of each handle, a palmette inverted.; | Type: pelike | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 25.40 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: calyx-krater — 470BC-440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured calyx-krater (a) Dionysos and two Maenads (?). Dionysos (bearded, long hair wreathed with a woollen fillet and ivy, Ionic chiton and mantle) moves to right, holding in left thyrsos, in right, clasped to his body, a cantharos of unusual form (silhouette). He looks back at a Maenad who holds thyrsos in left and oinochoe in right. On right stands a woman (another Maenad?), holding in her right a long torch (?). On left a woman like the one on right in (a) moves away, holding a thyrsos, looking back and raising her left in surprise. Good period, but careless drawing. Attica, Fikellura grave 121, Greece

properties.title: lekanis — 440BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured lekanis with lid. The design forms a broad frieze on the lid, around the handle, between two bands of rays. The drawing is of a good period, but careless. White is used for the hair and beard and tail of the old Seilenos (bearded satyr) and the wreaths of the young Seilenos and Satyr. Brown inner markings. Seileni, a Satyr, and Maenads. An old bent Seilenos, holding a keras, moves haltingly to right, propping his steps with a thyrsos in his right hand; he looks round at a Maenad in a long chiton with apoptygma tied, and looped-up hair, who runs towards him, holding in front of her in each hand a torch. She is followed by a black-haired Seilenos wreathed with ivy, who holds out in his right a keras. Behind him a beardless wreathed Satyr walks to left, his left hand resting on his hip, and holding upright in his right a thyrsos. Towards him comes a Maenad like the first, but with a nebris knotted round her waist and over the left shoulder, so that the hind leg hangs down in front; she has a torch in her right hand, her left is extended, and she looks round at the old Seilenos.; | Type: lekanis | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 19.05 centimetres; 13.97 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Athens, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 460BC-440BC
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured neck-amphora. (a) Departure of a youth. A beardless figure in deep-bordered chlamys, petasos hanging at back, sword at thigh, long wavy hair bound with fillet, stands to front, left hand on hip, right resting on two spears. He looks to left towards an old man, bald on the crown and bearded, who leans forward, with mantle and left arm resting against staff, and from the gesture of his right seems to address the youth; he wears a fillet. The spears have in the centre a thong (άγκύλη). (b) Ephebos and girl with lyre and flutes. The ephebos on right, wearing mantle and fillet, stands resting right on a staff. The woman on left seems to offer him in right a chelys, in left a pair of flutes; she wears a chiton schistos and earrings, and her hair is looped up with a fillet. The figure of the woman in b is very long in proportion to the head, being about nine heads. The figures in a are larger than those in b. Below each design, a strip of maeander.; | Type: neck-amphora | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 34.00 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Nola, Greece

properties.title: neck-amphora — 450BC-430BC
properties.notes:

properties.title: kylix — 430BC (circa)
properties.notes:
Pottery: red-figured kylix. Exterior: (a) Two youths wrestling, beside a stele on the left. This group seems to represent an intermediate stage between the two scenes shown on BM Vase Ε94, the relative positions of the combatants being reversed. Here the left hand athlete has gripped his opponent with his right hand under the right armpit, and chin pressed upon the shoulder, rendering this arm of his adversary helpless: passing his left arm across his adversary's back, he pulls his body sideways, so that it is in three-quarter face: the next stage will correspond to that shown in Ε94 b (a very similar vase), where the victor has suddenly twisted round, and using his adversary's arm over his own shoulder as a support, pitches him head first over his own head. nodes.name: Reicher Stil (Greece, 429 BC–399 BC)
nodes.title: Reicher Stil (Greece, 429 BC–399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 429 BC–399 BC] Reicher Stil. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The 'Rich Style' of late fifth-century Greek sculpture, in which drapery becomes an end in itself — clinging, transparent, breaking into deep swirling folds that reveal the body beneath. The Nike balustrade on the Athenian Acropolis is its showpiece, along with a wave of elegant grave stelai and small-scale reliefs. Emerging as Athens fought and lost the Peloponnesian War, it turns away from the calm authority of the Parthenon towards elaborate surface and emotional grace.

In the centre a youthful warrior is seated on a mantle spread on high ground beside his shield; he has long hair and wears a helmet with visor and cheek-pieces; he holds out in his right hand a sword in its scabbard towards a tree-trunk on the right, which is already decorated with a short chiton, a cuirass and a shield seen in foreshortening; a spear pointing obliquely downwards is attached to the right shoulder, and a conical helmet rests on the top. This helmet is being nailed in position by Nike, who advances from the right, holding the nail in her left and brandishing the hammer in her right; she wears a long chiton and bracelets, and her hair is knotted behind. On the left a woman leans forward with her left foot on rising ground, holding in each hand a greave decorated with a spiral; she wears a long chiton, a necklace, bracelets, and a saccos decorated over the forehead with an ornament. Beneath her, a plant with fruits, and between Nike and the trophy a long tendril with spirals rises from the ground. Graceful drawing. The flesh of Nike and the woman is painted white with brown details, on the red ground; their d | Type: squat lekythos | Medium: pottery; gold | Dimensions: 16.51 centimetres; | Culture: Attic

Attica, Athens, Greece

Pottery: red-figure stemless kylix. Interior: Nereid on Hippocamp with greave of Achilles. Through the sea (indicated by wavy lines) the Hippocamp moves to right, bearing on its back, side-saddle, a Nereid in long chiton with apoptygma tied, long hair tied at the back and wreathed with olive, and earrings: she holds upright on her left palm, by its lower end, a greave, and extends her right as if directing the animal; it has the head and fore-quarters of a horse, wide open jaws with teeth, a spiny back in place of mane, and fins in place of fore-legs. The exergue is left red. Exterior: (a) Three youthful athletes: one in the centre sits on a bema of two steps, talking to one on right, who confronts him: on the left a third stands scraping his left arm with a strigil (apoxyomenos). nodes.name: hochhellenistisch (Greece, 229 BC–149 BC)
nodes.title: hochhellenistisch (Greece, 229 BC–149 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 229 BC–149 BC] hochhellenistisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

The mature phase of the Hellenistic world, when the Antigonid, Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms and the Achaean and Aetolian leagues fought each other into exhaustion while Rome, drawn in as an ally, steadily became the arbiter of Greek affairs. Sculpture and architecture reached their most theatrical, emotionally charged form, seen in works like the Great Altar of Pergamon. The sequence of Macedonian wars ended with the sack of Corinth and the reduction of Greece to Roman control.

nodes.name: späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC)
nodes.title: späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechenland, 149 BC–29 BC] späthellenistisch. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Roman power closed over the Greek world: Corinth was destroyed in 146 BC, Athens was sacked by Sulla, and Mithridates' wars ravaged Asia Minor and the Aegean. Kings and cities became clients or provinces, artists and philosophers migrated to Rome, and the last independent Hellenistic kingdom ended with Cleopatra's defeat at Actium.

nodes.name: Früheisenzeit (Rome, 999 BC–619 BC)
nodes.title: Früheisenzeit (Rome, 999 BC–619 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rom, 999 BC–619 BC] Früheisenzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Iron working spread through the Italian peninsula while communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in hut-shaped urns. Villanovan villages in Etruria and Latial hut settlements on the hills above the Tiber grew, merged and hardened into towns, and imported Greek and Phoenician goods appear in increasingly rich graves. Out of this came the Etruscan city-states and the small settlement that Romans later remembered as the founding of their city.

nodes.name: Archaische Zeit (Rome, 619 BC–508 BC)
nodes.title: Archaische Zeit (Rome, 619 BC–508 BC)
nodes.description: [Rom, 619 BC–508 BC] Archaische Zeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

nodes.name: Republikanische Zeit (Rome, 508 BC–30 BC)
nodes.title: Republikanische Zeit (Rome, 508 BC–30 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rom, 508 BC–30 BC] Republikanische Zeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

After the expulsion of the kings, Rome was governed by annually elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and assemblies of citizens, a system built as much on custom as on law. In under five centuries the city went from one player among many in central Italy to master of the Mediterranean, absorbing Carthage, Greece and much of Gaul and the Near East. The wealth and armies that conquest produced eventually broke the system itself, in a century of civil war that ended with Augustus.

nodes.name: frührepublikanisch (Rome, 508 BC–366 BC)
nodes.title: frührepublikanisch (Rome, 508 BC–366 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rom, 508 BC–366 BC] frührepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

After driving out its kings, Rome spent a century and a half as one middling Latin city among many, fighting neighbours in the hills while plebeians wrung concessions from the patrician aristocracy. The Twelve Tables put law in public writing, the Gauls sacked the city around 390 BC, and the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 finally opened the consulship to plebeians. The institutions improvised in these struggles — consuls, tribunes, the Senate's authority — became the machinery of Mediterranean empire.

nodes.name: mittelrepublikanisch (Rome, 366 BC–201 BC)
nodes.title: mittelrepublikanisch (Rome, 366 BC–201 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rom, 366 BC–201 BC] mittelrepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Rome moved from being one central Italian power among many to master of the western Mediterranean, absorbing the Samnites, Etruscans and Greek cities of the south, then surviving Hannibal. Plebeians won access to the consulship and the senatorial governing class took its classic shape. Conquest brought slaves, silver and provinces, remaking Roman society as thoroughly as it remade the map.

nodes.name: spätrepublikanisch (Rome, 201 BC–30 BC)
nodes.title: spätrepublikanisch (Rome, 201 BC–30 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rom, 201 BC–30 BC] spätrepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Victory over Carthage and the eastern kingdoms brought Rome enormous wealth, slaves and provinces – and a political system unable to manage them. Land struggles, the murders of the Gracchi, civil wars between Marius and Sulla, and generals with private armies culminated in Caesar's dictatorship and assassination, ending with Octavian's supremacy and the birth of the empire.

nodes.name: Frühe Kaiserzeit (Rome, 30 BC–AD 68)
nodes.title: Frühe Kaiserzeit (Rome, 30 BC–AD 68)
nodes.description:
[Rom, 30 BC–AD 68] Frühe Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Augustus turned the wreckage of the civil wars into a monarchy dressed as a restored republic, and his successors made the arrangement permanent. Provinces were reorganised, a standing army and professional bureaucracy took shape, and the Mediterranean enjoyed unusually uninterrupted peace and trade. It was also the age of Virgil, Ovid and Livy, of the imperial cult, and of the dynastic scandals under Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero that ended when the last Julio-Claudian killed himself.

nodes.name: Mittlere Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 69–AD 192)
nodes.title: Mittlere Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 69–AD 192)
nodes.description:
[Rom, AD 69–AD 192] Mittlere Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Rome's high imperial century and a bit more, running from the chaos of the four emperors of AD 69 through the Flavian dynasty and the so-called Five Good Emperors to the murder of Commodus. The empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan, hardened its frontiers under Hadrian, and spread a shared urban culture of baths, amphitheatres and aqueducts from Britain to Syria - the Colosseum, Pantheon and Trajan's Column all belong here. Citizenship and imperial office opened to provincials, so that emperors themselves came from Spain and North Africa, while trade goods and coinage circulated across an unprecedented single market.

nodes.name: Späte Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 193–AD 306)
nodes.title: Späte Kaiserzeit (Rome, AD 193–AD 306)
nodes.description:
[Rom, AD 193–AD 306] Späte Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

From the Severan dynasty to the tetrarchy, the empire lurched through soldier-emperors, currency debasement, plague and simultaneous invasions on the Rhine, Danube and Persian frontiers. Provinces broke away as the Gallic and Palmyrene empires before being reconquered. Diocletian's reforms — a divided command, a swollen bureaucracy and a fixed tax system — rebuilt the state on far more authoritarian lines.

nodes.name: Spätantike (Rome, AD 306–AD 395)
nodes.title: Spätantike (Rome, AD 306–AD 395)
nodes.description:
[Rom, AD 306–AD 395] Spätantike. Spatial coverage: Rome, ancient Rome. No end date for this period provided in the chronological chart, probably because Hölscher does not provide an explicit end date in his chronological chart. We have provided a value of 0395, following Hölscher, so that the temporal coverage can be visualized. Period definition from Archäologie und Chronologie : eine Einführung — Balbina Bäbler, 2004.

Constantine's rise ended the tetrarchic experiment, legalised Christianity and founded a new capital on the Bosphorus; by the reign of Theodosius, Christianity was the state religion and the empire was permanently administered as eastern and western halves. Art, coinage and government all took on the hierarchical, ceremonial character we call late Roman, and bishops became figures of political weight.

nodes.name: Gumelnița Culture (Romania, 4199 BC–3699 BC)
nodes.title: Gumelnița Culture (Romania, 4199 BC–3699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, 4199 BC–3699 BC] Gumelnița Culture. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Copper Age farmers who lived on tells built up by generations of rebuilt mud-brick houses, some ringed by ditches and palisades. They made graphite-painted pottery and clay figurines, and their smiths worked copper and gold on a scale unmatched anywhere at the time, linked to the goldwork of the Varna cemetery. Their tells were abandoned in a widespread collapse that ended settled life in the region for centuries.

nodes.name: Hamangia Culture (Romania, 5199 BC–4599 BC)
nodes.title: Hamangia Culture (Romania, 5199 BC–4599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, 5199 BC–4599 BC] Hamangia Culture. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Neolithic villages along the western Black Sea coast, sustained by cereals, cattle, fishing and shellfish, and remarkable for their art. Their extensive inhumation cemeteries and their strikingly modern-looking clay figurines, above all the seated Thinker of Cernavodă, are among the best-known finds of Old Europe. The culture eventually merged into the copper-using Gumelnița world that followed.

nodes.name: Boian Culture (Romania, 4499 BC–3999 BC)
nodes.title: Boian Culture (Romania, 4499 BC–3999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, 4499 BC–3999 BC] Boian Culture. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Farming communities of the lower Danube plain and southeastern Romania, living in villages of rectangular houses and burying their dead in flat cemeteries beside the settlements. They are recognised by dark burnished pots incised with meanders and spirals filled with white paste, and by an economy of cereals, cattle and pigs. Their late phases feed directly into the Gumelnița culture, which took copper and gold working much further.

nodes.name: Middle Archaic (Romania, 619 BC–559 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Archaic (Romania, 619 BC–559 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, 619 BC–559 BC] Middle Archaic. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

A warmer, drier climate shrank wetlands and shifted forests, and people responded by concentrating on rivers and shoals rich in fish, mussels and nuts. Ground and polished stone tools, notched projectile points and the first substantial refuse middens appear, marking a shift from wide-ranging mobility toward repeated use of favoured valley locations.

nodes.name: High Classical (Romania, 449 BC–399 BC)
nodes.title: High Classical (Romania, 449 BC–399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, 449 BC–399 BC] High Classical. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

The decades after the Persian wars when Athens, funded by its maritime empire, rebuilt the Acropolis and put up the Parthenon under Pheidias's direction. Sophocles and Euripides were writing for the theatre, Socrates was arguing in the agora, and sculptors worked out an idealised human figure that European art would copy for two thousand years. The same era brought the Peloponnesian War, plague, and the collapse of Athenian power in 404.

nodes.name: Late Classical (Romania, 399 BC–322 BC)
nodes.title: Late Classical (Romania, 399 BC–322 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, 399 BC–322 BC] Late Classical. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

In the Greek cities of the south, this was the era of grand Apulian and Lucanian red-figure vases, tomb painting, and lavish burials, even as Oscan and Lucanian peoples took over cities like Poseidonia. Central Italy saw Etruscan power ebb and Rome fight its way through the Latin and Samnite wars, absorbing neighbours and building the first roads and aqueducts. By the end of the century the peninsula's future belonged to Rome rather than to the Greek or Etruscan cities.

nodes.name: Middle Hellenistic II (Romania, 199 BC–99 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Hellenistic II (Romania, 199 BC–99 BC)
nodes.description: [Dobruja, 199 BC–99 BC] Middle Hellenistic II. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

nodes.name: Late Roman (Romania, AD 330–AD 641)
nodes.title: Late Roman (Romania, AD 330–AD 641)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, AD 330–AD 641] Late Roman. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Britain settled into a mature provincial society of walled towns, mosaic-floored country villas and industrial-scale pottery production, while new forts along the southeast coast guarded against seaborne raiders. The province was split into smaller units, coinage circulated in enormous quantities, and Christianity appeared alongside older cults. Around 410 the central administration and army pay ceased, and the whole system – towns, coins, mass-produced pottery – unravelled within a generation.

nodes.name: Ottoman (Romania, AD 1420–AD 1878)
nodes.title: Ottoman (Romania, AD 1420–AD 1878)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, AD 1420–AD 1878] Ottoman. closeMatch with. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Ottoman victory at Kosovo opened the way to the absorption of the Serbian lands, completed with the fall of the Despotate in the fifteenth century. For some three hundred years Serbia was a frontier province, its peasants organised under the timar system and its Orthodox Church tolerated as a religious community, with a great migration of Serbs northwards after the failed Habsburg advance of the 1690s. Uprisings from 1804 won autonomy and set the country on the road to full independence.

nodes.name: World War I (Romania, AD 1916–AD 1918)
nodes.title: World War I (Romania, AD 1916–AD 1918)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, AD 1916–AD 1918] World War I. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Romania stayed neutral for two years before joining the Allies in August 1916, hoping to win Transylvania from Austria-Hungary. The offensive collapsed within months; German and Bulgarian armies took Bucharest and the government fled to Iasi, holding a rump of Moldavia until Russia's collapse forced a punitive peace in 1918. Romania re-entered the war days before the armistice and emerged doubled in size, gaining Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina to form Greater Romania.

nodes.name: Interwar (Romania, AD 1918–AD 1941)
nodes.title: Interwar (Romania, AD 1918–AD 1941)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, AD 1918–AD 1941] Interwar. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Britain emerged from the Great War victorious, indebted and short of a generation of young men, and spent the following two decades wrestling with mass unemployment, the General Strike, the slump and the slow retreat from the gold standard. It was also the age of the wireless and the cinema, suburban semis and arterial roads, votes for all women in 1928, and the abdication crisis. Rearmament and the failure of appeasement brought it to a close.

nodes.name: World War II (Romania, AD 1941–AD 1945)
nodes.title: World War II (Romania, AD 1941–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, AD 1941–AD 1945] World War II. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

Romania joined the Axis under Marshal Ion Antonescu and sent large armies east alongside Germany in 1941, recovering Bessarabia and occupying territory beyond the Dniester. Romanian and German forces carried out mass killings of Jews and Roma in Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transnistria, one of the war's largest national contributions to the Holocaust outside Germany itself. After catastrophic losses at Stalingrad and with the Red Army on the frontier, King Michael arrested Antonescu in August 1944 and switched sides, opening the way to Soviet occupation and a communist state.

nodes.name: Post-Communist (Romania, AD 1989–AD 2020)
nodes.title: Post-Communist (Romania, AD 1989–AD 2020)
nodes.description:
[Dobruja, AD 1989–AD 2020] Post-Communist. Period definition from Romanian Dobruja Periodization for ARIADNEplus — Institute of Archaeology "Vasile Pârvan", 2020.

The violent overthrow and execution of Nicolae Ceaușescu in December 1989 ended one of the harshest regimes in the Eastern bloc and opened a rough transition: privatisation, mass emigration, hyperinflation and the closing of the huge state factories built by communist industrial policy. Institutions were rebuilt to meet Western criteria, bringing NATO membership in 2004 and European Union accession in 2007. Communist-era housing blocks, unfinished megaprojects and the Palace of the Parliament remain the most visible legacy in Romanian cities.

nodes.name: Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.title: Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III (Greece, 3199 BC–2099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 3199 BC–2099 BC] Frühe Ägäische Bronzezeit I-III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from the title of the chronological table on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Farming villages around the Aegean began working bronze, sailing longer routes and accumulating wealth in metal. This is the age of the Cycladic marble figurines, of fortified coastal settlements and of the first monumental buildings in mainland Greece, such as the House of the Tiles at Lerna. Widespread destructions and disruption at the end of the period cleared the way for the palace societies of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.

nodes.name: Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 2099 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 2099 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 2099 BC–1699 BC] Mittlere Ägäische Bronzezeit. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

On Crete the first great palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia - sprawling complexes of storerooms, workshops and courts that ran regional economies and used the still-undeciphered Linear A script. Cretan pottery, frescoes and seafaring reached across the Aegean to Thera and the Cyclades, while the Greek mainland remained comparatively modest until the spectacular shaft graves of Mycenae appear at the period's close. The wealth, bureaucracy and long-distance trade built up here became the foundation of Mycenaean civilisation.

nodes.name: MM / MH I-II (Greece, 2099 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.title: MM / MH I-II (Greece, 2099 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 2099 BC–1799 BC] MM / MH I-II. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Alte Paläste, Kreta. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

On Crete the first great palaces rose at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, with central courts, vast storage magazines, the Kamares polychrome pottery style and the earliest Cretan writing. The Greek mainland was poorer and simpler, its villages producing grey Minyan ware and burying their dead in modest cist graves. The contrast between palatial Crete and rustic mainland Greece defines the age.

nodes.name: MM / MH III (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: MM / MH III (Greece, 1799 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1799 BC–1699 BC] MM / MH III. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Neue Paläste, Kreta. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The first Cretan palaces were destroyed and immediately rebuilt on a grander scale, opening the brilliant Neopalatial era of frescoes, seal-stones and Linear A administration. On the mainland the first shaft graves at Mycenae appear, packed with gold, weapons and imported goods — the earliest sign of the warrior elites who would later dominate the Aegean.

properties.title: jar — 1850BC-1700BC
properties.notes:
Pottery jar decorated with two circles in black, made from Egyptian clay in Middle Minoan II style.; | Type: jar | Medium: pottery | Dimensions: 4.00 centimetres base ; 6.50 centimetres rim ; 7.80 centimetres; 145.00 grammes; 8.60 centimetres; | Culture: Middle Minoan II

Egypt, Lahun, el-, Greece

nodes.name: Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 1699 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit (Greece, 1699 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1699 BC–1049 BC] Späte Ägäische Bronzezeit. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The age of the Cretan palaces at their height and then of the Mycenaean citadels — Linear B archives, shaft graves, tholos tombs and warrior kings who traded with Egypt and the Levant. Thera's eruption and the fall of Knossos shifted power to the Greek mainland. Around 1200 BC the palace system collapsed everywhere, taking writing and monumental building with it.

nodes.name: SM I A / SH I (Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: SM I A / SH I (Greece, 1699 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1699 BC–1599 BC] SM I A / SH I. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Schachtgräber Mykene, Eruption Thera. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The height of Minoan Crete: rebuilt palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, elegant frescoed towns, and pottery painted with dark spiralling plants on light clay. The eruption of Thera, which buried the town of Akrotiri, falls within these years. On the mainland the first Mycenaean elites announce themselves in the shaft graves of Mycenae, heaped with gold masks, weapons and imported goods.

nodes.name: SM I B / SH II A (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: SM I B / SH II A (Greece, 1599 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1599 BC–1499 BC] SM I B / SH II A. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Zerstörung der Neuen Paläste". Date range noted as "außer Knossos". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The moment of the Marine Style, with octopuses and argonauts sprawling across Cretan jars, and of intense Aegean contact with Egypt, where Keftiu envoys appear in Theban tomb paintings. It closes with widespread burning and abandonment of Cretan country houses and towns, while on the mainland the Mycenaeans begin building monumental tholos tombs.

hints.label: SM I B / SH II A

nodes.name: SM II / SH II B (Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC)
nodes.title: SM II / SH II B (Greece, 1499 BC–1449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1499 BC–1449 BC] SM II / SH II B. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Knossos alone remains a functioning palace, now run by a mainland-linked elite: Linear B tablets record Greek, warrior graves are furnished with swords and boar's-tusk helmets, and stiff, formal Palace Style jars replace the earlier fluid decoration. The balance of Aegean power has swung from Crete to the mainland.

nodes.name: SM III A1 / SH III A1 (Greece, 1449 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.title: SM III A1 / SH III A1 (Greece, 1449 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1449 BC–1399 BC] SM III A1 / SH III A1. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Mycenaean Greece consolidates into palace states, with the great citadels and their bureaucracies taking shape and Mycenaean pottery turning up in quantity in Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt. Crete is administered from Knossos in its final palatial phase, and standardised Mycenaean styles spread so widely that regional differences blur across the Aegean.

hints.label: SM III A1 / SH III A1

nodes.name: SM III A2 / SH III A2 (Greece, 1399 BC–1349 BC)
nodes.title: SM III A2 / SH III A2 (Greece, 1399 BC–1349 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1399 BC–1349 BC] SM III A2 / SH III A2. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Zerstörung u. Wiederaufbau von Knossos. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The high point of Mycenaean power on the mainland, when palace centres like Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns were rebuilt on a grand scale and Knossos on Crete lay under mainland-style control. Standardised Mycenaean pottery was exported the length of the Mediterranean, turning up in Egypt at Amarna, along the Levantine coast and in Italy, and this uniform tableware is what lets archaeologists date sites hundreds of miles apart to the same generation.

hints.label: SM III A2 / SH III A2

nodes.name: SM III B / SH III B (Greece, 1349 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: SM III B / SH III B (Greece, 1349 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1349 BC–1199 BC] SM III B / SH III B. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "myken. Burgen um 1200 zerstört". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The palace system reached its most bureaucratic form: Linear B tablets recording rations, textiles, chariot wheels and offerings, roads, dams and drained basins, and the massive Cyclopean walls thrown up around the citadels of Mycenae and Tiryns. Those fortifications, and hoarded valuables, hint at rising insecurity. Around 1200 BC nearly every mainland palace burned within a few decades, ending centralised record-keeping in Greece for some four hundred years.

hints.label: SM III B / SH III B

nodes.name: SM III C / SH III C (Greece, 1199 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: SM III C / SH III C (Greece, 1199 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1199 BC–1049 BC] SM III C / SH III C. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Ende der myken. Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Life after the palaces: no more tablets, no more frescoed throne rooms, but people carried on in smaller, scattered settlements, some perched in defensible spots like Lefkandi, Perati and the Cretan mountain refuges. Potters produced some of the liveliest Mycenaean painting yet, including ships, warriors and the famous octopus jars, while population fell sharply and long-distance trade thinned. The period ends with the shift to Protogeometric styles and the beginning of the Greek Iron Age.

hints.label: SM III C / SH III C

nodes.name: Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche (Greece, 1049 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche (Greece, 1049 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 1049 BC–999 BC] Subminoische/-mykenische Epoche. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Dark Ages" provided as gloss in English for this period in chart. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The last flicker of Bronze Age Aegean traditions after the palaces at Knossos and on the mainland had fallen: potters still worked in degenerate Minoan and Mycenaean shapes, but writing, monumental building and centralised administration were gone. Communities were small, burial customs shifted toward single graves and cremation, and iron began to appear alongside bronze. Out of this impoverished interval grew the Protogeometric style and the reorganised Greece of the early Iron Age.

nodes.name: Protogeometrische Epoche (Greece, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Protogeometrische Epoche (Greece, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 999 BC–899 BC] Protogeometrische Epoche. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athenian workshops reinvented vase decoration after the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, using a compass and multiple brush to lay out precise concentric circles and banded zones. Cremation burial became standard in Attica and iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons. The style spread across the Aegean and to the new Greek settlements on the Anatolian coast.

nodes.name: Geometrische Epoche (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Geometrische Epoche (Greece, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 899 BC–699 BC] Geometrische Epoche. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Greek communities rebuilt after the fall of the Mycenaean world, and their pottery — meanders, zigzags, concentric circles, then silhouetted mourners and horses on monumental grave vases — gives the age its name. Sanctuaries at Olympia and Delphi began receiving dedications, the alphabet was borrowed from the Phoenicians, and the first western colonies were founded. The polis and the Homeric epics emerged from this world.

nodes.name: frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC) [p0wz8jkpxx8]
nodes.title: frühgeometrisch (Greece, 899 BC–849 BC) [p0wz8jkpxx8]
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 899 BC–849 BC] frühgeometrisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athenian potters imposed a strict new order on their vases — bands of meanders, concentric circles and zigzags covering black-glazed surfaces — in the first coherent Greek art style after the collapse of the Mycenaean world. Populations were growing again, iron working was routine, and cremation burials with modest metal goods hint at families asserting rank. The Lefkandi hero-burial shows how much wealth and long-distance contact could still be commanded.

nodes.name: mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC) [p0wz8jk2fqt]
nodes.title: mittelgeometrisch (Greece, 849 BC–759 BC) [p0wz8jk2fqt]
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 849 BC–759 BC] mittelgeometrisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athenian potters tightened the geometric repertoire inherited from the previous century, filling vases with meanders, zigzags and the first tentative silhouette animals. Behind the pottery lies a society climbing out of the post-Mycenaean slump: population growing, metalwork and burial goods richer, contacts with Cyprus and the Levant resuming. The stage is being set for the huge grave-marker amphorae and figured scenes of the Late Geometric, and for the eighth-century surge of colonisation and writing.

nodes.name: spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC) [p0wz8jkgsxv]
nodes.title: spätgeometrisch (Greece, 759 BC–699 BC) [p0wz8jkgsxv]
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 759 BC–699 BC] spätgeometrisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Entstehung der Polis-Kultur, Erste Gründungen von 'Kolonie'-Städten". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Painters filled Athenian grave vases with meanders, chariot processions and rows of mourners – the first narrative scenes in Greek art after centuries of abstraction. Population and settlement grew sharply, sanctuaries filled with dedications, the alphabet was adopted from Phoenician traders, and Greeks began founding colonies in Italy and Sicily as the polis took shape.

nodes.title: früharchaisch (Greece, 699 BC–619 BC) [p0wz8jk6r9h]

[Griechische Kultur, 699 BC–619 BC] früharchaisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Greek communities emerged from centuries of isolation to trade and settle across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, absorbing Near Eastern art, myth and technology in the process. The alphabet was put to work on Homer and on the first written laws; the first monumental stone temples and life-size statues appeared; and the citizen militia of massed hoplites began to reshape who held power in the polis.

nodes.title: mittelarchaisch (Greece, 619 BC–559 BC) [p0wz8jk7j96]
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 619 BC–559 BC] mittelarchaisch. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Athens and Corinth turned out black-figure vases traded across the Mediterranean, sculptors carved the first life-size marble kouroi and korai, and cities replaced timber shrines with stone temples. Tyrants seized power in many poleis, while Solon's reforms reshaped Athenian law and citizenship. Colonies planted from the Black Sea to Spain spread Greek language, coinage and the alphabet.

properties.notes:
Black-figure painted pottery situla. Designs in black on buff panels on the neck, with incised lines and accessories of purple. Behind the hare stands a larger bird to right, and in the field above is a grasshopper, also crosses and dots, as in (a). On either side is a square, as on (a). The one on the left has a border of rosettes, as before; in it is a star of four points, shaded, with segments of circles and rows of dots filling up the angles; in the field, crosses and dots. nodes.name: Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC) [p0wz8jkvm9p]
nodes.title: Hochklassik (Greece, 449 BC–429 BC) [p0wz8jkvm9p]
nodes.description:
[Griechische Kultur, 449 BC–429 BC] Hochklassik. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "Kimon, Perikles". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The high point of Athenian art and confidence, funded by tribute from the Delian League under Pericles: the Parthenon and the Propylaia rose on the Acropolis, Phidias made his colossal cult statues, and Polykleitos worked out the canon of ideal bodily proportion. Sculpture achieved the balanced, idealised naturalism that later ages took as the definition of classical beauty. It ended with the outbreak of war with Sparta and the plague that killed Pericles himself.

[Griechische Kultur, 429 BC–399 BC] Reicher Stil. Spatial coverage: Greece, Turkey. "431-404 Peloponnes. Krieg". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The 'Rich Style' of late fifth-century Greek sculpture, in which drapery becomes an end in itself — clinging, transparent, breaking into deep swirling folds that reveal the body beneath. The Nike balustrade on the Athenian Acropolis is its showpiece, along with a wave of elegant grave stelai and small-scale reliefs. Emerging as Athens fought and lost the Peloponnesian War, it turns away from the calm authority of the Parthenon towards elaborate surface and emotional grace.

[Griechische Kultur, 229 BC–149 BC] hochhellenistisch. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Syria, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur", together with the areas defined by the note on kingdoms. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

The mature phase of the Hellenistic world, when the Antigonid, Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms and the Achaean and Aetolian leagues fought each other into exhaustion while Rome, drawn in as an ally, steadily became the arbiter of Greek affairs. Sculpture and architecture reached their most theatrical, emotionally charged form, seen in works like the Great Altar of Pergamon. The sequence of Macedonian wars ended with the sack of Corinth and the reduction of Greece to Roman control.

nodes.title: späthellenistisch (Greece, 149 BC–29 BC) [p0wz8jkzd2q]

[Griechische Kultur, 149 BC–29 BC] späthellenistisch. Spatial coverage: Egypt, Greece, Syria, Turkey. Spatial coverage inferred from title of chronological chart on p. 34-35: "Griechische Kultur", together with the areas defined by the note on kingdoms. Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Roman power closed over the Greek world: Corinth was destroyed in 146 BC, Athens was sacked by Sulla, and Mithridates' wars ravaged Asia Minor and the Aegean. Kings and cities became clients or provinces, artists and philosophers migrated to Rome, and the last independent Hellenistic kingdom ended with Cleopatra's defeat at Actium.

nodes.name: Früheisenzeit (Italy, 999 BC–619 BC)
nodes.title: Früheisenzeit (Italy, 999 BC–619 BC)
nodes.description:
[Römische Kultur, 999 BC–619 BC] Früheisenzeit. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Iron working spread through the Italian peninsula while communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in hut-shaped urns. Villanovan villages in Etruria and Latial hut settlements on the hills above the Tiber grew, merged and hardened into towns, and imported Greek and Phoenician goods appear in increasingly rich graves. Out of this came the Etruscan city-states and the small settlement that Romans later remembered as the founding of their city.

nodes.name: Republikanische Zeit (Italy, 508 BC–30 BC)
nodes.title: Republikanische Zeit (Italy, 508 BC–30 BC)
nodes.description:
[Römische Kultur, 508 BC–30 BC] Republikanische Zeit. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

After the expulsion of the kings, Rome was governed by annually elected magistrates, a powerful Senate and assemblies of citizens, a system built as much on custom as on law. In under five centuries the city went from one player among many in central Italy to master of the Mediterranean, absorbing Carthage, Greece and much of Gaul and the Near East. The wealth and armies that conquest produced eventually broke the system itself, in a century of civil war that ended with Augustus.

nodes.name: frührepublikanisch (Italy, 508 BC–366 BC)
nodes.title: frührepublikanisch (Italy, 508 BC–366 BC)
nodes.description:
[Römische Kultur, 508 BC–366 BC] frührepublikanisch. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

After driving out its kings, Rome spent a century and a half as one middling Latin city among many, fighting neighbours in the hills while plebeians wrung concessions from the patrician aristocracy. The Twelve Tables put law in public writing, the Gauls sacked the city around 390 BC, and the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 finally opened the consulship to plebeians. The institutions improvised in these struggles — consuls, tribunes, the Senate's authority — became the machinery of Mediterranean empire.

nodes.title: mittelrepublikanisch (Italy, 366 BC–201 BC)
nodes.description:
[Römische Kultur, 366 BC–201 BC] mittelrepublikanisch. "264-241 1. punischer Krieg"; "218-201 2. punischer Krieg". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Rome moved from being one central Italian power among many to master of the western Mediterranean, absorbing the Samnites, Etruscans and Greek cities of the south, then surviving Hannibal. Plebeians won access to the consulship and the senatorial governing class took its classic shape. Conquest brought slaves, silver and provinces, remaking Roman society as thoroughly as it remade the map.

nodes.name: spätrepublikanisch (Italy, 201 BC–30 BC)
nodes.title: spätrepublikanisch (Italy, 201 BC–30 BC)
nodes.description:
[Römische Kultur, 201 BC–30 BC] spätrepublikanisch. Spatial coverage: France, Greece, Italy, Roman Republic, Spain, Tunisia, Turkey. "149-146 3. punischer Krieg"; "146 Eroberung Korinths"; "133 'Schenkung' von Pergamon an Rom"; "Marius, Sulla; Pompeius, Caesar". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Victory over Carthage and the eastern kingdoms brought Rome enormous wealth, slaves and provinces – and a political system unable to manage them. Land struggles, the murders of the Gracchi, civil wars between Marius and Sulla, and generals with private armies culminated in Caesar's dictatorship and assassination, ending with Octavian's supremacy and the birth of the empire.

nodes.name: Frühe Kaiserzeit (Italy, 30 BC–AD 68)
nodes.title: Frühe Kaiserzeit (Italy, 30 BC–AD 68)
nodes.description:
[Römische Kultur, 30 BC–AD 68] Frühe Kaiserzeit. Spatial coverage: Albania, Algeria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Egypt, France, Greece. Spatial coverage inferred from historical developments and title of chronological chart on p. 40-41: "Epochengliederung der römischen Kultur". Period definition from Klassische Archäologie : Grundwissen — Tonio Hölscher, 2002.

Augustus turned the wreckage of the civil wars into a monarchy dressed as a restored republic, and his successors made the arrangement permanent. Provinces were reorganised, a standing army and professional bureaucracy took shape, and the Mediterranean enjoyed unusually uninterrupted peace and trade. It was also the age of Virgil, Ovid and Livy, of the imperial cult, and of the dynastic scandals under Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero that ended when the last Julio-Claudian killed himself.
