nodes.name: Talamanca Phase (Panama, 4599 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.title: Talamanca Phase (Panama, 4599 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.description: [Rio Chiriquí region, 4599 BC–2299 BC] Talamanca Phase. This definition is provided in a contribution by Ranere to the edited volume: A. Ranere, “Preceramic shelters in the Talamancan Range”, pp. 16-43. Period definition from Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1980.

nodes.name: Boquete Phase (Panama, 2299 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: Boquete Phase (Panama, 2299 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description: [Rio Chiriquí region, 2299 BC–299 BC] Boquete Phase. This definition is provided in a contribution by Ranere to the edited volume: A. Ranere, “Preceramic shelters in the Talamancan Range”, pp. 16-43. Period definition from Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1980.

nodes.name: Tropical Forest Archaic (Panama, 4799 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Tropical Forest Archaic (Panama, 4799 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Chiriquí region, 4799 BC–499 BC] Tropical Forest Archaic. This definition is provided in Linares' concluding chapter, but makes reference to the preceding chapters, including Ranere's: O. Linares, "Conclusions", pp. 233-247. Period definition from Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama — Olga F. Linares, 1980.

Preceramic foragers in the Panamanian lowlands hunted, fished and gathered palm nuts while gradually taking up cultivation, burning clearings in the forest for early maize, manioc and arrowroot. Traces come mostly from rockshelters and their charred plant remains and starch grains, which push the beginnings of tropical farming back much earlier than pottery-using villages. The slow shift from foraging to gardening here helped carry domesticated crops between the Americas.

nodes.name: Talamanca phase (Panama, 5999 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.title: Talamanca phase (Panama, 5999 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.description: [Greater Chiriqui, 5999 BC–2999 BC] Talamanca phase. Spatial coverage: Costa Rica, Panama. The older of the two preceramic phases, Talamanca, has been dated by Ranere (1975b: 177) to before 3000 B.C., while Cooke (1976a:22) suggested a dating between 5000 and 3000 B.C. Taking the corrected C14 dates into account, 6000 to 3000 B.C. seems appropriate.” (p. 236). Period definition from The Archaeology of Greater Chiriqui — Wolfgang Haberland, 1984.

nodes.name: Boquete phase (Panama, 2999 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Boquete phase (Panama, 2999 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description: [Greater Chiriqui, 2999 BC–999 BC] Boquete phase. Spatial coverage: Costa Rica, Panama. The Boquete lithic assemblage “stratigraphically overlies the Talamanca phase at the Casita de Piedra and Trapiche rockshelters (Ranere 1975b: 176-77). The single C14 date, slightly later than 3000 B.C. when adjusted, came from the top of layer D at Casita de Piedra and either antedates the Boquete phase or reflects its very beginning (Linares and Ranere 1971: 350). The end should be around 1000 B.C., since SI-1844 is said to date the transition to the following ceramic phase at Casita de Piedra. Boquete represents a gradual development out of the Talamanca phase.” (p. 237). Period definition from The Archaeology of Greater Chiriqui — Wolfgang Haberland, 1984.

nodes.name: Prehistoria Reciente (Europe, 5550 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.title: Prehistoria Reciente (Europe, 5550 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–1150 BC] Prehistoria Reciente. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

Galicia's landscape filled with monuments: megalithic tombs under earthen mounds, then, in the Bronze Age, thousands of open-air rock carvings of deer, weapons and cup-marks on granite outcrops. Metalworkers produced flat axes, halberds and remarkable gold ornaments, some deposited in hoards or bogs. By the end of the period people were gathering into fortified hilltop settlements, the seeds of the castro culture.

nodes.name: Neolítico (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.title: Neolítico (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–3050 BC] Neolítico. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

The first farmers in the peninsula grew cereals and pulses and kept sheep, goats and cattle, spreading along the Mediterranean coast with distinctive shell-impressed Cardial pottery and inland through cave and open-air settlements. Burial in caves and, increasingly, in megalithic tombs marks a new concern with ancestors and place. Rock art and the earliest large communal monuments belong to these centuries.

nodes.name: Calcolítico (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC)
nodes.title: Calcolítico (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 3350 BC–1850 BC] Calcolítico. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

Copper metallurgy spread across the Iberian peninsula alongside the first walled settlements, such as Los Millares in the southeast, with bastioned enclosures, collective tholos and megalithic tombs, and rich grave goods of ivory, ostrich eggshell and Atlantic amber. Communal burial and long-distance exchange point to societies growing more unequal and more organised, while irrigation and metalworking reshaped the countryside. Near its end came the Bell Beaker phenomenon, whose distinctive drinking vessels and archer's kit turn up from Portugal to central Europe. The fortified towns and copper daggers of these centuries set the stage for the Bronze Age El Argar culture.

nodes.name: Edad del Bronce (Asia, 1850 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.title: Edad del Bronce (Asia, 1850 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 1850 BC–1150 BC] Edad del Bronce. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from PeriodO — 2020.

Metalworking in copper and tin spread across the peninsula, and in the southeast the El Argar culture built fortified hilltop towns with rectangular houses, buried its dead in jars beneath house floors, and marked out sharp differences of wealth in silver and bronze grave goods. Elsewhere communities raised cairns and stelae, worked gold, and traded along Atlantic and Mediterranean routes. It was the first period in Iberia with clearly stratified societies controlling metal and land.

nodes.name: Roman Climate Optimum (Roman Empire, 199 BC–AD 150)
nodes.title: Roman Climate Optimum (Roman Empire, 199 BC–AD 150)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, 199 BC–AD 150] Roman Climate Optimum. Spatial coverage: Europe, Roman Empire. "The empire reached its maximal extent and prosperity in the folds of a late Holocene climate period called the Roman Climate Optimum (RCO)." (p.14). Period definition from The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire — Kyle Harper, 2019.

A long stretch of warm, wet and unusually stable conditions across the Mediterranean, when glaciers retreated and farming pushed into higher and drier ground. Reliable harvests underpinned dense cities, big armies and the grain fleets that fed Rome. The end of this favourable spell coincided with epidemics, harvest failure and political strain, a reminder of how closely the empire's economy tracked its weather.

hints.label: Roman Climate Optimum
hints.source: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire

nodes.name: Roman Transitional Period (Roman Empire, AD 150–AD 450)
nodes.title: Roman Transitional Period (Roman Empire, AD 150–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 150–AD 450] Roman Transitional Period. Spatial coverage: Europe, Roman Empire. "... a period of climate disorganization covering three centuries (AD 150-450) set in, which we will propose to call the Roman Transitional Period." (p.15). Period definition from The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire — Kyle Harper, 2019.

A phase of unsettled climate between the reliable warmth of the earlier empire and the sharp cold of late antiquity, marked by shifting rainfall and repeated bad harvest years. It coincides with the Antonine plague, the third-century civil wars and the movements of peoples along the northern frontiers. Historians debate how far the weather drove these crises, but the correlation makes it one of the most argued-over episodes in climate history.

hints.label: Roman Transitional Period
hints.source: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire

nodes.name: Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empire, AD 450–AD 700)
nodes.title: Late Antique Little Ice Age (Roman Empire, AD 450–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 450–AD 700] Late Antique Little Ice Age. Spatial coverage: Europe, Roman Empire. "... from the later fifth century, we sense the stirrings of a decisive reorganization that culminated in the Late Antique Little Ice Age. A spasm of volcanic activity in the AD 530s and 540s brought on the most frigid spell in the entire Late Holocene." (p. 15). Period definition from The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire — Kyle Harper, 2019.

A cluster of massive volcanic eruptions beginning in 536 dimmed the sun and pushed temperatures down across the northern hemisphere for well over a century, a cooling recorded in tree rings and ice cores. Contemporaries described a year without summer, failed harvests and famine, and in 541 the Justinianic plague arrived to kill a large share of the Mediterranean population. Historians link the combined shock to the collapse of Justinian's reconquest, the weakening of Rome and Persia, and upheavals from the steppe to Scandinavia.

hints.label: Late Antique Little Ice Age
hints.source: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire

nodes.name: Pre-Christian Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Pre-Christian Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Iceland, AD 870–AD 1000] Pre-Christian Iceland. Iceland was Christianized in the year 1000 CE, when Christianity became the religion by law. In Icelandic, this event is known as the kristnitaka (literally, "the taking of Christianity"). (from. Period definition from The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries — Gunnar Karlsson, 2019.

Norse and Hiberno-Norse settlers claimed an uninhabited island during the landnám, clearing birch woods, building turf longhouses and running sheep and cattle over land that eroded quickly under them. Without a king, chieftains (goðar) organised law and feud through local assemblies and, from about 930, the annual Althing at Þingvellir. Farmsteads of this era preserve pagan burials with horses and weapons, and the memory of the period shaped the sagas written centuries later.

hints.label: Pre-Christian Iceland
hints.source: The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries

nodes.name: Settlement Period, Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–AD 930)
nodes.title: Settlement Period, Iceland (Iceland, AD 870–AD 930)
nodes.description:
[Iceland, AD 870–AD 930] Settlement Period, Iceland. Traditionally, the Icelandic Age of Settlement is considered to have lasted from 874 to 930, at which point most of the island had been claimed and Alþingi (Althingi), the assembly of the Icelandic Commonwealth, was founded at Þingvellir (Thingvellir). (from. Period definition from The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries — Gunnar Karlsson, 2019.

Norse and Hiberno-Norse families, many arriving via Norway, the Hebrides and Ireland, claimed land across an uninhabited island, felling birch woods and turning livestock loose on fragile volcanic soils. Within two generations the best land was taken and the settlers established a system of local chieftains that culminated in the founding of the Althing assembly. The period is unusually well documented for an early medieval migration, thanks to the Book of Settlements and the family sagas written down later.

hints.label: Settlement Period, Iceland
hints.source: The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries

nodes.name: Cenozoic Era (World, 65998050 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Cenozoic Era (World, 65998050 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[World, 65998050 BC–AD 1950] Cenozoic Era. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The era that began when the asteroid impact and its aftermath wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs, leaving mammals and birds to fill the empty ecological space. India collided with Asia to raise the Himalaya, grasslands spread as the world cooled, and by the last few million years ice sheets were advancing and retreating across the northern continents. Primates evolved within it, and every human being who has ever lived belongs to its final sliver.

nodes.name: Holocene Epoch (World, 9750 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Holocene Epoch (World, 9750 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[World, 9750 BC–AD 1950] Holocene Epoch. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The current warm interglacial, beginning as ice sheets retreated and sea levels rose by more than a hundred metres, flooding continental shelves and land bridges. Within a few thousand years people in several unconnected regions began cultivating plants and herding animals, leading to villages, cities, writing and states. Almost all of recorded human achievement, and the mass extinctions and atmospheric change of recent centuries, fall inside this single epoch.

nodes.name: Meghalayan Age (World, 2250 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Meghalayan Age (World, 2250 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[World, 2250 BC–AD 1950] Meghalayan Age. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The most recent slice of geological time, defined by a severe drought roughly 4,200 years ago that is recorded in a stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave in northeast India. The same climate shift is blamed for the collapse or reorganisation of early civilisations in Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus valley and China. It is the first geological unit whose starting point is tied to a cultural event, and it runs up to the mid-twentieth century.

nodes.name: Northgrippian Age (World, 6250 BC–2250 BC)
nodes.title: Northgrippian Age (World, 6250 BC–2250 BC)
nodes.description:
[World, 6250 BC–2250 BC] Northgrippian Age. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

The middle stage of the Holocene, bracketed by two abrupt climate events recorded in Greenland ice — the cold, dry 8.2-kiloyear pulse at its start and the 4.2-kiloyear drying at its end. It covers the warmest part of the present interglacial, when the Sahara was green and grassland, sea levels stabilised, and farming spread across Eurasia. Cities, writing, metallurgy and the first states all appear within it.

nodes.name: Quaternary Period (World, 2578050 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.title: Quaternary Period (World, 2578050 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[World, 2578050 BC–AD 1950] Quaternary Period. Period definition from Geologic Time Scale (2020) — International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2020.

Begins with the onset of the great northern ice ages, when the world's climate swung between glacial and interglacial states roughly every hundred thousand years, reshaping coastlines, rivers and the distribution of every living thing. Our own genus spread out of Africa across the globe during it, and everything humans have made lies within its deposits.

nodes.name: Post-Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1375–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Post-Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1375–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1375–AD 1450] Post-Classic Period. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

The last pre-contact century in southern Arizona saw the great Hohokam irrigation communities come apart: platform-mound villages and multi-storey compounds such as Casa Grande were abandoned, canal systems fell out of use, and populations dispersed into smaller settlements. Flooding, drought and canal failure are all argued as causes, along with social strain within crowded valley communities. When Spanish explorers arrived, they found the O'odham living among the ruins of those earlier towns.

hints.label: Post-Classic Period
hints.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

nodes.name: Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375)
nodes.title: Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1375] Classic Period. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

Hohokam communities in the Sonoran Desert moved into walled adobe compounds and built platform mounds, while the older ballcourts fell out of use - signs of a more hierarchical society. The vast irrigation canal networks of the Salt and Gila valleys reached their greatest extent, and multi-storey great houses such as Casa Grande were raised, aligned to solar and lunar events. Within a few generations the canal systems and the large settlements were abandoned.

hints.label: Classic Period
hints.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

nodes.name: Late Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1200–AD 1275)
nodes.title: Late Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1200–AD 1275)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1200–AD 1275] Late Soho Phase. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

Hohokam Classic-period communities of the Salt and Gila valleys, living in walled adobe compounds clustered around earthen platform mounds instead of the older ballcourts. Ceramics shift to plain and red wares with Salado polychromes arriving from outside, and burial practice moves from cremation toward inhumation. The changes point to a more hierarchical society and closer ties with peoples to the east and north.

hints.label: Late Soho Phase
hints.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

nodes.name: Early Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Early Soho Phase (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1200] Early Soho Phase. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

Hohokam settlement changed shape: ballcourts fell out of use and people moved into walled adobe compounds clustered around platform mounds, with above-ground houses replacing the older pit dwellings. The change suggests tighter control by a small elite over land, water and ritual, and a more inward-looking, defensive kind of village. Irrigation continued on a huge scale, setting the stage for the great houses of the following century.

hints.label: Early Soho Phase
hints.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

nodes.name: Early Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1275)
nodes.title: Early Classic Period (Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1275)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1100–AD 1275] Early Classic Period. Period definition from Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes — David R. Abbott, 2019-04.

In the Hohokam world of southern Arizona, ballcourts fell out of use and platform mounds became the focus of communities, suggesting a more hierarchical society with restricted ritual space. Above-ground adobe compounds replaced pithouses, and populations concentrated along the great irrigation canal systems of the Salt and Gila valleys.

hints.label: Early Classic Period
hints.source: Calculating Hohokam Domestic Architecture Building Costs to Test an Environmental Model of Architectural Changes

nodes.name: Sedentary Period (Arizona, AD 950–AD 1100)
nodes.title: Sedentary Period (Arizona, AD 950–AD 1100)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 950–AD 1100] Sedentary Period. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam settlements in the Salt and Gila valleys reached their widest reach, sustained by hundreds of kilometres of hand-dug irrigation canals that watered maize, beans, cotton and agave. Ball courts served as gathering places across a network of villages, and craftspeople made red-on-buff pottery, carved shell jewellery etched with acid, and traded for macaws and copper bells from Mexico. Around 1100 the ball courts fell out of use and platform mounds took their place.

hints.label: Sedentary Period
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Late Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1070–AD 1100)
nodes.title: Late Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1070–AD 1100)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1070–AD 1100] Late Sacaton Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

The final stretch of Hohokam Sedentary-period life in the Phoenix and Gila basins, when red-on-buff pottery, ballcourts and vast hand-dug irrigation canals were at their height. Within a generation or two the ballcourt network collapsed and communities began building walled adobe compounds and platform mounds instead, opening the Classic period. Visitors can see the scale of the canal systems, some tens of kilometres long, that supported one of North America's largest desert farming populations.

hints.label: Late Sacaton Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Middle Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1000–AD 1070)
nodes.title: Middle Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 1000–AD 1070)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 1000–AD 1070] Middle Sacaton Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam farmers in the Salt and Gila valleys maintained the largest irrigation canal systems in prehistoric North America, some running for tens of kilometres. Villages centred on oval ballcourts, which drew people together for games, ritual and exchange, and craftworkers produced red-on-buff pottery, carved stone bowls and shell jewellery etched with acid. The ballcourt network linked settlements across much of southern Arizona before this way of life was reorganised around platform mounds.

hints.label: Middle Sacaton Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Early Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 950–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Early Sacaton Phase (Arizona, AD 950–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 950–AD 1000] Early Sacaton Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam villages along the Gila and Salt rivers reached their widest reach, tied together by ballcourts where communities gathered and traded, and fed by irrigation canals dug for kilometres across the desert. Red-on-buff pottery, shell jewellery worked with acid etching, and copper bells and macaws from Mesoamerica circulated through the network. Population and canal systems were at their peak before the shift to walled compounds and platform mounds.

hints.label: Early Sacaton Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Colonial Period (Arizona, AD 750–AD 950)
nodes.title: Colonial Period (Arizona, AD 750–AD 950)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 750–AD 950] Colonial Period. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Hohokam communities in the Sonoran Desert expanded rapidly, extending their irrigation canals across the Salt and Gila valleys and settling new districts. This is when ballcourts appear in numbers, hosting gatherings that linked scattered villages, alongside red-on-buff pottery, carved stone palettes, shell jewellery traded from the Gulf of California and cremation burial. Visitors can see the distinctive Gila Butte and Santa Cruz style pottery that defines the phase.

hints.label: Colonial Period
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Santa Cruz Phase (Arizona, AD 850–AD 950)
nodes.title: Santa Cruz Phase (Arizona, AD 850–AD 950)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 850–AD 950] Santa Cruz Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A high point of the Hohokam Colonial period in southern Arizona, when villages spread out from the Gila and Salt river cores and the great irrigation canals were extended. Oval ballcourts became standard village features, tying scattered settlements into a network of gatherings and exchange, and potters produced finely painted red-on-buff vessels covered in tiny repeated human and animal figures. Shell from the Gulf of California, some of it etched with acid, moved widely through the region.

hints.label: Santa Cruz Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Late Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 800–AD 850)
nodes.title: Late Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 800–AD 850)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 800–AD 850] Late Gila Butte Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A Hohokam phase in the Gila and Salt river valleys, when irrigation canals lengthened, ballcourts spread between villages, and red-on-buff pottery carried repeating scroll and life-form designs. Trade brought shell from the Gulf of California, worked into bracelets and pendants in astonishing quantities.

hints.label: Late Gila Butte Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Early Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 750–AD 800)
nodes.title: Early Gila Butte Phase (Arizona, AD 750–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 750–AD 800] Early Gila Butte Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A Hohokam phase in the Phoenix Basin when desert farmers extended their canal systems and began building the large oval ballcourts that drew people together for games and exchange. Red-on-buff pottery, carved shell jewellery from the Gulf of California and cremation burial are its hallmarks.

hints.label: Early Gila Butte Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Pioneer Period (Arizona, AD 450–AD 750)
nodes.title: Pioneer Period (Arizona, AD 450–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 450–AD 750] Pioneer Period. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

The earliest recognised stage of Hohokam life in the Sonoran Desert, when villages of shallow pit houses clustered around central plazas along the Salt and Gila rivers. Farmers began digging the irrigation canals that would eventually water thousands of acres, and potters produced plain and red-slipped wares before the buff pottery of later centuries. These small settlements were the foundation of the largest indigenous canal system in North America.

hints.label: Pioneer Period
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Snaketown Phase (Arizona, AD 650–AD 750)
nodes.title: Snaketown Phase (Arizona, AD 650–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 650–AD 750] Snaketown Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

Named for the great village on the Gila River, this phase of the Hohokam sequence saw settlements grow larger and more formally arranged, with clusters of pithouses around open plazas and the dead cremated with offerings. Distinctive red-on-buff painted pottery came into its own, and irrigation canals were extended across the desert floor — the engineering that made dense settlement possible in one of North America's harshest environments.

hints.label: Snaketown Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Sweetwater Phase (Arizona, AD 600–AD 650)
nodes.title: Sweetwater Phase (Arizona, AD 600–AD 650)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 600–AD 650] Sweetwater Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

A phase of the early Hohokam sequence in the Sonoran Desert, when villages of shallow pithouses clustered around plazas and farmers extended irrigation canals off the Gila and Salt rivers. Potters began decorating buff and gray wares with red painted designs, an early step toward the distinctive red-on-buff tradition of later centuries. Shell ornaments from the Gulf of California show trade links already in place.

hints.label: Sweetwater Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Estrella Phase (Arizona, AD 500–AD 600)
nodes.title: Estrella Phase (Arizona, AD 500–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 500–AD 600] Estrella Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

An early stage of Hohokam life in the Phoenix Basin, when small groups of pit-house dwellers farmed the Salt and Gila floodplains and dug the first substantial irrigation canals. It is recognised chiefly by its pottery, plain and red-on-gray wares whose painted designs are among the earliest decorated ceramics in the Sonoran Desert. Everything the later Hohokam became famous for, ballcourts, vast canal systems, shell jewellery traded from the Gulf of California, grew out of these modest beginnings.

hints.label: Estrella Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Vahki Phase (Arizona, AD 450–AD 500)
nodes.title: Vahki Phase (Arizona, AD 450–AD 500)
nodes.description: [South-Central Arizona, AD 450–AD 500] Vahki Phase. Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

hints.label: Vahki Phase
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: Red Mountain (Arizona, AD 50–AD 450)
nodes.title: Red Mountain (Arizona, AD 50–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[South-Central Arizona, AD 50–AD 450] Red Mountain. Listed in source as unknown started date. For these purposes a tentative start date for the Red Mountain period can be based off of the end date of the Early Agricultural Period (EAP). Period definition from Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona — David R. Abbott, 2009-07.

The earliest recognised phase of Hohokam settlement in the Phoenix Basin, when scattered clusters of shallow pit houses appeared along the Salt and Gila rivers. Villagers grew maize, made undecorated brown pottery and began the small-scale ditching that would later grow into the largest canal systems in prehistoric North America. Because the remains are deeply buried under later occupations and modern Phoenix, the phase is known from only a handful of excavated sites.

hints.label: Red Mountain
hints.source: Extensive and Long-Term Specialization: Hohokam Ceramic Production in the Phoenix Basin, Arizona

nodes.name: 縄文時代 (Honshu, 10999 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: 縄文時代 (Honshu, 10999 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州・北海道, 10999 BC–299 BC] 縄文時代. Spatial coverage: Hokkaidō, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Added alternative spelling with macrons. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

One of the world's longest-lasting hunter-gatherer cultures, sustained by acorns, chestnuts, salmon, deer and rich coastal shellfish beds rather than farming. Its people made some of the earliest pottery anywhere, built settled villages with pit dwellings and vast shell middens, and left striking clay figurines and flame-shaped vessels. The sheer stability of the way of life challenges the assumption that agriculture is a necessary step toward complex society.

hints.label: 縄文時代
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: 縄文時代早期 (Honshu, 8999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 8999 BC–4999 BC] 縄文時代早期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. start確認. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

As the last glaciation ended and the islands were cut off by rising seas, people adapted to new forests of oak and chestnut with bows, pit traps, fish hooks and a growing reliance on shellfish. Pointed-base and rounded pots suited to cooking over hearths appear, and the first large shell middens begin to accumulate along the drowned coastlines.

hints.label: 縄文時代早期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.title: 縄文時代前期 (Honshu, 4999 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 4999 BC–2999 BC] 縄文時代前期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Sea levels reached their highest point and warm waters pushed deep inland, leaving shell mounds now stranded far from the coast. Settlements grew larger and more permanent, with horseshoe-shaped arrangements of pit houses, and pottery shifted to flat-bottomed, cylindrical forms decorated with rolled cord impressions.

hints.label: 縄文時代前期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: 縄文時代中期 (Honshu, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 2999 BC–1999 BC] 縄文時代中期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

The warm, resource-rich centuries when Jomon population peaked in central and eastern Honshu, with large villages laid out around open plazas and monumental sites like Sannai-Maruyama. Potters produced the most exuberant vessels of the whole era, including the flame-rimmed jars of the Shinano basin, alongside numerous clay figurines and stone rods that suggest an active ritual life.

hints.label: 縄文時代中期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: 縄文時代後期 (Honshu, 1999 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 1999 BC–999 BC] 縄文時代後期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

A cooling climate scattered the large inland villages, and people moved toward the coasts and river valleys. Ritual activity became more visible: stone circles such as Oyu, elaborate burial grounds, and finely finished pottery and lacquerware suggest communities investing heavily in ceremony as conditions grew harder.

hints.label: 縄文時代後期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC)
nodes.title: 縄文時代晩期 (Honshu, 999 BC–299 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 999 BC–299 BC] 縄文時代晩期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

The final Jomon centuries saw exquisitely crafted Kamegaoka pottery and the famous goggle-eyed dogu figurines in the north, while in the west rice agriculture was already taking hold. The overlap of the two worlds - foragers and the first farmers - marks the transition into the Yayoi era.

hints.label: 縄文時代晩期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC)
nodes.title: 弥生時代前期 (Honshu, 299 BC–199 BC)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 299 BC–199 BC] 弥生時代前期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. stopの期間はおおよそ. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Wet-rice paddy farming, spread from the Korean peninsula through northern Kyushu and up into western Honshu, along with bronze and iron tools, weaving and new burial customs using jars and dolmen-like stone markers. Villages became permanent and were often ditched or palisaded, a sign that stored grain surpluses were worth fighting over. The plain, wheel-finished pottery that gives the era its name replaced the elaborate cord-marked wares of the preceding age.

hints.label: 弥生時代前期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 弥生時代中期 (Honshu, 199 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: 弥生時代中期 (Honshu, 199 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description:
[本州・四国・九州, 199 BC–AD 1] 弥生時代中期. Spatial coverage: Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku. startの期間はおおよそ。. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Rice farming was now well established across Honshu, supporting large moated settlements, storehouses on stilts and the first clear signs of hereditary rank. Bronze was used for display rather than tools: ritual bells cast in the east, weapon-shaped objects in the west, deliberately buried on hillsides. Imported Chinese mirrors and coins in elite graves show communities plugged into networks reaching the Han commanderies in Korea, while defensive ditches and injured skeletons point to competition between them.

hints.label: 弥生時代中期
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: 旧石器時代 (Okinawa Islands, 31999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[沖縄, 31999 BC–4999 BC] 旧石器時代. 大陸から現生人類が日本列島に渡り、居住を始める
炭素14年代測定法による校正年代では、Start label：B.C.36000. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

Hunter-gatherers occupied the limestone caves and fissures of the Ryukyus, leaving some of the oldest human skeletal remains in Japan, including the Minatogawa and Shiraho-Saonetabaru finds. The islands' limestone preserves bone far better than the acidic soils of the main islands, which is why so much of what is known about Pleistocene people in Japan comes from here. Sea crossings were required to reach these islands, implying seafaring capability tens of thousands of years ago.

hints.label: 旧石器時代
hints.source: Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020

nodes.name: 貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: 貝塚時代前期 (Okinawa Islands, 10999 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[沖縄, 10999 BC–999 BC] 貝塚時代前期. Added alternative translation. Period definition from Exhibition of Excavations in the Japanese Archipelago 2020 — Agency for Cultural Affairs, Government of Japan, 2020.

The long era in which Ryukyuan islanders lived off coral-reef fish, shellfish and wild plants, leaving huge accumulations of discarded shell. Pottery and stone tools followed their own island trajectory, distinct from the Jomon sequence of the main islands, showing how differently the subtropical south developed.

While the main islands took up rice farming, people in the Ryukyus stayed with fishing, shellfish gathering and foraging along the reefs, leaving the deep shell middens that name the era. Their shell ornaments and tools travelled north into Kyushu, showing long-distance exchange between the islands and the emerging Yayoi world.

nodes.title: Early period (Roman Noricum) (Austria, 14 BC–AD 117)

[Noricum, 14 BC–AD 117] Early period (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. Adapted from the source. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. (page 369) originally include the whole reign of emperor Augustus (BC 31/27–AD 14) for this phase, for Noricum the occupation of the Alps (15 BC) was chosen as the starting date. The Celtic kingdom of Noricum, long a friendly trading partner supplying Rome with its prized iron, was absorbed into the empire under Augustus. Roman administration replaced hillfort centres with planned towns such as Virunum, and roads over the Alpine passes tied the region to Italy and the Danube. Latin, coinage and Mediterranean building styles spread quickly among a population that kept much of its Celtic identity.

[Noricum, AD 117–AD 284] Imperial period (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. Adapted from the original source. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. Period definition from A Controlled Vocabulary for a Simple and Basic Chronology for the Roman Province of Noricum — Hagmann, Dominik, 2021.

The Alpine province supplied the empire with iron - the famed ferrum Noricum - and with cattle, salt and gold, worked from towns like Virunum, Flavia Solva and Ovilava. Veterans, traders and Celtic-speaking locals mingled in a thoroughly Romanised landscape of villas, tombstones and hill sanctuaries where the goddess Noreia was still honoured. Third-century civil war and raids across the Danube ended the quiet prosperity.

[Noricum, AD 68–AD 69] Year of the Four Emperors (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. During the so-called Year of the Four Emperors (AD 68/69) Galba (AD 68–69), Otho (AD 69), Vitellius (AD 69) and Vespasian (AD 69–79) laid claim to power in the Roman Empire; cf. "Gassner, Verena; Pülz, Andreas (ed.) (2015): Der römische Limes in Österreich. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. < pages 300–301.

Period definition from A Controlled Vocabulary for a Simple and Basic Chronology for the Roman Province of Noricum — Hagmann, Dominik, 2021.

Nero's suicide opened a scramble for the throne in which Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each held power within a year. The provinces learned, as Tacitus put it, that an emperor could be made outside Rome, and legions on the Rhine and Danube became kingmakers. Alpine Noricum lay on the marching routes between the Danube armies and Italy, so the civil war passed close to its roads and towns.

The Danube frontier province enjoyed a prosperous stretch under the Severans, with towns such as Virunum, Ovilava and Lauriacum gaining monumental buildings and civic status, and the Second Italic Legion settled at Lauriacum guarding the river. Noric iron and trade along the amber routes fed the wider empire. The peace ended after 235, when the frontier wars and civil strife of the third century reached the province.

The Alpine kingdom of Noricum, long a trading partner of Rome and a source of the prized 'Norican iron', was absorbed peacefully into the empire under Augustus and administered as a district before becoming a full province. Towns such as Virunum and Teurnia were laid out with forums, baths and temples, roads crossed the passes, and Celtic aristocrats took Roman names while continuing to worship local gods.

nodes.name: Flavian dynasty (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 69–AD 96)
nodes.title: Flavian dynasty (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 69–AD 96)
nodes.description:
[Noricum, AD 69–AD 96] Flavian dynasty (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. Adapted from the original source. Vespasian and his sons reorganised the Alpine and Danubian provinces, granting municipal status to towns such as Flavia Solva and boosting Virunum, Teurnia and Iuvavum. Stone building, road improvement and formal town charters replaced the older Celtic settlement pattern, and the iron and salt trade drew the region firmly into the imperial economy. Military attention shifted toward the Danube frontier facing the Germanic tribes.

nodes.name: Late antiquity (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 284–AD 488)
nodes.title: Late antiquity (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 284–AD 488)
nodes.description:
[Noricum, AD 284–AD 488] Late antiquity (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. While Gassner et al. (pages 371–372) define Late Antiquity in their book form AD 284 until AD 610, at this place AD 488, when Odoaker ordered parts of the remaining Roman people moving from Noricum to Italy (page 372), is used as a stop of the period. AD 488 is the commonly used date for marking the definite end of *Roman* Noricum and the beginning of the Early Medieval Period in that area (although the Western Roman Empire ceased to be in AD 476); nevertheless, various settlements continued in the Early Medieval Period, as well as seemingly not all Romans moved to Italy and stayed instead in Noricum. Period definition from A Controlled Vocabulary for a Simple and Basic Chronology for the Roman Province of Noricum — Hagmann, Dominik, 2021.

Diocletian split the province into Noricum ripense along the Danube and Noricum mediterraneum in the Alpine interior, backed by a chain of forts facing pressure from beyond the river. As security frayed, people moved from open valley towns to fortified hilltop settlements, and Christianity spread with bishops and early churches. The Life of Saint Severinus describes the last decades of Roman life here, ending when Odoacer ordered the remaining Roman population evacuated to Italy.

hints.label: Late antiquity (Roman Noricum)
hints.source: A Controlled Vocabulary for a Simple and Basic Chronology for the Roman Province of Noricum

nodes.name: Adpotive Emperors/Antonine dynasty (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 96–AD 192)
nodes.title: Adpotive Emperors/Antonine dynasty (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 96–AD 192)
nodes.description:
[Noricum, AD 96–AD 192] Adpotive Emperors/Antonine dynasty (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. Adapted from the original source. Under Trajan, Hadrian and the Antonines, the Alpine province of Noricum enjoyed its most prosperous stretch, exporting its famous iron and supplying recruits to the legions. Towns such as Virunum and Ovilava gained forums, baths and stone monuments, and Roman law and Latin spread among the descendants of the Celtic Norici. The peace broke with the Marcomannic Wars under Marcus Aurelius, when Germanic raiders crossed the Danube and permanent legionary garrisons were installed.

nodes.title: Barracks Emperors (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 235–AD 284)

Emperors were made and unmade by the army, dozens of them in half a century, while plague, debased coinage and invasion tore at the frontiers. In the Alpine and Danube provinces this meant raids across the river, hoards buried and never recovered, and communities pulling back from open valley towns onto defensible hilltops. Diocletian's accession ended the chaos and brought a reorganised, more militarised province.

Diocletian's reorganisation split the Danubian province of Noricum into two smaller units, ripaense along the river frontier and mediterraneum in the Alpine interior, each with its own governor. Forts and towns were rebuilt in heavier, more defensible form as pressure from beyond the Danube grew, and the imperial arms factories and iron of the region supplied the frontier armies.

hints.source: A Controlled Vocabulary for a Simple and Basic Chronology for the Roman Province of Noricum

nodes.name: Second Year of the Four Emperors (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 193–AD 193)
nodes.title: Second Year of the Four Emperors (Roman Noricum) (Austria, AD 193–AD 193)

[Noricum, AD 193–AD 193] Second Year of the Four Emperors (Roman Noricum). Spatial coverage: Austria, Germany, Italy, Roman Empire, Slovenia. Adapted from the original source. The murder of Commodus set off a scramble for the throne in which Pertinax was killed by the Praetorians, the office was notoriously auctioned to Didius Julianus, and rival armies proclaimed their own commanders. Septimius Severus marched on Rome from the Danube and won, founding a dynasty built openly on military loyalty. Frontier provinces like Noricum, astride the route from the Danube legions to Italy, felt the passage of armies directly.

Along the Danube here, the fourth century meant fortification: watchtowers, granaries and thick-walled forts replacing the open garrison towns of earlier centuries, as the province was split into a militarised riverside zone and a quieter Alpine interior. Christian churches and cemeteries appear in the towns for the first time, while coin hoards mark the raids and troop movements that increasingly disturbed provincial life.

The Danube frontier through this province was rebuilt on a large scale, with new burgi, watchtowers and granaries strung along the river to watch the crossings. Military spending and troop movements shaped the towns behind the line, and the archaeology of the period is dominated by late fortifications, coin hoards and hastily repaired walls. Within a generation of the dynasty's end the garrisons were unpaid and the provincial population began drifting south.

The last stretch of functioning Roman administration in the Alpine and Danube province, dated archaeologically by the coinage of Theodosius I and his successors, which is the latest imperial money to reach the region in quantity. Frontier garrisons went unpaid and unreplaced, low-lying towns shrank, and populations shifted to fortified hilltop settlements and church complexes. It closes with the collapse of imperial control after the Hunnic wars, the world described a generation later in the Life of Severinus.

The Germanic commander who deposed the last western emperor in 476 ruled Italy as king, and the Roman provincials of Noricum along the Danube fell within his orbit. Frontier life there is vividly recorded in the Life of Saint Severinus: shrinking garrisons, unpaid soldiers, raids and towns emptying out. In 488 Odoacer ordered the remaining Romans evacuated south to Italy, effectively ending Roman civil administration on this stretch of the Danube.

The period subsumes from the overarching periods defined for Roman Noricum ("Early Period," "Imperial Period," and "Late Antiquity"; derived from Hagmann 2021, < Furthermore, this overarching period takes into account the early pre-occupation activities in the area of the urban settlement at the Magdalensberg ("Stadt auf dem Magdalensberg", Carinthia/AUT), the beginning of which is put around 50 BC (cf., Gassner et al. 2002–2003, 70. 369). The Celtic kingdom of Noricum, long a friendly trading partner supplying Rome with its prized 'Noric iron', was absorbed under Augustus without a war. Roman towns such as Virunum and Teurnia replaced hilltop centres like the Magdalensberg, and mining, ironworking and the amber route brought wealth. Late in the period the province was Christianised and increasingly militarised as pressure grew along the Danube.

Rome took control of the Alpine and Danube lands after Augustus's campaigns of 15 BC, absorbing the Norican kingdom largely without a fight. Early Roman presence shows as military posts, new road links and the first traders and administrators arriving at native hilltop centres such as the Magdalensberg. The old oppida were gradually abandoned in favour of planned towns in the valleys.

nodes.title: Die Frühzeit (Austria, 30 BC–AD 117)

[Donauprovinzen, 30 BC–AD 117] Die Frühzeit. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Rome absorbed the Celtic kingdom of Noricum without a fight and conquered Pannonia by force, pushing the frontier to the Danube and turning the region into a corridor between Italy and the northern provinces. Legions and auxiliary forts appeared along the river, the amber road carried Baltic goods south, and native hilltop centres such as the Magdalensberg gave way to Roman towns. It was the foundation of four centuries of Roman life in the eastern Alps and the Vienna basin.

hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.title: Die neuen Provinzen (Austria, AD 41–AD 68)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, AD 41–AD 68] Die neuen Provinzen. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Under Claudius the Alpine kingdom of Noricum was formally organised as a procuratorial province and its main native centres — Virunum, Celeia, Teurnia, Aguntum, Iuvavum — were promoted to Roman municipia. Local elites gained citizenship and adopted Latin, monumental building and Roman religion, while iron and salt continued to flow south. Provincial administration and urban life arrived here largely by agreement rather than conquest.

hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Zeit der späten Republik (Austria, 224 BC–39 BC)
nodes.title: Zeit der späten Republik (Austria, 224 BC–39 BC)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, 224 BC–39 BC] Zeit der späten Republik. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

As Rome expanded across the Mediterranean, its republican institutions buckled under the strain of army commanders, civil wars and vast new wealth. In the eastern Alps this was the era of the kingdom of Noricum, whose famous iron drew Italian merchants to the trading settlement on the Magdalensberg long before the region was formally annexed. Roman goods, coinage and inscriptions appear here generations ahead of Roman troops.

hints.label: Zeit der späten Republik
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Die flavisch-traianische Zeit (Austria, AD 69–AD 117)
nodes.title: Die flavisch-traianische Zeit (Austria, AD 69–AD 117)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, AD 69–AD 117] Die flavisch-traianische Zeit. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

Timber camps on the Danube were rebuilt in stone as the frontier hardened into a permanent military zone, with legions installed at Carnuntum and a new fortress at Vindobona, the seed of Vienna. Trajan divided Pannonia into two provinces in 106 and drew troops from the region for his Dacian wars, while veteran settlement and trade turned garrison towns into civilian cities. The road and fort network laid down here shaped settlement in the area for centuries.

hints.label: Die flavisch-traianische Zeit
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Von Hadrian bis Commodus (Austria, AD 117–AD 192)
nodes.title: Von Hadrian bis Commodus (Austria, AD 117–AD 192)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, AD 117–AD 192] Von Hadrian bis Commodus. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

The high imperial period on the Danube frontier, when Carnuntum and Vindobona grew into major garrison towns with amphitheatres, baths and civilian settlements, and Noricum's iron and Pannonia's grain fed the army. Prosperity was interrupted by the Marcomannic Wars, when Germanic groups broke across the river and Marcus Aurelius spent years campaigning from Carnuntum, where he is said to have written part of his Meditations. The wars, and the plague that came with them, marked the point at which the frontier stopped being simply a place of profit.

hints.label: Von Hadrian bis Commodus
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Die Zeit der Severer (Austria, AD 193–AD 235)
nodes.title: Die Zeit der Severer (Austria, AD 193–AD 235)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, AD 193–AD 235] Die Zeit der Severer. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

Carnuntum was where the Pannonian legions proclaimed their governor, Septimius Severus, emperor in 193, and the province was rewarded with favour for the rest of the dynasty. Towns received city charters, soldiers' pay and privileges rose, and the Danube settlements reached their greatest extent, with stone amphitheatres, baths and imported cults such as Mithras and Jupiter Dolichenus. It was the high point of provincial prosperity before the crises of the mid-third century.

hints.label: Die Zeit der Severer
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Zeit der Soldatenkaiser (Austria, AD 235–AD 284)
nodes.title: Zeit der Soldatenkaiser (Austria, AD 235–AD 284)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, AD 235–AD 284] Zeit der Soldatenkaiser. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

Roman emperors were made and unmade by their armies at bewildering speed, while invasions, plague and a collapsing silver coinage strained the empire to breaking point. Along the Danube in Noricum the pressure was felt directly: towns contracted behind walls, hilltop sites were reoccupied and rural villas were abandoned or fortified. Diocletian's accession ended the cycle and imposed a new, more militarised order.

hints.label: Zeit der Soldatenkaiser
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Die Spätantike (Austria, AD 284–AD 610)
nodes.title: Die Spätantike (Austria, AD 284–AD 610)
nodes.description:
[Donauprovinzen, AD 284–AD 610] Die Spätantike. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Österreichische Geschichte 15 v. Chr.–378 n. Chr. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

Diocletian's reforms redrew the provinces and stiffened the Danube defences with new forts, watchtowers and river fleets, while Christianity spread and bishoprics appeared in the Alpine towns. From the fourth century the frontier came under mounting pressure, and the Life of Saint Severinus paints a vivid picture of shrinking towns, unpaid garrisons and negotiated survival among barbarian neighbours. The Roman population was evacuated to Italy in 488, and Bavarians, Lombards, Slavs and Avars filled the space that remained.

hints.label: Die Spätantike
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.title: Odoaker (Austria, AD 475–AD 476)

[Donauprovinzen, AD 475–AD 476] Odoaker. Adapted from the original source. "Gassner, Verena; Jilek, Sonja; Ladstätter, Sabine (2002–2003): Am Rande des Reiches. Die Römer in Österreich. Vienna: Ueberreuter. < is one of the most important contributions which still represents the most comprehensive account of the Roman period's archaeology for the former Roman provinces on the territory of present-day Austria. This is especially true for the holistic presentation of all aspects of archaeology concerning the province of Noricum. Period definition from Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich — Verena Gassner, 2002–2003.

The moment when a Germanic officer of the imperial army removed Romulus Augustulus and sent the western regalia to Constantinople, taking the title of king rather than emperor. For the Danube provinces it meant the last thread of imperial authority snapped, leaving communities to negotiate with barbarian neighbours on their own, as the Life of Saint Severinus describes.

hints.label: Odoaker
hints.source: Am Rande des Reiches: Die Römer in Österreich

nodes.name: Período Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1573–AD 1620)
nodes.title: Período Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1573–AD 1620)
nodes.description:
[Córdoba (provincia, Argentina), AD 1573–AD 1620] Período Colonial Temprano. Period definition from Las sociedades indígenas y su incorporación al proceso de producción de textiles en el período colonial temprano (Córdoba, 1573-1620) — Borrastero, Lucas, 2015.

The first generation of Spanish town-founding, land grants and forced labour drafts, met by fierce indigenous resistance in the Andean valleys. Native settlements were relocated to mission towns, populations collapsed under epidemics and warfare, and European livestock, wheat and vines began transforming the landscape.

hints.label: Período Colonial Temprano
hints.source: Las sociedades indígenas y su incorporación al proceso de producción de textiles en el período colonial temprano (Córdoba, 1573-1620)

nodes.name: Mesolithic (Portugal, 9999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolithic (Portugal, 9999 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 9999 BC–4999 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

nodes.name: Neolithic (Portugal, 4999 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Portugal, 4999 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 4999 BC–2999 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

nodes.name: Chalcolithic (Portugal, 2999 BC–2199 BC)
nodes.title: Chalcolithic (Portugal, 2999 BC–2199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 2999 BC–2199 BC] Chalcolithic. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The copper-using centuries before the first cities, and one of the most visually striking periods in the southern Levant: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of over four hundred cast copper maceheads and standards, the sanctuary at Ein Gedi, carved ivory figurines and bone-box ossuaries for secondary burial. Villagers such as those at Teleilat Ghassul added olives and dates to their fields and made cheese and wool from their herds. The whole system collapsed before the walled towns of the Early Bronze Age appeared.

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Portugal, 2199 BC–700 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Portugal, 2199 BC–700 BC)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 2199 BC–700 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

nodes.name: Iron Age (Portugal, 799 BC–25 BC)
nodes.title: Iron Age (Portugal, 799 BC–25 BC)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 799 BC–25 BC] Iron Age. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The formative era of the southern Levant, when the Canaanite city-state system gave way to territorial kingdoms - Israel, Judah, Philistia, Phoenician ports and the Transjordanian states. Iron tools became common, olive oil and wine were produced on an industrial scale, and alphabetic script came into everyday administrative use. The period closes with conquest by Assyria and Babylon and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, the setting for much of the Hebrew Bible.

nodes.name: Roman Period (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 476)
nodes.title: Roman Period (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 25 BC–AD 476] Roman Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Crete was joined with Cyrenaica in a single province governed from Gortyn, which grew into a large city with a praetorium, theatres and the famous inscribed law code reused in its buildings. The island prospered on grain, oil, wine and its position on shipping lanes, and Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony. Earthquakes repeatedly levelled its towns, and the rebuilt remains are among the best preserved in the Aegean.

nodes.name: Early Roman Empire (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 305)
nodes.title: Early Roman Empire (Portugal, 25 BC–AD 305)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, 25 BC–AD 305] Early Roman Empire. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Augustus reorganised the far west of Iberia into provinces, and the territory that would become Portugal was drawn into a network of roads, towns and taxation centred on new foundations such as Bracara Augusta and Emerita Augusta. Villas, mines, fish-salting works and garum factories tied the Atlantic coast into Mediterranean markets, while local elites took Roman names, Roman citizenship and Roman gods. Latin, urbanism and the road system left permanent marks on the landscape.

nodes.name: Late Roman Empire (Portugal, AD 305–AD 476)
nodes.title: Late Roman Empire (Portugal, AD 305–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 305–AD 476] Late Roman Empire. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Diocletian's and Constantine's reforms reorganised the provinces, taxation and army, and Christianity moved from persecuted sect to favoured religion, leaving churches and Christian burials across the region. Wealth concentrated in large rural estates whose villas were decorated with elaborate mosaics, while towns contracted behind new walls. In the fifth century the frontier gave way and Suebic and Visigothic groups took control of the peninsula's west.

nodes.name: Late Antiquity (Portugal, AD 401–AD 800)
nodes.title: Late Antiquity (Portugal, AD 401–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 401–AD 800] Late Antiquity. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The Roman provinces along the lower Danube and in Thrace became a frontier zone under constant pressure, with Goths, Huns and other groups crossing the river while emperors fortified cities and roads. Christianity spread fast: basilicas and bishoprics appeared at Serdica, Philippopolis and elsewhere, and Serdica hosted a major church council. After the empire split, these lands fell to the eastern half, setting up their long Byzantine future.

nodes.name: Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1415)
nodes.title: Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1415)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 601–AD 1415] Middle Ages. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman rule in the west and the Renaissance saw Latin Christendom take shape: monasteries preserved and reworked classical learning, kingdoms hardened into states, and lords, peasants and towns settled into new legal relationships. Population and cultivated land grew steadily until plague and famine reversed it in the fourteenth century. Cathedrals, universities, guilds, parliaments and the vernacular literatures of Europe all date from this span.

nodes.name: Late Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 1100–AD 1415)
nodes.title: Late Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 1100–AD 1415)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1100–AD 1415] Late Middle Ages. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

A frontier county broke away from León to become a kingdom, and its rulers pushed south with Templar and Cistercian help until the capture of the Algarve completed the Reconquest and fixed borders that have barely moved since. Lisbon and Porto grew on Atlantic trade, and Portuguese replaced Latin in royal documents. A succession crisis brought the House of Aviz to power at Aljubarrota, and the seizure of Ceuta in 1415 opened the era of overseas expansion.

nodes.name: Early Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1100)
nodes.title: Early Middle Ages (Portugal, AD 601–AD 1100)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 601–AD 1100] Early Middle Ages. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

The Visigothic kingdom governed the west of Iberia until Muslim armies crossed from North Africa in 711, making the region the Gharb of al-Andalus, with Islamic administration, agriculture and urban life in the south. From the ninth century Christian rulers from the north pushed the frontier back down the Douro and Mondego, repopulating Braga, Porto and Coimbra. The county of Portucale that emerged from this frontier zone became the kingdom of Portugal in the twelfth century.

nodes.name: Medieval Islamic Period (Portugal, AD 711–AD 1249)
nodes.title: Medieval Islamic Period (Portugal, AD 711–AD 1249)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 711–AD 1249] Medieval Islamic Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Umayyad armies crossed from North Africa in 711 and within a few years held most of the Iberian peninsula; the western territories became al-Andalus's Gharb, with Silves, Mértola and Lisbon as centres of irrigated agriculture, ceramics and Mediterranean trade. New crops, water-lifting technology and urban forms arrived, and Arabic left a deep mark on Portuguese vocabulary and place names. Christian kings pushed south over three centuries, and Afonso III's capture of Faro in 1249 completed the conquest and fixed Portugal's modern borders.

nodes.name: Medieval Christian Period (Portugal, AD 1200–AD 1415)
nodes.title: Medieval Christian Period (Portugal, AD 1200–AD 1415)
nodes.description: [Portugal, AD 1200–AD 1415] Medieval Christian Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

nodes.name: Modern Age (Portugal, AD 1415–AD 1789)
nodes.title: Modern Age (Portugal, AD 1415–AD 1789)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1415–AD 1789] Modern Age. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Beginning with the seizure of Ceuta, Portugal pushed south along the African coast and then round it, reaching India and Brazil and building a seaborne empire of trading forts stretching to Macau. Wealth from spices, sugar, gold and the Atlantic slave trade poured through Lisbon, funding Manueline architecture and a court culture of global reach, even as the crown passed to Spain for sixty years and the empire's centre shifted to Brazil. The 1755 earthquake levelled Lisbon and gave the Marquis of Pombal his chance to rebuild the city and remake the state along Enlightenment lines.

nodes.name: Contemporary Period (Portugal, AD 1789–AD 2021)
nodes.title: Contemporary Period (Portugal, AD 1789–AD 2021)
nodes.description:
[Portugal, AD 1789–AD 2021] Contemporary Period. Period definition from DB-HERITAGE historical periods — DB-HERITAGE project, 2021.

Napoleonic invasion drove the Portuguese court to Brazil, and the country came back to a liberal revolution, civil war and the loss of its largest colony. A republic replaced the monarchy in 1910, gave way to Salazar's long authoritarian Estado Novo, and the Carnation Revolution of 1974 ended both the dictatorship and the African empire, opening the way into Europe.

nodes.name: 弥生時代 (Japan, 299 BC–AD 300)
nodes.title: 弥生時代 (Japan, 299 BC–AD 300)
nodes.description:
[Japan, 299 BC–AD 300] 弥生時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Wet-rice agriculture arrived from the Asian mainland along with bronze and iron, transforming a foraging society into one of paddy fields, granaries and permanent villages. Surpluses meant inequality: some settlements were ringed with ditches and palisades, and skeletons show wounds from organised fighting. Chinese histories record dozens of small kingdoms sending envoys to the Han and Wei courts, among them Queen Himiko's Yamatai.

hints.label: 弥生時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 大和時代 (Japan, AD 300–AD 600)
nodes.title: 大和時代 (Japan, AD 300–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 300–AD 600] 大和時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Rulers based in the Nara basin built enormous keyhole-shaped burial mounds, the largest earthworks ever raised in Japan, filled with mirrors, armour, horse gear and clay haniwa figures. This was when a paramount lineage extended control over much of the archipelago and maintained close ties with the kingdoms of the Korean peninsula. Immigrants brought iron working, horses, sericulture, writing and eventually Buddhism, laying the groundwork for a Chinese-style state.
