nodes.name: 飛鳥時代 (Japan, AD 600–AD 709)
nodes.title: 飛鳥時代 (Japan, AD 600–AD 709)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 600–AD 709] 飛鳥時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Buddhism, Chinese writing, Chinese law and continental court ritual took hold as the Yamato rulers reshaped themselves into an emperor's government. Prince Shotoku's reforms and the Taika edicts introduced ranked officials, registered land and taxation, and the first great temples such as Horyuji rose with the oldest surviving wooden architecture in the world.

hints.label: 飛鳥時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 奈良時代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 794)
nodes.title: 奈良時代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 794)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 710–AD 794] 奈良時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Japan's first lasting capital, Heijo-kyo, was laid out on a Chinese grid, and the state ran on the ritsuryo law codes, censuses and rice taxes. Emperor Shomu poured national resources into Buddhism, casting the colossal bronze Buddha at Todai-ji and founding provincial temples. The court's earliest books date from these years: the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and the Man'yoshu poetry anthology, alongside the treasures still preserved in the Shosoin storehouse.

hints.label: 奈良時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 平安時代 (Japan, AD 794–AD 1192)
nodes.title: 平安時代 (Japan, AD 794–AD 1192)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 794–AD 1192] 平安時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

With the capital settled at Heian-kyo, the Fujiwara family ruled through marriage alliances with emperors while the formal Chinese-style administration decayed. Court life produced the kana syllabary and a literature largely written by women, including The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book, alongside esoteric Tendai and Shingon Buddhism and a widespread belief in Amida's paradise. In the provinces, warrior clans grew strong enough to fight the Genpei War and hand real power to the samurai.

hints.label: 平安時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 古代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 1192)
nodes.title: 古代 (Japan, AD 710–AD 1192)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 710–AD 1192] 古代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Japan's classical age, governed by an imported Chinese-style legal code with a capital first at Nara and then at Heian-kyo, modern Kyoto. Buddhism was state-sponsored and monumental, but courtiers also developed a distinctly Japanese culture: kana writing, waka poetry, and prose such as The Tale of Genji. Behind the elegance, tax-free private estates and provincial warrior bands were quietly draining the court's power.

hints.label: 古代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 鎌倉時代 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333)
nodes.title: 鎌倉時代 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1192–AD 1333] 鎌倉時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Power shifted from the court in Kyoto to a warrior government in the east, with the shogun and later the Hojo regents ruling through networks of vassals. The two Mongol invasions were beaten back with the help of storms later called the kamikaze, though the cost strained the regime. Zen Buddhism and the popular Pure Land and Nichiren movements took root, and a stark, muscular style appeared in sculpture and war tales.

hints.label: 鎌倉時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 室町時代 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573)
nodes.title: 室町時代 (Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1336–AD 1573] 室町時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The Ashikaga shoguns governed from Kyoto, close to the imperial court, presiding over a lucrative trade with Ming China and over steadily weakening central control. Their patronage produced some of Japan's most enduring culture: noh drama, linked verse, ink landscape painting, flower arranging, and the Golden and Silver Pavilions. The Onin War of 1467 wrecked the capital and unleashed a century of provincial warfare in which retainers routinely overthrew their lords.

hints.label: 室町時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 中世 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573)
nodes.title: 中世 (Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1192–AD 1573] 中世. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Power passed from the court aristocracy to warrior houses ruling from Kamakura and later Kyoto, with the emperor reduced largely to a ceremonial role. Estates, temples and armed leagues carved up authority; Zen, Pure Land and Nichiren Buddhism spread among ordinary people; and the Mongol invasions were beaten off with help from storms remembered as the kamikaze. The era ends in a century of open civil war among regional warlords, which also produced the tea ceremony, noh theatre and ink painting.

hints.label: 中世
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 安土・桃山時代 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603)
nodes.title: 安土・桃山時代 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1573–AD 1603] 安土・桃山時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Three decades of dramatic unification, as Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi broke the power of independent warlords, monasteries and free cities. Hideyoshi's sword hunt and land surveys froze the boundary between samurai and peasants, and his two invasions of Korea ended in costly failure. The mood shows in the art: soaring stone-based castles, gold-leaf screens, and by contrast the deliberate rusticity of Sen no Rikyu's tea ceremony.

hints.label: 安土・桃山時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 江戸時代 (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868)
nodes.title: 江戸時代 (Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1603–AD 1868] 江戸時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Under the Tokugawa shoguns Japan enjoyed two and a half centuries without major war, with the country closed to most foreign contact and society divided into fixed hereditary ranks. Cities boomed - Edo became one of the largest in the world - and with them came kabuki, woodblock prints, popular fiction and a widely literate merchant public. The order finally cracked under fiscal strain and the arrival of American warships.

hints.label: 江戸時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 近世 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868)
nodes.title: 近世 (Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1573–AD 1868] 近世. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The age from the warlord reunification under Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi through the Tokugawa peace: castles, cadastral surveys, disarmed peasants and a fixed status order. Cities, road networks and a money economy grew rapidly, producing a rich urban culture even as contact with the outside world was tightly restricted.

hints.label: 近世
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 明治時代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912)
nodes.title: 明治時代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1912] 明治時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

In little more than four decades Japan dismantled the samurai order, built railways, factories, a conscript army and a written constitution, and turned itself from a country forced open by foreign gunboats into a power that defeated Russia. Domains became prefectures, commoners took surnames, and Western dress, science and law were adopted wholesale while Shinto was reworked into a state ideology around the emperor. The speed of the change made it a model, and a warning, for modernisers everywhere.

hints.label: 明治時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 大正時代 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926)
nodes.title: 大正時代 (Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1912–AD 1926] 大正時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

A brief, liberal-feeling interlude often called Taisho democracy: party cabinets, universal male suffrage in 1925, mass-circulation newspapers, cafés, cinema and the 'modern girl'. Japan profited from the First World War and joined the great powers at Versailles, while labour unrest, rice riots and socialist agitation grew at home. The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 flattened Tokyo and Yokohama and killed over a hundred thousand people, and the same year's security laws pointed towards the harder decades ahead.

hints.label: 大正時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 昭和時代 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989)
nodes.title: 昭和時代 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1989] 昭和時代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The longest imperial reign in Japanese history spanned militarism, empire, catastrophic defeat, occupation and then the fastest sustained economic growth the world had seen. A visitor can trace the same country from the invasion of Manchuria and the atomic bombings to bullet trains, transistor radios and the Tokyo Olympics within a single lifetime.

hints.label: 昭和時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 近代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989)
nodes.title: 近代 (Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1868–AD 1989] 近代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Japan's era as a modern state, from the Meiji reforms and industrialisation through empire-building in Korea, Taiwan and China, to war, defeat and postwar reconstruction. The whole arc - constitution, conscription, factories, colonies, ruin and recovery - unfolded in barely more than a century.

hints.label: 近代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 昭和時代戦前 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945)
nodes.title: 昭和時代戦前 (Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1926–AD 1945] 昭和時代戦前. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Economic crisis, assassinations of politicians and the growing independence of the army pushed Japan from party government toward military domination. Expansion into Manchuria and China led into the Pacific War, ending with firebombed cities, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and unconditional surrender. Material from these years - propaganda posters, rationing goods, air-raid gear - shows how thoroughly civilian life was mobilised.

hints.label: 昭和時代戦前
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 昭和時代戦後 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988)
nodes.title: 昭和時代戦後 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1946–AD 1988] 昭和時代戦後. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Occupation reforms brought a new constitution renouncing war, land redistribution, votes for women and the dissolution of the great business combines. From the ruins came decades of double-digit growth built on steel, shipbuilding, cars and electronics, producing the consumer society of televisions, apartment blocks and commuter trains that still shapes Japan.

hints.label: 昭和時代戦後
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 平成時代 (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019)
nodes.title: 平成時代 (Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1989–AD 2019] 平成時代. The source did not have an end label for the Heisei era because the era ended 5 years after its publication. I added the date because it is undisputed. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

The era opened just as the asset bubble burst, ushering in the 'lost decades' of stagnant wages, deflation and an ageing, shrinking population. It saw the Kobe earthquake, the Tokyo subway sarin attack, and the 2011 tsunami and Fukushima nuclear disaster, alongside the global spread of Japanese games, anime and food. It ended with the first abdication of a Japanese emperor in two centuries.

hints.label: 平成時代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: 現代 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019)
nodes.title: 現代 (Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019)
nodes.description:
[Japan, AD 1946–AD 2019] 現代. Period definition from 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典 — Momoo Yamaguchi, 2014.

Postwar Japan under a pacifist constitution became the world's second-largest economy, then faced the bursting of its asset bubble, an ageing population and disasters like Kobe and Fukushima. It is also the era of Japanese cultural export - cameras, cars, video games, manga and anime reaching a global audience.

hints.label: 現代
hints.source: 日本の文化・観光・歴史辞典

nodes.name: Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Neuquén Province, 200 BC–AD 1400] Período Alfarero Temprano. Period definition from  Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina. — Pérez, Alberto E., 2020.

Farming hamlets appear with pottery, stone hoes, grinding equipment and pens for llamas, set among field walls and irrigation channels. Households were largely self-sufficient but exchanged obsidian, shell, metal and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia over long distances, laying the agricultural and technological groundwork for the crowded towns of later centuries.

hints.label: Período Alfarero Temprano
hints.source: Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina.

nodes.name: Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1001–AD 1900)
nodes.title: Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1001–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[Neuquén Province, AD 1001–AD 1900] Período Alfarero Tardío. Period definition from  Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina. — Pérez, Alberto E., 2020.

Communities consolidated into large agglomerated towns of stone-walled rooms, often perched on defensible spurs above terraced fields, with cemeteries of urns holding infant burials. Painted Santa María and Belén jars, metalwork and evidence of raiding point to competition between valley polities, which were later drawn into the Inca road system and then shattered by the Spanish invasion and the Calchaquí wars.

hints.label: Período Alfarero Tardío
hints.source: Alfarería arqueológica del centro sur de Chile y la Patagonia Noroccidental argentina.

nodes.name: Período Alfarero (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1900)
nodes.title: Período Alfarero (Argentina, 200 BC–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[Neuquén Province, 200 BC–AD 1900] Período Alfarero. Period definition from Crono-categorías culturales Argentina. Base de Datos. — Izeta, Andrés Darío, 2021.

The long stretch in which fired pottery, cultivated crops and llama herding became the basis of life across northwestern Argentina. Scattered hunting camps gave way to permanent villages with storage, irrigation and cemeteries, and later to large fortified towns that were absorbed first by the Inca and then by Spain. Ceramics are the backbone of the chronology here: styles change often enough that a broken bowl can date a site to within a century or two.

hints.label: Período Alfarero
hints.source: Crono-categorías culturales Argentina. Base de Datos.

nodes.name: Recent Prehistory (Europe, 5550 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.title: Recent Prehistory (Europe, 5550 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–1150 BC] Recent Prehistory. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The stretch from the spread of farming to the end of the Bronze Age, when Europe filled with villages, fields and herds, and communities began raising megaliths and burial mounds over their dead. Copper and then bronze metallurgy created long-distance trade in ore, amber and finished weapons, and with it visible differences of wealth and rank. By its close, fortified centres, chariots, warrior burials and shared prestige styles linked much of the continent to the Mediterranean palace world.

hints.label: Recent Prehistory
hints.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

nodes.name: Neolithic (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Europe, 5550 BC–3050 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 5550 BC–3050 BC] Neolithic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

hints.label: Neolithic
hints.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

nodes.name: Calcolithic (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC)
nodes.title: Calcolithic (Europe, 3350 BC–1850 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 3350 BC–1850 BC] Calcolithic. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The centuries when copper working spread across Europe alongside continued heavy use of stone tools, bringing the first metal axes, daggers and ornaments and the first specialised miners. Ploughs, wheeled vehicles, wool sheep and horses transformed farming and travel, while megalithic tombs, richly furnished individual graves and hilltop enclosures point to sharpening inequality and conflict. It is the world of the Iceman, of Corded Ware and Bell Beaker pottery, and of the population movements that reshaped the continent's ancestry before bronze became standard.

hints.label: Calcolithic
hints.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Europe, 1850 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Europe, 1850 BC–1150 BC)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 1850 BC–1150 BC] Bronze Age. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

hints.label: Bronze Age
hints.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

nodes.name: Holocene (Europe, 9050 BC–AD 2021)
nodes.title: Holocene (Europe, 9050 BC–AD 2021)
nodes.description:
[Eurasia, 9050 BC–AD 2021] Holocene. Spatial coverage: Asia, Europe. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The warm interval since the last glaciation, in which rising seas cut Britain off from the continent and drowned the plain now beneath the North Sea. Tundra gave way to birch, pine and then dense mixed woodland; hunter-gatherers were followed by farmers, and every monument, field system, town and road in the country belongs to this sliver of geological time. Its later part is marked worldwide by human alteration of climate, soils and species.

hints.label: Holocene
hints.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

nodes.name: MIS 1 (Earth, 12050 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.title: MIS 1 (Earth, 12050 BC–AD 1950)
nodes.description:
[World, 12050 BC–AD 1950] MIS 1. Period definition from Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH — Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH, 2021.

The current warm interval in the ocean-sediment record, beginning as the last ice age ended, ice sheets melted and sea level rose more than a hundred metres, drowning coastlines and land bridges such as Doggerland and Beringia. Stable, comparatively mild conditions accompanied the spread of farming, cities, writing and every recorded civilisation. It is the climatic stage humans still live in.

hints.label: MIS 1
hints.source: Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana, CENIEH

nodes.name: Quaternaire (France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Quaternaire (France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[France, 2580000 BC–AD 2000] Quaternaire. Le Quaternaire est la troisième période géologique de l'ère du Cénozoïque et la plus récente sur l'échelle des temps géologiques. Cette période se caractérise par le retour des glaciations, l'extension du genre Homo et l'extinction des faunes de l'Holocène. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The most recent stretch of geological time, defined by repeated ice ages in which glaciers advanced and retreated across northern Europe, sea levels rose and fell by more than a hundred metres, and mammoth, reindeer and woolly rhinoceros ranged over the continent. It is also the age of humanity: the whole story of stone tools, cave painting, farming and cities falls inside it.

hints.label: Quaternaire
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Chronologie américaine (France, 23000 BC–AD 1492)
nodes.title: Chronologie américaine (France, 23000 BC–AD 1492)
nodes.description: [France, 23000 BC–AD 1492] Chronologie américaine. Employer ce terme pour les périodes entre la préhistoire et l'arrivée des Espagnols (BL). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

hints.label: Chronologie américaine
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Holocène (France, 9700 BC–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Holocène (France, 9700 BC–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[France, 9700 BC–AD 2000] Holocène. L'Holocène (du grec ancien holos - ὅλος : entier, et kainos - καινός : récent) est une époque géologique s'étendant sur les 10 000 dernières années, toujours en cours de nos jours. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The postglacial warm period in which the ice caps withdrew, the Atlantic rose to something near its present level, and reindeer-hunting steppe gave way to oak and hazel forest. Mesolithic foragers adapted to the new woodlands and coasts before farming spread from the Mediterranean and the Danube, bringing megaliths, metal, and eventually towns. Everything from the painted caves' aftermath to the present belongs to this interval.

hints.label: Holocène
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Préhistoire (France, 800000 BC–3001 BC)
nodes.title: Préhistoire (France, 800000 BC–3001 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 800000 BC–3001 BC] Préhistoire. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The long arc from the first hominins in Europe - the half-million-year-old skull from Tautavel, the Neanderthal burials of the Dordogne - to the eve of metal and writing. Its most famous legacy is the painted caves of Chauvet, Lascaux and Pech Merle, made by Ice Age hunters with charcoal and ochre. After the glaciers retreated, farming spread up the Rhône and along the Mediterranean, and communities began raising the megaliths and standing stones of Brittany, including the thousands of alignments at Carnac.

hints.label: Préhistoire
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Néolithique (France, 6000 BC–2201 BC) [p02chr4ghc6]
nodes.title: Néolithique (France, 6000 BC–2201 BC) [p02chr4ghc6]
nodes.description:
[France, 6000 BC–2201 BC] Néolithique. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Herding of sheep, goats and cattle, together with pottery and cultivated grain, spread across the Moroccan coast, the Rif and the Atlas, taking hold among populations descended from earlier hunter-gatherers. Cardial-impressed pottery in the north points to contact across the Strait with Iberia, while cave sites and shell middens show a mixed economy of farming, herding, fishing and gathering. Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.

hints.label: Néolithique
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Néolithique moyen (France, 5300 BC–4501 BC) [p02chr4m92t]
nodes.title: Néolithique moyen (France, 5300 BC–4501 BC) [p02chr4m92t]
nodes.description:
[France, 5300 BC–4501 BC] Néolithique moyen. English label not present in original source but required for data entry via  client. Obtained via Google translate. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Farming communities across France moved beyond the tightly uniform longhouse villages of the first settlers into a patchwork of regional groups with their own pottery and burial customs. In the west, people began raising long earthen mounds and stone chambered tombs – among the earliest monumental architecture in Europe – while enclosures ringed by ditches and palisades appeared in the north and the Paris basin. Cattle herding, flint mining and long-distance movement of polished stone axes tied these communities together.

hints.label: Néolithique moyen
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Néolithique récent (France, 4500 BC–2201 BC)
nodes.title: Néolithique récent (France, 4500 BC–2201 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 4500 BC–2201 BC] Néolithique récent. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Farming communities across France grew denser and more organised, raising megalithic tombs and long stone alignments, digging flint mines, and building enclosures ringed by ditches and palisades. Pottery styles and burial customs became strongly regional, from the collective gallery graves of the Paris Basin to the passage tombs of Brittany. Toward the end, copper objects and the first Beaker pottery signal the shift into the metal ages.

Lion Point, France

nodes.name: Néolithique final (France, 4500 BC–3951 BC)
nodes.title: Néolithique final (France, 4500 BC–3951 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 4500 BC–3951 BC] Néolithique final. Correspond au Chalcolithique sans métal. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The closing stage of the Neolithic in France, when the landscape filled with people: hilltop and ditched enclosures, large collective tombs and rock-cut hypogea, extensive flint mines and polished-axe workshops. Copper was worked in the south, and networks moving axes, flint and ornaments stretched across the country. These societies, denser and more competitive than what came before, were the ones absorbed into the Bell Beaker world at the threshold of the Bronze Age.

hints.label: Néolithique final
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Sub-boréal (France, 3710 BC–851 BC)
nodes.title: Sub-boréal (France, 3710 BC–851 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 3710 BC–851 BC] Sub-boréal. Avant-dernier étage paléoclimatologique de l'Holocène, le Subboréal s'étend de - 5000 ans à - 2500 ans avant le présent. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

A climatic phase in the northern European sequence, drier and somewhat cooler than the warm Atlantic period that preceded it, traced through shifts in pollen: beech and hornbeam spreading, lime declining, and clear signals of forest clearance for fields and pasture. It spans the arrival and consolidation of farming, the megalith builders and the whole of the Bronze Age. Peat bogs and lake cores from this interval are the main archive for reconstructing how much of the landscape change was climate and how much was people.

hints.label: Sub-boréal
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Chronologie antillaise (France, 3000 BC–AD 1915)
nodes.title: Chronologie antillaise (France, 3000 BC–AD 1915)
nodes.description: [France, 3000 BC–AD 1915] Chronologie antillaise. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

hints.label: Chronologie antillaise
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC) [p02chr42bc7]
nodes.title: Chalcolithique (France, 3000 BC–2201 BC) [p02chr42bc7]
nodes.description:
[France, 3000 BC–2201 BC] Chalcolithique. Parfois appelé Énéolithique, ou encore plus rarement Épinéolithique, période de la protohistoire originellement définie comme une transition entre le Néolithique et l'âge du bronze. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Copper working spread through late Neolithic communities in France, while the great megalithic tomb-building traditions continued and collective burial in hypogea and gallery graves reached its height. Toward the close of the period, Bell Beaker pottery and archery equipment arrived from the wider European network, bringing new metalworking skills and burial customs that led into the Bronze Age.

hints.label: Chalcolithique
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Protohistoire (France, 2200 BC–51 BC)
nodes.title: Protohistoire (France, 2200 BC–51 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 2200 BC–51 BC] Protohistoire. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Covers the Bronze and Iron Ages in Gaul, from the first metal-using communities through the tumulus and urnfield traditions to Hallstatt princely burials and the La Tène world of the Celts. These societies built hillforts and oppida, minted coins and traded wine with the Mediterranean, but wrote almost nothing about themselves, so they are known through excavation and through what Greeks and Romans said about them. The sequence ends with Caesar's conquest, which brought Gaul into recorded history.

hints.label: Protohistoire
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: âge du Bronze (France, 2200 BC–801 BC) [p02chr4bdf4]
nodes.title: âge du Bronze (France, 2200 BC–801 BC) [p02chr4bdf4]
nodes.description:
[France, 2200 BC–801 BC] âge du Bronze. La chronologie de l'âge du Bronze faisant référence est celle de J.-J. Hatt « Nouveau projet de chronologie pour l’âge de bronze en France » in : Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française, p. 304-306, 1958, vol. 55, no 5-6. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Copper and tin alloyed into bronze pulled the region into long-distance exchange networks running from Cornwall and Brittany to central Europe and the Mediterranean. Warrior elites were buried under tumuli with daggers and axes, and later centuries produced enormous hoards of scrap and finished metalwork, deliberately buried or thrown into rivers. By the closing phase, cremation in urnfields, fortified hilltop sites and mass-produced socketed axes point to the more crowded, competitive world that iron would inherit.

hints.label: âge du Bronze
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–1601 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze ancien (France, 2200 BC–1601 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 2200 BC–1601 BC] Bronze ancien. Correspond à l’apparition de la métallurgie, avant le Ve millénaire av. J.‑C. en Anatolie mais vers le IIe millénaire av. J.‑C. en Europe occidentale comme en France. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The first true tin bronze came into general use in France, made into flanged axes, triangular daggers and pins. Elite burials under mounds appear in Brittany and the Rhône valley, stocked with weapons, gold ornaments and amber that show long-distance contacts with Wessex and central Europe. Settlement remained dispersed, but control of metal and its trade routes was starting to create visible social ranks.

hints.label: Bronze ancien
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: époque mycénienne (France, 1650 BC–1101 BC)
nodes.title: époque mycénienne (France, 1650 BC–1101 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 1650 BC–1101 BC] époque mycénienne. après 1400 av. J.-C.- vers 1200 av. J.-C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Fortified palace citadels at Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns ruled mainland Greece, administering their territories with Linear B tablets in an early form of Greek. Their shaft graves and beehive tombs held gold masks, weapons and imports showing wide Mediterranean contacts. The palaces burned around 1200 BC and writing was lost for centuries, but the memory of these kings survives in Homer.

hints.label: époque mycénienne
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–1401 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze moyen (France, 1600 BC–1401 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 1600 BC–1401 BC] Bronze moyen. Appelé aussi l’« âge du Bronze véritable », il correspond à la culture des tumulus protoceltiques ce qui en Europe centrale se situe vers le IIe millénaire av. J.-C. et vers 1500 av. J.-C. en France. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Tumulus burial with weapons and ornaments spread widely, and metalworkers turned out palstave axes, torcs, bracelets and the first long swords. Regional workshops in Brittany, the Rhône and the north each developed recognisable styles while sharing forms with central Europe and Britain. Deliberate deposition of metal in rivers and hoards became a regular practice.

hints.label: Bronze moyen
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–801 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze final (France, 1400 BC–801 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 1400 BC–801 BC] Bronze final. Marqué par le début des grandes invasions, principalement celtiques, il se confond en Europe centrale avec la culture des champs d’urnes. Il commence en Europe occidentale comme en France vers le XIIe siècle av. J.-C. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Cremation replaced inhumation across much of France as the Urnfield tradition spread from central Europe, leaving large cemeteries of ash-filled pots. Bronze production reached industrial levels, with sheet-metal vessels, leaf-shaped swords and enormous scrap hoards along the Atlantic and Rhône corridors. Hilltop sites were fortified, and by the closing generations the first iron objects appear, leading directly into the Hallstatt Iron Age.

hints.label: Bronze final
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Hallstatt (France, 1200 BC–475 BC)
nodes.title: Hallstatt (France, 1200 BC–475 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 1200 BC–475 BC] Hallstatt. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Central Europe's Early Iron Age, named after the Austrian salt-mining village whose cemetery yielded a thousand richly furnished graves. Iron replaced bronze for weapons and tools, while chieftains were buried under great mounds with four-wheeled wagons, horse harness, and wine-drinking gear imported from Greek and Etruscan traders. Hilltop "princely seats" such as the Heuneburg and Mont Lassois show wealth concentrating in a few hands before the whole system gave way to the La Tène world.

hints.label: Hallstatt
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Bronze récent (France, 1200 BC–1001 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze récent (France, 1200 BC–1001 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 1200 BC–1001 BC] Bronze récent. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last phase of bronze-working in France, when Urnfield practices spread west: cremation in urn cemeteries largely replaced inhumation, and metalworkers turned out sheet-bronze vessels, socketed axes and slashing swords in huge numbers. Enormous hoards of scrap and finished tools were buried across the country, evidence of long-distance exchange in copper, tin and finished goods. Hillforts and fortified settlements multiplied, foreshadowing the iron-using societies of the Hallstatt world.

hints.label: Bronze récent
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.title: Bronze récent I (France, 1200 BC–1101 BC)

nodes.name: époque orientalisante (France, 1000 BC–701 BC)
nodes.title: époque orientalisante (France, 1000 BC–701 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 1000 BC–701 BC] époque orientalisante. de 750 à 600 pour les archéologues. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Contact with Phoenician and Near Eastern traders flooded the Greek and Italian world with new imagery — griffins, sphinxes, lions, palmettes — and new techniques in ivory, gold and bronze. Greek potters and metalworkers absorbed these motifs and made them their own, and the alphabet arrived by the same routes. It marks the point at which the Mediterranean became a single connected cultural zone.

nodes.name: Subatlantique (France, 850 BC–AD 2000)
nodes.title: Subatlantique (France, 850 BC–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[France, 850 BC–AD 2000] Subatlantique. Sur l'échelle des temps géologiques, le Subatlantique est le dernier étage géologique de l'Holocène. Succédant au Subboréal, il s'étend depuis environ -850 (tant que la proposition de création de l'Anthropocène n'est pas retenue). (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The current climatic phase, opening with a cool, wet downturn around the start of the Iron Age that raised bog surfaces and pushed settlement off some upland ground. Beech and hornbeam dominate the pollen record where woodland survives, but the overwhelming story is human: sustained clearance, cereal and weed pollen, and eventually a landscape more managed than natural. It covers everything from Celtic Europe through the Roman world and the medieval warm period to the Little Ice Age and industrialisation.

hints.label: Subatlantique
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–51 BC) [p02chr45626]
nodes.title: âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–51 BC) [p02chr45626]
nodes.description:
[France, 800 BC–51 BC] âge du Fer. Période chronologique caractérisée par l'usage de la métallurgie du fer et faisant généralement suite à l'âge du bronze. Cependant, les limites chronologiques de l'âge du fer varient considérablement selon l'aire culturelle et géographique considérée. Ainsi peut-il être considéré comme appartenant à la Préhistoire, à la Protohistoire ou l'Histoire selon les aires géographiques considérées. L'âge du fer débute vers 1100 av. J.-C. dans le monde méditerranéen, vers 800 à 700 av. J.-C. dans le nord de l'Europe et vers 500 av. J.-C. en Afrique. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Iron, cheap and widely available, replaced bronze for tools and weapons and changed who could arm and equip themselves. Princely burials, Mediterranean wine imports and later the fortified oppida trace the rise of Celtic chiefdoms with coinage, towns and craft specialisation. It ends with Caesar's conquest, which folded Gaul into the Roman world.

hints.label: âge du Fer
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Italie archaïque (France, 800 BC–401 BC)
nodes.title: Italie archaïque (France, 800 BC–401 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 800 BC–401 BC] Italie archaïque. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Archaic Italy, when Etruscan city-states dominated the centre of the peninsula, Greek colonies ringed the south, and Rome was still ruled by kings. Etruscan bronze vessels, black-glaze pottery and wine amphorae travelled north and west along trade routes to southern Gaul, where they turn up in native settlements and princely graves.

hints.label: Italie archaïque
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 BC)
nodes.title: Premier âge du Fer (France, 800 BC–451 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 800 BC–451 BC] Premier âge du Fer. Correspondant à la culture de Hallstatt, le Premier âge du Fer est une culture du centre-ouest de l'Europe qui dure d'environ -1200 à -500. Elle succède à l'âge du bronze final et précède la période de La Tène ou Second âge du Fer (fin de la Protohistoire). (D'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Iron working spread through Gaul, and with it a new social order: chieftains buried under great mounds with wagons, gold torcs and imported Mediterranean bronzes. The Vix krater and the princely seat at Mont Lassois show how Greek and Etruscan traders reached deep into the interior in exchange for tin, salt and slaves. Hillfort strongholds controlled the river routes, laying the groundwork for the Celtic societies Caesar would later meet.

hints.label: Premier âge du Fer
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: interglaciaire Riss-Würm (France, 800 BC–451 BC)
nodes.title: interglaciaire Riss-Würm (France, 800 BC–451 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 800 BC–451 BC] interglaciaire Riss-Würm. Avant-dernière période interglaciaire du Quaternaire. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last warm interval before the final glaciation, when temperatures in Europe briefly ran warmer than today. Deciduous forest spread to the far north and animals now associated with Africa and the Mediterranean, including hippopotamus, straight-tusked elephant and lion, lived in the river valleys of France. Neanderthals were the human population of the time, and their tool assemblages and butchered animal bones from this interval show them hunting large game in dense woodland.

hints.label: interglaciaire Riss-Würm
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: époque archaïque (France, 800 BC–481 BC)
nodes.title: époque archaïque (France, 800 BC–481 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 800 BC–481 BC] époque archaïque. Ne concerne que le monde grec : de 800 à 480 pour les historiographes et de 600 à 480 pour les archéologues. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The Greek world recovered from its dark age and remade itself: the polis emerged, the alphabet was adopted, colonies were planted from the Black Sea to Marseille, and monumental stone temples and kouros statues appeared. Coinage, written law and the first philosophers date from these centuries. Everything the Classical period is famous for was invented, in rough form, here.

hints.label: époque archaïque
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Transition Bronze/Fer (France, 775 BC–725 BC)
nodes.title: Transition Bronze/Fer (France, 775 BC–725 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 775 BC–725 BC] Transition Bronze/Fer. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The generations in which iron working spread through Gaul and the bronze-hoarding world of the Late Bronze Age gave way to the early Hallstatt chieftains. Cremation urnfields continue, but a new elite marks itself out with long iron slashing swords, horse harness and four-wheeled wagons buried under mounds - the beginning of the princely burial tradition that would culminate at Vix and Hochdorf.

hints.label: Transition Bronze/Fer
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499) [p02chr4ws55]
nodes.title: Antiquité (France, 600 BC–AD 499) [p02chr4ws55]
nodes.description:
[France, 600 BC–AD 499] Antiquité. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The long stretch in which Gaul moved from Iron Age chiefdoms trading with Mediterranean merchants to a fully Roman province and then to a Christianised, increasingly fragmented late-imperial society. It covers Greek colonial contact on the southern coast, Caesar's conquest, the Gallo-Roman towns with their forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, and the arrival of Frankish and Visigothic settlers. Most of France's monumental ancient remains, from Nîmes to Vienne, belong to it.

hints.label: Antiquité
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Antiquité gréco-romaine (France, 600 BC–AD 499)
nodes.title: Antiquité gréco-romaine (France, 600 BC–AD 499)
nodes.description:
[France, 600 BC–AD 499] Antiquité gréco-romaine. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

A combined label for the classical Mediterranean world as it reached and reshaped Gaul, from the first Greek colonies on the coast to the end of Roman rule. It spans the shared culture of city life, temple architecture, sculpture and inscribed stone that Greeks established and Romans spread across the whole of western Europe. Museum collections use it for material that sits on either side of that continuum.

hints.label: Antiquité gréco-romaine
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Antiquité grecque (France, 600 BC–229 BC)
nodes.title: Antiquité grecque (France, 600 BC–229 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 600 BC–229 BC] Antiquité grecque. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Greek traders and colonists from Phocaea founded Massalia and a string of coastal settlements, bringing wine, olive oil, coined money and writing to southern Gaul. Their goods travelled far inland up the Rhône, and Greek imports turn up in the richest Celtic burials of the interior. The category also covers Greek objects held in French collections, from painted vases to sculpture.

hints.label: Antiquité grecque
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: République romaine (France, 509 BC–27 BC)
nodes.title: République romaine (France, 509 BC–27 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 509 BC–27 BC] République romaine. 509 av. J.-C. - 27 av. J.-C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The last generation of the Roman Republic, when Caesar's newly conquered Gaul was absorbed into a state tearing itself apart in civil war. Gallic communities were reorganised, taxed and drawn into Roman military recruitment, and local elites began the shift to Latin, coinage and Roman-style towns that would define the provinces under the empire that followed.

hints.label: République romaine
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: époque pré-classique grecque (France, 490 BC–461 BC)
nodes.title: époque pré-classique grecque (France, 490 BC–461 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 490 BC–461 BC] époque pré-classique grecque. Abbreviation ép (for époque) not present in PACTOLS thesaurus, but present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. The generation after the Persian Wars, when Greek sculptors abandoned the fixed archaic smile for the sober, weight-shifting figures of the Severe Style. Athens, its city sacked and rebuilt, emerged at the head of a naval league that would become an empire. The bronze Charioteer of Delphi and the Riace warriors belong to these decades.

nodes.description:
[France, 480 BC–323 BC] époque classique grecque. L’Époque classique est une période de l'histoire de la Grèce antique, située entre l'époque archaïque et l'époque hellénistique. Elle correspond à la majeure partie des ve et ive siècles av. J.-C., c'est-à-dire depuis la victoire athénienne de Salamine contre les Perses en -480 jusqu'à la mort d'Alexandre le Grand en -323. (WP le 07/11/18). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The century and a half between the repulse of Persia and the death of Alexander, when Athens built the Parthenon, staged its tragedies and experimented with democracy. Sculpture reached the idealised naturalism later ages kept copying; Socrates, Plato and Thucydides worked in these decades. It was also an age of ruinous warfare between Greek cities that left them open to Macedonian takeover.

Neck zone has six repeats of a defined key motif in black or dark red, i.e. bichrome positive. nodes.title: La Tène (France, 450 BC–51 BC) [p02chr4qkk2]
nodes.description:
[France, 450 BC–51 BC] La Tène. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Named after a votive deposit of weapons in a Swiss lake, this culture spread across Gaul with a new elite of horse-riding warriors buried with chariots, swords and imported wine services. Its curvilinear art, all tendrils, palmettes and hidden faces, is the most recognisable Celtic style. By the final century large fortified towns, coinage and mass production were emerging, and it all ended with the Roman conquest.

nodes.name: Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC)
nodes.title: Second âge du Fer (France, 450 BC–51 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 450 BC–51 BC] Second âge du Fer. Correspondant à la culture de La Tène, le Second âge du Fer se développe en Europe entre environ 450 av. J.-C. et 25 av. J.-C. Considéré comme l'apogée de la civilisation celtique, il succède au Premier âge du Fer (Hallstatt, 1300-400 av. J.-C.) et s'achève avec la conquête romaine et les migrations germaniques. Son nom provient du site archéologique de La Tène découvert en 1857 à Marin-Epagnier, sur les bords du lac de Neuchâtel en Suisse. (D'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The La Tène era, when Gaulish societies produced the swirling curvilinear art found on scabbards and torcs, struck their own coinage, and built fortified towns, the oppida, with markets and workshops. Trade with the Mediterranean brought wine by the amphora-load, and Gaulish warbands raided as far as Italy and Greece. It closed with Caesar's conquest and the siege of Alesia.

nodes.name: La Tène A (France, 450 BC–261 BC)
nodes.title: La Tène A (France, 450 BC–261 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 450 BC–261 BC] La Tène A. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The opening phase of the La Tène Iron Age, when a wealthy elite in the Rhine, Moselle and Marne regions buried its dead with two-wheeled chariots, gold neck-rings and imported Etruscan and Greek wine service. Out of contact with those Mediterranean imports came the Early Style of Celtic art, which took palmettes, lotus buds and lion masks and reworked them into the swirling, ambiguous designs seen on the Glauberg and Reinheim finds. The old Hallstatt hillfort centres further west collapsed at about this time, and power shifted north.

nodes.description:
[France, 323 BC–30 BC] époque hellénistique. 323-31 av. J.C. - Période de l'Antiquité qui suit la conquête d’une partie du monde méditerranéen et de l’Asie par Alexandre le Grand jusqu’à la période romaine. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Alexander's conquests scattered Greek cities and Greek as a common language from Egypt to the Indus, and his generals carved the empire into rival kingdoms. Alexandria and Pergamon became centres of scholarship, libraries and mathematics; art turned dramatic, emotional and often colossal. Rome absorbed these kingdoms one by one, inheriting their culture along with their territory.

Gaul in the full La Tène Iron Age: warrior aristocracies, elaborate metalwork with curving abstract ornament, and farming communities scattered across the countryside. Gallic bands raided deep into Italy, Greece and Asia Minor, and mercenary service brought home Macedonian gold coins that local smiths began to copy, launching the first native coinages. Trade in wine, salt and metals with the Mediterranean world grew steadily, laying the ground for the fortified towns and Roman contact of the following century.

nodes.name: La Tène B (France, 260 BC–151 BC)
nodes.title: La Tène B (France, 260 BC–151 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 260 BC–151 BC] La Tène B. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The phase of the great Celtic migrations, when war bands from the north moved into the Po valley, the middle Danube and the Balkans; the sack of Rome and the raid on Delphi belong to these generations. Large flat cemeteries of inhumations replace the earlier princely tumuli, with men buried with sword, spear and shield and women with brooches and rings. Metalworkers developed the Waldalgesheim or Vegetal Style, a flowing tendril ornament that spread across Europe with astonishing uniformity.

hints.label: La Tène B
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: La Tène D (France, 150 BC–51 BC)
nodes.title: La Tène D (France, 150 BC–51 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 150 BC–51 BC] La Tène D. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The final Iron Age phase, dominated by the oppida: huge walled towns with streets, workshops, mints and imported Roman wine. Political life sharpened into named tribes with magistrates and coinage, and the archaeological record ends with the Gallic Wars and the absorption of the region into the Roman world.

hints.label: La Tène D
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: La Tène C (France, 150 BC–51 BC)
nodes.title: La Tène C (France, 150 BC–51 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 150 BC–51 BC] La Tène C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The middle La Tène, when the long slashing sword hung from an iron chain belt becomes the standard warrior's equipment and cremation begins to replace inhumation over much of the region. Large open settlements and craft centres grew, gold and silver coinage struck in imitation of Macedonian and Roman types came into use, and trade with the Mediterranean intensified. The decorated scabbards of this phase, in the so-called Sword Style, are among the finest Celtic metalwork.

nodes.name: époque tardo-républicaine (France, 133 BC–27 BC)
nodes.title: époque tardo-républicaine (France, 133 BC–27 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 133 BC–27 BC] époque tardo-républicaine. Abbreviation ép (for époque) not present in PACTOLS thesaurus, but present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Included as it is a commonly used alternative in French language. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Rome's last century as a republic, and the century in which Gaul became Roman. Armies moved north to protect the route to Spain, the province of Gallia Transalpina was organised around Narbo, and Caesar's campaigns of the 50s BC brought the rest of the territory under Roman control. Towns, roads, coinage and villa estates spread quickly, and the civil wars that ended the Republic were fought partly with Gallic manpower and money.

nodes.name: Ier siècle av. J.-C. (France, 100 BC–1 BC)
nodes.title: Ier siècle av. J.-C. (France, 100 BC–1 BC)
nodes.description:
[France, 100 BC–1 BC] Ier siècle av. J.-C.. Alternative punctuation for av J-C was present in list of dated terms received from INRAP. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Caesar's campaigns between 58 and 51 BC broke the Gallic confederations, ending with Vercingetorix's defeat at Alesia and the loss of enormous numbers of lives and captives. What followed was rapid reorganisation: new provincial boundaries, roads, taxation and colonies of veterans. Gaulish oppida gave way to Roman towns, and the local elite began the shift to Latin and Roman citizenship.

nodes.name: Antiquité romaine (France, 50 BC–AD 499) [p02chr4964n]
nodes.title: Antiquité romaine (France, 50 BC–AD 499) [p02chr4964n]
nodes.description:
[France, 50 BC–AD 499] Antiquité romaine. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

After Caesar's conquest, Gaul was reorganised into provinces, laid out with roads, and filled with towns modelled on Rome; local elites adopted Latin, togas and civic office while keeping many indigenous gods. Aqueducts, arenas, theatres and villa estates transformed the landscape, and cities such as Lugdunum became imperial centres in their own right. The Gallo-Roman synthesis that resulted underlies later French language, law and settlement patterns.

hints.label: Antiquité romaine
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Haut-Empire romain (France, 50 BC–AD 299)
nodes.title: Haut-Empire romain (France, 50 BC–AD 299)
nodes.description:
[France, 50 BC–AD 299] Haut-Empire romain. Il constitue, avec le Bas-Empire, une des deux découpes historiographiques de l'Empire romain telle que vue par les historiens français. Ces termes sont des concepts très usuels, mais leurs limites chronologiques respectives ne sont pas fixées de façon unanime. Elle désigne la première période de l’Empire romain, qui débute en 27 av. J.-C. avec le principat d'Auguste, et inclut le règne idéalisé des Antonins. (Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul under the Principate, when Roman rule turned a patchwork of Celtic peoples into a network of chartered towns linked by paved roads. Cities like Lugdunum, Nemausus and Arelate acquired forums, aqueducts, amphitheatres and Latin inscriptions, while villa estates reorganised the countryside for grain, wine and pottery export. Local gods were paired with Roman ones and native aristocrats bought into imperial careers, leaving the monumental ruins that still anchor southern French towns.

nodes.name: Empire romain d'Occident (France, 27 BC–AD 476)
nodes.title: Empire romain d'Occident (France, 27 BC–AD 476)
nodes.description:
[France, 27 BC–AD 476] Empire romain d'Occident. jusqu'en 476. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul spent five centuries as a set of Roman provinces, and the transformation was thorough: grid-planned cities with forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, a road network binding the Rhine frontier to the Mediterranean, villa estates exporting grain and wine, and Latin displacing Gaulish speech. Lyon, Arles, Nîmes and Trier became major imperial centres, and Christianity spread through them from the third century on. When central authority collapsed in the west, the bishops, estates and Latin language it left behind became the foundations of Frankish Gaul.

nodes.name: époque augustéenne (France, 27 BC–AD 14)
nodes.title: époque augustéenne (France, 27 BC–AD 14)
nodes.description:
[France, 27 BC–AD 14] époque augustéenne. 27 av. J-C à 14 ap. J.C. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The reign of Rome's first emperor, when the machinery of the Republic was quietly repurposed into one-man rule. Augustus rebuilt Rome in marble, sponsored Virgil and Horace, and imposed a long peace that let provincial cities be laid out on Roman lines with forums, theatres and aqueducts. In Gaul the period saw an intense burst of urban foundation and road building whose grid plans still shape modern towns.

hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Ier siècle (France, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.title: Ier siècle (France, AD 1–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 1–AD 100] Ier siècle. De l'an 1 à l'an 100. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul, conquered only decades earlier, became thoroughly Roman: new cities laid out on grids, aqueducts, amphitheatres and roads, with Lugdunum as the administrative hub and the site of the annual assembly of the Gallic provinces. Local aristocracies took Roman names and citizenship while Gaulish gods were paired with Roman ones. The pottery, glass and wine trades made the region one of the wealthiest parts of the western empire.

hints.label: Ier siècle
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: IIe siècle (France, AD 100–AD 199)
nodes.title: IIe siècle (France, AD 100–AD 199)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 100–AD 199] IIe siècle. De l'an 101 à l'an 200. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul at the peak of Roman prosperity, with no wars on its soil and cities like Lugdunum, Nemausus and Arelate building amphitheatres, baths and aqueducts. Wealth came from grain, wine, pottery and river trade, and it shows in the sprawling villas and their mosaics. Latin, Roman gods and Roman dress mixed with Gallic traditions to make a distinctly Gallo-Roman culture.

hints.label: IIe siècle
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: IIIe siècle (France, AD 200–AD 299)
nodes.title: IIIe siècle (France, AD 200–AD 299)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 200–AD 299] IIIe siècle. De l'an 201 à l'an 300. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Roman Gaul went from prosperity to crisis: plague, civil war, currency collapse and Germanic raiding across the Rhine. For fourteen years the region broke away as a separate Gallic Empire under Postumus and his successors, and towns that had sprawled unwalled for two centuries pulled back behind hastily built ramparts made partly of tombstones and monuments. The century also brought the first Christian communities and bishops to Gaul, and the peasant Bagaudae revolts that Diocletian's reforms were meant to end.

hints.label: IIIe siècle
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Antiquité tardive (France, AD 300–AD 499)
nodes.title: Antiquité tardive (France, AD 300–AD 499)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 300–AD 499] Antiquité tardive. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Imperial authority thinned, cities shrank behind hastily built walls, and bishops emerged as the effective leaders of urban communities. Christianity became the dominant religion, with the first basilicas and pilgrimage cults, while Franks, Burgundians and Visigoths settled and formed kingdoms out of the western provinces. It is the period in which Roman Gaul becomes medieval France, more by transformation than by sudden collapse.

hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Bas-Empire romain (France, AD 300–AD 499)
nodes.title: Bas-Empire romain (France, AD 300–AD 499)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 300–AD 499] Bas-Empire romain. Il constitue avec le Haut-Empire une des deux découpes historiographiques de l'Empire romain dans l'historiographie romaine vue par les historiens français. Ces termes sont des concepts très usuels, mais leurs limites chronologiques respectives ne sont pas fixées de façon unanime. On fixe la plupart du temps cette période entre les années 284 et 476.(Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

A militarised, heavily taxed empire, defended by field armies and frontier troops that increasingly included Germanic recruits. In Gaul the countryside consolidated into great estates while walled towns became administrative and episcopal centres, and imperial authority weakened until it dissolved into successor kingdoms.

nodes.title: IVe siècle (France, AD 300–AD 399)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 300–AD 399] IVe siècle. De l'an 301 à l'an 400. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Late Roman Gaul was a frontier province turned political centre, with emperors residing at Trier and armies stationed along the Rhine. Cities shrank behind thick new walls while great rural estates flourished. Christianity became the official religion and spread fast in the countryside under figures like Martin of Tours, and by the century's end Germanic peoples were settling inside the frontier as often as raiding across it.

nodes.name: Ve siècle (France, AD 400–AD 499)
nodes.title: Ve siècle (France, AD 400–AD 499)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 400–AD 499] Ve siècle. De l'an 401 à l'an 500. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Roman authority in Gaul dissolved over four generations: the Rhine was crossed in 406, the field armies withdrew, and Visigoths, Burgundians, Alans and Franks settled as federates who soon ruled in their own names. Villas were abandoned or fortified, cities shrank behind late walls, and bishops became the leading figures in urban life. By the end of the century Clovis had defeated the last Roman commander in the north and begun assembling the Frankish kingdom.

nodes.name: époque mérovingienne (France, AD 481–AD 751)
nodes.title: époque mérovingienne (France, AD 481–AD 751)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 481–AD 751] époque mérovingienne. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The first Frankish dynasty, descended from Clovis, ruled Gaul as it shifted from a Roman province to a Germanic kingdom. Its cemeteries are famous: the dead buried dressed, with weapons, belt buckles and garnet-inlaid brooches, giving archaeologists an unusually rich picture of costume and status. Real power drifted to the mayors of the palace, one of whose families eventually took the crown outright.

nodes.name: époque carolingienne (France, AD 751–AD 999)
nodes.title: époque carolingienne (France, AD 751–AD 999)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 751–AD 999] époque carolingienne. De 751 à 987 en France ou 911 en Germanie (Rob.). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Under Charlemagne and his heirs a Frankish dynasty assembled an empire spanning much of western Europe and revived the title of emperor in the West. Monastic scriptoria produced a legible new script, Carolingian minuscule, and copied the classical texts that survive today largely because of it. The empire split among his grandsons, sketching the outlines of later France and Germany.

hints.label: époque carolingienne

nodes.name: époque médiévale (France, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.title: époque médiévale (France, AD 500–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 500–AD 1500] époque médiévale. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The thousand years between the end of Roman rule in the West and the Renaissance, when Christianity, feudal landholding and the manor structured European life. Towns revived after the year 1000, cathedrals and castles rose in stone, universities were founded, and plague in the fourteenth century killed perhaps a third of the population. Most of Europe's villages, parish churches and field boundaries were laid down in these centuries.

hints.label: époque médiévale
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: Haut Moyen Âge (France, AD 500–AD 999) [p02chr4scv9]
nodes.title: Haut Moyen Âge (France, AD 500–AD 999) [p02chr4scv9]
nodes.description:
[France, AD 500–AD 999] Haut Moyen Âge. Période historique qui commence en 476 par la chute du dernier empereur romain d'Occident, et s'achève en l'an 1000. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman authority and the year 1000, when Frankish kings — first Merovingian, then Carolingian — built kingdoms out of the western provinces. Charlemagne's coronation in 800 revived the idea of a western empire and sponsored a revival of Latin learning and manuscript production in monastic scriptoria. Viking, Muslim and Magyar raids and the break-up of the Carolingian inheritance then shifted real power to counts and castellans, laying the ground for feudal society.

hints.label: Haut Moyen Âge
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: VIe siècle (France, AD 500–AD 599)
nodes.title: VIe siècle (France, AD 500–AD 599)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 500–AD 599] VIe siècle. De l'an 501 à l'an 600. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Clovis's sons and grandsons carved Gaul into competing Merovingian kingdoms, absorbed Burgundy and Provence, and fought long dynastic feuds that Gregory of Tours recorded in vivid, gossipy detail. Roman civic institutions faded while bishops, drawn from the surviving senatorial families, took over the running of towns. Gold coinage, villa estates and long-distance trade in Mediterranean goods persisted, but on a shrinking scale.

hints.label: VIe siècle
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: VIIe siècle (France, AD 600–AD 699)
nodes.title: VIIe siècle (France, AD 600–AD 699)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 600–AD 699] VIIe siècle. De l'an 601 à l'an 700. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Gaul was divided among rival Merovingian kingdoms — Neustria, Austrasia and Burgundy — whose queens and factions fought bitter civil wars; Dagobert I briefly reunited them. Afterwards effective power drained to the mayors of the palace, the aristocratic officials who would become the Carolingians. Irish and Frankish monasticism spread rapidly in the wake of Columbanus, planting abbeys such as Luxeuil and Corbie that became centres of learning and landholding.

hints.label: VIIe siècle
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: époque islamique (France, AD 622–AD 750)
nodes.title: époque islamique (France, AD 622–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 622–AD 750] époque islamique. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Beginning with the Hijra, the community founded by Muhammad in Arabia expanded within a century across Syria, Egypt, Iran, North Africa and Spain, absorbing the Sasanian empire and half of Byzantium's territory. A new religion, a new script and a new political order spread through cities that were often the old Roman and Persian ones under new management. Raids reached as far as southern Gaul before being checked in the eighth century.

hints.label: époque islamique
hints.source: PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data

nodes.name: époque des Omeyyades (France, AD 661–AD 750)
nodes.title: époque des Omeyyades (France, AD 661–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 661–AD 750] époque des Omeyyades. époque du règne de la dynastie arabe des Omeyyades sur le monde musulman de 661 à 750. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The first hereditary Islamic dynasty, ruling from Damascus over an empire that stretched from Spain to Central Asia within a single lifetime of conquest. Arabic became the language of administration, the first Islamic coinage was struck, and the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus set the template for mosque architecture. Overthrown by the Abbasids in 750, a surviving branch went on to rule al-Andalus.

nodes.name: VIIIe siècle (France, AD 700–AD 799)
nodes.title: VIIIe siècle (France, AD 700–AD 799)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 700–AD 799] VIIIe siècle. De l'an 701 à l'an 800. Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

Real power had passed from the Merovingian kings to the Carolingian mayors of the palace: Charles Martel checked an Arab raiding army near Poitiers, and his son Pippin deposed the last Merovingian and had himself anointed king with papal blessing. That alliance between the Frankish crown and Rome culminated in Charlemagne's conquests of Lombardy, Saxony and Bavaria, and his imperial coronation at the century's end. Monastic scriptoria began producing the clear Caroline minuscule script that preserved much of Latin literature.

hints.label: VIIIe siècle

nodes.name: époque abbasside (France, AD 750–AD 1258)
nodes.title: époque abbasside (France, AD 750–AD 1258)
nodes.description:
[France, AD 750–AD 1258] époque abbasside. Epoque du califat sunnite qui gouverna le monde musulman de 750 à 1258. Sous les Abbassides, le centre de gravité de l'islam se déplace de la Syrie vers l'Irak où une nouvelle capitale est fondée en 762 : Bagdad. (d'après Wikipédia). Period definition from PACTOLS chronology periods used in DOLIA data — INRAP: Institut National de Recherches Archeologiques Preventive, 2021.

The caliphate that overthrew the Umayyads and moved the centre of Islamic power east to Baghdad, a new round city built to be the hub of an empire. Its early centuries saw an extraordinary flowering of science, translation of Greek learning, and long-distance trade linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean. Political control fragmented long before the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, but Abbasid art, ceramics and scholarship set the standards imitated everywhere.
