nodes.name: Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1650)
nodes.title: Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1650] Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional. Period definition from "No tan simples": Pesca y horticultura entre grupos originarios del Norte de Mendoza. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2013.

The final centuries of independent valley societies, marked by nucleated settlements, defensive locations and strongly regional ceramic styles. Populations here experienced Inca conquest and then the Spanish invasion within a few generations, and their sites often contain the debris of both. Indigenous life continued at these places until the mid-seventeenth-century deportations emptied them.

hints.label: Período Prehispánico Tardío Regional
hints.source: "No tan simples": Pesca y horticultura entre grupos originarios del Norte de Mendoza.

nodes.name: Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1301–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Prehispánico Tardío (Argentina, AD 1301–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1301–AD 1500] Prehispánico Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

Densely populated valleys of the northwest supported farming communities that terraced hillsides, irrigated fields and built stone villages, some perched on defensible ridges as pukaras. Painted urns of the Santa María style, used to bury children beneath house floors, are the signature artefacts. Warfare and competition among these polities were cut short by Inca conquest and then by Spanish arrival.

hints.label: Prehispánico Tardío
hints.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

nodes.name: Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1501–AD 1601)
nodes.title: Colonial Temprano (Argentina, AD 1501–AD 1601)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1501–AD 1601] Colonial Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

Spanish expeditions pushed in from Peru and Chile, founding towns like Santiago del Estero, Mendoza and Córdoba and imposing the encomienda on indigenous communities. Native populations collapsed under warfare, forced labour and epidemic disease, though groups in the Calchaquí valleys and the southern plains resisted for generations. European livestock and metal goods spread far beyond the reach of actual Spanish settlement.

hints.label: Colonial Temprano
hints.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

nodes.name: Colonial Medio (Argentina, AD 1601–AD 1701)
nodes.title: Colonial Medio (Argentina, AD 1601–AD 1701)
nodes.description: [Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1601–AD 1701] Colonial Medio. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

hints.label: Colonial Medio
hints.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

nodes.name: Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1800)
nodes.title: Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1701–AD 1800] Colonial Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

Bourbon reforms reorganised Spanish administration, and the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776 turned Buenos Aires from a smuggling outpost into a legal port of empire. Cattle hides, mules and silver routed from Potosí drove the economy, while Jesuit expulsion in 1767 broke up the mission system. Creole grievances built here toward the revolutions that followed.

hints.label: Colonial Tardío
hints.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

nodes.name: Republicano (Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861)
nodes.title: Republicano (Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1801–AD 1861] Republicano. Period definition from Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI. — Chiavazza Horacio, 2009.

The decades after Argentina broke with Spain, when the question was not independence but what kind of country would follow. Buenos Aires and the interior provinces fought a long series of civil wars between centralists and federalists, dominated for two decades by the caudillo Juan Manuel de Rosas, and settled only after Rosas fell and the province of Buenos Aires was reconciled with the Confederation. Out of this came the constitutional framework and territorial shape of the modern Argentine state.

hints.label: Republicano
hints.source: Arqueología de una formación urbana. Los registros en una ciudad de desarrollo continuo: Mendoza en el siglo XVI.

nodes.name: Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1350] Alfarero Medio. Period definition from Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina). — Ots María José, 2020.

The centuries when farming villages in the Argentine northwest became fully settled and hierarchical, relying on irrigated maize, llama herding and long-distance exchange across the Andes. This is the era of Ciénaga and Aguada pottery, with its dense feline and shamanic imagery, and of the first substantial stone-built settlements in the valleys of Catamarca and La Rioja.

hints.label: Alfarero Medio
hints.source: Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina).

nodes.name: Tardío-Incaico (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1550)
nodes.title: Tardío-Incaico (Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1550)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1550] Tardío-Incaico. Period definition from Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina). — Ots María José, 2020.

The last pre-Hispanic phase in northwest Argentina, joining the era of local valley chiefdoms with their conquest by the Inca, who made the region the far southern edge of Collasuyu. Inca roads, storehouses, high-altitude shrines and administrative centres were grafted onto existing towns, and the arrangement lasted barely a lifetime before Spanish expeditions arrived.

hints.label: Tardío-Incaico
hints.source: Grabados rupestres, paisaje y prácticas sociales en la cuenca del Río de Las Tunas (Mendoza, Argentina).

nodes.name: Período Colonial (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Período Colonial (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1700] Período Colonial. Period definition from Articulaciones del Corredor Trasandino Meridional: El río Tunuyán en el Valle de Uco Mendoza, Argentina. — Ots María José, 2015.

Spanish towns, encomiendas and Catholic missions were imposed on indigenous societies, with native labour drafted for farming, textile workshops and the mule trade supplying the silver mines of Potosí. Epidemics, warfare and forced relocations dismantled the old valley communities, while African slavery and mixed-descent populations reshaped who lived where. Colonial-era sites often show indigenous cooking pots sitting alongside Spanish majolica and iron.

hints.label: Período Colonial
hints.source: Articulaciones del Corredor Trasandino Meridional: El río Tunuyán en el Valle de Uco Mendoza, Argentina.

nodes.name: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media (Argentina, AD 401–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media (Argentina, AD 401–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 401–AD 1400] Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media. Period definition from Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2013.

The long middle stretch of village farming life in the Argentine Northwest, when maize and quinoa agriculture, llama herding and pottery-making supported permanent settlements in the valleys and puna. Craftwork became strikingly ambitious: bronze and copper metallurgy, elaborate painted and engraved ceramics, and the feline and warrior imagery associated with the Aguada tradition. Communities grew larger and more differentiated, setting the stage for the fortified chiefdoms of later centuries.

hints.label: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Media
hints.source: Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza).

nodes.name: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía (Argentina, AD 1401–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía (Argentina, AD 1401–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1401–AD 1700] Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía. Period definition from Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2013.

The final centuries of indigenous village society in the Argentine Northwest, when dense settlements clustered on defensible hilltops and irrigated terraces climbed the valley slopes. Local chiefdoms with distinctive painted urn styles were absorbed into the Inca empire in the later 1400s, then confronted by Spanish colonists, whose arrival brought decades of resistance in the Calchaquí valleys.

hints.label: Etapa Agro-Alfarera Regional Tardía
hints.source: Caracterización de la frontera suroriental del Tawantinsuyu (sur de San Juan-norte y centro de Mendoza).

nodes.name: Precerámico (Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC)
nodes.title: Precerámico (Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 699 BC–600 BC] Precerámico. Period definition from Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2005.

A catch-all label for communities that had not yet taken up pottery, known instead from stone tools, grinding equipment, hearths and burials. Hunting, foraging and, in some regions, early herding and small-scale cultivation supported these groups, and their camps and rockshelters — some with painted walls — are the main evidence of the deep human past across Argentina.

hints.label: Precerámico
hints.source: Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza).

nodes.name: Agroalfarero Tardío Local (Argentina, AD 1201–AD 1700)
nodes.title: Agroalfarero Tardío Local (Argentina, AD 1201–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1201–AD 1700] Agroalfarero Tardío Local. Period definition from Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2005.

Farming and llama-herding communities in the Andean northwest consolidated into large, densely packed settlements, many perched on defensible hilltops behind walls, a sign of chronic conflict over land and water. Painted urns and bowls, metalwork in bronze, and irrigated terraces mark the local chiefdoms of these centuries. Their independence ended in stages, first under Inca provincial rule and then under Spanish encomienda and forced resettlement.

hints.label: Agroalfarero Tardío Local
hints.source: Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza).

nodes.name: Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local (Argentina, AD 501–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local (Argentina, AD 501–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 501–AD 1200] Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local. Period definition from Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza). — Ots María José, 2005.

Settled villages of farmers and camelid herders produced their own pottery and worked copper and bronze, living in scattered residential compounds beside irrigated fields. Long-distance exchange moved obsidian, shell, metal and hallucinogenic snuffs across the Andes, tying local groups into wider networks. The elaborate iconography of the period — felines, masked figures, trophy heads — shows a shared religious language spreading well beyond any one valley.

hints.label: Agroalfarero Temprano-Medio Local
hints.source: Prospección arqueológica de la Cuenca del Río de las Tunas (Dptos. Tupungato-Tunuyán, Mendoza).

nodes.name: Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 250 BC–AD 450)
nodes.title: Período Alfarero Temprano (Argentina, 250 BC–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 250 BC–AD 450] Período Alfarero Temprano. Period definition from Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.  — Carosio Sebastián, 2020.

Farming hamlets appear with pottery, stone hoes, grinding equipment and pens for llamas, set among field walls and irrigation channels. Households were largely self-sufficient but exchanged obsidian, shell, metal and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia over long distances, laying the agricultural and technological groundwork for the crowded towns of later centuries.

hints.label: Período Alfarero Temprano
hints.source: Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.

nodes.name: Período Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Período Alfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 450–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1500] Período Alfarero Medio. Period definition from Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.  — Carosio Sebastián, 2020.

The centuries when village societies in the northwest grew denser, more hierarchical and more artistically ambitious. This is the era associated with La Aguada imagery — jaguar-faced figures, sacrificed and trophy heads, finely burnished black ceramics and cast bronze — followed by the breakup of that tradition into regional chiefdoms with their own valley identities.

hints.label: Período Alfarero Medio
hints.source: Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.

nodes.name: Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1450–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Período Alfarero Tardío (Argentina, AD 1450–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1450–AD 1600] Período Alfarero Tardío. Period definition from Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.  — Carosio Sebastián, 2020.

Communities consolidated into large agglomerated towns of stone-walled rooms, often perched on defensible spurs above terraced fields, with cemeteries of urns holding infant burials. Painted Santa María and Belén jars, metalwork and evidence of raiding point to competition between valley polities, which were later drawn into the Inca road system and then shattered by the Spanish invasion and the Calchaquí wars.

hints.label: Período Alfarero Tardío
hints.source: Prácticas de manufactura cerámica de las comunidades del centro de Mendoza (Argentina) entre 1500 y 450 años AP.

nodes.name: Expansión Inkaica (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533)
nodes.title: Expansión Inkaica (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533] Expansión Inkaica. Period definition from La presencia inka en el extremo suroriental del Kollasuyo. Investigaciones en las tierras bajas de Mendoza y San Juan y el Valle de Uco -Rca. Argentina-. — Cahiza Pablo Andrés, 2002.

The Inca state pushed south into the valleys of northwest Argentina, absorbing local chiefdoms into the province of Collasuyu. Roads, waystations, storehouses and administrative centres were laid out, high mountain summits received capacocha sacrifices, and populations were resettled as mitmaqkuna to work fields and mines. The whole arrangement lasted barely two generations before Spanish conquest dismantled it.

hints.label: Expansión Inkaica
hints.source: La presencia inka en el extremo suroriental del Kollasuyo. Investigaciones en las tierras bajas de Mendoza y San Juan y el Valle de Uco -Rca. Argentina-.

nodes.name: Dominación Inka (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533)
nodes.title: Dominación Inka (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1533] Dominación Inka. Period definition from Ictioarqueología de las Lagunas de Guanacache (Mendoza, Argentina). Identificación y estacionalidad de captura a partir de análisis de otolitos sagitales. — Cahiza Pablo Andrés, 2003.

The southernmost expansion of the Inca empire, reaching the Andean valleys and the edge of the Cuyo region as part of Collasuyu. Roads, storehouses and garrison-like installations tied scattered local chiefdoms into a tribute system, and metalworkers and farmers were relocated to serve state projects. High-altitude mountain shrines, including capacocha burials on peaks above 6,000 metres, mark the frontier of imperial ritual. Spanish conquest cut the system short within two generations.

hints.label: Dominación Inka
hints.source: Ictioarqueología de las Lagunas de Guanacache (Mendoza, Argentina). Identificación y estacionalidad de captura a partir de análisis de otolitos sagitales.

nodes.name: Período Incaico (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1533)
nodes.title: Período Incaico (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1533)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1533] Período Incaico. Period definition from Sinopsis de investigaciones arqueológicas en el N.O. de la Provincia de Mendoza: Secuencias estratigráficas y cronología absoluta. — Bárcena Joaquín Roberto, 1982.

Under Inca rule the valleys and puna were tied into an imperial network of highways, waystations, farmland and metal production feeding Cuzco. Local Diaguita, Omaguaca and other groups kept their own pottery styles but adopted imperial forms, and some populations were resettled outright. The period closes with the collapse of Inca authority as the Spanish advanced from Peru.

hints.label: Período Incaico
hints.source: Sinopsis de investigaciones arqueológicas en el N.O. de la Provincia de Mendoza: Secuencias estratigráficas y cronología absoluta.

nodes.name: Período Precerámico (Argentina, 5999 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: Período Precerámico (Argentina, 5999 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 5999 BC–AD 1] Período Precerámico. Period definition from Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza. — Bárcena Joaquín Roberto, 1974.

Millennia of hunting and gathering before pottery, from the first peopling of the region through Holocene camelid hunters using caves, rockshelters and open camps. Stone projectile points, grinding tools and vivid rock art record shifting prey and expanding social networks. Towards its end, the taming of llamas and cultivation of highland crops began the slow move to settled village life.

hints.label: Período Precerámico
hints.source: Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza.

nodes.name: Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Período Cerámico (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1–AD 1536] Período Cerámico. Period definition from Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza. — Bárcena Joaquín Roberto, 1974.

Defined by the appearance and spread of fired clay vessels, which accompanied settled farming villages, storage of maize and beans, and camelid herding. Pottery styles, burial urns and metal ornaments allow archaeologists to trace regional traditions right up to the Spanish conquest.

hints.label: Período Cerámico
hints.source: Nuevos testimonios de la presencia humana prehistórica en el noroeste de la provincia de Mendoza.

nodes.name: Período Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Período Agropecuario Tardío (Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1480] Período Agropecuario Tardío. Period definition from Barrio Ramos I: prácticas funerarias en el inicio del período de dominación inca del valle de Uspallata (Mendoza, Argentina). — Durán Víctor, 2018.

Farming and herding communities in the northwest lived in large agglomerated stone settlements, often perched on defensible high ground above terraced and irrigated fields. Regional ceramic styles, extensive bronze metallurgy and burials in painted urns mark the period, along with signs of frequent conflict between neighbouring valley groups. It closes with Inca expansion into the region.

hints.label: Período Agropecuario Tardío
hints.source: Barrio Ramos I: prácticas funerarias en el inicio del período de dominación inca del valle de Uspallata (Mendoza, Argentina).

nodes.name: Período de Dominación Incaica (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1532)
nodes.title: Período de Dominación Incaica (Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1532)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1532] Período de Dominación Incaica. Period definition from Estudios Arqueológicos sobre sus ocupantes prehispánicos. — Durán Víctor, 2011.

The southern reach of Tawantinsuyu, administered through the road system, provincial centres and the resettlement of labourers far from their homelands. The Inca were drawn by metals - copper, silver, gold - and by the region's farmland, and left mountaintop sanctuaries at extraordinary altitudes. Their rule collapsed with the Spanish capture of Atahualpa, leaving local groups to face a new conqueror.

hints.label: Período de Dominación Incaica
hints.source: Estudios Arqueológicos sobre sus ocupantes prehispánicos.

nodes.name: Período Agroalfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 750–AD 1050)
nodes.title: Período Agroalfarero Medio (Argentina, AD 750–AD 1050)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 750–AD 1050] Período Agroalfarero Medio. Period definition from Variabilidad alfarera y procesos ambientales en un sitio de límite cultural. Estilos tecnológicos de la cerámica del río Desaguadero (PA68) (Mendoza, centro-oeste argentino). — Prieto Olavarría Cristina, 2016.

Village farming societies in the northwest valleys grew denser and more hierarchical, with the Aguada tradition setting the tone: finely burnished black pottery incised with feline and dancing-warrior figures, bronze axes and plaques, and imagery hinting at shamanic ritual and hallucinogenic snuff use. Ceremonial precincts and the movement of goods across the Andes point to leaders who drew authority from ritual as much as farmland.

hints.label: Período Agroalfarero Medio
hints.source: Variabilidad alfarera y procesos ambientales en un sitio de límite cultural. Estilos tecnológicos de la cerámica del río Desaguadero (PA68) (Mendoza, centro-oeste argentino).

nodes.name: Período Agroalfarero (Argentina, AD 350–AD 1650)
nodes.title: Período Agroalfarero (Argentina, AD 350–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 350–AD 1650] Período Agroalfarero. Period definition from Resultados preliminares del análisis petrográfico de la cerámica de los períodos agroalfarero medio y tardío del Norte de Mendoza. — Prieto Olavarría Cristina, 2015.

The long era in northwest Argentina when people lived in permanent villages, farmed maize, beans and squash, herded llamas and made pottery. Irrigation canals, terraced fields and stone-walled house compounds spread through the valleys, and copper, bronze and gold metallurgy developed alongside elaborate painted and incised ceramics. It ends with the Inca annexation of the region and the Spanish invasion that followed.

hints.label: Período Agroalfarero
hints.source: Resultados preliminares del análisis petrográfico de la cerámica de los períodos agroalfarero medio y tardío del Norte de Mendoza.

nodes.name: Etapa Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Etapa Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1850] Etapa Hispano-Indígena. Period definition from La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 2004.

The centuries after Spanish forces subdued the Northwest, when indigenous communities were resettled into reducciones, granted as encomiendas and drawn into the labour economy supplying Potosí. Native pottery and building traditions persisted alongside imported glazes, iron tools and Christian ritual, producing a distinctly hybrid material culture. Prolonged resistance in the Calchaquí valleys ended in mass deportations, permanently reshaping the region's population.

hints.label: Etapa Hispano-Indígena
hints.source: La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel

nodes.name: Premapuche (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650)
nodes.title: Premapuche (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650] Premapuche. Period definition from La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 2004.

The generations in northern Patagonia and the Pampas before Mapuche language and culture spread east of the Andes. Local hunting peoples were already being reshaped by two forces arriving from outside: the horse, which transformed mobility and warfare, and the pressure of Spanish colonial settlement to the north.

hints.label: Premapuche
hints.source: La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel

nodes.name: Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche (Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1850)
nodes.title: Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche (Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1850)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1850] Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche. Period definition from La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 2004.

Mapuche groups spread east of the Andes into the Argentine plains and northern Patagonia, absorbing or reshaping earlier local societies in the process known as araucanización. Horses transformed everything: mounted raiding, long-distance cattle droving to Chile, large chiefdoms and a frontier trade in silver, textiles and captives. Archaeological sites from this time mix traditional pottery and stone tools with European glass, metal and horse gear, and the era closed with the Argentine and Chilean military campaigns of the later nineteenth century.

hints.label: Neoaraucanense o Neomapuche
hints.source: La posible significación mágica del arte rupestre en el Atuel

nodes.name: Cultura Agrelo (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100)
nodes.title: Cultura Agrelo (Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 299 BC–AD 100] Cultura Agrelo. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

Early farming and herding communities of the Mendoza valleys, identified by dark incised pottery and by pit dwellings and storage features. Their appearance marks the shift in the region from mobile foraging to settlements combining cultivation, camelid herding and continued hunting.

hints.label: Cultura Agrelo
hints.source: Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante.

nodes.name: Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial (Argentina, AD 100–AD 700)
nodes.title: Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial (Argentina, AD 100–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 100–AD 700] Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

The first centuries of settled village life with pottery: modest clusters of circular houses, agricultural terracing, llama herds and burials accompanied by simple modelled and incised vessels. Exchange networks moving obsidian, metal and coastal shell were already in place, linking the valleys to the puna and the eastern lowlands.

hints.label: Período Cerámico Temprano Inicial
hints.source: Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante.

[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450] Período Cerámico Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología y ambiente natural de los valles del Atuel y Diamante. — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1974.

Dispersed hamlets gave way to dense, walled settlements on defensible ground, surrounded by terraces and irrigated fields. Painted urns, bronze axes and disc-shaped ornaments circulated widely, and the fortified layouts and weapon finds suggest chronic conflict between valley groups in the generations before Inca expansion.

hints.label: Período Cerámico Tardío

nodes.name: Etapa Arcaica (Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 BC)
nodes.title: Etapa Arcaica (Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 6050 BC–2050 BC] Etapa Arcaica. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Hunter-gatherer bands ranged across the puna, valleys and steppe, hunting guanaco and vicuña, gathering wild plants and camping repeatedly in rock shelters whose walls they sometimes painted. Over these millennia the tools grew more specialised and the first steps were taken towards herding camelids and tending useful plants. These slow shifts are what made the later farming villages possible.

hints.label: Etapa Arcaica
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Etapa de proto-productores (Argentina, 2050 BC–350 BC)
nodes.title: Etapa de proto-productores (Argentina, 2050 BC–350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 2050 BC–350 BC] Etapa de proto-productores. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

A long transitional stage in which people still hunted and gathered but increasingly tended plants and managed camelid herds, moving less and storing more. Rock shelters show repeated seasonal occupation, and the first cultivated species and evidence of domesticated llamas appear. It is the slow groundwork for the fully agricultural villages that followed.

hints.label: Etapa de proto-productores
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, 300 BC–AD 250] Etapa de Productores de Alimentos. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The point at which food production, rather than hunting and gathering, became the basis of life: cultivated fields, stored harvests and herded camelids supporting settled communities. Pottery, weaving and permanent dwellings accompany the change, and populations grew denser than ever before.

nodes.name: Etapa Agroalfarera (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1551)
nodes.title: Etapa Agroalfarera (Argentina, AD 1–AD 1551)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1–AD 1551] Etapa Agroalfarera. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The span in which farming and pottery-making defined life across much of what is now Argentina, from early village communities through to the Spanish conquest. Maize, beans and squash agriculture, llama caravans, weaving and metalwork underpinned settlements that grew from scattered hamlets into large, defended towns. It ends abruptly with European invasion, which cut short indigenous political development and reorganised the countryside around encomiendas and missions.

hints.label: Etapa Agroalfarera
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Temprano (Argentina, AD 1–AD 650)
nodes.title: Período Temprano (Argentina, AD 1–AD 650)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1–AD 650] Período Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Farming villages became the normal way of life: people settled in one place, grew maize, beans and squash, herded llamas, made pottery and began working copper and gold. Small clusters of round or rectangular houses spread through the valleys, with grinding stones, carved stone menhirs and the first metal ornaments. The social groundwork for the later valley chiefdoms was laid here.

hints.label: Período Temprano
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Medio (Argentina, AD 650–AD 950)
nodes.title: Período Medio (Argentina, AD 650–AD 950)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 650–AD 950] Período Medio. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.

hints.label: Período Medio
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Tardío (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450] Período Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.label: Período Tardío
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Inca (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551)
nodes.title: Período Inca (Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1551] Período Inca. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Cuzco's armies incorporated the Northwest into Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, roughly a lifetime before the Spanish arrived. Roads, tambos, storage complexes and administrative centres were built, local lords were co-opted, and mitmaqkuna colonists were moved in to work fields and mines. Cuzco-style polychrome pottery and bronze appear in local villages, and mountain summits were turned into shrines.

hints.label: Período Inca
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1875)
nodes.title: Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1875)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1875] Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The colonial and early national economy, when the Argentine interior was tied into long-distance trade: mules and textiles moving north to the mines, hides and later wool moving out through the Atlantic ports. Towns, haciendas, sugar mills and cart roads reorganised the landscape, and imported ceramics, glass and metal goods appear throughout archaeological deposits. It ends as railways and mass immigration transformed the country's economy again.

hints.label: Etapa de Expansión Mercantilista
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650)
nodes.title: Período Hispano-Indígena (Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1551–AD 1650] Período Hispano-Indígena. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The generation after the Spanish arrival, when conquistadors, missionaries and encomenderos imposed themselves on the agricultural communities of the Andean Northwest. Native settlements continued to be lived in, but their rubbish now mixes local pottery with imported glaze, metal blades and European livestock. Epidemics, forced labour and repeated rebellion reshaped populations that the Inca had ruled only decades earlier.

hints.label: Período Hispano-Indígena
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1750)
nodes.title: Período Colonial Tardío (Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1750)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1750] Período Colonial Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

A settled colonial order of estancias, obrajes and mission towns, tied into the long mule and cart routes that linked the Río de la Plata with Upper Peru. Indigenous survivors of earlier wars and resettlements lived as tributaries and labourers, and material culture becomes increasingly hybrid — local earthenware beside imported glazed wares, glass and metal tools.

hints.label: Período Colonial Tardío
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Histórico Institucional Temprano (Argentina, AD 1750–AD 1810)
nodes.title: Período Histórico Institucional Temprano (Argentina, AD 1750–AD 1810)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1750–AD 1810] Período Histórico Institucional Temprano. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

Late colonial decades reshaped by the Bourbon reforms and the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, which turned Buenos Aires into a legal port and drew the interior into wider Atlantic commerce. Jesuit expulsion emptied major mission complexes, while cattle ranching, mule trade and mining supply routes structured rural settlement. Excavated sites from these years are full of imported European tableware, clay pipes and bottle glass among locally made wares.

hints.label: Período Histórico Institucional Temprano
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: Período Histórico Institucional Tardío (Argentina, AD 1810–AD 1875)
nodes.title: Período Histórico Institucional Tardío (Argentina, AD 1810–AD 1875)
nodes.description:
[Mendoza, Argentina, AD 1810–AD 1875] Período Histórico Institucional Tardío. Period definition from Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura — Lagiglia Humberto Antonio, 1997.

The break with Spain, followed by decades of caudillo warfare between Buenos Aires and the interior provinces before a national state was consolidated. Old colonial towns, estancias and mission sites were rebuilt, abandoned or absorbed by new frontier forts and immigrant settlement. Material culture shifts sharply towards mass-produced British ceramics and glass arriving through expanding river and later rail trade.

hints.label: Período Histórico Institucional Tardío
hints.source: Arqueología de cazadores-recolectores cordilleranos de altura

nodes.name: IIe millénaire AEC (Earth, 1999 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.title: IIe millénaire AEC (Earth, 1999 BC–1000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Earth, 1999 BC–1000 BC] IIe millénaire AEC. The Gregorian calendar is used as a reference for dating in years by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects.
The nomenclature used in periods names refers to the Common Era. The dating goes from -1 to +1, year 0 does not exist.
The sub-division in half and quarter of some centuries are dating periods used by some researchers.

Le calendrier Grégorien est utilisé comme référence pour les datations en années par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOPEN.
La nomenclature utilisée pour les noms des périodes fait référence à l'Ere Commune. La datation passe de -1 à +1 l'année 0 n'existe pas.
Les sub-division en moitié et quart de certains siècles sont des périodes de datation utilisés par certains chercheurs. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The great age of Bronze Age palaces and empires: Hammurabi's Babylon, Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs, the Hittites in Anatolia, Mycenaean citadels in Greece and the Shang in the Yellow River valley, all linked by long-distance trade in copper, tin and luxury goods. Writing spread and simplified, with the first alphabets appearing among Semitic workers in the Levant. Around 1200 BC much of this network collapsed within a generation, destroying kingdoms and scripts and clearing space for the smaller iron-using societies that followed.

The Third Dynasty of Ur had collapsed, and its bureaucratic empire gave way to competing Amorite kingdoms at Isin, Larsa and elsewhere, with Sumerian surviving as a scholarly language. In Egypt the Twelfth Dynasty restored strong central rule, colonised Nubia and reorganised the provinces. The Indus cities were losing population and their script and seals fell out of use, while Anatolia became the destination for a booming Assyrian tin and textile trade.

Mari's palace archives, burned when he sacked the city, preserve thousands of letters about diplomacy, prophecy and trade. In Egypt central authority weakened and Hyksos rulers took the Delta, bringing horses and chariots, while Crete's palaces were rebuilt after earthquake and Minoan influence spread through the Aegean.

In China the Zhou court fled east, beginning the long slide into rule by competing states.

This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a general chronology from the Paleolithic to the present day, of a central-western part of continental Europe. The territory covered by this chronology extends from the eastern part of France in the west to Moldavia in the east, and from the south of the UK through southern Germany to Slovenia and central France on a north/south axis.

Rock engravings and painted shelters of these centuries record the animals people now depended on.

Farming communities across France moved beyond the tightly uniform longhouse villages of the first settlers into a patchwork of regional groups with their own pottery and burial customs. Cattle herding, flint mining and long-distance movement of polished stone axes tied these communities together.

In the Aegean this is the age of Europe's first literate, palace-based societies: Minoan Crete with its labyrinthine complexes, frescoes and Linear A script; the marble-figurine cultures of the Cyclades; and the Mycenaean citadels of the mainland with their shaft graves, gold masks and Linear B archives. Long-distance trade carried Aegean pottery and metalwork across the Mediterranean and brought in copper, tin and ivory. The collapse of the palaces around 1200 BC ended writing and centralised rule for centuries, but left the legends that Homer later drew on.

Deliberate deposition of metal in rivers and hoards became a regular practice.

Marqué par le début des grandes invasions, principalement celtiques, il se confond en Europe centrale avec la culture des champs d’urnes. Il commence en Europe occidentale comme en France vers le XIIe siècle av. J.-C. (Wikipédia). Cremation replaced inhumation across much of France as the Urnfield tradition spread from central Europe, leaving large cemeteries of ash-filled pots. Bronze production reached industrial levels, with sheet-metal vessels, leaf-shaped swords and enormous scrap hoards along the Atlantic and Rhône corridors. Hilltop sites were fortified, and by the closing generations the first iron objects appear, leading directly into the Hallstatt Iron Age.

After the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, Greece rebuilt from small, scattered communities — the era once called the Dark Age. Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons, cremation burials and Protogeometric then Geometric pottery mark a new visual language, and by its end the alphabet had been adapted from Phoenician, the first monumental temples were rising, and the polis was taking shape. The climax and collapse of Hallstatt society. Fortified "princely seats" like the Heuneburg, with its Mediterranean-style mudbrick wall, controlled trade in Greek wine, bronze vessels and coral, while nearby mounds held spectacular burials such as the woman of Vix with her huge Greek bronze krater. Long swords gave way to short daggers, and by the end of the phase the centres were abandoned and the La Tène style was taking shape.

The opening phase of the La Tène Iron Age, when a wealthy elite in the Rhine, Moselle and Marne regions buried its dead with two-wheeled chariots, gold neck-rings and imported Etruscan and Greek wine service. Out of contact with those Mediterranean imports came the Early Style of Celtic art, which took palmettes, lotus buds and lion masks and reworked them into the swirling, ambiguous designs seen on the Glauberg and Reinheim finds. The old Hallstatt hillfort centres further west collapsed at about this time, and power shifted north.

The phase of the great Celtic migrations, when war bands from the north moved into the Po valley, the middle Danube and the Balkans; the sack of Rome and the raid on Delphi belong to these generations. Large flat cemeteries of inhumations replace the earlier princely tumuli, with men buried with sword, spear and shield and women with brooches and rings. Metalworkers developed the Waldalgesheim or Vegetal Style, a flowing tendril ornament that spread across Europe with astonishing uniformity.

The middle La Tène, when the long slashing sword hung from an iron chain belt becomes the standard warrior's equipment and cremation begins to replace inhumation over much of the region. Large open settlements and craft centres grew, gold and silver coinage struck in imitation of Macedonian and Roman types came into use, and trade with the Mediterranean intensified. The decorated scabbards of this phase, in the so-called Sword Style, are among the finest Celtic metalwork.

Archaeologists date this phase closely using brooch types and imported wine containers.

Selon Wikipédia: "À sa mort [de Théodose Ier], en 395, l'Empire fut définitivement réparti entre un Occident et un Orient romains. La disparition de l'Empire romain d'Occident est conventionnellement située au moment de l'abdication de l'empereur-usurpateur Romulus Augustule, le 4 septembre 476." (Wikipédia,. Gaul spent five centuries as a set of Roman provinces, and the transformation was thorough: grid-planned cities with forums, amphitheatres and aqueducts, a road network binding the Rhine frontier to the Mediterranean, villa estates exporting grain and wine, and Latin displacing Gaulish speech. Lyon, Arles, Nîmes and Trier became major imperial centres, and Christianity spread through them from the third century on. When central authority collapsed in the west, the bishops, estates and Latin language it left behind became the foundations of Frankish Gaul.

Augustus turned victory in civil war into a durable one-man rule dressed in republican forms, creating the Principate that governed Rome for the next three centuries. Peace at home paid for a rebuilt capital of marble, a professional standing army, new provinces to the Danube and Spain, and the poetry of Virgil, Horace and Ovid. The disaster in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 fixed the empire's northern limit and ended the dream of conquering Germany.

The closing years of Augustus's long reign, when the machinery of one-man rule was settling into routine and the Mediterranean world enjoyed a peace it had not known for a century. Deaths in the imperial family forced the ageing princeps to adopt Tiberius as heir, and the annihilation of three legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 halted expansion beyond the Rhine for good. Augustus's death in AD 14 tested whether the position he had invented could actually be inherited.

nodes.name: Haut-Empire (Roman Empire, AD 15–AD 235)
nodes.title: Haut-Empire (Roman Empire, AD 15–AD 235)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 15–AD 235] Haut-Empire. Il constitue, avec le Bas-Empire, une des deux découpes historiographiques de l'Empire romain telle que vue par les historiens français. Ces termes sont des concepts très usuels, mais leurs limites chronologiques respectives ne sont pas fixées de façon unanime. Elle désigne la première période de l’Empire romain, qui débute en 27 av. J.-C. avec le principat d'Auguste, et inclut le règne idéalisé des Antonins. (Wikipédia). Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The high point of the Principate, from the settled succession of Augustus's heirs through the Antonines and Severans. Frontiers were fixed on the Rhine, Danube and Euphrates, citizenship was gradually extended to the provinces until Caracalla granted it to nearly everyone, and a single currency and legal system let goods and people move from Britain to Syria. This is the Rome of monumental building, long-distance trade and provincial cities, before the political and military crises of the third century.

The Augustan settlement hardened into a hereditary monarchy under the Julio-Claudians, survived the bloody year of four emperors in 69, and continued under the Flavians. Britain was invaded, the Rhine and Danube frontiers were fortified, and Judaea rose in revolt and was crushed. For most inhabitants it meant peace, tax, Roman law and a building boom of forums, baths and theatres from Syria to Spain.

The Julio-Claudian emperors turned Augustus's improvised settlement into a working system: a professional standing army on fixed frontiers, salaried provincial governors, imperial cult temples in every town, and roads and aqueducts built to a common template. Provincial elites bought into Roman citizenship and Latin, and mass-produced goods like Gallic red-gloss tableware and Spanish oil amphorae moved across the whole Mediterranean. The conquest of Britain under Claudius showed the machine still expanding.

The Severan emperors leaned openly on the army, raising pay and courting the legions while the Senate's influence shrank. In 212 Caracalla extended Roman citizenship to almost every free inhabitant of the empire, ending a distinction that had shaped provincial life for centuries. The murder of Severus Alexander in 235 opened the door to fifty years of military anarchy.

nodes.title: Bas-Empire (Roman Empire, AD 236–AD 395)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 236–AD 395] Bas-Empire. Période de l’histoire européenne et méditerranéenne qui commence à la fin du IIIe siècle mais dont le terme est beaucoup plus flou. Elle n’est employée qu’en référence aux pays ayant appartenu au monde romain : les régions d’Europe occidentale, orientale et méridionale, d’Asie et d’Afrique autour du bassin méditerranéen mais se prolonge bien au-delà de la fin de l’Empire romain d’Occident en 476. The reforms of Diocletian and Constantine reshaped Gaul into smaller provinces run by an expanded bureaucracy, with Trier serving as an imperial capital. Cities shrank behind hastily built walls, villas were fortified or abandoned, and Christianity moved from tolerated cult to the religion of the state, leaving bishops as the effective leaders of urban life. By the end of the period Frankish and Visigothic settlers were established inside the frontier.

Fifty years of soldier-emperors, assassinations, debased coinage and frontier breaches nearly destroyed the empire, and for a time separate Gallic and Palmyrene states ruled its edges. Cities across the west threw up hasty defensive walls, often built from the rubble of their own monuments. Aurelian and then Diocletian pulled the pieces back together, dividing rule between four emperors and rebuilding the army, taxation and administration on new, more rigid lines.

The decades when the empire's political stability broke down: soldier-emperors were raised and killed by their own troops, coinage was steadily debased, and pressure mounted on the Rhine, Danube and eastern frontiers. Decius ordered the first empire-wide requirement to sacrifice to the gods, producing the first general persecution of Christians. Towns began to invest in walls, and coin hoards from these years are a common archaeological marker of the insecurity.

nodes.description:
[Parts of central continental western Europe, AD 401–AD 476] Ve siècle apr. J.-C. - Fin Bas-Empire. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, England, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy. This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a general chronology from the Paleolithic to the present day, of a central-western part of continental Europe. It allows to link the relative chronology to the Gregorian calendar.
The territory covered by this chronology extends from the eastern part of France in the west to Moldavia in the east, and from the south of the UK through southern Germany to Slovenia and central France on a north/south axis.

Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie générale du Paléolithique à nos jours, d'une partie centrale-occidentale de l'Europe continentale. Elle permet de rattacher la chronologie relative au calendrier grégorien.
Le territoire recouvert par cette chronologie s'étend de la partie orientale de la France, à l'ouest, jusqu'à la Moldavie à l'est, et du sud du Royaume-Uni en passant par l'Allemagne méridionale jusqu'à la Slovénie et le centre de la France sur un axe nord/sud. The last decades of imperial rule in Gaul, beginning with the Rhine crossing of 406 and the collapse of the northern frontier. Visigoths were settled in Aquitaine in 418, Burgundians on the Rhône, and the emperors' authority came to depend on generals bargaining with these kings; Attila was checked near Chalons in 451. Coin circulation thins out, villas are abandoned, and towns contract inside their walls before the western title lapses in 476.

The last decades of Roman rule in Gaul: after Attila's Huns were checked on the Catalaunian Plains in 451, imperial authority north of the Alps became a fiction maintained by treaties with Visigoths, Burgundians and Franks. Roman landowners and bishops kept the machinery of towns and estates running while generals like Aegidius and Syagrius governed in the emperor's name with no emperor left behind them. Villas contract, cemeteries change, and Christian basilicas become the new focus of urban life.

A thousand years running from the collapse of Roman authority through Merovingian and Carolingian kingdoms to the age of cathedrals, and on into the plague, the Hundred Years' War and recovery under Charles VII and Louis XI. Latin Christianity, feudal lordship and the manorial countryside gave the era its framework, while towns, guilds and universities gradually grew inside it. By its end a recognisably French kingdom, language and royal state had emerged.

The centuries between the collapse of Roman authority and the year 1000, when Frankish kings — first Merovingian, then Carolingian — built kingdoms out of the western provinces. Charlemagne's coronation in 800 revived the idea of a western empire and sponsored a revival of Latin learning and manuscript production in monastic scriptoria. Viking, Muslim and Magyar raids and the break-up of the Carolingian inheritance then shifted real power to counts and castellans, laying the ground for feudal society.

The Roman order in Gaul is gone and the Frankish kings are the new power: Clovis defeated Syagrius at Soissons in 486 and pushed south and east against Alamanni, Burgundians and Visigoths. Burials of this generation are furnished with weapons, belt fittings and brooches in a new Germanic taste, while Gallo-Roman bishops kept churches, Latin and civic memory alive. It is the hinge between the ancient world and Merovingian Gaul.

Justinian tried to put the Roman Empire back together, retaking Africa and Italy, codifying Roman law into a text that would shape European legal systems for a millennium, and building Hagia Sophia. Then plague arrived from the east and killed a vast share of the Mediterranean population, wrecking the effort. In the west the Franks consolidated Gaul, India's Gupta order broke up under Hunnic pressure, and Buddhism reached Japan.

Justinian's reconquest of Italy and Africa proved brittle: plague had emptied the cities, and the Lombards overran much of Italy within a generation. Avars and Turks reshaped the steppe, Byzantium and Persia bled each other in endless war, and the Sui dynasty reunified China after centuries of division. Muhammad was born around 570; Gregory the Great sent missionaries to England in 597.

Byzantium and Sasanian Persia fought a war so exhausting that it hollowed out both; into the gap came the armies of the new Muslim community, taking Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Iran within twenty years of Muhammad's death. A single religion and Arabic administration now stretched from the Nile to the Iranian plateau. In East Asia the Tang dynasty was founded and grew into the era's model empire, while Harsha briefly reunited much of northern India.

Arab armies finished off the Sasanian empire and pressed across North Africa, while civil war among Muslims produced the Sunni-Shi'a split and the Umayyad caliphate at Damascus. Constantinople survived repeated sieges with the help of Greek fire, and the Dome of the Rock announced the new faith in monumental stone. The last stretch of Capetian confidence, when Philip the Fair humiliated the papacy, moved it to Avignon and destroyed the Templars to seize their wealth. Royal lawyers built up an administration and a treasury that treated the kingdom as a state rather than a bundle of lordships. Then came catastrophic harvest failures and famine, and in 1328 the direct male line ran out — opening the succession dispute that led to war with England.

War with England, recurring plague and rural depopulation dominated these generations, yet they also produced a stronger royal state: standing armies, permanent taxation and a crown that emerged from the Hundred Years' War far more powerful than before. Towns rebuilt in flamboyant Gothic, printing arrived in the 1470s, and the marriage politics of the 1490s folded Brittany into the kingdom.

Royal taxation became permanent and standing companies of soldiers appeared, but so did peasant and urban revolts against the cost. Charles V clawed back much of the lost territory before the century closed with a king descending into madness.

The Capetian direct line failed in 1328, bringing the Valois to the throne and giving Edward III of England a pretext to claim it; open war followed from 1337. French armies were shattered at Crécy in 1346 and Calais fell the next year, and in 1348 plague swept up from Marseille through a countryside already weakened by famine and heavy war taxation. Villages emptied, wages and prices lurched, and the confident growth of the previous two centuries came to an abrupt end.

A century that began in crisis: torrential rains brought the Great Famine of 1315–17 to northern Europe, and the Black Death arrived from Central Asia in 1347, killing perhaps a third of Europeans within a few years. England and France began the long dynastic struggle later called the Hundred Years' War, while the popes ruled from Avignon rather than Rome. Elsewhere Mansa Musa's Mali made its legendary pilgrimage to Cairo, the Mongol Yuan grip on China loosened, and Giotto's frescoes signalled a new naturalism in painting.

Europe lived through the aftershocks of the Black Death: labour shortages raised wages and broke old obligations, and revolts swept France, Flanders and England. The papacy split into rival lines in 1378, the Hundred Years' War ground on, and Chaucer wrote in English rather than French or Latin. In Asia the Ming expelled the Mongols from China in 1368 and Timur carved out an empire from Central Asia to Delhi.

The Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Roman Empire in the east and pushed Europeans to seek sea routes around the Muslim world, leading to Columbus's landfall in 1492 and Vasco da Gama's arrival in India in 1498. Spain completed the Reconquista and expelled its Jews, Italy's cities funded the height of the Renaissance, and the Aztec and Inca empires reached their peak just before contact.

A century of dramatic reinvention: Diocletian's reforms and Constantine's rise remade imperial government, the capital shifted east to Constantinople, and Christianity went from illegal to official. Coinage was stabilised, the army restructured, and a vast new bureaucracy grew up around the emperor. It ended badly, with the disastrous defeat at Adrianople in 378 and Gothic groups settled inside the frontiers as armed communities.

The last decades in which one man could rule the whole Roman world. Julian's brief pagan revival failed, the defeat at Adrianople in 378 forced the settlement of Goths inside the frontiers, and Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the state religion while suppressing the old cults. His death in 395 left the east and west under separate courts, a split that proved permanent.

The Greek world emerged from its dark age with an explosion of energy: the alphabet was adopted, cities sent out colonies from Spain to the Black Sea, coinage spread, and the polis became the basic unit of political life. Monumental stone temples, life-size kouros statues and the poetry of Sappho and Homer's written text all belong here, as do the first tyrants and the first experiments in citizen government at Athens. It ends with the Persian invasions, which the Greeks improbably survived.

Between the defeat of the Persian invasion and the death of Demosthenes, the Greek city-states reached their political and artistic peak and then exhausted themselves. Athens built the Parthenon, staged the great tragedies and experimented with direct democracy while fighting Sparta in the Peloponnesian War; Plato and Aristotle founded schools that shaped philosophy for two thousand years. Macedonian victory at Chaeronea ended the independence of the city-states and opened the Hellenistic age.

When Theodosius I died in 395 the empire passed to his two young sons, and the division between east and west became permanent. The western provinces, including the Atlantic edge of Iberia, still functioned as Roman territory with villas, towns and bishops, but the army guarding the Rhine was already stretched thin. Within a decade the frontier would break and the western provinces would begin slipping out of imperial control.

nodes.title: Lithique (Bahamas, 4599 BC–3000 BC)
nodes.description:
[Antilles, 4599 BC–3000 BC] Lithique. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge lithique est marqué par un mode de vie nomade, vivant de chasse et de pêche, sans cultures végétales identifiées, sans utilisation de céramique, et avec une utilisation d’outils en pierre taillés et non polis.
Les sites sont concentrés uniquement dans les Grandes Antilles et à Trinidad.

The Lithic Age is marked by a nomadic lifestyle, living from hunting and fishing, with no identified plant crops, no use of ceramics, and the use of carved and unpolished stone tools.
Sites are concentrated only in the Greater Antilles and Trinidad. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Caribbean archaeologists use this label for the earliest human presence in the islands, when small bands of foragers who made chipped stone blades and used no pottery moved out from the mainland by sea. They lived on shellfish, fish, land crabs and wild plants, leaving thin scatters of flint and shell rather than villages. It marks the moment when island chains that had never seen people were first entered.

[Antilles, 499 BC–AD 1491] Céramique. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge Céramique correspond à l’occupation formative des Antilles par une migration depuis le bassin de l’Orénoque. L’utilisation de la Céramique se développe très fortement, ainsi que l’horticulture. The Ceramic Age corresponds to the formative occupation of the West Indies by a migration from the Orinoco basin. The use of ceramics developed very strongly, as did horticulture. If the first phase concerns only the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico, the following phases concern the whole Caribbean arc. nodes.title: Céramique ancien (Bahamas, 499 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Antilles, 499 BC–AD 400] Céramique ancien. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. Les occupations du Céramique ancien sont caractérisées par une localisation côtière de villages de taille modeste, dont la subsistance se base essentiellement sur la pêche, ainsi que l’horticulture et la chasse d’espèces importées du continent. Les productions matérielles tranchent avec l’âge précédent et son plutôt homogène sur l’aire concernée, en particulier à travers les céramique de type Saladoïde (huecan et cedrosan), la production importante d’éléments de parure en pierres diverses, et un outillage sur coquille de lambi.

The Early Ceramic occupations are characterised by a coastal location of modest-sized villages, whose subsistence is based essentially on fishing, as well as horticulture and the hunting of species imported from the continent. The material production contrasts with the previous age and is rather homogeneous in the area concerned, in particular through Saladoid type ceramics (huecan and cedrosan), the important production of various stone ornaments, and lambi shell tools. Le Céramique moyen montre une évolution essentiellement endogène des pratiques des sociétés amérindiennes. L’appropriation du territoire se fait plus intense, avec un nombre de sites plus importants dont certains plus à l’intérieur des terres. The Middle Ceramic period shows an essentially endogenous evolution of the practices of Amerindian societies. The appropriation of the territory was more intense, with a greater number of sites, some of which were further inland. Ceramics were modified, as was symbolic expression, with the appearance of the three-pointed stick and, probably, the first rock representations. Society became more complex and hierarchical, and specialised sites, including ceremonial centres, were found, particularly in the Greater Antilles. nodes.name: Historique (Bahamas, AD 1492–AD 2050)
nodes.title: Historique (Bahamas, AD 1492–AD 2050)
nodes.description:
[Antilles, AD 1492–AD 2050] Historique. Spatial coverage: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Colombia. L’âge Historique début avec les premiers contacts entre les colons européens et les Amérindiens et se poursuit jusqu’à l’actuel, en passant par la période coloniale. Ces quelques siècles ont vu une révolution démographique, culturelle, environnementale, se dérouler dans cette région du monde, qui, d’un point de vue archéologique, reste encore largement à étudier, afin de s’affronter aux connaissances textuelles très importantes dont nous disposons sur cette période.

The Historical Age begins with the first contacts between the European settlers and the Amerindians and continues until the present day, passing through the colonial period. These few centuries have seen a demographic, cultural and environmental revolution take place in this region of the world, which, from an archaeological point of view, remains largely unstudied, in order to confront the very important textual knowledge that we have on this period. European contact begins here: Columbus's first Atlantic landfall was on a Lucayan island, and within about twenty-five years Spanish slave raiding for labour in Hispaniola's mines and pearl fisheries had emptied the archipelago of its indigenous people. The islands lay largely abandoned until English settlers arrived in the seventeenth century, followed by wreckers, pirates, and Loyalist planters with enslaved Africans after the American Revolution. The archaeology of this span is one of ruined plantations, harbour defences, shipwrecks and colonial towns rather than of continuity with the Lucayan past.

Egypt's Old Kingdom built the Giza pyramids, Sumerian city-states gave way to Sargon's Akkadian empire, the Indus civilisation laid out Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, and writing, bronze metallurgy and long-distance trade in tin, lapis and copper linked them all. Farther west and north, societies without writing raised megalithic tombs and stone circles and began working copper.

Around 2200 BC a phase of drought and instability, often called the 4.2 ka event, coincided with political collapse across several of these regions.

nodes.name: IIIe millénaire AEC – Fin Néolithique (France, 3299 BC–2200 BC)
nodes.title: IIIe millénaire AEC – Fin Néolithique (France, 3299 BC–2200 BC)
nodes.description:
[Parts of central continental western Europe, 3299 BC–2200 BC] IIIe millénaire AEC – Fin Néolithique. Spatial coverage: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, England, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy. This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a general chronology from the Paleolithic to the present day, of a central-western part of continental Europe. It is used to connect the relative chronology to the gregorian calendar.
The territory covered by this chronology extends from the eastern part of France in the west to Moldavia in the east, and from the south of the UK through southern Germany to Slovenia and central France on a north/south axis.

Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie générale du Paléolithique à nos jours, d'une partie centrale-occidentale de l'Europe continentale. Elle est utilisée pour rattachée la chronologie relative au calendrier grégorien.
Le territoire recouvert par cette chronologie s'étend de la partie orientale de la France, à l'ouest, jusqu'à la Moldavie à l'est, et du sud du Royaume-Uni en passant par l'Allemagne méridionale jusqu'à la Slovénie et le centre de la France sur un axe nord/sud. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The closing centuries of the Neolithic, when farming villages spread across the whole country and communities built collective tombs — passage graves, gallery graves and hypogea — in which hundreds of ancestors were laid together. Copper working appears, flint mining and axe production reach an industrial scale, and fortified and ditched enclosures suggest growing competition over land. It ends with the arrival of Bell Beaker pottery, archery equipment and metalwork, the prelude to the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–616 BC)
nodes.title: Rois latins et sabins (Latium, 752 BC–616 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 752 BC–616 BC] Rois latins et sabins. Durant cette première période 4 rois tour à tour Latin et Sabin mettent sur pied les fondations des institutions politiques et religieuses de la ville.
La ville est organisée en **curies**, le **Sénat** et les **comices** deviennent officiels. Les 4 premiers rois sont élus.

During this first period, 4 kings, in turn Latin and Sabine, laid the foundations of the city's political and religious institutions. The city was organised into **curies**, and the **Senate** and **comices** became official. The first 4 kings were elected. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The first four kings of Rome in legend — Romulus the founder, Numa the lawgiver of religion, the warlike Tullus Hostilius and Ancus Marcius — belong to a tradition that Romans themselves told to explain their institutions. Archaeology shows a real village cluster on the hills growing into a town in these centuries, but the named kings and their deeds are later reconstruction rather than record.

nodes.name: Romulus (Latium, 752 BC–714 BC)
nodes.title: Romulus (Latium, 752 BC–714 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 752 BC–714 BC] Romulus. **Romulus** : Petit-fils du roi d'Albe-la-Longue, il fonde Rome et organise l’enlèvement des Sabines, agrandissant ainsi son territoire sur le Quirinal, colline appartenant à l’origine aux Sabins. Régna de -753 à -715 (38 ans).

**Romulus**: Grandson of the king of Alba-Longa, he founded Rome and organised the abduction of the Sabine women, thus extending his territory onto the Quirinal, a hill originally belonging to the Sabines. Reigned from 753 BC to 715 BC (38 years).

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The reign ascribed by tradition to Rome's legendary founder, who was said to have marked out the city's boundary, killed his brother Remus, seized wives from the Sabines and created the Senate and the first legions. No archaeology confirms the man, but early huts on the Palatine and a defensive wall show a real settlement forming at just this time. Romans treated the story as their charter myth, endlessly reworked to explain their institutions and their appetite for absorbing outsiders.

hints.label: Romulus
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Numa Pompilius (Latium, 714 BC–671 BC)
nodes.title: Numa Pompilius (Latium, 714 BC–671 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 714 BC–671 BC] Numa Pompilius. **Numa Pompilius** : roi d’origine sabine, pacifique et religieux, il crée le collège des Pontifes, fait construire le temple de Janus et fixe les fêtes religieuses dans un calendrier de douze mois.
Régna de -715 à -673 (42 ans).

**Reigned from 715 BC to 673 BC (42 years)**. A peaceful and religious king of Sabine origin, he created the College of Pontiffs, built the Temple of Janus and established religious festivals in a twelve-month calendar.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The second of Rome's legendary kings, remembered as the peaceful counterpart to the warlike Romulus. Roman tradition credited him with inventing the city's religious framework: the priestly colleges, the Vestal Virgins who tended the sacred fire, the office of pontifex maximus, and a reformed twelve-month calendar. Whether or not he existed, later Romans used him to explain why their state religion looked the way it did.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Tullus Hostilius (Latium, 671 BC–640 BC)
nodes.title: Tullus Hostilius (Latium, 671 BC–640 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 671 BC–640 BC] Tullus Hostilius. **Tullus Hostilius** : roi romain, guerrier, il organise l’armée, détruit Albe-la-Longue et conquiert tout le Latium.
Régna de -672 à -641 (31 ans).

**Reigned from 672 BC to 641 BC (31 years).** A Roman king and warrior, he organised his army, destroyed Albe-la-Longue and conquered the whole of Lazio.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Rome's legendary third king, remembered as a warrior in contrast to the pious Numa. Tradition credits him with the destruction of Alba Longa — decided, in the story, by the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii triplets — and the transfer of its people to Rome, along with the building of the first senate house, the Curia Hostilia. The tales are later constructions, but they encode how Rome absorbed its Latin neighbours and grew by incorporation.

hints.label: Tullus Hostilius
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Ancus Marcius (Latium, 639 BC–615 BC)
nodes.title: Ancus Marcius (Latium, 639 BC–615 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 639 BC–615 BC] Ancus Marcius. **Ancus Marcius** : roi sabin, petit-fils de Numa Pompilius, il est pacifique et religieux. C’est un bâtisseur : Rome ayant intégré les peuples latins, il fait construire un mur et un pont sur le Tibre, fait fonder **Ostie** vers -640 et favorise l’essor du commerce.
Régna de -640 à -616 (24 ans).

Reigned from 640 BC to 616 BC (24 years). A Sabine king and grandson of Numa Pompilius, he was a peaceful and religious man. He was a builder: as Rome had integrated the Latin peoples, he built a wall and a bridge over the Tiber, founded Ostia around 640 BC and encouraged the growth of trade.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The fourth of Rome's legendary kings, remembered as a builder rather than a conqueror. Tradition credits him with the first bridge over the Tiber, a prison on the Capitoline, the port of Ostia at the river mouth, and the resettlement of defeated Latins on the Aventine — a step that shaped Rome's later habit of absorbing its enemies as citizens. The details come from writers centuries later, so the man is half history, half national myth.
