nodes.title: Rois étrusques (Latium, 615 BC–509 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 615 BC–509 BC] Rois étrusques. Durant cette seconde période, 3 rois étrusques entament une politique de conquête, et la monarchie devient héréditaire.

During this second period, 3 Etruscan kings began a policy of conquest, and the monarchy became hereditary. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Roman tradition assigns the city's last three kings to an Etruscan-influenced line, credited with the great drainage of the Forum, the Circus, the Capitoline temple and the first city walls — the works that turned Rome into a real urban centre. The expulsion of Tarquin the Proud became the founding myth of the Republic and of Roman hostility to monarchy.

nodes.name: Tarquin l'Ancien (Latium, 615 BC–577 BC)
nodes.title: Tarquin l'Ancien (Latium, 615 BC–577 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 615 BC–577 BC] Tarquin l'Ancien. **Tarquin l'Ancien** : roi étrusque, tuteur des enfants d'Ancus Marcius, il est un grand bâtisseur : il embellit Rome en agrandissant ses murailles, en créant le forum , il fait commencer la construction du Capitole, équipe la Ville de la Cloaca Maxima, grand égout qui traverse Rome, et du Circus Maximus, le grand Cirque. Il est cependant assassiné car il veut transmettre son pouvoir à l’un de ses protégés, Servius Tullius, alors que les descendants d’Ancus Martius revendiquent sa succession.
Régna de -616 à -578 (38 ans).

Reigned from 616 BC to 578 BC (38 years). An Etruscan king and tutor to the children of Ancus Marcius, he was a great builder: he embellished Rome by extending its walls, creating the Forum, starting construction of the Capitol, equipping the city with the Cloaca Maxima, the great sewer that runs through Rome, and the Circus Maximus, the great Circus. However, he was assassinated because he wanted to pass on his power to one of his protégés, Servius Tullius, while the descendants of Ancus Martius claimed his succession.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The reign of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the first of Rome's Etruscan kings in the traditional list, remembered for turning a hill settlement into a city: draining the forum valley, laying out the Circus Maximus and beginning the great Capitoline temple. Whether or not the details are historical, they reflect a real period when Etruscan wealth and engineering reshaped early Rome.

nodes.name: Servius Tullius (Latium, 577 BC–533 BC)
nodes.title: Servius Tullius (Latium, 577 BC–533 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 577 BC–533 BC] Servius Tullius. **Servius Tullius** : roi étrusque, c’est un grand administrateur. Il divise le peuple en quatre tribus territoriales et en sept classes en fonction de leur fortune, le cens. Il organise l'armée en centuries et fait construire la muraille de Rome, dite « de Servius Tullius ». Il crée aussi la première Constitution romaine. Il est cependant assassiné par sa propre fille et son gendre.
Régna de -578 à -534 (44 ans).

Reigned from 578 BC to 534 BC (44 years). This Etruscan king was a great administrator. He divided the people into four territorial tribes and seven classes according to their wealth, the cens. He organised the army into centuries and built the walls of Rome, known as the ‘walls of Servius Tullius’. He also created the first Roman Constitution. However, he was assassinated by his own daughter and son-in-law.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The sixth king in Rome's traditional list, remembered as a reformer who reorganised citizens into classes based on wealth rather than birth and created the assembly that voted by centuries. Tradition also credits him with the city's first great defensive wall and the census. Whether or not the man is historical, the institutions attributed to him structured Roman voting and military service for centuries.

nodes.name: Tarquin le Superbe (Latium, 533 BC–508 BC)
nodes.title: Tarquin le Superbe (Latium, 533 BC–508 BC)
nodes.description:
[Latium, 533 BC–508 BC] Tarquin le Superbe. **Tarquin le Superbe** : roi étrusque, fils de Tarquin l’Ancien, il achève l'œuvre de son père en poursuivant sa politique de grands travaux, fait bâtir le temple de Jupiter. Il est cependant guerrier et, son fils étant impliqué dans le viol de Lucrèce, la femme de Tarquin Collatin (neveu du roi), il est renversé, à cause de ses violences, par le peuple. Après vingt-cinq ans de règne, il est exilé et remplacé par deux consuls : Tarquin Collatin et Brutus, l’un de ses proches.
Régna de -534 à -509 (25 ans).

Reigned from 534 BC to 509 BC (25 years). Etruscan king, son of Tarquin the Elder, he completed his father's work by continuing his policy of major works, building the temple of Jupiter. However, he was a warrior and, as his son was involved in the rape of Lucrezia, the wife of Tarquin Collatin (the king's nephew), he was overthrown by the people because of his violence. After reigning for twenty-five years, he was exiled and replaced by two consuls: Tarquin Collatin and Brutus, one of his relatives.

Credit : Chrystelle BERTHON.  . 16/01/2022. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The reign of Tarquinius Superbus, Rome's seventh and last king, cast by later writers as a tyrant who ruled by murder and fear. His overthrow — triggered in legend by his son's rape of Lucretia — ended the monarchy and founded the Republic, and Romans afterwards treated the very word 'king' as a political insult.

nodes.name: Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia (Rome, 508 BC–287 BC)
nodes.title: Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia (Rome, 508 BC–287 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 508 BC–287 BC] Lex Valeria à la Lex Hortensia. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Tite-Live rapporte qu’apres l'expulsion de Tarquin le Superbe deux consuls furent élus par les comices centuriates présidés par le préfet de la Ville, conformément aux commentarii de Servius Tulli. Selon la tradition antique, qui est unanime sur ce point, la premiere loi votée par les comices centuriates sous la présidence d'un consul fut la Lex Valeria de prouocatione, qui interdisait à tout magistrat de faire exécuter ou de faire fouetter un citoyen romain sans lui laisser le droit d'en appeler au peuple“. Comme le dit Cicéron dans le De legibus (Leg. 3, 6), la prouocatio ad populum avait pour róle de limiter le pouvoir de coercitio des magistrats supérieurs, pouvoir qui les autorisait à punir les citoyens qui refusaient de leur obéir. C'est aussi Cicéron qui fait dans le De oratore l’éloge de la prouocatio qu'il qualifie de sauvegarde de la cité et de rempart de la liberté“. 

Titus Livius reports that after the expulsion of Tarquin the Superb, two consuls were elected by the centuriate comices presided over by the prefect of the city, in accordance with the commentarii of Servius Tulli. According to ancient tradition, which is unanimous on this point, the first law passed by the comices centuriates under the presidency of a consul was the **Lex Valeria de prouocatione**, which prohibited any magistrate from executing or whipping a Roman citizen without giving him the right to appeal to the people’. As Cicero says in De legibus (Leg. 3, 6), the purpose of prouocatio ad populum was to limit the coercive power of the higher magistrates, which allowed them to punish citizens who refused to obey them. It was also Cicero who, in his De oratore, praised the prouocatio as a safeguard for the city and a bulwark of freedom. -

Credit : Adalberto Giovannini « Les institutions de la République romaine des origines à la mort d’Auguste ». (2015). nodes.name: Ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–367 BC)
nodes.title: Ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–367 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 508 BC–367 BC] Ère patricienne. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Ère patricienne (-509 -367 AEC)
Durant la période consécutive à la révolution ayant entraîné la chute du dernier roi de Rome, le Sénat et les assemblées ont aussi peu de pouvoirs que sous la Royauté. La devise traditionnelle de la république est **Senatus populusque Romanus (SPQR)**, « le Sénat et le peuple romain ». Elle symbolise l'union consensuelle du Sénat, où siègent les sénateurs (patres) à l'origine les familles de l'élite économique et politique de la cité, et de l'ensemble des citoyens romains, qui par son vote adopte les lois, confère leurs pouvoirs aux magistrats, et consent au versement des impôts et à la levée des armées.

During the period following the revolution that led to the fall of the last king of Rome, the Senate and the Assemblies had as few powers as they did under the monarchy. The traditional motto of the republic is **Senatus populusque Romanus (SPQR)**, ‘the Senate and the Roman people’. It symbolises the consensual union of the Senate, where the senators (patres), originally the families of the city's economic and political elite, sit, and all Roman citizens, who by voting pass laws, confer their powers on magistrates, and consent to the payment of taxes and the raising of armies. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

In the first century and a half of the Republic, the patrician clans monopolised the consulship, the priesthoods and the interpretation of law, while the plebeians organised their own tribunes and assemblies to push back. The long 'Conflict of the Orders' produced the Twelve Tables and a series of concessions, ending when the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 BC forced the consulship open to plebeians. Rome in these years was still a modest central-Italian city fighting its neighbours, and was sacked by the Gauls in 390 BC.

nodes.name: Début de l'ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–500 BC)
nodes.title: Début de l'ère patricienne (Rome, 508 BC–500 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 508 BC–500 BC] Début de l'ère patricienne. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. D'après la tradition, Junius Brutus, le neveu du dernier roi, Tarquin le Superbe, aurait été le fondateur de la République romaine, en 509 av. J.-C., aux côtés de Tarquin Collatin, membre de la famille des Tarquins et mari de Lucrèce, dont le viol par Sextus Tarquin, fils du roi, est l'élément déclencheur de la révolution. La tradition mentionne deux noms supplémentaires : Lucretius Tricipitinus, père de la victime, et Valerius Publicola, dont l'existence est attestée par la découverte d'une inscription sur un bloc de tuf (le lapis Satricanus). Selon les annalistes, Tarquin le Superbe est renversé parce qu'il use de ses pouvoirs pour instituer une tyrannie (il multiplie les exécutions arbitraires) et qu'il gouverne seul sans tenir compte du Sénat. C’est cette atteinte à la souveraineté du Sénat, plutôt qu’une tyrannie intolérable, qui pousse les patriciens - d’avantage que le peuple entier - à chasser le dernier roi. Comme le suggère la légende, cette monarchie historique est probablement très vite remplacée et les changements les plus importants qui ont lieu immédiatement après concernent le responsable de l’exécutif. Le Sénat décide d'élire deux chefs, appelés « préteurs » (les magistrats romains qui deviennent le consulat républicain). Les consuls possèdent les mêmes pouvoirs que le roi, avec deux limitations : chacun a un droit de veto sur les actes de son collègue et le mandat de leur magistrature est limité à une seule année. Ces deux restrictions limitent leur pouvoir et réduisent les risques d'établissement d'une autre tyrannie.

According to tradition, Junius Brutus, the nephew of the last king, Tarquin the Superb, was the founder of the Roman Republic in 509 BC, along with Tarquin Collatin, a member of the Tarquin family and husband of Lucrezia, whose rape by Sextus Tarquin, the king's son, was the catalyst for the revolution. Tradition mentions two more names: Lucretius Tricipitinus, the victim's father, and Valerius Publicola, whose existence is attested by the discovery of an inscription on a block of tufa (lapis Satricanus). According to the annalists, Tarquin the Superb was overthrown because he used his powers to institute a tyranny (he increased the number of arbitrary executions) and ruled alone without taking the Senate into account. It was this infringement of the Senate's sovereignty, rather than an intolerable tyranny, that prompted the patricians - rather than the people as a whole - to oust the last king. As the legend suggests, this historic monarchy was probably replaced very quickly and the most important changes that took place immediately afterwards concerned the head of the executive. The Senate decided to elect two chiefs, known as ‘praetors’ (the Roman magistrates who became the republican consulate). The consuls had the same powers as the king, with two limitations: each had the right to veto the actions of his colleague and their term of office was limited to a single year. These two restrictions limited their power and reduced the risk of another tyranny being established. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The first years after the expulsion of the last king, when Rome replaced monarchy with two annually elected consuls and a Senate dominated by a closed circle of patrician families. Power over priesthoods, law and office was monopolised by that group, and plebeian resentment at debt-bondage and exclusion soon produced the long Conflict of the Orders. The traditions of this moment, from Brutus to the war with Lars Porsenna, were later told as founding legends of Roman liberty.

nodes.name: Fin de l‘ère patricienne (Rome, 374 BC–367 BC)
nodes.title: Fin de l‘ère patricienne (Rome, 374 BC–367 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 374 BC–367 BC] Fin de l‘ère patricienne. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a chronology presenting the institutions and their representatives in the Roman-Byzantine world. From the year of the foundation of Rome by Romulus (the Ab Urbe Condita was defined by the monk Denys the Lesser). Until the fall of Constantinople and the death of Constantin XI Palaeologus, Dragases.

The 3 successive regimes - Monarchy, Republic and Empire - are presented in different periods. These periods are themed according to different criteria: the origin and family of the reigning ruler, the development of the law and changes to the institutions of the regime in place. This chronology is not exhaustive. The annual mandates of the consuls, reigns of less than a year or in chaotic succession are not presented. This chronology is numerical. For technical reasons, some end dates differ from historical dates to give priority to the start date of the following period. The historical dates are indicated in the period descriptions.

The information assembled and presented is taken from the following open sources: Adalberto GIOVANNINI, Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, Library of Congress, Ministère de l'éducation nationale, Wikipedia.

---

Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie qui présente les institutions et leurs représentants dans le monde romain-byzantin. À partir de l'année de la fondation de Rome par Romulus (l'Ab Urbe Condita a été définie par le moine Denys le Petit). Jusqu'au jour de la chute de Constantinople et à la mort de Constantin XI Paléologue, Dragasès.

Les 3 régimes successifs la Monarchie, la République, puis l'Empire sont présentés en différentes périodes.
Ces périodes sont thématiques suivant les différents critères que sont l'origine et la famille du régnant, l’évolution du droit et la modification des institutions du régime en place.
Cette chronologie n'est pas exhaustive. Les mandats annuels des consuls, les règnes de moins d'un an ou dans une succession chaotique ne sont pas présentés.
Cette chronologie est numérique. Pour des raisons techniques, certaines dates de fin son différentes des dates historiques pour donner la priorité de la date à la date de début de la période suivante. Les dates historiques sont indiquées dans les descriptions des périodes.

Les informations assemblées et présentées sont issues des sources ouvertes suivantes : Adalberto GIOVANNINI, Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, Library of Congress, Ministère de l'éducation nationale, Wikipedia. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Years of blocked elections and agitation ended with the Licinio-Sextian laws, which required that one consul each year be a plebeian and capped how much public land any citizen could hold. The patrician monopoly on Rome's highest office was broken, and over the following decades plebeians gained access to the other magistracies and priesthoods. The result was not democracy but a new mixed nobility of office-holding families that would govern the Republic through its conquest of the Mediterranean.

nodes.name: Crises patricio-plébéiennes (Rome, 366 BC–287 BC)
nodes.title: Crises patricio-plébéiennes (Rome, 366 BC–287 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 366 BC–287 BC] Crises patricio-plébéiennes. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. **Guerre des ordres patriciens et plébéiens (-367 à -287 AEC)**
Cette période voit l’émergence de tendances alarmantes pour l'équilibre politique de l’État, tel que le rapprochement continu des tribuns et des sénateurs. Le Sénat commence à donner aux tribuns un réel pouvoir, tel que la reconnaissance officielle de leur droit de veto. Les tribuns se sentent alors redevables au Sénat. Comme les tribuns et les sénateurs se rapprochent de plus en plus, les sénateurs plébéiens sont souvent en mesure de réserver le tribunat aux membres de leurs propres familles. De plus, en 342 av. J.-C., deux lois importantes sont ratifiées : la première rend illégal le fait de cumuler les magistratures, la deuxième impose un délai de dix ans avant la réélection à une même magistrature. Ces deux lois introduisent un nouveau point faible dans le fonctionnement des institutions, qui peut éventuellement être interprété comme l’amorce du déclin de la République et facilite l’avènement de l’Empire.

War between the patrician and plebeian orders (-367 to -287 AEC) This period saw the emergence of alarming trends for the political balance of the state, such as the continued rapprochement of the tribunes and senators. The Senate began to give the tribunes real power, such as the official recognition of their right of veto. The tribunes then felt indebted to the Senate. As tribunes and senators became increasingly close, plebeian senators were often able to reserve the tribune seat for members of their own families. In addition, in 342 BC, two important laws were ratified: the first made it illegal to hold more than one magistracy, and the second imposed a ten-year time limit on re-election to the same magistracy. These two laws introduced a new weakness into the functioning of the institutions, which could be interpreted as the beginning of the decline of the Republic and facilitated the advent of the Empire. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The closing rounds of the struggle between patricians and plebeians, opened by the Licinio-Sextian laws that reserved a consulship for plebeians and capped holdings of public land. Successive measures abolished debt-bondage, opened the priesthoods, and finally, with the Lex Hortensia, made resolutions of the plebeian assembly binding on all Romans. The outcome was not democracy but a merged patrician-plebeian nobility that would govern Rome through its wars of conquest.

nodes.name: Lois licinio-sextiennes (Rome, 366 BC–350 BC)
nodes.title: Lois licinio-sextiennes (Rome, 366 BC–350 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 366 BC–350 BC] Lois licinio-sextiennes. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Les **lois licinio-sextiennes (Leges Liciniae Sextiae)** sont des lois romaines votées en -367 AEC. et qui prennent effet l'année suivante, en -366. Ces lois portent le nom de leurs deux auteurs, les tribuns de la plèbe Caius Licinius Stolon et Lucius Sextius Lateranus.
Elles restaurent définitivement le consulat, dont obligatoirement un des deux magistrats suprêmes doit être plébéien, elles imposent une limitation des possessions de l'ager publicus, et elles comprennent sûrement quelques dispositions pour diminuer les charges pesant sur les débiteurs.

The **Licinio-Sextian Laws (Leges Liciniae Sextiae)** were Roman laws passed in -367 BC and came into effect the following year, -366. These laws were named after their two authors, the tribunes of the plebs Caius Licinius Stolon and Lucius Sextius Lateranus. They definitively restored the consulship, in which one of the two supreme magistrates had to be a plebeian, they imposed a limit on the possessions of the ager publicus, and they certainly included a few provisions to reduce the burdens on debtors. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

After a decade of obstruction by two plebeian tribunes, Rome adopted laws opening the consulship to plebeians, capping the amount of public land any one man could hold, and easing debts. They broke the patrician monopoly on the highest office and set the shape of Republican politics, in which a mixed noble class competed for annual magistracies. The land clauses would be invoked again by the Gracchi two centuries later.

nodes.name: Lex Ogulnia (Rome, 299 BC–287 BC)
nodes.title: Lex Ogulnia (Rome, 299 BC–287 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 299 BC–287 BC] Lex Ogulnia. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Vers un statut politique égal entre plébéiens et patriciens.
La **lex Ogulnia** est une loi romaine adoptée en 300 av. J.-C. qui a ouvert les différents sacerdoces aux plébéiens (aux fonctions religieuses de pontifes et d’augures).  Elle fut une étape importante dans la longue lutte entre les plébéiens (plebs) et les patriciens (patricii) et vit l'abolition d'un des derniers privilèges des patriciens. Elle constitue une étape majeure dans l'élaboration des institutions patricio-plébéiennes de la République romaine.

Towards equal political status for plebeians and patricians. The **lex Ogulnia** was a Roman law passed in 300 BC that opened up the various priesthoods to plebeians (to the religious functions of pontiffs and augurs).  It was an important step in the long struggle between the plebeians (plebs) and the patricians (patricii) and saw the abolition of one of the last privileges of the patricians. It was a major stage in the development of the patricio-plebeian institutions of the Roman Republic. nodes.name: Lex Hortensia à la mort de César (Rome, 286 BC–43 BC)
nodes.title: Lex Hortensia à la mort de César (Rome, 286 BC–43 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 286 BC–43 BC] Lex Hortensia à la mort de César. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Gräce à Polybe, Tite-Live et Cicéron, complétés et parfois corrigés par de nombreux autres auteurs et par des inscriptions, les institutions de la Rome républicaine nous sont bien connues depuis la Lex Hortensia de -287. qui rendit contraignantes pour tous les citoyens les lois promulguées par l'assemblée de la plébe. En dépit de certains changements et de divers désordres survenus à partir du tribunat des Gracchus en -133, les principes généraux qui régissaient la vie politique romaine et la gestion de l'Empire restèrent assez stables jusqu'à la dictature de César et à son assassinat en -44.

Thanks to Polybius, Titus Livius and Cicero, supplemented and sometimes corrected by numerous other authors and inscriptions, the institutions of republican Rome are well known to us from the Lex Hortensia of 287 BC, which made the laws enacted by the assembly of the plebs binding on all citizens. Despite certain changes and various disorders that arose from the Gracchus tribunate in 133 BC onwards, the general principles that governed Roman political life and the management of the Empire remained fairly stable until Caesar's dictatorship and his assassination in 44 BCE.

Credit : Adalberto Giovannini « Les institutions de la République romaine des origines à la mort d’Auguste ». (2015). nodes.name: Institutions patricio-plébéiennes (Rome, 286 BC–133 BC)
nodes.title: Institutions patricio-plébéiennes (Rome, 286 BC–133 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 286 BC–133 BC] Institutions patricio-plébéiennes. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Promulguée en -287, la **Lex Hortensia**, connue également sous l'appellation de lois hortensiennes, est le résultat d'un conflit entre les patriciens et les plébéiens nommé le conflit des ordres.
La plèbe se retire sur le Janicule pour obtenir l’assignation des terres sabines nouvellement conquises. Quintus Hortensius, nommé dictateur et soutenu par Manius Curius Dentatus, promulgue les lois Hortensiennes qui favorisent la plèbe pour qu’elle revienne dans la cité. Elles amnistient et allègent les dettes et donnent aux plébiscites décidés par les concilia plebis force de loi pour le peuple entier (suppression de la ratification sénatoriale traditionnelle, l’auctoritas patrum[réf. Nécessaire]).
Le conseil de la plèbe obtient le droit de faire voter un **plébiscite** ( proclamé ou discuter sur une loi par le peuple sans passer par les autres ordres ).
Gräce à Polybe, Tite-Live et Cicéron, complétés et parfois corrigés par de nombreux autres auteurs et par des inscriptions, les institutions de la Rome républicaine nous sont bien connues depuis la /ex Hortensia de 287 av. J.-C. qui rendit contraignantes pour tous les citoyens les lois promulguées par l'assemblée de la plébe. En dépit de certains changements et de divers désordres survenus à partir du tribunat de Ti. Gracchus en 133 av. J.-C., les principes généraux qui régissaient la vie politique romaine et la gestion de l'Empire restèrent assez stables jusqu'à la dictature de César et à son assassinat en 44.

Promulgated in 287 BC, the **Lex Hortensia**, also known as the Hortensian Laws, was the result of a conflict between the patricians and plebeians known as the Conflict of Orders. The plebs withdrew to the Janiculum to obtain the assignment of the newly conquered Sabine lands. Quintus Hortensius, appointed dictator and supported by Manius Curius Dentatus, promulgated the Hortensian laws, which favoured the plebs to return to the city. They granted amnesty and debt relief and gave the plebiscites decided by the concilia plebis the force of law for the entire people (abolition of the traditional senatorial ratification, the auctoritas patrum [ref. Necessary]). The council of the plebs obtained the right to vote a **plebiscite** (proclaimed or discussed on a law by the people without going through the other orders). Thanks to Polybius, Titus Livius and Cicero, supplemented and sometimes corrected by numerous other authors and inscriptions, the institutions of republican Rome are well known to us from the /ex Hortensia of 287 BC, which made the laws enacted by the assembly of the plebs binding on all citizens. Despite certain changes and various disorders that arose from the time of Ti. Gracchus in 133 BC, the general principles governing Roman political life and the management of the Empire remained fairly stable until Caesar's dictatorship and his assassination in 44.

Credit : Adalberto Giovannini « Les institutions de la République romaine des origines à la mort d’Auguste ». (2015). Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

After the last of the plebeian secessions, decisions of the plebeian assembly became binding on all Romans, formally ending the long struggle between the orders. In practice power settled on a mixed nobility of patrician and rich plebeian families who monopolised the consulship and the Senate. Under this arrangement Rome conquered Italy, defeated Carthage and took over the eastern Mediterranean, until the strains of empire broke into open violence with the Gracchi.

nodes.name: Lois hortensiennes (Lex Hortensia) (Rome, 286 BC–250 BC)
nodes.title: Lois hortensiennes (Lex Hortensia) (Rome, 286 BC–250 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 286 BC–250 BC] Lois hortensiennes (Lex Hortensia). Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. This period is used by the ArkeoGIS and ArkeOpen projects, in the framework of a chronology presenting the institutions and their representatives in the Roman-Byzantine world. From the year of the foundation of Rome by Romulus (the Ab Urbe Condita was defined by the monk Denys the Lesser). Until the fall of Constantinople and the death of Constantin XI Palaeologus, Dragases.

The 3 successive regimes - Monarchy, Republic and Empire - are presented in different periods. These periods are themed according to different criteria: the origin and family of the reigning ruler, the development of the law and changes to the institutions of the regime in place. This chronology is not exhaustive. The annual mandates of the consuls, reigns of less than a year or in chaotic succession are not presented. This chronology is numerical. For technical reasons, some end dates differ from historical dates to give priority to the start date of the following period. The historical dates are indicated in the period descriptions.

The information assembled and presented is taken from the following open sources: Adalberto GIOVANNINI, Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, Library of Congress, Ministère de l'éducation nationale, Wikipedia.

---

Cette période est utilisée par les projets ArkeoGIS et ArkeOpen, dans le cadre d'une chronologie qui présente les institutions et leurs représentants dans le monde romain-byzantin. À partir de l'année de la fondation de Rome par Romulus (l'Ab Urbe Condita a été définie par le moine Denys le Petit). Jusqu'au jour de la chute de Constantinople et à la mort de Constantin XI Paléologue, Dragasès.

Les 3 régimes successifs la Monarchie, la République, puis l'Empire sont présentés en différentes périodes.
Ces périodes sont thématiques suivant les différents critères que sont l'origine et la famille du régnant, l’évolution du droit et la modification des institutions du régime en place.
Cette chronologie n'est pas exhaustive. Les mandats annuels des consuls, les règnes de moins d'un an ou dans une succession chaotique ne sont pas présentés.
Cette chronologie est numérique. Pour des raisons techniques, certaines dates de fin son différentes des dates historiques pour donner la priorité de la date à la date de début de la période suivante. Les dates historiques sont indiquées dans les descriptions des périodes.

Les informations assemblées et présentées sont issues des sources ouvertes suivantes : Adalberto GIOVANNINI, Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, Library of Congress, Ministère de l'éducation nationale, Wikipedia. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A law passed after the plebeians walked out of Rome in protest at debt, making resolutions of the plebeian assembly binding on the whole citizen body without senatorial approval. It closed the long struggle between patricians and plebeians and gave Rome the legislative machinery it would use for the rest of the Republic. In practice the old aristocracy adapted rather than lost power, blending with wealthy plebeian families into a new governing elite.

In the years between the destruction of Carthage and Corinth and the tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus, Rome mastered the Mediterranean and began to be pulled apart by its own success. Plunder and slaves poured in, great estates squeezed out smallholders who were also the army's recruiting pool, and a slave war erupted in Sicily. Gracchus's land bill and his murder in 133 BC opened a century of political violence that would end the Republic.

nodes.name: Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43 BC)
nodes.title: Crise de la République (Rome, 132 BC–43 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 132 BC–43 BC] Crise de la République. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. Rome est devenue la première puissance du bassin méditerranéen, mais les guerres longues et lointaines et les conquêtes sont sources de tensions sociales : le système du paysan-soldat n’est plus adapté, le blé à bas prix qui afflue de Sicile, de Sardaigne, puis d'Afrique ruine les petits propriétaires, les classes populaires s’appauvrissent.
Le clivage patricien/plébéien s’est effacé de la vie politique, mais la classe sénatoriale monopolise le pouvoir politique et la richesse foncière, et s’oppose aux affairistes de l’ordre équestre, négociants, publicains et banquiers enrichis par l’exploitation des provinces.

Rome had become the leading power in the Mediterranean basin, but long and distant wars and conquests were a source of social tension: the peasant-soldier system was no longer appropriate, cheap wheat from Sicily, Sardinia and Africa was ruining small landowners, and the working classes were becoming poorer. The patrician/plebeian divide had disappeared from political life, but the senatorial class monopolised political power and land wealth, and opposed the businessmen of the equestrian order, merchants, publicans and bankers enriched by the exploitation of the provinces.

Credit : Adalberto Giovannini « Les institutions de la République romaine des origines à la mort d’Auguste ». (2015). Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Beginning with the murder of Tiberius Gracchus, Roman politics turned repeatedly to street violence, proscription and civil war as generals with loyal armies—Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar—outgrew the institutions meant to contain them. Land hunger, the demands of Italian allies and slave revolts strained a city-state constitution now governing a Mediterranean empire. The killing of Caesar solved nothing, and the triumvirs' proscriptions of 43 BC closed the era of genuine republican rule.

nodes.name: Tribunats des Gracques (Rome, 132 BC–120 BC)
nodes.title: Tribunats des Gracques (Rome, 132 BC–120 BC)
nodes.description:
[Rome, 132 BC–120 BC] Tribunats des Gracques. Spatial coverage: Ancient Rome, Rome. **Gracques** est le nom donné à deux frères et hommes d'État romains, Tiberius Gracchus et Caius Gracchus, connus pour leur tentative infructueuse de réformer le système social romain durant la deuxième moitié du IIe siècle av. J.-C. : Tiberius en 133 av. J.-C., puis Caius entre 123 et 121.

**Grachicus** is the name given to two brothers and Roman statesmen, Tiberius Gracchus and Caius Gracchus, who were known for their unsuccessful attempts to reform the Roman social system during the second half of the 2nd century BC: Tiberius in 133 BC, then Caius between 123 and 121. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Tiberius and then Gaius Gracchus used the tribunate to push land redistribution, grain subsidies and court reform past a hostile Senate, appealing directly to the popular assembly. Both were killed by their opponents, Tiberius clubbed down on the Capitol and Gaius dying in a bloodbath on the Aventine. Political murder had entered Roman public life, and the split between populares and optimates opened here would run all the way to the civil wars and the end of the Republic.

nodes.name: Nerva (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98)
nodes.title: Nerva (Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 96–AD 98] Nerva. **Règne du 18 septembre 96 au 27 janvier 98 (1 an)**.
Proclamé empereur par le Sénat après le meurtre de Domitien.

**Reigned from 18 September 96 to 27 January 98 (1 year)**.
Proclaimed emperor by the Senate after the murder of Domitian. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An elderly senator raised to the throne after Domitian's assassination, he governed briefly and uneasily, hemmed in by a Praetorian Guard that forced him to hand over Domitian's killers. His lasting act was to adopt the general Trajan as his heir, a choice that steadied the state and gave Rome its succession of "adoptive" emperors. The precedent — merit rather than birth, at least in appearance — shaped nearly a century of comparatively stable rule.

nodes.name: Lucius Aurelius Verus (Roman Empire, AD 161–AD 169)
nodes.title: Lucius Aurelius Verus (Roman Empire, AD 161–AD 169)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 161–AD 169] Lucius Aurelius Verus. **Règne du 7 mars 161 à janvier 169 (~ 7 ans)**.
Fils adoptif et héritier d'Antonin le Pieux. Co-empereur avec Marc Aurèle jusqu'à sa mort.

**Reigned from 7 March 161 to January 169 (~ 7 years)**.
Adopted son and heir of Antoninus the Pious. Co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius until his death. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Adopted alongside Marcus Aurelius, he became Rome's first co-emperor, an experiment in shared rule that would be repeated for centuries. He nominally commanded the long war against Parthia in the east, whose returning armies carried back the devastating Antonine Plague. He died of a stroke while campaigning on the Danube.

[Roman Empire, AD 211–AD 216] Caracalla. **Règne de 198 au 8 avril 217 (~ 19 ans)**.
Coempereur avec **Sévère** depuis 198, avec Sévère et **Geta** de 209 à février 211, avec Geta jusqu'en décembre 211.

**Reigned from 198 to 8 April 217 (~ 19 years)**.
Co-emperor with **Severus** from 198, with Severus and **Geta** from 209 to February 211, with Geta until December 211. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

He came to power alongside his brother Geta and secured it by having him murdered, then bought the army's loyalty with huge pay rises. His Antonine Constitution granted Roman citizenship to nearly every free inhabitant of the empire, ending a distinction that had shaped provincial life for centuries. He also left Rome its most spectacular bath complex, and was cut down by his own soldiers on campaign in the east.

nodes.name: Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère (Orient) (Roman Empire, AD 305–AD 306)
nodes.title: Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère (Orient) (Roman Empire, AD 305–AD 306)
nodes.description:
[Roman Empire, AD 305–AD 306] Constance 1er Chlore (Occident) - Galère (Orient). Constance Chlore : **Règne du 1er mai 305 au 25 juillet 306 (~1 an)**. Adopté en tant que « César » de l'Occident et héritier par Maximien en 293 « Auguste » de l'Occident jusqu'en 306.
Galère : **Règne du 1er mai 305 – mai 311 (~ 6 ans)**. Adopté en tant que « César » de l'Orient et héritier par Dioclétien de 293 à 305 « Auguste » de l'Orient de 305 à 307.

Constantius Chlorus: **Reigned from 1 May 305 to 25 July 306 (~1 year)**. Adopted as ‘Caesar’ of the West and heir by Maximian in 293 ‘Augustus’ of the West until 306.
Galerius: **Reign from 1 May 305 - May 311 (~ 6 years)**. Adopted as ‘Caesar’ of the East and heir by Diocletian from 293 to 305 ‘Augustus’ of the East from 305 to 307. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The tetrarchy's first test: after Diocletian and Maximian stepped down together, power passed to their deputies, who divided the empire between a western and an eastern Augustus. It lasted barely a year. When Constantius died at York in 306 his troops proclaimed his son Constantine, wrecking the orderly succession Diocletian had designed and opening two decades of civil war.

nodes.name: Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient (Byzantine Empire, AD 477–AD 517)
nodes.title: Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient (Byzantine Empire, AD 477–AD 517)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 477–AD 517] Empire byzantin – Empire romain d’Orient. **Empire byzantin - Empire romain d’Orient** : À l'Est, l'Empire romain d'Orient fut confronté aux migrations de nombreux peuples venus d'Asie et d'Europe du Nord. Toutefois, la partie orientale de l'empire n'avait pas connu l'exode qui avait dépeuplé les villes de la partie occidentale et sa prospérité économique lui permit d'acheter la paix. Théodose II (401-450) fortifia les murailles de Constantinople. Elles résistèrent à tous les assauts jusqu'en 1204.
**Antiquité tardive** : Période de l’histoire européenne et méditerranéenne qui commence à la fin du IIIe siècle mais dont le terme est beaucoup plus flou. Elle n’est employée qu’en référence aux pays ayant appartenu au monde romain : les régions d’Europe occidentale, orientale et méridionale, d’Asie et d’Afrique autour du bassin méditerranéen mais se prolonge bien au-delà de la fin de l’Empire romain d’Occident en 476.

**Byzantine Empire - Eastern Roman Empire**: In the east, the Eastern Roman Empire was faced with the migration of many peoples from Asia and Northern Europe. However, the eastern part of the empire had not experienced the exodus that had depopulated the cities of the western part, and its economic prosperity enabled it to buy peace. Theodosius II (401-450) fortified the walls of Constantinople. They withstood all assaults until 1204. **Late Antiquity**: A period in European and Mediterranean history that began at the end of the 3rd century, but for which the term is much more vague. It is only used in reference to countries that once belonged to the Roman world: the regions of Western, Eastern and Southern Europe, Asia and Africa around the Mediterranean basin, but extends well beyond the end of the Western Roman Empire in 476. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

With the western provinces gone, the eastern half of the Roman Empire carried on from Constantinople with its taxes, bureaucracy and Latin legal tradition intact. Emperors such as Anastasius left a full treasury while the church tore itself apart over the nature of Christ, splitting Egypt and Syria from the capital. This was the platform from which Justinian would launch his attempt to reunite the Roman world.

nodes.name: Empire byzantin - Empire romain universel (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 716)
nodes.title: Empire byzantin - Empire romain universel (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 716)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 716] Empire byzantin - Empire romain universel. Justinien est parfois considéré comme le dernier empereur romain, avant que l'Empire byzantin (Empire romain d'Orient) ne commence à se différencier de l'Empire romain dont il est le continuateur direct. Il est le dernier empereur à chercher à rétablir l'unité et l'universalité de l'Empire romain, ce qui l'amène à mener des guerres expansionnistes, principalement en Italie et en Afrique, tout en défendant victorieusement les frontières contre les Perses ou les Slaves. 
Jusqu'à l'avènement d'Héraclius en 610, l'Empire romain d'Orient est la continuation directe de l'Empire romain qu'il tente de reconstituer, guidé dans cette politique par la volonté de retrouver son imperium (« emprise, contrôle, souveraineté ») sur l’Orbis romana (« monde romain »). Toutefois, le fait que l'Empire romain d'Orient règne principalement sur des régions où c'est le grec qui sert de langue commune et qui sont profondément christianisées, en fait un État original combinant structure romaine de l'État, culture hellénique et foi chrétienne.

Justinian is sometimes regarded as the last Roman emperor, before the Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) began to differentiate itself from the Roman Empire, of which he was the direct successor. He was the last emperor to seek to re-establish the unity and universality of the Roman Empire, which led him to wage expansionist wars, mainly in Italy and Africa, while successfully defending the borders against the Persians and Slavs. 
Until the advent of Heraclius in 610, the Eastern Roman Empire was a direct continuation of the Roman Empire, which it attempted to reconstitute, guided in this policy by the desire to regain its imperium (‘hold, control, sovereignty’) over the Orbis romana (‘Roman world’). However, the fact that the Eastern Roman Empire reigned mainly over regions where Greek was the common language and which were deeply Christianised made it an original state combining Roman state structure, Hellenic culture and Christian faith. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Justinian's reconquests briefly restored Roman rule over Italy, North Africa and southern Spain, and his jurists compiled the Corpus Juris Civilis that became the foundation of European law. Hagia Sophia was raised in five years as the largest domed interior in the world. Plague, exhaustion and then the Persian and Arab wars stripped away most of these gains within a century, leaving an empire fighting for survival.

nodes.name: Dynastie Justiniens (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 609)
nodes.title: Dynastie Justiniens (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 609)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 609] Dynastie Justiniens. La dynastie justinienne est une dynastie ayant régné sur l'Empire byzantin de 518 à 610. Fondée par Justin Ier, elle se termine avec Maurice. Les prénoms « Justin », « Justinien » et « Germanus » y sont courants.

The Justinian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 518 to 610. Founded by Justin I, it ended with Maurice. The first names ‘Justin’, ‘Justinian’ and ‘Germanus’ were common. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Justinian I dominates the period: he codified Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots, and reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, at ruinous cost and just before the plague of 541 emptied the treasury and the countryside. His successors, Justin II, Tiberius, and the capable Maurice, struggled to hold Italy against the Lombards and the Balkans against Avars and Slavs while fighting Persia. Maurice's murder by the soldier Phokas opened the crisis that ended the dynasty.

hints.label: Dynastie Justiniens
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Justin Ier (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 526)
nodes.title: Justin Ier (Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 526)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 518–AD 526] Justin Ier. **Règne du 10 juillet 518 au 1er août 527 (9 ans)**.
Général de basse extraction proclamé empereur par acclamation sur proposition du Sénat à la suite de la mort sans héritier d'Anastase Ier. Associa à son trône son neveu Justinien.

**Reigned from 10 July 518 to 1 August 527 (9 years)**. General of low extraction proclaimed emperor by acclamation on the proposal of the Senate following the death of Anastasius I without heir. He associated his nephew Justinian with his throne. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An illiterate Balkan peasant who rose through the palace guard and was acclaimed emperor in his late sixties, Justin ended the Acacian Schism and restored communion between Constantinople and Rome after nearly forty years of rupture. His most consequential act was promoting his nephew Justinian, who effectively ran the government and succeeded him.

nodes.title: Phocas (Byzantine Empire, AD 602–AD 609)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 602–AD 609] Phocas. **Règne du 23 novembre 602 au 5 octobre 610 (7 ans)**.
Soldat dans l'armée des Balkans, usurpateur désigné par ses troupes révoltées.

**Reigned from 23 November 602 to 5 October 610 (7 years)**.
Soldier in the Balkan army, usurper appointed by his revolting troops. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A junior officer raised to the throne by mutinying Danube troops, whose reign began with the murder of Emperor Maurice and ended with his own public dismemberment. The Balkans were abandoned to Slavs and Avars while the Persians overran the eastern provinces, using Maurice's death as their pretext. His overthrow by Heraclius left an empire in crisis that would soon face the Arab conquests.

nodes.name: Dynastie Héraclides (Byzantine Empire, AD 610–AD 694)
nodes.title: Dynastie Héraclides (Byzantine Empire, AD 610–AD 694)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 610–AD 694] Dynastie Héraclides. La dynastie des Héraclides (610 – 711) a vu se succéder six empereurs qui ont régné pendant un siècle, allant du fondateur de la dynastie, Héraclius (610–641), jusqu’au deuxième renversement de Justinien II en 711.

The Heraclian dynasty (610 - 711) was succeeded by six emperors who reigned for a century, from the founder of the dynasty, Heraclius (610-641), to the second overthrow of Justinian II in 711. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Heraclius overthrew Phokas, fought a desperate war that destroyed Sasanian Persia and recovered the True Cross, and then watched the exhausted empire lose Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa to the Arab conquests within a generation. What survived was a smaller, poorer, more militarised state organised around the themes, with Greek replacing Latin as the language of government and Constantinople twice holding off Arab siege. The religious compromises attempted in these years, monothelitism above all, deepened the split with Rome and the eastern churches.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Constantin IV Pogonate (Byzantine Empire, AD 668–AD 684)
nodes.title: Constantin IV Pogonate (Byzantine Empire, AD 668–AD 684)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 668–AD 684] Constantin IV Pogonate. **Règne du 15 septembre 668 au 14 septembre 685 (16 ans)**.
Règne après l'assassinat de son père Constant II, défait l'usurpateur Mézézios en Sicile.

**Reigned from 15 September 668 to 14 September 685 (16 years)**.
Reigns after the assassination of his father Constant II, defeats the usurper Mezezios in Sicily. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Constantinople survived years of Arab attack, and Greek fire, the empire's incendiary secret weapon, made its terrifying debut against enemy fleets. With the eastern threat blunted, the emperor summoned the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which condemned monothelitism and healed the rift with Rome. In the Balkans, though, he was forced to recognise a new Bulgar state south of the Danube.

nodes.name: Anarchie impériale (Byzantine Empire, AD 695–AD 716)
nodes.title: Anarchie impériale (Byzantine Empire, AD 695–AD 716)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 695–AD 716] Anarchie impériale. L’expression « Anarchie impériale » est utilisée en français pour désigner la période de grande instabilité politique à laquelle fut confrontée l’Empire byzantin lorsque plusieurs empereurs se succédèrent sur le trône entre la dynastie des Héraclides et la dynastie des Isauriens entre 695 et 717.

The Twenty Years' Anarchy is a historiographic term used by some modern scholars for the period of acute internal instability in the Byzantine Empire marked by the rapid succession of several emperors to the throne between the first deposition of Justinian II in 695 and the ascent of Leo III the Isaurian to the throne in 717, marking the beginning of the Isaurian dynasty. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Between the overthrow of Justinian II and the rise of Leo III, seven emperors seized and lost the Byzantine throne in barely twenty years, most ending blinded, mutilated or dead. Arab armies exploited the chaos, taking Carthage and raiding deep into Anatolia, and the empire lost North Africa for good. The turmoil ended only when Leo III took power and beat off the great Arab siege of Constantinople in 717-718.

hints.label: Anarchie impériale
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénisé (Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 1203)
nodes.title: Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénisé (Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 1203)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 717–AD 1203] Empire byzantin - Empire romain hellénisé. Cette période s’étend du début du VIIIe siècle jusqu’à la prise de Constantinople par les croisés en 1204 lors de la quatrième croisade. Elle vit une succession de reculs et d’expansions de l’Empire sous cinq dynasties : les Isauriens, les Amoriens, Macédoniens, les Comnènes et les Anges. Durant cette période, seuls les hellénophones des côtes, des grandes villes, de l'Hellade et d'Asie mineure occidentale (Grecs), les romanophones des Balkans (Dalmates, Valaques) et les arménophones d'Asie mineure orientale (Arméniens) se considérèrent encore comme des Romains (en grec Ρωμαίoί ou « Romées »). L'état empire multinational se transforma ainsi en un empire plus homogène ethniquement, tandis que les institutions subirent de profondes transformations pour faire face aux diverses menaces.

This period stretched from the beginning of the 8th century until the capture of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204 during the Fourth Crusade. It saw a succession of retreats and expansions of the Empire under five dynasties: the Isaurians, the Amorians, the Macedonians, the Comnenes and the Angels. During this period, only the Greek-speaking people of the coasts, large cities, Helladia and western Asia Minor (Greeks), the Roman-speaking people of the Balkans (Dalmatians, Vlachs) and the Armenian-speaking people of eastern Asia Minor (Armenians) still considered themselves Romans (in Greek Ρωμαίoί or ‘Romées’). The multinational empire state was thus transformed into a more ethnically homogenous empire, while institutions underwent profound transformations to cope with the various threats. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The empire that emerged from the Arab onslaught was smaller, Greek-speaking and organised around military provinces, its army and administration rebuilt for permanent defence. It fought out the iconoclast controversy over religious images, then under the Macedonian emperors recovered territory in the Balkans and Syria and sent missionaries who brought Slavic peoples into Orthodox Christianity. The schism with Rome in 1054 and the defeat at Manzikert in 1071 opened the way to the Crusades and to the catastrophe of 1204.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 775–AD 780] Léon IV le Khazar. **Règne du 14 septembre 775 au 8 septembre 780 (4 ans)**.
Fils du précédent.

**Reigned from 14 September 775 to 8 September 780 (4 years)**.

Son of an iconoclast emperor and a Khazar princess, Leo IV pursued a milder line on religious images than his father, easing persecution of monks before turning against icon supporters late in his short reign. His early death left his widow Irene as regent for their young son, and it was she who summoned the council that restored icon veneration.

[Byzantine Empire, AD 780–AD 797] Constantin VI. **Règne du 8 septembre 780 au 18 août 797 (17 ans)**.
Fils du précédent et d'Irène l'Athénienne.

**Reigned from 8 September 780 to 18 August 797 (17 years)**.

He came to the throne as a child under the regency of his mother Irene, who in 787 assembled the Second Council of Nicaea and restored the veneration of icons after decades of iconoclasm. His attempt to rule alone ended badly: after military failures and a scandalous second marriage, Irene had him seized and blinded in the same room where he had been born, and took the throne herself.

nodes.name: Dynastie Nicéphoriens (Byzantine Empire, AD 802–AD 812)
nodes.title: Dynastie Nicéphoriens (Byzantine Empire, AD 802–AD 812)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 802–AD 812] Dynastie Nicéphoriens. La dynastie nicéphorienne de l'Empire byzantin a débuté après la déposition de l'impératrice Irène d'Athènes. Le trône de l'Empire byzantin passe à une dynastie relativement éphémère, la dynastie des Niképhores, du nom de son fondateur, Nicéphore Ier . 

The Nikephorian dynasty of the Byzantine Empire began following the deposition of the Empress Irene of Athens. The throne of the Byzantine Empire passed to a relatively short-lived dynasty, the Nikephorian dynasty, named after its founder, Nikephoros I. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Nikephoros I seized power from the empress Irene and set about repairing state finances with unpopular new taxes and land registers, while resettling populations in the Balkans to reassert control there. His campaign against the Bulgar khan Krum ended in ambush and his own death in 811, his skull reportedly made into a drinking cup. His short-lived successors, including Michael I Rangabe, could not stop Krum and the throne passed to Leo the Armenian.

nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 802–AD 811] Nicéphore Ier le Logothète. **Règne du 31 octobre 802 au 26 juillet 811 (8 ans)**.
Usurpateur

**Reigned from 31 October 802 to 26 July 811 (8 years)**. Usurper. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The imperial treasurer who overthrew the empress Irene and set about repairing Byzantine finances with a battery of unpopular new taxes and fiscal controls that chroniclers, mostly monks he had also taxed, remembered as 'vexations'. He resettled populations in the Balkans to rebuild imperial control there and refused to buy peace with the Bulgars. His army was ambushed and annihilated at the Vărbica pass, and Khan Krum had his skull mounted in silver as a drinking cup.

nodes.title: Michel Ier Rhangabé (Byzantine Empire, AD 811–AD 813)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 811–AD 813] Michel Ier Rhangabé. **Règne du 2 octobre 811 au 10 juillet 813 (2 ans)**.
Renverse, avec l'aide des sénateurs, son beau-frère incapable de régner à cause de ses blessures.

**Reigned from 2 October 811 to 10 July 813 (2 years)**. With the help of the senators, overthrew his brother-in-law, who was unable to reign due to his injuries. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A pious, generous emperor raised to the throne after his father-in-law Nikephoros I was killed in battle against the Bulgars, Michael I spent his short reign trying and failing to contain Khan Krum. To win Frankish recognition of Byzantine rights in the Adriatic he acknowledged Charlemagne as basileus — a landmark concession that effectively admitted a second emperor in the West. His army's collapse at Versinikia ended him: he abdicated, was tonsured as a monk, and lived on quietly for decades while Leo V reopened the war on icons.

nodes.name: Dynastie Amoriens (phrygienne) (Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 867)
nodes.title: Dynastie Amoriens (phrygienne) (Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 867)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 867] Dynastie Amoriens (phrygienne). La dynastie amorienne fut fondée par Michel l’Amorien en 820. Elle règnera sur l'Empire byzantin jusqu’à l'assassinat de Michel III par son chambellan Basile le Macédonien en 867.

The Amorian dynasty was founded by Michael the Amorian in 820. It ruled the Byzantine Empire until Michael III was assassinated by his chamberlain Basil the Macedonian in 867. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Three emperors from Amorion in Phrygia presided over the last phase of iconoclasm and its abandonment: in 843 the empress Theodora restored the veneration of images in the ceremony still marked as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Militarily the period was hard, with the loss of Crete to Arab corsairs and the slow Muslim conquest of Sicily, yet Constantinople saw a revival of learning around Leo the Mathematician and dispatched Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs. It ended when Basil the Macedonian murdered his patron Michael III and seized the throne.

hints.label: Dynastie Amoriens (phrygienne)
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Michel II l'Amorien (Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 829)
nodes.title: Michel II l'Amorien (Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 829)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 820–AD 829] Michel II l'Amorien. **Règne du 24 décembre 820 au 2 octobre 829 (9 ans)**.
Général condamné à l'exécution par Léon V, proclamé empereur par les assassins de Léon V et couronné par le patriarche Théodote Ier le même jour.

**Reigned from 24 December 820 to 2 October 829 (9 years)**.
General sentenced to execution by Leo V, proclaimed emperor by Leo V's assassins and crowned by Patriarch Theodotus I on the same day. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A rough-spoken soldier from Amorion who came to the throne by having his former comrade Leo V murdered in the palace chapel, founding a dynasty that lasted three generations. He spent his first years fighting the massive revolt of Thomas the Slav, which besieged Constantinople itself, and could not prevent Arab forces from seizing Crete and beginning the long conquest of Sicily. In religion he kept a moderate iconoclast line, persecuting little but refusing to restore the images.

nodes.name: Théophile (Byzantine Empire, AD 829–AD 842)
nodes.title: Théophile (Byzantine Empire, AD 829–AD 842)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 829–AD 842] Théophile. **Règne du 2 octobre 829 au 20 janvier 842 (12 ans)**.
Fils de Michel II, co-empereur depuis le 12 mai 821.

**Reigned from 2 October 829 to 20 January 842 (12 years)**.
Son of Michael II, co-emperor since 12 May 821. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Theophilos was the last emperor to enforce iconoclasm, banning religious images while presiding over a court famous for its luxury — golden automata, mechanical birds and a roaring lion beside the throne. He fought a grinding war with the Abbasid caliphate that culminated in the sack of Amorion, his family's ancestral city, and he rebuilt Constantinople's walls and founded new palaces. Within a year of his death his widow Theodora restored the icons for good, ending the controversy that had split the church for over a century.

nodes.name: Michel III (Byzantine Empire, AD 842–AD 867)
nodes.title: Michel III (Byzantine Empire, AD 842–AD 867)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 842–AD 867] Michel III. **Règne du 20 janvier 842 au 24 septembre 867 (25 ans)**.
Fils de Théophile, co-empereur depuis le 16 mai 840. Il règne sous la régence de sa mère Théodora jusqu'au 15 mars 856.

**Reigned from 20 January 842 to 24 September 867 (25 years)**.
Son of Theophilos, co-emperor since 16 May 840. Ruled under his mother's regency Theodora until 15 March 856. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Remembered by hostile later historians as 'the Drunkard', Michael presided over a genuine Byzantine revival. Iconoclasm was formally abandoned in 843, the empire went on the offensive against the Arabs, and the missions of Cyril and Methodius carried Slavonic Christianity to Moravia and Bulgaria while Patriarch Photios opened a lasting rift with Rome. He was assassinated in 867 by his favourite Basil the Macedonian, who took the throne and whose dynasty had every reason to blacken his memory.

nodes.name: Dynastie Macédoniens (Byzantine Empire, AD 867–AD 1057)
nodes.title: Dynastie Macédoniens (Byzantine Empire, AD 867–AD 1057)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 867–AD 1057] Dynastie Macédoniens. La dynastie macédonienne régna pendant presque deux siècles à Constantinople, soit de 867 à 1057.
Elle doit son nom à son fondateur, Basile Ier qui naquit dans le thème byzantin de Macédoine (district administratif correspondant à la région d'Andrinople en Thrace). Elle a compté plus de vingt souverains.

The Macedonian dynasty ruled Constantinople for almost two centuries, from 867 to 1057. It owes its name to its founder, Basil I, who was born in the Byzantine theme of Macedonia (an administrative district corresponding to the region of Andrinople in Thrace). It has had more than twenty sovereigns. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Under Basil I's line the empire went on the offensive, retaking Crete, Antioch and much of Syria, and Basil II destroyed the Bulgarian state after decades of campaigning. It was also an age of law and letters, with the Basilika code, encyclopaedic compilations and a revival of classical art known as the Macedonian Renaissance, while missionaries drew the Rus and the Slavs into the Orthodox world. The dynasty's last decades saw the frontier armies neglected and the schism with Rome of 1054, leaving problems that broke out under its successors.

hints.label: Dynastie Macédoniens
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Zoé Porphyrogénète (Byzantine Empire, AD 1028–AD 1050)
nodes.title: Zoé Porphyrogénète (Byzantine Empire, AD 1028–AD 1050)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1028–AD 1050] Zoé Porphyrogénète. **Règne du 11 novembre 1028  à juin 1050 (22 ans)**.
Fille du précédent. Après que Basile II ait tenté sans succès de la marier à l'empereur romain germanique Otton III, Constantin VIII l'oblige à épouser Romain Argyre. A la mort de ce dernier en 1034, elle épouse Michel le Paphlagonien, puis adopte le neveu de celui-ci Michel le Calfat, et épouse enfin Constantin Monomaque en 1042.

**Reigned from 11 November 1028 to June 1050 (22 years)**. Daughter of the previous king. After Basil II tried unsuccessfully to marry her off to the Germanic Roman Emperor Otto III, Constantine VIII forced her to marry Roman Argyre. On his death in 1034, she married Michael the Paphlagonian, then adopted his nephew Michael the Calfat, and finally married Constantine Monomachus in 1042. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Born in the purple chamber as an emperor's daughter, Zoe inherited the Byzantine throne in middle age and passed imperial legitimacy to three successive husbands and an adopted son, none of whom could rule without her. A popular uprising in Constantinople restored her when one of them tried to shut her away in a convent, and she ended up reigning jointly with her sister Theodora. Her reign is famous for court intrigue, lavish spending, and the vivid, gossipy portrait left by the historian Michael Psellos.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Constantin IX Monomaque (Byzantine Empire, AD 1042–AD 1055)
nodes.title: Constantin IX Monomaque (Byzantine Empire, AD 1042–AD 1055)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1042–AD 1055] Constantin IX Monomaque. **Règne du 12 juin 1042 au 11 janvier 1055 (12 ans)**.
Sénateur issu de l'aristocratie byzantine, il est choisi par Zoé comme époux après la chute de Michel le Calfat.

**Reigned from 12 June 1042 to 11 January 1055 (12 years)**.
A senator from the Byzantine aristocracy, he was chosen by Zoe as her husband after the fall of Michael the Calfat. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An emperor of court intrigue, lavish building and learned patronage, who refounded the law school at Constantinople and endowed churches while the army was allowed to decay. In 1054 papal legates and the patriarch exchanged excommunications, the moment conventionally taken as the split between Catholic and Orthodox Christendom. Meanwhile Seljuk Turks began raiding Armenia, the frontier the empire had just annexed and demilitarised.

nodes.title: Théodora Porphyrogénète (Byzantine Empire, AD 1055–AD 1056)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1055–AD 1056] Théodora Porphyrogénète. **Règne du 11 janvier 1055 au 31 août 1056 (1 an)**.
Fille de Constantin VIII.

**Reigned from 11 January 1055 to 31 August 1056 (1 year)**. Daughter of Constantine VIII. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The last ruler of the Macedonian dynasty, an elderly imperial princess who took sole power rather than marry again and governed with a circle of officials of her own choosing. Her brief reign was marked by resistance to the court aristocracy and by the schism between Rome and Constantinople in 1054. Her death without an heir opened the succession crises that led to the disasters of the 1070s.
