nodes.name: Michel VI Bringas (Byzantine Empire, AD 1056–AD 1057)
nodes.title: Michel VI Bringas (Byzantine Empire, AD 1056–AD 1057)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1056–AD 1057] Michel VI Bringas. **Règne du 31 août 1056 au 30 août 1057 (1 an)**.
Issu d'une famille de hauts fonctionnaires, logothète des armées, il est désigné comme le successeur de Théodora. Une rébellion militaire conduite par Isaac Comnène met un terme définitif à la dynastie macédonienne, après quoi l'empereur abdique pour finir ses jours dans un monastère.

**Reign from 31 August 1056 to 30 August 1057 (1 year)**. Born into a family of high-ranking civil servants and a logothete of the armies, he was designated as Theodora's successor. A military rebellion led by Isaac Comnenus put a definitive end to the Macedonian dynasty, after which the emperor abdicated to end his days in a monastery. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An elderly palace treasurer handed the throne by the dying Empress Theodora, Michael VI was the last ruler of the Macedonian line's political settlement and the last chosen by the civil bureaucracy against the army's wishes. He insulted a delegation of generals seeking promotions and rewards, and they proclaimed Isaac Komnenos emperor within months. His forced abdication marked the moment the military aristocracy of Anatolia seized control of the empire's destiny.

hints.label: Michel VI Bringas
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Isaac Ier Comnène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1057–AD 1059)
nodes.title: Isaac Ier Comnène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1057–AD 1059)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1057–AD 1059] Isaac Ier Comnène. **Règne du 1er septembre 1057 au 22 novembre 1059 (2 ans)**.
Commandant de l'armée d'Orient, il prend la tête d'une conspiration de généraux et vainc les troupes de Michel VI. Il est couronné empereur par le patriarche Michel Cérulaire après que celui-ci ait contraint Michel VI à abdiquer.

**Reigned from 1 September 1057 to 22 November 1059 (2 years)**.
As commander of the army of the East, he led a conspiracy of generals and defeated Michael VI's troops. He was crowned emperor by Patriarch Michael Cerularius after the latter had forced Michael VI to abdicate. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A general raised to the purple by a revolt of the Anatolian military aristocracy against the civil bureaucracy of Constantinople, and the first of the Komnenos family to rule. He cut court expenditure, confiscated church and monastic property to refill the treasury, and forced the removal of the overmighty patriarch Michael Keroularios. Ill and politically isolated, he abdicated to a monastery after barely two years, but his family would return to dominate the empire for a century.

hints.label: Isaac Ier Comnène
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Dynastie Doukas (Byzantine Empire, AD 1060–AD 1080)
nodes.title: Dynastie Doukas (Byzantine Empire, AD 1060–AD 1080)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1060–AD 1080] Dynastie Doukas. Les Doukas (en grec, masculin : Δούκας, féminin : Δούκαινα, pluriel : Δούκαι) forment une ou plusieurs familles ayant appartenu à l'aristocratie byzantine. Le nom apparaît dans les textes au IXe siècle, mais son origine est incertaine. Une branche régna sur l'Empire de 1059 à 1081. Le nom devint avec le temps synonyme de noblesse et fut associé à d'autres noms comme celui des Comnène et Doukas d'Épire et de Thessalonique. Les liens de parenté entre les générations sont souvent difficiles à établir ou douteux, de telle sorte qu'il est impossible d'affirmer avec certitude que tous les personnages ayant porté ce nom aient effectivement appartenu à une seule famille.

The Doukas (Greek, masculine: Δούκας, feminine: Δούκαινα, plural: Δούκαι) are one or more families who belonged to the Byzantine aristocracy. The name appears in texts in the ninth century, but its origin is uncertain. One branch ruled the Empire from 1059 to 1081. Over time, the name became synonymous with nobility and was associated with other names such as the Comnenes and Doukas of Epirus and Thessalonica. Intergenerational links are often difficult to establish or doubtful, so it is impossible to say with certainty that all the people who bore this name belonged to a single family. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A short, troubled dynasty of civilian aristocrats whose reduced spending on the army coincided with disaster: in 1071 the emperor Romanos IV was defeated and captured by the Seljuks at Manzikert, and Bari, the last Byzantine city in Italy, fell to the Normans the same year. Under Michael VII the coinage was debased, Anatolia was lost piecemeal to Turkish bands, and rival generals rose in revolt. The crisis ended only with the accession of Alexios I Komnenos.

hints.label: Dynastie Doukas
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Constantin X (Byzantine Empire, AD 1059–AD 1067)
nodes.title: Constantin X (Byzantine Empire, AD 1059–AD 1067)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1059–AD 1067] Constantin X. **Règne du 24 novembre 1059 au 22 mai 1067 (8 ans)**.
Empereur avec son frère Jean Doukas comme César.

**Reigned from 24 November 1059 to 22 May 1067 (8 years)**.
Emperor with his brother John Doukas as Caesar. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A civilian aristocrat who cut military spending and slighted the frontier armies just as Seljuk Turks pressed into Anatolia and Norman adventurers finished off Byzantine Italy. The neglect is usually blamed for the catastrophe that followed at Manzikert a few years after his death.

nodes.name: Romain IV Diogène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1068–AD 1071)
nodes.title: Romain IV Diogène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1068–AD 1071)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1068–AD 1071] Romain IV Diogène. **Règne du 1er janvier 1068 au 24 octobre 1071 (3 ans)**.
Pour prévenir un coup d'état, Eudocie Makrembolitissa, veuve de Constantin X, épouse Romain Diogène qui devient co-empereur avec les enfants mineurs de Constantin X, Michel, Constance et Andronic.

**Reign from 1 January 1068 to 24 October 1071 (3 years)**.
To prevent a coup d'état, Eudocie Makrembolitissa, Constantine X's widow, married Roman Diogenes, who became co-emperor with Constantine X's minor children Michael, Constantius and Andronicus. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A soldier-emperor raised to the throne by marriage, he marched east to halt Seljuk raiding and was defeated and captured at Manzikert in 1071 — a battle lost partly through treachery in his own ranks. Released by the sultan, he was overthrown, blinded and left to die, while the resulting civil wars let Turkish groups settle across Anatolia, permanently shrinking Byzantine power.

hints.label: Romain IV Diogène
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Michel VII Doukas (Byzantine Empire, AD 1071–AD 1078)
nodes.title: Michel VII Doukas (Byzantine Empire, AD 1071–AD 1078)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1071–AD 1078] Michel VII Doukas. **Règne du 24 octobre 1071 au 24 mars 1078 (7 ans)**.
Fils de Constantin X et d'Eudocie Makrembolitissa Déjà co-empereur avec ses frères dès le règne de Constantin X, son règne personnel commence à la chute de Romain Diogène. Il nomme son fils Constantin co-empereur (celui-ci redeviendra à nouveau co-empereur sous Alexis 1er).

**Reigned from 24 October 1071 to 24 March 1078 (7 years)**.
Son of Constantine X and Eudocie Makrembolitissa Already co-emperor with his brothers during the reign of Constantine X, his personal reign began with the fall of Roman Diogenes. He appointed his son Constantine co-emperor (he would become co-emperor again under Alexius I). Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Michael VII took power in the wreckage of Manzikert and presided over the loss of Anatolia, as Turkish warbands settled the interior unopposed and Bari fell to the Normans, ending five centuries of Byzantine rule in Italy. Bookish and dominated by his ministers, he debased the coinage so badly that grain measures shrank and Constantinople nicknamed him "Parapinakes" — "minus a quarter." Revolts on every frontier drove him into a monastery, and his reign is usually taken as the low point from which the Komnenian recovery had to begin.

hints.label: Michel VII Doukas
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Nicéphore III Botaniatès (Byzantine Empire, AD 1078–AD 1081)
nodes.title: Nicéphore III Botaniatès (Byzantine Empire, AD 1078–AD 1081)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1078–AD 1081] Nicéphore III Botaniatès. **Règne du 4 mars 1078 au 4 avril 1081 (3 ans)**.
Chef militaire ayant déjà participé au soulèvement de 1057 contre Michel VI, il se rebelle à nouveau en 1071 face à la dégradation de la situation en Anatolie à la suite de la bataille de Manzikert. Il se fait couronner empereur, contraint Michel Doukas à rentrer dans un monastère, et épouse Marie d'Alanie.

**Reigned from 4 March 1078 to 4 April 1081 (3 years)**.
A military leader who had already taken part in the 1057 uprising against Michael VI, he rebelled again in 1071 in the face of the deteriorating situation in Anatolia following the battle of Manzikert. He was crowned emperor, forced Michael Doukas to return to a monastery and married Mary of Alania. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

An elderly Anatolian general who marched on Constantinople and unseated Michael VII, inheriting an empire hollowed out after Manzikert. He faced constant revolts, bought off Turkish warbands with land and titles, and debased the coinage still further as Norman attacks began in the west. Alexios Komnenos deposed him within three years and packed him off to a monastery, beginning a dynasty that would stabilise the empire.

hints.label: Nicéphore III Botaniatès
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Alexis II Comnène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1180–AD 1183)
nodes.title: Alexis II Comnène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1180–AD 1183)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1180–AD 1183] Alexis II Comnène. **Règne du 24 septembre 1180 à octobre 1183 (3 ans)**.
Fils de Manuel Ier, co-empereur depuis 1171

**Reign from 24 September 1180 to October 1183 (3 years)**.
Son of Manuel I, co-emperor since 1171. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A boy emperor whose brief reign collapsed into factional struggle around his regent mother, the Latin princess Maria of Antioch. Resentment of Western merchants exploded in the 1182 massacre of Constantinople's Italian residents, and his cousin Andronikos seized power and had the child strangled. The murder ended the stable Komnenian succession and began the slide towards 1204.

hints.label: Alexis II Comnène
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Andronic Ier Comnène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1183–AD 1185)
nodes.title: Andronic Ier Comnène (Byzantine Empire, AD 1183–AD 1185)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1183–AD 1185] Andronic Ier Comnène. **Règne de septembre 1183 au 12 septembre 1185 (2 ans)**.
Fils d'Isaac Komnenos, fils d'Alexios Ier. Renverse la régence d'Alexios II en avril 1182, est couronné co-empereur en 1183 et fait assassiner Alexios II peu après.

**Reign from September 1183 to September 12, 1185 (2 years)**.
Son of Isaac Komnenos, a son of Alexios I. Overthrew the regency of Alexios II in April 1182, crowned co-emperor in 1183 and shortly thereafter had Alexios II murdered. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Andronikos I Komnenos seized power as regent for a child emperor and made himself sole ruler amid the massacre of Constantinople's Latin merchants. He terrorised the great landowning families with executions and confiscations while posing as a defender of the provincial poor. When a Norman army sacked Thessalonica, the city turned on him and he was torn apart by a mob — the violent end of the Komnenian dynasty that had held the empire together for a century.

hints.label: Andronic Ier Comnène
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Isaac II Ange (Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1195)
nodes.title: Isaac II Ange (Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1195)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1185–AD 1195] Isaac II Ange. **Règne du 12 septembre 1185 au 8 avril 1195 (9 ans)**.
Arrière-petit-fils d'Alexis Ier. Résiste à l'ordre d'arrestation d'Andronikos Ier, après quoi il est proclamé empereur par le peuple de Constantinople. Capture et tue Andronikos Ier.

**Reign from 12 September 1185 to 8 April 1195 (9 years)**.
Great-grandson of Alexios I. Resisted an order of arrest issued by Andronikos I, after which he was proclaimed emperor by the people of Constantinople. Captured and killed Andronikos I. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Isaac II came to the throne when a Constantinople mob lynched the tyrannical Andronikos I. His reign saw a heavy tax revolt in Bulgaria that succeeded, re-establishing an independent Bulgarian state, and the awkward passage of Frederick Barbarossa's crusading army through Byzantine territory. Blinded and deposed by his own brother, his cause later gave the Fourth Crusade its pretext for turning on Constantinople.

nodes.name: Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée (Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1260)
nodes.title: Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée (Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1260)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1260] Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée. Vestige de l’Empire byzantin ayant résisté à la prise de Constantinople par les croisés en 1204, l’empire de Nicée, le plus étendu des États grecs, occupait, en Asie Mineure occidentale, une large bande de terre s’étendant de la mer Égée à la mer Noire. Si Nicée demeura sa capitale et le siège du patriarcat pendant toute sa brève histoire (1204-1261), les empereurs établirent leur résidence et le siège du gouvernement à Nymphaion (aujourd’hui Kemalpaşa), ville de Lydie, moins exposée aux armées ennemies.
Les historiens modernes reconnaissent la lignée des empereurs de la dynastie des Laskaris, régnant à Nicée, comme les empereurs romains légitimes pendant cette période, car l'Empire nicéen a fini par reprendre Constantinople. Pour d'autres lignées d'empereurs prétendants, voir Liste des empereurs trapézantins et Liste des empereurs thessaliens.

A remnant of the Byzantine Empire that resisted the capture of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204, the Empire of Nicaea, the largest of the Greek states, occupied a wide strip of land in western Asia Minor stretching from the Aegean Sea to the Black Sea. While Nicaea remained its capital and the seat of the patriarchate throughout its brief history (1204-1261), the emperors established their residence and seat of government at Nymphaion (today's Kemalpaşa), a city in Lydia that was less exposed to enemy armies.
Modern historians recognize the line of emperors of the Laskaris dynasty, reigning in Nicaea, as the legitimate Roman emperors during this period because the Nicene Empire eventually retook Constantinople. For other lines of claimant emperors, see List of Trapezuntine emperors and List of Thessalonian emperors. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204 and carved the empire into Latin fiefs, driving the Byzantine court into exile. At Nicaea a rump state rebuilt an army, a treasury and a patriarchate, outmanoeuvred its rivals at Epirus and Trebizond, and cultivated learning at its provincial capital. In 1261 its troops walked into a lightly guarded Constantinople and restored the empire, though it never recovered its former strength.

hints.label: Empire byzantin – Empire de Nicée
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Théodore Ier Lascaris (Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1222)
nodes.title: Théodore Ier Lascaris (Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1222)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1204–AD 1222] Théodore Ier Lascaris. **Règne du 19 mars 1205 à novembre 1222 (16 ans)**.
Gendre d'Alexis III. Époux d'Anna Komnène Angelina, fille d'Alexios III. Organise la résistance contre l'Empire latin à Nicée et est proclamé empereur en 1205 après la bataille d'Adrianople, couronné par le patriarche Michel IV le 6 avril 1208.

**Reigned from 19 March 1205 to November 1222 (16 years)**.
Son-in-law of Alexis III. Husband of Anna Komnene Angelina, a daughter of Alexios III. Organized resistance against the Latin Empire in Nicaea and proclaimed emperor in 1205 after the Battle of Adrianople, crowned by Patriarch Michael IV on 6 April 1208. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

After the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, he gathered Byzantine refugees in western Anatolia and built a functioning state at Nicaea, having himself crowned emperor by a patriarch in exile. He fought off the Latin emperors, the Seljuks of Rum and rival Greek claimants, defeating and killing the sultan in single combat at Antioch on the Meander. The realm he founded became the base from which the Byzantines retook their capital in 1261.

hints.label: Théodore Ier Lascaris
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Jean III Doukas Vatatzès (Byzantine Empire, AD 1222–AD 1254)
nodes.title: Jean III Doukas Vatatzès (Byzantine Empire, AD 1222–AD 1254)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1222–AD 1254] Jean III Doukas Vatatzès. **Règne du 15 décembre 1222 au 3 novembre 1254 (32 ans)**.
Gendre du précédent. Époux d'Irene Laskarina, fille de Théodore I.

**Reigned from 15 December 1222 to 3 November 1254 (32 years)**.
Son-in-law of the former. Husband of Irene Laskarina, a daughter of Theodore I. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Ruling the Empire of Nicaea while Latin crusaders held Constantinople, he expanded into Thrace, Macedonia and the Aegean islands, reducing the Latin emperors to little more than their capital. He is remembered for careful economic management — encouraging farming, limiting luxury imports, filling the treasury — and for founding schools and hospitals. His work made the recapture of Constantinople a few years after his death possible, and the Orthodox Church later venerated him as a saint.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Théodore II Lascaris (Byzantine Empire, AD 1254–AD 1258)
nodes.title: Théodore II Lascaris (Byzantine Empire, AD 1254–AD 1258)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1254–AD 1258] Théodore II Lascaris. **Règne du 3 novembre 1254 au 18 août 1258 (3 ans)**.
Fils du précédent. Fils de Jean III et petit-fils de Théodore Ier, co-empereur depuis environ 1235.

**Reigned from 3 November 1254 to 18 August 1258 (3 years)**.
Son of the previous Emperor. Son of John III and grandson of Theodore I, co-emperor since around 1235. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

Emperor of the exiled Byzantine state at Nicaea, a scholar-ruler who wrote philosophy and promoted men of talent over the great landed families. He held off Bulgarian and Epirote challenges and strengthened the army, but chronic illness and quarrels with the aristocracy dogged his short reign. His death left a child heir, whom Michael Palaiologos pushed aside before recapturing Constantinople.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Jean IV Lascaris (Byzantine Empire, AD 1258–AD 1261)
nodes.title: Jean IV Lascaris (Byzantine Empire, AD 1258–AD 1261)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1258–AD 1261] Jean IV Lascaris. **Règne du 18 août 1258 au 25 décembre 1261 (3 ans)**.
Fils du précédent. Fils et co-empereur de Théodore II.

**Reigned from 18 August 1258 to 25 December 1261 (3 years)**.
Son of the previous. Son and co-emperor of Theodore II. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

A boy emperor of Nicaea who never really ruled: the general Michael Palaiologos made himself co-emperor and monopolised power. After Michael's forces retook Constantinople in 1261, he had the eleven-year-old blinded and shut away in a fortress. The patriarch excommunicated him for it, and the crime shadowed the legitimacy of the Palaiologan dynasty for generations.

hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: Empire byzantin tardif (Byzantine Empire, AD 1261–AD 1453)
nodes.title: Empire byzantin tardif (Byzantine Empire, AD 1261–AD 1453)
nodes.description:
[Byzantine Empire, AD 1261–AD 1453] Empire byzantin tardif. L'Empire byzantin a été gouverné par la dynastie des Paléologues entre 1261 et 1453, depuis la restauration de l'autorité byzantine à Constantinople par l'usurpateur Michel VIII Paléologue après sa reprise à l'Empire latin, fondé après la quatrième croisade (1204), jusqu'à la chute de Constantinople aux mains de l'Empire ottoman. Cette période est connue sous le nom d'Empire byzantin tardif.

The Byzantine Empire was ruled by the Palaiologos dynasty in the period between 1261 and 1453, from the restoration of Byzantine rule to Constantinople by the usurper Michael VIII Palaiologos following its recapture from the Latin Empire, founded after the Fourth Crusade (1204), up to the Fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire. This period is known as the late Byzantine Empire. Period definition from ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment. — ArkeoGIS authors, 2022.

After the recapture of Constantinople from the Latins, the restored empire under the Palaiologos dynasty was a shrunken state hemmed in by Serbs, Venetians and the rising Ottomans, wracked by civil wars and unable to pay for its own defence. Attempts to buy Western aid by submitting to the pope were rejected by most of the clergy and people. Yet these were decades of extraordinary art, learning and theological debate, and scholars fleeing westward carried Greek manuscripts into Italy, feeding the Renaissance.

hints.label: Empire byzantin tardif
hints.source: ArkeOpen chronology periods used in ArkeoGIS, a FAIR platform based on ontology organized spatiotemporal data about archaeology, history and environment.

nodes.name: History (Austria, AD 1–AD 2000)
nodes.title: History (Austria, AD 1–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 1–AD 2000] History. History as opposed to prehistory. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The span in which the region enters the written record, first through Roman authors and inscriptions from the provinces of Noricum, Raetia and Pannonia, then through medieval charters and chronicles. Roman roads, forts and towns gave way to migration-period kingdoms, Carolingian marches, the Babenberg and Habsburg lands, and finally the modern republic. Archaeology here works alongside archives, so sites can often be tied to named people and events.

hints.label: History
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Prehistory (Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1)
nodes.title: Prehistory (Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1)
nodes.description:
[Austria, 300000 BC–AD 1] Prehistory. Prehistory as opposed to history. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Runs from the earliest Palaeolithic occupation of the Danube corridor — including the mammoth hunters who carved the Venus of Willendorf — through Neolithic farming, copper mining in the Alps and the salt-and-iron wealth of the Hallstatt cemetery. Austria's Iron Age communities grew rich controlling Alpine salt and metal routes, and their culture was absorbed into the Roman Empire at the end of the period.

hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 500–AD 1100] Early Middle Ages. Early Medieval period in Austria as used in THANADOS from the end of the Late Roman period until the 11th Century. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The Visigothic kingdom governed the west of Iberia until Muslim armies crossed from North Africa in 711, making the region the Gharb of al-Andalus, with Islamic administration, agriculture and urban life in the south. From the ninth century Christian rulers from the north pushed the frontier back down the Douro and Mondego, repopulating Braga, Porto and Coimbra. The county of Portucale that emerged from this frontier zone became the kingdom of Portugal in the twelfth century.

hints.label: Early Middle Ages
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 822)
nodes.title: Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 822)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 568–AD 822] Avar Period. Period of Avar burials in Austria. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Horse-riding nomads from the Eurasian steppe built a khaganate centred on the Carpathian basin, drawing tribute from Byzantium and pressing Slavic peoples westward into the Alpine lands. Their graves are unmistakable: warriors buried with their mounts, cast bronze belt fittings covered in griffins and tendrils, stirrups and composite bows. Charlemagne's Frankish campaigns from 791 broke the khaganate and plundered its legendary treasure ring, leaving the region open to Frankish and Slavic settlement.

hints.label: Avar Period
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Early Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 630)
nodes.title: Early Avar Period (Austria, AD 568–AD 630)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 568–AD 630] Early Avar Period. Early Avar Period in Austria. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Steppe horsemen from Inner Asia seized the Carpathian Basin after the Lombards left for Italy and built a khaganate that extracted tribute and gold from Constantinople for decades. Their graves are unmistakable: warriors buried with their horses, stirrups, composite bows and pressed gold ornaments, alongside farming Slavic and local populations they dominated. The failed siege of Constantinople in 626 broke Avar prestige and ended the period of expansion.

hints.label: Early Avar Period
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Middle Avar Period (Austria, AD 630–AD 680)
nodes.title: Middle Avar Period (Austria, AD 630–AD 680)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 630–AD 680] Middle Avar Period. Dated after P. Stadler 2010. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

After the failed Avar siege of Constantinople in 626 cut off the flow of Byzantine tribute, burial customs in the Carpathian Basin changed: gold gave way to different ornaments and new metalwork styles, and fresh groups from the eastern steppe appear to have arrived. Graves from this phase are a key argument in the long debate over whether the Avar realm was reinforced by newcomers. It bridges the early Avar khaganate and the later griffin-and-tendril horizon.

hints.label: Middle Avar Period
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Late Avar Period (Austria, AD 680–AD 822)
nodes.title: Late Avar Period (Austria, AD 680–AD 822)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 680–AD 822] Late Avar Period. Dated after P. Stadler 2010. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The Avar khaganate in the Carpathian basin settled into a dense agricultural society, buried with the cast bronze belt sets whose griffin and tendril ornament defines the era. Cemeteries of thousands of graves show a mixed population of steppe descendants and local farmers. Charlemagne's campaigns from 791 destroyed the khaganate's power and looted its treasure, opening the region to Frankish and later Slavic control.

hints.label: Late Avar Period
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Carolingian Era (Austria, AD 751–AD 919)
nodes.title: Carolingian Era (Austria, AD 751–AD 919)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 751–AD 919] Carolingian Era. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

Frankish armies destroyed the Avar khaganate and pushed the frontier down the Danube, organising the conquered lands into marches settled by Bavarian colonists. Bishoprics at Salzburg and Passau took charge of converting the Slavs of Carantania and Pannonia, tying the region to the Latin west rather than Byzantium. Magyar raids from the east wrecked this frontier order in the early tenth century.

hints.label: Carolingian Era
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Merovingian Era (Austria, AD 450–AD 750)
nodes.title: Merovingian Era (Austria, AD 450–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 450–AD 750] Merovingian Era. Time span in which Merovingian period finds occur in grave finds from Austria. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

With Roman authority gone from the Danube provinces, Bavarian and Slavic settlers moved into the valleys and buried their dead in row-grave cemeteries furnished with weapons, brooches and glass beads. Irish and Frankish missionaries such as Rupert and Virgil worked out of Salzburg, and the Agilolfing dukes of Bavaria drew the region into the Frankish orbit. It is the period when the ethnic and religious map of the eastern Alps was redrawn, setting up the later Carolingian conquest of Carantania.

hints.label: Merovingian Era
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Arpadian Age (Austria, AD 890–AD 1250)
nodes.title: Arpadian Age (Austria, AD 890–AD 1250)
nodes.description:
[Austria, AD 890–AD 1250] Arpadian Age. Period definition from THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures — Stefan Eichert, 2022.

The Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin, raided deep into western Europe until crushed at the Lechfeld, then converted to Christianity and built a kingdom under Stephen I. Their descendants ruled a realm of stone churches, royal counties and market towns whose western frontier ran along the Austrian borderlands, a zone of repeated warfare with the German rulers. The dynasty's Mongol catastrophe of 1241 forced a wave of castle-building that reshaped the landscape.

hints.label: Arpadian Age
hints.source: THANADOS - The Anthropological and Archaeological Database of Sepultures

nodes.name: Пре династије Немањића (Serbia, AD 700–AD 1167)
nodes.title: Пре династије Немањића (Serbia, AD 700–AD 1167)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Vlastimirović Dynasty, Vojislavljević Dynasty, Vukanović Dynasty, AD 700–AD 1167] Пре династије Немањића. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Slavic groups settled the Balkan interior after Byzantine control lapsed, organising into župas and small principalities such as Raška, Duklja, Zahumlje and Travunija. Christianisation from the 9th century tied the region to Constantinople and to the Cyrillic literacy spreading from Bulgaria, and the Miroslav Gospel and Duklja's brief kingship under Mihailo mark its high points. Overlordship shifted repeatedly between Byzantium, Bulgaria and Hungary until the rise of the Nemanjići.

nodes.name: Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина (Serbia, AD 1167–AD 1267)
nodes.title: Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина (Serbia, AD 1167–AD 1267)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Serbian Grand Principality, Rascia, Byzantine Empire, AD 1167–AD 1267] Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Stefan Nemanja united the Serbian lands and founded the dynasty that would rule for two centuries, endowing monasteries at Studenica and Hilandar and retiring as a monk. His son Sava secured an autocephalous Serbian church in 1219 and his brother a royal crown in 1217, binding church and monarchy together. The frescoed monastery churches of this era — Mileševa's White Angel, Sopoćani — are among the finest Byzantine-style painting anywhere.

hints.label: Од Стефана Немање до краља Милутина

nodes.name: Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства (Serbia, AD 1267–AD 1371)
nodes.title: Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства (Serbia, AD 1267–AD 1371)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Kingdom of Serbia, Byzantine Empire, AD 1267–AD 1371] Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Milutin pushed the frontier deep into Byzantine Macedonia and spent lavishly on churches, marrying into the imperial family; his successors continued the expansion. Stefan Dušan conquered Albania, Epirus and Thessaly, had himself crowned emperor of Serbs and Greeks in 1346 and issued a famous law code. His empire outgrew its foundations, and after his death in 1355 it fragmented among quarrelling lords — a collapse sealed by the Ottoman victory on the Marica in 1371.

hints.label: Од краља Милутина до распада Српског царства

nodes.name: Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт (Serbia, AD 1371–AD 1459)
nodes.title: Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт (Serbia, AD 1371–AD 1459)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Serbian Empire, Serbian Despotate, Byzantine Empire, AD 1371–AD 1459] Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Regional lords replaced the empire, and Prince Lazar's stand against the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389 — where both rulers died — became the founding tragedy of Serbian memory. Under Stefan Lazarević and Đurađ Branković the Despotate survived as an Ottoman and Hungarian vassal, prospering from the Novo Brdo silver mines and producing a late flowering of literature and art. Belgrade was rebuilt as a capital, then given up; the fall of Smederevo in 1459 extinguished the state.

hints.label: Од распада Српског царства до пада под турску власт

nodes.name: Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1690)
nodes.title: Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1690)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Ottoman Empire, AD 1459–AD 1690] Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

With Smederevo's surrender the Serbian state disappeared and the land became Ottoman provincial territory, its nobility gone, its peasants paying tithe and the child-levy. The Orthodox Church, its Patriarchate at Peć restored in 1557, became the main institution holding a Serbian identity together. Austro-Ottoman wars repeatedly swept the region, and the failed Habsburg advance of 1689–90 ended in reprisals and mass flight northward.

hints.label: Од пада под турску власт до Велике сеобе Срба

nodes.name: Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка (Serbia, AD 1690–AD 1804)
nodes.title: Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка (Serbia, AD 1690–AD 1804)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Ottoman Empire, Habsburg Monarchy, AD 1690–AD 1804] Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Patriarch Arsenije III led tens of thousands of Serbs north into Habsburg territory as Ottoman armies returned, shifting the demographic centre of the nation into what became Vojvodina. There, under imperial privileges, Serbs served as military frontiersmen and developed printing, schools and a merchant class, while the lands under Ottoman rule grew poorer and more violent. Abuses by renegade janissaries at the end of the period pushed the peasantry of the Belgrade Pashalik towards revolt.

hints.label: Од Велике сеобе Срба до Првог српског устанка

nodes.name: Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата (Serbia, AD 1804–AD 1914)
nodes.title: Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата (Serbia, AD 1804–AD 1914)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Principality of Serbia, Kingdom of Serbia, Ottoman Empire, Habsburg Monarchy, Austrian Empire, Austro-Hungarian Empire , AD 1804–AD 1914] Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Karađorđe's 1804 rising and Miloš Obrenović's second uprising won autonomy from the Sultan, and a modern state was assembled — a constitution, ministries, a capital at Belgrade, and the departure of Ottoman garrisons in 1867. Full independence came at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and a kingdom was proclaimed in 1882, though the rival Obrenović and Karađorđević dynasties fought bitterly, ending in the regicide of 1903. Victories in the Balkan Wars doubled Serbia's territory and sharpened the confrontation with Austria-Hungary that led to Sarajevo.

hints.label: Од Првог српског устанка до Првог светског рата

nodes.name: Камено доба (Serbia, 2599999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.title: Камено доба (Serbia, 2599999 BC–3499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, 2599999 BC–3499 BC] Камено доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Neanderthals and then modern humans hunted the Danube valley and Balkan uplands for hundreds of millennia before farming arrived from Anatolia. Along the Iron Gates gorge, the fisher-foragers of Lepenski Vir built trapezoidal houses and carved boulders into fish-faced human figures. Later Starčevo and Vinča farming villages grew into some of Europe's largest, producing distinctive burnished pottery, figurines and inscribed signs, and digging copper ore at Rudna Glava.

nodes.name: Метално доба (Serbia, 3499 BC–AD 150)
nodes.title: Метално доба (Serbia, 3499 BC–AD 150)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, 3499 BC–AD 150] Метално доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Copper, then bronze, then iron reshaped the Balkans: metal wealth concentrated in the hands of chiefs, hillforts appeared, and hoards of bronze weapons and ornaments were buried across the Danube plain. Iron Age tribes — Triballi, Dardanians, Autariatae — were joined after 300 BC by Celtic Scordisci, who founded a settlement at the site of Belgrade. Rome absorbed the whole region by the early 1st century AD, ending local independence and knitting it into a provincial economy.

nodes.name: Енеолит (Serbia, 3499 BC–2199 BC)
nodes.title: Енеолит (Serbia, 3499 BC–2199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Baden Culture, Kostolac Culture, Vučedol Culture, 3499 BC–2199 BC] Енеолит. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Copper metallurgy became routine across the central Balkans, with cast axes and hammer-axes replacing the small ornaments of earlier centuries. The great tell villages of the Vinča world gave way to the Baden, Kostolac and Vučedol cultures, who often chose fortified hilltops and produced boldly incised, encrusted pottery. Kurgan burials and new pastoral practices signal contact with steppe populations moving up the Danube, foreshadowing the Bronze Age.

nodes.name: Бронзано доба (Serbia, 2199 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Бронзано доба (Serbia, 2199 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Urnfield Culture, Vatin Culture, Somogyvár-Vinkovci Culture, Mureș Culture, Cruceni-Belegiš Culture, 2199 BC–1099 BC] Бронзано доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Farming and herding communities along the Danube, Sava and Morava adopted bronze metallurgy, and groups such as the Vatin culture built substantial settlements and buried their dead under mounds. Enormous hoards of bronze axes, sickles and ornaments testify to a region sitting on the trade routes that carried metal and amber between the Aegean, the Carpathians and central Europe. Fortified sites and the growing quantity of weaponry point to increasingly hierarchical, warlike societies.

nodes.name: Гвоздено доба (Serbia, 1099 BC–AD 150)
nodes.title: Гвоздено доба (Serbia, 1099 BC–AD 150)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Bosut Culture, Brnjica Culture, 1099 BC–AD 150] Гвоздено доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Iron replaced bronze for tools and weapons among the hillfort communities of the central Balkans, ancestors of the tribes the Greeks and Romans knew as Triballi, Dardani and Autariatae. Princely burials with imported Greek bronzes and jewellery show elites plugged into Mediterranean trade, and from the 3rd century BC the Celtic Scordisci settled around the mouth of the Sava and struck their own coinage. The era closes with the Roman conquest and the absorption of the region into the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia.

nodes.name: Стари век (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 700)
nodes.title: Стари век (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, 299 BC–AD 700] Стари век. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Celtic Scordisci and Illyrian and Thracian tribes held the Danube and Morava valleys before Roman armies absorbed the area into the empire, founding cities, roads and river fortresses that made it a strategic corridor between Italy and the East. Mining, military recruitment and imperial patronage brought prosperity, and Christianity arrived early enough for local bishops to matter in church councils. The era ends as the Danube defences collapsed and Avar and Slavic groups settled the countryside.

nodes.name: Предримско доба (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 100)
nodes.title: Предримско доба (Serbia, 299 BC–AD 100)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Triballi, Dardani, Autariatae, Scordisci, Moesi, 299 BC–AD 100] Предримско доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Celtic Scordisci settled the Danube–Sava confluence after the failed Balkan invasion of 279 BC, founding Singidunum and minting their own coinage alongside the older Triballi and Dardanian communities. Hillforts, imported Greek wine and Italian bronze vessels show a trading world linked to the Mediterranean. Roman campaigns from the late 1st century BC broke local power and created the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia, bringing roads, legionary camps and Latin.

nodes.name: Римско доба (Serbia, AD 100–AD 700)
nodes.title: Римско доба (Serbia, AD 100–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, Ancient Rome, Byzantine Empire, AD 100–AD 700] Римско доба. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia, ancient Rome. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Roman armies pushed the frontier to the Danube, and the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia became one of the empire's most militarised and productive zones, with legionary bases, silver and lead mines, and paved roads carrying troops toward the east. Sirmium, Viminacium and Naissus grew into major cities, and the region produced a remarkable run of emperors, Constantine the Great among them. Mosaics, tombs painted with Christian imagery and the ruins of Danube fortresses show both the wealth and the anxiety of the later centuries, before Avar and Slavic incursions ended provincial life.

nodes.name: Средњи век (Serbia, AD 700–AD 1459)
nodes.title: Средњи век (Serbia, AD 700–AD 1459)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, AD 700–AD 1459] Средњи век. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Byzantine Empire, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Slavic settlement and gradual conversion to Christianity gave way to competing principalities, then to the Nemanjić dynasty, which built an independent kingdom with its own archbishopric and endowed monasteries such as Studenica and Dečani, whose frescoes rank among the finest in Byzantine art. Under Stefan Dušan the state briefly reached the Aegean before fragmenting after his death. Ottoman pressure grew after the battle on the Kosovo field, and the period ends with the fall of the fortress capital of Smederevo.

nodes.name: Нови век (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1914)
nodes.title: Нови век (Serbia, AD 1459–AD 1914)
nodes.description:
[Serbia, Balkans, AD 1459–AD 1914] Нови век. Spatial coverage: Balkans, Serbia. Period definition from  Cultural Monuments in Serbia Timeline — Mathematical Institute SANU, 2022.

Ottoman rule after the fall of Smederevo turned the Serbian lands into a frontier province, fought over repeatedly by Istanbul and Vienna and drained by migrations north. The Patriarchate of Peć and village life preserved a distinct identity through centuries without a state. From 1804 uprisings won autonomy, then full independence in 1878 and a kingdom that expanded in the Balkan Wars — ambitions that helped ignite a world war.

nodes.name: Iron I / II (Levant, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Iron I / II (Levant, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Levant, 999 BC–899 BC] Iron I / II. Transitional period, usually subsumed within Iron Ib or Iron IIA. Period definition from Levantine Chronology — Ilan Sharon, 2013.

The transitional century when highland villages began to consolidate into territorial polities and coastal and inland centres were rebuilt with fortifications and public buildings. Traditionally the era of Israel's early monarchy, its dating is one of the most fiercely contested problems in Levantine archaeology, with radiocarbon results pulling against the biblical chronology.

nodes.name: Iron III/Persian (Levant, 529 BC–329 BC)
nodes.title: Iron III/Persian (Levant, 529 BC–329 BC)
nodes.description:
[Levant, 529 BC–329 BC] Iron III/Persian. The historical end date (332 BCE) falls within the Persian/Hellenistic transition period. Period definition from Levantine Chronology — Ilan Sharon, 2013.

Achaemenid rule reorganised the Levant into satrapal provinces, with Phoenician cities like Sidon and Tyre prospering as naval and commercial powers and Jerusalem rebuilt on a small scale as the temple city of Yehud. Greek pottery and locally minted silver coins circulate widely, evidence of a coast integrated into Mediterranean trade well before Alexander arrived in 332 BC.

nodes.name: Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 474 BC–329 BC)
nodes.title: Cypro-Classical (Cyprus, 474 BC–329 BC)
nodes.description:
[Cyprus, 474 BC–329 BC] Cypro-Classical. Period definition from Levantine Chronology — Ilan Sharon, 2013.

Under Persian suzerainty the island's kings played Greek and Persian interests against each other, most famously Evagoras I of Salamis, who fought a long war for independence and promoted Greek language and art. Cypriot syllabic writing survived alongside the Greek alphabet and Phoenician, and royal tombs at Salamis were furnished with chariots, horses and Homeric-looking grave goods. The kingdoms ended when Ptolemy I abolished them and absorbed Cyprus into his empire.

nodes.name: Early Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 168–AD 210)
nodes.title: Early Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 168–AD 210)
nodes.description:
[Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 168–AD 210] Early Mithraeum. End of pre-mithraeum phase, start of EM phase determined by inscription YUAG accession # 1935.97, WD QID Q98270560; end of EM and start of MM phase determined by the inscription referring to the rebuilding of a temple to mithras under Antonius Valentinus (CIMRM 1.53; AE 1940.220; PR VII + VIII no. 847, p. 85). Period definition from  Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935 — M. I. Rostovtzeff, 1939.

A small private shrine to Mithras installed in a house in a Roman garrison town, apparently by Palmyrene archers serving in the army—one of the very few mithraea whose whole history can be traced. Its dated reliefs of Mithras slaying the bull, set up by Palmyrene officers, are among the earliest firmly dated Mithraic monuments anywhere. The building was later enlarged and painted, then buried when the city's defences were reinforced, which is why it survives.

hints.label: Early Mithraeum
hints.source: Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935

nodes.name: Middle Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 210–AD 240)
nodes.title: Middle Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 210–AD 240)
nodes.description: [Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 210–AD 240] Middle Mithraeum. End of EM and start of MM phase determined by the inscription referring to the rebuilding of a temple to mithras under Antonius Valentinus (CIMRM 1.53; AE 1940.220; PR VII + VIII no. 847, p. 85). Period definition from  Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935 — M. I. Rostovtzeff, 1939.

hints.label: Middle Mithraeum
hints.source: Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935

nodes.name: Late Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 240–AD 256)
nodes.title: Late Mithraeum (Dura-Europos, AD 240–AD 256)
nodes.description:
[Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 240–AD 256] Late Mithraeum. Date for the destruction of the building determined by the date of Sasanian siege c. 256 CE; Mithraeum went out of use when commandeered for the construction of a defensive embankment along wall street. Period definition from  Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935 — M. I. Rostovtzeff, 1939.

The final rebuilding of the temple of Mithras in a Roman garrison town on the Euphrates, enlarged and richly painted before the city was destroyed by Sasanian attack. Its frescoes show Mithras hunting on horseback and robed magi, and its walls carry graffiti left by soldiers of the Roman army. Buried in the defensive embankment thrown up during the final siege, it survived almost intact for excavators to find in the 1930s.

hints.label: Late Mithraeum
hints.source: Excavations at Dura-Europos, Seventh and eight seasons, 1933-1934, 1934-1935

nodes.name: Brief period of Roman control (Dura-Europos, AD 116–AD 117)
nodes.title: Brief period of Roman control (Dura-Europos, AD 116–AD 117)
nodes.description:
[Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 116–AD 117] Brief period of Roman control. The brief period of Roman control of the site under Trajan is attested by an inscription from a triumphal arch dedicated to Trajan whose remains were excavated outside the walls of Dura--see Preliminary Report 7/8: 128–129, no. 868; Baird also notes: "While historical sources outside Dura are silent on Rome’s intervention at the site under Trajan, a single Greek inscription tells us that it was not a quiet nor unnoticed handover: in 116/17 CE, the inscription records that a man called Alexander (he was also known as Ammaios, it reports), who was the son of one Epinicus, renovated the naos of a temple, as his father had, and that he replaced at his own expense the temple doors, the originals having been taken away by the Romans. So, there was damage to the site (and the seizure of booty) by Roman forces, and the Romans were recorded by name as having desecrated a temple, all within Dura’s Arsacid period; this was an explicit judgement against the Romans" (p. 23). Period definition from  Dura-Europos — Jennifer A. Baird , 2018.

Trajan's Parthian campaign carried Roman armies down the Euphrates and briefly placed the caravan city under Roman command. The occupation collapsed almost immediately: Hadrian abandoned the new eastern conquests on his accession, and the city returned to Parthian hands for another sixty years.

nodes.name: Phase A (Dura-Europos, AD 180–AD 200)
nodes.title: Phase A (Dura-Europos, AD 180–AD 200)
nodes.description: [Dura-Europos, Syria, AD 180–AD 200] Phase A. One of at least two wall painting phases belonging to Mithraeum I; authors note that phases of wall decoration and structural changes to buildings do not always correspond to the same moment of intervention (169, 176). Note 33 to p. 169: "If the final decoration is dated to 209/10, the other two phases are perhaps to be dated to around 200 and 180 CE respectively.". Period definition from Rethinking the Dura-Europos Mithraeum — Lucinda Dirven, 2020.

nodes.name: Middle Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5799 BC–4749 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5799 BC–4749 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 5799 BC–4749 BC] Middle Neolithic Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Farming villages in Thessaly and central Greece grew into tells, occupied so long that the debris of mud-brick houses piled into artificial hills. This is the era of Sesklo, with rectangular houses, red-on-white painted pottery and finely made stone tools, and of the small clay figurines that fill museum cases. The settlements show a settled, prosperous farming society centuries before anything resembling a town appeared in the Aegean.

nodes.name: Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4799 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic I Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4799 BC] Late Neolithic I Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Thessalian villages such as Arapi and Otzaki flourished, producing the painted and black-burnished wares that define the phase, while similar communities spread through Macedonia and southern Greece. Farmers kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs and grew cereals and pulses, living in mudbrick houses on tells. Melian obsidian moved widely, evidence of regular seafaring around the Aegean.

hints.label: Late Neolithic I Greece
hints.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

nodes.name: Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic II Greece (Greece, 4799 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 4799 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic II Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

The era of Dimini in Thessaly, with its concentric enclosure walls and central court, and of the elaborate incised and polychrome wares that bear its name. Settlements were denser and more differentiated than before, and copper and gold objects begin to appear in small numbers. These developments set the stage for the Final Neolithic dispersal of settlement and the start of the Bronze Age.

hints.label: Late Neolithic II Greece
hints.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

nodes.name: Late Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic Greece (Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Villages across Thessaly, Macedonia and the south expanded, some into substantial tell settlements with enclosure ditches and walls, while distinctive regional pottery styles proliferated. Obsidian from Melos and Spondylus shell ornaments circulated over long distances. Copper working and increasingly elaborate figurines point to social changes that would culminate in the Final Neolithic and Bronze Age.

hints.label: Late Neolithic Greece
hints.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

nodes.name: Late Neolithic Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 5299 BC–4499 BC] Late Neolithic Crete. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Crete remained thinly settled, with the long-lived village at Knossos its best-documented community, along with cave sites used for shelter and burial. Pottery turned to dark burnished wares with incised and pattern-burnished decoration. The deep Neolithic mound at Knossos became the foundation on which the Bronze Age palace would later rise.

hints.label: Late Neolithic Crete
hints.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

nodes.name: Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic I Crete (Crete, 5299 BC–4899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crete, 5299 BC–4899 BC] Late Neolithic I Crete. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Occupation on Crete stayed concentrated at a few places, above all the growing settlement mound at Knossos, with caves used episodically elsewhere. Dark burnished pottery with incised and rippled decoration is characteristic. The island's isolation kept its material culture distinct from mainland Greek assemblages.

nodes.name: Late Neolithic Northern Greece (Greece, 5499 BC–3249 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic Northern Greece (Greece, 5499 BC–3249 BC)
nodes.description:
[Northern Greece, 5499 BC–3249 BC] Late Neolithic Northern Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

Farming villages in Thessaly and Macedonia grew into long-lived tells, their mudbrick houses rebuilt on the rubble of earlier ones until settlements like Sesklo and Dimini stood as low mounds above the plain. Potters produced fine painted and burnished wares, and obsidian from Melos and Spondylus-shell ornaments moved along exchange routes reaching deep into the Balkans. It is the phase in which village life in the southern Balkans reached its densest and most settled form, setting the stage for the metal-using societies that followed.

hints.label: Late Neolithic Northern Greece
hints.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece

nodes.name: Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece (Greece, 4499 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.title: Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece (Greece, 4499 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Greece, 4499 BC–2999 BC] Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece. Period definition from The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece — British School at Athens, 2022.

A long transitional stretch between the settled farming villages of the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, when copper and silver working took hold, settlement scattered into caves and small upland sites, and seafaring links across the Aegean grew stronger. Burial and craft practices become more varied, and some communities began to show clearer differences in wealth. It is the seedbed of the Early Bronze Age societies of the mainland and islands.

hints.label: Final Neolithic or Chalcolithic Greece
hints.source: The British School at Athens: archaeological periods of Greece
