Its metalwork and pottery link the region to the wider Urnfield world spreading across the middle Danube at the time.

nodes.name: Tamoani (Teleorman County, 1099 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Tamoani (Teleorman County, 1099 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description: [Muntenia de sud, Dobrogea de sud, 1099 BC–999 BC] Tamoani. Spatial coverage: Bucharest, Constanța County, Călărași County, Giurgiu County, Ialomița County, Ilfov County, Teleorman County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Insula Banului (Bucharest, 999 BC–799 BC)
nodes.title: Insula Banului (Bucharest, 999 BC–799 BC)
nodes.description: [Muntenia, Oltenia, 999 BC–799 BC] Insula Banului. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County, Călărași County, Dolj County, Dâmbovița County, Giurgiu County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Babadag (Tulcea County, 1049 BC–649 BC)
nodes.title: Babadag (Tulcea County, 1049 BC–649 BC)
nodes.description:
[Dobrogea, 1049 BC–649 BC] Babadag. Spatial coverage: Constanța County, Tulcea County. Babadag I, Babadag II, Babadag III. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Iron Age culture of the Dobruja and lower Danube, known from fortified hilltop settlements and thick refuse layers rather than rich graves. Its hallmark is dark burnished pottery decorated with channelling and, later, stamped concentric circles and spirals. The communities farmed and herded on the Black Sea steppe fringe and traded with Thracian and Aegean worlds before disruption around the time steppe horsemen appeared in the region.

nodes.name: Mezocsat (Bihor County, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Mezocsat (Bihor County, 899 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crisana, 899 BC–699 BC] Mezocsat. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Iron Age group of the eastern Carpathian Basin known mainly from its cemeteries, where inhumation burials replaced the cremation rite of the preceding Urnfield world. Graves contain horse harness, bronze and iron weapons and steppe-style ornaments, and the shift is usually read as evidence of eastern horse-riding populations, often linked to the Cimmerians, moving into the Tisza region. It marks the moment when steppe influence began reshaping the cultures of the middle Danube.

nodes.name: Kalaca (Timiș County, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Kalaca (Timiș County, 999 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description: [Banat, 999 BC–899 BC] Kalaca. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Gornea (Timiș County, 899 BC–799 BC)
nodes.title: Gornea (Timiș County, 899 BC–799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Banat, 899 BC–799 BC] Gornea. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A settlement horizon of the Danube gorges in the Banat, associated with the Gornea–Kalakača group that marks the transition from the Late Bronze Age to the earliest Iron Age in the middle Danube. Its dark burnished pottery with fluted and channelled decoration replaced older Bronze Age styles and spread widely along the river, signalling the reorganisation of communities that preceded the Hallstatt world.

nodes.name: Teleac (Sălaj County, 1049 BC–799 BC)
nodes.title: Teleac (Sălaj County, 1049 BC–799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Transilvania, 1049 BC–799 BC] Teleac. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Bistrița-Năsăud County, Brașov County, Cluj County, Covasna County, Harghita County, Hunedoara County, Mureș County. Teleac I, Teleac II, Teleac III.  Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Named after a vast fortified hilltop settlement in Transylvania, enclosed by earthen ramparts and ditches on a scale unmatched in the region. Belonging to the transition from the Late Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age, it shows large-scale communal labour, metalworking and the channelled black pottery of the Gáva tradition, and appears to have been destroyed by fire.

nodes.name: Hallstatt timpuriu cu ceramica canelata (Mehedinți County, 999 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Hallstatt timpuriu cu ceramica canelata (Mehedinți County, 999 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Muntenia, Oltenia, Moldova, 999 BC–699 BC] Hallstatt timpuriu cu ceramica canelata. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Bacău County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County, Călărași County, Dolj County, Dâmbovița County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The opening stage of the Iron Age along the lower Danube, recognised above all by its pottery: dark, highly burnished bowls and urns decorated with broad fluted grooves and bosses instead of paint. Cremation in urnfields was the normal burial rite, and bronze remained common while iron slowly spread. The uniformity of this channelled ware over a huge area from the Tisza to the Danube gorges points to shared workshops, tastes and exchange networks.

nodes.name: Stoicani (Bacău County, 799 BC–749 BC)
nodes.title: Stoicani (Bacău County, 799 BC–749 BC)
nodes.description: [Moldova centrala si de sud, Estul Munteniei, Dobrogea, 799 BC–749 BC] Stoicani. Spatial coverage: Bacău County, Brăila County, Buzău County, Constanța County, Călărași County, Galați County, Ialomița County, Tulcea County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Soldanesti (Bacău County, 799 BC–699 BC)
nodes.title: Soldanesti (Bacău County, 799 BC–699 BC)
nodes.description: [Moldova centrala si de sud, Estul Munteniei, 799 BC–699 BC] Soldanesti. Spatial coverage: Bacău County, Brăila County, Buzău County, Călărași County, Galați County, Ialomița County, Vaslui County, Vrancea County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Basarabi (Sălaj County, 799 BC–649 BC)
nodes.title: Basarabi (Sălaj County, 799 BC–649 BC)
nodes.description:
[Transilvania, Moldova, Muntenia, Oltenia, Dobrogea, Banat, 799 BC–649 BC] Basarabi. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Argeș County, Bacău County, Bistrița-Năsăud County, Brașov County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County. Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Iron Age culture of the middle and lower Danube, instantly recognisable from its pottery: burnished dark surfaces covered with stamped and incised spirals, meanders and channelled fluting, the lines filled with white paste. Its remarkably uniform style spread across a wide swathe of the Balkans and Carpathian basin, marking a period of shared taste and exchange among the communities usually identified with the early Thracians.

nodes.name: Gulmenița (Argeș County, 4499 BC–3699 BC)
nodes.title: Gulmenița (Argeș County, 4499 BC–3699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Muntenia, Nord-estul Olteniei, Sudul Moldovei, Bugeac, Dobrogea, 4499 BC–3699 BC] Gulmenița. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County, Constanța County, Călărași County, Dâmbovița County, Galați County. Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (2), p. 156-161. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Farming communities of the lower Danube and its tributaries who lived on tells - mounds built up from generations of mud-brick houses on the same spot. They produced graphite-painted pottery, fired clay figurines and some of the earliest large-scale copper and gold work in Europe, part of the same world that produced the astonishingly rich Varna cemetery. The culture collapsed toward the end of the fourth millennium as settlements were abandoned across the region.

nodes.name: Sălcuța (Caraș-Severin County, 4499 BC–3999 BC)
nodes.title: Sălcuța (Caraș-Severin County, 4499 BC–3999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Estul Banatului, Oltenia, Vestul Munteniei, 4499 BC–3999 BC] Sălcuța. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Caraș-Severin County, Dolj County, Gorj County, Mehedinți County, Olt County, Teleorman County, Vâlcea County. Altfel la pg 166 este amintit complecul cultural Salcuta IV-Baile Herculane-Cheile Turzii-Hunyadihalom. Salcuta-Krivodol-Bubanj. Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (2), p.161. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Copper Age culture of the lower Danube in what is now Oltenia and neighbouring Serbia and Bulgaria, part of the wider Balkan world that produced Europe's earliest large-scale copper metallurgy. Its people lived in tell-like settlements, made dark burnished and graphite-painted pottery, and cast heavy copper hammer-axes. Its later phases coincide with the disruption and collapse of the old Balkan tell societies.

nodes.name: Petresti (Mureș County, 4999 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Petresti (Mureș County, 4999 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Centrul si sud-vestul Transilvaniei, Banat, 4999 BC–4499 BC] Petresti. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Caraș-Severin County, Hunedoara County, Mureș County, Sibiu County, Timiș County. Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (2), p.161-162. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Copper Age culture of the Transylvanian uplands, known above all for finely made pottery painted before firing in bold bichrome and trichrome designs, among the most accomplished ceramics of prehistoric southeastern Europe. Its communities lived in settled villages, farmed and herded, and worked the copper that was becoming widely available across the Balkans. It grew out of the Vinča tradition and stands alongside the better-known Cucuteni-Tripolye world to the east.

nodes.name: Cucuteni (Moldova, 4599 BC–3699 BC)
nodes.title: Cucuteni (Moldova, 4599 BC–3699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Moldova, Sud-estul Transilkvaniei, 4599 BC–3699 BC] Cucuteni. Spatial coverage: Bacău County, Brașov County, Covasna County, Galați County, Iași County, Moldova, Neamț County, Vaslui County. Cucuteni A. Cucuteni A-B. Cucuteni B. Cucuteni-Ariusd-Tripolie/Ariusd-Cucuteni-Tripolje. Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (2), p.162-166. Epoca de final poate sa fie pe la 3000 a.Chr. si intra in Epoca timpurie a bronzului. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Farming communities of the forest-steppe famous for their painted pottery—spirals and bands in red, white and black on vessels of remarkable size and precision—and for clay figurines and house models. Villages could be very large, laid out in concentric rings of houses, and many were deliberately burned at intervals and rebuilt, a practice still argued over. Together with Trypillia to the east this was one of the densest concentrations of population in Neolithic Europe.

nodes.name: Schneckerberg (Covasna County, 2699 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.title: Schneckerberg (Covasna County, 2699 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.description: [Sud-estul Transilvaniei, nord-estul Munteniei, 2699 BC–2399 BC] Schneckerberg. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Brașov County, Covasna County, Dâmbovița County, Prahova County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (1), p. 235; Gogâltan, F.,  2015, p. 69; Băjenaru 2014, p. 258. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Glina (Argeș County, 2699 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.title: Glina (Argeș County, 2699 BC–2399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Muntenia, Oltenia, Sudul si sud-estul Transilvanieei, 2699 BC–2399 BC] Glina. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Argeș County, Brașov County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County, Covasna County, Călărași County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (1), p. 235-236. Pentru zona Banatului (Valea inferioară a Mureșului) Gogâltan 2015 datează elemente Glina între 2700 și 2500 a. Chr. (Gogâltan 2015, p. 63). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Bronze Age culture of the lower Danube and Wallachian plain, known for coarse handmade pottery with knobbed and fingertip-impressed decoration and for small settlements on terraces and hilltops. Its people herded cattle and sheep, buried some of their dead under low tumuli, and belonged to the wider network of communities through which metalwork and steppe influences spread into southeastern Europe.

nodes.name: Yamnaya (Neamț County, 3399 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.title: Yamnaya (Neamț County, 3399 BC–2499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Moldova, Muntenia, Dobrogea, Banat, Crișana, Câmpia de Vest, Depresiunea Transilvaniei, 3399 BC–2499 BC] Yamnaya. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Arad County, Argeș County, Bacău County, Bihor County, Brașov County, Brăila County, Bucharest. Gogâltan, F., 2015, p. 63; Frânculeasa, A., 2019, p. 129-168. Pentru spațiul cuprins între Banat, bazinul inferior al Mureșului, Crișana și valea Someșului Mic, Gogâltan datează structuri Yamna între 2800 - 2500 a. Chr. (Gogâltan 2015 p. 63). Cele mai timpurii urme Yamnaya datate C14 au fost descoperite la Galați (3400 cal BC)) și Baia Hamangia (3380-3010 cal BC) (A. Frânculeasa 2013, p. 43). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Pastoralists from the Pontic-Caspian steppe, known from the pit graves under low earth mounds that they scattered across the grasslands, the dead laid on their backs with knees raised and dusted with red ochre. Wagons, cattle and horses let them exploit open country that farmers had largely ignored, and burials in the lower Danube region mark their westward push. Ancient DNA has tied this expansion to a massive movement of steppe ancestry into Europe and to the spread of Indo-European languages.

nodes.name: grupul Gornea-Foeni (Timiș County, 2199 BC–1949 BC)
nodes.title: grupul Gornea-Foeni (Timiș County, 2199 BC–1949 BC)
nodes.description:
[Banat, 2199 BC–1949 BC] grupul Gornea-Foeni. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 2015, p. 63. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Bronze Age community of the Banat plain and Danube gorges, known mainly from settlement pottery with channelled and incised decoration. Its sites document the local reworking of older Copper Age traditions as new metal-using networks spread up the Danube.

nodes.name: grupul Sănislău (Satu Mare County, 2899 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.title: grupul Sănislău (Satu Mare County, 2899 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Câmpia Careilor, 2899 BC–2299 BC] grupul Sănislău. Gogâltan, F., 2017, p. 32. Este datat în Bronzul Timpuriu III sau 2300 - 1950 a. Chr, conform cronologiei propuse de Florin Gogâltan (F. Gogâltan 2017, p. 32). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Bronze Age group of the sandy Nyírség borderland of north-west Romania, closely tied to related groups across the Hungarian plain. Its low settlement mounds and cremation burials, with textile-impressed and incised pottery, mark the period when herding communities of the Tisza lowlands took on a distinctly Bronze Age character.

nodes.name: Vučedol (Timiș County, 2499 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.title: Vučedol (Timiș County, 2499 BC–2299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Banat, Valea inferioară a Mureșului, 2499 BC–2299 BC] Vučedol. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Hunedoara County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 71-72. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A late Copper Age culture of the middle Danube known for dark burnished pottery with white-encrusted geometric designs, including the famous vessel long read as a calendar. Its people worked copper on a substantial scale using two-piece moulds and lived in fortified hilltop settlements, and their expansion and ceramic styles fed into the early Bronze Age cultures of central Europe.

nodes.name: grupul Orlea-Gornești (Timiș County, 2299 BC–2149 BC)
nodes.title: grupul Orlea-Gornești (Timiș County, 2299 BC–2149 BC)
nodes.description: [Banat, Valea inferioară a Mureșului, 2299 BC–2149 BC] grupul Orlea-Gornești. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Hunedoara County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 72-73. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Wietenberg (Sălaj County, 1999 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Wietenberg (Sălaj County, 1999 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Transilvania, 1999 BC–1499 BC] Wietenberg. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Bistrița-Năsăud County, Brașov County, Cluj County, Covasna County, Harghita County, Hunedoara County, Mureș County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 255-258. Studiul lui Gabriel Bălan, Collin Quinn și Gregory Hodgins propune  o periodizare a culturii Wietenberg în trei faze distincte bazate pe formele și ornamentele ceramice: timpurie, clasică și târzie. ornamentele ceramice: timpurie, clasică și târzie. Faza timpurie se clasifică  printr-o ceramică cu tradiții în bronzul timpuriu final  și este similară fazelor I-II potrivit periodizării lui N. Chidioșan și fazelor A1-2 definite de N. Borofka.  Conform datelor C14, această fază poate fi datată în invervalul secolelor XX-XVIII a. Chr. Faza clasică prezintă noi forme și ornamente ceramice, evidențiate în ultimele două niveluri din așezarea de la Derșida. Vase bogat ornamentate, care au stat la baza definirii culturii. Similară fazelor III Chidioșan și B-C Boroffka și poate fi datată în intervalul secolelor XVIII- XVI a. Chr conform datelor C14. Faza târzie prezintă forme și ornamente ceramice diferite de cele din faza clasică. Faza de locuire este restrânsă în jumătatea de vest a spațiului locuit anterior, fapt ce poate fi pus în legătură cu apariția culturii Noua. Este similară fazelor IV Chidioșan și D Boroffka. Conform datelor C14 perioada este cuprinsă între secolele XVI și XV a. Chr. In Ciugudean, H., Quinn, C., 2015, p. 147-178 si Palincaș, N., et all 2019, p. 38-51 este realizata o impartire in patru faze; N. Palincaș propune incheierea fazei a IV-a din Cultura Wietenberg dupa 1400 a.Chr. Dupa Gogâltan, F.,  2009, p. 45-70 este datata faza a patra a culturii Wietenberg in secolul XIII a.Chr. In Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 73-78. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of the Transylvanian basin, best known for pottery covered in tightly incised spirals, meanders and running scrolls — some of the most elaborate ornament of Bronze Age Europe. Its communities lived in hilltop and terrace settlements, worked local gold and copper, and exchanged goods along routes that link them to the Carpathian and Mycenaean worlds.

nodes.name: Wietenberg faza timpurie (Mureș County, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.title: Wietenberg faza timpurie (Mureș County, 1999 BC–1799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Centrul Transilvaniei - bazinul carpatic, 1999 BC–1799 BC] Wietenberg faza timpurie. Spatial coverage: Brașov County, Mureș County, Sibiu County. Bălan, G., Quinn, C.,  Hodgins G., 2016, p. 67-92. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The formative stage of the Transylvanian Bronze Age culture, when its settlements and pottery styles emerged out of the preceding Early Bronze Age communities of the region. Decoration is simpler than in the later phases, with the incised spiral ornament that would define the culture still developing.

nodes.name: Wietenberg faza clasică (Mureș County, 1799 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.title: Wietenberg faza clasică (Mureș County, 1799 BC–1599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Centrul Transilvaniei - bazinul carpatic, 1799 BC–1599 BC] Wietenberg faza clasică. Spatial coverage: Brașov County, Mureș County, Sibiu County. Bălan, G., Quinn, C.,  Hodgins G., 2016, p. 67-92. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The mature stage of the Transylvanian Bronze Age culture, when its characteristic spiral and meander ornament on dark burnished pottery reached its most complex form, including hearths and vessels decorated with sun and wheel motifs. Metalwork and gold objects from this horizon show wide-ranging contacts across the Carpathian basin.

nodes.name: Wietenberg faza târzie (Mureș County, 1599 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Wietenberg faza târzie (Mureș County, 1599 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Zona de ocupație se restrânge la Mureșul Mijlociu, Someșul Cald și Someșul Rece., 1599 BC–1499 BC] Wietenberg faza târzie. Spatial coverage: Cluj County, Mureș County. Bălan, G., Quinn, C.,  Hodgins G., 2016, p. 67-92. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The closing stage of the Transylvanian Bronze Age culture, when decoration becomes sparser and vessel forms shift, and settlement patterns change under pressure from new groups moving into the Carpathian basin. It gives way to the Noua culture and its very different herding-oriented ash-mound settlements.

nodes.name: Otomani (Arad County, 1699 BC–1249 BC)
nodes.title: Otomani (Arad County, 1699 BC–1249 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1699 BC–1249 BC] Otomani. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Vulpe, Al. 2001, p. 249-250, 258-260; Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Cultura Otomani- Fuzesabony a  apărut în zona bazinului Tisei, extinzându-se spre vestul României, Slovacia de est, nord-estul Ungariei, Ucraina Transcarpatică și sud-estul Poloniei (Gankarski 2002, p. 8).  Pe teritoriul României: nordul Crișanei, bazinul inferior al Someșului, Câmpia de Vest. Întregul areal cultural este încadrat între 2150 a. Chr și 1250 a. Chr.. Maria Gimbutas încadrează faza timpurie a culturii Otomani la începutul mileniului II î.Chr, faza clasică între 1550- 1400 î.CHr, și faza finală până la 1100 î.Chr. (Gimbutas 1965; Fazecaș 1999, p. 53). Dumitru Berciu (1965) împărțea cultura Otomani în patru faze. (Fazecaș 1999). Ordenlitch revine asupra acestei probleme și împarte prima fază în două subfaze: Ia, încadrată în Br A1 și Ib în Br A2, menținând pentru  celelalte încadrarea propusă anterior. (Ordenlitch 1973, 15, Fazecaș 1999). T. Bader pornește de la cronologia  lui Ordenlitch și propune împărțirea în patru etape menținând limitele Br A-D (Bader 1978, 61; Fazecaș 1999). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age culture of the Carpathian Basin, known for tightly packed settlements protected by ditches and ramparts, some of them built up into tells occupied for generations. Its metalworkers produced bronze weapons, ornaments and horse gear traded far across central Europe, and its fortified sites suggest chiefly elites competing for control of the routes carrying copper, tin and gold. Excavated houses, storage pits and rich metal hoards make it one of the best-documented Bronze Age societies of the region.

nodes.name: Otomani A (Arad County, 1699 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.title: Otomani A (Arad County, 1699 BC–1549 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1699 BC–1549 BC] Otomani A. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Br. A2 Central European (Reinecke). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The formative stage of the culture, when communities in the Tisza and Mureș lowlands settled into long-lived villages and began enclosing them with ditches and banks. Pottery styles and the first substantial bronze working mark a break with the preceding Early Bronze Age groups.

nodes.name: Periam-Pecica (Mureș County, 2199 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Periam-Pecica (Mureș County, 2199 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Valea inferioara a Muresului, 2199 BC–1699 BC] Periam-Pecica. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 261-265; Vulpe, Al., 2010, p. 257; Nicodemus,  O`Shea, J.,  2015, p. 691-702. Datări C14 din cimitirul Mokrin, din Banatul sârbesc, sugerează un interval de timp între 2200 și 1700 a. Chr. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Bronze Age farmers of the lower Mureș valley who lived in long-occupied tell settlements, rebuilding house on house until the mounds stood metres above the floodplain. Excavations at Pecica revealed workshops for bronze casting and bone working, horse gear, and imported goods showing links to the Mycenaean world and the Carpathian metal trade. Their fine burnished pottery with knobs and spiral decoration is a hallmark of the Maros culture.

nodes.name: Vatina (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Vatina (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Banat, 1899 BC–1499 BC] Vatina. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Ljustina, M., Dmitrovic, K., 2015, p. 37-47;Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79. Cultura Vatin s-a întins din sudul Câmpiei Panonice până în nord-vestul Peninsulei Balcanice, în Banatul sârbesc și Banatul românesc. Cronologia generală pentru întreg arealul cultural este cuprinsă între 2000 și 1500 a. Chr.; Dupa Ljustina, M., Dmitrovic, K., 2015, p. 37-47aceasta cultura avea 3 faze, dupa Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79 exista doua faze. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of the Banat plain and the middle Danube, known from long-lived tell settlements and cemeteries with cremation urns. Its fine dark burnished pottery, incised and channelled with spirals and encrusted with white paste, is among the most distinctive of the region. Bronze weapons and ornaments in its graves show it was plugged into exchange networks running from the Carpathians towards the Aegean.

nodes.name: Vatina faza timpurie (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1649 BC)
nodes.title: Vatina faza timpurie (Timiș County, 1899 BC–1649 BC)
nodes.description: [Banat, 1899 BC–1649 BC] Vatina faza timpurie. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Ljustina, M., Dmitrovic, K., 2015, p. 37-47;Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79. Bronz A2 central European, Helladicul târziu (mormintele cu puț). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Vatina faza clasică (Timiș County, 1649 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Vatina faza clasică (Timiș County, 1649 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description: [Banat, 1649 BC–1499 BC] Vatina faza clasică. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Timiș County. Gogâltan, F., 1999, p. 78-79. O parte din A3 central european și Bronz B1 european. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Verbicioara (Gorj County, 1899 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Verbicioara (Gorj County, 1899 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Oltenia , 1899 BC–1499 BC] Verbicioara. Spatial coverage: Dolj County, Gorj County, Mehedinți County, Olt County, Vâlcea County. 3-5 faze. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 265-267; Vulpe, Al., 2010, p. 261. B. Hansel contestă existența fazelor IV și V ale culturii Verbicioara pe care le include în grupul Govora, atestat mai ales în nordul și estul Olteniei. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age culture of Oltenia and the Danube valley in south-western Romania, known chiefly from its settlements and its dark, highly burnished pottery decorated with incised spirals and meanders, often filled with white paste. Its people farmed and herded in small tell-like and open villages, and their bronze- and goldwork shows links running down the Danube to the Balkans and the Aegean world.

nodes.name: Tei (Călărași County, 2199 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.title: Tei (Călărași County, 2199 BC–1499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Muntenia  si sud-estul Transilvaniei, 2199 BC–1499 BC] Tei. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Brașov County, Brăila County, Bucharest, Buzău County, Covasna County, Călărași County, Dâmbovița County. primele 3 faze. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2),, p. 267-269; Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300. Fazele IV și V prezintă multe discrepanțe față de cele precedente, precum și strânse asemănări cu grupul Govora din Oltenia, încât cercetătoarea Nona Palincaș a propus denumirea grupului cultural Govora-Fundeni, care evoluează în Bronzul târziu sub forma unei sinteze sub ceramica de tradiția Verbicioara și Tei. (N. Palincaș 1996, p. 239-295). Dupa A. Laszlo (Laszlo, A. 2001, p. 300) faza a cincea a culturii Tei se prelungeste pana pe la 1100 a.Chr.. Dupa Gavrilă, E., 2013, p. 153-168; Leahu, V., 2003, p. 42-43, 202-208 cultura Tei ar fi situata intre 2000/1900 a.Chr. si 1520/1410 a.Chr. iar aria de raspandire este sud-estul României și Bulgaria între Stara Planina (sud) și Carpații Meridionali în nord, bazinul superior al Ialomiței și Mostiștea în est și râul Vedea în Vest. Descoperiri și în sud-estul Transilvaniei. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Middle Bronze Age culture of the lower Danube plain, known from settlement mounds and cemeteries around Bucharest and the Wallachian lowlands. Its people farmed and herded on the plain and made dark burnished pottery with incised and encrusted geometric decoration, part of the network of Carpathian-Balkan communities linked by bronze exchange.

nodes.name: Monteoru (Buzău County, 2499 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Monteoru (Buzău County, 2499 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Nord-estul Munteniei, sudul Moldovei, 2499 BC–1099 BC] Monteoru. Spatial coverage: Brăila County, Buzău County, Galați County, Vrancea County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 250-254; Motzoi-Chicideanu, I., Șandor-Chicideanu, M.,  2015, p. 9-53. 2500 a. Chr. posibil si mai devreme; data de final post 1500 a. Chr.. Ocupă un spațiul cuprins între curbura Carpaților, până spre câmpie, pentru ca în faza de maximă expansiune, să ocupe cea mai mare parte a sudului și centrului Moldovei, cu unele pătrunderi spre est, dincolo de Prut, unde intră în contact cu manifestările culturale Mnogovalikovaja. (Bolohan 2016, p. 98). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age culture of the sub-Carpathian hills, known for terraced hilltop settlements defended by ditches and ramparts, and for cemeteries of crouched inhumations. Its pottery, with spiral and channelled decoration, and its bronze and bone ornaments show contacts stretching from the Carpathian Basin to the steppe. The type site at Sărata Monteoru, with its long stratified sequence, remains the yardstick for dating the Bronze Age of eastern Romania.

nodes.name: Gârla Mare (Caraș-Severin County, 1649 BC–1249 BC)
nodes.title: Gârla Mare (Caraș-Severin County, 1649 BC–1249 BC)
nodes.description:
[Sudul Banatului și Oltenia, 1649 BC–1249 BC] Gârla Mare. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Dolj County, Gorj County, Mehedinți County, Vâlcea County. are patru faze. Șandor-Chicideanu, M., 2003. cultura Zuto-Brdo-Gârla Mare; Ion Motzoi Chicideanu in  2009,  consideră că prima etapă a culturii Gârla Mare începe cu faza a III-a a culturii Verbicioara. El propune o cronologie intre 1900 si 1400 a.Chr. Sfârșitul este marcat de apariția grupului cultural Bistreș-Ișalnița. Verbicioara III. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Bronze Age community of the lower Danube, best known for cremating its dead in urns and for extraordinary clay figurines: bell-shaped female statuettes covered in incised spirals and meanders that seem to record costume, jewellery and tattooing. The pottery is richly decorated and often encrusted with white paste. The figurines remain the fullest picture we have of how people in this region dressed and adorned themselves.

nodes.name: Suciu (Satu Mare County, 1599 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Suciu (Satu Mare County, 1599 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tara Lapusului, Maramuresul istoric, 1599 BC–1199 BC] Suciu. Spatial coverage: Bistrița-Năsăud County, Maramureș County, Mureș County, Satu Mare County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (1), p. 224; Vulpe, Al. 2001 (2), p. 261; Petrescu-Dȋmboviţa, M. 2001 (3), p.280-281; Petrescu-Dȋmboviţa, M., 2019, p. 274. Unii cercetători o denumesc faza a treia a culturii Suciu cultura Culciu Mare. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Late Bronze Age culture of the upper Tisza basin, recognised above all by its dark burnished pottery covered in incised spirals and meander patterns. Its people cremated their dead, worked bronze on a large scale, and left hoards of tools, weapons and ornaments that show them plugged into the metal trade networks running between the Carpathians and central Europe.

nodes.name: Coslogeni (Călărași County, 1349 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.title: Coslogeni (Călărași County, 1349 BC–1049 BC)
nodes.description:
[Sud-estul Munteniei, Dobrogea, 1349 BC–1049 BC] Coslogeni. Spatial coverage: Constanța County, Călărași County, Ialomița County, Tulcea County. 3 faze. Sabatinovka-Noua-Coslogeni/Noua-Sabatinovka-Coslogeni sau grupul Coslogeni-Yagnilo. Petrescu-Dȋmboviţa, M. 2001 (3), p.285-286; Bojadziev, J., 1992, p. 17;Bolohan 2016, p, 160. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Late Bronze Age herding culture of the lower Danube and Dobrudja, part of the wider Noua-Sabatinovka-Coslogeni complex that stretched east across the steppe. Its most recognisable sites are the so-called ash mounds, low heaps of grey settlement debris packed with cattle and sheep bone, that mark seasonal camps of a heavily pastoral economy.

nodes.name: Otomani B (Arad County, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.title: Otomani B (Arad County, 1549 BC–1399 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1549 BC–1399 BC] Otomani B. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Br. B Central European (Reinecke). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The classic stage, with heavily fortified settlements and tell mounds, dense house plots and a flourishing bronze industry producing weapons, ornaments and harness fittings. Wealth differences visible in burials and hoards point to an established warrior elite controlling metal supply and trade.

nodes.name: Otomani C (Arad County, 1399 BC–1249 BC)
nodes.title: Otomani C (Arad County, 1399 BC–1249 BC)
nodes.description:
[Crisana, Maramures, 1399 BC–1249 BC] Otomani C. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County. Gankarski, J., Mykenami, M., 2002; Fazecaș, G., 1999, p. 51-65. Br. C Central European (Reinecke). Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The late stage, when the great fortified tells were abandoned or reduced and material culture shifted under influence from the Tumulus groups spreading through central Europe. Metalwork remained abundant, but settlement broke up into smaller, more dispersed sites as the Middle Bronze Age order gave way.

nodes.name: Cehăluț (Cluj County, 1299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.title: Cehăluț (Cluj County, 1299 BC–1199 BC)
nodes.description:
[între Câmpia Careiului și Colinele Tășnadului, în nord și râurile Crasna și Barcău, în sud, 1299 BC–1199 BC] Cehăluț. Spatial coverage: Bihor County, Cluj County, Satu Mare County, Sălaj County. grupul cultural Cehăluț-Pișcolt-Hajdúbagos. Gogâltan, F., 2009, p. 45-70; Nemeti, J., 2008, p. Este contemporan Bronzului C/D din cronologia lui Reinecke. T. Bader considera grupul cultural Cehăluț-Pișcolt faza a IV-a a culturii Otomani. Suciu de Sus II și Lăpuș I. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Late Bronze Age group of northwestern Romania and the neighbouring Hungarian plain, usually paired with the Hajdúbagos finds across the border. It is known mainly from cremation cemeteries with urns and from dark burnished pottery with channelled and knobbed decoration, part of the wider shift in the Carpathian basin towards urnfield burial rites.

nodes.name: Gava (Timiș County, 1349 BC–999 BC)
nodes.title: Gava (Timiș County, 1349 BC–999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Maramureș, Banat, 1349 BC–999 BC] Gava. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Maramureș County, Satu Mare County, Timiș County. complexul cultural Gava-Holihrady. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A late Bronze Age world of the eastern Carpathian Basin recognised by its channelled pottery, black and glossy outside with a deep orange interior, and by cremation burials in urnfields. Its communities buried enormous hoards of bronze and were among the first in the region to work iron, forming a bridge between the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age cultures of the Danube and Transylvania.

nodes.name: Poienesti-Lukasevka (Romania, 199 BC–19 BC)
nodes.title: Poienesti-Lukasevka (Romania, 199 BC–19 BC)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 199 BC–19 BC] Poienesti-Lukasevka. Babes, M. 2001, p. 522-528; Iarmulschi 2018, p. 36. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An archaeological culture of the lands between the Carpathians and the Dniester whose cremation cemeteries, brooches and pottery show strong links to the Jastorf world of northern Europe. It is generally identified with the Bastarnae, Germanic-speaking migrants who moved southeast and appear in Greek and Roman accounts as mercenaries and raiders in the Balkans. Its remains document one of the earliest large-scale Germanic migrations into southeastern Europe.

nodes.name: cultura geto-dacica clasica (Romania, 174 BC–AD 106)
nodes.title: cultura geto-dacica clasica (Romania, 174 BC–AD 106)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 174 BC–AD 106] cultura geto-dacica clasica. Babes, M. 2010, p. 805-808. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The height of Dacian civilisation, when Burebista and later Decebalus welded the tribes north of the Danube into a kingdom powerful enough to alarm Rome. Its centre was the mountain complex around Sarmizegetusa Regia, with stone-walled citadels, circular sanctuaries, ironworking on an industrial scale and hoards of silver ornaments and Greek and Roman coin. Trajan's two wars ended it, and the conquered kingdom became the Roman province of Dacia.

nodes.name: Lipita (Romania, AD 1–AD 200)
nodes.title: Lipita (Romania, AD 1–AD 200)
nodes.description: [Romania, AD 1–AD 200] Lipita. Babes, M. 2010,  p. 806; Ionita, I. 2001 (2), p. 432-437. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Regatul Traciei (Romania, 27 BC–AD 46)
nodes.title: Regatul Traciei (Romania, 27 BC–AD 46)
nodes.description:
[Romania, 27 BC–AD 46] Regatul Traciei. (Observatii) Marquardt 1892, p. 198; Premerstein 1898, col. 183; Filow 1906, p. 3-4; Weiss 1911, p. 32; Pârvan, V. 1921, p. 193; Patsch 1937, p. 145-146; Condurachi, E. 1954, p.53; Florescu 1958, p. 7; Stoian 1962, p.38; Pippidi 1965, p. 306-307; Vulpe, R. 1938, p. 48-49. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The last decades of the Thracian kingdom as a client state of Rome, ruled by the Sapaean dynasty with Roman backing and Roman troops propping up unpopular kings. Dynastic murders and a revolt of the mountain tribes repeatedly forced imperial intervention, until Claudius ended the arrangement and annexed the territory outright as the province of Thracia.

nodes.name: Vinca timpurie (Timiș County, 5499 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.title: Vinca timpurie (Timiș County, 5499 BC–4999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Banat, Vestul Olteniei, Tara Hategului, 5499 BC–4999 BC] Vinca timpurie. Spatial coverage: Caraș-Severin County, Dolj County, Gorj County, Hunedoara County, Mehedinți County, Timiș County. fazele A si B. Ursulescu, N. 2001 (2), p.135-139. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

The formative phase of the Vinča culture in the Banat, as farming communities settled into long-lived villages of substantial rectangular houses. Fine dark burnished pottery and clay figurines appear from the start, marking a clear change from the earlier Starčevo–Criș tradition that preceded it.

nodes.title: Iclod (Bistrița-Năsăud County, 4899 BC–4599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Bazinul Somesului mijlociu (nordul Transilvaniei), 4899 BC–4599 BC] Iclod. Spatial coverage: Bistrița-Năsăud County, Cluj County, Mureș County, Sălaj County. Este denumita cand cultura cand grup. Ursulescu, N. 2001 (2) p.134-135, 147; Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (1), p.149; Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (2), p. 166-167. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Late Neolithic farming communities of the Transylvanian plateau, known from ditched settlements and, unusually, from orderly flat cemeteries of extended inhumations furnished with pottery. Their fine dark burnished and painted wares link them to wider Carpathian networks of the period.

Spatial coverage: Alba County, Arad County, Bihor County, Caraș-Severin County, Cluj County, Hunedoara County, Sălaj County, Timiș County. Grupul ceramicii liniare din Campia Tisei. Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (1), p.152. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.title: Suplac (Romania, 4899 BC–4599 BC)
nodes.description: [Romania, 4899 BC–4599 BC] Suplac. Este denumita cand cultura cand grup. Ursulescu, N. 2001 (1), p.121; Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (2)., p.166-167. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Stoicani-Aldeni (Vrancea County, 4799 BC–4599 BC)
nodes.title: Stoicani-Aldeni (Vrancea County, 4799 BC–4599 BC)
nodes.description:
[Sudul Moldovei, vestul Buceagului, Nord-estul Munteniei, 4799 BC–4599 BC] Stoicani-Aldeni. Spatial coverage: Brăila County, Buzău County, Galați County, Tulcea County, Vrancea County. Petrescu-Dambovita, M. 2001 (1), p. 152-153. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A Copper Age cultural group of the lower Danube and southern Moldavia, occupying the ground where the Gumelnița and Cucuteni-Tripolye worlds met and mixing traits from both. Its tell-like settlements and painted and incised pottery show how fluid the boundaries between the great Balkan farming cultures could be.

nodes.name: Ciumbrud (Cluj County, 649 BC–449 BC)
nodes.title: Ciumbrud (Cluj County, 649 BC–449 BC)
nodes.description:
[Transilvania, 649 BC–449 BC] Ciumbrud. Spatial coverage: Alba County, Bistrița-Năsăud County, Brașov County, Cluj County, Covasna County, Harghita County, Hunedoara County, Mureș County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (4), p. 473; Vulpe 1967; Vulpe 1977, 81-111. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

A distinctive burial group in the Transylvanian basin marking the arrival of steppe nomad culture west of the Carpathians. Its inhumation graves contain akinakes daggers, trilobate arrowheads, bronze mirrors and animal-style ornaments of Scythian type, alongside local pottery, and are often linked with the Agathyrsi described by Herodotus. The mixture shows incomers and indigenous communities merging rather than one simply replacing the other.

nodes.name: Vekerzug (Bihor County, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Vekerzug (Bihor County, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[ Campia Tisei, Crisana, 649 BC–499 BC] Vekerzug. Spatial coverage: Arad County, Bihor County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (4), p. 473. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Iron Age culture of the Great Hungarian Plain and neighbouring regions in which steppe fashions arrived in the Carpathian Basin: bridle bits and harness ornaments, iron akinakes daggers, trilobate arrowheads and animal-style decoration. Its cemeteries mix inhumation and cremation and sometimes include horse burials, and wheel-made grey pottery appears alongside handmade wares. The culture marks contact between the settled Carpathian populations and Scythian groups from the east.

nodes.name: Ferigile (Prahova County, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Ferigile (Prahova County, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Nordul Munteniei si nord-estul Olteniei, 649 BC–499 BC] Ferigile. Spatial coverage: Argeș County, Brăila County, Buzău County, Dâmbovița County, Prahova County, Vâlcea County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (4), p. 473. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

An Early Iron Age burial culture of the northern Oltenian foothills, known chiefly from large cemeteries of tumuli covering cremated remains. Graves held iron weapons, horse gear and ornaments that mix local Thracian traditions with Scythian and Hallstatt-world influences, evidence of warrior elites in contact with the steppe and the Danube. These communities are generally seen as ancestors of the Getae who later confronted Greeks and Persians on the lower Danube.

nodes.name: Barsesti (Vrancea County, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Barsesti (Vrancea County, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Moldova de sud, 649 BC–499 BC] Barsesti. Spatial coverage: Galați County, Vrancea County. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (4), p. 473. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

Known chiefly from tumulus cemeteries in the Carpathian foothills, where cremated remains were buried under earth mounds with iron weapons, horse gear and dark burnished pottery. The group belongs to the northern Thracian world of the later Hallstatt period, when iron working, mounted warriors and contacts with the steppe and the Greek Black Sea coast reshaped local society.

nodes.name: Vraca (Bulgaria, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Vraca (Bulgaria, 649 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description: [nordul Bulgariei, 649 BC–499 BC] Vraca. Vulpe, Al. 2001 (4), p. 473. Period definition from Institutul Național al Patrimoniului periodizare — Bogdan Șandric, 2023.

nodes.name: Prehistory (Tuscany, 2500000 BC–2101 BC)
nodes.title: Prehistory (Tuscany, 2500000 BC–2101 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 2500000 BC–2101 BC] Prehistory. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Runs from the earliest Palaeolithic occupation of the Danube corridor — including the mammoth hunters who carved the Venus of Willendorf — through Neolithic farming, copper mining in the Alps and the salt-and-iron wealth of the Hallstatt cemetery. Austria's Iron Age communities grew rich controlling Alpine salt and metal routes, and their culture was absorbed into the Roman Empire at the end of the period.

hints.label: Prehistory
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età protostorica (Tuscany, 2100 BC–721 BC)
nodes.title: Età protostorica (Tuscany, 2100 BC–721 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 2100 BC–721 BC] Età protostorica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The long stretch between prehistory proper and the first written records, covering the Bronze and early Iron Ages. Communities moved from scattered hamlets to large fortified hilltop settlements, adopted cremation burial, exploited local copper and iron, and gradually developed the hierarchies and concentrated populations that produced the Etruscan cities.

hints.label: Età protostorica
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età Etrusca (Tuscany, 720 BC–90 BC)
nodes.title: Età Etrusca (Tuscany, 720 BC–90 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 720 BC–90 BC] Età Etrusca. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscany was the heartland of the Etruscans, whose independent cities, Volterra, Chiusi, Populonia, Vetulonia and Arezzo among them, grew wealthy on the iron of Elba, copper mining and Mediterranean trade. Their painted and chamber tombs, banqueting scenes, bronze mirrors and alabaster urns give an unusually vivid picture of daily life and belief, and their inscriptions preserve a language still only partly understood. Roman conquest and, finally, the grant of citizenship after the Social War dissolved them into Italy.

hints.label: Età Etrusca
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età Romana (Tuscany, 89 BC–AD 337)
nodes.title: Età Romana (Tuscany, 89 BC–AD 337)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 89 BC–AD 337] Età Romana. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Etruria was absorbed into the Roman state after the Social War, its cities granted citizenship and its language and script fading within a few generations. Roman roads, centuriated field systems, colonies like Florentia and Luca, and coastal villas producing wine and oil reshaped the landscape; marble from Luni was shipped across the empire. Much of what survives above ground in Tuscan towns - street grids, theatres, aqueducts, baths - dates from these centuries.

hints.label: Età Romana
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età tardoantica (Tuscany, AD 338–AD 600)
nodes.title: Età tardoantica (Tuscany, AD 338–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 338–AD 600] Età tardoantica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscany in these centuries shifted from a landscape of Roman villas and municipal towns to one of fortified hilltop settlements, shrinking cities and Christian basilicas. Estates were consolidated, coinage and long-distance pottery imports thinned out, and bishops took over much of the administrative role once held by civic magistrates. The Gothic War of the mid-sixth century wrecked much of the region, and the Lombard arrival at its close reshaped who held the land.

hints.label: Età tardoantica
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età Altomedievale (Tuscany, AD 601–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Età Altomedievale (Tuscany, AD 601–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 601–AD 1000] Età Altomedievale. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Following the Gothic wars, Tuscany passed to the Lombards, who made Lucca a ducal seat, and then to the Carolingian counts and the powerful margraves who succeeded them. Roman towns shrank, but monasteries, rural parish churches and the first fortified hilltop villages took shape, laying the settlement pattern still visible today. Trade never disappeared entirely: pilgrims and merchants moving along the Via Francigena kept the region connected to the wider world.

hints.label: Età Altomedievale
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età bassomedievale (Tuscany, AD 1001–AD 1499)
nodes.title: Età bassomedievale (Tuscany, AD 1001–AD 1499)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1001–AD 1499] Età bassomedievale. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscan towns broke free of feudal lords and organised themselves as communes, growing rich on wool, banking and long-distance trade; Florence, Siena, Pisa and Lucca fought each other as much as they fought outsiders. The florin became an international currency, and merchant wealth paid for cathedrals, town halls and the first generation of painters and poets who would define the Renaissance. Plague in 1348 killed perhaps half the population and permanently altered the balance between the surviving cities.

hints.label: Età bassomedievale
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età moderna (Tuscany, AD 1500–AD 1799)
nodes.title: Età moderna (Tuscany, AD 1500–AD 1799)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1500–AD 1799] Età moderna. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The Medici turned Florence into a hereditary duchy and then a grand duchy, draining marshes, developing the free port of Livorno and governing a unified Tuscan state. The dynasty died out in 1737 and the Habsburg-Lorraines took over, bringing Enlightenment reform - most famously the abolition of the death penalty in 1786, the first anywhere. Meanwhile the region's political weight in Europe steadily faded even as its art and science drew visitors from everywhere.

hints.label: Età moderna
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età contemporanea (Tuscany, AD 1800–AD 2050)
nodes.title: Età contemporanea (Tuscany, AD 1800–AD 2050)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1800–AD 2050] Età contemporanea. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The grand duchy gave way to Napoleonic rule, restoration, and then absorption into a united Italy, with Florence serving briefly as the national capital. Railways, land reclamation in the Maremma, marble and mining industries, and mass emigration transformed a largely agricultural region, while sharecropping estates that had shaped the countryside for centuries were finally dismantled after the Second World War.

hints.label: Età contemporanea
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età eneolitica (Tuscany, 3700 BC–2101 BC)
nodes.title: Età eneolitica (Tuscany, 3700 BC–2101 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 3700 BC–2101 BC] Età eneolitica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Copper metallurgy arrived among still largely Neolithic farming communities, and with it new weapons - daggers, halberds, arrowheads - that appear in male burials and in the carved stone stelae of the Lunigiana. Rinaldone-culture groups buried their dead in rock-cut chamber tombs, often with ochre and flint blades, marking a growing emphasis on individual status.

hints.label: Età eneolitica
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età neolitica (Tuscany, 6000 BC–3701 BC)
nodes.title: Età neolitica (Tuscany, 6000 BC–3701 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 6000 BC–3701 BC] Età neolitica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Farming, pottery and permanent villages replaced a hunting and gathering way of life, spreading up the Tyrrhenian coast and inland along the river valleys. Communities kept sheep, goats and cattle, grew cereals, and traded obsidian from Sardinia and the Aeolian islands along with polished stone axes over long distances.

hints.label: Età neolitica
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età del bronzo (Tuscany, 2100 BC–926 BC)
nodes.title: Età del bronzo (Tuscany, 2100 BC–926 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 2100 BC–926 BC] Età del bronzo. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Over roughly a millennium, scattered farming hamlets grew into fortified hilltop communities with specialised metalworkers, and cremation cemeteries replaced older collective tombs. Copper and iron ores in the hills inland of the coast drew the region into Mediterranean trade, laying the economic groundwork on which Etruscan civilisation would be built.

hints.label: Età del bronzo
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età del Bronzo antica (Tuscany, 2100 BC–1701 BC)
nodes.title: Età del Bronzo antica (Tuscany, 2100 BC–1701 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 2100 BC–1701 BC] Età del Bronzo antica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Small farming and herding communities settled on defensible hilltops and in caves, working copper and tin alloys and burying their dead in collective rock-cut and natural chambers. Metal ores in the Colline Metallifere and on Elba began to attract attention, setting up a resource base that would make the region wealthy for the next two thousand years.

hints.label: Età del Bronzo antica
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età del bronzo media (Tuscany, 1700 BC–1301 BC)
nodes.title: Età del bronzo media (Tuscany, 1700 BC–1301 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 1700 BC–1301 BC] Età del bronzo media. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Apennine-culture communities herded livestock across upland pastures and lived in stable villages, leaving distinctive incised and inlaid pottery in caves and open settlements. Bronze tools and weapons became widespread, and networks moving metal and salt across the peninsula grew steadily denser.

hints.label: Età del bronzo media
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età del Bronzo recente (Tuscany, 1300 BC–1151 BC)
nodes.title: Età del Bronzo recente (Tuscany, 1300 BC–1151 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 1300 BC–1151 BC] Età del Bronzo recente. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Villages grew larger and more permanent, and the distinctive Subapennine pottery with its horned and crested handles spread across central Italy. Mycenaean goods reaching Tyrrhenian shores show these communities were plugged into a Mediterranean exchange network, and local elites were beginning to emerge from control of metal supplies.

hints.label: Età del Bronzo recente
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età del Bronzo finale (Tuscany, 2100 BC–926 BC)
nodes.title: Età del Bronzo finale (Tuscany, 2100 BC–926 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 2100 BC–926 BC] Età del Bronzo finale. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Settlement shifted towards larger, well-defended hilltop sites, and cremation in urn cemeteries became the normal way to bury the dead - the practice that gives the wider 'Protovillanovan' horizon its name. Bronze hoards, sophisticated metalwork and long-distance contacts along the Tyrrhenian coast point to communities already organising themselves around control of ore and trade, immediately foreshadowing the rise of Etruscan centres.

hints.label: Età del Bronzo finale
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età del ferro (Tuscany, 925 BC–721 BC)
nodes.title: Età del ferro (Tuscany, 925 BC–721 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 925 BC–721 BC] Età del ferro. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The Villanovan phase: large clusters of huts on the plateaus that would become Etruscan cities, with cemeteries of biconical urns holding cremated ashes, sometimes capped by a helmet. Iron working spread rapidly, populations concentrated dramatically into a few big centres, and the differences between rich and poor graves show a society sorting itself into ranks - the direct ancestor of the Etruscan city-states.

hints.label: Età del ferro
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età orientalizzante (Tuscany, 720 BC–581 BC)
nodes.title: Età orientalizzante (Tuscany, 720 BC–581 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 720 BC–581 BC] Età orientalizzante. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Contact with Phoenician and Greek traders flooded Etruria with eastern styles and technologies - gold granulation, ivory carving, writing, the banquet and the chariot. Enormously rich princely tombs under earth mounds show aristocratic families displaying wealth drawn from metal ore and trade, and the Villanovan villages consolidated into recognisable cities.

hints.label: Età orientalizzante
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età orientalizzante antica (Tuscany, 720 BC–681 BC)
nodes.title: Età orientalizzante antica (Tuscany, 720 BC–681 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 720 BC–681 BC] Età orientalizzante antica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The first phase of the eastern-influenced boom, when imported Levantine and Greek objects began appearing in the graves of an emerging aristocracy and local craftsmen started imitating them. Alphabetic writing was adopted from Greek colonists, and the earliest Etruscan inscriptions date from around this time.

hints.label: Età orientalizzante antica
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età orientalizzante media (Tuscany, 680 BC–631 BC)
nodes.title: Età orientalizzante media (Tuscany, 680 BC–631 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 680 BC–631 BC] Età orientalizzante media. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Aristocratic display reached its peak in enormous tumulus tombs stocked with gold jewellery, ivories, bronze cauldrons and imported pottery. Workshops in the Etruscan cities produced luxury goods of extraordinary technical skill, and the settlements that supported these elites were taking on genuinely urban form.

hints.label: Età orientalizzante media
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età orientalizzante recente (Tuscany, 630 BC–581 BC)
nodes.title: Età orientalizzante recente (Tuscany, 630 BC–581 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 630 BC–581 BC] Età orientalizzante recente. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The exuberant princely burials gave way to more restrained, standardised tombs as power shifted from individual dynasts towards civic institutions. Cities were laid out with streets, drains and stone-built houses, sanctuaries were monumentalised, and the political map of archaic Etruria took its lasting shape.

hints.label: Età orientalizzante recente
hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: Età etrusca arcaica (Tuscany, 580 BC–481 BC)
nodes.title: Età etrusca arcaica (Tuscany, 580 BC–481 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 580 BC–481 BC] Età etrusca arcaica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The height of Etruscan power, when cities like Vulci, Volterra, Chiusi and Populonia controlled the Tyrrhenian sea and traded intensively with Greeks and Carthaginians. Painted tombs, monumental temples with terracotta decoration, black bucchero ware and imported Attic vases fill the archaeological record; writing in the Etruscan alphabet becomes common. Etruscan kings ruled Rome for much of this period, until their expulsion around 509 BC.

nodes.name: Età etrusca classica (Tuscany, 480 BC–324 BC)
nodes.title: Età etrusca classica (Tuscany, 480 BC–324 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 480 BC–324 BC] Età etrusca classica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Naval defeat at Cumae in 474 BC and pressure from Celts in the north cost the Etruscans their sea power and their northern colonies, and coastal cities declined while inland centres such as Chiusi, Volterra and Perugia held on. Art absorbed Greek classical models, and rising Rome began the long series of wars that would end Etruscan independence.

nodes.name: Età etrusca ellenistica (Tuscany, 323 BC–90 BC)
nodes.title: Età etrusca ellenistica (Tuscany, 323 BC–90 BC)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 323 BC–90 BC] Età etrusca ellenistica. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

City by city the Etruscan states fell to Rome, keeping local institutions and language while losing political freedom. Wealthy families built family tombs filled with carved alabaster and terracotta ash urns, and Volterra and Chiusi produced some of the most distinctive sculpture of the period; the era closes with the granting of Roman citizenship and the swift Latinisation of the region.

nodes.name: Età tardorepubblicana (Tuscany, 89 BC–AD 32)
nodes.title: Età tardorepubblicana (Tuscany, 89 BC–AD 32)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 89 BC–AD 32] Età tardorepubblicana. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

After the Social War, the Etruscan towns received Roman citizenship, and Latin, Roman law and Roman coinage rapidly displaced Etruscan civic life. Sulla's veteran colonies at places like Arretium and Faesulae redistributed land, while the countryside filled with slave-run villa estates producing wine and oil for wider markets. Visitors see the last Etruscan-language inscriptions and urns alongside the first thoroughly Roman townscapes.

nodes.name: Prima età imperiale (Tuscany, 31 BC–AD 68)
nodes.title: Prima età imperiale (Tuscany, 31 BC–AD 68)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, 31 BC–AD 68] Prima età imperiale. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Augustus turned the exhausted Roman Republic into a monarchy in all but name, and his Julio-Claudian heirs ruled to Nero's fall. Etruria was reshaped by veteran colonies, new road building and vast senatorial estates worked by slaves, while its old cities became comfortable Roman municipia. Marble public buildings, imperial portrait statues and mass-produced Arretine red-gloss pottery from Arezzo, exported as far as India, define the material world of these decades.

nodes.name: Media età imperiale (Tuscany, AD 69–AD 192)
nodes.title: Media età imperiale (Tuscany, AD 69–AD 192)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 69–AD 192] Media età imperiale. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The Flavians and the Antonines brought stability after the civil wars of 69, with the Empire at its widest extent under Trajan and a long stretch of peace under Hadrian and the Antonines. In Etruria this shows in prosperous villas, brick-stamped building booms, and the exploitation of marble and terracotta industries feeding Rome's construction. Roman citizenship spread widely through the provinces, and the era closes with Commodus's murder and a return to civil war.

nodes.name: Tarda età imperiale (Tuscany, AD 193–AD 337)
nodes.title: Tarda età imperiale (Tuscany, AD 193–AD 337)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 193–AD 337] Tarda età imperiale. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

From the Severan emperors through the third-century crisis to Constantine, the Roman world weathered civil war, inflation, plague and frontier collapse, and re-emerged reorganised under Diocletian and his successors. In Italy, coastal villas were fortified or abandoned, town councils buckled under fiscal pressure, and large estates absorbed smallholders. The period ends with a Christian emperor and a new capital in the east, leaving Italy politically sidelined.

nodes.name: VII sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 601–AD 700)
nodes.title: VII sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 601–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 601–AD 700] VII sec. d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscany lay under Lombard rule, governed from ducal seats such as Lucca and Chiusi by warrior elites whose weapon-filled graves are among the region's most distinctive finds. Roman towns shrank to a fraction of their former size, aqueducts and public buildings fell out of use, and settlement shifted toward hilltops and rural estates. The Lombards gradually converted from Arianism to Catholicism, setting up the church networks that would organise the countryside for centuries.

nodes.name: VIII sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 701–AD 800)
nodes.title: VIII sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 701–AD 800)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 701–AD 800] VIII sec. d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Lombard Tuscany reached its most organised phase, with Lucca a wealthy ducal capital, a revival of stone church building, and a boom in monastic foundations that generated the parchment archives historians still rely on. In 774 Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom, and Frankish counts replaced Lombard dukes, tying the region into a north-European empire. Written wills, land charters and craft workshops show an economy reviving after two centuries of contraction.

nodes.name: IX sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 801–AD 900)
nodes.title: IX sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 801–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 801–AD 900] IX sec. d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Under Carolingian rule Tuscany was governed as a march from Lucca, with Frankish and Lombard counts holding land alongside powerful bishops and monasteries. Church building, land charters and monastic estates shaped the countryside, while coastal towns had to cope with Saracen raiding from the sea. The great families who emerged here would dominate Italian politics for the next two centuries.

nodes.name: X sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 901–AD 1000)
nodes.title: X sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 901–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 901–AD 1000] X sec. d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscany was governed as a march under counts appointed by Italian and German kings, with real power draining towards local lords who were beginning to fortify hilltops and gather peasants into walled villages. Bishops and monasteries such as those around Lucca and Arezzo held huge estates and acted as centres of law and literacy. The century's castle-building set the settlement pattern that still shapes the Tuscan landscape.

nodes.name: XI sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1001–AD 1100)
nodes.title: XI sec. d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1001–AD 1100)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1001–AD 1100] XI sec. d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The march of Tuscany reached its height under the Canossa family, culminating in Countess Matilda, whose castle hosted the emperor's submission to the pope in 1077 during the investiture struggle. Pisa turned to the sea, raiding Muslim ports and building a fleet that would make it a Mediterranean power, and began its marble cathedral in 1063. Church reform, growing towns and new markets were loosening the old rural order.

nodes.name: XII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1101–AD 1200)
nodes.title: XII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1101–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1101–AD 1200] XII secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscan towns turned themselves into self-governing communes, run by elected consuls and bound by oath rather than by counts or bishops, and promptly began fighting each other over land and roads. Pisa and Genoa contested the sea; Florence, Siena, Lucca and Arezzo expanded into their countryside and pulled down rival castles. Money economy, long-distance cloth trade and the Romanesque churches of the period all date from this surge of urban confidence.

nodes.name: XIII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1201–AD 1300)
nodes.title: XIII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1201–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1201–AD 1300] XIII secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscan cities became European financial centres, with Sienese and Florentine bankers handling papal revenues and Florence minting the gold florin in 1252, a coin trusted from London to Constantinople. Guelf and Ghibelline factions split the region in wars that ended with Florence's dominance after Benevento, and popular guilds pushed the old nobility out of government. The same decades produced Dante's early years, Giotto's teachers, and the great mendicant churches and civic palaces still standing in Florence and Siena.

nodes.name: XV secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1401–AD 1500)
nodes.title: XV secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1401–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1401–AD 1500] XV secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Florence became the workshop of the Renaissance: Brunelleschi raised a dome no one knew how to build, Masaccio and Donatello reinvented perspective and the human figure, and scholars hunted down Greek and Latin manuscripts. Banking wealth, above all the Medici's, paid for it, and Cosimo and then Lorenzo ran the republic without ever holding a crown. The city also absorbed Pisa and gained a sea outlet, before Savonarola's brief theocracy and French invasion upended everything at century's end.

hints.source: Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili

nodes.name: XVI secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1501–AD 1600)
nodes.title: XVI secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1501–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1501–AD 1600] XVI secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The republic finally died: Medici dukes returned with imperial backing, and Cosimo I built a centralised state, crushed Siena and had himself made Grand Duke. Vasari laid out the Uffizi and wrote the first history of art, while Michelangelo, Cellini and Giambologna worked for princely patrons rather than guilds. Livorno was developed as a free port open to Jews, Greeks and other outsiders, and the Tuscan countryside settled into the sharecropping pattern that lasted for centuries.

nodes.name: XVII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1601–AD 1700)
nodes.title: XVII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1601–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1601–AD 1700] XVII secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

The old wool and banking wealth drained away as northern Europeans took over Mediterranean trade, and plague in 1630–31 hit the cities hard. Grand-ducal Florence nonetheless kept a scientific edge: Galileo worked under Medici patronage, and the Accademia del Cimento pioneered experimental method with thermometers and barometers. Livorno thrived as a cosmopolitan port while the rural economy stagnated, and the last Medici rulers grew increasingly devout and indebted.

nodes.name: XVIII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1701–AD 1800)
nodes.title: XVIII secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1701–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1701–AD 1800] XVIII secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

With the Medici line extinct, Tuscany passed to the house of Lorraine and became a laboratory of enlightened reform under Grand Duke Peter Leopold, who freed the grain trade, dissolved guilds, reorganised the church and in 1786 abolished the death penalty — the first state in the world to do so. Land was drained and redistributed, and economists in Florence argued about free trade with an audience across Europe. The reforms ended abruptly with French armies and a peasant backlash at the century's close.

nodes.name: XIX secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1801–AD 1900)
nodes.title: XIX secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1801–AD 1900)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1801–AD 1900] XIX secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

French occupation under Napoleon swept away the old Grand Duchy before the Lorraine dynasty returned, ruling a quiet, largely agricultural state famous for its mild government and its foreign residents. Marsh drainage in the Maremma and Val di Chiana, new roads and the first railways reshaped the countryside, while Livorno remained the region's commercial window. Tuscany voted itself into the new Italian kingdom, and Florence briefly served as its capital, gaining boulevards and piazzas at the cost of its medieval centre.

nodes.name: XX secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1901–AD 2000)
nodes.title: XX secolo d.C. (Tuscany, AD 1901–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Tuscany, AD 1901–AD 2000] XX secolo d.C.. Period definition from Report 1.2: Modello dati, applicativo web e servizi erogabili — MAPPA Lab, 2022.

Tuscany passed from a united Italy's liberal monarchy through Fascism, wartime occupation and the bitter fighting along the Gothic Line, which shattered Florence's bridges and many hill towns. Postwar reconstruction brought industry to the Arno valley, mass emigration from the countryside, and the 1966 flood that swamped Florence's libraries and galleries and launched a global rescue of its art. Tourism and heritage protection became central to the region's economy.

nodes.name: Prehispánico Tardío (Córdoba, AD 450–AD 1550)
nodes.title: Prehispánico Tardío (Córdoba, AD 450–AD 1550)
nodes.description:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1550] Prehispánico Tardío. Period definition from Géneros rituales: figuras sexuadas en cerámica y arte rupestre de las sierras de Córdoba (Argentina) — Sebastián Pastor, 2015.

Densely populated valleys of the northwest supported farming communities that terraced hillsides, irrigated fields and built stone villages, some perched on defensible ridges as pukaras. Painted urns of the Santa María style, used to bury children beneath house floors, are the signature artefacts. Warfare and competition among these polities were cut short by Inca conquest and then by Spanish arrival.

nodes.name: Late pre-Hispanic Period (Córdoba, AD 450–AD 1590)
nodes.title: Late pre-Hispanic Period (Córdoba, AD 450–AD 1590)
nodes.description:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1590] Late pre-Hispanic Period. Period definition from Bone tool and tuber processing: a multi-proxy approach at Boyo Paso 2, Argentina — Matías Medina, 2018-08.

In the Sierras and plains of Córdoba, small groups lived in semi-subterranean pit houses, growing maize and beans while still relying heavily on hunting guanaco and gathering algarrobo pods. They ground food in bedrock mortars, made simple incised pottery, and left painted and engraved rock art in the sierra rockshelters. Spanish chroniclers met their descendants, the Comechingones and Sanavirones, when Córdoba was founded in 1573.
