nodes.title: late pre-Hispanic period (Córdoba, AD 450–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1600] late pre-Hispanic period. Period definition from Archaeobotany in central Argentina: macro- and microscopic remains at several archaeological sites from early Late Holocene to early colonial times (3,000–250 bp) — M. Laura López, 2017-07-29.

Small agricultural communities settled the sierras, combining maize and bean cultivation with hunting, gathering of algarrobo, and llama herding. Pit dwellings, grinding hollows worn into bedrock outcrops and painted rock shelters are the most visible traces they left. The sequence runs right up to the Spanish arrival, when these populations were recorded as Comechingones and Sanavirones.

nodes.title: late Pre-Hispanic Period (Córdoba, AD 800–AD 1500)

[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 800–AD 1500] late Pre-Hispanic Period. Period definition from The first quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa Willd) macrobotanical remains at Sierras del Norte (Central Argentina) and their implications in pre-Hispanic subsistence practices — M. Laura López, 2016-08.

In the sierras and valleys, farming communities grew maize, beans and squash, stored grain in pits, and lived in semi-subterranean pit houses clustered in small hamlets. Bedrock mortars ground wild algarrobo pods, llamas provided wool and transport, and painted rock shelters such as Cerro Colorado record the imagery of these groups. Their descendants, the Comechingones and Sanavirones, were the peoples the Spanish encountered.

[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 450–AD 1650] Prehispánico Tardío. Period definition from Informe sobre el sitio El Cajón (Serrezuela, Córdoba, Argentina). La ocupación prehispánica de los micro-ambientes áridos próximos a las Salinas Grandes.  — Sebastián Pastor, 2009.

Densely populated valleys of the northwest supported farming communities that terraced hillsides, irrigated fields and built stone villages, some perched on defensible ridges as pukaras. Painted urns of the Santa María style, used to bury children beneath house floors, are the signature artefacts. Warfare and competition among these polities were cut short by Inca conquest and then by Spanish arrival.

hints.source: Informe sobre el sitio El Cajón (Serrezuela, Córdoba, Argentina). La ocupación prehispánica de los micro-ambientes áridos próximos a las Salinas Grandes.

nodes.name: Late Prehispanic Period (Córdoba, AD 600–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Late Prehispanic Period (Córdoba, AD 600–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Córdoba, Argentina, AD 600–AD 1600] Late Prehispanic Period. Period definition from Colonial rock art: A reflection on resistance and cultural change (16th and 17th century-Córdoba, Argentina) — Andrea Recalde, 2014-09-11.

The hills and plains of central Argentina were occupied by groups later known to the Spanish as Comechingones and Sanavirones, who lived in semi-subterranean pit dwellings, grew maize, beans and squash, and hunted and gathered alongside their crops. They made plain and incised pottery, ground stone tools and mortars in bedrock outcrops, and left painted rock art in the sierras. The period closes with Spanish colonisation and the collapse of these communities under encomienda.

hints.label: Late Prehispanic Period
hints.source: Colonial rock art: A reflection on resistance and cultural change (16th and 17th century-Córdoba, Argentina)

nodes.name: Mesolithic (Poland, 9150 BC–2950 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolithic (Poland, 9150 BC–2950 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 9150 BC–2950 BC] Mesolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 1, 500 000 - 5500 BC — 2016.

After the ice sheets withdrew, birch and then dense oak forest spread over Britain, and hunter-gatherers followed the red deer, wild pig and fish into it. They worked tiny flint microliths into composite arrows and harpoons, built shelters at places like Star Carr, and burned back woodland to draw game into clearings. For most of these millennia Britain was joined to the continent by the drowned plain of Doggerland, and the sea's final closure around 6000 BC turned the population into islanders.

hints.label: Mesolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 1, 500 000 - 5500 BC

nodes.name: Late Mesolithic (Poland, 6050 BC–2950 BC)
nodes.title: Late Mesolithic (Poland, 6050 BC–2950 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 6050 BC–2950 BC] Late Mesolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 1, 500 000 - 5500 BC — 2016.

Hunter-gatherers in dense post-glacial woodland made tiny geometric microliths set into composite arrows and worked the coasts, rivers and clearings with fire to draw in game. Rising seas finally drowned Doggerland during this period, cutting Britain off from the Continent and leaving its foragers on an island. Their world ended with the arrival of farming, and the debate over how much they contributed to what came next is still unresolved.

hints.label: Late Mesolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 1, 500 000 - 5500 BC

nodes.name: Neolithic (Poland, 5499 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Neolithic (Poland, 5499 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 5499 BC–1999 BC] Neolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

In the southern Levant this is where farming villages first take hold: wheat, barley, sheep and goats replace foraging, and settlements like Jericho grow to unprecedented size behind stone walls and a tower. Households plastered their floors, kept the skulls of their dead under them and modelled faces onto them in plaster, and at 'Ain Ghazal produced large human statues of lime plaster over reed frames. Pottery arrives only in the later centuries, long after the farming economy itself.

hints.label: Neolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Early Neolithic (Poland, 5499 BC–4099 BC)
nodes.title: Early Neolithic (Poland, 5499 BC–4099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lesser Poland, Lublin Region, Silesia, Kuyavia, 5499 BC–4099 BC] Early Neolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

Farming, pottery and domesticated animals arrived in Britain, and within a few generations people were building monuments: earthen long barrows over the bones of the dead, ditched causewayed enclosures for gatherings and feasts, and deep flint mines. Woodland was cleared for cereals and pasture, beginning the long transformation of the British landscape. These communities laid the groundwork for the great henge and stone circle building that followed.

hints.label: Early Neolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Middle Neolithic (Poland, 4099 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Neolithic (Poland, 4099 BC–2999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lesser Poland, Lublin Region, Silesia, Kuyavia, Pomerania, Masovia, 4099 BC–2999 BC] Middle Neolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

Communal long barrows and causewayed enclosures fell out of use, and people began building cursus monuments – enormous parallel-ditched avenues running for miles across the landscape – along with the first great henges. Pottery grew heavier and more elaborately decorated, and forest clearance and herding reshaped the countryside. The earthwork phase of Stonehenge belongs to the end of this stretch of time.

hints.label: Middle Neolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Late Neolithic (Poland, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Late Neolithic (Poland, 2999 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 2999 BC–1999 BC] Late Neolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

Farming villages in Greece grew larger and more numerous, some piling up into tells occupied for centuries, and new pottery styles - black-burnished, matt-painted and polychrome wares - mark out distinct regional groups. Trade in Melian obsidian and Spondylus shell linked the Aegean to communities as far away as central Europe. The first copper objects and elaborate figurines appear, foreshadowing the metal-using societies of the following millennium.

hints.label: Late Neolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Eneolithic (Poland, 4099 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.title: Eneolithic (Poland, 4099 BC–1999 BC)
nodes.description:
[Silesia, Greater Poland, Kuyavia, Lesser Poland, Lublin Region, 4099 BC–1999 BC] Eneolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

Copper working and long-distance exchange transformed farming communities that had already been settled for centuries in tells and villages. This is the world of Cucuteni and Gumelnita painted pottery, clay figurines, and the astonishing gold of Varna across the Danube, some of the earliest worked gold anywhere. The tell settlements were abandoned around the later fourth millennium as steppe pastoralist influence and new burial customs spread into the region.

hints.label: Eneolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Early Eneolithic (Poland, 4099 BC–3799 BC)
nodes.title: Early Eneolithic (Poland, 4099 BC–3799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lesser Poland, Lublin Region, Kuyavia, Silesia, 4099 BC–3799 BC] Early Eneolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

Farming communities on the Polish lowlands began using copper — mostly small ornaments and tools traded in from the south — while stone remained the working material. Villages of Funnel Beaker and related groups cleared woodland with ard ploughs and cattle traction, and began building the long earthen barrows and communal monuments that mark the landscape.

hints.label: Early Eneolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Late Eneolithic (Poland, 3799 BC–2799 BC)
nodes.title: Late Eneolithic (Poland, 3799 BC–2799 BC)
nodes.description:
[Lesser Poland, Lublin Region, Silesia, Greater Poland, Kuyavia, 3799 BC–2799 BC] Late Eneolithic. Period definition from The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC — 2017.

Farming communities across the Polish lands shifted towards herding, wagons and copper metallurgy, with Funnel Beaker settlements giving way to Globular Amphora groups and then the widely dispersed Corded Ware culture. Burial changes are striking: single graves under barrows, men with stone battle-axes, women with beads. This is the horizon linked to steppe-derived ancestry spreading into central Europe.

hints.label: Late Eneolithic
hints.source: The past societies : polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the early middle ages. 2, 5500-2000 BC

nodes.name: Bronze Age (Poland, 1999 BC–749 BC)
nodes.title: Bronze Age (Poland, 1999 BC–749 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 1999 BC–749 BC] Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Pile-dwelling villages on the Ljubljana Marshes and hilltop settlements to the east mark a landscape of small farming communities well connected to the Alpine and Pannonian metal trade. From the later centuries the Urnfield tradition took hold, with cremation cemeteries and large hoards of bronze axes, sickles and weapons buried in the ground. These hoards are among the region's richest prehistoric finds and hint at both ritual deposition and the workshops of travelling smiths.

nodes.name: Middle Bronze Age (Poland, 1299 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.title: Middle Bronze Age (Poland, 1299 BC–1099 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 1299 BC–1099 BC] Middle Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Across the Thracian lands, settlement grew more dispersed and mobile, with mound burials and stock-raising economies leaving fewer of the great tells that had dominated earlier millennia. Metalworking continued in bronze, and contacts ran south towards the Aegean world and north across the Danube. It is a comparatively thin archaeological record that sets the stage for the rich warrior burials and gold-bearing elites of the later Bronze Age in the region.

nodes.name: Younger Bronze Age (Poland, 1099 BC–899 BC)
nodes.title: Younger Bronze Age (Poland, 1099 BC–899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 1099 BC–899 BC] Younger Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Lusatian communities cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large, orderly cemeteries, some holding thousands of graves. Settlements grew larger and some were ringed with timber-and-earth ramparts; bronze was plentiful enough to be deposited in hoards in rivers and bogs. The pottery, sheet-bronze vessels and pins show close links across a broad Central European world stretching from the Elbe to the Carpathians.

hints.label: Younger Bronze Age
hints.source: The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC

nodes.name: Late Bronze Age (Poland, 899 BC–749 BC)
nodes.title: Late Bronze Age (Poland, 899 BC–749 BC)
nodes.description:
[Poland, 899 BC–749 BC] Late Bronze Age. Period definition from The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC — 2017.

Farming communities in the Danube, Sava and Morava basins turned to cremation burial in urnfields and produced bronze on a large scale, leaving hoards of swords, axes and ornaments buried in the ground. Fortified settlements on river terraces and along trade routes carrying Baltic amber and Transylvanian metal mark the era. Its groups feed directly into the Iron Age cultures of the central Balkans.

hints.label: Late Bronze Age
hints.source: The past societies : Polish lands from the first evidence of human presence to the Early Middle Ages. 3, 2000 - 500 BC

nodes.name: młodszy okres wpływów rzymski (Poland, AD 160–AD 310)
nodes.title: młodszy okres wpływów rzymski (Poland, AD 160–AD 310)
nodes.description:
[Poland, AD 160–AD 310] młodszy okres wpływów rzymski. Period definition from Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period — Piotr Kaczanowski, 2014.

The Przeworsk and Wielbark cultures flourished on the amber route running from the Baltic to the Danube, and Roman coins, glass, bronze vessels and sigillata reached Polish lands in quantity. Wielbark cemeteries with stone circles and unburnt burials are linked to the Goths, whose southward movement in the third century reshaped the region. Local iron smelting, notably in the Holy Cross Mountains, worked on a scale rarely matched in barbarian Europe.

hints.label: młodszy okres wpływów rzymski
hints.source: Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period

nodes.name: późny okres wpływów rzymskich (Poland, AD 310–AD 375)
nodes.title: późny okres wpływów rzymskich (Poland, AD 310–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Poland, AD 310–AD 375] późny okres wpływów rzymskich. Period definition from Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period — Piotr Kaczanowski, 2014.

Communities of the Przeworsk and Wielbark cultures in the Vistula and Oder basins were still tied to the Roman world by the amber route, importing coins, glass, bronze vessels and weaponry, and burying their dead with them. Local ironworking and pottery production reached an industrial scale in places, notably the smelting centres of the Holy Cross Mountains. The arrival of the Huns on the Black Sea steppe at the end of the fourth century broke these networks and pushed groups westward.

hints.source: Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period

nodes.name: faza C1 okresu wpływów rzymskich (Poland, AD 160–AD 260)
nodes.title: faza C1 okresu wpływów rzymskich (Poland, AD 160–AD 260)
nodes.description:
[Poland, AD 160–AD 260] faza C1 okresu wpływów rzymskich. Period definition from Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period — Piotr Kaczanowski, 2014.

The Late Roman period opens with the aftermath of the Marcomannic Wars, when the frontier trade that had funnelled Roman coin, bronze vessels and glass into the Vistula basin was disrupted and reorganised. Przeworsk communities kept burying their dead with weapons, while Wielbark groups pushed south-east towards the Black Sea — the movement that ancient writers describe as the migration of the Goths. Grave goods from this phase are the richest in Polish Iron Age cemeteries.

A short, unsettled phase matching the crisis decades of the Roman Empire, when the flow of denarii northwards dried up and local craftsmen copied Roman forms rather than importing them. Barbarian raiding across the Danube and Black Sea coasts brought new booty and new fashions in brooches and belt fittings back to the Vistula. Settlement in some areas thins out as populations shifted south and east.

hints.label: faza C2 okresu wpływów rzymskich
hints.source: Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period

nodes.name: faza C3 okresu wpływów rzymskich (Poland, AD 310–AD 375)
nodes.title: faza C3 okresu wpływów rzymskich (Poland, AD 310–AD 375)
nodes.description:
[Poland, AD 310–AD 375] faza C3 okresu wpływów rzymskich. Period definition from Uwagi o chronologii absolutnej początków młodszego okresu wpływów rzymskich w kulturze przeworskiej = Some remarks about the absolute chronology of the beginning of the younger Roman period — Piotr Kaczanowski, 2014.

Contacts with the Roman world revived under the recovered empire of Constantine and his successors, and new brooch and buckle types spread rapidly across the barbarian lands. Przeworsk and Wielbark settlements continued, but the phase closes abruptly around 375 with the arrival of the Huns on the Pontic steppe, the shock that set the Migration Period in motion.

nodes.name: Mesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 9299 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 9299 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 9299 BC–3899 BC] Mesolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. This is a wider term encompassing all the source's Mesolithic sub-periods. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

As the ice retreated and the sea flooded the land bridges, Denmark's hunter-gatherers passed through the Maglemose, Kongemose and Ertebølle traditions, moving from inland lake and bog camps to a rich life on the coast. Waterlogged sites preserve an extraordinary record: dugout canoes, leister prongs, bows, fish weirs, and huge shell middens of oyster and cockle. Ertebølle communities were settled enough to build cemeteries and make pottery while still living entirely by hunting and fishing, and they traded with farming neighbours for generations before taking up farming around 4000 BC.

hints.label: Mesolitikum
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Neolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Neolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 3899 BC–1699 BC] Neolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. This is a wider term encompassing all the source's Neolithic sub-periods. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Farming reached the Oslofjord region only patchily; for most of these millennia people continued to hunt, fish and gather while adopting pottery, polished axes and, eventually, small-scale cereal growing and stockkeeping. Funnel Beaker influences appear early along the coast, followed by Battle Axe/Corded Ware groups with their distinctive shafthole axes and burials. It shows how the agricultural package thinned out and changed shape at the northern edge of Europe.

hints.label: Neolitikum
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Seinmesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.title: Seinmesolitikum (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 6299 BC–3899 BC] Seinmesolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Hunter-fisher groups worked the rising, rebounding coastline of the Oslo fjord, living off seals, fish and wild game and leaving shore-bound camps that are now stranded well inland. Ground and pecked stone axes of Nøstvet type appear alongside blade tools, and sites become larger and more repeatedly used, hinting at a more settled rhythm of life. Farming had not yet arrived.

hints.label: Seinmesolitikum
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Mesolitikum, Fase 3 (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolitikum, Fase 3 (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC] Mesolitikum, Fase 3. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Along a coast still rising rapidly from the sea, hunter-fisher groups settled on shorelines that shifted with every few centuries of land uplift, leaving beach terraces stacked like a staircase inland. This phase is marked by ground stone adzes of greenstone and a heavy reliance on marine resources, seals, fish and sea birds. The strandline dating of these sites gives Norwegian archaeologists an unusually precise chronological tool.

hints.label: Mesolitikum, Fase 3
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Mesolitikum, Fase 4 (Eastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.title: Mesolitikum, Fase 4 (Eastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC] Mesolitikum, Fase 4. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

The last hunter-gatherer centuries in eastern Norway, when coastal settlements grew larger and more repeatedly occupied, and contacts reached south towards the pottery-using fishers of the Baltic and Denmark. Ground stone tools and specialised marine hunting continued right up to the point when farming and Neolithic material culture began to filter northwards.

hints.label: Mesolitikum, Fase 4
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Nøstvetfasen (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.title: Nøstvetfasen (Eastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 6299 BC–4499 BC] Nøstvetfasen. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Coastal hunter-fisher groups along the Oslo Fjord, named for the Nøstvet site, worked greenstone into distinctive pecked and ground core axes—the first heavy woodworking tools in the region. Settlements cluster on what were then shorelines, now stranded well inland by land uplift, and shell and bone refuse points to seal hunting, fishing and boat use. The technology marks a Middle Mesolithic world of stable, resource-rich coastal life before pottery and farming reached Scandinavia.

hints.label: Nøstvetfasen
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.title: Kjeøyfasen (Eastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC)
nodes.description: [Southeastern Norway, 4499 BC–3899 BC] Kjeøyfasen. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

hints.label: Kjeøyfasen
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Tidligneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–3299 BC)
nodes.title: Tidligneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3899 BC–3299 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 3899 BC–3299 BC] Tidligneolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Farming reached the interior and coastlands of eastern Norway in a piecemeal way: cereals, domestic animals and polished flint axes appear alongside continuing hunting, fishing and sealing. Pottery and burial customs echo the Funnel Beaker world of southern Scandinavia, but settlement stayed mobile and small-scale, and many communities kept living much as their Mesolithic ancestors had. The interest lies in the mixture — a frontier zone where the Neolithic package arrived as an option rather than a replacement.

hints.label: Tidligneolitikum
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Mellomneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3299 BC–2349 BC)
nodes.title: Mellomneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 3299 BC–2349 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 3299 BC–2349 BC] Mellomneolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

In the Oslofjord region farming and Funnel Beaker traditions took hold, while inland and along the coast hunting, fishing and pecked-slate technology continued much as before. The later part of the period brought the Battle Axe culture, with single graves, corded pottery and polished boat-shaped axes, and with it new connections south to Denmark and east to Sweden. The mix makes eastern Norway a frontier zone where farmers and foragers lived side by side.

hints.label: Mellomneolitikum
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Mellomneolitikum A (Eastern Norway, 3299 BC–2849 BC)
nodes.title: Mellomneolitikum A (Eastern Norway, 3299 BC–2849 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 3299 BC–2849 BC] Mellomneolitikum A. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Funnel Beaker influence reached the Oslofjord, bringing pottery, polished flint axes and the first traces of cultivation and stock-keeping to eastern Norway. Away from the fjord, communities kept to hunting, fishing and a rich slate and quartzite tool tradition, so the archaeological picture is one of contrast rather than a clean transition to farming.

hints.label: Mellomneolitikum A
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Mellomneolitikum B (Eastern Norway, 2849 BC–2349 BC)
nodes.title: Mellomneolitikum B (Eastern Norway, 2849 BC–2349 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 2849 BC–2349 BC] Mellomneolitikum B. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

The Battle Axe culture arrived, recognisable from its cord-decorated beakers and polished boat-shaped stone axes, buried with individuals rather than in collective tombs. Herding and a more mobile, cattle-centred economy spread through the lowlands, part of the wider Corded Ware expansion that reshaped populations across northern Europe.

hints.label: Mellomneolitikum B
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Seinneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 2349 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.title: Seinneolitikum (Eastern Norway, 2349 BC–1699 BC)
nodes.description:
[Southeastern Norway, 2349 BC–1699 BC] Seinneolitikum. Spatial coverage: Eastern Norway, Southern Norway. Period definition from Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum — Hege Damlien, 2021-11-15.

Farming and herding took firm hold in eastern Norway, along with a new material culture centred on finely pressure-flaked flint daggers imitating the metal blades of the Continent. Two-aisled longhouses appear, along with burials under cairns and the first regular use of bronze objects obtained through southern Scandinavian networks. The groundwork for the Nordic Bronze Age was laid here.

hints.label: Seinneolitikum
hints.source: Steinalderen i Sørøst-Norge: Faglig program for steinalderundersøkelser ved Kulturhistorisk museum

nodes.name: Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena (Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1660)
nodes.title: Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena (Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1660)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1660] Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena. Period definition from Investigations at Pichao: Introduction to Studies in the Santa María Valley, North-western Argentina — Acreche Noemí, 2001.

Spanish entradas from Peru and Chile pushed into the valleys of the Northwest, founding short-lived towns and imposing encomienda tribute on Diaguita and other communities. Resistance was fierce and prolonged, culminating in the Calchaquí wars; defeat brought forced relocation of whole populations, and settlement sites from these decades mix indigenous pottery with European glass, iron and glazed ware.

hints.label: Periodo de contacto hispano-indígena
hints.source: Investigations at Pichao: Introduction to Studies in the Santa María Valley, North-western Argentina

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1500] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Desarrollo del asentamiento del sitio STucTav 5 (El Pichao), provincia de Tucumán, comentarios sobre dataciones de 14C y luminiscencia — Cornell Per, 1993.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Desarrollo del asentamiento del sitio STucTav 5 (El Pichao), provincia de Tucumán, comentarios sobre dataciones de 14C y luminiscencia

nodes.name: Spanish Native Period (Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Spanish Native Period (Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1600)
nodes.description: [Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1530–AD 1600] Spanish Native Period. Period definition from The excavation of the cemeteries 1991-1992 — Johansson Nils , 2001.

nodes.name: Late Pre-agricultural Period (Tucumán, 5999 BC–499 BC)
nodes.title: Late Pre-agricultural Period (Tucumán, 5999 BC–499 BC)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 5999 BC–499 BC] Late Pre-agricultural Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

Mobile hunting and gathering groups worked the valleys, high puna and eastern forest margins of northwest Argentina, hunting camelids and deer with stone-tipped weapons and returning repeatedly to rock shelters and open camps. Their traces are chipped stone tools, grinding equipment, hearths and painted or engraved rock art. Over these millennia people began cultivating and herding, gradually leading into the settled farming villages of the region.

hints.label: Late Pre-agricultural Period
hints.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

nodes.name: Archaic Period (Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC)
nodes.title: Archaic Period (Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 499 BC–199 BC] Archaic Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

The island's many small city-states — Knossos, Gortyn, Dreros, Lyktos — produced the earliest surviving Greek law inscribed on stone, and a strong tradition of hammered bronze work and Daedalic sculpture that influenced sculptors on the mainland. Votive deposits in the Idaean Cave and the temples of Dreros and Prinias show a distinctive local blend of Greek and Near Eastern forms. Crete then turned inward, staying out of the Persian Wars and playing little part in the classical politics that followed.

hints.label: Archaic Period
hints.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

nodes.name: Regional Development Period (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Regional Development Period (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1480] Regional Development Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

After the collapse of the wide-reaching Aguada style, the valleys of the Argentine northwest split into competing local polities with their own pottery, dress and burial customs. Populations concentrated in dense hillside settlements and fortified pukaras, farming irrigated terraces and burying infants in painted funerary urns. The Inca conquest at the end of the period absorbed these chiefdoms into Collasuyu, resettling populations and building roads and administrative centres among them.

hints.label: Regional Development Period
hints.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

nodes.name: Imperial Period (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Imperial Period (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1536] Imperial Period. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

Inca armies pushed south into the valleys of northwest Argentina, absorbing local chiefdoms into the province of Qollasuyu. Roads, waystations, hilltop administrative centres and relocated groups of settlers changed how people lived, and imperial-style pottery and metalwork appear alongside older local wares. Spanish entradas arrived while this system was still young, and it collapsed quickly.

hints.label: Imperial Period
hints.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

nodes.name: Spanish Contact Periods (Tucumán, AD 1536–AD 1660)
nodes.title: Spanish Contact Periods (Tucumán, AD 1536–AD 1660)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1536–AD 1660] Spanish Contact Periods. Period definition from An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection — Stenborg Per, 1999.

Spanish expeditions pushing south from Peru and east from Chile met dense, fortified farming communities in the valleys of northwest Argentina. Encomienda demands, mission settlement and forced resettlement provoked the long Calchaquí wars, which kept parts of the region outside colonial control for over a century. Sites of the period mix indigenous pottery with glass beads, iron and European animal bone, before whole populations were deported and dispersed.

hints.label: Spanish Contact Periods
hints.source: An attempt at further classification of parts of the material belonging to the 1930.39 collection

nodes.title: Formativo (Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800)
nodes.description: [Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 800] Formativo. Period definition from Consideraciones acerca de la variabilidad formal en el diseño de las plantas de arquitectura en el NOA durante las Etapas Formativa y de Desarrollos Regionales — Giani Laura Margarita, 1999.

hints.label: Formativo
hints.source: Consideraciones acerca de la variabilidad formal en el diseño de las plantas de arquitectura en el NOA durante las Etapas Formativa y de Desarrollos Regionales

nodes.name: Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1470] Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Nuevos avances en las prospecciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de los Cardones — Rivolta Gustavo Mario, 2005.

After the collapse of earlier region-wide styles, distinct local polities emerged across the Northwest, each with its own pottery and territory. Populations concentrated in large settlements and hilltop pukarás, irrigation and terracing expanded, and warfare left its mark in fortifications and weapons. Painted funerary urns for infant burials are among the most recognisable objects of the era, which closed with the Inca annexation of the region.

hints.label: Etapa cultural de los Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Nuevos avances en las prospecciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de los Cardones

nodes.name: Período Arcaico (Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC)
nodes.title: Período Arcaico (Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 7050 BC–550 BC] Período Arcaico. Period definition from Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina) — Gómez Augier Julián Patricio , 2020-11-30.

Small mobile bands hunted guanaco and deer, gathered algarrobo pods and chañar, and camped in rockshelters and open sites across the ranges and valleys. Over these millennia grinding stones, storage and the first tended plants and camelids appear, marking the slow shift from foraging to food production that made settled village life possible.

hints.label: Período Arcaico
hints.source: Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Formativo (Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 750)
nodes.title: Período Formativo (Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 750)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, 550 BC–AD 750] Período Formativo. Period definition from Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina) — Gómez Augier Julián Patricio , 2020-11-30.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.

hints.label: Período Formativo
hints.source: Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500] Período Tardío. Period definition from Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina) — Gómez Augier Julián Patricio , 2020-11-30.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.source: Análisis multitemporal de las formas de ocupación del espacio prehispánico en el Sector Occidental de las Cumbres Calchaquíes de la provincia de Tucumán (Argentina)

[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1480] Período Tardío. Period definition from Distribución espacial de los asentamientos de los Períodos de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca en el tercio central de la Sierra de Quilmes (Valle de Yocavil-Tucumán — Maldonado Mario Gabriel, 2014.

nodes.name: Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Santa María, Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1535] Período Inca. Period definition from Distribución espacial de los asentamientos de los Períodos de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca en el tercio central de la Sierra de Quilmes (Valle de Yocavil-Tucumán — Maldonado Mario Gabriel, 2014.

Cuzco's armies incorporated the Northwest into Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, roughly a lifetime before the Spanish arrived. Roads, tambos, storage complexes and administrative centres were built, local lords were co-opted, and mitmaqkuna colonists were moved in to work fields and mines. [Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 299 BC–AD 500] Cultura Tafí. Period definition from Investigaciones arqueológicas en la Quebrada de la Ciénaga (Dpto. Tafí, Tucumán) — Cremonte María Beatriz, 1996.

The first settled farming villages of the Tucumán highlands, whose people lived in circular stone houses grouped around patios and grew maize on terraced slopes. Farming villages took root in the valleys of Tucumán, with stone-walled house compounds, cultivated terraces and llama herds. The Tafí communities of the highland valleys left standing menhirs and carved stone monuments, while the Candelaria groups of the wooded eastern slopes made distinctive modelled pottery. Pottery, weaving and early metalwork all appear here for the first time in the region.

The stage when people in the Argentine Northwest settled into permanent farming hamlets, growing maize and other crops on terraced slopes and keeping llamas. Circular stone house compounds, grinding stones, ceramic vessels and the carved menhirs of the Tafí valley all belong to this world. It marks the shift from mobile foraging to the rooted village life on which all later Andean societies in the region were built.

[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 199 BC–AD 850] Formative Period. Period definition from Dynamic places, durable structures: Early Formative agropastoral settlements of the southern Andes, Argentina — Salazar Julián, 2016-11-21.

Farming villages took hold in the valleys and piedmont of northwestern Argentina, with maize, beans and squash cultivated alongside herds of llamas. nodes.name: Regional Developments Period (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Regional Developments Period (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1480] Regional Developments Period. Period definition from Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis — Páez María Cecilia, 2014-05-14.

After the collapse of the wide-reaching Aguada style, the valleys of the Argentine northwest split into competing local polities with their own pottery, dress and burial customs. Populations concentrated in dense hillside settlements and fortified pukaras, farming irrigated terraces and burying infants in painted funerary urns. The Inca conquest at the end of the period absorbed these chiefdoms into Collasuyu, resettling populations and building roads and administrative centres among them.

hints.label: Regional Developments Period
hints.source: Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis

nodes.name: Inca Period/Late Horizon (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1530)
nodes.title: Inca Period/Late Horizon (Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1530)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 1480–AD 1530] Inca Period/Late Horizon. Period definition from Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis — Páez María Cecilia, 2014-05-14.

The Inca state absorbed the valleys and puna of the far south, tying them to Cusco through roads, tambos and administrative centres and reorganising labour for farming and mining. Imperial pottery styles and architecture appear at local sites, mixed with long-established regional traditions. The arrangement lasted barely two generations before Spanish expeditions arrived from Peru and Chile.

hints.label: Inca Period/Late Horizon
hints.source: Changes in pottery production under Inca rule in a frontier site in the Tafí Valley, Argentina: a mineralogical analysis

nodes.name: Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 900–AD 1430] Período Tardío. Period definition from Desafiando esencialismos. Las vasijas globulares negro sobre rojo del Valle de Tafí (Tucumán, Argentina) — Páez María Cecilia, 2023-02-10.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.label: Período Tardío
hints.source: Desafiando esencialismos. Las vasijas globulares negro sobre rojo del Valle de Tafí (Tucumán, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1430–AD 1530)
nodes.title: Período Inca (Tucumán, AD 1430–AD 1530)
nodes.description:

Cuzco's armies incorporated the Northwest into Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, roughly a lifetime before the Spanish arrived. Roads, tambos, storage complexes and administrative centres were built, local lords were co-opted, and mitmaqkuna colonists were moved in to work fields and mines. Cuzco-style polychrome pottery and bronze appear in local villages, and mountain summits were turned into shrines.

nodes.title: Tafí Culture (Tucumán, 359 BC–AD 800)

[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, 359 BC–AD 800] Tafí Culture. Period definition from Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina — Sampietro Vattuone María Marta, 2009.

The first settled farming villages of the highland valleys of northwest Argentina, whose people grew maize and herded llamas around clusters of circular stone-walled house compounds. They are best known for carved stone menhirs, some over two metres tall, set up in ceremonial spaces and marked with stylised human and feline faces. Their terraces and field walls laid the groundwork for the later, larger societies of the region.

nodes.name: Santa María Culture (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Santa María Culture (Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Tafí, Tucumán, AD 1000–AD 1400] Santa María Culture. Period definition from Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina — Sampietro Vattuone María Marta, 2009.

A society of the Calchaquí valleys of northwest Argentina, known above all for its large painted funerary urns, which held the remains of infants and are decorated with staring faces, toads, snakes and rheas. Its people lived in dense stone-built towns, many perched on defensible hilltops behind walls, farming maize on terraces and herding llamas. The fortified settlements point to endemic warfare; the Inca absorbed the region in the fifteenth century, and its descendants fought the Spanish for over a hundred years.

hints.label: Santa María Culture
hints.source: Relationships between archaeology and landscape in two preandean valleys from northwest Argentina

Early village life in the valleys and eastern slopes of Tucumán, best known from the Tafí valley with its circular stone house compounds, terraced fields and carved stone menhirs set in ceremonial spaces. Households farmed maize and kept llamas, ground their food with stone mortars, and buried their dead in cists near the home. In the humid piedmont to the east, related communities produced the modelled funerary urns of the Candelaria tradition.

nodes.title: Candelaria II (Tucumán, AD 200–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Piedemonte Oriental - Tierras Bajas, Tucumán, AD 200–AD 400] Candelaria II. Period definition from Investigaciones Arqueológicas en el sector meridional de las Selvas Occidentales — Heredia Osvaldo R., 1974.

In the humid wooded eastern slopes of northwest Argentina, farming communities lived in dispersed hamlets and buried their dead in large ceramic urns. Their grey-black pottery, often modelled with human and animal faces, links them to neighbouring valley cultures and shows how maize agriculture and settled village life spread down from the highlands into the yungas forest.

hints.label: Candelaria II
hints.source: Investigaciones Arqueológicas en el sector meridional de las Selvas Occidentales

nodes.name: Candelaria III (Tucumán, AD 400–AD 700)
nodes.title: Candelaria III (Tucumán, AD 400–AD 700)
nodes.description:
[Piedemonte Oriental - Tierras Bajas, Tucumán, AD 400–AD 700] Candelaria III. Period definition from Investigaciones Arqueológicas en el sector meridional de las Selvas Occidentales — Heredia Osvaldo R., 1974.

The later centuries of the urn-burial tradition in the forested eastern ranges, with continuing village agriculture and modelled grey pottery. Contact with the valleys to the west is visible in the ceramics, and the population that emerged from these communities occupied the region until the Inca and then the Spanish arrived.

hints.label: Candelaria III
hints.source: Investigaciones Arqueológicas en el sector meridional de las Selvas Occidentales

nodes.name: Candelaria IV (Tucumán, AD 700–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Candelaria IV (Tucumán, AD 700–AD 1000)

[Piedemonte Oriental - Tierras Bajas, Tucumán, AD 700–AD 1000] Candelaria IV. Period definition from Investigaciones Arqueológicas en el sector meridional de las Selvas Occidentales — Heredia Osvaldo R., 1974.

The final stretch of the Candelaria ceramic tradition in the wooded eastern foothills of the Andes, made by farming communities who grew maize, kept llamas and lived in scattered hamlets. They are best known for their dark burnished pottery and modelled human faces and figures, including large burial urns used for the dead. Their world was eventually absorbed into the denser, more fortified settlement patterns of the late pre-Inca centuries.

hints.label: Candelaria IV
hints.source: Investigaciones Arqueológicas en el sector meridional de las Selvas Occidentales

nodes.title: Desarrollos Regionales (Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500)

[Piedemonte Oriental - Tierras Bajas, Tucumán, AD 750–AD 1500] Desarrollos Regionales. After the Tiwanaku-influenced horizon faded, the valleys and highlands of northwest Argentina broke into a mosaic of local polities, best known through the Santa María and related groups. Communities clustered in dense, walled hilltop settlements — pukaras — with terraced fields below, buried their dead in painted urns, and worked copper and bronze. Warfare and competition between chiefdoms shaped the landscape until Inca armies absorbed the region in the late fifteenth century.

nodes.description:
[Piedemonte Oriental - Tierras Bajas, Tucumán, 999 BC–AD 1000] Estilo Candelaria. Period definition from Vida y muerte de los instrumentos musicales prehispánicos de las tierras bajas del Noroeste Argentino — Caria Mario Alejandro, 2021-07-21.

The Candelaria peoples farmed the humid eastern slopes and valleys below the Andes, growing maize in forest clearings and living in scattered hamlets rather than towns. They are best known for their pottery: grey and blackish vessels with modelled human faces and animal forms, and large urns in which the dead were buried in a crouched position. Their material culture links the highland Andean world with the tropical lowlands to the east.

hints.label: Estilo Candelaria
hints.source: Vida y muerte de los instrumentos musicales prehispánicos de las tierras bajas del Noroeste Argentino

nodes.name: 2° milenio d.C. (Tucumán, AD 1001–AD 2000)
nodes.title: 2° milenio d.C. (Tucumán, AD 1001–AD 2000)
nodes.description:
[Piedemonte Oriental - Tierras Bajas, Tucumán, AD 1001–AD 2000] 2° milenio d.C.. Period definition from La alimentación prehispánica en las tierras bajas de Tucumán (Argentina): una primera aproximación a su análisis — Caria Mario Alejandro , 2020-12-23.

In the valleys of northwestern Argentina, farming communities of the Santa María and related traditions built dense stone settlements, terraced fields and painted funerary urns before the Inca absorbed the region into Collasuyu in the late 1400s. Spanish colonisation from the 1550s brought encomiendas and the long Calchaquí wars, ending with the forced removal of whole populations in the 1660s. Later centuries saw Tucumán become a sugar-growing province and the site of Argentina's declaration of independence in 1816.

nodes.name: Período de expansión incaica-Inca Imperial (Santiago del Estero, AD 1475–AD 1532)
nodes.title: Período de expansión incaica-Inca Imperial (Santiago del Estero, AD 1475–AD 1532)
nodes.description:
[Santiago del Estero, AD 1475–AD 1532] Período de expansión incaica-Inca Imperial. Period definition from Posibles influencias incaicas en Santiago del Estero — Gramajo de Martínez Moreno Amalia Josefina, 1982.

The Inca state absorbed the southern Andes into Collasuyu, its southeastern quarter, extending roads, way stations and administrative centres far beyond the Cuzco heartland. Local populations were counted, taxed in labour and sometimes resettled as mitmaqkuna colonists, and Cuzco-style pottery and architecture appear at provincial sites. In the eastern lowlands the imperial presence was thinner, an indirect frontier zone rather than a fully governed province — and it lasted barely two generations before the Spanish arrival.

hints.label: Período de expansión incaica-Inca Imperial
hints.source: Posibles influencias incaicas en Santiago del Estero

nodes.name: Late pottery-making and farming (Santiago del Estero, AD 1150–AD 1550)
nodes.title: Late pottery-making and farming (Santiago del Estero, AD 1150–AD 1550)
nodes.description: [Santiago del Estero, AD 1150–AD 1550] Late pottery-making and farming. Period definition from First Approach to Study the Presence of Domesticated Camelids (Lama glama) in the Chaco‐Santiago Region, a Marginal Zone of the South Central Andes — del Papa Luis Manuel , 2012-08-15. Farming communities of the Dulce and Salado floodplains grew maize, squash and beans on seasonally flooded land, living in villages built on low mounds above the water. They made the distinctive incised and painted wares of the Sunchituyoj and Averías traditions, including modelled zoomorphic vessels and urn burials. The sequence ends with the arrival of Spanish expeditions, who found dense riverine populations here before disease and encomienda broke them up.

hints.label: Late pottery-making and farming
hints.source: First Approach to Study the Presence of Domesticated Camelids (Lama glama) in the Chaco‐Santiago Region, a Marginal Zone of the South Central Andes

nodes.name: Formativo Inferior (Salta, 599 BC–AD 400)
nodes.title: Formativo Inferior (Salta, 599 BC–AD 400)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, 599 BC–AD 400] Formativo Inferior. Period definition from Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos) — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 1983.

Settled agricultural life in the valleys and eastern piedmont of the Argentine Northwest, based on maize, quinoa and camelid herding. Communities lived in small dispersed hamlets with round stone-walled houses and cultivation plots, made incised and painted pottery, and worked copper and gold. Regional exchange networks carried pottery styles, obsidian and Amazonian and Pacific goods across the Andes.

hints.label: Formativo Inferior
hints.source: Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos)

nodes.title: Formativo Superior (Salta, AD 400–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 400–AD 900] Formativo Superior. Period definition from Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos) — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 1983.

The later stage of village farming society in the Argentine Northwest, when settlements grew larger and more clustered, agricultural terraces and irrigation spread, and craft production in ceramics and metal became more specialised. Distinct regional pottery styles emerged, and differences in burial goods hint at growing inequality. These communities are the direct ancestors of the fortified towns and chiefdoms of the following Regional Development period.

hints.label: Formativo Superior

nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Salta, 899 BC–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, 899 BC–AD 1470] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos) — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 1983.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.

nodes.name: Período Inka (Salta, AD 1470–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Período Inka (Salta, AD 1470–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 1470–AD 1535] Período Inka. Period definition from Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos) — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 1983.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.

hints.label: Período Inka
hints.source: Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos)

nodes.name: Período Hispano-Indigena (Salta, AD 1535–AD 1660)
nodes.title: Período Hispano-Indigena (Salta, AD 1535–AD 1660)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 1535–AD 1660] Período Hispano-Indigena. Period definition from Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos) — Raffino Rodolfo Adelio, 1983.

Spanish entradas into the valleys of the Northwest collided with Diaguita-Calchaquí communities, producing a century of encomienda demands, refounded towns and repeated uprisings. Archaeologically it shows as indigenous villages with European glass beads, iron tools, horse and cattle bone and majolica alongside traditional urn burials and painted wares. It ends with the crushing of the last Calchaquí resistance and the forced relocation of whole communities far from their homelands.

hints.source: Sitios arqueológicos del Valle Calchaquí Medio (Departamentos de Molinos y San Carlos)

nodes.name: Período Medio (Salta, AD 600–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Período Medio (Salta, AD 600–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 600–AD 1000] Período Medio. Period definition from Nuevos aportes a la prehistoria del valle Calchaquí. Noroeste argentino — Pollard Gordon, 1983.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.

nodes.name: Formativo de las sociedades agrícolas en el Sur del Valle Calchaquí (Salta, 899 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Formativo de las sociedades agrícolas en el Sur del Valle Calchaquí (Salta, 899 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Sur, Salta, 899 BC–AD 1000] Formativo de las sociedades agrícolas en el Sur del Valle Calchaquí. Period definition from El Alisar y El Divisadero. Dos Sitios Arqueológicos con Pinturas Rupestres en Cafayate, Salta. — Ledesma Rossana Elizabeth, 2004.

Agricultural communities settled the southern Calchaquí valley, farming maize and squash on terraced and irrigated plots and pasturing llama herds on the surrounding slopes. Their villages of stone-walled compounds, with grinding stones, storage cists and painted pottery, show a way of life that lasted well over a millennium. Later in the sequence settlements grew and clustered, foreshadowing the dense fortified towns of the Calchaquí chiefdoms.

hints.label: Formativo de las sociedades agrícolas en el Sur del Valle Calchaquí
hints.source: El Alisar y El Divisadero. Dos Sitios Arqueológicos con Pinturas Rupestres en Cafayate, Salta.

nodes.name: Período Formativo (Salta, AD 1–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Período Formativo (Salta, AD 1–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Sur, Salta, AD 1–AD 1000] Período Formativo. Period definition from La figura humana en el arte rupestre en el sur del valle Calchaquí (Salta, Argentina) — Ledesma Rossana , 2015.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.

hints.label: Período Formativo
hints.source: La figura humana en el arte rupestre en el sur del valle Calchaquí (Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Tardío (Salta, AD 900–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Tardío (Salta, AD 900–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 900–AD 1400] Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Tardío. Period definition from El Valle Calchaquí Medio (Salta, Argentina) durante los siglos XV-XVII: aportes desde el registro arqueológico y las fuentes documentales — Castellanos María Cecilia, 2016-03.

Local polities in the Calchaquí and neighbouring valleys built agglomerated stone settlements, some heavily fortified, and farmed terraced slopes with irrigation. Each group developed its own ceramic style, and bronze ornaments and weapons became widespread. Population growth and visible defence works point to sustained competition before Inca rule imposed a new order.

hints.source: El Valle Calchaquí Medio (Salta, Argentina) durante los siglos XV-XVII: aportes desde el registro arqueológico y las fuentes documentales

nodes.name: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca (Salta, AD 900–AD 1500)
nodes.title: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca (Salta, AD 900–AD 1500)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 900–AD 1500] Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca. Period definition from Aproximación a la tecnología cerámica y metalúrgica en las quebradas altas del Noroeste Argentino. El caso de Tacuil, valle Calchaquí medio, Salta, Argentina. — Castellanos María Cecilia, 2020-12-28.

Centuries of independent valley polities, with terraced agriculture, nucleated settlements and defensive pukaras, followed by their absorption into the Inca empire. Local painted wares and urn burials continued while imperial roads, tambos and administrative sites were grafted onto the landscape. The sequence ends on the eve of European contact.

hints.label: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca
hints.source: Aproximación a la tecnología cerámica y metalúrgica en las quebradas altas del Noroeste Argentino. El caso de Tacuil, valle Calchaquí medio, Salta, Argentina.

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Salta, AD 400–AD 900)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (Salta, AD 400–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Medios, Salta, AD 400–AD 900] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from “Era la tierra doblada con que se peleó arriesgadamente…”: Paisajes de guerra y resistencia indígena en Gualfín hacia mediados del siglo XVII (Valle Calchaquí, Gobernación del Tucumán) — Castellanos María Cecilia, 2022-08-02.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: “Era la tierra doblada con que se peleó arriesgadamente…”: Paisajes de guerra y resistencia indígena en Gualfín hacia mediados del siglo XVII (Valle Calchaquí, Gobernación del Tucumán)

nodes.name: Período previo a la conquista inka (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1430)
nodes.title: Período previo a la conquista inka (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1430)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Sur, Salta, AD 1000–AD 1430] Período previo a la conquista inka. Period definition from Nuevos datos sobre la prehistoria local en la quebrada de Tolombón. Pcia. De Salta. Argentina — Williams Verónica Isabel, 2003.

Valley communities lived in large stone-built settlements, many of them perched on defensible heights with encircling walls, farming terraced slopes and herding llamas. Distinctive urn burials and painted funerary ceramics mark the period, and warfare between neighbouring groups appears to have been frequent. These independent polities retained strong local identities right up to their absorption by the Inca state.

hints.label: Período previo a la conquista inka
hints.source: Nuevos datos sobre la prehistoria local en la quebrada de Tolombón. Pcia. De Salta. Argentina

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Sur, Salta, AD 1000–AD 1536] Período de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca. Period definition from El uso del espacio a nivel estatal en el sur del Tawantinsuyu — Williams Verónica Isabel, 2010.

Independent valley societies with their own ceramic styles and fortified settlements were drawn, in the final century, into the Inca empire. Imperial roads, tambos and mountaintop shrines were built across the region, and high-altitude ritual sites here have preserved some of the most remarkable Inca offerings known. The sequence closes with Spanish entry into the Calchaquí valleys.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales e Inca
hints.source: El uso del espacio a nivel estatal en el sur del Tawantinsuyu

nodes.name: Período Medio (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Período Medio (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1000–AD 1450] Período Medio. Period definition from Experiencia de la muerte y la representación de las personas en las prácticas funerarias del valle Calchaquí Norte — Acuto Felix, 2011-06-01.

The centuries when the Aguada tradition dominated the Northwest, famous for its dark polished ceramics engraved with feline, serpent and sacrificer imagery. Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.

hints.label: Período Medio
hints.source: Experiencia de la muerte y la representación de las personas en las prácticas funerarias del valle Calchaquí Norte

nodes.name: Late Intermediate period (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Late Intermediate period (Salta, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1000–AD 1450] Late Intermediate period. Period definition from Recognising strategies for conquered territories: a case study from the Inka North Calchaquí Valley — Acuto Felix Alejandro, 2012-12.

Following the collapse of Tiwanaku-linked influence, valley populations grew and reorganised into competing local chiefdoms, farming irrigated terraces and herding llamas. Settlements shifted onto defensible heights, and elaborately painted funerary urns for infants are among the most distinctive finds. The sequence ends with Inca conquest, which overlaid an imperial administration on these local polities.

hints.label: Late Intermediate period
hints.source: Recognising strategies for conquered territories: a case study from the Inka North Calchaquí Valley

nodes.name: Inka occupation (Salta, AD 1450–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Inka occupation (Salta, AD 1450–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1450–AD 1536] Inka occupation. Period definition from Recognising strategies for conquered territories: a case study from the Inka North Calchaquí Valley — Acuto Felix Alejandro, 2012-12.

Inca administrators extended the royal road and a network of tambos and fortified centres through the Calchaquí and Lerma valleys, drawing local communities into imperial tribute and mining. Mountaintop sanctuaries, including some of the highest sacrificial sites known, mark the state's presence on the peaks. Spanish entradas found these arrangements still in place, and the valleys' peoples resisted them for well over a century.

hints.label: Inka occupation
hints.source: Recognising strategies for conquered territories: a case study from the Inka North Calchaquí Valley

nodes.name: Late Intermediate Period (Salta, AD 1250–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Late Intermediate Period (Salta, AD 1250–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1250–AD 1450] Late Intermediate Period. Period definition from Death, personhood, and relatedness in the South Andes a thousand years ago — Acuto Felix Alejandro, 2014-07-08.

With no overarching state, communities in the northwestern Andean valleys built dense hilltop settlements and defensive pukaras, a sign of chronic conflict over land and water. Santa María painted urns, irrigated terracing and llama caravan trade tie the valleys into a wide exchange network. Inca armies absorbed the whole region at the close of the period, imposing roads, garrisons and forced resettlement.

hints.label: Late Intermediate Period
hints.source: Death, personhood, and relatedness in the South Andes a thousand years ago

nodes.name: Período Tardío (Salta, AD 900–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (Salta, AD 900–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 900–AD 1470] Período Tardío. Period definition from El sitio Mariscal (SSalCac5): Investigaciones sobre la vida cotidiana en una aldea prehispánica del valle Calchaquí Norte — Kergaravat Marisa, 2014.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.label: Período Tardío
hints.source: El sitio Mariscal (SSalCac5): Investigaciones sobre la vida cotidiana en una aldea prehispánica del valle Calchaquí Norte

nodes.name: Período Intermedio Tardío (Salta, AD 900–AD 1460)
nodes.title: Período Intermedio Tardío (Salta, AD 900–AD 1460)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 900–AD 1460] Período Intermedio Tardío. Period definition from Las vasijas y su potencial como sujetos estabilizadores de seres incompletos: Prácticas mortuorias de infantes durante el período Tardío en el Valle Calchaquí Norte — Amuedo Claudia, 2015-06.

After the collapse of the Middle Period order, populations in the valleys built dense settlements, extensive terraced fields and irrigation systems, and increasingly clustered in defensible hilltop pukaras. Regional identities are visible in distinct painted pottery styles and in urn burials of infants beneath house floors. The rising evidence for warfare and territorial competition sets the stage for Inca conquest.

hints.source: Las vasijas y su potencial como sujetos estabilizadores de seres incompletos: Prácticas mortuorias de infantes durante el período Tardío en el Valle Calchaquí Norte

After the collapse of the Middle Period order, populations in the valleys built dense settlements, extensive terraced fields and irrigation systems, and increasingly clustered in defensible hilltop pukaras. Regional identities are visible in distinct painted pottery styles and in urn burials of infants beneath house floors. The rising evidence for warfare and territorial competition sets the stage for Inca conquest.
