hints.source: ¿Qué, cómo y quiénes comen a través de un ushnu? Historias de comensalidad en el ushnu de Guitián (Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período de contacto hispano-indígena (Salta, AD 1535–AD 1664)
nodes.title: Período de contacto hispano-indígena (Salta, AD 1535–AD 1664)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1535–AD 1664] Período de contacto hispano-indígena. Period definition from ¿Qué, cómo y quiénes comen a través de un ushnu? Historias de comensalidad en el ushnu de Guitián (Salta, Argentina) — Amuedo Claudia, 2020-12-19.

Spanish expeditions pushing down from Peru and across from Chile met the fortified valley communities of the northwest, and the encounter lasted more than a century. Encomienda labour demands, missionaries and epidemic disease reshaped indigenous life, while repeated uprisings — the Calchaquí wars — kept whole valleys outside colonial control until the 1660s, when the defeated populations were deported wholesale to distant settlements. Archaeologically the period shows up as mixed assemblages: European glass, glazed ware and iron alongside traditional pottery.

hints.label: Período de contacto hispano-indígena
hints.source: ¿Qué, cómo y quiénes comen a través de un ushnu? Historias de comensalidad en el ushnu de Guitián (Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Inka (Salta, AD 1430–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Período Inka (Salta, AD 1430–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1430–AD 1535] Período Inka. Period definition from Recrear el cosmos en la cocina: cocción y comensalidad en el sitio Guitián (Salta, Argentina) — Amuedo Claudia, 2022-08-06.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.

hints.label: Período Inka
hints.source: Recrear el cosmos en la cocina: cocción y comensalidad en el sitio Guitián (Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Formativo en el Valle Calchaquí Norte (Salta, 750 BC–AD 450)
nodes.title: Período Formativo en el Valle Calchaquí Norte (Salta, 750 BC–AD 450)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, 750 BC–AD 450] Período Formativo en el Valle Calchaquí Norte. Period definition from Primeros entierros y primeros cultivos en el Valle Calchaquí: Los inicios del Holoceno y del primer milenio en el sitio Puente del Diablo (SSalLap20) — Lema Verónica Soledad , 2022-05-19.

Farming settlements filled the northern Calchaquí valley, building stone-walled house compounds and vast fields bounded by rock alignments and terraces along the river terraces and alluvial fans. Residents cultivated maize, quinoa and beans, herded llamas and traded obsidian and other goods across the puna, creating the agrarian landscape that later towns would inherit.

hints.label: Período Formativo en el Valle Calchaquí Norte
hints.source: Primeros entierros y primeros cultivos en el Valle Calchaquí: Los inicios del Holoceno y del primer milenio en el sitio Puente del Diablo (SSalLap20)

nodes.name: Formativo Temprano (Salta, 1550 BC–450 BC)
nodes.title: Formativo Temprano (Salta, 1550 BC–450 BC)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, 1550 BC–450 BC] Formativo Temprano. Period definition from El espacio doméstico en las ocupaciones aldeanas del valle Calchaquí Norte (Salta, Argentina) — Rivolta María Clara, 2017.

The transition from mobile hunting and gathering to settled life in the valleys of the Argentine Northwest. People began cultivating maize, beans and quinoa, herding llamas, storing crops in pits and cists, and making the region's first pottery, while continuing to hunt guanaco and vicuña. Small, widely spaced hamlets of round houses replaced the earlier rock-shelter camps.

hints.label: Formativo Temprano
hints.source: El espacio doméstico en las ocupaciones aldeanas del valle Calchaquí Norte (Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Desarrollos Regionales (Salta, AD 900–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Desarrollos Regionales (Salta, AD 900–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 900–AD 1480] Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Paisaje y Materialidad en el Formativo del Valle Calchaquí Norte — Rivolta María Clara, 2020-12-19.

After the Tiwanaku-influenced horizon faded, the valleys and highlands of northwest Argentina broke into a mosaic of local polities, best known through the Santa María and related groups. Communities clustered in dense, walled hilltop settlements — pukaras — with terraced fields below, buried their dead in painted urns, and worked copper and bronze. Warfare and competition between chiefdoms shaped the landscape until Inca armies absorbed the region in the late fifteenth century.

hints.label: Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Paisaje y Materialidad en el Formativo del Valle Calchaquí Norte

nodes.name: Ocupación incaica (Salta, AD 1480–AD 1520)
nodes.title: Ocupación incaica (Salta, AD 1480–AD 1520)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1480–AD 1520] Ocupación incaica. Period definition from Paisaje y Materialidad en el Formativo del Valle Calchaquí Norte — Rivolta María Clara, 2020-12-19.

Inca armies extended Tawantinsuyu into the far south, incorporating the valleys and puna of the northwest Argentine Andes as part of Qollasuyu. The state built roads, waystations and administrative centres, resettled populations of mitmaqkuna, and pressed local labour into mining and farming. Mountaintop shrines from this drive include the frozen child sacrifices of Llullaillaco; the whole system lasted barely two generations before Spanish arrival.

hints.label: Ocupación incaica
hints.source: Paisaje y Materialidad en el Formativo del Valle Calchaquí Norte

nodes.name: Late Period (Salta, AD 900–AD 1430)
nodes.title: Late Period (Salta, AD 900–AD 1430)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 900–AD 1430] Late Period. Period definition from Irrigation canals from the Calchaqui valley (province of Salta, Argentina) — Páez María Cecilia, 2019-10.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

hints.label: Late Period
hints.source: Irrigation canals from the Calchaqui valley (province of Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Inca Period (Salta, AD 1430–AD 1530)
nodes.title: Inca Period (Salta, AD 1430–AD 1530)
nodes.description:
[Valles Calchaquíes Norte, Salta, AD 1430–AD 1530] Inca Period. Period definition from Irrigation canals from the Calchaqui valley (province of Salta, Argentina) — Páez María Cecilia, 2019-10.

Cusco's armies incorporated the valleys of the Calchaquí and the Andean south into Qollasuyu, installing garrisons, administrative sites and roads linked to the great highland highway. Local communities kept their own pottery and burial customs while paying labour tribute and, in places, being moved wholesale as mitmaqkuna colonists. Mining and metalworking in the region were of particular interest to the state.

hints.label: Inca Period
hints.source: Irrigation canals from the Calchaqui valley (province of Salta, Argentina)

nodes.name: Formativo Superior (La Rioja, 599 BC–AD 900)
nodes.title: Formativo Superior (La Rioja, 599 BC–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, 599 BC–AD 900] Formativo Superior. Period definition from Un tipo de estratégia de localización en el oeste riojano (Villa Castelli) — Callegari Adriana , 1991.

The later stage of village farming society in the Argentine Northwest, when settlements grew larger and more clustered, agricultural terraces and irrigation spread, and craft production in ceramics and metal became more specialised. Distinct regional pottery styles emerged, and differences in burial goods hint at growing inequality. These communities are the direct ancestors of the fortified towns and chiefdoms of the following Regional Development period.

hints.label: Formativo Superior
hints.source: Un tipo de estratégia de localización en el oeste riojano (Villa Castelli)

nodes.name: Periodo Medio (La Rioja, AD 550–AD 900)
nodes.title: Periodo Medio (La Rioja, AD 550–AD 900)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 550–AD 900] Periodo Medio. Period definition from Materialización de la Ideología, Ceremonialismo y Complejidad Social. Un Caso de Estudio: La Cuestecilla (Famatina, La Rioja) — Callegari Adriana , 2000.

The time of the Aguada tradition in the Argentine Northwest, when scattered farming villages shared a strikingly uniform art style: black incised and polychrome pottery, cast bronze plaques and discs, and repeated images of felines, shamans and trophy heads. Craft specialisation and metallurgy reached new heights, and the imagery suggests ritual leaders and a widely shared belief system linking valleys across the region.

hints.label: Periodo Medio
hints.source: Materialización de la Ideología, Ceremonialismo y Complejidad Social. Un Caso de Estudio: La Cuestecilla (Famatina, La Rioja)

nodes.name: Período Temprano o Formativo (La Rioja, 599 BC–AD 550)
nodes.title: Período Temprano o Formativo (La Rioja, 599 BC–AD 550)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, 599 BC–AD 550] Período Temprano o Formativo. Period definition from Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja — Callegari Adriana , 2007.

Mobile hunting gave way to settled village farming, with irrigation, maize and camelid herding supporting permanent hamlets. Pottery, weaving and early copper metallurgy appear, alongside elaborate burials and long-distance trade in shell, obsidian and hallucinogenic snuff paraphernalia. Everything that later valley societies built on - fields, herds, kin-based villages - takes shape in these centuries.

hints.label: Período Temprano o Formativo
hints.source: Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja

nodes.name: Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional (La Rioja, AD 550–AD 1100)
nodes.title: Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional (La Rioja, AD 550–AD 1100)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 550–AD 1100] Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional. Period definition from Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja — Callegari Adriana , 2007.

Named for the way distant valley communities came to share one visual language – the feline and shaman imagery of the Aguada style – on pottery, bronze and rock walls. Farming villages grew, irrigation and llama herding expanded, and metalworkers produced fine cast plaques and axes. The unity dissolved towards the end of the period, giving way to more localised, competitive societies.

hints.label: Periodo Medio o de Integración Regional
hints.source: Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja

nodes.name: Período Tardío o de los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1100–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Período Tardío o de los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1100–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1450] Período Tardío o de los Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja — Callegari Adriana , 2007.

After the collapse of the earlier Aguada-style unity, the western valleys broke into competing local chiefdoms with their own pottery styles, among them the Sanagasta and Angualasto traditions. Villages of stone-walled compounds spread across irrigated valley floors, some perched on defensible heights, and dead children were buried in painted ceramic urns beneath house floors. These were the societies the Inca armies later absorbed, and whose descendants the Spanish met as the Diaguita.

hints.label: Período Tardío o de los Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja

nodes.title: Período Inka (La Rioja, AD 1450–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1450–AD 1535] Período Inka. Period definition from Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja — Callegari Adriana , 2007.

nodes.title: Período Hispano Indígena (La Rioja, AD 1535–AD 1700)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1535–AD 1700] Período Hispano Indígena. Period definition from Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja — Callegari Adriana , 2007.

The contact era, when indigenous communities of the western valleys encountered Spanish settlers, encomenderos and priests. Sites from this time mix local hand-made pottery with glazed European wares, glass beads and iron, and record the resistance, forced resettlement and demographic collapse that ended independent indigenous polities in the region.

hints.label: Período Hispano Indígena
hints.source: Los Recursos Arqueológicos de Villa Castelli. Dto. General La Madrid, La Rioja

Metallurgy flourished, with cast bronze plaques and axes, and shared iconography suggests ritual specialists and networks of exchange linking widely separated valleys. Contacts with the Bolivian altiplano and Tiwanaku world brought hallucinogenic snuff kits and camelid caravan goods.

hints.label: Período Medio
hints.source: Más de 1000 años de explotación minera en la Sierra de Famatina. La Rioja, Argentina

nodes.name: Período Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período Tardío. Period definition from Más de 1000 años de explotación minera en la Sierra de Famatina. La Rioja, Argentina — Callegari Adriana , 2012.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.label: Período Tardío
hints.source: Más de 1000 años de explotación minera en la Sierra de Famatina. La Rioja, Argentina

nodes.name: Formativo (La Rioja, 199 BC–AD 1200)
nodes.title: Formativo (La Rioja, 199 BC–AD 1200)
nodes.description: [La Rioja, Argentina, 199 BC–AD 1200] Formativo. Period definition from Tras las Huellas del Formativo. Norte de la Provincia de La Rioja. — Callegari Adriana , 2015.

hints.label: Formativo
hints.source: Tras las Huellas del Formativo. Norte de la Provincia de La Rioja.

nodes.name: Período Temprano (La Rioja, 99 BC–AD 600)
nodes.title: Período Temprano (La Rioja, 99 BC–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, 99 BC–AD 600] Período Temprano. Period definition from Estrellas Riojanas. Geoglifos del norte de la provincia de La Rioja, Argentina — Callegari Adriana , 2019-06.

Farming villages became the normal way of life: people settled in one place, grew maize, beans and squash, herded llamas, made pottery and began working copper and gold. Small clusters of round or rectangular houses spread through the valleys, with grinding stones, carved stone menhirs and the first metal ornaments. The social groundwork for the later valley chiefdoms was laid here.

hints.label: Período Temprano
hints.source: Estrellas Riojanas. Geoglifos del norte de la provincia de La Rioja, Argentina

nodes.name: Período Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1350] Período Tardío. Period definition from Estrellas Riojanas. Geoglifos del norte de la provincia de La Rioja, Argentina — Callegari Adriana , 2019-06.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.label: Período Tardío
hints.source: Estrellas Riojanas. Geoglifos del norte de la provincia de La Rioja, Argentina

nodes.name: Tardío 0 o de transición (La Rioja, AD 800–AD 1350)
nodes.title: Tardío 0 o de transición (La Rioja, AD 800–AD 1350)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 800–AD 1350] Tardío 0 o de transición. Period definition from Arquitectura y asentamiento de las sociedades tardías del sector centro-norte del Valle de Vinchina, La Rioja. — Spengler Gisela , 2017.

A transitional stage in the northwest Argentine sequence, between the collapse of the Aguada-style ceremonial tradition and the emergence of the densely settled Late Period communities. Villages became more dispersed and agricultural, decorated pottery styles simplified and diversified regionally, and the political landscape fragmented into local groups.

hints.label: Tardío 0 o de transición
hints.source: Arquitectura y asentamiento de las sociedades tardías del sector centro-norte del Valle de Vinchina, La Rioja.

nodes.name: Tardío I (La Rioja, AD 1350–AD 1430)
nodes.title: Tardío I (La Rioja, AD 1350–AD 1430)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1350–AD 1430] Tardío I. Period definition from Arquitectura y asentamiento de las sociedades tardías del sector centro-norte del Valle de Vinchina, La Rioja. — Spengler Gisela , 2017.

The first full Late Period stage in the western valleys, when farming communities clustered into larger nucleated settlements, often on defensible ground, and irrigated fields and terraces were extended across the valley floors. Regional ceramic styles and local chiefly leadership crystallised in the generations just before Inca armies reached the region.

hints.label: Tardío I
hints.source: Arquitectura y asentamiento de las sociedades tardías del sector centro-norte del Valle de Vinchina, La Rioja.

nodes.name: Tardío II (La Rioja, AD 1430–AD 1636)
nodes.title: Tardío II (La Rioja, AD 1430–AD 1636)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1430–AD 1636] Tardío II. Period definition from Arquitectura y asentamiento de las sociedades tardías del sector centro-norte del Valle de Vinchina, La Rioja. — Spengler Gisela , 2017.

Covers the incorporation of these valley communities into the Inca empire's southern province and then their violent absorption into the Spanish colonial world. Inca roads, tambos and administrative sites overlay existing settlements, and after the 1530s came encomienda, forced resettlement and the long indigenous resistance in the Calchaquí valleys.

hints.label: Tardío II
hints.source: Arquitectura y asentamiento de las sociedades tardías del sector centro-norte del Valle de Vinchina, La Rioja.

nodes.name: Período Precerámico (La Rioja, 9999 BC–AD 600)
nodes.title: Período Precerámico (La Rioja, 9999 BC–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, 9999 BC–AD 600] Período Precerámico. Period definition from Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja — Raviña María Gabriela , 1988.

Millennia of hunting and gathering before pottery, from the first peopling of the region through Holocene camelid hunters using caves, rockshelters and open camps. Stone projectile points, grinding tools and vivid rock art record shifting prey and expanding social networks. Towards its end, the taming of llamas and cultivation of highland crops began the slow move to settled village life.

hints.label: Período Precerámico
hints.source: Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja

nodes.name: Formativo Inferior (La Rioja, 599 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Formativo Inferior (La Rioja, 599 BC–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, 599 BC–AD 1000] Formativo Inferior. Period definition from Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja — Raviña María Gabriela , 1988.

Settled agricultural life in the valleys and eastern piedmont of the Argentine Northwest, based on maize, quinoa and camelid herding. Communities lived in small dispersed hamlets with round stone-walled houses and cultivation plots, made incised and painted pottery, and worked copper and gold. Regional exchange networks carried pottery styles, obsidian and Amazonian and Pacific goods across the Andes.

hints.label: Formativo Inferior
hints.source: Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja

nodes.name: Formativo Superior (La Rioja, AD 600–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Formativo Superior (La Rioja, AD 600–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 600–AD 1000] Formativo Superior. Period definition from Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja — Raviña María Gabriela , 1988.

The later stage of village farming society in the Argentine Northwest, when settlements grew larger and more clustered, agricultural terraces and irrigation spread, and craft production in ceramics and metal became more specialised. Distinct regional pottery styles emerged, and differences in burial goods hint at growing inequality. These communities are the direct ancestors of the fortified towns and chiefdoms of the following Regional Development period.

hints.label: Formativo Superior
hints.source: Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja

nodes.name: Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1470] Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja — Raviña María Gabriela , 1988.

After the Tiwanaku-influenced horizon faded, the valleys and highlands of northwest Argentina broke into a mosaic of local polities, best known through the Santa María and related groups. Communities clustered in dense, walled hilltop settlements — pukaras — with terraced fields below, buried their dead in painted urns, and worked copper and bronze. Warfare and competition between chiefdoms shaped the landscape until Inca armies absorbed the region in the late fifteenth century.

hints.label: Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja

nodes.name: Período Inka (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Período Inka (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1470–AD 1535] Período Inka. Period definition from Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja — Raviña María Gabriela , 1988.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.

hints.label: Período Inka
hints.source: Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja

nodes.name: Período Hispano Indígena (La Rioja, AD 1535–AD 1660)
nodes.title: Período Hispano Indígena (La Rioja, AD 1535–AD 1660)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1535–AD 1660] Período Hispano Indígena. Period definition from Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja — Raviña María Gabriela , 1988.

The contact era, when indigenous communities of the western valleys encountered Spanish settlers, encomenderos and priests. Sites from this time mix local hand-made pottery with glazed European wares, glass beads and iron, and record the resistance, forced resettlement and demographic collapse that ended independent indigenous polities in the region.

hints.label: Período Hispano Indígena
hints.source: Mapa arqueológico de la provincia de La Rioja

nodes.name: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Arte rupestre entre las sierras y Los Llanos riojanos: localidad arqueológica Palancho — Falchi María Pía , 2011-12-01.

Local chiefdoms in the valleys built dense villages, extensive field systems and hilltop refuges, each with recognisable pottery and burial customs. Long-distance caravan traffic kept them supplied with obsidian, metals and altiplano goods, while competition over land and water drove fortification. Their leaders were the intermediaries through whom the Inca later governed.

hints.label: Período Tardío o de Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Arte rupestre entre las sierras y Los Llanos riojanos: localidad arqueológica Palancho

nodes.name: Período de Integración Regional (La Rioja, AD 550–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Período de Integración Regional (La Rioja, AD 550–AD 1000)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 550–AD 1000] Período de Integración Regional. Period definition from Arte rupestre en la localidad arqueológica El Chiflón- Punta de la Greda (Parque Natural Provincial El Chiflón, La Rioja) en su contexto regional. — Falchi María Pía , 2017.

Farming villages across the western valleys grew denser and more organised, tied together by shared styles of decorated pottery, textiles and cast bronze. This is the horizon of the Aguada tradition, whose black incised vessels carry stylised feline and warrior imagery that suggests shamanic ritual and an emerging elite. Metallurgy, llama herding and irrigation agriculture all became firmly established, setting the economic base for the later chiefdoms of the region.

hints.label: Período de Integración Regional
hints.source: Arte rupestre en la localidad arqueológica El Chiflón- Punta de la Greda (Parque Natural Provincial El Chiflón, La Rioja) en su contexto regional.

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1450] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Arte rupestre en la localidad arqueológica El Chiflón- Punta de la Greda (Parque Natural Provincial El Chiflón, La Rioja) en su contexto regional. — Falchi María Pía , 2017.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Arte rupestre en la localidad arqueológica El Chiflón- Punta de la Greda (Parque Natural Provincial El Chiflón, La Rioja) en su contexto regional.

nodes.name: Late Period (La Rioja, AD 900–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Late Period (La Rioja, AD 900–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1470] Late Period. Period definition from Temporal dynamics of La Rioja village landscapes, Argentina — Cahiza Pablo , 2021-10.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

hints.label: Late Period
hints.source: Temporal dynamics of La Rioja village landscapes, Argentina

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1470] Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío. Period definition from Análisis ceramológicos de la Tambería de Guandacol (dpto. Felipe Varela, provincia de La Rioja). Avances para el conocimiento de las prácticas de manufactura. — Carosio Sebastián , 2011.

Farming communities in the western valleys reached their greatest extent, irrigating fields, terracing slopes and living in dense stone-built settlements. Distinct regional ceramic traditions and infant urn burials mark the period, along with widespread copper-bronze metallurgy. Growing evidence of conflict - walls, lookouts, weapons - accompanies the rise of local chiefly authority.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío
hints.source: Análisis ceramológicos de la Tambería de Guandacol (dpto. Felipe Varela, provincia de La Rioja). Avances para el conocimiento de las prácticas de manufactura.

nodes.title: Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1200–AD 1470)

[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1470] Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Cadena operativa y tradición tecnológica cerámica durante Desarrollos Regionales en el extremo sur del Noroeste Argentino (ca. 1200-1470 AD). Un aporte desde el estilo tecnológico Sanagasta/Angualasto del sitio Tambería de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja). — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

After the Tiwanaku-influenced horizon faded, the valleys and highlands of northwest Argentina broke into a mosaic of local polities, best known through the Santa María and related groups. Communities clustered in dense, walled hilltop settlements — pukaras — with terraced fields below, buried their dead in painted urns, and worked copper and bronze. Warfare and competition between chiefdoms shaped the landscape until Inca armies absorbed the region in the late fifteenth century.

hints.source: Cadena operativa y tradición tecnológica cerámica durante Desarrollos Regionales en el extremo sur del Noroeste Argentino (ca. 1200-1470 AD). Un aporte desde el estilo tecnológico Sanagasta/Angualasto del sitio Tambería de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja).

nodes.name: Período de Dominio Incaico Regional (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1533)
nodes.title: Período de Dominio Incaico Regional (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1533)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1470–AD 1533] Período de Dominio Incaico Regional. Period definition from Estudios preliminares de Pigmentos en Cerámicas Arqueológicas Tardías Mediante Microscopio de Barrido Electrónico (MEB-EDS). Aportes para el Conocimiento Tecnológico Alfarero de las Sociedades de la Tambería de Guandacol (Oeste de la Provincial de La Rioja). — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

Imperial administration reached the western valleys, imposing tribute in labour, redirecting agriculture and mining, and tying local settlements into the Andean road network. Local pottery continued but adopted imperial shapes and motifs, evidence of negotiated rather than total control. The arrangement lasted only decades before Spanish forces arrived.

hints.label: Período de Dominio Incaico Regional
hints.source: Estudios preliminares de Pigmentos en Cerámicas Arqueológicas Tardías Mediante Microscopio de Barrido Electrónico (MEB-EDS). Aportes para el Conocimiento Tecnológico Alfarero de las Sociedades de la Tambería de Guandacol (Oeste de la Provincial de La Rioja).

nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período de Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Patrimonio arqueológico en el Valle de Guandacol (provincia de La Rioja, Argentina): Estudios exploratorios de los procesos de alteración natural y cultural.  — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

Sharply distinct local traditions emerged across the valleys, each with its own pottery, architecture and territory. Settlements grew into agglomerated stone towns with terraced fields and defensive walls, and the dead were interred with painted urns and bronze goods. Interpretation of the period turns on whether these were warring chiefdoms or looser village confederations.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Patrimonio arqueológico en el Valle de Guandacol (provincia de La Rioja, Argentina): Estudios exploratorios de los procesos de alteración natural y cultural.

nodes.name: Período del Dominio Inca (La Rioja, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Período del Dominio Inca (La Rioja, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1535] Período del Dominio Inca. Period definition from Patrimonio arqueológico en el Valle de Guandacol (provincia de La Rioja, Argentina): Estudios exploratorios de los procesos de alteración natural y cultural.  — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

Inca officials incorporated the valleys into the empire, taking control of mineral sources, imposing labour tribute and installing garrisons and storage facilities along the road system. Imperial pottery and architecture appear alongside continuing local traditions, and high-altitude mountain shrines in the region attest to state-sponsored ritual. The arrangement collapsed with the Spanish invasion, though Inca administrative geography shaped how the colonisers first understood the area.

hints.label: Período del Dominio Inca
hints.source: Patrimonio arqueológico en el Valle de Guandacol (provincia de La Rioja, Argentina): Estudios exploratorios de los procesos de alteración natural y cultural.

nodes.name: Periodo Agroalfarero Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1200–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Periodo Agroalfarero Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1200–AD 1470)
nodes.description: [La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1470] Periodo Agroalfarero Tardío. Period definition from Una aproximación a las trayectorias estilísticas cerámicas del valle de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja): Continuidades y rupturas entre los siglos XIII y XVIII. — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

hints.label: Periodo Agroalfarero Tardío
hints.source: Una aproximación a las trayectorias estilísticas cerámicas del valle de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja): Continuidades y rupturas entre los siglos XIII y XVIII.

nodes.name: Dominación Inca (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Dominación Inca (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1470–AD 1535] Dominación Inca. Period definition from Una aproximación a las trayectorias estilísticas cerámicas del valle de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja): Continuidades y rupturas entre los siglos XIII y XVIII. — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

Inca armies pushed south into the valleys of northwest Argentina, folding them into Collasuyu, the empire's southern quarter. The state built roads, waystations and administrative centres, moved populations of resettled colonists (mitmaqkuna) to work fields and mines, and imposed labour tribute on local chiefdoms. Traces survive as hilltop sanctuaries, stretches of the Qhapaq Ñan and imperial-style pottery mixed into local wares. It lasted only a few decades before Spanish forces arrived.

hints.label: Dominación Inca
hints.source: Una aproximación a las trayectorias estilísticas cerámicas del valle de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja): Continuidades y rupturas entre los siglos XIII y XVIII.

nodes.name: fase transicional del Formativo a los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 600–AD 1200)
nodes.title: fase transicional del Formativo a los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 600–AD 1200)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 600–AD 1200] fase transicional del Formativo a los Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Una aproximación a las trayectorias estilísticas cerámicas del valle de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja): Continuidades y rupturas entre los siglos XIII y XVIII. — Carosio Sebastián , 2017.

Farming villages of the Argentine Northwest, long organised around small irrigated plots and llama herding, gave way to denser and more hierarchical settlement, with distinctive regional ceramic styles and, in this stretch of the Andes, the spread of Aguada iconography of felines and warriors. Metallurgy in copper and bronze became a marker of status, and communities began fortifying and clustering in defensible spots. The pattern of competing local polities set here is what the Inca later found and absorbed.

hints.label: fase transicional del Formativo a los Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Una aproximación a las trayectorias estilísticas cerámicas del valle de Guandacol (Provincia de La Rioja): Continuidades y rupturas entre los siglos XIII y XVIII.

nodes.name: Período Intermedio Tardío o Período de los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1430)
nodes.title: Período Intermedio Tardío o Período de los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1430)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1430] Período Intermedio Tardío o Período de los Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Primeros resultados del estudio bioarqueológico de restos óseos humanos de La Rioja (Argentina). — Gheggi María Soledad , 2019.

With no unifying horizon style, communities in the western valleys developed their own pottery traditions, settlement layouts and leadership. Farming spread across terraced slopes and irrigated valley floors, supporting larger, more nucleated villages, while fortified sites and weapon-related finds point to conflict between groups. These local polities were the societies the Inca later absorbed.

hints.label: Período Intermedio Tardío o Período de los Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Primeros resultados del estudio bioarqueológico de restos óseos humanos de La Rioja (Argentina).

nodes.name: Período de los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1100–AD 1470)
nodes.title: Período de los Desarrollos Regionales (La Rioja, AD 1100–AD 1470)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1470] Período de los Desarrollos Regionales. Period definition from Prospecciones arqueológicas en el valle de Guandacol, depto. Felipe Varela, La Rioja. — Iniesta María Lourdes , 2013.

With the collapse of the earlier integrative traditions, communities fragmented into distinct local groups, each with its own pottery styles and territory. Settlements moved to defensible spurs and hilltops, walls and lookouts multiplied, and skeletal trauma points to endemic raiding over land and water. These were the densely populated valley chiefdoms that the Inca armies would later conquer and reorganise.

hints.label: Período de los Desarrollos Regionales
hints.source: Prospecciones arqueológicas en el valle de Guandacol, depto. Felipe Varela, La Rioja.

nodes.name: Período de Dominación Inca (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Período de Dominación Inca (La Rioja, AD 1470–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1470–AD 1536] Período de Dominación Inca. Period definition from Prospecciones arqueológicas en el valle de Guandacol, depto. Felipe Varela, La Rioja. — Iniesta María Lourdes , 2013.

Inca armies and administrators extended Tawantinsuyu into the western valleys, linking them by road to Cuzco and reorganising labour for mining and farming. Storehouses, waystations and high-altitude shrines appear alongside existing local settlements, and communities were sometimes resettled as mitmaqkuna. Imperial control lasted barely two generations before Spanish invasion dismantled it.

hints.label: Período de Dominación Inca
hints.source: Prospecciones arqueológicas en el valle de Guandacol, depto. Felipe Varela, La Rioja.

nodes.name: Período de los Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Período de los Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período de los Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío. Period definition from Investigaciones arqueológicas sobre las sociedades tardías del Valle de Guandacol (Departamento Felipe Varela, oeste de La Rioja): Espacio, estilos tecnológicos cerámicos y cronología — Iniesta María Lourdes , 2014.

Populations grew and clustered into large agglomerated villages surrounded by terraced fields and irrigation canals, each region developing its own recognisable ceramic style. Fortified hilltop sites and evidence of violence suggest competition between neighbouring polities, while long-distance exchange in metal and hallucinogenic plants continued. This mosaic of independent valley societies was the political landscape the Inca encountered.

hints.label: Período de los Desarrollos Regionales o Agroalfarero Tardío
hints.source: Investigaciones arqueológicas sobre las sociedades tardías del Valle de Guandacol (Departamento Felipe Varela, oeste de La Rioja): Espacio, estilos tecnológicos cerámicos y cronología

nodes.name: Período Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1300–AD 1440)
nodes.title: Período Tardío (La Rioja, AD 1300–AD 1440)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1300–AD 1440] Período Tardío. Period definition from Configuración del paisaje tardío (ca. 1300-1440 d.c.) en el Valle de Guandacol (Felipe Varela, oeste de la provincia de La Rioja) — Iniesta María Lourdes , 2016.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

nodes.name: Período de Dominación Incaica (La Rioja, AD 1475–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Período de Dominación Incaica (La Rioja, AD 1475–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[La Rioja, Argentina, AD 1475–AD 1536] Período de Dominación Incaica. Period definition from Investigaciones arqueológicas en la sierra de Famatina (Prov. de La Rioja) — Schobinger Juan , 1966.

The southern reach of Tawantinsuyu, administered through the road system, provincial centres and the resettlement of labourers far from their homelands. The Inca were drawn by metals - copper, silver, gold - and by the region's farmland, and left mountaintop sanctuaries at extraordinary altitudes. Their rule collapsed with the Spanish capture of Atahualpa, leaving local groups to face a new conqueror.

hints.label: Período de Dominación Incaica
hints.source: Investigaciones arqueológicas en la sierra de Famatina (Prov. de La Rioja)

nodes.name: Cultura de Los Morrillos (San Juan, 5899 BC–2199 BC)
nodes.title: Cultura de Los Morrillos (San Juan, 5899 BC–2199 BC)
nodes.description:
[San Juan, Argentina, 5899 BC–2199 BC] Cultura de Los Morrillos. Period definition from Textilería incaica en la provincia de San Juan: Los ajuares de los cerros Mercedario, Toro y Tambillos — Catalina Teresa Michieli, 1990.

Hunter-gatherers of the high Andean valleys who camped in rock shelters, hunted guanaco and vicuña, and left painted and engraved rock art on the cliffs around their sites. The exceptionally dry conditions preserved wooden tools, cordage and burials, making these caves one of the fullest records of archaic life in the southern Andes.

hints.label: Cultura de Los Morrillos
hints.source: Textilería incaica en la provincia de San Juan: Los ajuares de los cerros Mercedario, Toro y Tambillos

nodes.name: Cultura de Ansilta (San Juan, 1799 BC–AD 550)
nodes.title: Cultura de Ansilta (San Juan, 1799 BC–AD 550)
nodes.description:
[San Juan, Argentina, 1799 BC–AD 550] Cultura de Ansilta. Period definition from Textilería incaica en la provincia de San Juan: Los ajuares de los cerros Mercedario, Toro y Tambillos — Catalina Teresa Michieli, 1990.

Early cultivators of the high western Andes who combined hunting guanaco with small-scale gardening of maize and squash, living in caves and rock shelters. Their dry burial sites have preserved extraordinary twined textiles and netted bags, giving an unusually detailed picture of clothing and craft in a period that otherwise leaves little behind.

hints.label: Cultura de Ansilta
hints.source: Textilería incaica en la provincia de San Juan: Los ajuares de los cerros Mercedario, Toro y Tambillos

nodes.name: Cultura Angualasto (San Juan, AD 1200–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Cultura Angualasto (San Juan, AD 1200–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1450] Cultura Angualasto. Period definition from Nuevas evidencias textiles del período tardío en el valle fronterizo de Iglesia (San Juan, Argentina) y sus relaciones con el norte de Chile y noroeste argentino — Catalina Teresa Michieli, 2001.

Farmers of the arid Andean valleys who irrigated maize and beans, stored grain in stone silos, and buried their dead in dry caves where textiles and basketry survive remarkably well. Their distinctive plain and incised pottery marks the last centuries of local independence before Inca armies absorbed the region.

hints.label: Cultura Angualasto
hints.source: Nuevas evidencias textiles del período tardío en el valle fronterizo de Iglesia (San Juan, Argentina) y sus relaciones con el norte de Chile y noroeste argentino

nodes.name: Cultura de la Aguada (San Juan, AD 650–AD 1050)
nodes.title: Cultura de la Aguada (San Juan, AD 650–AD 1050)
nodes.description:
[San Juan, Argentina, AD 650–AD 1050] Cultura de la Aguada. Period definition from Textilería Aguada en el Valle de Iglesia, provincia de San Juan — Catalina Teresa Michieli, 2001.

Known for dark, polished pottery and bronze plaques covered in feline and jaguar-man imagery, this was the great artistic tradition of northwest Argentina. Its craftsmen mastered metallurgy, its iconography suggests shamanic ritual and human sacrifice, and its motifs echo those of Tiwanaku far to the north, hinting at long-distance religious connections across the Andes.

hints.label: Cultura de la Aguada
hints.source: Textilería Aguada en el Valle de Iglesia, provincia de San Juan

nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1200] Período Tardío. Period definition from  Identificacion y Analisis de Pigmentos y Pinturas en Ceramicas Arqueológicas Sanagasta (ca. 900 1200 AD) e Inka (ca. 1480 1532 AD) a traves de MEB-EDS y Microespectroscopia de Raman (Abaucan, Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina). — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2010.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. nodes.name: Período Agroalfarero Tardío (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Período Agroalfarero Tardío (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1450] Período Agroalfarero Tardío. Period definition from  Identificacion y Analisis de Pigmentos y Pinturas en Ceramicas Arqueológicas Sanagasta (ca. 900 1200 AD) e Inka (ca. 1480 1532 AD) a traves de MEB-EDS y Microespectroscopia de Raman (Abaucan, Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina). — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2010.

After the collapse of the Aguada tradition, the valleys of the northwest filled with sizeable, densely packed settlements built of stone, many of them fortified hilltop pukaras overlooking terraced fields. Distinct regional styles emerged, such as the Santa María funerary urns painted with staring anthropomorphic faces and the Belén ceramics, and bronze working reached its peak. Warfare between valley polities was common, and the era closed with their incorporation into the Inca empire.

hints.source: Identificacion y Analisis de Pigmentos y Pinturas en Ceramicas Arqueológicas Sanagasta (ca. 900 1200 AD) e Inka (ca. 1480 1532 AD) a traves de MEB-EDS y Microespectroscopia de Raman (Abaucan, Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina).

nodes.name: Período Inka (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1532)
nodes.title: Período Inka (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1532)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1532] Período Inka. Period definition from Cronología por Termoluminiscencia (TL) de Cerámicas pertenecientes al Horizonte Inka (ca. AD 1480-AD 1532) y el Período Tardío (ca. AD 900-AD 1450) en el sur del Valle de Abaucán: Análisis Comparativos y Resultados Preliminares (Tinogasta, Catamarca). — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2010.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.

hints.label: Período Inka
hints.source: Cronología por Termoluminiscencia (TL) de Cerámicas pertenecientes al Horizonte Inka (ca. AD 1480-AD 1532) y el Período Tardío (ca. AD 900-AD 1450) en el sur del Valle de Abaucán: Análisis Comparativos y Resultados Preliminares (Tinogasta, Catamarca).

nodes.name: Late Period (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1450)
nodes.title: Late Period (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1450)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1450] Late Period. Period definition from Urns, Bowls, and Ollas: Pottery-Making Practices and Technical Identity in the Southern Andes During the Late Period (ca. A.D. 900—A.D. 1450) (Catamarca, Northwestern Argentine Region, Argentina) — Guillermo A. De La Fuente, 2011-06.

Egyptian kings ruled again from Sais after the Assyrian withdrawal, reviving Old Kingdom art and burial customs in a deliberate archaising style, while Greek and Carian mercenaries and traders settled in the Delta at Naukratis. Persian conquest in 525 BC made Egypt a satrapy, interrupted by brief native dynasties, until Alexander took the country in 332 BC. The period is where Egypt becomes fully entangled with the Mediterranean world that would later record its history.

hints.label: Late Period
hints.source: Urns, Bowls, and Ollas: Pottery-Making Practices and Technical Identity in the Southern Andes During the Late Period (ca. A.D. 900—A.D. 1450) (Catamarca, Northwestern Argentine Region, Argentina)

nodes.name: Inca Period (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1530)
nodes.title: Inca Period (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1530)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1530] Inca Period. Period definition from Chemical and Petrographic Analysis of Pre-Hispanic Pottery from the Southern Abaucán Valley, Catamarca, Argentina — de La Fuente Guillermo Adrián, 2014-02-16.

Cusco's armies incorporated the valleys of the Calchaquí and the Andean south into Qollasuyu, installing garrisons, administrative sites and roads linked to the great highland highway. Local communities kept their own pottery and burial customs while paying labour tribute and, in places, being moved wholesale as mitmaqkuna colonists. Mining and metalworking in the region were of particular interest to the state.

hints.label: Inca Period
hints.source: Chemical and Petrographic Analysis of Pre-Hispanic Pottery from the Southern Abaucán Valley, Catamarca, Argentina

nodes.name: Período Tardío Inicial (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1300)
nodes.title: Período Tardío Inicial (Catamarca, AD 900–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1300] Período Tardío Inicial. Period definition from Prácticas alfareras, tecnología y cronología durante los períodos Tardío e Inca en el sector meridional del Valle de Abaucán. Tradiciones y rupturas: el caso de Costa de Reyes N°5 (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina) — Vera Sergio David, 2019-03.

The opening phase of the late sequence, when Aguada-era patterns gave way to new regional communities in the Catamarca valleys. Settlements grew more nucleated, agricultural terracing and irrigation expanded, and distinctive local pottery traditions such as early Belén wares took shape. Signs of defence and conflict begin to appear in settlement locations.

hints.label: Período Tardío Inicial
hints.source: Prácticas alfareras, tecnología y cronología durante los períodos Tardío e Inca en el sector meridional del Valle de Abaucán. Tradiciones y rupturas: el caso de Costa de Reyes N°5 (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Intermedio Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Período Intermedio Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1300–AD 1480] Período Intermedio Tardío. Period definition from Prácticas alfareras, tecnología y cronología durante los períodos Tardío e Inca en el sector meridional del Valle de Abaucán. Tradiciones y rupturas: el caso de Costa de Reyes N°5 (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina) — Vera Sergio David, 2019-03.

After the collapse of the Middle Period order, populations in the valleys built dense settlements, extensive terraced fields and irrigation systems, and increasingly clustered in defensible hilltop pukaras. Regional identities are visible in distinct painted pottery styles and in urn burials of infants beneath house floors. The rising evidence for warfare and territorial competition sets the stage for Inca conquest.

hints.label: Período Intermedio Tardío
hints.source: Prácticas alfareras, tecnología y cronología durante los períodos Tardío e Inca en el sector meridional del Valle de Abaucán. Tradiciones y rupturas: el caso de Costa de Reyes N°5 (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Tardío-Inca (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1600)
nodes.title: Período Tardío-Inca (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1600)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1600] Período Tardío-Inca. Period definition from Prácticas alfareras, tecnología y cronología durante los períodos Tardío e Inca en el sector meridional del Valle de Abaucán. Tradiciones y rupturas: el caso de Costa de Reyes N°5 (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina) — Vera Sergio David, 2019-03.

The last stretch of independent valley life overlapped with, and was overtaken by, imperial rule and then Spanish invasion. Inca administrative sites, road segments and storehouses were grafted onto existing Belén and Santa María settlements, and local potters began mixing imperial shapes and designs into their own work. The sequence ends in the long indigenous resistance of the Calchaquí Wars.

hints.label: Período Tardío-Inca
hints.source: Prácticas alfareras, tecnología y cronología durante los períodos Tardío e Inca en el sector meridional del Valle de Abaucán. Tradiciones y rupturas: el caso de Costa de Reyes N°5 (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Agroalfarero Temprano (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD 600)
nodes.title: Período Agroalfarero Temprano (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD 600)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, 199 BC–AD 600] Período Agroalfarero Temprano. Period definition from Aproximación a los estudios de traza. El caso de las urnas funerarias estilo Saujil (Catamarca, noroeste argentino). — Vera Sergio David, 2018.

The first settled farming villages of northwest Argentina, when maize agriculture, llama herding and pottery making took hold across valleys and puna. Communities such as those at Tafí built circular stone house compounds around patios, carved standing stone monoliths, and produced modelled and painted ceramics, while early copper and gold work appears in graves. Populations remained small and dispersed, without the fortifications and towns of later centuries.

hints.label: Período Agroalfarero Temprano
hints.source: Aproximación a los estudios de traza. El caso de las urnas funerarias estilo Saujil (Catamarca, noroeste argentino).

nodes.name: Período Hispano Indígena (Catamarca, AD 1535–AD 1690)
nodes.title: Período Hispano Indígena (Catamarca, AD 1535–AD 1690)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1535–AD 1690] Período Hispano Indígena. Period definition from Ultimas etapas del desarrollo cultural indigena (1480-1690) en el valle de Abaucan, Tinogasta, Provincia de Catamarca — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1973.

The contact era, when indigenous communities of the western valleys encountered Spanish settlers, encomenderos and priests. Sites from this time mix local hand-made pottery with glazed European wares, glass beads and iron, and record the resistance, forced resettlement and demographic collapse that ended independent indigenous polities in the region.

hints.label: Período Hispano Indígena
hints.source: Ultimas etapas del desarrollo cultural indigena (1480-1690) en el valle de Abaucan, Tinogasta, Provincia de Catamarca

nodes.name: Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 950–AD 1000)
nodes.title: Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 950–AD 1000)
nodes.description: [Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 950–AD 1000] Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

hints.label: Fase IX o Punta Colorada-Guanchín
hints.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

nodes.name: Fase XII o Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Fase XII o Guanchín (Catamarca, AD 1300–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1300–AD 1480] Fase XII o Guanchín. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

The late pre-Inca centuries in the Abaucán valley, when farming communities lived in dispersed stone-walled settlements, irrigated the desert bottomlands and buried their dead with painted vessels. It was a time of local chiefdoms without any overarching state, the world the Inca armies would encounter when they pushed south into the Argentine Northwest.

hints.label: Fase XII o Guanchín
hints.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

nodes.name: Fase XIII o Guatungasta (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.title: Fase XIII o Guatungasta (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1535] Fase XIII o Guatungasta. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

Incorporation into the Inca empire brought the valley roads, way-stations and a new administrative overlay on communities that had been independent. Imperial pottery styles and reorganised labour appear alongside older local traditions, marking the far southern edge of Tawantinsuyu.

hints.label: Fase XIII o Guatungasta
hints.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

nodes.name: Fase XIV o Tinogasta (Catamarca, AD 1535–AD 1630)
nodes.title: Fase XIV o Tinogasta (Catamarca, AD 1535–AD 1630)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1535–AD 1630] Fase XIV o Tinogasta. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

Spanish expeditions crossing from Chile and Peru broke the Inca order and imposed encomiendas, mission priests and tribute on the valley's inhabitants. Indigenous households kept making their own pottery while European animals, metal and disease reshaped everyday life.

hints.label: Fase XIV o Tinogasta
hints.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

nodes.name: Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD 1630–AD 1637)
nodes.title: Fase XV o Cerro Encantado (Catamarca, AD 1630–AD 1637)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1630–AD 1637] Fase XV o Cerro Encantado. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

A few violent years coinciding with the great indigenous uprising that swept the Calchaquí and neighbouring valleys, when communities abandoned lowland sites for defensible heights and Spanish control briefly collapsed. The revolt was crushed and its leaders executed, and the region never regained that measure of independence.

hints.label: Fase XV o Cerro Encantado
hints.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

nodes.name: Fase XVI o Abaucán (Catamarca, AD 1637–AD 1690)
nodes.title: Fase XVI o Abaucán (Catamarca, AD 1637–AD 1690)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1637–AD 1690] Fase XVI o Abaucán. Period definition from Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).  — Sempé de Gómez Llanes María Carlota, 1977.

The decades after the failed rebellion, when surviving communities were resettled, put to work under encomenderos and steadily absorbed into colonial parish and estate life. Indigenous ceramic traditions thinned out and the distinctive archaeological record of the valley effectively comes to an end.

hints.label: Fase XVI o Abaucán
hints.source: Las culturas agroalfareras prehispánicas del Valle de Abaucan (Tinogasta—Catamarca).

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1200–AD 1400)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1200–AD 1400)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Abaucán, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1200–AD 1400] Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío. Period definition from Colores y surcos: Una propuesta metodológica para el análisis de las representaciones plásticas de la región de Fiambalá (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina) — Mara Basile, 2011.

A time of assertive local polities between the collapse of the Aguada horizon and Inca conquest, each valley producing its own recognisable pottery and settlement pattern. People concentrated in fortified villages overlooking terraced land, and craft production in ceramics and bronze intensified. The archaeology suggests competition over land and water in an increasingly crowded landscape.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales o Período Intermedio Tardío
hints.source: Colores y surcos: Una propuesta metodológica para el análisis de las representaciones plásticas de la región de Fiambalá (Tinogasta, Catamarca, Argentina)

nodes.name: Período Formativo (Catamarca, 1999 BC–AD 200)
nodes.title: Período Formativo (Catamarca, 1999 BC–AD 200)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina, 1999 BC–AD 200] Período Formativo. Period definition from Continuidad y ruptura en procesos de diferenciación social en comunidades aldeanas del valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina (s. IV-X dC) — Laguens Andrés Gustavo, 2006-12.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. The Tafí tradition of this era left carved stone menhirs and stone-lined house compounds, while snuff trays, metal ornaments and exotic materials show ties reaching to the puna, the Pacific coast and the forested lowlands.

hints.label: Período Formativo
hints.source: Continuidad y ruptura en procesos de diferenciación social en comunidades aldeanas del valle de Ambato, Catamarca, Argentina (s. IV-X dC)

nodes.title: Período de Integración Regional (Catamarca, AD 300–AD 1000)

Named for the way distant valley communities came to share one visual language – the feline and shaman imagery of the Aguada style – on pottery, bronze and rock walls. [Sierra de el Alto-Ancasti, 499 BC–AD 600] Formative Period. Period definition from New insights into South American camelid management strategies at El Alto-Ancasti mountain range (Catamarca, Argentina) during the first millennium of the Common Era — Moreno Enrique, 2022-07-07.

Farming villages took hold in the valleys and piedmont of northwestern Argentina, with maize, beans and squash cultivated alongside herds of llamas. People built permanent stone and adobe houses, made pottery and ground-stone tools, and buried their dead beneath house floors and in stone cists. Exchange along the mountain corridors moved obsidian, shell and snuff-taking equipment over long distances, laying the base for the later fortified towns of the region.

Settled valley communities in the Argentine northwest coalesced into larger, more organised societies, best known through the Aguada tradition. Metalworkers produced cast bronze plaques and axes, and potters covered black burnished vessels with jaguar-headed figures and sacrificing warriors – imagery that hints at shared ritual beliefs across a wide region. Irrigated fields and llama herding supported growing populations that later fragmented into the fortified settlements of the following era.

Valley farmers of the Argentine northwest were now fully settled, irrigating maize fields and herding llamas from villages of stone-walled compounds. This is the era of Aguada art, with its jaguar-men, sacrificers and severed heads incised on black polished pottery and cast in bronze plaques – imagery suggesting warfare, hallucinogen use and a shared religious world stretching across the Andean foothills.

Catamarca's valleys were the heartland of Aguada, whose distinctive engraved and painted ceramics and jaguar iconography spread across the Northwest. Villages of agriculturalists and llama herders grew, metalworkers produced elaborate bronze objects, and ritual paraphernalia points to a shared belief system uniting scattered communities. The dominant culture of northwest Argentina's valleys during the Middle Period, unified less by political control than by a shared and unmistakable art style. Its black incised pottery, carved stone and cast bronze plaques are covered with feline and jaguar-man imagery, warriors and trophy heads, hinting at ritual specialists and hallucinogen use. Irrigated fields, llama caravans and metalworking supported dense settlement before the style dissolved around AD 1000.

Village farming and herding communities across the valleys of Catamarca, living in round stone-walled houses with adjoining fields and corrals. This is the era of the Condorhuasi, Ciénaga and Alamito traditions, known for modelled and polychrome pottery, carved stone bowls, early copper metallurgy and elaborate equipment for taking hallucinogenic snuff. Long-distance llama caravans tied the valleys to the puna and the eastern lowlands.

A long era of continuity in the valleys of Catamarca, when dispersed farming and herding hamlets, stone-walled fields and household craft production persisted with only gradual change. Ceramic styles shifted through the Condorhuasi, Ciénaga and Aguada traditions, copper and bronze working developed, and ritual objects such as carved stone bowls and snuff tablets circulated widely. Treating it as one long span emphasises how slowly, rather than how dramatically, these societies were transformed.

Dense agricultural settlements of stacked stone rooms, terraces and canals filled the valleys, associated with the Belén and Santa María pottery traditions and their tall painted funerary urns. Metalworking in bronze reached its height, producing axes, discs and plaques. Rising population and visible fortification suggest competition between valley polities, a landscape the Inca would later reorganise rather than replace.

[Valle del Bolsón, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 900–AD 1600] Tardío Prehispánico. Period definition from “Atravesando fronteras”: Prácticas compartidas e identidades sociales negociadas durante el tardío prehispánico. Una discusión desde la alfarería ordinaria del valle del Bolsón (Belén, Catamarca). — Puente Verónica, 2012.

The centuries of the Santa María and Belén traditions, when the valleys of Catamarca filled with large agglomerated settlements of stone-walled houses, extensive terraced fields and hilltop pukaras. Painted funerary urns, bronze working and evidence of raiding mark a crowded, competitive landscape that was eventually taken over by the Inca and then dismantled by the Spanish.

After the long era of village farming, populations in the valleys and puna of northwest Argentina gathered into larger, often defended settlements with dense stone architecture and terraced fields. Distinctive painted urns and black-on-red wares mark regional polities that were later absorbed into the Inca empire, which built roads, waystations and high-altitude shrines here. Spanish conquest and the long indigenous resistance close the sequence.

Salta's valleys and high puna became part of Collasuyu, crossed by the Qhapaq Ñan and dotted with tambos, agricultural terraces and administrative sites. The most spectacular legacy is high-altitude ceremonial architecture, including the summit sanctuaries where children were sacrificed and preserved by the cold. Local communities supplied labour and were sometimes uprooted and resettled to serve the state.

Local chiefdoms in the valleys built dense villages, extensive field systems and hilltop refuges, each with recognisable pottery and burial customs. Long-distance caravan traffic kept them supplied with obsidian, metals and altiplano goods, while competition over land and water drove fortification. Their leaders were the intermediaries through whom the Inca later governed.

nodes.name: recent Colonial period (Catamarca, AD 1650–AD 1800)
nodes.title: recent Colonial period (Catamarca, AD 1650–AD 1800)
nodes.description:
[Valle del Bolsón, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1650–AD 1800] recent Colonial period. Period definition from An Early Hispanic-Indigenous Contact Event at the Los Viscos Archaeological Site in the South-Central Andes: A Zooarchaeological Perspective — Árias María Florencia, 2021-10-16.

Following the long Calchaquí Wars and the forced deportation of surviving indigenous communities, the valleys of northwestern Argentina were reorganised around Spanish towns, encomiendas and haciendas. Estates raised cattle and mules for the mining economy of Upper Peru, adobe chapels and rural churches spread, and indigenous, Spanish and mestizo populations merged into a new rural society. Excavated sites of the era show European ceramics and metal goods used alongside persisting local pottery traditions.

nodes.name: Fase I de Alamito (Catamarca, AD 240–AD 360)
nodes.title: Fase I de Alamito (Catamarca, AD 240–AD 360)
nodes.description:
[Campo del Pucará, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 240–AD 360] Fase I de Alamito. Period definition from  Aproximación a la funcionalidad de un determinado tipo de recintos presentes en campo del Pucará (Depto Andalgalá, Catamarca), desde una perspectiva geoarqueológica.  — Gianfrancisco María Soledad, 2005.

The earliest layer of the distinctive Alamito settlements on the Campo del Pucará, where houses were arranged as a ring of low mounds around an open plaza with paired ceremonial mounds and a sunken patio. The plan is one of the most formalised village layouts in the pre-Hispanic Argentine northwest, and the workshops found in it show craftspeople working stone and copper for exchange with neighbouring valleys.

hints.label: Fase I de Alamito
hints.source: Aproximación a la funcionalidad de un determinado tipo de recintos presentes en campo del Pucará (Depto Andalgalá, Catamarca), desde una perspectiva geoarqueológica.

[Campo del Pucará, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 360–AD 480] Fase II de Alamito. The full flowering of the Alamito settlement pattern, with its ring of dwelling mounds facing a plaza and ceremonial precinct. Stone sculpture, notably the crouching 'suplicante' figures, and intensive craft production in stone and metal belong to this stretch, before the sites were abandoned and the region's population shifted towards the emerging Aguada world.

The opening stage of the Ciénaga tradition in the valleys of Catamarca, when small farming and herding hamlets took shape and potters began producing the incised dark ware with hatched geometric designs that defines the culture. It marks the transition out of the earlier Condorhuasi world and the beginning of a sequence that would culminate in Aguada.

The later stage of the Ciénaga tradition, when farming hamlets of the Catamarca valleys were well established and their potters were turning out the dark burnished bowls incised with hatched geometric panels and stiff, stylised human and feline figures that make Ciénaga ware instantly recognisable. Copper working, llama herding and maize agriculture all deepen in this stretch, setting the stage for the more hierarchical Aguada society that followed.

Known for dark, polished pottery and bronze plaques covered in feline and jaguar-man imagery, this was the great artistic tradition of northwest Argentina. Its craftsmen mastered metallurgy, its iconography suggests shamanic ritual and human sacrifice, and its motifs echo those of Tiwanaku far to the north, hinting at long-distance religious connections across the Andes.

nodes.title: Belén I (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1300)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1300] Belén I. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

Farming and herding communities of the Catamarca valleys developed the bold black-on-red pottery — tall urns with stylised faces and geometric bands — that gives this culture its name. Villages of stone-walled compounds sat near irrigated fields of maize and quinoa, with llama caravans linking the valleys to the puna and beyond.

A time of growing conflict and concentration, when communities moved onto defensible hilltops and built walled settlements overlooking their fields. Belén urns and metalwork circulated widely across northwestern Argentina, and local chiefly leaders emerged in the valleys of Hualfín and Abaucán.

nodes.title: Belén III (Catamarca, AD 1480–AD 1535)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1480–AD 1535] Belén III. Period definition from Cronología arqueológica del Valle de. Hualfín, Pcia. De Catamarca, Argentina. Obtenida mediante el uso de computadoras.  — González Rex Alberto, 1975.

The Inca empire absorbed the Catamarca valleys, imposing roads, storehouses and administrative centres and resettling labour for state mines and fields. Local Belén pottery continued but now alongside imperial Cuzco-style vessels. Spanish invaders arrived within a generation, touching off the long Calchaquí wars that ended with the forced removal of the valley populations.

The mature phase of Ciénaga village life in the Hualfín and neighbouring valleys, marked by incised grey-black pottery covered in fine hatched geometry and schematic human and animal figures. Its farming, herding and copper metallurgy formed the base on which the later Aguada culture, with its jaguar imagery and sharper social divisions, was built.

nodes.title: Período Tardío (Catamarca, AD 1100–AD 1480)

[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1100–AD 1480] Período Tardío. Period definition from La cultura de La Ciénaga y el período temprano. — Sempé María Carlota, 2005.

Following the end of the Middle Period, the Northwest fragmented into competing local polities with their own painted ceramics, cemeteries and territories. Agriculture intensified on terraces and irrigated land, populations concentrated in large villages, and fortified pukaras multiplied on ridges and hilltops. These chiefdoms were still expanding when the Inca arrived.

hints.source: La cultura de La Ciénaga y el período temprano.

Permanent farming villages spread through the valleys: houses and patios enclosed by stone walls, terraced fields, llama corrals and communal cemeteries. nodes.title: Período de Integración (Catamarca, AD 650–AD 950)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 650–AD 950] Período de Integración. Period definition from Contextos temáticos y ordenamientos funerarios en el cementerio Aguada orilla norte. — Sempé María Carlota, 2002.

The Aguada tradition spread a shared visual language across the valleys - felines, sacrificers and geometric designs incised on fine black pottery and cast in bronze. Ceremonial spaces, elaborate burials and the circulation of prestige goods point to emerging ranked societies and shared ritual practice over a wide area. Its breakdown gave way to the fragmented regional polities of later centuries.

hints.label: Período de Integración
hints.source: Contextos temáticos y ordenamientos funerarios en el cementerio Aguada orilla norte.

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales del Noroeste argentino (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales del Noroeste argentino (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1480)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1480] Período de Desarrollos Regionales del Noroeste argentino. Period definition from La Loma de Ichanga: Visibilidad, defensibilidad y abandono en el valle de Hualfín (Depto. De Belén, Prov. De Catamarca, Argentina). — Balesta Bárbara, 2010.

Valley communities developed strongly local identities visible in ceramics, burial practice and architecture, building agglutinated stone villages and extensive terrace systems. Painted urns holding infant burials, worked bronze and defensive site placement are the period's signature finds. These regional polities were the political units the Inca later incorporated as provinces.

hints.source: La Loma de Ichanga: Visibilidad, defensibilidad y abandono en el valle de Hualfín (Depto. De Belén, Prov. De Catamarca, Argentina).

nodes.name: Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1536)
nodes.title: Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka (Catamarca, AD 1000–AD 1536)
nodes.description:
[Valle de Hualfín, Catamarca, Argentina, AD 1000–AD 1536] Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka. Period definition from La configuración del paisaje Belén (valle de Hualfín, Catamarca). — Balesta Bárbara, 2011.

Spans the era of independent valley chiefdoms and their incorporation into Tawantinsuyu. Local Belén and Santa María communities continued to make their own pottery and bury children in urns while working within Inca demands for labour, metal and maize. Imperial roads and installations laid over older villages make the two phases hard to separate in the ground.

hints.label: Período de Desarrollos Regionales/Inka
hints.source: La configuración del paisaje Belén (valle de Hualfín, Catamarca).

nodes.title: Temprano Inicial (Catamarca, 199 BC–AD 200)
